# Dedication.

praise of Your exuberant mildness <note>original: "Mildigkeit." In this 18th-century religious context, this refers to God's gentle mercy and compassionate kindness.</note>. You have united Yourself with them; You have lived in them and through them; for that reason—yes, for that reason alone—they lived holy lives. If I praise them, I praise only Your gifts. All deeds, all virtues, all lights, all graces, and wonders that we see in them are Your graces and Your works. This they themselves most humbly recognized while on earth; and even at this hour they still confess it in heaven, as they lay down the crowns of their holiness and glory at Your feet.

Ah, then grant also to me that I may likewise most submissively present and dedicate to You these few pearls that we still have remaining here below from their crown. I have found these jewels <term>Kleinodien<gloss>Precious gems or treasures; here used metaphorically to describe the valuable spiritual examples of the saints.</gloss></term> and I have loved them; I recognize this as Your singular grace, and offer You public thanks for both. Yes, I have even ventured to gather them, so that I might present them to You and Your congregation as a testimony of my gratitude.

I pray fervently for the most gracious approval of this my undertaking, so that I may require no other approbation <note>original: "Approbation." While the book received a legal "Approbation" from the censors on the previous page, the author here seeks a higher, divine approval.</note>. Note in grace the frailty of what I have done; and nonetheless, take both me, unworthy as I am, and this little work into Your high protection. Protect and defend that which is Yours; accompany and strengthen it in my heart and the hearts of all readers, so that only You may be recognized, loved, and praised in Your saints.

<page-num>VI.</page-num>
<header>Preface.</header>

<image-desc>An ornate horizontal woodcut headpiece featuring symmetrical scrolling acanthus leaves, floral blossoms, and a central shell-like decorative motif.</image-desc>

# Preface.

->To all those who pursue holiness and peace: grace and salvation!<-

->1.<-

Beyond what is reported in the specific introductory reports of the following biographies, I consider it necessary to briefly explain here my intentions in preparing this work; then, to clear away some difficulties and scruples <note>In this context, "scruples" refers to hesitant doubts or moral objections readers might have regarding the portrayal of these figures.</note> against it; and finally, to provide some encouragement and guidance for its useful application. For this presentation, I ask for God’s grace and for a little patience from the favorable and discerning reader before he hastens to the reading or judging of these matters.

---

->I.<-

<margin>(a) Tertullian, *On Patience*, Chapter 10.</margin>
<margin>(b) 1 Peter 2:9.</margin>

2. If anyone asks me, *What is the purpose of this work?* I answer briefly: *For the glory of God and for the edification of the community of Jesus Christ;* to which I believe this work can and will be conducive, under God's blessing. For it is an honor to God that His works and mysteries be revealed; and it provides an occasion to praise the Father in heaven when one beholds the good works of the saints. What that teacher of the Church (a) says of Job and his patience, we must say of all the saints and of every one of their virtues: *What a trophy of victory against the devil has God raised up in this man; what a banner of honor has He planted against the enemy of His glory,* since this man said nothing else in response to all the harsh news but: *Praise be to God.* All the graces, all the gifts, all the virtues and deeds of the saints—indeed, the saints themselves—are but the effects and representations of the great deeds of God, to proclaim the virtues of Him who has called them (b). Let us then represent and behold the saints as shining works and masterpieces of His hand, to the honor and praise of the great Master Craftsman <term>Werkmeister<gloss>A traditional term for God as the supreme architect or artisan of the human soul.</gloss></term>.

<meta>catchword: 3. Contem-</meta>

<summary>The author opens his preface by stating that the biographies of saints are intended to glorify God and edify the Christian community. He argues that the virtues of holy people are essentially "masterpieces" created by God to demonstrate His power over the devil.</summary>
<keywords>preface, edification, glory of God, Job, Tertullian, Master Craftsman, holiness, masterpieces of God</keywords>

--- Page 15 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's Preface from page VI, moving from the general purpose of the work (the glory of God) to the specific benefit these "examples" or biographies provide to the spiritual community.</meta>

<page-num>VII.</page-num>
<header>Preface.</header>

<margin>(a) 1 Corinthians 3:22, 23.</margin>

3. If we consider the saints in relation to ourselves, they are members of the community of Jesus Christ. Everything that God has given to them, He has given to the entire community; what He has worked in them and through them—indeed, they themselves in their entirety—belongs to the body of Jesus Christ. *Whether it be Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas <note>Cephas is the Aramaic name for the Apostle Peter.</note>, all is yours, and you are Christ's* (a). Just as I then desire, in the preparation of this work, to give to God what is God’s; so I also wish to give to the Church what belongs to her, namely these models of the saints, as precious church-ornaments <note>original: "Anathemata" [Luke 21:5]. In this context, it refers to sacred gifts or votive offerings used to decorate a temple, rather than the modern sense of a curse.</note> with all their various distributions and gifts, for the common benefit; for it is One Body. If only no one, out of sectarian self-love, would push away this gift of God, and rob himself of this good to his own harm!

4. That the presentation of examples of pious and holy people contributes greatly to the edification of the community of Christ—that it penetrates more powerfully and more sweetly than a mere lecture or sermon—has been testified by others in many ways, and is otherwise confirmed by experience. What is required in a lecture only as appropriate and necessary, but which is perhaps neither done nor experienced by the one who teaches it, is shown by these examples to be both possible and feasible—indeed, actually experienced and done. At the same time, the glorious benefit and outcome of such a way of life shines before one's eyes everywhere as a powerful attraction. What one finds presented in other writings only as general doctrines and instructions is often misunderstood and even more poorly applied when it is to be applied to specific cases, contrary to the writer's intention; such writings are like a <term>pharmacy</term> <note>original: "Apothecke." The author compares abstract theology to a room full of medicine that is dangerous if the user does not know which bottle fits which illness.</note> to one who is untrained. In these examples, however, one sees everything applied to specific stations and cases; one hears the sick themselves describing their illnesses with all their symptoms <note>original: "Symptomatibus."</note> or circumstances, how they behaved therein, and what harmed or helped them: and that gives their fellow patients a clearer and more reliable report. It is true that an example might very rarely be found that agrees in every particular circumstance with the condition and guidance of a reader: however, it would be just as rare to find an example in which a God-seeking reader would not encounter one or another case or report, even very specific ones, that served his own station or circumstances; not to mention that the primary conditions, the general leadings and experiences, are the same in all the pious.

<margin>(b) *Confessions*, Book VIII, Chapters 6, 7, 8.</margin>

5. If one wished to confirm the utility of reading the biographies of pious people with specific examples, one would have to write a large book instead of a preface. I shall mention only a single, yet twofold instance, which St. Augustine (b) describes: namely, that two prominent court officials of the Emperor, while out walking, happened to find the *Life of Anthony* <note>St. Anthony the Great (c. 251–356), often considered the father of Christian monasticism.</note> in a hermit’s cottage, and were so moved by it that they instantly renounced the world, wishing to think of nothing further but their salvation. His words regarding this are as follows: One of them began to read; he

<sig>† 4</sig>
<meta>The catchword "ver:" indicates the next page begins with "verändert" (changed) or "verlassen" (left/abandoned), continuing the story of the court officials' transformation.</meta>

<summary>The author argues that the lives of saints belong to the whole Church and serve as practical, "medical" case studies for spiritual health, more effective than abstract teaching. He cites the conversion of two imperial officials via the Life of St. Anthony as proof of the power of biography.</summary>
<keywords>communal property, body of Christ, religious examples, spiritual medicine, St. Augustine, St. Anthony the Great, edification</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the Preface from page VII, specifically concluding an anecdote about St. Augustine's conversion and transitioning into the author’s motivations for collecting these biographies.</meta>

<page-num>VIII.</page-num>
<header>Preface.</header>

...was amazed, he was set on fire; indeed, while reading, he considered that he too wished to begin such a life and serve God by renouncing worldly service. He read, he was changed inwardly, and his spirit was liberated from the world. This was told to St. Augustine by an eyewitness of this history; and the narrative had almost the same effect on him as the reading had on the aforementioned courtiers, so that he also, turning to his friend, cried out in total consternation: "What is happening to us? What does this mean? What are we hearing? The unlearned <note>Augustine refers here to simple, uneducated monks like St. Anthony, whose biography had inspired the courtiers.</note> rise up and seize heaven for themselves: and behold, we, with all our learning, without heart or courage, where do we lie, drowned in fleshly desires? Should we be ashamed to follow because they have gone before us? Is it not rather a shame to us that we do not even want to follow?" And thereupon this dear man tells further how he, through this means, came to a full breakthrough <note>A "breakthrough" (Durchbruch) is a common Pietist term for the definitive moment of spiritual conversion.</note>.

6. Since the blessing in the use of such life-descriptions is obvious, then certainly those have rendered no small service to the community of God who have collected and shared such histories. However, one does not always proceed with equal faithfulness and judgment. Most remain within the boundaries of their own party <note>meaning their specific denomination or sect</note> and write according to their particular dogmas: everyone canonizes their own saints. One leaves everything at its own value; but meanwhile, one is assured that these souls, whose paths are shared here, have long since been inscribed and accepted into the register of saints by the higher Mother Church (a): for which reason their teachings and conduct are rightly presented and praised publicly for the benefit of the universal Church on earth.

7. But see what considerations moved me further toward this work and gave me occasion for it. When I look at the misery of our times, how so few living examples of holy souls are to be found, one might well strike up David’s lamentation: *Help, Lord, the godly are diminished* (b); since for the most part people allow themselves to be satisfied with the very first letters of Christian teaching, and the Israel that has departed <note>referring to those who have left the "Egypt" of a sinful life</note>, each in his tribe, lies securely by his miserable resting places, and is lulled further to sleep by false scouts <note>A reference to the spies in the Book of Numbers who gave a discouraging report of the Promised Land.</note> (as if it were not possible to get this or that far, or to reach this or that state on earth); what is then more necessary than to present a cloud of holy witnesses (c), who not only, at their initial conversion, left the Egypt of this world, but also wandered through the entire wilderness, went through all trials, and finally truly reached the blessed rest that remains for the people of God (d)—the Promised Land, the essential communion with God—and who now show us its fruits, praise the land, and promise certain victory: *The land is very good, let us go up, we are able to overcome it: if the Lord is gracious to us, He will bring us into that same land,* etc. Numbers <note>The original German citation incorrectly lists this as 5. Mos. (Deuteronomy), but the text quoted is from Numbers 13 and 14.</note> Chapters 13 and 14.

8. What do <term>awakened souls</term><note>German: *erweckte Seelen*. A term used in Pietism for individuals who have undergone a spiritual "awakening" or conversion and seek a deeper, more personal faith.</note> occupy themselves with these days, after they have walked the first paths of repentance for a little while? Is it not often with either merely external exercises and literal knowledge; or with an untimely mania for conversion, with a violent <term>storming of Babylon</term><note>German: *Babelstürmen*. A radical Pietist metaphor for attacking the perceived corruption and confusion of the established institutional church, which they likened to the biblical Babylon.</note>, with all sorts of strange opinions or higher speculations, each according to his own kind? And then one might even grasp a mystical image, praise it, and chatter about it; but who actually tackles the matter that truly counts? Real practice and experience are generally lacking. Not to mention those who, after having finished their studies in theology, lose themselves in the <term>Hermetic golden mountains</term><note>A reference to alchemy and the search for the "philosopher's stone." The author is criticizing those who turn to esoteric or occult secrets instead of simple inward holiness.</note>: what is more useful to all such people (and to us all together) than to have the examples of such souls placed before our eyes? Souls who applied everything external only to its proper goal—namely, the promotion of the <term>inner life</term>; such souls who considered only the one thing needful: how they might find God’s essential communion within themselves again through the dying away of all self-life; in short, such souls who practiced and experienced that of which we perhaps only have the images?

<margin>(a) G. Arnold, Preface to the *Lives of the Faithful*. See Weismann’s *Church History* cited below.</margin>

9. Furthermore, when I consider that the life-descriptions of such souls not only shed a great light upon church history, but are themselves the *true* church history, I have viewed this work as no less useful and necessary for that purpose. Those historians who know how to distinguish between the shell and the kernel have judged likewise:
> "I am of the opinion," (so goes the judgment of one (a) among them,) "the more precisely one could get behind the secret life of such persons, and discover the same for the shaming of common <term>state Christianity</term><note>German: *Statistisches Christenthum*. This refers to a nominal, institutional faith required by the state, rather than a living, personal conviction.</note> and the so-widely encroaching hypocrisy, the more necessary it would be to investigate this piece of church history by those who still have the desire, time, and ability for it. For such histories of such true members of Christ might with much better right be called a 'Church History' than the narrative of the endless wars of words of corrupt teachers."

10. Since I have now, through God’s goodness, found the rich treasure of grace, truths, and wonders of God in these golden vessels of honor, I regret nothing more than that such noble writings and persons remain so unknown and disregarded in the world. I saw clearly that this good belonged to the community of Christ, and it would not be fair that it be withheld from them in any way; I would have gladly granted everyone the influence of these stars of heaven, which I had found so lovely and healing for myself. But what was to be done? I saw various things standing in the way of recommending such matters from more than one side. The books themselves are rare and unknown, so much so that in large cities and otherwise well-stocked bookshops, one can hardly ask for a single one of them. <note>original: "Mystica sunt"</note> "They are mystical things," is the hollow answer one carries away. Also, not everyone can buy or read so many books, since they are, moreover, mostly composed in foreign languages. Many of them are far too long-winded, especially those that have published collections of such life-descriptions; so much so that—

...short excerpts already make up a few large volumes. The many secondary matters mixed in by various <term>factions</term><note>German: *Parthey*. To test everything, and to keep and publish only what is good—who wants to apply their time and strength to that? Human reason, being sharp and prone to taking offense, balks at such subject matter in every place; it finds nothing there but darkness and disgust; it rejects the good along with the bad. And it is no wonder, since such writings give such hard lessons to one's own ego and carnal senses. Even if someone should find a taste for it themselves, and gladly wish to grant others such "good pasture," how many human intentions hold them back?

11. Considering this, I have finally had to resolve, because the opportunity was given to me, to take this work upon myself in God’s name; so that I might keep no guilt upon me before God and in my conscience, as if I had kept these <term>heavenly lights</term> hidden <term>under a bushel</term><note>A reference to Matthew 5:15. The author feels a moral obligation to share these spiritual insights rather than keeping them to himself.</note> out of low esteem or fear of man. These lights, as it seemed, were given to me for the purpose that I should set them out upon the lampstand, so that they might shine for all who are in the house of God. May the Lord grant that such a blessing, because of my own unworthiness or unfitness, be in no way withheld!

12. If people have not known such writings or individuals until now; if they have been able to obtain or understand such books either not at all, or perhaps only this or that one with great effort; then let them herewith be made known to all <term>seekers of salvation</term><note>German: *Heils-Begierigen*. Those earnestly desiring to find the path to spiritual peace or heaven.</note>, presented as a gift, and most highly recommended for fruitful use. If people have not wanted to begin reading such books because of their long-windedness and great size; see, here they are summarized, yet in such a way that it is hoped this brevity will cause no noticeable obscurity to the history or the subject matter. If people have hitherto felt a disgust for them because of this or that <term>Popish</term><note>German: *Päbstischen*. A derogatory Protestant term for Catholic practices. 13. To be sure, I know well that by publishing and recommending such things, many will take occasion to be offended; and I will obtain little honor or thanks from most, but rather must expect contempt and slander. However, the high esteem and certainty of these divine truths, the love for their expansion, and the benefit that I promise myself others will draw from them, far outweigh those concerns for me. Furthermore, because of my <term>physical frailty</term><note>The author frequently mentions his poor health and proximity to death as a reason for his honesty and haste in finishing the work.</note>, I have every reason to think that I could soon be taken from the judgment of this lower world and be placed in a state where all human intentions—favor or disfavor, along with the entire <term>polemical theology</term><note>German: *Streit-Theologie*. 14. So that every offense and <term>scruple</term><note>A feeling of doubt or hesitation with regard to the morality or propriety of a course of action.</note> might be avoided, as much as possible, while reading this work, we wish to briefly resolve some of the difficulties that arise. "Who knows if it is all true?" many will undoubtedly object; "whether these things are not partly invented, partly embellished, or exaggerated? There are so many legends and fables in the world," etc. Now, one can by no means deny that many historians—driven by gullibility, <term>superstition</term>, self-love, or other human intentions—have forged many little stories and tales, some uncertain and some clearly invented, wishing perhaps to create a <term>Golden Legend</term><note>Original: *güldene Legende*. This refers to the *Legenda Aurea*, a famous medieval collection of lives of the saints that was often criticized by later scholars for including fantastical elements.</note>. I confess that I myself have looked wearily about in a vast forest of impressive books and found almost everything so dry that I could gather neither grapes nor figs; or else it appeared so painted and adorned that a mere glance soon showed these were no fruits grown from the stem. It is even more offensive when truth is obscured and error propagated with the most tasteless fables; through which, truly, much has been conceded to the unbelieving reason and the <term>atheistic mind</term> of the human heart, to say nothing of other consequences.

15. But what then? If some uncertain things have been told to us, or if someone has added something of their own, should we therefore reject everything? Because this or that person has reported something incorrectly in a few matters (which perhaps do not take away from the core of the subject), should no man therefore speak the truth? Far be it. A modest investigation is necessary; a rash condemnation is highly harmful. One leaves curiosity regarding unnecessary trifles and secondary matters to the unwise wasters of time, and dwells only on what is fundamental and useful. We should then call upon the Father for the spirit of discernment, and thereafter <term>test all things and hold fast to that which is good</term><note>A reference to 1 Thessalonians 5:21, a common refrain in Pietist literature emphasizing individual spiritual discernment.</note>. Whatever does not please the vain mind in these days must be called a "fable" or a "legend"; willful reason wants to master everything. Yet it is certain that human reason and a merely natural judgment, without the Spirit of God, harm the salvation of souls a thousand times more than superstition and "godly fables" whose content and basis are otherwise harmless. And however much one may feel disgust for such books—whose titles announce the biographies of the saints—because of the aforementioned objections, there is still merit in what a godly historian of our time says: *I (a) have no doubt that many beautiful things and the core of a better church history are hidden in such writings; and it is to be lamented that this part of Church History is so greatly neglected among us Protestants and regarded as lost.*

16. But to come closer to the point, and to answer the objection with specific regard to these present <term>biographies</term><note>Original: *Lebens-Beschreibungen*. Literally "descriptions of lives," a common term for spiritual biographies in the 18th century.</note>, it is first of all evident from the appearance and title that these are biographies chosen or selected with care and judgment; therefore, they are not to be compared with other mixed and uncertain histories. Furthermore, for each one in particular, indubitable records, testimonies, and evidence are provided. Secondly, no fictional <term>panegyrics</term><note>Original: *Lob-Reden*. High-flown speeches or writings meant to praise someone, often exaggerating their virtues.</note> are to be found here; rather, the saints for the most part tell of their own lives and conduct here themselves. At the very least, we have primarily reflected their own words and reports. And where another <term>historian</term><note>Original: *Historicus*.</note> speaks, it is not someone who lived several centuries after them or far removed from them; rather, they are eyewitnesses and earwitnesses, and indeed those from whose godliness one can expect nothing other than truth and faithfulness. Thirdly, for my part, my conscience also clears me, for I have intentionally falsified nothing, embellished nothing, made nothing too great, nor attributed any foreign meaning to the history when I have had to add a few things for the sake of the <term>context</term><note>Original: *Connexion*.</note> or otherwise; which, moreover, has been done sparingly and is mostly enclosed in brackets. In translating or quoting the saints' own words, I have strived to use even greater faithfulness out of due respect. Should one object that I have only cited the best, but kept silent about the bad and the faults of the saints, it speaks for itself that whoever makes an extract cannot or must not write everything—nor even the worst—of what he finds. I have omitted much that was good, but also much that I did not consider so edifying, especially what concerned certain particular customs or opinions of the <term>sects</term><note>Original: *Partheyen*. This refers to different religious denominations or factions.</note>, and this according to the rule of Saint Paul:

> Test all things, and hold fast to that which is good.

The faults and weaknesses of the saints, as many as were encountered, I have never intentionally omitted where circumstances allowed; rather, I have intentionally included them so that the greatness of the <term>grace of God</term><note>Original: *Gnade GOttes*.</note> might shine forth all the more.

17. Fourthly, and so that I may bring an end to answering this objection, the <term>subjects</term><note>Original: *Matherien*.</note> found in this writing are of three kinds: namely, partly historical, partly special or extraordinary, and partly essential matters. What foundation those things have which properly belong to history has just been mentioned; whoever desires more certainty must look into the work itself, and indeed into the cited testimonies and records, before he judges indiscreetly. Moreover, I relate such matters as I find them; they rest entirely on the responsibility of those authors; they are external and not essential things. I will not waste my time defending everything and anything to everyone—not only that it happened thus, but also that what happened was good and laudable—(as no sensible person can demand of me), even if I might <term>approve</term><note>Original: *approbiren*.</note> of it for my own part.

...If [God] has shown or said something to this or that soul in a vision, and the revelation is in itself a truth that is according to Scripture—indeed, holy and divine—then I have no reason to doubt that it should come from God, the origin of all good. However, he who nevertheless casts doubt upon such a vision, revelation, etc., can nonetheless hold fast to the truth presented therein for his own **edification**, without focusing on the extraordinary nature of the event.

19. The essential truths of the **inner life** <note>Original: *inwendigen Lebens*. A key term in Pietism referring to the soul's direct, internal relationship with God.</note>, such as the complete renunciation of the world, the dying to self, the paths of prayer, the fundamental virtues, and God’s guidance over His **chosen ones** <note>Original: *Auserwählten*. Those who have surrendered themselves to God's refining process.</note> to cleanse them of their self-will, to unite them with Himself, and to reveal the wonders of His grace and love in and through them—these necessary and essential matters have been particularly noted in the histories of these saints. Indeed, to praise these matters was the actual purpose of this work; everything else was added only as a pleasant **vehicle** <note>original: "vehiculum"</note> to help infuse these things which are so distasteful to human nature. Let all the rest then stand or fall; if one only reads, approves, and practices this **one thing**, then God and the author have reached their goal. For we are not in the world to brood or to quarrel, but to live holily. These truths, however, are truths of faith, grounded in God’s Word and in experience; they are of no concern to natural reason and criticism. The judgment of the latter in such matters is to be respected even less than the judgment of a blind man regarding color. Only those alone who do the will of God shall experience that these things are of God.

20. Be that as it may, one will further object: why does one occupy oneself with **Roman Catholic** <note>In the 18th century, Protestant readers were often suspicious of Catholic "mystics," fearing they were tainted by "popery." I shall leave it to its own place whether **sectarian self-love** <note>Original: *Sectirische Selbst-Liebe*. The tendency to value one's own religious group over the universal truth of the Gospel.</note> makes this objection; but why does one look askance because God is so kind that He allows Himself to be hindered by no name, nor intellectual concepts, nor external ceremonies and customs from communicating His grace and continuing His work in the hearts of those who fear Him and do right among all kinds of people (a)? Such are pleasing to Him (b); why should they not also be dear and precious to us? The Church is nothing other than the assembly of the saints, or those souls gathered back to God from their distraction in the creature and self-will, and united with Him in Christ. Any other name or distinction is worth nothing before God. If you now say: "These holy souls are not of my party," you thereby cut yourself off from the fellowship of both the Head and the members.

26. The **monastic life** of several of these souls should likewise not serve as an offense to modest readers. It is well known that many Protestant theologians (d) have judged that, during the Reformation, the monasteries should not have been abolished, but only improved. The decay that prevails today even among these so-called clergy is obvious, and is even confessed and lamented by sensible people within the Roman Church itself. However, that does not concern these [holy] souls. Indeed, I say it freely: had the monasteries been of such a character as those established by **Teresa** <note>St. Teresa of Avila (1515–1582), a Spanish mystic who reformed the Carmelite Order to focus on poverty and mental prayer.</note> at the time of the Reformation, no one would have abolished them without a heavy offense against God. How miserably must seriously resolved souls among the Protestants sometimes drag themselves along, scattered and confused by worldly business and other distractions! How are they not entangled, now here, now there, in the vanities of this world! And what would it be, then, if some of them, who were of one mind in Christ, in order that they might care only for what belongs to the Lord, and be holy both in body and in spirit, and so that they could remain constantly attached to the Lord without being pulled hither and thither in such a way—if they, I say, out of such an intention, drawn by God, also joined together externally? If they did so without partisanship, without coercion of conscience, without stubbornness, without harmful idleness, living together in harmony and community as brothers; if they also sought to arrange both their domestic affairs and the physical exercises of divine service into a fitting order and subordination; would such an undertaking then be so blame-

...worthy thing? 27. The final and very apparent objection and scruple, which I also foresaw from the beginning, is this: that through the publication and recommendation of such writings and persons, one or another might be moved to go over to the **Papacy**; therefore, this would seem to be dangerous, especially in these days and current circumstances, when some here and there are indeed already allowing themselves to be misled into it. It is known to God what political or other intentions such persons have had in re-embracing the Papacy; but I fear that it did not happen to the end that they might live as holily as these souls have done; for they could certainly have done that outside the communion of the Roman Church; indeed, I fear that few among them will read such writings, much less love such a life. I leave them to the Lord, but in no way do I approve of their actions.

<margin>R</margin>
28. But so that all feared misuse of this work, also in this regard, may be prevented as much as possible, one should only consider that between such undoubtedly pious and holy souls, and between the Papacy, as Papacy, there is a great distinction, indeed, an antagonism. 

<margin>R!</margin>
It is evident to the eye that these souls, through inner enlightenment and experience, have clearly understood, powerfully testified to, and practiced the fundamental truths of the Gospel, quite differently from how the school-teachers <note>Original: "Schul-Lehrer," referring to scholastic theologians who prioritized logic and dogma over personal experience.</note> and the greatest crowd in the Papacy recognize or tolerate them. The dominant Roman Church (and would to God she were the only one!) has at all times viewed with suspicion, suppressed, and persecuted these God-beloved, inward souls and writings that were among her, under various pretenses. The recent **Quietist controversies** <term>Quietism: A 17th-century movement emphasizing internal stillness and the passive contemplation of God, which was eventually condemned by the Catholic Church.</term> and the dispute over **Pure Love** <term>Pure Love: The theological idea that God should be loved for His own sake, without any regard for reward or punishment.</term> are active proofs of this. One need only read the life of **John of the Cross**, **Teresa**, **Fenelon**, **Madame Guyon**, and the like, to be fully convinced of this, even though, for other reasons, the "graves of the prophets" are sometimes decorated. <note>A biblical allusion to Matthew 23:29, suggesting that the institutional church honors saints after they are dead while having persecuted them in life.</note> The writings of the last-named [Guyon] may not be read; those of **Bernieres**, **Canfeld**, and similar, otherwise approved and beautiful books, have met a similar fate. 

<margin>R!</margin>
There one sees indeed that they cannot be children of this **step-mother** <note>The author uses "step-mother" as a derogatory term for the institutional Roman Church, suggesting it does not truly nurture these "holy souls."</note>; who then would wish to be in her bosom? If such souls are cast out, what remains of Rome? Is not nakedness and abomination manifest in all parts? but to speak of this more extensively here will be unnecessary.

<margin>R!</margin>
29. Let one judge for oneself whether one who stands outside this party <note>Meaning those outside the Catholic Church, specifically the author's Protestant audience.</note> cannot use both the Holy Scripture, and also all the gifts and benefits which God has given to His saints in the Roman Church, much more easily, purely, and usefully than others who live in her communion under such distressing **coercion of conscience**, upon whom the good is forced along with the trivial or useless, and who dare not look with even one eye upon what this church rejects, unless they [wish to feel] the effects of her...

<meta>catchword: 33. This</meta>

<margin>R</margin>
...experienced their tyranny. Not to mention that general love and the "communion of saints" <note>The "communion of saints" refers to the spiritual union of all Christian believers.</note> are nowhere more difficult to practice than in the bosom of the Roman Church, which accepts nothing as good except what has grown within its own fence; and especially, upon joining it, everything else must be condemned and abjured. This is terrifying, and is alone sufficient to keep a truly Christian soul from selling its freedom of spirit so dearly and breaking the sacred bond of love.

### III.

30. Therefore, whoever seeks nothing other than the thorough edification and nourishment of their soul may step into this pasture without hesitation. There is no danger to be feared here; no deceptive will-o'-the-wisps <note>original: "Irr-Lichter," referring to misleading spiritual delusions</note> are presented; nothing dry, harmful, or poisonous is to be found here. Instead, there are Divine lights, wholesome truths, living examples, and encouragements toward true sanctification and union with God in Christ Jesus.

31. Not that one must imitate all the particular and outward exercises of these holy souls; for through such mimicry <note>original: "Nachäffung," literally 'aping'</note>, we would place the greatest obstacle in the way of the Spirit of Grace in His free operation and governance, and could fall into a harmful hypocrisy. Each of these souls practiced their faith in such a way as the time, station, and circumstances—in which they found themselves externally or internally—suggested. We look only to the foundation of their virtue and grace, within which they did this or that, and to their intention and goal, which they kept in view in all things. And thus, beholding their (a) purpose and end, we follow (not this or that externally performed work, but) their faith, and practice ourselves in the same, according to the circumstances in which we find ourselves through God’s providence, following the correct instruction of the Spirit of Grace.

32. Just as little should we try to model ourselves internally after the particular paths of this or that saint, nor force ourselves into this or any other state without a Divine drawing; much less, out of self-love, desire some extraordinary graces, which would only vainly disturb us, darken us, and lead us off the path. God leads His saints according to His free pleasure and purpose, and indeed, wonderfully (b). In this work, one encounters holy souls of various kinds: in terms of the foundation, principal states, and goal, everything is the same in all; but in the particular leadings and experiences, there is a noticeable difference, for the revelation of the manifold wisdom, wonders, and riches of God. These diverse gifts serve the common benefit. We rejoice in them and praise God in His saints; yet at the same time, we pay all the more careful attention to the discipline and operation of His Spirit in our own hearts, and surrender ourselves to Him in simplicity, so that we live not for ourselves, or for some other, but that He Himself may be the "will and the work" <note>original: "das Wollen und das Wirken," a reference to Philippians 2:13: "For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure."</note> within us.

33. This only I wished, dear reader: that these precious witnesses of the truth, through God’s cooperation, might impress and confirm the following in your heart and mine: (1) That the true Christian life is certainly a precise and **inward life**; (2) That even now, through God’s grace, it is possible to practice and experience such a life and being in this time; and indeed (3) in all **stations of life** <note>original: "Ständen," referring to one's social class, profession, or status in life</note> in which we might find ourselves outwardly, according to God’s will. Oh, how exceedingly necessary are these reflections in these days, and how powerfully these examples can prove them!

34. Yes, here we see true saints who, each in his own measure, have through God actually done and experienced those things about which we perhaps doubt whether they are possible in this state of mortality. We see people who have brought all created things under their feet; who lived no longer for themselves, but for God—yes, in whom and through whom Christ lived. We see people who walked with God, and in whom God also dwelt and walked; who beheld Him and loved Him purely, and were loved by Him in return, united into one spirit, and made partakers of His **Divine Nature** (a) <note>original: "Göttlichen Natur," a reference to the mystical union where the soul participates in God's characteristics</note>, according to the most precious promises of God in the Scriptures. But we also see the path through which they traveled to reach this goal: that it is a narrow path, a path of the most exact **self-denial** <note>original: "Verläugnung," the act of setting aside one's own will</note> of all things, a path of the most thorough **dying away** <term>Absterbung: the spiritual process of "killing" the ego or worldly desires so the soul can be filled by God</term> of all self-life, a path of the cross and of bitter suffering from all sides. If we then look with high esteem and admiration at the glorious outcome of their conduct, well then, let us follow their faith and let no sour path discourage us; but rather, forgetting what lies behind, let us reach out for the noble prize of **essential sanctification** and communion with God. If we die with Him, we shall also be glorified with Him (b).

35. Should a weak and timid <note>original: "blödes," which in this period meant shy, simple, or faint-hearted rather than its modern derogatory meaning</note> but sincere soul become discouraged by considering the precise conduct, the great faithfulness, the perfect virtues, and the advanced sanctification which these souls allow to shine from themselves everywhere—since that same soul perceives its own misery and inability so greatly in all things—then let one only consider: (1) That these saints also had their weak beginnings and failings, which are also touched upon here and there. The stages of their sanctification, from beginning to end, are soon read through, but not so soon traveled through. They were not perfected in a single day, and we must not imagine it so. After they were faithful in small things, they were set over much; let us only confidently do the same through the power of Him who is called the **Author and Finisher of our Faith**. (2) The saints themselves looked upon themselves and their actions with entirely different eyes than we do now. Their life was hidden, not only from the world but also mostly from themselves, especially during those inner trials and states of suffering of which they all became partakers. We rightly hold all of this in high esteem, but who knows how they might have felt in their own minds at the time? We see the glorious outcome of their journey, which was mostly hidden from them. And therefore—

<page-num>XX</page-num>
<header>Preface.</header>

...according to (3), let it be far from us that their holiness should dismay or deter us; rather, our faith should be powerfully strengthened when we see by their example what a desired end all these dark paths of humiliation and purification take, and how finally a peaceable fruit of righteousness grows out of the barrenness. Indeed, when we see in them what grace can do where one abandons oneself unconditionally to its faithful guidance, we realize that we must not always remain stuck in our lamenting beginnings. Instead, we should know what is the hope of our calling, and what is the richness of the glory of His inheritance in His saints, and what is the surpassing greatness of His power in us who believe, according to the inner working of His mighty strength (a).

36. Let all flesh henceforth be silent before the Lord, and say no longer: "Who can live like this?"—a weak shield <note>The author uses the metaphor of a "loose shield" (losen Schilde) to describe a flimsy excuse used to deflect the truth.</note> with which people seek to reject and render powerless all testimonies of the truth. Here are irreproachable examples of such people who lived in this way. If only those sanctified from the mother's womb could attain this, or if learning, art, or human strength were required, then one would have a fair reason to complain and excuse oneself. However, the (b) saints were human beings, subject to the same passions just as we are; we are all formed from the same lump of clay. Christians are made, not born <note>original: "Fiunt, non nascuntur Christiani"</note>, says Tertullian <note>Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus (c. 155 – c. 220 AD), an early Christian author from Carthage.</note>; they were once sinners but became saints. Indeed, they were mostly unlearned, simple people and weak women whose entire "art" was love—but a pure, vigorous love <note>original: "männliche Liebe," literally "manly love," used here in the archaic sense of being strong, mature, and courageous rather than sentimental.</note> which rooted out all worldly love and self-love from within them.

37. It is well known what happened to St. Augustine; how, at the time of his conversion, the enemy tried to deter him by presenting the difficulty and impossibility of the matter. His own words on this are as follows:

> (c) Virtue, in the form of self-restraint <note>original: "Enthaltung," usually translated as "Continence" in English versions of Augustine's *Confessions*.</note>, presented herself to me with a majestic, serene, and deeply joyful presence; and with friendly glances she invited me to come and have no hesitation. She stretched out her ready arms to receive and embrace me. There with her was a great multitude of good examples; there were youths and maidens, men and women of every age, honorable widows and aged virgins, and in all of them was self-restraint herself. . . She smiled at me in an encouraging way, as if she were saying: "Could you not do what these youths and maidens have done? Or do you think that they could do it of themselves, and not rather in the Lord their God? Why do you stand so long within yourself and waver? Cast yourself into Him; do not fear, He will not withdraw His hand so that you fall. Cast yourself into Him with confidence; He will receive you and heal you," etc.

38. Furthermore, let none of us lay the blame on our <term>station</term> <note>original: "Stand"; referring to one's social rank, profession, or state of life (e.g., married or single).</note>, location, business, or any external thing, provided it is not in itself contrary to the order and will of GOD. For, although faithfulness to grace requires us to lay aside not only sin but also every weight (a) that would make us sluggish, we must not proceed in this according to our own will. GOD exercises His saints through many different means; the cause of our hindrance and unrest is to be sought deeper within. The various examples of the saints show that God’s inner workings do not depend on any external circumstances: here we see saints in the palace, and saints in the wilderness; saints in the state of marriage, and saints in the monastery; saints in the church, in the chamber, in the kitchen, on the streets, and in all places. Ah, therefore, let no one lose heart in their perhaps distressed circumstances, as if the path to a thorough <term>sanctification</term> <note>original: "Heiligung"; the process of being made holy.</note> were blocked for them because of it. If we only have GOD and the <term>Cross</term> <note>Referring to the spiritual practice of embracing suffering or difficulty as a means of growth.</note>, we have means enough for perfect holiness: and what prison could bar these two from us? GOD is not far from every one of us. Only faithfully employ the present opportunities and means which Providence puts into our hands: if the LORD finds us faithful therein, it is a small thing for Him to deliver us. GOD wants to have saints in all stations of life: let everyone strive to become such a person in their own station, and build no castles in the air through uncertain thinking and waiting for the future.

39. Especially in these times, when we—to the praise of GOD—begin to see that the truths of the <term>inner life</term> <note>original: "inwendigen Lebens"; the spiritual focus on the heart's relationship with God rather than outward ritual.</note> are being loved and practiced more and more, not just in this or that party, rank, or corner, but among those of all religious affiliations, stations, and places, to the noticeable decline of dry <term>scholastic theology</term> <note>original: "Schul-Theologie"; academic, theoretical divinity that the author views as spiritually lifeless.</note>. Yes, the times are approaching when this Gospel (b) of the Kingdom of GOD, which is within us, shall be proclaimed in the whole world as a testimony to all nations. So let us no longer believe those who say, "Look here, look there is Christ"; let us not run out to seek Him in the desert, in the chamber, or in any merely external thing. Where we lose the creatures <note>Meaning the excessive attachment to created things or worldly distractions.</note>, there GOD is found; within our hearts the Word of Life is near to us; there, where the carcass is, the eagles gather. The GOD of Israel, (c) who is wonderful in His saints, will give power and strength to His people. Blessed be GOD!

40. Wishing for this, I conclude with that important reminder from the 9th chapter of the *German Theology* <note>original: "Teutschen Theologie"; a famous 14th-century mystical treatise highly regarded by Martin Luther and the Pietists.</note>, which may the Lord Himself confirm and make fruitful in our hearts!

<meta>This page provides the "Preliminary Report" or introduction to the life of Gregory Lopez, following the title page. It outlines the historical transmission of his biography from Spanish to French and eventually into this German edition, while also situating Lopez within the controversial 17th-century mystical movement known as Quietism.</meta>

# Preliminary Report.

->I.<-

1. This following biography was originally written by Francisco Losa, the former pastor of the main church in Mexico City in the West Indies <note>The "West Indies" here refers to the Spanish colonies in the Americas, specifically New Spain (modern-day Mexico).</note>, who associated intimately with Gregory Lopez for 18 years. After resigning from his office, he lived in the same house with him at Santa Fe (two miles from Mexico City) until the seventh year. Later, this life was expanded by another very close friend of Lopez, Johannes a Sancto Jacobo, and printed in the Spanish language in Madrid in 1658. From that version, the famous Arnauld d'Andilly <note>Robert Arnauld d'Andilly (1589–1674) was a French writer associated with the Jansenist movement, known for translating lives of saints.</note> published it in French, first in Paris in 1673, and shortly thereafter among his *Diverse Works* in 1675. Following that same edition, Mr. Poiret <note>Pierre Poiret (1646–1719) was a French mystic and philosopher who promoted the works of spiritual writers like Lopez and Madame Guyon.</note> had it published again in Amsterdam in the year 1717, providing it with an edifying preface under the title: *The Holy Solitary of the Indies* <note>original: "Le Saint solitaire des Indes."</note>.

2. This latter edition was used for this translation and excerpt. The translation, especially the specific words of this saint, has been done with the greatest possible faithfulness. The reader will find the most essential and useful parts in this excerpt, though it will not amount to a third of the full book. Furthermore, it will likely not be necessary to remind the reader that, in publishing such biographies, one does not necessarily set before the eyes the extraordinary and peculiar aspects for imitation. Not everyone is called, with Lopez, to move to the Indies and live in total solitude; but everyone must, with him, give their heart to **GOD**, pray without ceasing, and have their "conversation in heaven"; <note>A reference to Philippians 3:20, implying that one's true citizenship or way of life is spiritual rather than worldly.</note> which is the essential thing this example is meant to teach us.

3. To cite all the testimonies, approvals <note>original: "Approbationes."</note>, and eulogies of this man here is considered superfluous; a great many of them stand printed at the front of the various editions. The Kings of Spain, Philip II and III, sought with all earnestness to promote the canonization <term>canonization</term> <note>The official process by which the Catholic Church declares a deceased person to be a saint.</note> of our saint with the Pope. However, after "Reason" began to dispute the pure and unswerving love of God and banish it from this life, Lopez was also placed on the register of the <term>Quietists</term> <note>Quietism was a 17th-century mystical movement that emphasized internal stillness and the passive contemplation of God; it was later condemned by the Catholic Church as a heresy.</note>; which, to the discerning, can already serve as a good recommendation. At the least, those who are commonly labeled with this name have held this man in high esteem. The famous Molinos (a) <note>Miguel de Molinos (1628–1696), the leading figure of Quietism, whose "Spiritual Guide" was highly influential before his arrest.</note> calls him an excellent man, gifted with deep knowledge in mystical theology <note>original: "geheimen Gottes-Gelehrtheit."</note>; a Seraph <note>A "Seraph" (plural Seraphim) is the highest order of angel, traditionally associated with burning love for God.</note> clothed in flesh and a deified human. Johannes Falconi (b) (likewise a Spaniard) gives him the title of a great man, a famous clergyman who very well understood the purity of the spirit, whose life was a perpetual prayer, etc., who seemed more to be a Seraph in a body than a human like others. The famous Madame Guyon (c) <note>Jeanne-Marie Bouvier de la Motte-Guyon (1648–1717), a prominent French mystic and advocate for "pure love."</note> calls the biography of Lopez excellent and counts him among the great saints.

4. 
> "But nothing" (I conclude with the words of the French publisher (d))
> "can better recommend this excellent little work than its own matter and the worthiness of its content,
> "which on the one hand sets before our eyes **GOD**, everywhere present, the only perfect
> "Being, and the highest Good, with His most precious divine and spiritual effects; and
> "on the other hand, the most worthy of His creatures, namely man, endowed with understanding
> "and will, presented here in the very best state in which he can find himself during the time of his life
> "here on earth; and all this in a solitary man whose understanding,
> "heart, inclinations, duties—in short, all the powers and acts of his spirit—through a thorough
> "and perpetual application, were occupied only with **GOD**, with His will, with His love, and with
> "the love of neighbor. This should serve in some measure to awaken people from the spiritual lethargy <note>original: "Schlaf-Sucht," literally "sleep-sickness."</note>
> "in which they exist regarding these things, and to move them to consider themselves
> "with all earnestness.

5. 
> "Truly, humans are created for **GOD**: they have received a heart from Him
> "so that they might love Him and receive Him in love into this heart of theirs; they have an understanding
> "so that they may contemplate Him; all kinds of spiritual inclinations and powers so that they might occupy
> "themselves with Him. . . But, one does not think of it! Transient vanities occupy all their
> "inclinations, and with these, they occupy themselves entirely; and thereafter, when it comes time to die,
> "one only then becomes aware of one's gross folly, when one sees all these vain childish things
> "disappear forever. . . Ah, what would one then not give or do to be able,
> "like our holy hermit, to say at the moment of death: *Everything is now clear; nothing is*
> "*hidden anymore; and it is a full noon for me!*" <note>A metaphor for entering the direct light of God’s presence, where there are no shadows or mysteries remaining.</note>

# Chapter One.
## Concerning the Origin and Life of Gregory Lopez, until his Journey to Mexico.

->1.<-

Gregory Lopez was born in Madrid, the capital city of Spain, on the 4th of July in the year 1542. From which family line he came, however, has never been able to be discovered. Some indeed have believed that he must have been of high and noble origin, because they saw him, in his interactions and manners, to be so noble, polite, and full of humble gravity; so much so that one could not sufficiently admire the frankness and composed seriousness in his speech; nevertheless, nothing certain could be learned of it.

<margin>(a) Matthew 23:9, 10.</margin>
And although we (says the author of his biography) often asked him about it, we were nonetheless unable to find out. To one who asked him about it, he gave as an answer with a singular seriousness: "Heaven is my fatherland, and God is my father, as He Himself taught us when He said: 'You shall call no one on earth father; for One is your Father, and your Master, who is in heaven'" (a).

A few days before his death, when I had intended to ask him for the names of his relatives, so that I might send them an account of his life and his death for their edification, and so they might rejoice over the graces shown to him by God, he gave me this answer: "Since I renounced everything to lead a solitary life, I have regarded God alone as my father; and as for my brothers, I do not doubt they will have already died by now, for I was the youngest of them all."

->2.<-

That he was from the city of Madrid, however, is evident from the following: Once I was with him (writes the aforementioned author) in the hospital at Guastepec <note>Also known as Huastepec or Oaxtepec, this was a location in Mexico famous for its hospital and gardens run by the Brothers of Charity.</note>, when a man who had recently come from Madrid recounted how several houses in a certain street there, which he named, had been burnt to ashes. As we were walking away, Lopez said to me: "You know what the man told us about the houses that burned down, and that they belonged to my father: I do not know if you noticed that I was moved by it." Yet, I had truly not perceived the slightest change in his countenance; indeed, he had not even inquired whether any people had also been burned, nor what damage this fire had caused: which was truly a sign of an extraordinary detachment <term>Abgestorbenheit: A mystical term meaning "mortification" or "deadness to the world," referring to a state where the soul is no longer affected by earthly news or personal loss.</term>.

<note>original: "Gregorius Lopes, Madrit, Spanien, Mexico, Guastepec, Matthäus 23, Abgestorbenheit, Biographie"</note>

First Part. The Life

<margin>(a) Lamentations of Jeremiah 3:27.</margin>
3. God called him to His service from his tender childhood. I once asked him whether he had begun to serve God from the time he first gained the use of his reason? To which he answered that he did not know for certain whether it happened then or a little thereafter; but it was the truth that God had shown him the grace of giving him a different mind, even at an early age, than children usually have. And he used to say often, as he had experienced it himself: "How blessed is the one who bears the yoke of the Lord from his youth" (a).

4. A trustworthy man also told me of him that when he was still quite young, without saying anything of it to his parents, he went into the Kingdom of Navarre, where he lived for more than six years with a pious hermit in great poverty, extreme humility, and perfect obedience. His father, however, who had searched for him with great care, finally found him and brought him to Valladolid, where the Royal Court was at that time, as he was to become a page (or noble youth) and, as he told me himself, was required to remain there for some time.

Regarding how he lived inwardly with God during this forced life at court, he once said that whenever his master sent him out to deliver a message, he strove to maintain such devotion to God that neither the persons of highest rank whom he encountered on the way, nor the many other temptations toward distraction <note>The original German "Vorwürfe der Zerstreuung" refers to objects or events that "throw" one off course or cause the mind to wander.</note> found at princely courts, could prevent him from thinking of God.

He had spent two or three years in this manner and had reached about the twentieth year of his age when he became minded to travel secretly to New Spain (or Mexico); which he also accomplished after he had prepared himself through much prayer and fasting and had recognized the will of God. As he then confessed, at that time during prayer, a grace so great was bestowed upon him by God as he had never before received, by which he was strengthened to carry out the resolution he had to be entirely for God. What else moved him to this long journey may be judged from these words, which he once gave in answer: that the primary cause which led him to this land was the honor of God. As he then certainly neglected nothing that could serve to further the same.

# Of Gregory Lopez. Chapter II.

...soon distributed everything he had brought with him, worth 8,400 reals, to the poor, thereby showing how little he esteemed the treasures of this New World; for instead of seeking to enrich himself there, he gave away even that which he still possessed.

From there he went to Mexico City. He stayed here for several days to earn enough by writing <note>He likely worked as a scribe or copyist, a common trade for educated men of the time.</note> so that he could travel further to Zacatecas, where he hoped to find a more suitable opportunity for the solitary life for which he so longingly yearned. He lodged with a man named Louis Zapata, as can be seen from a short letter that the same man wrote to him in the year 1591, with this content:

> "It is now 29 or 30 years since, while I was living in Mexico City on Tacuba Street, a certain nobleman came from Spain and lodged with me. He was dressed in serge <note>Serge is a durable, coarse wool fabric, often worn by the lower classes or as a sign of religious humility.</note>. And so that I may give you even more certain signs of what I am telling you, I add that throughout Lent he fasted on bread and water; and he was called Gregory Lopez. Since I have now been told that you bear this same name, I ask you to inform me whether you were that person, and to recommend me to God in your prayers."

To which Lopez wrote these words in reply: "I am the one of whom you write to me, and I will do as you desire of me."

2. When he arrived at Zacatecas, where the richest gold mines <note>original: "Goldgruben". While Zacatecas was primarily famous for its silver, the text uses "gold mines" to emphasize immense wealth.</note> are located, several wagons laden with silver were just about to depart for Mexico. There, amidst the great tumult of the people, he heard so many oaths and curses, and saw so much strife, contention, and bickering arise, that two Spaniards even murdered each other with their swords at the same time. The pain which this servant of God suffered, seeing two souls perish so miserably—and how they had lost an eternal good for the sake of a little silver, which is but earth—increased even more his desire to distance himself from all human society; for he considered into what infinite misfortune and misery people are brought by such vain things.

He therefore went eight miles further into the Valley of Amajac, which was inhabited by the Chichimeca <note>The Chichimeca were indigenous peoples of north-central Mexico, known by the Spanish for their fierce resistance to colonization.</note>, a kind of most cruel heathens. While he was searching thereabouts for a suitable place to put his intention into practice, he found a farmstead belonging to a captain named Carillo.

This Carillo was greatly astonished to see a young man in the prime of his years who intended to lead a solitary life in such a wilderness. Lopez, however, gave him good reason for this undertaking; he also said that as he had gone up the river, he had found a suitable place for it. Carillo offered him people to build him a hermitage, but Lopez declined this and only requested that he might lend him some tools for the purpose, which the captain willingly did. Lopez then built himself a small hut, in which the indigenous heathens <note>original: "Indianische Heyden"</note> helped him.

3. Now that he had stepped onto this field of battle <note>A common spiritual metaphor for the ascetic life as a struggle against the self and the devil.</note>, his first work was that he [placed] himself in

# First Part. The Life.

committed himself into the hands of God, and called upon Him for His assistance, saying among others these words:
> **Lord**, I come here solely to serve You, and to forget myself. If I go astray, You, and not I, will be the one to answer for it.

Lopes had surrendered himself and all his affairs so completely and thoroughly to God that his living faith—believing that God had accepted this sacrifice—caused him to speak of himself and his concerns as though they were no longer his own, but belonged to God alone.

He began his outward way of life quite harshly. His bed was a board, or the bare earth; he had nothing more than a wretched blanket to protect himself from the cold, and a stone for his pillow. This constituted the entire household furnishings of his little hut, which was decorated with several sayings written by his own hand to encourage him toward a holy life. He lived in constant abstinence; he ate only once a day, and even then, very little. For the most part, his food was only roasted <term>Maize</term> <note>original: "Türkisch Korn" (Turkish grain). In the 16th century, newly discovered corn from the Americas was often called "Turkish grain" in German-speaking lands because it was considered exotic.</note>, and now and then perhaps a completely raw salad, a turnip, or various herbs. He never ate meat; if it was given to him, he accepted it with thanks but did not consume it.

He taught the two sons of the aforementioned Captain Carillo to read and write, and at the same time sought to stir them toward the service and love of God through good exhortations. These children often found him on his knees in deep prayer, his hands crossed over one another, and his eyes cast down to the ground. They occasionally brought him small round loaves of bread baked from the aforementioned Indian corn; however, it did not please him when they brought more than one, saying that a single one was enough for eight days; he ate them even when they were hard and dry. Sometimes they found dead rabbits, quails, and figs in his hut, which are considered delicacies in that country. These presents, he said, were brought to him by his good friends, the wild <term>Chichimeca</term> <note>original: "Chichimequen". This was a collective term used by the Spanish for the various semi-nomadic indigenous peoples of northern Mexico who were often at war with the settlers.</note>, and he sent them on to the parents of these children.

He never used a candle, saying that he had no business for which he required one. He never went out to amuse himself or to visit his good neighbor; nor would he ever dine with him, no matter how much the neighbor pleaded with him to do so.

One of the Captain's sons, after the death of Lopes, testified under oath before the authorities that his brother-in-law, Martinus Moreno, once came away from Lopes entirely dissolved in tears; and when his wife asked him the reason, he answered that while he had intended to visit this holy man—who was then working at digging a ditch in his little garden—he had found him completely surrounded by angels. This had filled him with such wonder that he could not grow weary of praising and thanking God.

4. The various struggles, temptations, and attacks of the Enemy to weaken the courage of this young hero are known to the All-Knowing alone; yet he [Lopes] told me only...

<meta>This page continues the description of Gregory Lopez's ascetic life in the Mexican wilderness. Having established his humble hut, the narrative now shifts to his internal spiritual struggles and his interactions with both the Spanish military and the Indigenous populations.</meta>

<page-num>5</page-num>
<header>of Gregorius Lopes. Cap. II.</header>

He related that the Devil once attacked him in a visible form; and when I asked him what he had then done to defend himself against him, he answered: "Nothing else, but only, because I believed I could do nothing better than to continue in the purpose that God had put into my heart, that I resolved to practice it with all my power; and then this angel of darkness vanished, without ever attacking me in such a way again."

Constant prayer was his defense and weapon night and day. Especially for three years, this was his prayer:
> Thy will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. Amen, JESUS!
These words he used to repeat constantly in his heart and often aloud; indeed, he said that when he woke up, he never took two breaths before they came into his memory. If he occasionally fell into temptations and heavy suffering, such that he could not even take a book into his hands, then these words were his book:
> Thy will be done!
He would then fall to the ground and say:
> Lord, you are my Father, and everything happens in your presence, and according to your will;
whereby he was then strengthened anew in his course.

His temptations and trials were so fierce and manifold that he often told me he wondered how he had been able to persevere in his purpose, and that he could not remember the attacks without his hair standing on end. And another time he said that in these first three years, as he practiced this total <term>resignation</term> <note>In this context, "resignation" refers to the spiritual practice of "Gelassenheit" or "abandonment"—the complete surrender of one's own will to the will of God.</note>, God had led him through very difficult paths. Meanwhile, I have been able to learn little of this from him, so careful was he to hide everything; it only happened by chance that I learned one thing or another about it.

Outwardly, at that time, he also had his sufferings from men. The Spanish soldiers, who marched past his hut as they went to the war against the <term>Chichimeca</term> <note>The Chichimeca were a group of nomadic Indigenous peoples in north-central Mexico who fiercely resisted Spanish expansion in the "Chichimeca War" (1550–1590).</note>, called him partly a heretic and a Lutheran because he did not go to Mass; others said he was a fool for having settled in such a dangerous place. However, he had no danger to fear; for God had placed in the hearts of the barbarians such a fondness and reverence toward him that, even when they, according to their usual cruelty, murdered all other Spaniards they could get hold of, they greeted him kindly through signs which they made with their heads and hands, and brought him gifts, as we have mentioned above.

## He goes to *Mexico*, and from there to the lonely region of *Guasteca*. His sufferings and persecutions there. Of his stay and persecution at *Atrisco*, and finally at *Testuco*.

->I.<-

After *Lopes* had lived in this little hut in such a manner for three or four years, he moved, out of a spirit of accommodation <note>The original German word is *Herunterlassung*, which suggests a humble condescension or adapting his high spiritual standards to the needs or sensibilities of others.</note>, to a small village where he could go to church from time to time, because the people were so terribly offended by his strange way of life.

But he stayed there only two years, until God put it into his mind to return to his little hut. On the way, a man named *Sebastian Mexia* took him in, who was soon moved by his good example and wholesome reminders to begin a different life; this man developed such an affection for him that he wanted to make him his guide and the executor <note>original: *Executor*</note> of his last will <note>original: *Testaments*</note>, which *Lopes*, however, declined and went his way.

2. About seven years after he had begun to live in solitude, his little garment was so worn out that he necessarily had to have another. He could easily have received one as a gift if he had desired it: instead, he went and sought service with a gentleman whose household he managed with so much care, love, and humility that everyone admired his virtue. Once he had earned enough within two months to buy a simple garment, he requested his dismissal, and neither pleas nor tears, nor all the money offered to him, could keep him there any longer.

A certain good Dominican, named *Salazar*, urged *Lopes* to come to *Mexico* into his monastery, where he intended to give him a cell <note>original: *Celle*</note> so that he could live in complete freedom; he went there and was received with joy: however, because they would not give him a cell unless he also (as they say) became a cleric <note>original: *Geistlicher*; a member of the clergy or a monk</note>, he departed again and stayed in the lonely region of *Guasteca*, where he nourished himself on the fruits, herbs, and roots which the earth brings forth of its own accord, and continued in his holy practice of the love of God and neighbor.

3. From youth, *Lopes* had an uncommon love for the Holy Scripture; but now he applied himself so diligently to reading it that for four years in a row, he spent four hours daily on it, so that he knew it entirely by heart; for he had such a fortunate memory that he never forgot what he had once learned. He also loved other good books and read various ones on church history and spiritual matters. It was here (in *Guasteca*) that *Lopes* became very ill with the bloody flux <term>bloody flux</term> <note>original: *rothe Ruhr*; a historical term for dysentery, a severe intestinal infection.</note>, and after he had lain for several days in the greatest abandonment and want, so that he even had nothing to eat, Divine Providence, which

...who never abandons those who are devoted to Him, so that his condition became known to a priest in that same region named *Johannes Mesa*, who had him brought to his home and cared for him. After he had become healthy again, he wished to return at once to his solitude; but his kind host prevented this and kept him in his house for nearly four years, giving him a small room <note>original: *Kämmergen*, a diminutive of chamber or room</note> where he always kept to himself, edifying all who saw him through his holy conduct and powerful words.

Nevertheless, others—and especially spiritless clergymen—could not reconcile themselves to his way of life and suspected that he must be a heretic. A certain priest went to *Mexico City* and intended to report to the *Inquisition* that there was a man in *Guasteca* <note>Huasteca, a geographical and cultural region in northeastern Mexico</note> suspected of being a *Lutheran* because he carried no rosary, nor showed any other outward signs by which good Christians sought to prove their piety and pure faith (God have mercy!).

I asked this priest (these are the words of *Francisci Losa*, the author of this biography, who was then a preacher in *Mexico City*) whether *Lopez* spoke correctly and well regarding matters of faith, and how his life and conduct were? He answered: "As far as his faith is concerned, he seems to be irreproachable; he knows the entire Bible by heart; his life and conduct are blameless; he is almost always alone, as if he had great business to attend to, though he has dealings with no one. One has never been able to learn from him where he is from, who his parents are, nor anything of other worldly matters, just as if they were of no concern to him." I replied that I would be as angry with him as the priest *Eli* was with *Hannah*, the mother of *Samuel* <note>A reference to 1 Samuel 1, where Eli wrongly accuses the praying Hannah of being drunk.</note>. "If you," I said, "saw a robber without a rosary, you would certainly not take him for a heretic because of it," etc. And from then on, I conceived a high regard for *Lopez* and his way of life, of whom I had heard nothing until then.

4. The desire that *Lopez* had to remain unknown and hidden caused him to change his place of residence often; therefore, after he had been in *Guasteca* for four years and had become known and highly esteemed there among both the Spaniards and the Indians, he traveled to *Atrisco*. There, he stayed in a small room with an honest man named *Romero* and lived quite contentedly.

However, he could only remain here in peace for two years, as the evil enemy stirred up certain so-called clergymen against him. When these people saw in such a young man such good order in his life and conduct, such great detachment <note>original: *Abgestorbenheit*, a spiritual term referring to being "dead to the world" or completely detached from earthly desires</note> and wisdom, a virtue and knowledge that was most admirable in a man who had not studied at university, and who also wore no religious habit <note>The distinct clothing of a monk or friar</note>, etc., they were greatly offended. In their zeal, they accused him before the Archbishop of *Mexico City*, who conducted a legal inquiry into the matter; however, through this, the innocence, virtue, and great godliness of our *Lopez* were only made all the more manifest.
