Nevertheless, others—and especially certain soulless clergymen—could not reconcile themselves to his way of life and suspected that he must be a heretic. A certain priest came to Mexico City and wished to report it to the Inquisition <note>The Spanish Inquisition in Mexico was particularly vigilant against perceived "Lutheranism" or any deviation from outward Catholic ritual.</note> that there was a man in Guasteca whom people suspected of being a Lutheran, because he had no rosary, nor did he display any other outward signs by which good Christians sought to prove their piety and pure faith (**God** have mercy!). I asked this priest (these are the words of **Francisco Losa**, the author of this biography, who was then a preacher in **Mexico City**), whether **Lopez** spoke correctly and well regarding matters of faith, and how his life and conduct were. He answered: "As far as his faith is concerned, he seems to be blameless; he knows the entire Bible by heart; his life and conduct are irreproachable; he is almost always alone, as if he had great business to attend to, yet he has dealings with no one. One has never been able to learn from him where he is from, who his parents are, nor of any other things of this world, just as if they were of no concern to him." I replied that I would be as displeased with him as the priest **Eli** was with **Hannah**, the mother of **Samuel** <note>A biblical reference to 1 Samuel 1:12-17, where Eli mistakenly accuses the praying Hannah of being drunk because her lips moved but no sound came out.</note>. "If you," I said, "saw a robber without a rosary, you would surely not take him for a heretic because of it, etc." And from then on, I gained a high regard for **Lopez** and his way of life, of whom I had heard nothing until then.

4. The desire that **Lopez** had to be unknown and hidden caused him to change his place of residence frequently; therefore, since he had been in **Guasteca** for four years and had become known and highly esteemed there among both the Spaniards and the Indians, he traveled to **Atrisco** <note>Modern-day Atlixco, Mexico.</note>, where he stayed in a small room with an honest man named **Romero** and lived quite contentedly.

However, he could only remain here in peace for two years, as the evil enemy stirred up some so-called clergymen against him. When these people saw in such a young man such a good order in his life and conduct, such a great detachment <term>Abgestorbenheit: a mystical term referring to being "dead" to worldly desires</term> and wisdom, a virtue and knowledge which was most admirable in a man who had not studied at university, and who also wore no religious habit, etc., they were greatly offended by it and, in their zeal, accused him before the Archbishop of **Mexico**; who also held a judicial inquiry into the matter; through which, however, the innocence, virtue, and great godliness <term>Gottseligkeit: a deep, inward piety or devotion</term> of our **Lopez** were made only all the more manifest.

# Part One. The Life.

5. And with that, he took his leave from there and traveled to *Testuco* <note>Modern-day Texcoco, Mexico.</note>. Here he remained unknown for the first few months. He took extraordinary care to hide the grace he had received from GOD; therefore, he appeared outwardly to be a simple and foolish man, and no one noticed the treasure that GOD had hidden in his soul. It was later learned that because he fell into great poverty through this concealment, he was at times forced to sustain himself for several days on wild quinces. After some time, however, more notice was taken of him, and several devout people allowed him to eat with them. Now, some of those who saw his way of life were edified by him; others feared that there was something evil behind it. Indeed, some held him to be a hidden heretic and avoided his company—especially many among the outwardly pious of both sexes, who were highly regarded and seen as very spiritual because of their diligent observation of outward duties and ceremonies. Lopez, on the other hand, affected nothing singular or outward in his godliness, but concerned himself primarily with serving GOD in spirit and truth <note>A reference to John 4:24.</note>.

For this reason, he had to suffer much for several years afterward, since—as was said of the Savior JESUS in *John 7:12*—some said of him: "He is a good man"; but others said: "No, on the contrary, he deceives the people." But he bore everything with great patience. Meanwhile, he was once again examined here by order of the Bishop, through a pious Jesuit named *Alphonsus Sanchez*. Lopez satisfied him in all matters to such an extent that Sanchez said to the Archbishop: "In truth, I must confess that, in comparison with this man, I have not yet begun to learn the spiritual ABCs."

While Lopez was still here, various persons of high standing came to seek his counsel in their matters of conscience and spiritual affairs. They all went from him comforted and relieved of their doubts. It was then that people began to recognize that he had obtained a singular gift from GOD to comfort troubled souls and to set their minds at peace.

### Of Gregory Lopez. Chapter IV.

the Archbishop sent him one of his horses along with a servant to lead him there. He was also kindly received and cared for in that place. The entire morning he remained solitary in his little chamber; at midday he went into the dining room, always with his head bare, and one could not look upon him without admiring his inwardness and settled seriousness. He brought his little water jug, covered with a small napkin, with him and ate with great moderation <note>The German "Mässigkeit" refers to the virtue of temperance or restraint in eating.</note> without saying anything, even though the others spoke. After eating, he drank from his water which, because of the extreme weakness of his stomach, he had allowed to be warmed in the sun. When thanks had been given to GOD after the meal, he remained there for a while longer and spoke with those present about spiritual and edifying matters with such moderation and wisdom that one would have seen him as an angel rather than a man. As soon as the conversation was over, he withdrew again with a joyful countenance, with much politeness and great humility, and took his water jug and napkin back with him into his chamber, where he remained in his usual solitude until the same hour the following day.

2. Father Hermannus Ribera has related that when he was still a very young boy in this hospital and had to call Lopez to midday a meal, he sometimes found him outside of himself and in a state of ecstasy <note>The term "Entzückung" suggests a deep trance or rapturous prayer where the subject is oblivious to their surroundings.</note>, so that he did not answer when called; but when he continued to call him, he finally answered: "What do you wish, my son?" When he (Ribera) then said: "I have come to call you to the midday meal," he then went out of his little chamber and said: "GOD be praised!"

3. Because of his extreme physical weakness, he could not often visit the sick who were in this hospital; nevertheless, he encouraged others to do so and instructed them how they should conduct themselves in this task. In this, he spoke to them with such power that their zeal in this holy work and their devotion in the service of GOD were doubled; he also helped through his perpetual prayer where he could not do so through physical labor. Other sick persons whom he could visit, as well as those who were recovering, he comforted and strengthened in such a heart-stirring and lovely manner that everyone was edified by it, and all thanked God that they heard His servant speak in such a way. He had a singular gift for calming and satisfying those among the sick who—due to their ill temperament or the greatness of their suffering—fell into such annoyance and anger that they could not even bear their own attendants.

4. Just as it is nothing new, however, for the industrious Martha to complain about Mary’s sitting still <note>A reference to Luke 10:38–42, where Martha works while Mary listens to Jesus; Lopez is being compared to the contemplative Mary.</note>, so too did some who served in this hospital grumble about Lopez, holding him to be a man who was of no use. But those who took closer notice of him judged quite the opposite, based on the experience they themselves had of the benefit they received through his prayer, by which they gained great power and strength that they previously lacked to wait upon the sick day and night; this was in addition to the great gift they perceived in him for giving counsel and instruction to others, and the grace which GOD communicated to him to sweeten the pains of those who took refuge in him in their suffering and distress.

Finally, God arranged it so that I believed it was His will that I should take up this way of life; and in this way I actually arrived on Christmas Day, in the year 1589, at **S. Fé** <note>Santa Fe, a village founded as a social-religious community near Mexico City.</note>, to live with **Lopes**; where I remained with him until his death.

3. This mentioned above is related by **Franciscus Losa** himself, who described the life of **Lopes**. **Johannes von S. Jacob** adds that this **Losa**, a year before he came to live with our **Lopes**, asked him for advice on how he should proceed with his intention; for he was determined to obey him, even if he should command him to go onto a mountain and live there alone as a **hermit**; to which **Lopes** replied: **Remain living as a hermit in Mexico this year.** Upon these words, **Losa** felt such a change in himself that, in the midst of his distracting official duties, he always felt drawn to prayer and inner recollection, as powerfully as if he had already spent 50 years in this practice. He renounced all compliments, visits, and unnecessary social interaction. He gave up all the comforts of life, practiced self-denial, dismissed his servants, and gradually distributed more than sixty thousand **ducats** <term>A gold coin used for trade throughout Europe and the colonies; a very substantial fortune.</term> to the poor. When this year was over, he went to **Lopes** and said: "Behold, now the year is at an end in which I was to live as a **hermit**; what must I do now?" He answered only: **"Love God and your neighbor"**; and upon that they went their separate ways. As **Losa** reflected on **Lopes’s** reminder while on the way, he felt some resistance to practicing anew what **Lopes** had told him, as he thought himself already well-instructed in love, in which he had already practiced much; but as he remembered the powerful effect of the previous words of **Lopes**, he believed these must also contain more than he thought, and asked God to give him an understanding of their meaning and forgive him his pride. Immediately he heard a voice that said clearly to him in the depth of his soul: **"In order to be able to love God, you must strip yourself of yourself, and die to all things of this world"**; which words caused an incredibly great impression and change in him. In short, not long after, **Losa** resigned his office, along with 2,000 **ducats** of annual income, and came to **S. Fé** to live with **Lopes**. The first night he spent in this solitude, he had great temptations. When he told this to **Lopes** in the morning, the latter said to him: "I forgot you last night; it will not happen that way again in the future." For a year **Losa** lived quite contentedly, practiced prayer in his way almost constantly, and received many gifts of grace from God, so that he forgot to progress further. When **Lopes** noticed this, he spoke these words to him from the prophet **Isaiah: "You have found life; you have seen it in your hands; and have not troubled yourself to ask me," Chapter 57, 10.** <note>The author uses a specific German rendering of the Vulgate: *viam invenisti manus tuae propterea non rogasti*. Modern versions often translate this as "finding renewal of strength."</note> Which words opened his eyes in such a way as to bring him to a greater simplicity of spirit in his conduct, that he threw himself entirely into the immeasurable sea of the Divinity, and no longer held to any external means or inner feelings, in order to strip himself of everything that is not God. ->### of Gregory Lopez. Chapter V.<-

in this manner he lived seven years with **Lopez**, and provided for him from his very meager income which he had at **Santa Fe**, and served him until his death.

4. During this time (continues **Losa** himself to tell), I perceived many things which I recount in this description of his life, without him ever having told me anything of set purpose regarding what concerned himself, but only perhaps upon a occurring occasion, when he judged that it would be useful to me or others. Therefore, that which I say of it is very little in comparison with what I could have said; even though that which I saw in him was so wonderful that it cannot easily be told, like some other history. His life, however, was so uniform that one could almost judge from the arrangement of a single day what he did in entire months and years.

5. As soon as the day broke, he opened the window of his chamber; and after he had washed himself, he spent a quarter of an hour, or a little more, with the reading of the Bible, because it was the word of God, who commanded him to read such, and he had such a reverence toward the same that he took it as the daily rule of his conduct. And in this exercise he persevered with such constancy that he said to me a few days before his passing: **It is now ten days since I have read in the Bible; I do not remember that such has ever happened to me since the time of my seclusion.**

When he had finished this reading, he entered into such a deep <term>recollection<gloss>German: "Einsammlung"; a state of focused inward prayer where the soul gathers its faculties to be present with God.</gloss></term> that one could not recognize through any outward sign whether it was a prayer, or a meditation, or a contemplation; whether the objects with which he was occupied were sorrowful or joyful; whether he behaved actively or passively; whether he spoke with **God**, or whether **God** spoke to him. All that one could conclude from the stillness and devotion of his countenance was this: that he must be in a perpetual presence of **God**. He never spoke of this to a single person.

6. The Bishop of the Philippine Islands, **Salazar**, who loved him dearly, once asked him in what manner and way he actually occupied himself in his communion with **God**? To which he answered: his whole business was to love **God** and his neighbor. The Bishop replied: **You said that very same thing to me 25 years ago at Amajac: have you then since that time occupied yourself with nothing else but this single thing?** No, answered **Lopez**, I have always done one and the same thing, although my outward activities have been different.

7. See with what this servant of **God** spent the whole morning, the whole evening, and a great part of the night: these were his prayers, his meditations, and the bread with which he daily nourished his soul. Although he now exercised himself in the spirit in such a manner without ceasing, I nevertheless perceived that he was so occupied and permeated by it, especially in the morning, that he was quite

# First Part. The Life

...seemed to be outside of himself. He had no fixed place for this, nor a regulated posture of the body, but he generally stood upright, sometimes sat, or walked in his room; however, due to his great weakness in his final years, he could no longer remain on his knees.

8. At eleven o'clock, he emerged from this <term>recollection<gloss>German: "Einsammlung"; a state of focused inward prayer where the soul gathers its faculties to be present with God.</gloss></term>, took his small water pot and his little napkin, and we then ate together alone, unless some strangers had arrived. His moderation in eating was extraordinary, as we shall see hereafter. Over the meal we spoke of godly things, or sometimes of natural ones; whereby he took occasion to present very sublime truths.

9. After the midday meal we continued a little longer in our conversation. And when a clergyman happened to be present, it was a joy to hear **Lopez** speak with him, though he did so only by way of answering, or upon a occurring occasion; for he never began the conversation himself. Sometimes after the meal I would read to him the *Lives of the Saints*, which **Villegas** <note>Alonso de Villegas (1534–1603), a Spanish ecclesiastic and writer famous for his "Flos sanctorum," a collection of saints' lives.</note> described, or the *Chronicle of St. Francis*, or the *Spiritual Meadow* (a), or other such books, while he continued to remain in his union with God, which neither eating, nor conversing with men, nor his outward occupation, nor any other thing, could ever interrupt. It seldom happened that anyone visited him in the morning; but in the afternoon his door was open to everyone. He gave counsel, he comforted, and promised his intercession to those who desired it; as he was then visited very much in the final years of his life, not only by common people, but also by all kinds of persons of spiritual and worldly rank. Among the latter, the **Marquis of Salinas**, who was <term>Viceroy<gloss>The highest-ranking colonial official representing the Spanish King.</gloss></term> and President of the Royal Council of the Indies, visited him sometimes and would remain alone with him for perhaps two or three hours.

10. As soon as he was free of company, he returned again to his chamber, and did not come out again until the following day; he also never used a candle; at which many wondered, what he might be doing in the dark all that time.

He did not eat in the evening, but remained in silence until nine o'clock or half-past nine, and then wrapped himself in a wretched blanket, which was the best bed he had ever used. For at first he slept on the ground, and thereafter on sheepskins. But a few years before his death, I compelled him through my persistent begging to use a very thin cushion or <term>mattress<gloss>original: "Matelas"; a simple, thin sleeping pad.</gloss></term> alongside this miserable blanket. I do not believe that he slept more than two or three hours a night, but rather spent the remaining time in contemplation until the day broke, at which time he would, as said before, open his window again. And in this manner he lived, until it pleased God to take him into His eternal rest.

# The Sixth Chapter.

## The Knowledge of *Gregory Lopez* in Spiritual and Natural Matters.

->1.<-

Let us also recount a little of the divine virtues and graces with which **God** had endowed and adorned the soul of this His servant.

His science and knowledge of the Holy Scripture was truly supernatural. He knew all its histories by heart, word for word, the *Gospel of Matthew* and *John*, along with everything the other two Evangelists wrote, as well as all the *Epistles of Paul*, and the *Revelation of John*. In short, he knew the Scripture in such a way that whenever a text was discussed, he knew how to cite it immediately and with the greatest precision.

->2.<-

The *Vicar* <gloss>Latin: *Vicarius*; a representative or deputy of a high-ranking church official.</gloss> of the *Archbishop* once spoke with him about a certain scriptural passage that he could not find in the Bible. *Lopez* said to him: "The text is not in the Bible; there is one, however, that is nearly the same, which is this one"; he then opened the Bible and showed him the verse, which was indeed the one the *Vicar* was seeking. He was told of a certain man who knew the entire *Psalter* <note>The Book of Psalms.</note> by heart; to which he said: "The importance lies in being able to make use of it where it is necessary." His memory reminded him in an instant of all chapters and verses. He himself confessed that it was **God** who had given him the knowledge of the Scripture. Three *Doctors of Theology* <note>The highest academic rank in religious studies, usually requiring years of formal university training.</note>, to whom he explained several difficult scriptural passages at their request, were so astunted by it that they said:
> That is what it means to know: we all know nothing, and must say with *David*: Blessed is he whom You, **Lord**, teach Yourself. <note>A reference to Psalm 94:12.</note>

->3.<-

For those who only speak without doing are not wise; because divine wisdom begins with the doing, *Psalm 111, 10.* But *Lopez* had, as is written of the Savior, first done before he spoke. Therefore, it is not to be wondered at that he attained such a great measure of understanding in the **Holy** Scripture, so that all who heard him explain the darkest scriptural passages with such clarity had to confess that such high knowledge, in an unstudied man, must be attributed to a supernatural enlightenment and to <term>infused wisdom<gloss>Wisdom given directly by God into the soul, rather than acquired through human study.</gloss></term> from above. "How is it," one learned man said to another of his kind,
> "that we, who have spent our lives studying, still do not know nearly as much as this young, unlearned layman?"

->4.<-

...bring: whereupon he wrote about this whole dark book <note>The "dark book" refers to the Book of Revelation, traditionally considered the most difficult and obscure part of the Bible to interpret.</note> in less than eight days' time, and sent it to the same; who then could not sufficiently admire his ready understanding, science, and godliness therein. All the scholars who saw this writing admired it and stood quite confounded that a man who had not studied at a university would nevertheless be capable of writing such sublime things and making the darkest places so distinct and clear. He had written it without changing a single letter, as neat and beautiful as if it were printed.

5. Another man, who was acquainted with Lopez and was just then preaching at Zacatecas—where Lopez had lived for so long in solitude—said in a public sermon: "A man has lived here whose equal I would rather be than a King, Emperor, or Pope"; and added: "As I departed from him, I felt my soul permeated by the grace that I recognized in him."

6. Otherwise, he was far from showing himself masterly, or setting himself up as a judge among learned people, or pretending that one should follow his opinions, or engaging in disputations. A certain learned Jesuit, Antonius Arias, once disputed over the words of the Revelation of John, Chapter 21, verses 1 and 5: *Behold, I make all things new. And I saw a new heaven and a new earth* <note>original: "Ecce facio omnia nova. Et vidi cælum novum & terram novam."</note>; and said how some understood it according to the letter, that **God**, at the end of the world, would make a physical new heaven and earth; but others would have it that it is to be understood as the glorified bodies of the pious. To this, Lopez answered nothing more than: "When we are once there, then we shall see what will become of it."

7. In other sciences, he also possessed a wonderful knowledge. He knew both Church history and the history of all other religions and nations, together with their various provinces, cities, rivers, animals, plants, governments, manners, and customs. He understood astronomy, cosmography, and geography. He had manufactured a globe of the world and a general map of the entire world with his own hand, one cubit square <term>one cubit square: an "Elle ins Gevierte," roughly 24 by 24 inches.</term>, so neat and accurate that they seemed to be printed. He understood anatomy, medicine, and the powers and properties of plants, as well as through the infusion of which juices one could transform them into another and higher medicinal power, as I have seen the proof of with my own eyes; and he told me that if he knew a godly person who had a desire for it, he would gladly give him these recipes to use in love toward one's neighbor; but another would only misuse them.

8. Now although only "one thing is necessary" <note>A reference to the words of Jesus in Luke 10:42, suggesting that spiritual devotion is more important than worldly knowledge.</note>, and various interests are often a greater hindrance in the progress of godliness, yet it was quite otherwise with our Lopez. I once asked him if some of these things did not cause him distraction? To which he replied: "I find **God** just the same and as well in small things as in great things." Besides this, he could, without great effort or application, recognize and retain much, because **God** had bestowed upon him an uncommonly great understanding, a very lively concept, and such an extraordinarily firm memory.

## Chapter Seven.

### The light of discernment, and the grace in Gregory Lopez to give powerful counsel and instruction to other souls.

->I.<-

**But** even greater was his light in matters of the spirit, which he saw almost as clearly with his inner eyes as he saw physical things with his outer eyes. One could not sufficiently admire his precise insight in distinguishing between nature and grace—to strengthen the latter, and to suppress the former, both in himself and in others.

2. I can speak of this from my own experience. For several months in a row, I had applied myself to the practice of interior prayer <term>inwendiges Gebät: a form of silent, meditative prayer focused on the presence of God within the soul</term> and had found no small difficulty in it. Then an opportunity arose where I had to travel to perform a work of charity. Along the way, I found myself in such peace of mind and unusual joy that it seemed to me I was in heaven. When I returned to Santa Fe <note>S. Fè refers to Santa Fe, New Spain (modern-day Mexico), where Lopez lived for a time.</note>, I opened my heart to Lopez and said that my soul had poured itself out in joy. "My Father," he replied, "do not say that it was your soul, but your nature that poured itself out so." **God** also later enabled me to recognize how it had indeed been pleasing to nature <note>In the spiritual language of the time, "nature" refers to human ego, physical inclinations, or emotional impulses that can mimic spiritual experiences.</note> to perform outward works of charity and to speak of divine things; in these activities, nature was not as restricted as it was in interior prayer. Furthermore, on the journey, I encountered many changes and pleasant sights. Because of this, it caused me a much greater struggle than before when I tried to return to the practice of prayer.

3. Some people were once talking together in his presence about things that might serve to better awaken devotion. One said that he sometimes enjoyed a great sensation through music; another thought it was also very helpful to pray in the company of others. To this, Lopez did not answer a single word; I would have liked him to speak, however, in order to help these people out of their delusion, as I knew from experience that nature, under the pretext of spirituality <term>Geistlichkeit: here meaning the outward appearance of piety or religious feeling</term>, hides itself beneath all such external things. When these people had gone, I asked Lopez why he had given them no answer. He said: "That would be to condemn their path, which is like a staff to them, helping them to walk a little; otherwise, they would remain completely sitting still."

4. Regarding much speaking, he used to say: "It is not the love of **God**, but self-love <term>Eigen-Liebe: the egoistic preference for one's own desires and vanity</term> which causes many people to talk about **God**." He also said: "Just as the love of **God** consists entirely in doing, so too it speaks little, and sometimes nothing at all."

# First Part. The Life

5. To those who questioned him regarding their internal <term>inwendigen: relating to the inner spiritual life or the soul's state</term> affairs, he replied with very brief words, which were yet so full of wisdom and Divine power that they resolved the greatest difficulties and doubts.

6. A certain very troubled person came to Lopez and told him of his sufferings. He answered him with only these few words: "That is the fire of purification in which **God** wills that you should be." And these words were enough to comfort him and set his mind at rest.

7. Another asked him whether it might not be good for him to confess often, in order to quiet his mind regarding this or that scruple <note>In a religious context, a "scruple" is a persistent doubt or obsessive worry that one has committed a sin or performed a religious duty incorrectly.</note>? He answered: "It would be best if one had nothing to confess."

8. To another, who was in great suffering, he brought peace of mind through these words of the Revelation: "I counsel thee to buy of me gold tried in the fire, that thou mayest be rich." *Revelation 3:18*.

9. Again, another who was in the midst of great temptations was comforted by him only with these words: "The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force." <note>original: "Das Himmelreich leidet Gewalt, und die Gewalt thun, reissen es zu sich." A reference to Matthew 11:12, often interpreted in this period as the need for spiritual earnestness and "holy energy."</note>

10. Still another earnestly begged him to give him a direction for his path to **God**; to whom he only replied: "Go forth, my brother, **Jesus Christ** will be your Master and Guide." Through these words, the man perceived such a great change within himself as exists between being blind and seeing clearly: in that moment, he received a perfectly clear knowledge of himself and of the truths of the Gospel.

11. Another young man, who had good desires to progress, was very restless for five or six months, not knowing what way of life <note>original: "Lebens-Art." This likely refers to a "vocation," such as deciding whether to enter the priesthood, a monastery, or remain a layman.</note> he should choose; even the requested intercessions of other pious people had been fruitless for him. When he finally came to Lopez, he was completely calmed when Lopez said only these words to him: "Set your mind at rest; I will pray to **God** for you."

12. Whenever persons of high rank asked him what they must do to live rightly in their station, he answered: "Do that which you do out of love for **God**; that is enough."

13. To learned people, or those who were involved in many affairs, he commonly said: "Change your intention, and you will accomplish much." <note>Lopez emphasizes that the internal motivation—acting for God's sake—is more important than the external quantity of work.</note>

14. A certain very pious man desired from him a rule for praying well. To this man, he gave a paper on which he had written with his own hand the following words;

# Of Gregory Lopez. Chapter VII.

had: Our **Lord Jesus Christ** is the excellent Master, who can teach you the rule which you desire, to practice prayer; and this prayer is entirely contained within the Our Father. But, so that I give you no cause to complain that I am refusing you, I will tell you that you need only speak these few words, the meaning of which, however, encompasses much:

->**Lord**, my **God**, enlighten my soul, that I may know **Thee**, and that I may love **Thee** with my whole heart.<-

15. I have always attributed the great power of his words to his prayer—that is, to his inner communion with **God**; whereby his own life and activity were mortified, and he had become a passive and surrendered instrument of **God**. Therefore, when he spoke, his speeches, words, or pronouncements were those of **God**, spoken from **God**, and before **God**, in **Christ Jesus**. <note>The term "passive instrument" (*leidentliches Werkzeug*) refers to a mystical state where the soul ceases its own striving to allow God to act through it.</note>

16. Just as Lopez himself was spiritual, so too did he see in all things an image of the spiritual: for this reason, his speeches sometimes had a deeper meaning than fleshly eyes could see; (which is called allegorizing, and of which the entire Bible is full of examples.) When people, for instance, marveled at the beauty and pleasant scent of the flowers at Santa Fe, he said it was true that the flowers of Santa Fe had a pleasant scent: but Santa Fe means "Holy Faith"; and by the flowers, he understood the blessed in eternity, whose holiness had faith as its foundation, through which alone they pleased **God**. <note>Santa Fe was a community near Mexico City where Lopez resided. He frequently used the literal meaning of the name—"Holy Faith"—for spiritual metaphors.</note>

17. If one spoke of the beautiful springs and rivers between Santa Fe and Mexico, he said: The waters of Santa Fe (Holy Faith) are much better at their source than at Mexico; by this source he then understood **Jesus**, who is the source of true wisdom, and that the waters which one draws directly from this source are much purer and better than those which have flowed, as it were, like brooks through human reason; (by which he specifically aimed at the University in Mexico.) <term>Hohe Schule: Literally "High School," referring here to the Royal and Pontifical University of Mexico, then the center of academic and scholastic theology.</term>

18. If it was told that this or that person had been raised to a high rank (had become a Grandee of Spain), he said that true highness (grandeur) consisted in being a friend of **God**, hearing His Divine words, and accomplishing something great in His service. <note>original: "Grand d'Espagne." A Grandee was the highest rank of Spanish nobility.</note>

19. Once, a little dust rose up in Santa Fe, which is something quite unusual there. I asked him where it came from? He answered, pointing to the spiritual: There are pious people in Santa Fe (in Holy Faith) who are not yet perfect, and in whose actions something of the dust of the earth still clings: but as for those who are fully spiritual, they are entirely spirit. (a)

## Chapter Eight.

### A Brief Account of the Life of Don Ferdinand of Cordua.

1. Among all those who were blessed by the counsel and prayers of the servant of **GOD**, Gregory Lopez, Don Ferdinand of Cordua shines forth especially; he renounced his noble lineage, his blooming youth, and all his natural gifts and skills, and completely sacrificed himself to **GOD** and His service through the guidance of his faithful predecessor, Gregory Lopez.

2. He was the eldest son of this noble family and was born in **Mexico** on June 2, 1565. When he was ten years old, he began to study with great eagerness. He very quickly learned the **Latin** language and **rhetoric**, and made such good progress in his studies that he had already completed various translations of **Horace**, **Virgil**, **Homer**, and other poets. <note>original: "Horatio, Virgilio, Homero"</note> However, these occupations dampened in him all the good inclinations toward virtue that had lain in him during his childhood; and he began to behave according to the vain worldly fashions and in the manner of young lords, to which he was further led astray through his association with other noblemen.

3. Yet, in the midst of these vanities, **GOD** had His eyes fixed upon him and embittered the pleasures of the world for him, so that he was disgusted by them and felt a desire to leave them. Consequently, he fell into a deep <term>melancholy</term>, <note>In the 16th century, "melancholy" was often viewed as a spiritual crisis or a "divine sadness" that prompted a person to turn away from worldly vanities toward a religious life.</note> and he avoided the company of men, so that even his parents were placed in great unrest because of it; for this reason, they also sought to marry him off, which **GOD**, however, prevented.

4. All the pleasure of this young lord consisted in being able to be in prayer and in the company of pious people. Just as the name of Gregory Lopez was already very well known and famous at that time, Ferdinand also went and visited him at **Guasteca**. <note>The Huasteca is a geographical and cultural region in Mexico where Lopez lived for a time.</note> He was about 19 or 20 years old when he visited him. He remained with him for several days and opened the state of his soul to him; and through the conversations with Lopez, he felt such a change in his soul and such a fervent desire to please **GOD** that he found himself fully deter-

...oly, and began to follow the secluded lifestyle of this servant of **GOD**, his silence, his inward modesty, and his other virtues. He later said, thanking **GOD**, concerning this: "The Lord wished to instruct me through his servant: I myself did not know what I was seeking: I certainly felt that something was lacking, but I did not know what it was, and that was exactly what **GOD** wanted me to seek; and that made me so sad, restless, and melancholy. Oh Lord, how great was my pain! but You soon let it cease. I experience, without deserving it, the tenderness of your fatherly heart. <note>original: "väterlichen Eingeweide," literally "fatherly entrails," a traditional biblical expression for deep compassion or mercy.</note> You have come to my aid. Your true servant has enlightened my eyes, which did not see what was useful to me, through his light (which You placed in him); and his words have penetrated to the bottom of my heart. This change is an effect of your hand; may You be praised eternally for it!"

5. And in such a manner, Ferdinand returned to **Mexico** entirely inflamed with the love of **GOD**. He did great violence to himself to keep this great fire hidden in his heart; however, it soon broke through in the eyes of the world through the fruits of true repentance. He renounced all things that could hinder him in his purpose and watched with extreme care over all his actions. He shut himself in a chamber, where his eyes poured forth in tears and he sent up deep sighs in the presence of **GOD**. There he lamented with bitterness of heart his poorly spent years, and asked the Lord for forgiveness, with a firm resolution to rather die a thousand times than to offend Him, and to spend the rest of his life in His service alone.

6. Meanwhile, he soon returned secretly to **Lopez** in **Guastepec**, who then gave him further necessary instruction and comforted him through the promise of his intercession.

7. Ferdinand then received permission from his parents to live by himself in a house they had in **Tescuco**, seven miles from **Mexico**. He sold his horses, paid his debts, and gave the remaining money to the poor. He left his parents, his friends, his servants, and all the privileges that an eldest son can have in a rich house filled with every abundance.

the greatest part of the day he spent in prayer; and sleep did not prevent him from continuing in it at night, because he needed only a few hours for it, and comfort did not keep him in bed, as the same consisted only of a few boards, along with a blanket to protect himself from the cold.

2. **Jesus Christ** was the way in which he walked; and at the same time the guide who led him. The life, suffering, and virtues of this Savior of the world were the constant objects <note>original: "Vorwürfe." > "Lord, your will be done on earth as in heaven; Amen, **Jesus**!" 
whereby he had a great desire that these words might be fulfilled in him and in his neighbor.

3. He lived according to the inner as well as the outer man in great self-denial; therefore he gave his senses no nourishment. He ate little, and even then quite poor food, although he had been raised so delicately. He always lived secluded in his room, without going out for amusement <note>original: "Divertiren." Referring to worldly diversions or entertainment.</note>. His musical instruments, with which he had delighted himself in his vanity, he would no longer use. He burned all the verses <note>His poetry.</note> he had previously composed, and would not even remember the clever thoughts with which those who pass for "gifted minds" are enchanted.

His nature, to be sure, felt much annoyance in such things and wanted to resist; but the grace of **GOD** gained the victory: and whenever someone told him that he was going too far in this, he answered, 
> "he knew himself well, and must do no less than he did; for it was only right that his body, which had shared in sins, should also share in penance <note>original: "Busse." This refers to acts of atonement and the outward expression of repentance.</note>."

4. Although the parents of our **Ferdinand** saw their son continually proceeding in a life so far removed from the thoughts of the world, yet the great desire they had to marry him off caused them to press the matter often. This steadfastness of his in this matter greatly rejoiced **Lopez**, when he heard that he had so heroically renounced all the benefits and advantages (*advantages*) of his distinguished lineage. And thus he has won everything, as he left everything.

He never spoke of what he had left behind, nor of his noble lineage; because he believed it was a small thing that he had renounced all of it; and he said that, since **GOD** had given him some knowledge, he had not desired to have great advantages in the world except so that he might renounce them for **GOD**'s sake.

## Chapter Ten.
### Ferdinand’s final words, illness, and blessed passing.

->I.<-

After several years, when Ferdinand intended to put his plan of entering a monastery into action, and had traveled to Angelopolis <note>Angelópolis ("City of the Angels") is the historical name for Puebla, Mexico.</note> for that purpose to be initiated, he became so weak there that he had to be carried into the church and made to sit on a chair during the ceremony. Nevertheless, he fell into a faint; and when he came to himself again, he apologized to the Bishop for having hindered the ceremony in this way, and said he was nothing but earth, and would soon return to earth again.

The next day (which was the Sunday after Christmas) he was seized by a fever, which the physicians <note>original: "Medici"</note> did not consider to be very serious; meanwhile, he had to keep to his bed all that day and the following one, and on Monday he was so weak that he could hardly answer those who came to him; he only said to the Bishop: “This is truly celebrating a feast, when one is obedient to **GOD**.” At this, he seemed to lie entirely outside of himself and swallowed up in **GOD**.

Ferdinand said to his host, with the condition that he should tell no one: “I believe that our Lord will take me to Himself tomorrow morning: His will be done! I pray Him to forgive me for having served Him so poorly.”

Throughout the day he remained in his usual weakness; toward evening he broke out into these words: “O Lord, look here upon a poor man who is entirely covered with wounds. <note>This likely refers to the "wounds" of sin or a mystical identification with the suffering of Christ.</note> Have mercy on me, my God!” And turning his head to and fro, he repeated these words twice: “Alas! what a poor man, entirely covered with wounds! no one has compassion for me.”

2. At ten o'clock in the evening, he found himself extremely troubled: he began to sweat heavily, could hardly draw breath, turned his eyes toward his brother, and said: "The hour of the Lord has come," and so forth. He took his host by the hand and spoke: "I have need of help; let a confessor <note>original: "Beicht-Vater"</note> come."

He began to act piteously, with such deep and painful sighs that he could not restrain them. He tossed his body and arms to and fro, as if he were dealing with one who tortured him; he raised himself up, then let himself fall again, threw the blanket about, and often repeated these words: "**JESUS**, be with me! Stand by me, my **GOD**! What pain! Lord, it is time that You come to help me: what shall I do without You; oh, do not forsake me!"

He turned his head now to this side, now to that, as if entirely terrified, grasped those who were present by the hand, and repeated in this death-struggle <note>original: "Todes-Kampf"</note> these words: "My **GOD**! my Lord! what is happening to me?"

His confessor comforted him; and a good while later, as he lay with his eyes open and looking around in total dismay, he said: "O my Father, what terrible pains! I cannot express them. **GOD** has forsaken me; and what shall a weak and miserable sinner such as I am do, if He does not stand by me at such a time when I have so great a need of it, and when—if He does not show mercy—I must now be delivered over to the servants of His justice <note>In the mystical tradition, the "servants of justice" often referred to demons or purifying forces that test the soul before death.</note>. My **GOD**, be with me, and come to my aid in this terrible passage!"

He repeated with a strong voice, which did not seem to come from him, these words: "**JESUS**, be with me! Lord, what will become of me without You!"

He said to his confessor that his pains were the servants of **GOD** performing their office by tormenting him. His sighs were of such a nature that they seemed to come from a deep abyss; and his distraction and unrest increased to such an extent that it was thought they would suffocate him. But in such a terrible death-struggle, and in the midst of all his lamentations, his spirit always recovered itself again and united itself with **GOD'S** will, saying: "Lord, use only fire and sword against me, and spare me not in this life, only that You spare me in eternity."

This storm lasted in this manner for more than two hours, during which time he often repeated that **GOD** had forsaken him and delivered him to the servants of His justice; he also said, when they tried to comfort him: "O Lord, what pain! what dryness <note>original: "Dürre." In mystical theology, "dryness" or *ariditas* refers to a state where the believer feels no spiritual comfort or presence of God.</note>! what desertion! and what can a poor sinner like I am do without You? But if You have so ordained it, then let Your will be done!"

## Chapter Ten.

### Ferdinand’s Final Words, Illness, and Blessed Passing.

->I.<-

After several years, when Ferdinand intended to carry out his resolution to enter a monastery and had traveled to Angelópolis <note>The "City of Angels," now known as Puebla, Mexico.</note> for the purpose of being consecrated, he became so weak there that he had to be carried into the church and allowed to sit in a chair during the ceremony. ### First Part. The Life

3. Finally, the Lord relieved him. They put a fresh shirt on him, because the one he was wearing was completely wet from sweating, and he remained in a wonderful peace and tranquility, with his eyes directed toward heaven; his body, however, was so exhausted and as if battered <note>original: "zerschlagen," describing a body feeling bruised or shattered from the physical struggle of dying</note> that he could not move; his face, which had previously been quite glowing, now turned pale. When they wanted to turn him onto his side, as the doctors saw fit, he said twice: "**Jesus**, be with me! I surrender myself into your hands, and commend my soul to you;" and this Divine Savior took the same <note>referring to Ferdinand's soul</note> on the 28th of December 1589, at two o'clock in the morning.

4. He was only twenty-four years and six months old when he died; yet in the short time that he had spent in the service of God since his conversion, he had attained a high stage of grace and holiness, so that everyone had to admire his great faithfulness to the call of God. **Lopez** <note>referring to Gregory Lopez (1542–1596), the famous hermit and mystic</note> said in the presence of several persons: We will only recognize in heaven what kind of man **Ferdinand** was, and to what virtue God raised him in such early youth. In a few years, God shared with him the gift of an inward life in a higher degree and to a wider extent than many holy hermits have attained in many years of seclusion in the desert. God loved him greatly; and he also applied the graces that God bestowed upon him well to his own benefit.

On another occasion when **Lopez** spoke of the gifts, virtues, and earnestness of our **Ferdinand**, he lifted his eyes toward heaven and spoke: Praised be you, Lord, that you have bestowed such great graces upon him! We shall see him one day in your kingdom, when we depart from **Holy Faith** <note>original: "Sant Fé" (Spanish: Santa Fe); the text clarifies this as "the holy faith," but it also refers to the spiritual path Lopez and his companions followed</note>; and we will be reunited with him. And to **Don Francisco**, **Ferdinand’s** brother, he said: You have, my lord, a good intercessor in heaven, who rightly should be a great role model for those he has left behind.

5. It is said for certain that Father **Losa**, when he wanted to go to **Lopez** in his chamber on the very day that **Ferdinand** died, found him full of joy, with his eyes directed toward heaven, and heard him break out into these words: O blessed **Ferdinand**, all the choirs of heavenly spirits receive you with joy; so then take your place among them, etc. And when after several days, **Losa** received the news <note>original: "Zeitung," used here in the archaic sense of "news" or "report"</note> that **Ferdinand** had died, and he went to **Lopez** to make this known to him, and had hardly said the word, "He is dead," **Lopez** interrupted him and answered: Our friend **Ferdinand** is not dead, for he lives in heaven. Oh, how blessed he is, and what a good intercessor we have with God! Let us envy him (in a holy way); let us follow him; let us rejoice that we had him as a friend, and thank God for it.

# The Eleventh Chapter.

## How Gregory Lopez seemed to have recognized the thoughts of others.

1. IT appeared indeed that Lopez could see the thoughts of those who came to him. 
I was once (says Losa <note>Father Francisco Losa, the author of this biography and a close companion to Lopez.</note>) in the midst of a great temptation, which I disclosed to him, saying that I nonetheless hoped, through God's grace, I had not sinned in it. "Do not make yourself out to be so brave," he replied, "you were not such a hero as you say." He then added exactly what had been lacking and how I should have handled it.

2. Another man came from Angelopolis <note>A Latinized name for the city of Puebla, Mexico, "the City of Angels."</note> and told him of his spiritual doubts <note>original: "Gewissens-Scrupel," referring to scrupulosity or nagging anxieties about one's sins.</note>; whereupon Lopez answered him in such a way that the man said to him: "You have told me everything that was in my heart, and it was very necessary for me that you told me." Lopez replied: "Because God saw that it was so necessary for you, He moved my tongue to say to you what I have said."

3. Joseph of Vides, an advocate for the Royal Audience <note>term: "Royal Audience" (Real Audiencia), the high court and administrative body in the Spanish colonies.</note> in Mexico, who was moved by the prayers and the beneficial teachings of Gregory Lopez to give up his office after the death of his wife, said: "The words of Gregory seem to set fire to the hearts of those to whom he speaks; I have never left him without feeling a greater earnestness and resolve to serve God."

Once, this man went with another to Santa Fé <note>A village near Mexico City where Lopez lived for a period.</note>. Along the way, they spoke of matters concerning their consciences, which they intended to discuss with this servant of God. When they arrived at Lopez’s side, and before they had said anything about it, he spoke to them in such a way that they looked at each other in astonishment and thanked God that Lopez had answered everything so precisely and had satisfied them, just as if he had heard everything they had discussed with one another on the road.

4. 5. If people came to him out of idle curiosity, and not with the intention of applying his reminders to their improvement, he would answer nothing but: There are Doctors and Teachers in the Church.

A certain Dominican <note>A member of the Order of Preachers, a Catholic religious order.</note> came out of curiosity, and to dispute with Lopez over several passages of Scripture. 6. A certain pious man from Angelopolis <note>Latin for "City of Angels," referring to the city of Puebla, Mexico.</note>, who had a great desire to see our Lopez, once came to Santa Fe <note>A village near Mexico City where Lopez lived in seclusion.</note>, where he was received with all the friendliness and courtesy which Lopez was accustomed to show to everyone. This man's heart was then so inflamed with the love of God that he even asserted that Lopez appeared to him to be an apostle. As he then opened the state of his soul to him, Lopez spoke to him in such a way that his soul was filled with much comfort and joy, so much so that he could not refrain from saying so. This servant of God gave him the answer: thank our Savior for it. This man continued to visit him annually. Once, when he wished to reveal some doubts concerning his prayer, because they were causing him great distress, it happened upon his arrival that what he heard Lopez saying to other people who had arrived so comforted him that his suffering ceased entirely; and he could not sufficiently admire the man, because he perceived all virtues in him to such a high degree, especially humility, gentleness, patience, and love; and in short, he saw a completely heavenly man who walked among men.

7. A certain priest requested that he might pray to God for him; to whom he replied with a serious face: It would be better if you sought to serve God, and to walk on another path, in order to set your mind at rest. Whereupon this poor priest was so ashamed and dismayed that he did not dare to speak to Lopez afterward without first thinking of his conscience, as he himself later admitted.

8. Another, who was quite precise in his way, came to him and stayed with him for 14 days. But Lopez, who recognized in spirit that this man clung too much to those great gifts of grace <note>original: "Gnaden-Gaben," referring to spiritual favors or charismatic experiences.</note> which God showed him, in hopes of always obtaining more, said to him among other things: Let us take care that we do not exalt ourselves; for in truth, our lack of humility will cost us dearly in this world and the next.

9. A Franciscan, John of Saint James <note>original: "Iohannes von S. Iacob"</note>, who was greatly respected and loved by Lopez, once decided to go to Santa Fe to ask our blessed Lopez how he should go about remaining in a perpetual and pure act <note>original: "acte"</note> of the love of God, just as Lopez did, without being distracted from it by the occupations of his office; for he was a Vicar and a superior in the convent, and also had to preach regularly to both the Spaniards and the Indians. Several days before he departed, he wanted to see if he could perhaps manage it himself before seeking Lopez’s advice. He therefore applied, as he believed, all the powers of his soul to exercise an act of the love of God. However, because he entered into the denudation <note>A mystical term referring to the "stripping away" of worldly thoughts and self-will to reach a state of spiritual purity.</note> of the soul’s powers rather than the denudation of the soul itself (a), he exhausted himself greatly: for this way of exercising an act of love cannot well coexist with the outward occupations in which this man was placed. After he had thus spent all his efforts in vain to exercise this act of pure love, and having made the journey on foot, he arrived at Santa Fe at sunset; he was so faint and tired that Lopez had to give him something to eat immediately, and the conversation was postponed until early the next morning. He slept below in a chamber and asked the servant of God at what hour he should come to him? He answered: At whatever hour of the night you wish; for he slept so little that he was ready at all times. Accordingly, the Father stood up before sunrise, and as he was putting on his shoes to go to Lopez, he felt in the ground of his soul an inward light that completely illuminated him in everything about which he had intended to ask advice. This light made him truly exercise an act of the love of God in the interior of his soul, where no creature can reach (b). The same light also gave him to understand that the soul, through a supernatural grace communicated to it by God, can love Him without the help of the senses and without becoming weary; nothing could—

---

<note>(a) He wanted to turn away from all things by using the thoughts of his head and turn to God by force, clinging to Him with the coarse sensory inclinations of the outer man; which is a very human, laborious, and almost futile task. One must enter into a deeper denudation of the soul—that is, one leaves both the thoughts of the head and the coarse sensory emotions and inclinations outside in their place. Instead, one intentionally lets the innermost thoughts and inclinations of the heart focus on no other objects but God; rather, one keeps oneself, according to one's ability, from all attachment to creatures (even the most hidden); bare and set apart from all self-seeking and activity, and fundamentally yielded <term>Gelassenheit: a state of surrendered detachment or "letting be"</term> in the Will. One then turns with these same innermost thoughts and loving inclinations of the heart or the spirit, softly, simply, and lovingly toward God; beholding and embracing Him as present in the ground of the soul, and remaining in His presence, etc. This is the so-called active contemplation, and indeed one of the most useful and best kinds, because it is closest to passive contemplation. To practice such a thing uninterruptedly during ongoing business requires a passive and special drawing and effect of God in the inner ground, and a complete separation of the soul and the spirit. See more on this among the Mystic Writers.</note>

<note>(b) Behold, there he was suddenly placed into a kind of passive contemplation, which takes place in the ground of the soul; which for some is a passing experience, but for others is a more permanent state of the soul; and is also otherwise more or less passive, central, dark or light, bare or savory, according to how it pleases God and how the souls are disposed.</note>

...could even reach the point of darkening their light or making their love grow cold; and that this was the manner in which **God** wished to be loved, and how Lopez also loved Him with all his inner strength, without any created thing being able to hinder this act of love; and in this way, it could certainly coexist with outward works performed out of obedience or otherwise for the glory of **God** and the benefit of one's neighbor. This same light, which **God** granted him in the essence of his soul, communicated many other internal matters to him in that same moment, and rebuked him for seeking help from Lopez—who was, after all, a creature <note>In mystical theology, "creature" refers to any created being, including humans, as distinct from the Creator.</note>—when he should have expected it only from His Divine Majesty. For God was always essentially present in the essence of his soul to assist it with infallible certainty in all internal matters; for His hand was not yet shortened <note>original: "seine Hand wäre noch nicht verkürzet." A biblical idiom (Isaiah 59:1) meaning God’s power to help has not diminished.</note>. And since Lopez had nothing that he had not received from Him, God would be no less merciful toward the priest, provided he prepared himself properly to receive such great graces. This Father was, on one hand, almost ecstatic with wonder at such a great grace that **God** had shown him, and thanked Him for it with the deepest humility; but on the other hand, he did not know how he should now present his former doubt to Lopez, since **God** Himself had already enlightened him regarding it. In such a state, he went up to the chamber of the servant of **God**, who asked him with a smile: "What doubt do you have then?" He answered him: "To not hide the truth from you, I came to present a doubt to you, which **God** Himself has deigned to answer in the innermost part of my soul with divine clarity and certainty, and in that same moment, He gave me knowledge of many other entirely internal matters." When the priest then wanted to tell him about these things, Lopez helped him recount them. But because the priest said nothing of the rebuke **God** had given him, Lopez said to him: "Has our **Lord** not given you a good rebuke for coming and seeking a creature instead of placing your trust entirely in Him alone? Walk in the way He shows you, without ever (a) <margin>That is: in such a way that you would expect something from me as a creature and place your trust in me. For it is obvious that Lopez did not mean this absolutely or literally, nor did the priest take it that way, since he visited him often and socialized with him intimately until Lopez died, as he himself testifies in the *Life of Lopez, Chapter 29, Section 2.*</margin> coming to visit me further; for this is necessary, and our **Lord** does not wish it." The good Father stood there quite stunned and could not doubt that Lopez must have seen in **God** what had occurred within his soul.

# Of Gregory Lopez. Chapter XII.

...whoever does not stumble in word <note>original: "der in seinen Worten nicht fehlet." A reference to James 3:2: "If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man."</note>, then one may rightly have such thoughts of our Lopez. I lived with him in total fellowship for 18 years, and I deliberately paid close attention to all his words and actions to see if his virtue was a "mirror without spots," because I had resolved to follow his example; yet in all that time, I never heard a single blameworthy or unnecessary word from him. He spoke ill of no person, not even of pagans or heretics; he condemned the sins, but not the sinners.

2. Once, when he happened to recount a perverse deed from history and I then named the person he was speaking of, he answered me: "It is enough to condemn the deed without naming the one who committed it." If he was told that some spoke ill of him, his answer was: "We must believe that they have a good intention"; and he then excused them further, as best he could, saying that based on what people had heard about him, they were right to judge so. Indeed, he sought to excuse not only the people themselves but also their actions, without ever justifying himself; and sometimes he cleverly steered the conversation to something else.

3. A certain clergyman <note>original: "Geistlicher (wie man sie nennet)." The parenthetical "as they are called" hints at the narrator's distinction between those who hold the office and those who possess true spirit.</note> once rebuked him harshly for having no religious images in his chamber, saying that in this he was following the heretics <note>During this period, the absence of icons or devotional images was often viewed with suspicion by the Church as a sign of Protestant leanings.</note>; Lopez replied to him with a calm spirit: "Do not trouble yourself over this; if something offends you, there are superiors <note>original: "Vorsteher." Refers to Church authorities or regional overseers.</note> to whom you can report, and they will surely provide counsel in the matter."

4. He never spoke unless he was asked. A certain Bishop was advised by an acquaintance of Lopez to visit him while traveling through. The Bishop did so, came to Lopez, had him sit beside him, and also told those who had come with him to sit down. They spoke of various things among themselves without Lopez being specifically addressed, and therefore he said not a word. After a quarter of an hour, the Bishop left again. A few days later, the one who had arranged the visit asked what he thought of Lopez. He replied that Lopez seemed like a fool <note>original: "Narr." A term for a simpleton. In mystical traditions, being seen as a "holy fool" was often considered a mark of true humility.</note> to him. The friend asked further whether he had spoken of spiritual matters with him or asked him about them. When the Bishop answered "No," the other said: "I am not surprised that he answered nothing when he was asked nothing, and thus showed who he is." When Lopez heard this, he rejoiced that he had been taken for a fool, and said: "I would have judged just the same as he did about such a man as I am."

5. When learned men spoke of all kinds of sciences in his presence—which were excellently well known to him—he nevertheless did not open his mouth unless the speech was specifically directed to him and he saw it as necessary; so that one would have taken him for a peasant-like and ignorant man. And he did the same when spiritual matters were discussed, and with people who often

6. One day it rained very heavily; as I was standing by the window, I said: "Look, what a heavy rain!" and at that moment a fierce lightning bolt struck my hand, causing me great pain. When I told this to Lopez <note>original: "Lopes"</note>, I received the answer: "You have been paid what you deserved, because you spoke unnecessary words; for I could see well enough that it was raining hard." <note>This anecdote illustrates the strict ascetic view that even stating the obvious could be considered "idle talk," a concept derived from Matthew 12:36.</note>

7. Another time, when he reminded me of something important regarding my inner state, I asked him why, since he knew this, he had not told me sooner? He answered: "I do not say everything that I know, but only that which is necessary." And on another occasion he said to me: "I once lived for two years without opening my mouth, except to say good day to my host, whom I happened to see once every 24 hours."

8. Previously we have seen that Lopez never spoke unless he was asked; however, an exception was made whenever the honor of God <note>original: "GOtt"</note> or the love of one's neighbor particularly required it. If, for example, someone was in heavy inner or outer suffering and seemed to complain somewhat against God, one had to marvel at the emphasis with which he spoke to such a person to make them recognize their error, ignorance, and weakness, and to show what the depth of the wisdom and mercy of God is, which is hidden from the eyes of men in their tribulations, and how they are obligated to surrender themselves to His guidance and yield to His more than fatherly hands.

9. No less few were the words in his writing. I still have several of his letters, of five, six, or fewer lines, as we have already seen an example above. He wrote some to our Viceroy <note>The Spanish royal representative in Mexico.</note>, in response to those he received from him, and one of them consisted only of these words: "I will do what you desire of me." For people commonly requested him to present this or that matter to God in prayer <note>original: "Gebät"</note>.

10. Just as his speeches were short, they were, on the other hand—as was his conduct—full of great wisdom and prudence. He answered those who questioned him calmly and deliberately, or perhaps not at all, as he judged necessary. And since a question put to him often contained four or five other matters at once, he answered each of them so precisely and orderly that he did not skip a single point that he believed to be necessary.

### Of Gregory Lopez. Chapter XII.

...memory that everything he knew was present to him; yet he knew how to restrain himself in such a way that he never spoke unless he deemed it necessary.

12. A clergyman, who was a Doctor of Theology <note>original: "Doctor Theologiæ"</note>, once came to visit him and asked me to arrange for Lopez to speak with him about <term>God</term>. I did so, and the Doctor began first, delivering a long speech to draw Lopez out. When I saw that he did not answer anything, I signaled him to do so; but he answered me very softly, so that the Doctor, who was a little deaf, did not hear: **"My silence will edify him more than my words."** And although the Doctor stayed with him for two days and a night, he did not say a single word to him about <term>God</term>. I asked the Doctor as he was leaving what he thought of Lopez? He answered: "I have a great respect for his silence." Lopez told me afterward: **"My Father, I see that many speak well; but as for us, let us do good."**

13. When someone, in order to argue or to test him, presented something in the Latin language <note>original: "Lateinischer Sprache"</note>, Lopez would answer: **"Tell it to me, if it pleases you, in Spanish."** Once they had done so, he would say: **"Was that what you wanted to tell me?"** and thereby gave them to understand that he did not consider it necessary to respond.

14. When some asked him for advice—whether they should marry, whether they should return to Spain, or other such matters—he answered nothing further than: **"I will commend the matter to God in prayer."** <note>original: "Gebät"</note>

15. Regarding the externally secluded life compared to life among people, he said: **"A tree that is planted in an open field requires much stronger roots to preserve itself against the storm winds than another that stands in safety behind a mountain."** <note>This metaphor suggests that those living "in the world" require a deeper, more robust internal faith than those protected by the walls of a monastery or a hermitage.</note>

16. When subjects complained about the conduct of their princes, authorities, and judges, he said: **"If you were in that same position, you would perhaps not do as well as they do; and who has appointed you to judge them?"** But if they wanted to insist on their complaint—that the officials truly acted wrongly—he answered: **"Then it must be told to the person themselves; it is useless to speak of it here."** Otherwise, his answer was: **"My lord, you would not dare to say such a thing in his presence."**

17. When people who wished to be seen as pious spoke ill of someone, he said to them: **"I cannot believe that one is pious and virtuous if they wish to set themselves up as a judge over other people and speak to their detriment."** Or else: **"This is not the place to correct such things; that is not what we deal with here."**

# Part One. The Life

4. He concealed his virtues and graces <note>The German *Gnaden* refers to spiritual gifts or divine favors.</note> as much as he possibly could; and when I once remarked to him that such a task seemed so difficult to me, he replied: "It is not difficult for those who have faith to hide their virtues; for because they are certain that they are seen in Heaven, they care little that they are unknown in the world."

5. So Lopez also never rejoiced in any temporal thing; rather, all his joy was in God alone. "To us," he once said to me, "who live under the law of grace, it must be a great shame to love anything in the world after we have renounced everything; since Queen Esther, who was the wife of such a great monarch, said to God: *You know, Lord, that since I was brought here into this palace, I have never rejoiced except in you alone.*" <note>original: "Stücke in Esth. Cap. 3, 11. 12." This refers to the "Additions to Esther" found in the Apocrypha.</note>

6. He had never, he said, since the time he had taken up the solitary life, desired to see anything in this world—not even his relatives, his friends, his fatherland, and so forth.

7. He was free from all disordered attachment to people and trusted solely in God alone. From the day I came to know him until his death—eighteen years in succession—I sought to care for him and devoted myself to him as if I had been his slave. This was well known to him, and he was grateful to me for it. Nonetheless, I can assure you that I could never perceive that he was too attached to me or placed his trust in me; indeed, not even in himself, nor in his own works. He also wished that thanks should be given only to God and not to him, if he happened to advise or serve his neighbor.

8. He was detached from all spiritual gifts, feelings, and the like, and said the ecstasies <note>original: "Entzückungen"</note> he desired to have in this life were to unite himself with God and to make himself more and more conformed to His holy will, in order to obey it in all things.

He did not rejoice over the memory of his past difficult struggles and sufferings, nor his attained virtues and graces.

9. Just as he was poor in spirit, he also loved physical poverty; and he commonly used to say: "When a person takes pleasure in outward poverty, it is a sign that he is rich inwardly."

He never wanted to possess anything as his own property; he also remained always in this poverty, without paying attention to his present needs or worrying about them a single day in advance. I have never been able to perceive in him the slightest desire for created things.

### of Gregorio Lopez. Chapter XIII.

<margin>D 3</margin>

10. It was all the same to him what kind of clothing **God’s** Providence <note>German: *Vorsehung*; the theological concept of God's intervention and care for the world.</note> sent to him, though he otherwise handled it quite cleanly. For the first eleven years, he wore a garment that hung down to his feet; and afterwards, another dark brown coat was given to him, which he wore for the rest of his time until his end. He washed his clothes himself, as well as his feet, for which he—due to his frailty—previously warmed the water in the sun.

11. His food was poor and very little, and he used to say of it: The poor must take care of their health, for fear that if they commit excess in eating or drinking, they might become a burden to their neighbor.

12. In the earlier years, he ate no meat, as mentioned above; but later, when he had to interact more with people, he ate everything that was set before him, yet little, and only once a day: otherwise, even when he was sick, he never demanded anything else or better than what was reached to him.

13. His bed and chamber were poor, as we have seen above and will touch upon later. All his possessions consisted of a Bible, a map, and a globe <note>Lopez was known for his self-taught knowledge in geography and the natural sciences, despite his life as a hermit.</note>—both made with his own hand—and two other books which he had also written with his own hand.

14. He had also written excellent annotations on some of the white pages of his Bible. This Bible I lent to a priest at his request, but to my regret, I was never able to get it back.

15. It often happened that he had traveled the whole day on foot, and in the evening, quite tired and without food, he would lie down on the bare earth, and the next morning travel several miles further without any person daring to refresh him in his need; for in his manner, one would have taken him for a distinguished man <note>German: *vornehmen Mann*; implying he possessed a natural dignity or noble bearing that disguised his destitution.</note> rather than a needy person.

16. He also never wished to demand anything in his poverty. I asked him one day, if I should perhaps find myself in great want, whether I must not then humble myself and ask for alms? He answered: As for me, I would not do it. I replied: It seems to me I would do wrong if I did not ask for what is necessary where I lacked it. He said: You are right, and you would be able to do it with a free conscience. But as for me, I cannot do it; for **God** leads everyone as it pleases Him.

17. In his final years, he had to take a little wine every morning, or else he would suffer, if he omitted it, a violent colic <term>Colik: a severe, fluctuating pain in the abdomen</term> and stomach pains.

One day now, I saw him quite weak and pale, and when I asked him,

20. It was also a wonderful thing regarding his poverty that **GOD**, as it seemed, willed that he, as a truly poor man, should be nourished by that which is left over from others. For as often as something special was prepared for him, it caused him harm; as I have frequently experienced when I had something more nutritious prepared for him that might serve to strengthen him in his great weakness; hardly had he eaten it, before he felt worse, and he begged me not to do such things anymore. I thought at first he said this only so as not to be a burden to me, and I continued in it regardless; until he finally told me straight out that such was not the will of **GOD**. And in this manner, it seemed that **GOD** alone wished to be his housekeeper and caregiver <note>German: *Haushalter und Verpfleger*; terms emphasizing God's role as the primary provider of daily needs.</note>, without allowing humans to interfere in His office and work.

# The Fourteenth Chapter.

->On the inner and outer sufferings of Gregorio Lopez.<-

->I.<-

His great patience and unshakeable stillness of mind, in all internal and external sufferings, was extraordinary.

2. Of his internal sufferings, struggles, and trials, we have learned little or nothing; only **GOD** and His angels were spectators to them. And in this very thing his great strength and patience shine forth most clearly: that in his internal temptations and trials (which truly will have been neither few nor small), he said nothing about them to anyone, nor sought comfort from any creature <note>In the spiritual language of the time, "creature" refers to any created being, particularly other humans, as opposed to the Creator.</note>.
