He once told me that he did not believe his internal sufferings could have been any greater than they were; he could not think of them without trembling, and he would never reveal the specific circumstances to any human being.

3. Nevertheless, we can easily judge from the answers he gave to those who sought counsel from him regarding their own internal sufferings that he must have been uncommonly experienced in them. The most cruel torments, he said, that one can suffer in a physical martyrdom, pass quickly; but **GOD** allows spiritual martyrdoms to be suffered which far exceed those. As he also told me one day, **GOD** had led him through very heavy paths during the first three years when he practiced complete resignation <note>original: "völligen Resignation"; a central concept in mysticism referring to the total surrender of the self to God's will.</note>.

4. At another time I saw that he was very weak and looked very ill; therefore I went to him more often and stayed longer with him to see if I could refresh him in any way. I also asked him what sufferings he had? But he did not tell me. Finally, he confessed that he had very great and constant toothaches and other ailments. But I was not satisfied with this because I knew well that he was not telling me everything. I therefore persisted with him so long and urgently, and pressed him so hard, that he did something he had never done before, and revealed to me something of what he had to suffer internally from **GOD**, saying these words: "Lord, you know that for the sake of your love, I give no place to any creature in my heart; and yet you forsake me so that, though you see me enduring such great suffering and can heal me, you do not heal me; yes, though you could do it with a single word, you nevertheless bring me to the point where I must eat grass (a) with the beasts."

I was so dismayed that he told me something of what passed between **GOD** and him that I wrote it down immediately; and this happened on March 23rd, 1591.

5. Even when he had nothing to suffer for his own person, he took on the burden of his neighbor in such a way that he nevertheless had no less of a load to carry.

6. As I had observed with attention for several years that this man of **GOD** never grew tired of walking in the ways of virtue, I once said to him: "You surely have no rest in the ways you walk." To which he replied with a joyful and calm face: "It is true that I can have no rest as long as my brothers are in such great dangers, labor—"

7. Another time, when I said something about his sufferings and hardships, his answer was: "There are people who certainly carry much heavier burdens than these."

8. Regarding his external sufferings, he often suffered from violent stomach colic and toothaches, without complaining in the least or letting it be noticed; I could only become aware of it by his great weakness and at his meals.

9. One day I saw that he was completely worn down. I asked him what was the matter? He answered that it had already been 14 days that he had constantly had severe colic.

10. He often had the fever: the means to cure such was that he remained without eating for three, four, or five days; yet he never took to his bed.

11. In *S. Fé* <note>Santa Fe, Mexico, where Lopez lived in a small community.</note> he had toothaches for almost an entire year; and I did not notice it, except for the fact that twice he used certain herbs known to him, and that the pains were sometimes so violent that he could not eat at all.

12. He used to say: One must not desire sufferings; but endure them with brave courage when they arrive.

Just as we have never heard him state a single rule that he did not practice himself, so he also practiced this one with such patience that he seemed not to be moved by the sufferings at all.

13. Of his sufferings which were inflicted upon him through people's blasphemies, condemnations, and persecutions, mention has already been made several times above: we see here again how little he was disturbed by them. Some held him for a heretic, others for a fool, others for a vagabond <term>Land-Läuffer: a transient, tramp, or wandering beggar, often viewed with suspicion by authorities</term>, and so forth. He remained silent to everything and never made excuses for himself.

14. Once, when some of his good friends informed him that such a great noise was being made on his account, he answered: "God preserve me from spending my time so poorly as to concern myself with that."

15. A certain nobleman once spoke with me about the hospital at *Guastepec* <note>Oaxtepec, Mexico; site of a famous hospital run by the Brothers of Charity where Lopez resided.</note>, where *Lopez* was staying at the time. Among other things, I told him there was a man there named *Gregorius Lopez*, who was of great virtue, great understanding, and of high prayer. "What does he do then?" he asked. I said: "He spends his whole life in a small chamber, in prayer to God." He answered: "I would like to have someone give that fellow a couple of hundred lashes <term>Geissel-Streiche: strokes of a whip, traditionally used for punishment or as a severe form of penance</term> to put him in good spirits."

# The Fifteenth Chapter.
## Concerning Gregory Lopez’s Self-Denial and Mortification in Corporal and Spiritual Matters.

->I.<-

We shall see, in a few words, how our blessed Lopez denied himself in all things, and especially how he kept his senses in check and was dead to their desires <note>The term used is "Abgestorbenheit," a mystical concept referring to being "dead to the world" or completely detached from earthly cravings.</note>. He showed as little love or inclination toward any human affairs as if he were not like others—namely, a man of flesh and blood.

2. He looked upon people with a noble freedom, just as if they were souls without bodies, or inanimate forms. His modesty and reserve created an impression of reverence. He also denied himself the lusts of his eyes in everything else. Only once did he go with me to see the springs at Guastepec <note>Modern-day Oaxtepec, Mexico, known for its thermal springs and gardens.</note>, and he said then that he had done it merely to please me, because I had urged him so much to do so.

3. For more than six years that he lived in S. Fé <note>Santa Fe, a community near Mexico City.</note>, people often strongly urged him to go just once and see a garden that belonged to the house where he lived, which contained many beautiful waters, trees, and flowers; but he did not enter it, except only to draw water for drinking.

4. He did not seek out what was pleasant to the ears; but if he had to listen to it, he did not flee. "If," he said, "all the most beautiful music in the world were gathered together, I would not take a single step to hear it."

5. He had by nature a great aversion to foul odors; yet he never desired pleasant-smelling things. He rarely accepted flowers; or he only did so so that he might not grieve those who gave them to him.

6. He ate only for the maintenance of his life, but not to please his taste. Whenever I might suggest that he should eat something such as a melon, grapes, or figs—which are highly regarded and excellent in this land <note>Reference to the fruits of colonial Mexico, where Lopez lived</note>—he would merely smell the melon and say: "It is enough for this year." He said the same even if he had enjoyed only half a fig.

7. He preferred eating bread because it was the food of the poor; however, a few years before his death, he could not eat it unless he dipped it in warm water. One day he said to me: "My Father <note>original: "Pater"</note>, I think you have not noticed that as long as we have lived together, I have never eaten more on one day than on another."

8. As long as his health permitted, he had no other bed than the earth; later, he lay upon wretched sheepskins; until his great weakness and illnesses forced him to take a very thin and small cushion or mattress, along with a poor blanket; yet I had to urge him strongly to make use of it.

9. He slept no more than three hours, and one could not even call it a proper sleep; and yet he said, whenever someone asked him why he slept so little: "I sleep too much."

10. He took little care for his outer man; nor could he easily bear it when others did so.

11. The air in Santa Fe <note>S. Fé; a village near Mexico City where Lopez spent his final years</note> was quite unhealthy for him; but whenever he noticed my concern about it, he said: "I pray you, do not trouble yourself over it; **God** will provide."

12. Just as he gave no room to his own life in physical matters, so too did he allow no nourishment for it in spiritual matters. He made no display of his self-denials, nor did he delight in his own virtues and gifts; I never saw or heard him weep, nor sigh, nor complain, nor break out into words in his prayer and walk with **God**.

13. I once said to him: "How is it possible that, since you are always united with **God**, the presence of such Majesty never makes you sigh or speak; but that you are always as if buried in the abyss of His infinite goodness?" "That is not how it happens," he answered me; "for in truth, I groan and sigh a thousand times a day; I speak almost constantly to **God**; but inwardly. And it has been thirty years now that I have done it so. For I do not want to let Nature <note>In this context, "Nature" refers to the "lower self" or the ego, which seeks emotional satisfaction from spiritual experiences</note> know my feelings, now that I have recognized her tenderness and that she is only a thief; which proceeding is no small self-denial for her."

## The Sixteenth Chapter.
### Of Gregory Lopez's Prayer and Interior Exercise of Love.

->I.<-

Just as the primary practice and constant occupation of our Gregory consisted in interior prayer, or "walking with God," we shall be able to consider the description of his whole life most thoroughly and usefully if we describe this interior practice more clearly from the few things we find recorded about it.

2. We have already seen above how, from his childhood and tender youth, he practiced walking with God without allowing business or various external distractions to hinder him. We have also touched upon how he later practiced this interior prayer—specifically for three consecutive years, night and day—in the most inward surrender and conformity to the will of God, saying:
> Thy will be done, on earth as it is in heaven; Amen, JESUS!

After this time, and until his death, he practiced unswervingly to fulfill these words:
> You shall love God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength; and your neighbor as yourself:

and through this, he attained such a great love of God in a short time that he told me it would be very difficult for him to interrupt this holy practice even for a moment, whether it be while eating, speaking, or in any other activities of the mind or body.

3. The most precise report on how Gregory Lopez specifically practiced this love of God and neighbor internally is given to us by the aforementioned Franciscan, John of St. James, who was perhaps the most intimately acquainted and familiar with our Lopez, and who also, by all appearances, had the most light and experience in recognizing Lopez's internal states. This man speaks of him in the following manner:

He lived in a pure union, detached from all other things, which he maintained at all times with God in the "ground of his soul" <note>A term used by mystics to describe the deepest, most essential part of the human spirit where it meets the divine</note>, where this Highest Majesty establishes His dwelling and where no creature can reach (as Tauler <note>Johannes Tauler (c. 1300–1361), a famous German Dominican mystic whose writings influenced Lopez</note>

# The Sixteenth Chapter.

## Concerning Gregory Lopez's Prayer and Interior Practice of Love.

-> I. <-

Just as the main practice and perpetual occupation of our Gregory consisted in inward prayer or walking with God, we will be able to consider his entire biography most thoroughly and usefully if we describe this inner practice of his more clearly from the few things we find recorded about it.

2. We have already seen above how he practiced walking with God from his childhood and tender youth, without business or various external distractions being able to hinder him in it. We have also touched upon how he afterwards—specifically for three years in succession—practiced day and night in the most inward surrender and conformity to the will of God through this inward prayer:
> Thy will be done, on earth as it is in heaven; Amen, JESUS!

After this time, and until his death, he practiced unwaveringly to fulfill the words:
> You shall love God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength; and your neighbor as yourself:

and through this, he attained so great a love of God in a short time that he told me it would be very difficult for him to interrupt this holy practice even for a moment, whether it be while eating, speaking, or in any other activities of the mind or body.

3. The most precise report of how Gregory Lopez practiced himself inwardly, especially in this love of God and neighbor, is given to us by the aforementioned Franciscan, John of St. James <note>original: "Johannes von S. First Part. The Life.

(as the 34th chapter of the *Institutions* says) <note>original: "cap. 34. Instit. spricht"</note>, through this inward union, I say, he had raised himself above all created things. He was in a perpetual and so inward **Act of the Love of God**, and in which his soul, detached from everything, was so inwardly united with this Divine Majesty, that from this very source he received all the graces which the **Lord** communicated to him, and all the excellent heroic virtues which he possessed in such a high degree that one will hardly find his equal among the former saints.

4. I asked him whether he also had certain regulated hours to practice more fervently, or more than usual, in these **Acts of Love**, and whether he did not perhaps slacken in them during conversations or other occupations? He answered that he had no set time or hours for it, nor was it necessary for him to have them, because no created things were able to turn him away or hinder him in this perpetual **Act of the Love of God** and **of the Neighbor**, which had become, as it were, natural to him; and it was so far from being the case that he should regress in this union which **God** communicated to him, that he rather progressed further in it daily, by offering back and sacrificing all the graces which the Divine Majesty showed him through the **Act of Pure Love**, without appropriating any of it for himself: and this union was the fountainhead and origin of all that he knew. And thus it was **God** who had been his teacher, and not books; although it had been a great pleasure for him to read what *Tauler* <note>Johannes Tauler (c. 1300–1361), a famous German Dominican mystic.</note> and *Ruusbroec* <note>Jan van Ruusbroec (1293–1381), an influential Flemish mystic.</note> had written of those purely spiritual matters which **God** is accustomed to communicate according to His pleasure.

5. He also told me that **God** had given him to understand that the very greatest union which exists between **God** and the soul is this: when the soul stands in such a way that there is no mediation <gloss>interposition</gloss> <note>original: "interposition"</note> between **God** and it; and that **God** had let him see and comprehend the nature of this union through the example of that union found between light and air. For although these were two different things, each having its own distinct essence, they were yet united in such a way that no one but **God** alone could distinguish them. With how much greater right then is that union exact which is found between the pure essence of the soul and **God**, who is an infinitely pure Spirit.

6. When I asked him one day what he would have done if he had become a priest? He gave me this answer: I would have done what I do now. And if I were certain, he said, that I should die in a few hours, I would do nothing else than what I do now; for I truly sacrifice everything to **God** that is in my power through a perpetual **Act of Love**, and I can do nothing more, unless He Himself provides me with the means to do so.

### Of Gregorio Lopez. Chapter XVI.

7. This servant of **God** also told me in the course of our conversation that perfection does not consist in visions, revelations, and ecstasies <note>original: "Entzückungen"</note>, although **God** often graces His servants with them, because He works in each person according to their ability, according to what is necessary for them, and according to the state of soul in which they stand. He said that for those souls who are accustomed to practicing acts of pure love, no <term>suspension of the senses<note>original: "suspension des sens"; a mystical state where physical senses are temporarily deactivated or "frozen" during intense prayer</note></term> is necessary to have frequent communion with **God**, because the senses do not hinder them. He added that he never had revelations or ecstasies that deprived him of the use of his senses; nor had his senses ever caused him distractions, because they had been made completely <term>spiritualized<note>original: "spiritualises"; meaning the physical senses have been refined to serve spiritual purposes</note></term>, were fully subject to the intellect, and were entirely conformed to the will of **God**. Regarding this, he shared this example with me: As long as a master is not yet certain of the love and loyalty of a servant, he lets him go out and locks the door when he has important things to say to his wife. But when he has proof that this servant has such love for him—a love that should be called that of a son rather than a servant—then he speaks freely of the most secret matters in the servant's presence. And exactly so it happens in regard to my senses.

8. As we continued the conversation, Lopez said to me that he knew a soul who, for thirty-six years, had not for a single moment ceased to perform an act of the pure love of **God** to the best of their ability. And I am certain that he meant himself by this.

9. Finally, ever since I had come to know Gregorio Lopez and the high and pure union in which he always stood with **God**, and whenever I later read such remarkable and extraordinary things about such a union with **God** in spiritual books—such as those by <term>Tauler<note>Johannes Tauler (c. 1300–1361), a famous German Dominican mystic and theologian</term></note>, <term>Ruusbroec<note>Jan van Ruusbroec (1293–1381), an influential Flemish mystic</note></term>, and the like—and found in them the signs they give by which to recognize those who have reached this highest stage of <term>contemplation<note>original: "Beschauung"; the highest form of prayer involving a direct, wordless experience of God</note></term>; I then went diligently to visit Lopez and conversed with him about it. I then learned that **God** worked the fruits of perfect union, of which these books treat—and even others which the same books do not mention—in him in a sublime manner; and that this holy man was one of those special friends of **God** of whom the aforementioned Tauler speaks in the 25th chapter of his *Institutions*: "These holy people bring more benefit to Christendom in one hour than all others do in many years."

10. From this perpetual and fervent act of the love of **God**, from this so intimate union with **God**, and from this participation in the divine abundance, Lopez drew all the excellent virtues and graces that were seen in him. And from this it also came that, according to the command of Paul (1 Timothy 6:8), he allowed himself to be content with only food and clothing.

# First Part. The Life

He told me that, since **God** had placed him in this perpetual act of love, He had not allowed him to possess anything in the world, or to desire anything for himself, from whomever it might be, but rather to surrender himself entirely to Him. He also had little need, because he desired little.

11. As I always saw him without a hat and with a bare head, I once asked him if he did so out of reverence, because he was always in the presence of **God**? He answered that he did not do it for that reason; for his union with **God** was in the interior of his soul, and therefore he had no need to either cover or uncover himself; rather, he did it so that he might have as few things in the world as possible, and so as not to accustom his body to <term>softness<note>original: "zärtlich zu gewöhnen"; referring to the habit of seeking physical comfort or pampering the body.</note></term>.

12. From this also sprang his great humility, which he possessed in a very high degree, because he stood in such a close union with **God** and had such a clear insight into His infinite essence and into his own nothingness.

13. I also noted that this holy man had no need to practice patience during the annoyances, labor, and suffering that others caused him. This union with **God** meant that he could take all such things upon himself with the greatest peace and stillness of mind, and could even excuse such people without ever complaining about a single person.

14. From this also came his abstinence and moderation. When I saw him remain in the same devotion during a meal as at other times, I asked him if he remained in that same act of love toward **God** while eating? He answered: "I am always as devout in it as I possibly can be, not only during the meal, but at all other times."

15. From this also came his deep silence, his well-measured words, and his divine wisdom, which everyone who knew him admired in him; as well as the fact that he could see the state of other people's souls in **God**, in order to give each of those who asked him for counsel what was necessary for them.

16. He had no need to impose many external, severe penances upon himself. After our **Lord**, he said, had placed him in this perpetual act of internal love toward **God**, his senses, all parts of his body, and his nature had become weak, weary, and thin, because he always kept them in check without letting them take the slightest pleasure in any created thing: and therefore he could do nothing more than simply live in such a way that he did not need to wear them down through other harsh external rigors, which would not be pleasing to **God** because nature would <note>original: "darunter würde liegen bleiben"</note> succumb under them. External rigors serve only to tame nature and to subject the senses to reason; but his senses

Even though Lopez (so Losa <note>Francisco de Losa, Lopez's friend and biographer</note> continues) was always occupied to the best of his ability in this act of love for **God** and neighbor, this did not prevent him from also practicing other forms of prayer (all of which, however, are truly contained within this internal act of pure love for **God** and emerged from that very foundation).

2. I asked him once in what way and manner he practiced this love of **God** and neighbor? [Not as if he had spoken these words externally with his mouth, but he wished to make understood how, in the hidden sanctuary of his <term>soul's ground<note>original: "Seelen-Grund"; a mystical term for the deepest part of the soul where it remains in constant contact with the Divine.</note></term>, such veneration, praise, and worship of the eternal Godhead proceeded unceasingly in spirit and in truth. # First Part. The Life

[Not as if he had spoken these words externally with his mouth, but] spoke of the childhood, the life, and the death of our Savior. And this was also specifically the basis for his intercession <term>intercession: the act of praying to God on behalf of others</term> for others. For he used to offer the life, suffering, and death of **Jesus Christ**, the Son of **God** and our Savior, to the eternal Father—sometimes for the whole world, sometimes for this or that person in particular, according as he recognized it to be **God's** will. **God**, he said, still had various priests in this world who often during the day, in a spiritual manner, offered Him this sacrifice; and as for himself, he often practiced two types of communion. Namely, first, through a fervent desire to receive our **Lord Jesus Christ** in the Holy Supper <note>The sacrament of the Eucharist or Holy Communion</note>; and then, second, through an ardent longing to receive the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit into his soul, and in such a way to become a living and pure temple of the most holy **Trinity**, letting the same truly dwell in his heart so that they might remain and rest there at all times.

4. Everything that happened gave him cause for prayer; he saw everything in **God**, and everything led him to **God**. When he, for example, heard it said that the King in Spain was greatly feared (and respected) because of his great power and justice, and that he possessed his kingdoms in peace, he immediately turned to **God** and said: "**Lord**, You who are almighty and entirely just, all men must fear [and respect] You, and may You possess Your kingdom in peace!"

5. If he heard that a father was greatly loved by his children because of his goodness, he spoke to **God**: "You eternal Father, who are the fountainhead of all good, all Your children must love You!"

6. When he heard talk of heavy war and many who were slain, he lifted his heart to **God** and said: "See, **Lord**, into what a wretched state Your children and my brothers are brought, whom You so strictly command me to love!" In a word, nothing occurred to him, whether good or evil, from which he did not take occasion for prayer.

7. He said at times that in **God**, in one moment and with a single glance, he saw everything that was in the world.

8. In short, our **Lopez** had attained the most inward and immediate union with **God** in his inner being, and was so transformed in **God** that all those who closely observed his life and conduct, as I have done, could well say of him that he was, as it were, a portrait or image of **Jesus Christ**. This was true in his other virtues, and especially in his following of the Life of the Cross <note>original: *Creuz-Lebens*; a term for a life of suffering and self-denial in imitation of Christ's passion</note>, for **God** certainly led him—since He granted him no sensory comforts <note>referring to a lack of emotional or physical "good feelings" in his spiritual practice</note>—through such a path in which he had need of great bravery. 2. # First Part. The Life

...with his usual affectionate seriousness, saying he did not wish to rob the hospital in Mexico of this brother whom they needed. The superior, however, left him there anyway. Lopez remained for several days in this patience and courage, which he was also accustomed to showing in all his other illnesses; he never complained about his pains, even though they were very great. Afterward, he developed a very difficult time swallowing; his pulse became weak; he also took very little nourishment: so that I stood in fear that he would die unexpectedly. He said to Brother Sarmiento: "You well know what this difficulty in swallowing signifies." Almost until his death, he did not cease to get up by himself and dress himself, in order to attend to the needs of his illness, even though people were very willing to serve him.

4. He grew weaker from day to day; he could no longer eat anything and sustained his life merely with broths, which <term>persons of rank</term> <note>German: "Standes-Personen." Refers to the nobility or high-ranking Spanish officials in colonial Mexico.</note> from Mexico sent to him. When he heard that something was being sent to him by such people, he turned to Brother Sarmiento and said: "You are wonderful, my God, that since a man who possesses nothing in this world requires such food for the preservation of his life—food which befits only princes—people are found who send it to him without him even desiring it."

5. Now, as it seemed to me that he was near death, I told him so; whereupon he answered: "Behold then, O nature, now it is come to the point with you that you shall die!"

6. His close friend Ortigosa came to visit him and said to him: "Now you shall go hence to enjoy God." He thought, however, that Lopez would take this as an occasion to tell him the hour of his death. But this servant of God answered his thoughts and said: "Why do you ask me such things? It will happen then, when it shall please God."

7. Three or four days before his death, an indigenous woman from the <term>village</term> <note>German: "Flecken." Often used to describe a small market town or settlement, in this context likely a local native community.</note> came to see him; since I understood her language, he said to me: "Oh, listen to what she says, dear Father; for perhaps she wishes to give me a good reminder"; from which one sees how great his humility was, in that he believed an indigenous woman could give him a good reminder in the state in which he found himself.

8. He had such incredible pains in his illness that, when I asked how he found himself and where it pained him, he answered me that he felt great pains from his head to his feet.

A high-ranking military or administrative post in the service of the King of Spain.</note> in the King's service. # Of Gregory Lopez. Chapter XVIII.

...death of Lopez, to Santa Fe <note>S. Fé (Holy Faith), a community for the poor and indigenous people near Mexico City where Lopez spent his final years.</note>, and brought various things for the refreshment of the patient: for as disorderly as she otherwise was, she was nonetheless affectionate toward those who suffer. When I was given news of her arrival, I had her told that because she had made such poor use of the prayers that had been offered for her in this house, and had not put an end to her gambling and the scandal arising from it, she should simply go away; she could not see the sick man, and he would not accept her alms. She remained insistent, however, that she wanted to go to Lopez; and it lasted fully three or four hours that I continually turned her away, and she continually returned. Finally, however, because a pious man who had come with her, and others as well, assured me that she came with a great desire to improve herself and give up her gambling, I finally gave in. As she went in, one of her children said: "Madame, Father Losa <note>Father Francisco Losa, the author of the original biography and Lopez's close companion.</note> said you would not get in." To which she gave the answer: "He was quite right, but I will improve myself." When she saw Gregory Lopez, she showed great compassion for his illness; she fell on her knees before the bed, begged him with many tears that he might pray to GOD for her and care for her soul. She remained several days with him and served him with great humility and love.

10. In the morning and the evening, she had long conversations with Lopez: and it was then that she felt such a great change in her heart that one could visibly notice that GOD was working in her soul. She incessantly begged Lopez, with great contrition, to assist her with his prayer; which he then also promised her. In the meantime, however, she contracted the very same illness that Lopez had; and yet she remained for two more days and served him with very many tears, which came from a true penance. As her illness increased, however, she was forced to return to Mexico <note>Refers to Mexico City.</note>, yet entirely comforted. Upon parting, Lopez said to her: "Commended to GOD, Madame; our illnesses will ensure that we see each other no more in this life."

11. As soon as she arrived in Mexico, she wrote me such a letter from which I recognized that GOD was working powerfully within her. The more her illness increased, the more her sorrow and pain over her sins also increased; and I saw at the same time that the pains in Gregory Lopez were also increasing.

12. When this lady was extremely ill and near the end, she again urgently requested Lopez that he might remember her; to which he answered, just like a person who finds himself loaded with a heavy weight: "Yes, I do so; I carry this burden on my shoulders." This made me very dismayed because I had never heard him say that anything was a burden to him. He also said: "JESUS, assist me. My God, how harsh is this fire of purification!" <note>Original German: "Feuer der Läuterung." This refers to the spiritual cleansing or purgation of the soul through suffering.</note> This lady then died; and as soon as Lopez heard of it, he spoke: "GOD is almighty!"

### First Part. The Life

13. I asked him often during this final illness how things stood with the perpetual **act of love?** <term>act of love (That der Liebe): A central concept in Lopez's spirituality, referring to a continuous, internal state of devotion and mental union with God that persists regardless of external activity.</term> To which he answered that it still proceeded quite well.

14. Once I asked whether the great pains did not prevent him a little from remembering **GOD**? Not in the slightest, he answered.

15. Another time, when I saw that he was in heavy suffering, I said to him: Now it is time that one thinks of **GOD**; And of what else, he replied, should I think? As he already lay in the throes of death, I spoke to him: Are you now well united with **GOD**? He answered: Well enough.

16. Another time he emerged as if from a deep recollection <note>German: *Einsammlung*. A mystical state of gathering one's thoughts and senses inward to focus entirely on the Divine presence.</note>, turned to me, and spoke: Perseverance, paired with peace, is of great value. And as I comforted him, saying that **GOD** was leading him through a path of the cross, just as He had led His own Son through it; he answered me: I cannot thank Him enough for it, nor rejoice enough over it; may His holy will be fulfilled in me!

17. At the end I said further: Behold, now the time is here to go and see the mystery. But he answered me with a wonderful confidence: Everything is clear; nothing is hidden anymore; it is full noon for me. And in this confidence, this great servant and secret friend of **GOD** surrendered his pure soul into the hands of his Creator, in a wonderful peace and deep silence of his spirit, sinking into the immeasurable ocean of the love of **GOD**, there to continue perfectly and for all eternity that which he had spent the time of his mortal life doing here—namely, to exercise the purest acts of the love of **GOD** without interruption through every moment of endless eternity. He ended this Divine exercise on earth and began it in heaven on Saturday at noon, the 20th of July, 1596; when he was 54 years old and had lived 33 years in solitude.

> **GOD** has sent me into this world for one reason alone: to love Him; and through His great mercy <note>original: *Barmherzigkeit*</note> I have loved Him so much that I can no longer love Him after the manner of mortals. It is time that I go to Him, so that I may love Him in the manner of the blessed <note>original: *Seligen*; referring to those already in heaven</note> in heaven.

<meta>This page serves as the "Preface" or "Introduction" (Vorbericht) to the biography of Armelle Nicolas, which follows the account of Gregorio Lopez from the previous section. It establishes the authenticity of the text by explaining how her life story was recorded by a contemporary nun.</meta>

# Preface.

->1.<-

The Spirit drove Lopez into the deserts; and that very same Spirit drove the good Armelle out of the "deserts" of a quiet <margin>(a) Chapter VI.</margin> convent. This uneducated peasant woman and poor maidservant shall now teach us, by her example, that through Divine Grace it is indeed possible to do exactly what he did in solitude—namely, to love God steadily and with a perfect heart—even in the midst of the hustle and bustle of people and under the burdens of a heavy household.

2. A pious Ursuline nun <margin>(b) See *School of Pure Love*, Epistle serving as Preface, page 56 and following. <note>original: *Vid. Ecole du pur amour, Epitre servant de Préface pag. 56. seqq.*</note></margin> at Vannes, Jeanne de la Nativité, became intimately acquainted with our Armelle. Their frequent interaction allowed Armelle, in the presence of this friend, to sometimes give vent to her inner flames and simply speak of the wonders of Divine Love occurring in her heart. After several years of such interaction, the aforementioned sister felt a painful realization that such great graces should not be buried with Armelle in the grave of oblivion; she then began, in the name of God, to set down the life of Armelle. However, after she had written nine or ten chapters, she fell into doubt as to whether her memory might sometimes fail to provide the details of the events according to the full truth. Yet she did not dare to question Armelle too closely, for fear that she might notice her intention and thereafter cease to speak with her usual intimacy.

> "Since I was in this fear," (this is how the nun describes the outcome of the matter,) "and did not know how I might actually get to the truth, the Lord chose at that time to lead her into a completely Divine and supernatural life, and communicated Himself to her soul with such wonderful and overflowing infusions that she did not know how she could thank Him enough for it; she then received a strong impulse that these should also be known to others, etc. Thereupon I asked her if she would be content if one were to record such things? 'Yes,' she answered me with great fervor, 'and I would wish it were done with my own blood; yes, that all the blood in my veins and all the bones of my body were as many tongues and voices to testify before angels and men to the overwhelming goodness and mercy <note>original: *Barmherzigkeit*</note> of my God toward His worthless creature, so that they might help me to love, praise, and thank Him for all eternity.' Afterward she added: 'O, how contentedly I shall die, and what a joy it will be for me when I know that through me, my Love and my All could still be loved and honored!'

> "When I saw her of this mind, I no longer hesitated to tell her that her desire was already partially fulfilled; and I then read to her what I had written. From that time on, I always read the chapters to her as I wrote them, so as not to write anything that was not in every part consistent with the truth; and she was so careful in this that she immediately told me if I had written even the slightest thing differently than she had experienced it. But by the grace of God, this did not have to happen often; for my writing was so consistent with the truth that she herself marveled at it and said that if she herself had been able to describe the state of her soul, she would not have been able to do it more clearly or truthfully."

Behold, the origin of this biography, and at the same time the undeniable proof of the unadulterated truth of its contents.

3. Should anyone wish to disapprove of Armelle’s conduct in this, let them only consider the state in which this blessed creature was at that time: annihilated in herself, lost in God. Let them consider the examples of many previous saints—a David, a Paul, a Gertrude, an Angela of Foligno, and others—who, driven by the Spirit of God, left behind written accounts of the high graces shown to them by God.

---

2. This life has been printed twice in Paris under the title *The Triumph of Divine Love*. <note>original: *Der Thriumph der Göttlichen Liebe*</note>

printed, but not without errors. Mr. Poiret <note>Pierre Poiret (1646–1719) was a prominent French mystic and philosopher who edited and promoted the works of many spiritual writers.</note> has made it known anew in these lands through a clean edition published in Amsterdam in 1704. He gave it the title *The School of the Pure Love of God*, because he believed this title would be more effective in awakening a desire to read the book. To that end, in an edifying preface, he called all his fellow scholars to the school of this poor peasant maid, who could neither read nor write. However, it is to be feared that few such students appeared. The great masters in Israel do not easily become like children <note>A biblical allusion to Matthew 18:3, suggesting that intellectual pride often prevents learned people from attaining the simple faith of a child.</note>. Meanwhile, this book must have found admirers in our Germany, as the German translation has already been published three times: namely in 1708, 1719, and recently in 1731.

5. The single sheet <note>original: *einzele Bogen*. This refers to a small, inexpensive pamphlet or broadsheet intended for wide circulation.</note> concerning the daily walk of Armelle, which has been reprinted many times, seemed too short to some—and not without reason; whereas others complained about the long-windedness of the entire book. In this present excerpt, a middle path has been taken between the two. The daily walk of this God-loving soul is found here in chapters 17 and 18 in much more detail than in that short sheet. Furthermore, this excerpt presents not only her outward life and death, but primarily God's guidance of her soul and the successive, wonderful effects of His love within her.

6. The reliable testimonies regarding the holiness of this person and the truth of this history are printed in great number at the front of the editions of the complete biography and can be examined there. The well-known Rigoleve <note>Jean Rigoleuc (1595–1658), a Jesuit known for his asceticism and spiritual direction.</note> calls our Armelle "a coal from the sanctuary" <note>An allusion to Isaiah 6:6, signifying a soul purified and set on fire by God.</note>; the famous Guilloré <note>François Guilloré (1615–1684), a French Jesuit spiritual writer.</note> calls her "a living spectacle and martyr-image of love"; Vincent Huby, her guide, writes: "I have had the good fortune of knowing and serving this excellent soul for nearly 20 years; she was in truth a Seraphim <note>The highest order of angels, whose name implies "burning ones," associated with intense divine love.</note> on earth," etc.

> O Love-filled God, God of the simple soul, God of the holy Armelle, touch our ice-cold hearts with this coal from the sanctuary, so that we may finally recognize with emphasis, and never forget, that to love You is better than to know everything. Spoil for us the barren heath of busy reasoning <note>original: *Vernunft-Geschäftigkeit*. This refers to the restless activity of the intellect which can distract the heart from spiritual devotion.</note>, so that we may follow You, with this Your servant-maid, in the simple and straight way of the heart and of love, and that the word of Your mouth may be fulfilled in us: *If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him.* John 14:23.

# The First Chapter.

->Concerning the birth of the good Armelle; her devout childhood; her arrival at Ploërmel; how she sought service and finally reached the place where she was to be crucified <note>The author uses the term "crucified" metaphorically to describe a state of intense spiritual purgation or suffering through which Armelle believed the soul is united with Christ.</note>. She is drawn to the love of God through a profound impression of the Savior’s suffering.<-

->I.<-

The blessed Armelle was born on September 19 in the year 1606 in Brittany, a province of the Kingdom of France, specifically in the parish of Campeneac, near the town of Ploërmel. Her parents, Georg Nicolas and Francoise Neant, were peasants; and this, their eldest daughter, was gifted with uncommonly good, natural, and healthy sense, a friendly and sociable disposition, and an outward manner so well-composed and reserved that modesty and propriety <term>propriety: the quality of behaving in a socially and morally acceptable way</term> shone through in all her actions from that time onward.

2. From her youth, it was seen that she was inclined toward solitude and silence; therefore, her mother (as she grew a little older) sent her into the fields to tend the sheep and other cattle. This was more pleasant to her than all her other duties because she was alone there, away from the turmoil of the household, and had more time to recite her prayers. She spent most of the day in prayer, often withdrawing alone behind a fence while the other girls who were with her sought to amuse themselves with games and other pastimes. Even then, the Lord God began to draw her to Himself with many tender tokens of love and sweetness <note>In the language of 17th-century mysticism, "sweetness" (original: *Süssigkeiten*) refers to spiritual consolations or pleasant emotional experiences of divine love during prayer.</note>, which He imparted to her during her little exercises of devotion.

In particular, from that time on, He impressed upon her heart a sincere love and a very sensitive compassion for the pains that her dear Savior suffered on the cross, although she did not yet know the specific circumstances of His suffering.

3. When she had reached her twentieth or twenty-second year, her parents wished to marry her off and pressured her greatly to do so; but she would never agree to it. Because she had to endure much solicitation in this regard, and furthermore sometimes found herself forced to be among people who were too forward and lacked the modesty that suited her character, she began to feel such vexation in the countryside that she could not remain there in peace. She therefore sought every opportunity to live somewhere in the city. Soon after, it happened that a certain woman requested her for service; however, in that place, she experienced such great anguish of heart that she was forced to leave that house again.

3. And this continued to happen to her in several other places, until she finally reached the location where she was meant to be crucified <note>The author uses "crucified" as a metaphor for the "death of the self"—a painful but necessary spiritual process where a believer's ego is surrendered to God.</note> through various internal and external sufferings, as we shall see in the continuation of this history. As soon as she entered this house, she was relieved of the anxiety and mental torment <term>mental torment: *Gemüthsqvaal*, a term used in 17th-century Pietism to describe intense spiritual suffering or a "dark night of the soul"</term> that she had previously endured in all the other houses where she had been. She became entirely free and content within herself, which served to confirm that it was the will of God for her to remain in this house.

4. Now, since it was the custom in this house to read from the *Lives of the Saints* or another spiritual book of similar content every evening after dinner, she found great joy and edification in it. Furthermore, because she herself could neither read nor write, she asked one of the daughters of the household if she would occasionally read something to her; the young lady did so gladly, and by God’s providence, she once read her a book that concerned the Passion of our Lord and the sorrows He endured therein.

5. This was, as it were, the hook by which this heart was fully captured—a heart that, for its part, already possessed a great readiness for it. It is impossible to describe what wonderful and glorious effects this reading and this knowledge produced in her soul; by this means, she was so wounded and ignited by love that she was completely transported out of herself. At that same moment, all other images or thoughts, of whatever kind they might be, were so banished from her mind that she retained no other object of focus within it, by day or by night, except the suffering of her Savior. This caused her such great pain and sorrow that she wasted away and withered from heartache—not only in consideration of the great martyrdom He had endured but also because her sins had been the cause of it. For this was vividly impressed upon her mind at the same time, so that she did not know what to do or where to turn; for the internal heat and distress were so great that it felt as though she were in a consuming fire, which grew larger from day to day.

6. Since she was fearful of being deceived <note>Common in mystical literature, "deception" refers to the fear that spiritual visions or feelings might come from one's own imagination or the devil rather than from God.</note> in this strange state, she revealed it to a pious Carmelite <note>A monk of the Carmelite Order, known for their focus on contemplative prayer and mysticism.</note>; he, however, strengthened her in it and encouraged her to be faithful and to follow the movements of grace, etc. This good priest accordingly became her guide, whom she obeyed in all things as long as he was in the country; for from that time on, God gave her such a great desire to be governed in all things according to the will of another that these thoughts never left her heart:

### Of the Good Armelle. Chapter II.
L 2

had spent time in this way, God gave the Devil power to distress and torment her with many kinds of temptations, which were much more painful to her than death itself.

Instead of the powerful love which she had previously felt within herself toward God and toward everything belonging to His service, the **Adversary** <note>The "Adversary" is a common title for the Devil or Satan.</note> pressed into her heart a kind of hatred toward God and a turning away from Him. This came with a certain contempt and such a great and excessive loathing toward all kinds of good works that even the smallest thing concerning the practice of piety <term>piety: *Gottseligkeit*, a life devoted to religious duties and reverence for God</term> was unbearable to her. Instead of her former deep repentance and **contrition** <term>contrition: *Zerknirschung*, literally a "crushing" of the heart out of sorrow for sins</term>, she became as if unfeeling. Because she saw herself in such a wretched state, she was attacked in a quite unusual way by a fierce rage and despair over her salvation. Instead of the praise and glory she used to offer the Lord with such heartfelt, childlike love, she found herself violently attacked by a spirit of blasphemy. The inward vision and remembrance of the **Passion** <note>The "Passion" refers to the suffering and crucifixion of Jesus Christ.</note> of our Lord was entirely taken from her mind, so that not a single thought of it remained, just as if she had never heard mention of it. In its place, it felt to her as if she were always in the company of devils, who incessantly enticed her to surrender herself to them.

2. See there the wretched state into which she was brought by them in the short time that God had given them power over her.

But so that she might not entirely succumb under the heavy burden of so many fierce assaults, the **Divine Majesty** <note>A formal way of referring to God's supreme power.</note> impressed a certain fear of offending Him deep into her heart. Though this fear was imperceptible to her senses, it was nonetheless powerful enough to restrain her will, so that she did not consent to all these suggestions of the Devil. Otherwise, this alone excepted, she was just like a desperate and utterly abandoned person; she did not even have the ability to grasp the slightest thought or do the smallest thing through which she might obtain any comfort or encouragement.

3. Her only refuge was her **confessor** <note>original: *Beicht-Vater*; a priest who hears confessions and provides spiritual guidance</note>, to whom she revealed all her distress. He himself had even foretold this to her some time before it happened. He felt very great compassion for her and sought to comfort and encourage her, although mostly in vain.

4. Finally, it pleased the Lord to deliver her from this, after she had been in this state for about six or seven months. During this time, she had faithfully used all the help her confessor provided, despite the internal resistance she felt toward it. His Divine Majesty looked upon her misery with compassion and let His divine light rise in the depths of her heart, by which all the power of her enemies was scattered. This happened one evening, just as her distress and the Devil’s attacks were at their most violent; whereupon she cried out with a heart full of thanks and praise:

> "O my God, You have torn my bonds asunder, and me

5. Thus the enemy was finally forced to leave the field, whereupon the brightly burning fire of Divine Love began once again to burn perceptibly within her. Her heart was so pierced by the Divine **Arrow of Love** <note>The "Arrow of Love" is a common image in mystical literature, representing a spiritual wound that makes the soul long only for God.</note> that she was incessantly occupied with seeking the One who had wounded her; she sighed and wailed for Him day and night, without allowing herself any pause or rest in any thing of this world. Her spirit was so estranged from her, and as if outside of her, that she acted like one possessed; and anyone who had seen what she did would have considered her quite insane. Because she did not know where she should find and take hold of the One who had wounded her heart, she often ran from one chamber to another, thinking she would encounter Him there. At other times she cried out for Him! and called to Him with all her might; and the love she possessed forced her to speak such words and do such works which, according to the spirit of the world, would have been judged foolish and beyond all reason, although they were by no means beyond the measure of her love.

6. At that same time, she received such a powerful desire to die that it would have been enough to cause her death, had God not tempered it. Her greatest joy was to think of death as the only means to attain her desire. Whenever she heard the bells tolling for a funeral, or perhaps heard that someone had died, she felt great joy over it and said to herself: "O, would to God! I were in the place of this person, so that I might see the **object** <note>The original German word "Vorwurf" here refers to the "object" or "aim" of her contemplation, not a "reproach."</note> of my love."

> "O my God," (she used to say constantly in these first years,) "there must
> certainly be something truly lovable in You, because even though I do
> not know You, and do not know who or what You are, I nevertheless burn with
> love for You."

8. "In this manner I spent the whole of **Passiontide** <note>original: "Passions-Zeit"; the period of two weeks preceding Easter Sunday dedicated to the suffering of Christ.</note>. On **Good Friday**, however, I went to the sermon; I had not heard the preaching on the suffering of my **Savior** for even a quarter of an hour when my heart was already so touched and pierced by pain that, because I could no longer remain, I found myself compelled to leave; for I feared my heart might burst into pieces, or at the very least, reveal its violent agitation in one way or another. I then went home, where no one was at the time. I locked myself inside and soon after ran from one place to another, calling out until I was out of breath, like a woman possessed, or like one who is completely outside of herself. Afterward, I threw myself down upon the earth and cried: Mercy, LORD, mercy! And after I turned myself to GOD, I said to Him with flaming fervor: O my LORD and my GOD, behold, the day has come when I must be entirely Thine. Cleanse and wash me in Thy precious blood. Anoint my heart with the oil of Thy mercy. Pierce me with the arrows of Thy holy love. Receive me into the number of Thy female disciples <note>original: "Jüngerinnen"; Armelle specifically uses the feminine form of disciples.</note>. Show Thyself to me, and unite me with Thee.

9. "In the midst of such prayer, as I was saying these very words which were inwardly inspired and as if dictated to me (for I myself did not know what I was saying, nor did I understand the sense of these words, nor the mysteries contained therein; rather, I was as if compelled and forced to speak them; and this I did with such mighty violence that it seemed to me every word was a sharp, pointed arrow intended to penetrate into the heart of GOD): as I, I say, lay in the midst of such prayer, and had greatly tormented and worn myself out, I was in an instant led to the highest floor <note>The German "Boden" can refer to an attic or top floor, often used in mystical literature to signify a higher spiritual state or physical removal from the world.</note> of the house, without knowing how; I simply found myself there, without having thought of it before.

10. "When I was there, I threw myself upon the earth, because I could no longer hold or carry myself, so greatly was I brought into the outermost anguish and distress; and behold, in that same moment GOD let a ray of His Divine light shine in the depth of my heart, through which He revealed Himself to me and gave me clearly to know that the One for whom I had so greatly longed was entering into me and taking full possession of me. As this great demonstration of favor happened to me, I found myself entirely clothed and surrounded by light, and indeed with a terror that seized me at first, but lasted only a moment; then immediately my heart was set in safety again, and so changed that I no longer knew myself; and I felt such a satisfaction of all desires that I knew not whether I was in heaven or on earth. I remained for some time motionless, like a carved statue <note>original: "gehauen Bild"; common imagery for a soul rendered still by the presence of the Divine.</note>, so that I could not stir: and from that time on, all the powers of my soul remained so satisfied and contented, and in all my senses there was such a great peace, that I could in no way doubt that GOD had now united and bound Himself with me in the most intimate way, as I had hitherto so fervently desired. And this truth was as infallible and certain to me as

# The Third Chapter.

->She is tested through various very difficult and long-lasting mortifications<-
->and domestic trials.<-

->I.<-

The flame of this holy love, through its great intensity, soon brought her into the utmost weakness, so that shortly thereafter she was ill for five or six months with a persistent fever, and in a short time found herself so emaciated and weak that she could hardly stay upright. The Lord used this opportunity to let the high regard and friendship that her mistress had previously held for her grow cold. She then began to grow resentful at seeing Armelle always sick; and she imagined that idleness was the sole cause of her unknown illness; and therefore there was no other remedy for it than work. Furthermore, she believed all this heat, which was visible on her exterior, arose from untimely and immoderate devotion <term>Andacht: private or public religious exercise or piety</term>; and if she did not seek to moderate it, this person [Armelle] would become weak-minded and foolish: in which thoughts she was confirmed by a godly person who likewise assured her of this.

2. Accordingly, her mistress greatly increased her labor. For beyond what she had previously been required to perform—namely, keeping watch over the children and caring for them—she now wanted her to perform everything that was most difficult in the housework besides. To this end, she commanded her other maidservant that she should by no means spare Armelle, but should let her do all the arduous and coarse work alone; in such a way that from morning until evening she had neither cessation nor rest; whereby she became so weak through exhaustion from the work, along with the persistent fever, that she often collapsed from great weariness. But her mistress viewed all of this as the effects of empty imagination, as she, as mentioned above, firmly believed that work was the only remedy against everything that ailed her.

3. Her first task was that early in the morning she had to go out to the well, or to the spring, which was quite far from the town, and carry large tubs full of water home on her head; which caused <note>original: "verurs-"; completed by the catchword "sachte" as "verursachte" (caused)</note> her intolerable pain—

## The Third Chapter.

### She is tested through various very heavy and long-lasting mortifications and household crosses.
<note>German: *Tödtungen und Haus-Creutz*. "Mortifications" refers to the spiritual practice of subduing the body and will; "household crosses" is a traditional term for the trials and suffering endured within domestic life.</note>

### I.

The flame of this holy love, through its great intensity, soon brought her into extreme weakness, so that shortly thereafter she became ill with a persistent fever for five or six months. In a short time, she found herself so emaciated and weak from this that she could hardly keep herself upright. The Lord used this opportunity to let the high regard and friendship that her mistress had previously held for her grow cold. She then began to grow resentful at seeing Armelle always sick; she imagined that idleness <term>Müffiggang: a term for laziness or lack of industriousness</term> was the sole cause of her unknown illness, and therefore there was no other remedy for it than work. Furthermore, she believed that all this heat that was visible on her exterior arose from unseasonable and immoderate devotion; and if she did not seek to moderate it, this person would become weak-minded and foolish. She was confirmed in these thoughts by a certain pious person who assured her of the same.

2. Accordingly, her mistress greatly increased her work. For in addition to what she had had to perform until then—namely, looking after and caring for the children—she now wanted her to also perform everything that was most difficult in the housework. To this end, she commanded her other maid that she should by no means spare Armelle, but should let her do all the laborious and coarse work alone; in such a way that from morning until evening she had neither standstill nor rest. Thus, through the exhaustion from the work and the persistent fever, she became so weak that she often fell down from great fatigue. But her mistress looked upon all this as the effects of empty imagination, as she—as mentioned above—firmly believed that work was the only remedy against everything that ailed her.

### Second Part. The Life

that occurred to her, she could accept them so willingly in a spirit of gratitude; so that, as the priest once said to her, she might well leave this place, she replied with her usual fervor <note>original: *Brünstigkeit*—a term common in 17th-century mystical texts denoting an intense, burning devotion or spiritual ardor.</note>: “How, my Father, would you advise me to leave the cross that GOD has sent me, and flee? No, no, I shall never do that, unless you command it of me outright. 8. Meanwhile, the **evil enemy** <note>A common reference to the Devil.</note> often gave her such a powerful urge to answer back defiantly and make excuses for herself when she was punished by her mistress, that she had difficulty restraining herself and felt inwardly quite distorted and inflamed. Indeed, he had whispered to her that even if an angel from heaven were treated this way, he could not have forced himself not to answer; moreover, she was herself the cause of her own misfortune; for if she would only let her sensitivity be seen for once, people would surely be careful not to be so vexing to her: also, her silence would not be counted as a virtue, but as mere lack of understanding (as indeed it actually happened). However, she stopped her ears to all such talk: and whenever she sensed such an agitation within her, she never said a single word to justify herself; instead, she listened to everything with wonderful self-mastery, even when she had the best reasons in the world for her justification and was entirely innocent of that which she was accused.

9. Since the enemy could in no way or manner drive her from this house, he finally incited the mistress herself to get rid of her: and indeed, the good woman threatened her with this daily for a long time. However, she was not moved by this at all, but said to herself: “Well then, my GOD, your will be done! If you wish that I be driven from here, I am content: but I, for my part, will never seek it as long as I find opportunity here to suffer for the sake of my love.”

10. Several times it truly came to the point that she was supposed to leave, so much so that she had already said her farewells and had already packed her things: but the LORD ensured that something always got in the way to turn the matter back. Thus she remained in this house four or five years, of which she spent the first year and a half partly in vivid feeling, sadness, and anxiety over the suffering of her Savior and in weeping for her sins, partly in the powerful and hideous temptations with which the devils beset her, and partly also in the great thirst and excessive longing for union with her Beloved <note>Referring to Christ.</note>, whom she finally and happily found.

Regarding the remaining years, they passed in the illnesses, frequent labor, exhaustion, contempt, humiliations, and scorn that we have described here, and in many other hardships that we pass over in silence.

# Chapter Four.

## How her mistress comes to know her; and how they travel from there to Vannes.

->I.<-

After God had tested her in this way for over three years, He brought it to pass that the virtue of our Armelle was finally recognized by her mistress, which occurred in the following manner: It happened one day in the summer, while her mistress was in the country, that she had a desire to bathe. As she took this good soul <note>original: *dieses gute Mensch*—a humble term for a person, often used in a spiritual or pitying sense</note> with her and stood at the edge of the water, she noticed that Armelle was in an instant completely drawn into herself and inwardly enclosed, without speaking a word to her. At this, the mistress rebuked her and said: "Well, you stupid beast, what sort of whims <note>original: *Grillen*—literally 'crickets,' but used historically to mean melancholy, strange notions, or idle fancies</note> do you have now?" Armelle, who was as if she were waking from a deep sleep, answered with great meekness and simplicity, "she was thinking of the terrifying anguish and sadness that had pierced the heart of the Son of God as He crossed the Brook Kidron <note>The stream Jesus crossed on His way to the Garden of Gethsemane (John 18:1), symbolizing the beginning of His Passion.</note>, which she had been reminded of by this water." Her mistress replied in turn: "Who told you that the Son of God went over the Brook Kidron?" "I do not know," she answered, "only I am certain that it is true;" at which words her face began to be ignited with great fervor <note>original: *Brünstigkeit*—intense spiritual ardor</note>, and her eyes broke out into frequent tears.

2. Through this, the heart of her mistress was so moved that from that time on, she changed her mind and gradually recognized that she had done wrong by holding such a pious person so strictly. Her behavior, which before had been unbearable to the mistress, now seemed quite different to her. Her silence, her meekness, patience, and submission—which the mistress had always considered to be mere folly or lack of understanding, and for which Armelle had been forced to endure so much—now received entirely different names in the mistress's mind and were recognized as true virtues. In this way, she began to love her dearly and to trust her with every good thing.

3. Armelle, however, called this mistress—who had caused her so much suffering—her dear mother; and I have often heard her say with tears and with a truly grateful heart: "Yes indeed, she is my true mother, as she is the one who helped me to find the true life. And if I could give her the blood from my veins, I would do so with all my heart."

4. After God had fulfilled the purpose for which He had brought her into this house, and she had now attained a substantial foundation and constant proficiency in all virtues through all the adversities she had magnanimously endured therein, and everything now began to go according to her wishes, He gave her a desire and longing to leave this house.

5. Although her mistress was not at all willing to consent, an opportunity soon arose for her to depart; for at that very time, the eldest daughter of the house married a nobleman who had his primary residence in the countryside and stayed near the city of Vannes <note>Vannes is a cathedral city in Brittany, France, where the historical Armelle Nicolas spent much of her life.</note>. And because he desired to lead his new bride there, she entreated her mother to let this good maidservant go with her to oversee her household. The mother consented only with great difficulty, for she was loath to lose such a faithful servant.

6. But for her, the good Armelle, this turn of events was very welcome for several reasons, one of the foremost being that by this means she would get away from her relatives, her homeland, and all her acquaintances. She had long yearned for this, so that through the forgetting and removal of all things, she might give herself all the more freely to the service and love of God, wherein was all her wishing and desire. Furthermore, her relatives were constantly pressuring her to marry; therefore, she believed God had allowed this opportunity to arise to free her from their persistent assaults. In addition, since she had always felt a great desire and inclination for solitude, she hoped she would be in her element in the countryside, where she would have no hindrance to living for God alone and enjoying Him constantly according to her own desire. But this poor girl was not a little dismayed when she later found things to be quite different than she had imagined: although everything turned out to her advantage, it was through such paths that were far removed from her thoughts and hidden from all men, as the reader shall soon see.

This took place when she was approximately twenty-nine to thirty years old; as we shall now briefly hear in the following chapter.

were pleasing to her, she accepted and embraced them with very great gentleness and quiet rest. 2. However, a completely different struggle awaited her there than she had ever imagined. She had spent three or four years in the rest and pleasure of which we have just spoken. I call "pleasure" the time when she felt inwardly that she stood well with GOD and enjoyed His sweetness and comfort. And although at that same time she had much to suffer from her mistress—indeed, as much as she could possibly bear—yet that was, in view of what happened to her afterward, mere child's play, and only a small trial by which GOD wished to test her constancy. She said herself:

> "When the soul believes that it stands well with
> "GOD and feels the effects of His grace, then everything that can happen to it,
> "as much from the devil as from creatures, is very sweet and easy for it to bear; but
> "when GOD steps back and leaves it to itself, then there is unbelievably great distress;
> "especially when it sees itself plunged into such misery that every
> "moment it seems it falls into a sin against GOD, which it cannot
> "resist. Then one truly has cause to have compassion for such a soul,
> "which then has to suffer properly.

3. She spoke this not without reason, because her own experience had made her knowledgeable in this: for she found herself gradually abandoned and forgotten by GOD, without receiving any more sensible help from Him. All her great fervor vanished, so that not even the slightest thought that she had ever possessed it, nor any other memory of those graces and gifts she had previously received from GOD, remained with her. All this, I say, was taken from her memory in such a way that for two whole years not a single thought of it entered her mind. Moreover, the desire and love for virtue became so weak in her that it was as if she had never had any.

> "When the soul believes that it stands
> "well with GOD, and feels the effects of His grace, then everything that can happen to it,
> "whether from the devil or from created beings, is very sweet and easy for it to bear: but
> "when GOD steps back and leaves the soul to itself, then there is unbelievably great distress;
> "especially when it sees itself plunged into such a misery that it thinks every
> "moment it is falling into a sin against GOD, which it cannot resist.
> "Then one truly has cause to have compassion for such a soul,
> "as it then has to suffer in earnest."

3. She spoke this not without reason, because her own experience had made her knowledgeable in this: for she found herself gradually abandoned and forgotten by GOD, without receiving any more sensible help from Him. All her great fervor vanished, so that not even the slightest thought that she had ever possessed it, nor any other memory of those graces and gifts she had previously received from GOD, remained with her. All this, I say, was taken from her memory in such a way that for two whole years not a single thought of it entered her mind. Moreover, the desire and love for virtue became so weak in her that she felt as if she had never had any.

foul and detestable thoughts, and so forth; and her imagination was filled with the most gruesome ideas, such as hell itself might suggest. I cannot doubt that God gave the devils power—if not to possess her bodily, then at least to entirely occupy and overwhelm her mind <note>original: "Gemüth," a term encompassing the soul, temperament, and inner emotional life.</note>, considering the strange condition into which she fell for two years. I deem it unnecessary to dwell on a detailed description of it; it will be enough to say in a word that the devil used everything he could devise to torment a poor soul in all these matters, yet she never gave the slightest consent of her will to any of these shameful inspirations.

5. It was truly pitiful to behold how this poor heart, which before was so ignited by the love of God, now burned with a hellish fire. This heart, which had been like a temple of the Holy Spirit, was now a place where the evil spirit carried out all his most gruesome temptations. This heart, finally, which had always loved purity <note>original: "Reinigkeit," referring here to both moral chastity and spiritual singleness of heart.</note> so highly and had left its parents, friends, and acquaintances to preserve it, was for such a long time surrendered to the grim rage of the spirit of impurity.

If I were now to recount the powerful anguish and bitterness of this poor heart, it would be utterly impossible. When she used to think of it afterward, her hair stood on end.

6. All the good that still remained in her consisted of a fear of offending God, which she felt always deeply impressed upon the bottom of her heart: this fear never left her as long as the struggle lasted. Nevertheless, this fear did nothing for her relief; for the more and deeper the fear of offending God was impressed upon her soul, the greater was the anguish she felt, because, in her opinion, she saw that she acted against it daily. In short, God let her fall into such extreme misery and wretchedness that everything that served only to increase her martyrdom <note>original: "Marter," meaning intense suffering or torture, used here for her spiritual agony.</note> stood vividly before her eyes; but everything that could have given her the slightest relief was entirely denied her and taken away from her mind.

7. And above all this, she found no one in those two years to whom she could trust herself or to whom she could reveal the wretched state in which she found herself; and even when she had the opportunity to reveal herself to someone, God did not allow her to receive any relief from it; very often she herself could not make her condition known, or if she did so, she was not understood. However, seven or eight months before she emerged from her sad state, she had the opportunity to speak with her spiritual director <note>original: "geistlichen Führer," a priest acting as a mentor to guide a soul through spiritual difficulties.</note>, who sought to encourage her with the following words: "Go boldly, my daughter, and do not fear that God will abandon you. No, He will not do that for all eternity; rather, in whatever misery you may be, He will nevertheless always stand by you." The intensity of the struggle
