## Second Part. The Life

8. “I therefore conversed with Him constantly during my work: I loved Him and delighted in Him: I always went about with Him as with my trusted friend: and if the task was such that it required all my thoughts, I nevertheless kept my heart turned toward Him at all times; and as soon as the matter was at an end, I ran hurriedly back to Him; just like one does who loves a person intensely, whom they only half-leave during all their business. So it was with me and my **GOD**. It was, as it were, impossible for me to part from Him, especially since I could not live outside of His presence.”

9. “For I knew very well, and He Himself had taught me so, that as long as I would only look at Him, I could not offend Him, nor restrain myself from loving Him. The more I looked at Him, the more I recognized both His Divine perfections and my own nothingness and misery: <note>original: "mein eigen Nichts und Elend." In 17th-century mysticism, "nothingness" refers to the soul's total dependence on God, while "misery" or "wretchedness" describes the human condition apart from divine grace.</note> so that I forgot and abandoned myself, as a thing not worthy of being occupied with; so that I might rise above myself and above all created things, and thus unite myself with Him, and cling to Him incessantly.”

10. “My sole and constant intent was that I might please Him in all my doing, and guard myself against offending Him. In all my activities I thought of nothing else. And this I did not do for the sake of the benefit I might have from it, or to escape the evil which would have followed had I acted otherwise: no, all these intentions, and my own gain or loss, were so far removed from my mind <note>original: "Gemüthe"; refers to the inner spirit or disposition.</note> that I did not think of them in the slightest. Love alone wanted everything for itself: and if that alone was satisfied, then I was already content; but other than that, everything was indifferent to me.”

11. One of her leaders <note>referring to her spiritual directors</note> wondered how it could be possible that, in the midst of so many different activities, she could look upon God as present at all times; he therefore asked her how such a thing could be? To satisfy this question, this parable and these words were placed in her mouth at that very moment: “My Father,” (she said,) “if just now, while I am holding a conversation with you, someone came who wanted to say something to me; I would not turn my back to you, nor go away from you and toward this person. All I might do would be perhaps this: that I would turn my head a little to listen to him; whereupon I would immediately turn back to you and away from him, to continue our discourse which you, or I, had started: for then I would need no reflection or special consideration to remember that I had to turn back to you; rather, I would do this naturally, and without thinking further about it, by myself, simply because I know that you are present there before me. Even so is the habit I have of incessantly looking upon my **GOD**; it is so great that it has, as it were, become nature to me; and I always remain therein, even without thinking about it.”

### of the good Armelle. Chapter XVII.

12. This Divine Art she had learned from the Savior himself; as He then once spoke these words to her: “My daughter; as long as you look upon me, you will love me; as long as you look upon me, you will serve me; as long as you look upon me, you will follow me; and when you no longer look upon me, you will also no longer follow me.”

Therefore she also said afterwards, “that, if a soul could truly accustom itself to reject all looking at itself and other things, and look only upon **GOD** alone, it would arrive at a high perfection in a very short time; because (she said) there is nothing that gives us such courage, and strengthens us so much, as this Divine presence.

“When I then in the morning lit a great glow with a small spark of fire, I said: Ah, my Love, if only one would let you work in souls as you please, how soon would you have accomplished the same thing! <note>Armelle often used her mundane tasks in the kitchen, such as tending the hearth, as metaphors for the "fire" of divine love in the soul.</note>

13. “When I cut the meat of slaughtered animals and prepared it for eating, it seemed to me that I heard the voice of my Beloved, who said to me that He, to nourish and preserve me, had willed to suffer death, and thus become a food for my soul.

14. “When I took food and drink, I did so in His Divine presence, just like everything else; and there it seemed to me as if every morsel were dipped in His precious blood, and that He Himself reached them to me for my nourishment, to inflame me more and more in His love. One can easily imagine what kind of effects this produced in my poor soul. Ah, certainly, they are quite incomprehensible, and there is no one but **GOD** himself who could recount them. For even if I spent my whole life doing so, I would never come to an end with it.

15. “No creature (said this good Armelle) was so small that it did not lead me to **GOD**, and teach me after its own kind to love Him; so that I often cried out aloud and said to Him: O my Love and my All, if there were not a single person in the world who could tell me that one must love you, yet the animals and other creatures teach me this sufficiently: and if You yourself should hide from me, they would direct me to serve you and to find you. <note>The idea that nature acts as a "second book" or a "ladder" to God was a common theme in 17th-century Christian mysticism.</note>

16. “When I saw a poor dog, who never leaves his master; who is so faithful that he always follows his master; who for a morsel of bread gives him a thousand caresses; O most gracious **GOD**! what a powerful lesson <term>lesson: originally "Lection," referring to a spiritual reading or instructional example</term> that was for me, to do the very same toward my **GOD**, who had bound and obligated me to His service through so many benefits.”

## Second Part. The Life

17. “When I saw the little lambs in the field, who are so meek and peaceable, allowing themselves to be shorn and slaughtered without once crying out or bleating, I imagined my **Savior** <note>original: "Heyland"</note> before me, who had likewise let himself be led to the slaughter and to death without opening his mouth. Through them, He taught me to follow Him and to act just as He did in all things that are adverse and difficult for human nature to bear.

18. “When I saw the little chicks flee under the wings of their mother, it immediately occurred to me that my **JESUS** had compared himself to this little animal <note>A reference to Matthew 23:37, where Jesus laments over Jerusalem, wishing to gather her children as a hen gathers her chicks.</note> so that He might awaken in me a great trust in Him, and teach me to keep myself hidden and covered under the wings of His Divine Providence to escape the claws of the devil.

19. “When I contemplated the beautiful meadows and pastures, when they are finely green and full of flowers, I said to myself: My Beloved is a flower of Sharon, and a lily of the valley, <term>Song of Sol. 2:1</term> <note>original: "Hohel. 2, 1." referring to the Hohelied or Song of Solomon.</note>. He is a rose without thorns, though He willed to let Himself be covered and crowned with them. I begged Him fervently that He might make my soul His pleasure garden, and keep it so well-enclosed and sealed that no one but He alone could ever enter therein.

20. “When I looked at how the trees let themselves be bent and guided according to every movement of the wind, and how the sea never overstepped its boundaries, I said: O my **GOD**! Why am I not just as willing and ready to let myself be steered and led by the movement and impulse of the Divine Spirit? And ah, grant that I may never overstep the barriers of your adorable will.

21. “The fish, which swam in the sea and delighted themselves therein, taught me that I should likewise constantly immerse myself in my Divine Love and move within it.

22. “When I saw the land being tilled and sown, it seemed to me that I saw my Savior, who had endured so much sweat, trouble, and labor throughout His entire life to cultivate our souls and to sow the seed of His heavenly doctrine and Divine Love within them; although, despite all this, so little soil is found that bears good fruit; the latter caused me unspeakable pain.

23. “When at harvest time I saw the wheat being separated from the chaff, I was taught thereby that this very thing would happen on the Day of Judgment with the godly and the ungodly.

24. “In short, there was no creature in the world known to me that did not serve for my instruction, and from which I did not always learn something new. Therefore I often said to **GOD**: O my Love, how finely You have [instructed] my

# The Eighteenth Chapter.
## Continuation of the previous matter.

->1.<-

Just as this good Armelle was, in this manner, very wise and vigilant in discovering and destroying all the cunning and schemes of the flesh, she spoke further of it thus: "Because the devil seeks to catch us by presenting and suggesting a thousand excuses of necessity, weakness, hardship, and other such appearances of reason, to bring us into his snares and craftily seize us, it can very easily happen that one becomes entangled therein, unless one stands on guard with the utmost care. These occasions are far more dangerous than others where the danger itself is more obvious, because in those cases, one uses more caution to avoid them; but when they are linked with the preservation of health and life, oh, then without doubt great wisdom is required just to discover them, and great courage to avoid being overcome; for they are very nimble and subtle. I would never have suspected any danger in them if my Beloved had not revealed it to me; but He showed it to me so clearly that I could not doubt it in the least; indeed, in almost all occurrences, He taught me to distinguish what proceeded from <term>Grace</term> <note>Divine influence acting within the soul</note> or from <term>Nature</term> <note>The human ego or fallen self, which seeks its own comfort</note>, and also gave me the strength to follow the former and to overcome the latter.

->2.<-

"Oh, how often have I been full of joy and pleasure when I saw others being right, while I myself was despised and scorned even by the lowliest servants in the house; it was especially a great delight to me to submit myself to their will and to follow their inclinations. Ah, how dear and delightful such instances are to a heart in love! There was no one in the house, no, not even the small children, to whom I did not sometimes have to be obedient and submissive, out of the impulse and command of Love. And all this was sweet and pleasant to the spirit, namely because it was pleasing to Love, although it often felt difficult enough to Nature; but even then I did it with all the greater joy and pleasure, because I saw

"...that I pleased my Beloved <note>original: "Geliebten"; Armelle’s intimate term for Jesus Christ</note> thereby. There was no creature in the world so small or lowly to whom I would not have submitted myself as willingly as to the greatest Saint in heaven; for I never looked at the person whom I obeyed, but solely at Him for whose sake I did it.

3. "But if I were indeed sometimes not sufficiently on my guard, and allowed myself to be overtaken by a fault, oh, then I could not live until I had received forgiveness and peace was once again made between me and my God. I wept at His holy feet; I told Him of my fault, just as if He had not seen it; I confessed my weakness to Him; and I could not leave the spot until He had forgiven me, and our friendship had been confirmed anew, and indeed much more strongly than ever: which, through His great goodness and mercy, happened every time I fell into a fault, so that even this had to serve to ignite me all the more in His Divine Love afterward."

4. And such a childlike trust in the goodness of God she would have gladly impressed upon the hearts of all the faint-hearted. At times she was so taken by what she felt in her heart regarding this, that she could speak nothing but these words: **O trust! O infinite trust in an infinite goodness, which never leaves nor neglects those who hope in it!**

5. Whenever a useless word escaped her at times, she was immediately punished for it by her Love, and given to understand "that her tongue was sanctified and dedicated to the service of God." At other times she would also say to herself: **Loving is better than speaking.**

6. For this reason, she generally spoke very little, and used to say: "Commonly, as long as one speaks much, it is impossible to love much; because the soul that truly loves does not have enough in all its powers to love: and thus it takes care that it does not turn a part of these powers toward speaking and pour itself out in words; rather, it keeps itself so turned inward and collected <note>original: "versammet" / "versammelt"; a state of inner focus and spiritual concentration</note> that it wishes everything external might be transformed into pure love.

7. She further said: "The soul that is wounded by love finds great effort and difficulty in speaking, unless the overwhelming power of love forces it to speak; and then it pours itself out entirely, so that it cannot remain silent, and wishes that all creatures in heaven and on earth were present, so that it might speak to them of the perfections of its Divine Love; but otherwise, it would rather remain silent toward all, and never converse with any, even if it were an angel from heaven."

> "Nothing in this world is more lowly and wretched than a heart that makes itself a **slave to its desires** and follows the lusts of its flesh.

> "That the longer one stays behind and puts the matter off, the more difficult and vexing it appears to us; because <term>nature</term><note>In this mystical context, "nature" refers to the "lower nature" or the ego and bodily impulses that resist spiritual discipline.</note> always grows stronger, while the spirit becomes weaker and loses its strength.

> "Whoever wishes to obtain this victory must not indulge nature at all, allow it no advantage, nor grant it even the slightest benefit over oneself.

> "As soon as one permits it the slightest thing it demands, it becomes proud and unruly, so that one afterwards has much more trouble taking it away again than one would have had in granting nothing at all.

> "Finally, whoever wishes to enjoy the true life must incessantly **kill nature**, without sparing it or having compassion for it: on the other hand, he who has completely vanquished it has truly brought about for himself a kingdom of peace and an incomprehensible <term>blessedness</term><note>original: "Seligkeit"; implies both extreme happiness and the state of being saved.</note>."

9. Furthermore, she was also accustomed to saying, "To love God, and for His sake to be willing to suffer everything without aim or measure, are two inseparable things. ### Of the Good Armelle. Chapter XVIII.

...spear be wounded, and my feet, like yours, might be pierced with the nails! O my Jesus, oh, that my blood might surge forth together with yours! Be You in me, and let me be in You, and die with You on this **Holy Cross**! O my Jesus, grant me the grace that I might be sick, yes, even die, out of sheer holy love for You, and from heartfelt repentance for having offended You!

11. This refuge in her <term>crucified Love</term><note>A common mystical expression referring to Jesus Christ as the embodiment of Love sacrificed on the cross.</note> helped her then to endure and overcome all the misfortunes that befell her.

> “For (said the cross-loving Armelle) when people persecuted me through their slanders and other ill encounters, or even when the evil spirits persecuted me through their temptations and frivolous malice, I turned instantly to my **Divine Love**, who stretched out His holy arms toward me and showed me His heart and open wounds, so that I might hide myself therein and find my safety there. And then I betook myself into it, as into my true castle and fortress, and there I alone was much stronger than all of hell combined. Yes, if all creatures had set themselves against me at once, I would have feared them no more than a fly, because I was under the protection and shield of Love.

> “All my joy (she said), my delight, my life, and my strength, consisted in the Cross and in Love. When I saw myself nailed there with my Savior, oh then, then I had everything I desired; then I found myself strong, yes, so powerful that all of hell seemed like nothing to me; then I was truly in my element and in my fortress.”

12. Whenever she herself, or others, encountered something adverse, she always had these words in her mouth: **God be praised! one must have patience**: and all her speech was aimed solely and exclusively toward that end.

13. Among other things, there was a certain pain in which she took a singular pleasure; it never left her, and yet it was highly painful. This extended through the whole spine with such sensitivity that she could hardly bend or stoop without suffering great pain. And yet this pain was the most dear to her of all others,

> “because (she said) my God and my Love, at the time when He carried His cross, endured cruel pains in that very place, which I am constantly reminded of through this.”

Moreover, she sometimes had violent <term>colic pains</term><note>original: "Colic-Schmerzen"; refers to severe, fluctuating abdominal pain.</note>, through which she often came into the greatest distress; but when her pain was at its greatest, she always had these words in her mouth: **Live Jesus and his pains!**

14. However, she considered all insults done to her as a great grace, and could not refrain from most fervently loving her insulters, enemies, and adversaries, even though they caused her all manner of heartache, and doing them as much good as was ever possible for her. Therefore, she used to say often,

## Second Part. The Life

„[per]fection, torn out, and has made of me what I now am through His mercy. See, this is my way of life, which I have led for twenty years, without ever feeling the slightest lessening of the love that was poured into my heart at the very beginning of my total conversion. On the contrary, it has increased more and more from day to day, even though every day it seemed to me that I could not even endure the love I already found within me. Now I find myself satiated and satisfied in His infinite love; but previously, before I reached this point, my soul hungered for it daily, even though it seemed to me that I could neither have nor obtain more of it than I actually had at every moment.

22. „But I did not arrive there until it pleased Him, in His great goodness, to lead me into His house. For twenty years (she said), I had been in my own house, and during that time I lived as I have just written; but after that time had passed, He led me into His house, that is, into Himself. <note>In mystical theology, "one's own house" represents the soul's own efforts and self-will, while "His house" represents a state of complete surrender where the soul dwells entirely within the presence of God.</note>

„What has happened in me since then is so sublime, and so far surpasses everything that was in me before, that it is impossible to make it understandable. The <term>creature</term><note>A term used by mystics to refer to the human self or the individual ego as a created being, distinct from the Creator.</note> seems to be completely lost here; the spirit is raised so high above the earth that it no longer seems to be upon it; the peace is so unfathomable, and the joy so perfect, that the soul thinks it has already truly entered into the peace and joy of God, and is, as it were, transformed into God.

23. „Before this so great grace (she said further), God, through His great mercy, never left my sight, and my heart was unceasingly united with Him through love; however, there still remained two things which, although very closely joined together, could nevertheless still be separated from one another. But now God has hidden the creature, so that He alone is seen in me. Here He has adorned me with His Divine perfections, and led me to the possession of His goods; He is my life and my All. Therefore, do not wonder that you see me being what I am; and that I do nothing else but that I am <note>original: "krank bin und sterbe" — "sick and dying [of love]." This is a traditional mystical reference to the Song of Solomon 2:5, describing a soul overwhelmed by divine affection.</note> sick with His love and am dying. I would have to be worse than the devils themselves if, after so many graces and mercies that I have received from His Divine Majesty, I did otherwise; and if I were to neglect this, hell would be too little to punish me. But no, He will never permit this misfortune to happen to me again.

24. „If I am now asked: what do you do at each and every moment of the day, and with what are you constantly occupied? then I can answer nothing else but this: I love, I love fervently. This is all that I can do. With these few words I recount my whole life; for the same has been nothing else but a perpetual love and constant gratitude for all goodness and mercy—

of the good Armelle. Chapter XVIII.

„tender mercies of God toward me. See, this is my prayer, my task, and my life; beyond this, I have nothing more to say of it.„

25. We conclude this chapter with a brief testimony concerning the outward appearance of this soul, so beloved of God. Her form and gestures, and her entire being, displayed something—I know not what—divine and supernatural; and it seemed as if God made Himself known through everything she did, revealing Himself in and beneath all her movements. Indeed, I have heard many people say that if they had not believed there was a God, they would only have needed to look at the good Armelle to be fully convinced of it, so greatly did He manifest Himself in all her expressions. Others said that all her movements, even the very smallest, cried out to them: God is here! And truly, it would have been almost difficult to see Armelle without being simultaneously moved to a sense of reverence toward her, because all her gestures and expressions clearly showed that she was a dwelling of God and the temple of the Holy Spirit. For the <term>modesty</term><note>The original German "Sittsamkeit" implies a deep, composed inner decorum rather than just modern "shyness."</note> that was perceived in her was by no means a feigned or assumed manner; this gave her such a holy appearance that one could easily recognize that her soul was nourished solely and uniquely by God, who had, as it were, imprinted upon her a certain character of His holiness that cannot be described with words. Thus, despite her being only a poor <term>maidservant</term><note>Armelle spent most of her life working as a domestic servant and farm hand, which makes her "majestic" spiritual reputation all the more striking to her contemporaries.</note>, one nevertheless saw something majestic shining forth from her, from which one had to conclude that her soul had truly and blessedly become a partaker of the Divine nature and its attributes.

# The Nineteenth Chapter.

## How God permitted her to break a leg. Her final illness and blessed departure.

->I.<-

In order that we may finally return to the proper order, and thus to the conclusion of our intended history, we must not forget how the Savior allowed it to happen in the year 1666 that, as the good Armelle was once passing by a horse in the street, the animal kicked out behind her and threw her to the ground, whereby she broke a leg. This accident did not dismay her in the least; rather, she immediately thanked the Lord and praised Him for this grace. And although she endured very great pains, which lasted until her death, and the <term>surgeons</term><note>Original: "Wundärzte," literally "wound-doctors." In the 17th century, these were craftsmen who performed external surgeries and set bones, distinct from academic physicians.</note> had to remove several pieces of bone during the treatment, she nevertheless never showed the slightest sign or movement of any impatience or disquiet, despite the long duration of her suffering.

Others said that all her movements, even the very slightest, called out to them: God is here! For the modesty <note>The German word "Sittsamkeit" implies a combination of modesty, propriety, and a calm, virtuous demeanor.</note> one perceived therein was by no means a feigned or put-on manner; and this gave her such a holy appearance that one could easily recognize from it that her soul was nourished solely and uniquely by God, as if a certain character of His holiness—which cannot be described with words—had been imprinted upon her. Thus, despite her being only a poor maidservant, one nevertheless saw something majestic shining forth from her, from which one had to conclude that her soul had truly and blessedly become a partaker of the Divine nature and attributes.

### Part Two. The Life

„[forgotten]ness, torn out, and has made out of me what I now am through his mercy. See, this is my way of life, which I have led for twenty years, without ever feeling the slightest lessening of the love that was poured into my heart at the very beginning of my complete conversion. On the contrary, this same love has increased more and more from day to day, even though every day it seemed to me that I could not even bear the love I already found within me. Now I find myself satisfied and content in His infinite love; but before, before I reached this point, my soul hungered for it daily, even though it seemed to me that I could not have or obtain more of it than I actually had at every moment.

22. „But I did not arrive at this point until it pleased Him, according to His great goodness, to lead me into His house. For twenty years, (she said,) I had been in my own house, and had lived during that time as I have now written; but after that time had passed, He led me into His house, that is, into Himself.

„What has happened within me since then is so sublime, and so far surpasses everything that was in me before, that it is impossible to make it understood. The creature <note>Armelle uses the term 'creature' to refer to her own human nature and identity as a created being, as distinct from the Creator.</note> seems to be completely lost here; the spirit is raised so high above the earth that it seems to no longer be upon it; the peace is so unfathomable, and the joy so perfect, that the soul thinks it has already truly entered into the peace and joy of God, and is, as it were, transformed into God.

23. „Before this so great a grace, (she said further,) through His great mercy, God never left my sight, and my heart was unceasingly united with Him through love; however, there still remained two things which, although they were very closely joined together, could nonetheless still be separated from one another. But now God has hidden the creature, so that He alone is seen in me. Here He has adorned me with His divine perfections <note>technical term: "Vollkommenheiten" — refers to the divine attributes such as goodness, holiness, and love being reflected in the soul</note>, and led me to the possession of His goods: He is my life and my All. Do not wonder, therefore, that you see me being what I am; and that I do nothing but that I am sick with His love and am dying. I would have to be worse than the devils themselves if, after so many graces and mercies I have received from His Divine Majesty, I acted otherwise; and if I were to neglect this, hell would be too little to punish me. But no, He will never again permit this misfortune to happen to me.

24. „So if I am now asked: what do you do every moment of the day, and what are you constantly occupied with? I can answer nothing else but this: I love, I love fervently. This is all that I can do. With these few words I tell my whole life; for it has been nothing else but a perpetual love and constant gratitude for all the goodness and mer[cy]—

### Second Part. The Life.

...look with tranquility; which caused great wonder among all those who saw her suffer such intense pains with such great joy.

2. For more than 15 full months, she was unable to go out. During this time, a flux <note>original: *Fluß*; a historical medical term for an accumulation of bodily fluids or an inflammation</note> had settled in her other leg, which meant that not only could she not walk on it, but she also felt almost as much pain in it as in the one that had been broken. Throughout this whole time, she lay in bed or sat in a chair; she was only carried into the church on Sundays and feast days. The rest of the time she remained in a small corner in the kitchen to manage the household and to do some work for the benefit of the house, so that she was never idle. Many people, of both high and low status, came to visit her, to find refreshment in her company, and to enjoy her friendly conversation and good counsel. She gave them all great pleasure, as much through her holy speech as through the great patience with which she bore her misfortune. Yet it pleased **GOD** to grant her some relief in this regard, in that He gave her strength again so that she could walk; at first indeed on crutches, but afterward with a smaller stick; although her pains were by no means lessened because of it, but instead lasted constantly until her death, of which it will now finally be time to speak.

3. Our Savior sent her, around the 5th of the month of August in the year 1671, a severe double three-day fever <note>This refers to a recurring fever cycle, likely a form of malaria which was common in the 17th century</note>, which in a short time changed into a daily one. She had this for a whole month, continuously and without relief; therefore, it was believed that she would die from it. When the daughter of the nobleman with whom she lived—a very sensible and virtuous person—once said to her that she feared, because she was so weak, that this illness would take her away, she answered with great assurance: „The work is not yet finished; and she would still have much to suffer,” over which she then greatly rejoiced.

4. After the passage of a month, she felt somewhat better; yet she was not freed from the fever, but had it every night. This compelled her master to return with her from the country to the city all the sooner, in the hope that the change of air would assist her in regaining her health. Thus she came back to Vannes at the end of September. Her fever, however, persisted and came every night as before, by which she became so weak that she was forced to stay entirely in bed. Although her illness did not seem at all dangerous, she fully believed that she would not recover from it again. To that end, she gave the aforementioned daughter of the nobleman an account of all household matters, as well as of some other things that concerned her in particular. The daughter, however, laughed at this and said there was no danger in her current illness; it was not nearly as great as the one she had recently had. But she answered her that she would certainly die and would not recover.

### of the good Armelle. Chapter XIX.

...an inflammation of the throat was added to this, which meant that she could take no food at all, nor swallow the slightest thing, without very intense pain; yet she endured this with her usual patience, and at the same time asked all who visited her to thank our Savior for the grace He showed her. At the very last, she still called upon the Holy Name of JESUS; after which she spoke no more.

7. Finally, on Saturday, the 24th of October of the same year, between twelve and one o’clock at midday, she gave up the ghost; and passed away so gently that one hardly noticed it. Thus this blessed soul ended her days here, so that hereafter she might love her Creator in a blessed life, which has no other end or limit than eternity itself.

# Preface.

->1.<-

Divine Wisdom, which reaches mightily from one end to the other <note>A reference to the Book of Wisdom 8:1: "She reacheth from one end to another mightily: and sweetly doth she order all things."</note>, goes about among those of the lowest status, and enters into the holy soul of a poor, uneducated peasant woman and maidservant, and others like her, and does not leave them until she brings them a scepter and a kingdom; as we have seen in the example of the good Armelle <note>Armelle Nicolas (1606–1671), the subject of the previous biography in this collection.</note>. Yet, this impartial wisdom from above has never been so entirely barred from entering palaces that she has not also found some—if not many, then at least a few—among the highest ranks who have befriended and wedded her in a manner befitting their status; as Monsieur Renty, a high-born Marquis and clever State Councilor to the King of France, shall prove with his example in the following history.

->2.<-

The life of this man was initially described by Father Saint-Jure <note>original: "St. Jurius"</note>, of the Society of Jesus <note>original: "Soc. J."</note>, a pious, learned author known for various writings. Because he was Renty's spiritual guide, not only was Renty’s conduct and inner nature better known to him than to anyone else, but he also held Renty's own manuscripts and letters as irreproachable records. It is so far beyond all suspicion that anything in this history was exaggerated; rather, it is certain that both Renty and Saint-Jure kept the best parts hidden from us—the former out of humility, the latter out of excessive caution. (a)

->3.<-

This *Life* was printed in Paris shortly after Renty's death, read by countless eyewitnesses, and reprinted perhaps 8 or 10 times, until finally in Amsterdam in 1701, Mr. Poiret <note>Pierre Poiret (1646–1719), a famous French mystical theologian and editor.</note> published it under this new title: *The Real Christian* <note>original: "Le Chretien Réel"</note>, etc. It is from this beautiful edition that this extract has been translated into German; in which (as with the other biographies) the words of this saint have been preserved as much as possible and marked in the margin with the usual sign, especially since his own style of writing is neat, thorough, and edifying.

->4.<-

All of France saw and admired this shining light—namely, a true saint at the Royal Court and amidst the bustle of people, no less than in the church and the prayer chamber, entirely devoted to inner prayer, constantly occupied in the service of his neighbor for the glory of God. Let us then take this example to refute the seemingly plausible objection that the contemplative or inward life (*mystical theology* <note>original: "Theologia mystica"</note>) is useless to the Church and the Republic. For, to say nothing of the fact that a single such soul, with their secret prayer, promotes the conversion of men and the well-being of a land more than a thousand others who are regarded as pillars; so it also sometimes pleases God to send out these angels—who always behold the face of their heavenly Father—as ministering spirits for the service of those who shall inherit salvation. And those who are thus placed in union with God bear fruit, and their fruit remains: whereas those who think they are accomplishing such great things often only stain and confuse everything further, as that final Day will make clear.

->5.<-

In both the Roman (b) and Protestant (c) Church, some short extracts of this history already exist, through which it has already been sufficiently approved. We wish, however, to add a few more testimonies here, upon which some readers might reflect. The well-known Bernières-Louvigny says: (d) "Mr. Renty was my intimate friend. We had a very

(c) In Reitz's *History of the Born-Again* <note>original: "Hist. der Wiedergeb."</note>. Also, in London, John Wesley issued an extract in the English language in 1741. And our present extract was published in 1744 in Hoorn in the Dutch language.

<meta>This page continues the "Preface" (Vorbericht) regarding the life of the Marquis de Renty. The previous page discussed how divine wisdom is found in both the lowly (like Armelle Nicolas) and the high-born (like Renty), and introduced Father Saint-Jure as Renty's biographer.</meta>

...close connection of the soul with one another; and I regret that I made so little use of his company. When he died, I could not be grieved by it; on the contrary, my soul was embalmed with a good scent <note>A reference to the "odor of sanctity," a mystical fragrance believed to emanate from the bodies or memories of the holy.</note> that I do not know how to express; indeed, with a perceptible joy and a certain assurance of his salvation. The judgment of the English Bishop (a) **Burnet** <note>Gilbert Burnet (1643–1715), a well-known Scottish theologian and Bishop of Salisbury.</note> is no less favorable when he says: "Although very many pay attention to fables, one must confess that the life of Monsieur de **Renty** does not taste of them. One perceives in it such excellent virtues that one must rightly count the one who practiced them among the greatest examples that France has produced in this century." This famous man is also said to have translated and published this very life into English. The comfortable "fashion-Christian" <note>original: "Modechrist"; refers to those who follow Christianity only as a social custom rather than a deep conviction.</note> will say of **Renty** (these are the words of Mr. **Johann Heinrich Reitz**): "that was a fantastical <note>In this context, "fantastical" means someone caught up in delusions or irrational religious enthusiasm.</note> saint!" But on that day <note>A reference to the Day of Judgment.</note> it will be shown whether he was not a man pleasing to GOD and a true holy Christian. Yet, the example of JESUS, his Master, the Scripture, and almost all of France and England stand on his side. And here I must say freely that the works of love, mortification <term>mortification: the practice of self-discipline and "dying to the self" to overcome worldly desires</term>, humility, self-denial, and, in a word, the true imitation of Christ, are practiced more among the *mystics* of the Roman Church than among us Protestants. (b)

6. Read and judge for yourself, dear reader! And see to it how you make use of what you have read; and whether the earnest conduct of this man—who in the bloom of his years, in such a high station and reputation, when all the hoped-for advantages of the world came to meet him, and moreover in the state of marriage, among many businesses and people, yes, even at the Royal Court, lived so virtuously and holily as this history brings to light—I say, whether this example may not be able to shame our laziness and to incite everyone, according to their circumstances, to emulation through the cooperation of the grace of GOD!

## The First Chapter.
### Concerning the Ancestry, Childhood, Youth, Marriage, and Military Service of the Marquis of Renty.

->1.<-

The Lord of Renty descended from the ancient lineage of the Nobles of Renty, in the province of Artois, in the Netherlands. <note>Artois was a territory in northern France that historically shifted between French and Burgundian/Spanish control.</note> He was the only son of Charles of Renty and Madeleine of Pâtoureau; he was born in Beny, in Lower Normandy, in the year 1611, and was carried to his baptism by the poor of that place. This was a singular act of Divine Providence, that he should receive as godparents those very people for whom he would later serve as a leader, protector, and father throughout his entire life.

2. In the ninth year of his age, he was placed in the College of Navarre in Paris, <note>A prestigious constituent college of the University of Paris.</note> and afterward in the Jesuit College at Caen, under the direction of a tutor who was a Protestant. In his seventeenth year, he entered the University of Paris, where he applied himself with singular pleasure to mathematics; out of zeal for this science, he abstained from all the delights of youth, and consequently made great progress in it.

3. As he frequently visited the bookstore to buy books serving his purpose, the bookseller once presented him with the famous little book by *Thomas à Kempis* <note>Thomas à Kempis (c. 1380–1471) was a German-Dutch canon regular; his book "The Imitation of Christ" remains one of the most famous Christian devotional works.</note> on the *Imitation of Christ*, requesting that he read it. However, because his mind was set on other sciences, he made little of it this first time. But when the bookseller brought him some books on another occasion, he presented it to him once more and earnestly begged him to read it. He then consented, read it, and was so moved by it that he resolved to consider the salvation of his soul in earnest and to surrender himself to **GOD**. Therefore, it happened that Renty thereafter always carried this little book with him; indeed, out of a desire to leave the world entirely, he wished to enter a Carthusian monastery, <note>The Carthusians are one of the most austere and secluded religious orders in the Catholic Church.</note> despite the fact that he was the only son of his father and an heir to great estates, and possessed such qualities that the path to all worldly honors stood open to him. See what happened:

4. This occurred in the nineteenth year of his age; and a few days later, he wrote the following letter to his father:

# Preface.

...close connection of spirits with one another; and I regret that I made so little use of his company. When he died, I could not grieve over it; on the contrary, my soul was embalmed with a "good scent" <note>The author refers to the "odor of sanctity," a traditional spiritual concept where a person's life or death is perceived to leave a metaphorical or literal sweet fragrance, symbolizing divine grace.</note> which I cannot describe; yes, with a palpable joy and a certain assurance of his salvation. The judgment of the English Bishop (a) Burnet is no less favorable, where he speaks: "Even though very many pay heed to fables, one must still confess that the life of Monsieur de Renty does not taste of them. One perceives in it such excellent virtues that one must rightly count the man who practiced them among the greatest examples that France has produced in this century." This famous man <note>referring to Bishop Gilbert Burnet (1643–1715), a well-known Scottish theologian and historian.</note> is also said to have translated and published this very *Life* into English. The "Christian of fashion" <note>original: "Modechrist"; a person whose faith is superficial or follows social trends rather than deep conviction.</note> will say of Renty (these are the words of Mr. Johann Heinrich Reitz): "That was a fantastical saint!" <note>Johann Heinrich Reitz (1655–1720) was a German Pietist author whose work *History of the Reborn* was a landmark collection of spiritual biographies.</note> However, on that day <note>A reference to the Day of Judgment.</note> it will be shown whether he was not a man pleasing to God and a true, holy Christian. Indeed, the example of Jesus, his Master, the Scripture, and almost all of France and England stand on his side. And here I must say freely that works of love, mortification <note>original: "Castenung"; the practice of self-discipline and abstaining from worldly pleasures for spiritual growth.</note>, humility, self-denial, and, in a word, the true imitation of Christ, are practiced more among the mystics of the Roman Church than among us Protestants. (b)

6. Read and judge for yourself, dear reader! And see to it how you make use of what you have read; and whether the earnest life of this man—who, in the flower of his years, in such a high station and reputation, with all the hoped-for advantages of the world coming toward him, and moreover in the state of marriage, amidst many affairs and people, even at the Royal Court, lived so virtuously and holily as this history brings to light—I say, see whether this example might not be capable of shaming our laziness and inciting everyone, according to their circumstances, to emulation through the cooperation of the grace of God?

# Chapter One.

## Regarding the Marquis de Renty's Origin, Childhood, Youth, Marriage, and Military Service.

->I.<-

**M**r. de Renty descended from the ancient lineage of the Nobles of Renty, in the province of Artois, in the Netherlands. He was the only son of Charles de Renty and Madeleine de Pâtoureau; he was born in Beni, in Lower Normandy, in the year 1611, and was brought to his baptism by the poor of that place. This was a singular act of Divine Providence, that he should receive as godparents those very people for whom he would later serve as a leader, protector, and father for the rest of his life.

2. In the ninth year of his age, he was placed in the College of Navarre in Paris <note>The College of Navarre was one of the most prestigious colleges of the University of Paris, known for educating the French nobility and royalty.</note>, and afterward in the Jesuit College at Caen, under the direction of a tutor who was a Protestant. In his seventeenth year, he entered the University of Paris, where he applied himself with singular pleasure to mathematics, and, out of zeal for this science, he abstained from all the pleasures of youth; as a result, he made very great progress in it.

3. As he frequently visited the bookstore to buy books serving his purposes, the bookseller once presented him with the famous little book by Thomas à Kempis <note>Thomas à Kempis (c. 1380–1471) was a German-Dutch canon regular; his book *The Imitation of Christ* is one of the most influential Christian devotional works in history.</note> on the *Imitation of Christ*, with a request that he read it. However, because his mind was set on other sciences, he made little of it this first time. But when the bookseller brought him some books another time, he presented this one to him again and earnestly begged him to read it. He then agreed, read it, and was so moved by it that he resolved to seriously consider the salvation of his soul and to give himself to God. Because of this, it also happened that Renty thereafter always carried this little book with him; indeed, out of a desire to leave the world entirely, he wished to enter a Carthusian monastery <note>The Carthusians are a Catholic religious order of enclosed monastics, known for their extreme silence and austerity.</note>, regardless of the fact that he was the only son of his father and an heir to great estates, and also possessed such qualities that the path to all the high honors of the world stood open to her. See what happened:

4. Once, while he was sitting in the carriage with his lady mother in Paris, he stepped out with her permission, pretending that he wanted to buy something; however, he immediately withdrew from her sight and hurried with all diligence through all the side streets out of the city. This happened in the nineteenth year of his age; and a few days later he wrote the following letter to his father:

->My Lord,<-

> "I have no doubt that this change will cause you distress; since the first movements of the heart are not within human power,"

through God’s special providence into a house where a poor, old, and sick woman lay, who had been unable to flee with the others. After he had spiritually and physically refreshed and comforted her, she assured him that the Croats <note>Irregular light cavalry troops often used as scouts or skirmishers during the Thirty Years' War, known for their speed and ferocity.</note> would arrive within a few hours, and that he should depart in haste. This all came to pass exactly as she said. Had they held their ground for even three hours longer, they would surely all have been put to the sword. Thus the Lord watches over those who fear Him.

8. As long as Mr. Renty remained in military service, he practiced constant prayer and devotion: and as soon as he arrived at his quarters, his first task was to go to the church; and if there was a monastery in that same place, he always took his lodging there. He avoided all the dissolute company of others in the war and prevented such behavior wherever it was in his power: but he especially forbade his men from being a burden to their hosts. He never mounted his horse [to depart] until he had summoned his hosts before him, so that he might hear from their own mouths whether his men had done them any harm. Once, as he was already on his horse to move out and had questioned his hostess, she complained that one of his men had stolen a shirt from her. He immediately ordered the thief—who had already put the shirt on—to come before him and take it off in the presence of everyone to return it to the woman, even though several noblemen who were present attempted to oppose this.

9. God allowed him to fall into various disputes or disagreements with other noblemen; in these, however, he knew how to conduct himself so Christianly and wisely that he always extricated himself successfully. For the basic rules which he used to present to his people in such occurrences were these:

> “It is a greater bravery and nobility of soul to endure some injustice for the sake of the love of God than to commit one; to suffer something rather than to seek revenge; because the former is much more difficult: an ox also has a heart, but that is a brutish heart, whereas we, on the contrary, must have a rational and Christian heart.”

***

...cast [his influence], as well in Paris as in all places where he came. It happened through the Fathers of the Oratory <note>original: "Patres Oratorii"; a Catholic society of apostolic life founded in France in 1611, known for their focus on education and spiritual depth.</note>, whose General, Father de Condren, he also took as his spiritual director <note>original: "Seelen-Führer"</note>. De Condren was a learned, very devout man, well-versed in the "interior ways" <note>The "inner ways" refers to a tradition of mystical and contemplative prayer popular in 17th-century France.</note> of the soul. He guided our Renty for as long as he lived—which was about two years—with the greatest care, love, and blessing, so that he once said to a certain person: "Mr. Renty would in his time yet become a great saint."

2. Mr. Renty truly received so many graces through this new calling that he marked that time as the beginning of his complete conversion to God and total sacrifice to His service. To say nothing of his penitential exercises and his severity toward the flesh—which is the first struggle of those who are honestly converted to God (of which more will follow later)—he at once renounced the court and all vain, ambitious services, in order to occupy himself hereafter only with those things which might serve for the glorification of God and the service of his neighbor. He renounced all visits which consisted only of useless compliments; he applied himself to the practice of prayer, so that he always devoted two or three hours in the night to it, even in the coldest part of winter; he visited the poor, the sick, and prisoners, and joined himself to godly assemblies.

3. Every evening he had a prayer hour held in his house with his children and servants; and every Saturday he held a conversation with them regarding the Gospel of the following Sunday, so that he might impress upon them the fundamental teachings contained therein and instruct them in those things which served for their salvation; from which they drew great edification. If he drove out with his people, he prayed, read, and sang with them, and spoke with them—according to the occasion of the subjects <note>original: "Vorwürfe"; here used in the archaic sense of "topics" or "objects of contemplation."</note> that arose—of God, of His perfections and truths, so that he might sweetly lift their hearts to God. When he came to an inn, his first act was to kneel down in the room and worship God. If he saw something unseemly written on the walls, he erased it and put some edifying words in its place. He also always gave the house servants a good reminder before he departed again, as well as to the poor of that place whom he encountered, so that in this he followed his Savior, who did good wherever He traveled.

4. He especially sought to instill in his children a deep impression of the fear of God and, conversely, a disregard for the world; to show them that the principles of the world were entirely contrary to the spirit of Jesus Christ, and that true nobility consisted in virtue. On which matter he once wrote, among others, the following words to a lady:

## The Third Chapter.

### The origin of all his virtues was the union with Christ JESUS.

->1.<-

If we now wish to proceed in investigating the origin of these virtues and this 
godliness, we shall find that it was the intimate union which the blessed Renty had with the Savior Jesus Christ. His wise and enlightened guide, Father Condren <note>Charles de Condren (1588–1641), a prominent figure in the French School of Spirituality and Renty’s spiritual director.</note>, knew that union with the Lord JESUS is the foundation of our election, our justification, our sanctification, of all grace and all glory that we can ever participate in; that JESUS Christ is the Way, and that everything found outside of this way can be nothing but error; that He is the Truth, and that everything not conforming to this truth is but a lie; that He is the Life, and everything not quickened by this life, and not animated by the Spirit of JESUS Christ, is by no means living, but necessarily dead. Therefore, he also sought to place the Lord de Renty upon this Way, to bind him to this Truth, and to unite him with this Life.

->2.<-

This guidance he followed quite exactly, made great progress therein, and became daily more perfect in it until his death; in such a way that, just as the sun gives far greater heat when it rises to midday than when it first arose, so also the union of this excellent soul with the Lord JESUS was, in its final years, far different from that which it had in its beginnings. For then our Renty was completely perfected in Christ JESUS; he

->3.<-

This is what he aimed for when he wrote to his guide <note>his spiritual director</note> in the year 1646, among other things: "I feel that I want nothing else but **God**, and that I desire to bring all my honors to Him in union with our Savior **JESUS Christ**. Nevertheless, I know that from myself I am nothing other than sin; despite this, I experience our **Lord** within me, who is my strength, my life, my peace, and my everything. I pray to Him that He would be our fullness."

->4.<-

"It has been about fourteen days since the following words came into my mind, without my doing anything on my part: Seek the spring-vein of living waters. I saw that precisely there was the fountainhead from which the veins of living water flow down upon us, and that we must turn ourselves exactly toward that place."

# The Fourth Chapter.
## Concerning his mortification <note>In 17th-century spirituality, "mortification" refers to the practice of "dying" to worldly or physical desires to focus on the soul.</note> of sensual desires, the denial of himself, his social standing, and his possessions.

->I.<-

To this union, which the dear Renty had with the Lord Jesus Christ, we must ascribe all his other virtues, which we now wish to examine somewhat more specifically: and we are to view them as nothing other than little streams that have issued from this fountain.

2. First, let us consider the subduing of his body. For once and for all, those who belong to Jesus Christ have crucified their flesh, together with its lusts and desires. Mr. Renty sought from the beginning in every way to make his body subject to the spirit. For several years in a row, he ate only once a day, until later, because of his heavy labors in the service of his neighbor, another course was advised. Once when he came to Amiens <note>A city in northern France.</note>, where I also was, (says the author of this history,) and stayed with a very noble lady of that city, she had prepared a magnificent bed in a beautiful room for him, according to his rank; but he was only distressed by this and lay down on a bench to sleep. The next morning, as if ashamed, he gave me a reprimand for having led him into such a room; and if this lady wished to have the happiness of keeping him longer, she had to have a humbler bed and room prepared for him.

3. He always ate little and of the poorest food, and indeed with such inwardness and collection of his mind that one could easily notice that he was not focused on the food, but on God, his devotion, and his joy.

One of his friends in Caen, who was also a pious man, once gave him a midday meal with a bit of ceremony <note>Refers to the formal etiquette expected for a nobleman.</note>; but he ate very little and said afterward that it was a shame that Christians even prepared feasts, and that it was only a great torment to be at a table where there was such a multitude of dishes, and that in this, one acted entirely contrary to the poverty of Jesus Christ, which should nevertheless be our rule. "A little bread, a little bacon, and a little butter is enough," said this Marquis and Royal State Councilor <note>original: "Königliche Staats-Rath"</note> to his friends.

## The Fourth Chapter.
### On his mortification of sensual lusts, denial of himself, his status, and his goods.

->I.<-

To this union, which the dear Renty had with the Lord Jesus Christ, we must attribute all his other virtues, which we will now examine somewhat more specifically; and we are to view them as nothing other than little streams that have come forth from this fountain.

2. First, we consider the mortification <note>The German *Betäubung* (literally "numbing" or "deafening") is used here in the sense of *mortification of the flesh*: the spiritual practice of subduing bodily desires through self-discipline.</note> of his body. For once and for all, all those who belong to Jesus Christ have crucified their flesh, together with its lusts and desires. Mr. Renty sought from the beginning in every way to make his body subject to the spirit. For several years in a row, he ate only once a day, until later, because of his heavy labors in the service of his neighbor, he was advised otherwise. When he once came to Amiens, where I also was (says the author of this history), and stayed with a very noble lady of that same city, she had prepared for him a magnificent bed in a beautiful room, according to his rank; but he was only distressed by it and lay down on a bench to sleep. The next morning, as if ashamed, he gave me a reprimand for having led him into such a room; and if this lady wished to have the good fortune of keeping him longer, she had to have a humbler bed and room prepared for him.

3 He always ate little and of the coarsest food, and indeed with such a withdrawal and collection <note>Referring to *recollection*, a state of inner spiritual focus and prayerful silence.</note> of his mind that one could easily notice that he was not focused on the food, but on God, his devotion, and his joy.

One of his friends at Caen, who was also a pious man, once gave him—as a person of status—a midday meal with a little ceremony; but he ate very little and said afterward that it was a shame that Christians even prepared banquets, and it was only a great torment to be at a table where there was such a quantity of food, and that one acted therein entirely contrary to the poverty of Jesus Christ, which nevertheless must be our rule. "A little bread, a little bacon, and a little butter is enough," said this Marquis and Royal State Councilor <term>Staats-Rath: a high-ranking political advisor to the King</term> to his friends.

### Third Part. The Life

4. It happened many times in *Paris* that the performance of some work of charity led him so far from his house that he could not return for the midday meal. In such cases, he went quite alone and unknown into a common cookshop <note>A *Garküche* was a basic eating house for laborers and the poor.</note> or to a baker, ate a little bread and drank water with it, which concluded his entire meal, and then joyfully continued his charitable business.

5. Just as he did regarding his sense of taste, so he also did in the mortification <note>In this context, *mortification* (or "killing off") refers to the spiritual practice of subduing the physical senses to focus entirely on God.</note> of his other senses; like *Paul*, he always carried about in his body the dying of Jesus Christ, so that the life of Jesus might also be made manifest in his body. *2 Corinthians 4:10.* Everything that could please or flatter his senses was intolerable to him; thus, he once let slip to a trusted friend that God had given him a great hatred toward himself—so much so that his spiritual guide had to earnestly restrain him toward moderation. To this, he once replied in a letter: "I do not know why the reins are held so short on such a lazy beast, for whom the spurs are surely more necessary than the stirrup."

6. Meanwhile, he continued sufficiently to combat his senses, so that he reached a point where his body was as if dead and insensible to all things, which now made almost no impression on his senses. He ate without taste; all foods, he said himself, were the same to him. He saw without seeing: he had often been in well-decorated churches for long periods and had all these ornaments before his eyes, yet when asked if they were not beautiful, he said simply that he had seen nothing. Indeed, all such disagreeable things, from which others who still live for themselves and pamper their bodies would have shuddered, no longer caused him any trouble.

He had overcome himself with such earnestness and in all matters through grace that he once wrote to his guide that he could not understand what people called self-denial or *mortification* <note>original: "Verläugnung oder Mortification"</note>. When something very mortifying once happened to him—something that could have struck him powerfully had he still possessed a life of his own—and a certain trusted person expressed their concern about it to him, he said with a laughing mouth:
> “That goes quite well. One must strive to overcome oneself
> to such an extent that nothing is any longer a self-denial (or *morti-*
> *fication*), and to become as if insensible to everything.”

7. To a certain devout person, he wrote the following:
> “O, how much is it to
> be feared that we misuse the name and the appearance of devotion by
> placing our trust in our outward godly exercises, which we perhaps still
> perform quite lukewarmly. We perform them perhaps only in *speculation* <note>In the sense of intellectual theory or contemplation without action.</note>; but they do not
> come to *practice* and to the overcoming of ourselves. In the morning, we worship Je-
> sus Christ as our Master and Guide; but throughout the day, our lives
> are not any better ordered for it. We look upon Him as our model without
> following Him; we take Him as the rule and guideline for our senses, and
> yet we do not sacrifice our lusts to Him; we make Him the pattern of our...”

8. How detached and poor in spirit he was, despite all the wealth and honor he was forced to possess against his will, we shall hear many more testimonies of this from time to time. On several occasions, he said to me in confidence that „he was quite ashamed when he came into his house and saw himself so well-lodged in this world; and that it was one of his greatest sufferings to have so many goods and be so well cared for; that it would be his highest joy to see himself in such a state where he had only bread and water, and must furthermore earn such through the labor of his hands and in the sweat of his brow.“ <note>A reference to the biblical mandate in Genesis 3:19.</note> When I asked him one day how he could be so calm in all the hardship and vexations that befell him, he answered me, on the condition that „I should keep it secret,“ that he found himself, through the mercy of God, both in tribulations and in joys, in a state of peace and settled equanimity, and that he no longer had any sensitivity to fear or desire anything. And I have seen the certainty of this in such instances when the greater part of his property was in danger of being lost, without one being able to perceive the slightest movement of emotion in him. Therefore, he held the poor in their state to be blessed people. He honored, loved, and cared for them because of the advantage their state has in reaching the perfection of the New Covenant, and because of the similarity to the state of Jesus Christ here on earth.

9. Although he could not and was not permitted to leave all his goods and become truly poor <note>As a nobleman, Renty had legal and social obligations to his family and estate that prevented him from becoming a wandering beggar.</note>, he nevertheless rid himself of them as often as he had the opportunity through the greatest acts of charity to the poor; he also stripped himself of many other things and made himself, in a word, as poor as he could. He gave away his magnificently bound books. His clothes had to be simple and plain. What was superfluous, he did not use. In the beginning, I saw him riding in a carriage with a page and several lacqueys <note>A lacquey was a uniformed manservant.</note>; afterward with one lacquey and no page; then without a carriage and on foot with one lacquey; and finally alone without a lacquey, and thus also without himself. <note>The phrase "without himself" refers to the mystical concept of "self-annihilation" or the total removal of the ego.</note> In his own house, he regarded himself as a poor man who received only his necessities from God through the hand of his wife.

**F**rom this poverty of spirit follows humility; indeed, it is already one with it. 3. This virtue can be considered according to the heart, according to words, and according to works. This true follower of **JESUS Christ** possessed humility of the heart in a singular way. He had such low thoughts of himself that it would be difficult to express them. And although he possessed quite uncommon gifts and qualities, both natural and supernatural, he nevertheless saw nothing in himself but nothingness and sin; and through a true and sincere conviction, he esteemed himself to be the most unworthy among all men, commonly calling himself a sinner, and a great sinner, which he sometimes repeated with a truly humbled spirit.

4. A certain credible person gives the following testimony of him, which fits very well here: In those six years that I have had the fortune to know him, I have observed in him a very deep humility, which held him in a perpetual annihilation <term>annihilation: "Vernichtigung," a 17th-century spiritual term for the total surrendering of the self until one feels like "nothing" before the presence of God</term> before **GOD** and all creatures, and indeed in such a way as I have never seen in a single person, though I have known very holy souls. The majesty of **GOD** humbled him even into the abyss. “Is anything then great” (he said to me one day) “before this Greatness? I see myself there as so small and absolutely nothing.” And thereupon he lifted his heart to **GOD** in the feeling of this smallness, and said: “A speck of dust in the sun is indeed small; but I am even smaller in the presence of **GOD**, for I am nothing.” Afterward he humbled himself in another way, and said: “Alas! I am only far too much; I am a sinner, an unfaithful one, a curse, because of my misdeeds.”

Another time he wrote to this same person: “I think that I crush myself 
“before **GOD**, as if I were to stomp an egg into the earth with all my might; 
“is it even right that you still speak of me, and that I am even still 
“mentioned? That is indeed a strange thing.”

6. He took every opportunity to humble himself. He lowered himself greatly because of the knowledge of our natural weakness; concerning which he wrote the following words to a certain person: “It is a wretched thing with man and with his weakness; it is sometimes very useful for him to experience what he is, so that he does not forget what he is and what place is due to him; so that no flesh <note>original: *Fleiſch*; here referring to human nature or mortality</note> (a) may boast in His presence; so that, after he has been made so small in this way, annihilated, and become as something that no longer is, **Jesus Christ** may be the life of grace and holiness in him, awaiting the time of our redemption, namely, the entry into glory, and, as it is written, that he (b) who boasts, let him boast in the **Lord**.”

7. To another person he wrote: “The state of our poverty, and the sight of our miseries, makes us recognize the high necessity of grace, and grounds the soul in the annihilation of itself <note>A mystical concept where the ego is "made into nothing" to allow God to act fully within the person</note> and in the conviction of its inability to do anything good, and in this truth: that it has never been anything else, nor can it ever be anything else, than a hindrance and a reduction of the workings of **God** within it.”

8. The knowledge of his faults and sins humbled him even more. “I assure you,” (he once wrote to me) “that I have cause enough to humble myself, and to work on my improvement with all seriousness, though also with patience. For I experience, and see it quite clearly, that however much we work and wish to leave our imperfections behind, the **Lord** nevertheless leaves us in them for a considerable time, so that He may make us recognize our weakness and humble us.”

9. He arranged for a certain person, who was far below him in rank, to remind him by order of his spiritual director as often as he failed, or seemed to fail; he received this with thanksgiving as often as she did so.

10. His excellent gifts and graces humbled him no less than his imperfections and sins. The spirit of **Jesus Christ** that animated him made him even feel ashamed of his high social standing according to the world, and he often sighed to **God** that his standing should be truly humbling, and, in view of the spirit of **Jesus**, poor and lowly, and he was ashamed to the highest degree in His eyes to see himself in such a rank. 11. Regarding the Divine gifts and graces, they produced their proper effects in him; namely, that they indeed raised him up to **God**, but also lowered him in his own estimation; through his humility, he hid the gifts of **God** as much as he could: and this is the reason that a thousand beautiful deeds have remained unknown to us, which could have been of use to us in this history. He could not bear for people to look at him in all that he did or said.

To a certain person, who earnestly requested his visit, he wrote the following: “I can hardly bear that you hold my visits and conversations in such high regard. Let us visit **God** much, and bind ourselves unceasingly with **Jesus Christ**, so that we may learn from Him the deep annihilation of ourselves <note>A central theme in Renty’s spirituality: the total emptying of the self to make room for God</note>. O my **God**! when shall we no longer look upon ourselves, when shall we no longer speak of ourselves, and when shall all vanity be destroyed?”

And to another, he wrote: “I beg of you, that you will look upon nothing else in me but my weaknesses, and the ground of malice, and of the astounding pride that is within me. See, for that, everyone might rebuke me and punish me.”

He considered himself entirely unworthy of the least of **God’s** graces: but see here, in what manner he was only humbled by so many great graces with which his soul was filled: “The gifts of **God**” (he wrote to a trusted friend) “are sometimes so great that they set us, so to speak, above ourselves; and if we could find a place to escape to that was even further than Nothingness, we would go there. You see it among men, when one gives someone something that is equal to the status of such a person, he gives great thanks for it; but if a prince, according to the greatness of his fortune, gave a poor man either a sum of money or an office; you should see how this poor man would be startled and say: ‘Ah, my Lord, I believe that you do not know me; so much is not due to me; I am unworthy of it.’ It is exactly the same with the treasures of grace, which far exceed our hope, and which give us to know what we are, since we dare not lift up our eyes, so greatly does their radiance blind us, and so greatly does their magnitude dismay the soul.”

12. His humility meant that he not only thought little of himself, but also gladly wished to be despised by others; and that, when this happened, he accepted it not only with patience, but also with joy. When he once had to travel to Dijon because of a very vexing business matter, he wrote the following short letter from there to his guide, on July 24, 1643. “I am then in Dijon, as it has pleased **God**; where I have recognized, from the prejudices by which people were biased against me, what **God** had in view with my journey,

The rumors that have been spread about me—that I was a sanctimonious hypocrite, possessing only a cunning appearance of godliness to give my wickedness a beautiful color—caused me to remain very secluded in my room, fearing that if I came forward, I might give more offense than an example of virtue. I found a monastic community <note>original: *Klostergesellschaft*; likely referring to a specific religious order or house</note> here that appealed to the authorities against me; and these were the very ones from whom, it seems to me, for many fair reasons, I should have hoped for more help than from anyone else. I took great care to say nothing that could have brought me into their favor. In my cause, I did only what I owed to the truth; thereafter, I took everything else upon myself for my shame and condemnation, as is my duty. It seems to me that I am here like one who is under a ban, or like the scapegoat <note>original: *Bock im alten Testament* (the goat in the Old Testament); a reference to the ritual in Leviticus 16 where a goat is sent into the wilderness bearing the sins of the community</note> driven into the wilderness because of my abominable sins: it seems that **God** wills that I should do penance for them, not only through suffering alone, but through such sufferings as also carry shame with them. I tell you this only to provide information about it, but I will not dwell on it any longer; for my only intention is to love **God** and to condemn myself.”

13. Among so many letters that he wrote, there is not a single one in which a mark of his humility is not to be found. He also humbled himself in the same way in his speech and interaction. For although it was his intention to speak neither good nor evil of himself, the low opinion he held of himself made this almost impossible. It is indeed the truth that one can also speak evil of oneself out of pride, namely, so that one may be seen as humble: but no proud person will speak evil of himself in such a way as this man of **God** did, for it could be clearly seen that what he spoke came from the bottom of his heart and his true opinion. Yes, what is even more wonderful, various people have experienced and testified that his self-humiliations were paired with such grace that those who heard him were led into that same spirit of humility and smallness by his words.

2. Whenever he entered a church, he placed himself among the tradesmen and common people so that he might not be recognized; among whom he was often pushed and squeezed or otherwise inconvenienced, which he bore with joy.

3. During the time of the war in Paris <note>This likely refers to the Fronde (1648–1653), a period of civil war in France that caused great suffering in the city.</note>, he went out himself and bought bread for the poor, carrying it to them across the streets himself, as much as he was able to carry.

4. In a certain monastery which he visited frequently, they asked him that, if he wished to show them the kindness of visiting, he might take a carriage because of the great distance; but he replied with a certain politeness, "he did not like to use a carriage because it smacked a little of his 'Monsieur' status <note>The term "Monsieur" here refers to the social affectations and pride of a gentleman of the upper class</note>; one must strive to make oneself very small in all things." And so he always walked the long way on foot, all alone, and sometimes in wet weather and late in the evening; and when they told him they were concerned about his hardship, he said, "our Savior humbled himself much differently and took much greater trouble and labor upon himself for souls; He was his Master (Patron) and model."

5. But see here another fruit of his humility, of which he wrote the following to his guide on December 20, 1646. I did not expect such a thing at all. I sent word to her that I would do myself the honor of visiting her to offer my thanks that the Lord Chancellor deigned to remember me; that I honored everything that bore the mark of the King and came on his behalf far too much to not receive it with all respect. However, I wished to most humbly ask her one thing: that since I now lead a simple and common way of life, she might allow that, although I consider myself most strongly obligated to them, such an obligation might not extend to my being forced to accept these royal letters. It was pointed out to me that in certain cases a <term>Committimus</term> (a) <note>original: *Committimus*, a Latin legal term for a writ that moves a court case to a higher jurisdiction</note> might be necessary for me, and that two thousand Livres (about six hundred and sixty-six Reichsthalers) of annual income could serve me to give even more alms. Regarding the second point, God had given me more goods...
