In this manner did he conduct himself on this occasion. Nevertheless, some time afterward, upon the advice of godly persons, he was compelled to accept this honorary position for the glory of God and the comfort of the poor.

6. He highly valued "smallness of spirit," which all true children of God must strive for and attain; so that he often said: "Let us be small, yes, quite small. Oh, what a great thing is holy smallness!" In this spirit, he loved everything lowly and fled everything that had any outward splendor, in whatever form it might be, wherein, as he well knew, human nature so secretly seeks its own interest, even in spiritual and holiest things. For this reason, he also avoided everything extraordinary. Even in his spiritual discourses, he took care not to use any exalted, magnificent, or unusual words; he desired that neither in his actions nor in his speeches should anything have the appearance of highness or singularity.

7. Among all the marks of his humility, however, not the least was his humble conduct toward his spiritual guide <term>Seelen-Führer: a spiritual director or mentor who provided guidance on religious life and personal conduct</term>. He undertook nothing of importance concerning his own person without his advice. He presented matters to him, either orally or in writing, clearly and orderly, and desired his report, will, and blessing over his "resolution" (these were his expressions) with such great humility, dependence, and submission of his own opinion that it was to be admired. He followed the guide's judgment exactly and without any second-guessing; even though he himself (as is well known) possessed an excellent and very enlightened...

8. And this virtue of submission, this true follower of *Jesus Christ* had again learned from his Divine Master and Pattern; as he once revealed to a confidant in the following manner:

> “It is true, I received a great grace this morning as I meditated upon the subjection and dependence of the Son of *God* upon his foster-father Joseph, to whom he wished to submit himself in all things, as a child to his father. What an exaltation and grace this was for this Saint! But what a virtue and what an annihilation <note>original: "Vernichtigung" — in 17th-century mystical theology, this refers to the 'emptying' of the self or the ego to allow God to work through the person</note> it was in the *Lord Jesus Christ*! The Son of *God*, who is equal to his Father, is subject to a creature, and submissive to a poor carpenter, just as if he did not sufficiently know how he ought to live and walk. It was shown to me how we, through this example of the Son of *God*, are instructed in such an emphatic way—one so befitting this Master—how creatures must be dependent upon *God*, and how we are thereby bound in the most obligatory way to submit ourselves to the high power he has over us, and also to the government of other men; so much so, that our heart will find no rest except in this submission, in union with that which *Jesus Christ* practiced toward a creature. Oh, how deep is this mystery, and how greatly I am moved by it!”

Thereupon he paused a little in his speaking, as if completely taken by the greatness of this grace. When the person with whom he spoke said they felt some sharing of this grace, he threw himself upon his knees, and they worshipped *Jesus Christ* together in this state of dependence and submission, and offered themselves to Him to follow Him.

# Chapter Eight.
## Concerning his Patience and Love for Suffering.

-> I. <-

A humble man is also, without doubt, patient; because he always deems himself worthy of whatever he suffers. Just as we have considered the humility of the dear Renty in the previous chapter, so we will now hear the testimonies of his patience. Those who were with him for a long time, and associated with him, and diligently observed his actions, testify that they never heard him complain about anything, whatever it might be—neither about illness, nor loss, nor any other occasion in which he had to suffer. Rather, they always perceived in him an immovable constancy and invincible patience, which sometimes even reached the point of joy, together with such a great and wonderful equanimity <note>original: "Gleichmüthigkeit" — a calm, even-tempered soul</note> that on such occasions he did not speak a single word more heatedly than any other, nor were any gestures to be seen in him from which one could have perceived an indignation or agitation of his mind.

2. Once, as he was traveling to Dijon with his wife, he was overtaken by a very severe cold; <note>original: "Schnupfen" — here implying a heavy catarrh or respiratory infection</note> at the same time, his limbs became completely paralyzed. At his lodgings, he had to be put to bed; he walked quite bent and had to use a cane. Throughout the entire journey, he endured extraordinary pains without saying a word or complaining. At times he became as pale as a linen cloth, and then again completely flushed. And although people said to him that he must be suffering a great deal, he remained silent on the matter and spoke only with very poignant expressions of the great and unspeakable sufferings of Jesus Christ, and of the grace that God shows to a soul by allowing it to suffer something for His sake. "of my weakness. I surrender myself only to **God**, to all that He might desire of me, from the highest heaven to the lowest hell. At His command I will everything; with Him I can do everything; and that which He commands is always accompanied by His grace."

9. To another person he writes: "Suffering is a great grace. Generally, one is deceived in thinking that this grace is so very common; it is, rather, very rare. It is indeed true that many people suffer; but very few suffer in the disposition <term>disposition: the inner state of heart and mind (German: *Gemüths-Gestalt*)</term> in which **Jesus Christ** suffered. Very few suffer with a perfect consent to everything **God** does with them; very few suffer without some unrest, and without too great an attention of their mind upon the suffering; very few are they who leave all future events and the outcome of the suffering to **God**, without making reflections upon it, in order to occupy themselves entirely and alone with His praise, and to give Him room—through our quiet consent and submission—to take upon us every right He has over us.

10. At another time he wrote the following to a distressed person: "**God**, who knows our misery, takes away from us, for our own good, the cause of our evil—for example, one of our relatives, a child, or a husband—so that He may draw us to Himself through another evil, namely tribulation, and that He may give us to recognize that all attachments <note>original: "Anklebungen"—refers to emotional or spiritual attachments to worldly things that hinder spiritual growth</note>, whatever they may be, which distance us from Him, are such significant obstacles that we shall once more have to confess before all creatures <note>In 17th-century spiritual writing, "creatures" refers to any created thing or person, as opposed to the Creator.</note> that the greatest mercy He ever showed us was precisely this: that He freed us from such things. This is a wormwood <note>Wormwood is a proverbially bitter herb used in medicine; Renty uses it as a metaphor for a "bitter pill" that heals the soul.</note> which is bitter only to the senses and the mouth, but healthy to the heart. It kills the Adam <note>Referring to the "Old Adam," the sinful or fallen nature of humanity that must "die" for the spiritual self to grow.</note>, so that he may make **Jesus Christ** live. It is like a very cold winter, which is the means of preserving the beauty of the other seasons. However, one must take great care that we do not accept that which is given to us by grace as an accidental thing, or as a misfortune; for in that way we would turn the medicine into poison, and receive grace only to drive it away again.

11. "Let us enter into the holy and adorable disposition in which **Jesus Christ** always remained, when He willingly suffered for the glory of His Father and for our salvation. Is it not strange? People see well enough that the way **Jesus Christ** trod to reach glory was shame, pain, and the Cross; and yet those who call themselves His disciples and followers nonetheless desire and expect a different way for themselves? Is the disciple above his Master? And when it pleased the Head to go through such a way, what follows from that for the members? <note>Renty uses the common theological metaphor of Christ as the "Head" and his followers as the "members" of his body.</note> Must they not follow Him? Let us then walk after Him, and suffer according to His example. Blessed be sickness! Blessed be the loss of honor, of goods, and of relatives, and the separation from all creatures which kept us bent down toward the earth, whereas through loss and separation we are set upright again,"

<summary>The Marquis de Renty explains through letters that true spiritual suffering requires total submission to God's will without focusing on the pain itself. He describes earthly losses as a "bitter medicine" that kills the "Old Adam" and allows the life of Christ to flourish within a person.</summary>

# Chapter Nine.

### Concerning his love and readiness to serve his neighbor; and especially the poor, prisoners, and the sick.

->I.<-

Just as this holy soul, in all things and at all times, kept the most holy example and teaching of the Savior in view, and held himself united with Him, so it could not be otherwise: this same soul had to shine forth especially in the love and service of his neighbor <note>original: "Nächsten"—referring to the biblical "neighbor" as defined in the Commandment to love one's neighbor as oneself</note>; since the heart of **Jesus**, and His entire way of life, could so powerfully incite and urge him toward such love and services of charity.

2. "I have," (he writes to someone), "so great a vision of the goodness, of the love, and of all kinds of effects of love from the most holy soul of our Lord **Jesus**, that this inner being, which is pure friendliness, kindness, and love, reveals to me quite differently than ever before how we must also live in this Divine love toward mankind, and how in this love the entire law is truly and perfectly fulfilled."

3. And further he says: "Ah, how very good is the wilderness <note>original: "Wüste"—likely a reference to the desert where Jesus fasted, symbolizing a place of spiritual preparation</note>, when we are led into it by the Spirit of **God** after baptism with the Savior! From there the Savior goes forth to dwell among men, to instruct them, and to work for their salvation. Since we then make up one single **Jesus Christ** with Him—as we have the honor to be His members—we must lead His life, adopt His mind, and walk in His footsteps." In this, then, did this perfect disciple of **Jesus** diligently strive with all his might, in the wonderful love he bore for his neighbor, as we shall now recount more circumstantially.

4. First and foremost, one can say this of Mr. Renty in general and with truth: that neither in Paris, nor far around it, was there a single important and public work of charity to be found in which he did not have a very large part. There was no plan concerning the honor of **God** and the benefit of the neighbor of which he was not either the author, the promoter, the executor, or all of these together. He was, so to speak, the soul and the mover of all sorts of godly gatherings. He maintained correspondence throughout the entire kingdom regarding all works of charity to be performed therein. From all places he received

5. He loved everyone without distinction, as those created in the image of **God** and purchased by the blood of **Jesus**; he taught them, gave them good counsel, established peace, and helped them in every way, regarding both body and soul. His thoughts, his desires, his words, his works, and everything in him was love for his neighbor, such that he himself once said to a confidant: "It seems to me my soul is entirely love." And so that he might impress the qualities of this Divine love even deeper into his innermost self and observe them more precisely, he had—besides the New Testament, which he always carried with him—also specifically written down the following words of Paul and carried them with him: 

> (a) Love is long-suffering, it is kind; love is not envious; love is not reckless <note>original: "verwegen"—suggesting acting without due caution or humility</note>; it is not puffed up; it is not ambitious; it does not seek its own; it is not easily provoked; it thinks no evil; it does not rejoice in iniquity; but it rejoices with the truth; it bears all things; it believes all things, it hopes all things; it endures all things.

6. From the year 1641 onwards, he fed several poor people at his table one or two days a week, which he arranged in the following manner: He went in the morning to the St. Anthony’s Gate <note>original: "Antonius Pforte"—The Porte Saint-Antoine, a historic gateway in Paris where the displaced and poor often entered the city</note> in Paris and took home those he found first, after having greeted them most kindly. If it was winter, they first had to warm themselves, and always sit down. Then, with a heartfelt affection shining from his face and all his actions, and with wonderful skill, he began to instruct them in the mysteries of faith and a pious life. After this instruction, he gave them water to wash themselves and let them sit at the table, where he then served them himself with all respect, having his children carry the food to them. During the meal, everyone had to remain silent so that the poor could eat more freely and undisturbed. After the meal, he gave them a physical alms, along with good instruction, and then accompanied them back with all courtesy. This custom he maintained until his death.

7. He was a constant provider for all the poor in all of Paris, and far around, in every possible way. He sought to learn what they needed; he devised means to come to their aid, and where he could not do everything alone, he also made use of others for that purpose: he prayed for them; he himself bought what was necessary for them and then brought it to them. He sought out good service <note>referring to employment as domestic servants</note> for young people of both sexes, and even for children, where they had none; and when he could not manage to do so immediately, he sometimes kept some in his house for a considerable time until he had found a good opportunity for them.

### Third Part. The Life
<meta>catchword: has.</meta>

8. And what is more, when this wise man visited the poor and had seen their destitution in general, he also investigated with all wisdom their needs piece by piece, both in spiritual and bodily matters. He sought at once to perceive what inclinations, passions <note>in this context, "passions" refers to uncontrolled emotions or desires that were believed to lead to sin</note>, bad habits, reigning sins, etc., they had; so that according to the nature of their evil he could come to their aid, always exhorting them to live Christian lives and to make good use of their poverty.

9. Regarding temporal <note>meaning "worldly" or "material" as opposed to spiritual</note> matters, he searched out what each person was capable of, whether he knew a craft or some other trade. If they were craftsmen, he saw what tools they lacked, or what materials they needed to make their goods; and these he provided for them, and also saw to it that their wives and children had work. Then he gave them sustenance for two or three more days; he was also helpful in selling their goods. He even bought some from them himself and gave it away again to others as alms. He exhorted them to diligent work and visited them again from time to time to see if everything was still going well in the house.

10. Once he went with a good friend in Paris to a poor man in a cellar who made carrying-baskets and bread-baskets from willow <note>original: "Weyden"</note> and earned his bread thereby; there he himself, in the presence of this friend, finished a carrying-basket which he had begun several days before, with the intention of teaching the same to the poor in the countryside so that they could have their livelihood from it. He then left the basket to this man and gave him money for having shown it to him.

11. He especially visited and comforted the poor prisoners, gave them alms, and promoted their release when he could judge that it would be beneficial for them; for he said: Sometimes one helps such people out of prison who afterwards abuse their freedom to offend **God** and plunge themselves into damnation.

12. Toward the sick poor, however, his love and care were doubled. He was sometimes simultaneously, and in the very same visit, their benefactor, their physician, their pharmacist, their surgeon <note>original: "Wund-Arzt"—literally "wound-doctor"</note>, their preacher, their father, their brother, friend, and servant, as he came to their aid in all kinds of ways. In the year 1641, he learned bloodletting <note>a common medical practice of the time involving the withdrawal of blood to balance the body's "humors"</note> and other surgical actions and arts; he had himself instructed in the most eminent parts of medicine; thereafter, when he went through the city or across the country, he always carried some medicines for the most common diseases with him, as well as a box for his surgical instruments to let blood or perhaps to cut open a swelling, which he did with a wonderful skill and certainty, although, according to his extraordinary wisdom, he would undertake nothing that exceeded his knowledge.

13. He also taught others, who perhaps waited upon the sick in the monasteries, various excellent medicines which had been found to be of great power and virtue <note>original: "Tugend"—in historical medical texts, this refers to the inherent medicinal efficacy or "potency" of a remedy</note>

### Of the Marquis de Renty. Chapter IX.

has. He prepared them <note>referring to the meals for the poor mentioned on the previous page</note> himself, put them on the fire to cook them, just as some kitchen boy might have done. Indeed, he sometimes remained by a large fire with his face over the vessel, in all the smoke and foul odor, so that he became quite wet with sweat, without showing any sign of his discomfort by a single gesture; and where others wished to come to his aid, he knew how to refuse this quite skillfully and unnoticed.

14. When he visited the poor sick, he omitted none of those services which he recognized as necessary for them. He made their beds, helped them into them, settled them comfortably, made fires for them, cleaned their vessels <note>this likely refers to cleaning chamber pots or cooking basins</note>, put their meager household goods in order, and so on; all of which he did to gain an entrance into the hearts of these poor people, so that he might afterward, with so much more blessing, exhort them to patience and godliness.

15. In Dijon (which city was a true theater for his virtues during the several months he stayed there), he was seen one day with a flint in his hand at a house door, trying to get a little fire to warm a poor sick man who lay there abandoned. Since he had asked to be shown the poor sick in this city once or twice, he thereafter often went there alone, visited them, and came to their aid in all kinds of ways, both by night and by day.

16. Once in the year 1640, as he went out to visit several poor people in the city of Paris, he found a sister of a religious order who cared for the sick in the parish <note>original: "Parochie [oder Gemeine]"</note> of St. Paul, just as she was leaving a certain house, and he asked her what she sought in that house? She gave the answer that she sought the Lord Jesus therein, and that she came from a chamber where great love was to be shown. Mr. Renty was quite moved and gladdened by such an answer, and said that he also sought the Savior; and so they both went back into the chamber where various sick people lay. It was found, however, that he had already visited them that same day, made them a soup, and also straightened their beds. From there, this daughter <note>a term for a nun or sister of a charitable order</note> led him to various other places, where he instructed the sick and gave them alms. Since that time, he kept the custom of visiting the sick in this area once a week, to perform <term>bloodletting</term> <note>original: "zur Ader zu laſſen" — a standard medical practice of the 17th century intended to balance the body's fluids</note>, and to give medicines and alms, and no less to comfort them spiritually, to strengthen them, and to instruct them in godliness. When he was in Dijon, they sought him out in crowds and desired his help in all sorts of weaknesses and illnesses. In the year 1642, when he was on his estates in Normandy, he spent about four months (as long as he stayed there) incessantly in such works of mercy, in such a way that they came to him from all regions to seek help in their misery

### Part Three. The Life

8. And what is more, when this wise man visited the poor and saw their general needs, he also investigated their poverty piece by piece with all wisdom, both in spiritual and physical matters. He sought at once to perceive what inclinations, passions, evil habits, or ruling sins they possessed, so that he could come to their aid according to the nature of their misfortune—always exhorting them to live Christian lives and to make good use of their poverty <note>In the 17th-century context, "making good use of poverty" meant accepting it with patience and spiritual humility as a path to God</note>.

9. In regard to temporal matters, he researched what each person was skilled at, whether they knew a craft or some other trade. If they were craftsmen, he saw to it what tools they lacked or what materials they needed to make their goods; these he provided for them, and he also ensured that their wives and children had work. Then he gave them support for two or three days and assisted them in selling their wares. He even bought some from them himself and then gave them away again as alms. He exhorted them to diligent work and visited them again every now and then to see if everything was still going well in the household.

10. Once, he went with a good friend in Paris to a poor man in a cellar who made carrying-baskets and bread-baskets from willow and earned his bread thereby. There, in the presence of this friend, he himself finished a carrying-basket which he had begun several days before, with the intention of teaching this skill to the poor in the countryside so that they might have a livelihood from it. He then left the basket with the man and gave him money for having shown him how to do it.

11. ### Third Part. The Life of the Marquis, etc.

...to have; and there was almost always such a large number around him that one could not approach him: so that it went for this faithful servant-slave of Jesus just like his Master, of whom the Evangelists say, that they brought to him from all places those afflicted with all kinds of diseases and plagues, all of whom he made healthy.

18. When this man of God was at his Castle of Béni <note>Béni-sur-Orne, the family estate in Normandy</note>, he took in such poor people who were piteously afflicted with the itch <term>Kräze: scabies, a contagious skin condition then associated with poverty and poor hygiene</term>, placed them in a well-prepared and decorated chamber, gave them medicines, visited them, and tended to them with his own hands until they were healthy again. As I once went into the hall at Béni (says a credible witness), he had one under his hands who had an evil cancer, which one could not even look upon from afar without disgust and horror; but he suppressed all such natural feelings and tended to him with joy and reverence.

19. In Lower Normandy, people were most greatly astonished, as he was so occupied with his patients, that he gave medicines for all kinds of things, even unusual and incurable diseases, and that through these medicines, which sometimes amounted to almost nothing, the sick suddenly became healthy; therefore some believed he must heal diseases not so much through his medicines, but rather through a supernatural way. To the Mother Superior of the Carmelites, who was very well known and intimate with him, he once told that a few days prior a certain woman in childbed <note>a woman recovering from childbirth</note> had lain sick unto death: since she had been completely abandoned by the physician <term>Medico: a doctor or medical professional</term>, they had sought him out to see if he could provide some relief with his medicines in this extreme need: and I made her one, he said, of which I well knew that it had no power to heal such a disease; but what was to be done? I had nothing better. I asked God that He might give His blessing thereto, if it might be for His glorification and for the best of the patient; which He also did: for when I went to visit her, she found herself well again. The Superior asked him if he often did it thus? He answered: Yes, when I am requested to do so; for, he added, they are poor people who have nothing to help themselves, and neither do I: the Lord is not bound to medicinal means; where we are capable of nothing, we must have faith; and that is what God has given me through His goodness. She replied: That is then a miracle-work. How, he said, does God not perform miracles for us every day? And you, she spoke, then perform miracles for the poor. Whereupon he answered in humility and quite gracefully: Dear Mother, call that a miracle-work which the Lord does; as for me, I contribute nothing to it, except only that I give the poor what I have. Take it as you will, I do not reflect upon it, except only that I thank the Lord when they recover.

# Chapter Ten.
## Concerning his Love and Zeal for the Salvation of Souls.

->I.<-

The beloved Renty recognized quite well that the worthiness of a soul far exceeded that of a mortal body; and for that reason, his love for coming to the aid of immortal souls was even greater than his devotion to providing earthly assistance to his needy neighbors. Furthermore, the love of God and of His son Jesus Christ, with which he was so greatly set aflame, caused him to employ all means and all his strength so that the Lord might be recognized and loved by many, both in time and in eternity. Finally, since God so loved the world that He gave them His only begotten Son—to whom immortal souls proved to be so dear—this disciple of Jesus also had to love them and seek their salvation with earnestness and zeal.

2. This love and earnestness of his was universal and impartial, extending over all people; so much so that he once said to a confidant, "he was entirely willing to serve all people, excluding not a single one, and, if it were necessary, to give up his life for any one of them."

He would have converted the whole world, enlightened it with the knowledge of God, set it aflame with His love, and made it holy and blessed, had it been within his power. In the great and mighty city of Paris, which is a microcosm <note>original: "kurzer Begriff," meaning a summary or representative sample of the whole world</note> of the world, he went through all parts and streets of the city and investigated everything that was either to be removed or established for the honor of God and the salvation of souls. The Spirit of God, who guided him in this investigation, blessed his work and gave him grace to bring disordered things into good order, to support the good that was wavering, and to preserve that which was in good condition; to destroy evil and to establish good. This he did in so many and various ways that it would be impossible to recount them all. But what can an earnest man not do, when he is freed from self-interest and filled with God?

3. In all places where he was able, he established godly assemblies <note>these "assemblies" were often religious societies or confraternities intended for lay spiritual growth</note> for more than one purpose. In the year 1648, he wrote the following to me, among other things: "Now I have arrived here again from Burgundy, according to God's good pleasure. Our journey was mostly spent helping to establish various societies, both of men and of women, who have a great desire to serve God uprightly."

From Caen they wrote: Monsieur Renty has arranged several assemblies here of certain persons, to whom he gave the counsel to meet every week to discuss ways and means to come to the aid of the poor and to prevent God from being offended; which has had wonderful progress and benefit.

It details his organizational efforts in Paris, Burgundy, and Caen to establish religious societies dedicated to social work and moral reform.</summary>

...and to what end God had created you? And he instructed her further in what was necessary for her, with such skill that this person not only sincerely confessed her ignorance to him—and that she had never once thought of her salvation until then—but also testified that from now on she would truly take it to heart and direct her earnest care toward it.

**13.** Once, when he was traveling back from Dijon with two of his friends who wished to accompany him for a few miles, he stopped at least three or four times on the road to catechize <note>to teach the principles of Christian faith through a series of questions and answers</note> poor travelers; and once he went out of his way to visit some laborers, so that he might likewise instruct them and provide guidance on how to sanctify <note>to make holy or dedicate to God</note> their work.

**14.** In this zeal he was courageous and untiring: he conducted his business in such a way as if he had three bodies; and indeed, he accomplished more in half an hour than others would have achieved in several days; for he was not only strong, such that he could endure all kinds of fatigues <note>original: "Fatiguen," referring to physical and mental exhaustion</note>, but he could also quickly decide and execute a matter.

**15.** However, he also possessed a very patient zeal. He endured with the greatest gentleness and steadfastness all kinds of burdens, complaints, bitterness, rejections, contempt, and mockery from the poor people he exhorted. Let us hear a few examples of this patience: One day he went to speak with a man who, out of jealousy and evil suspicion he had conceived against his wife, had treated her cruelly, even to the point of stabbing her with a knife. As he now confronted this man with his fault, the man received him very poorly, even raised his fist to strike him, spat out a heap of blasphemous words against him, and tried to drive him from the house by force. Mr. <term>Renty</term> <note>Gaston de Renty (1611–1649) was a French aristocrat who famously abandoned a life of luxury to serve the poor and sick.</note> endured all this without saying a word; afterward, he went to him, embraced him, and spoke to him with such soothing and heart-stirring expressions that the man finally came to peace. He visited him several more times afterward and saw to it that he went to confession <note>original: "beichtete"</note>—which he had not done in twelve years—brought him back to a good understanding with his wife, and from that time on, the man lived a Christian life and died a blessed death.

**16.** Another time he visited a poor and elderly sick man with whom he wished to speak, according to his custom, of what served for his salvation. This man, however, who was made irritable by old age as well as poverty and illness, instead of listening to him, became inflamed with anger against him and said that he knew more about it than Renty, and would even teach Renty himself if he would only listen. Renty said: "With all my heart"; and actually listened to him. But after he had let him speak to the end with great patience, he afterward wisely used the man's own words (however awkward and full of blindness they had been) to convince him; which succeeded so happily that from that time on, and for the remaining days of his life, the man took the salvation of his soul to heart with much care.

### Of the Marquis of Renty. Chapter X.

**17.** If some showed a far too immoderate zeal against the wicked, he would say: "Our Savior did not take away all evil from the earth while He walked upon the earth; we will also likely be compelled to leave much upon it; and God allows such things to happen at times, both for the exercise and refinement of the pious, as well as for the punishment of the ungodly."

**18.** Such patience he had to endure the faults of his neighbor; he sought to diminish them with a soothing word; he excused and covered them as much as he possibly could. Someone once confessed to him that he had practiced a certain trickery <note>original: "Schalkheit," implying a mix of malice, mischief, or deceit</note> against him; whereupon he, with great skill and humility, said nothing else but: "Yes, it is I who practice trickery; I commit trickery against my God." And thereupon he began to speak of an entirely different matter.

**19.** When he wished to punish others, he usually accused himself first; or he asked the other person to tell him his own faults as well. One day he intended to admonish someone; and to reach this goal, he began to speak of the union of minds <term>Vereinigung der Gemüther: a spiritual concept of deep, transparent friendship and mutual accountability</term>, and how one must have an open heart toward the other, and also tell each other the truth; and that, where such did not happen, one merely carried his sins within him like whitewashed tombs <note>A biblical reference to Matthew 23:27, describing outward righteousness that masks internal corruption</note>; and he would consider himself very much obliged to him if he would show him this love. The other felt that through these words his heart was opened, and he asked him that, if he saw anything in him that he needed to know, he should please tell him, which he then did.

**20.** However, Mr. Renty also knew well how to distinguish that gentle words did not serve all sinners. "Take care," he once said to one of his friends regarding an ungodly man, "that you do not humble yourself before him; such would harm him and the cause of God; speak sharply with him."

**21.** And thus, alongside his zeal, he also possessed great wisdom and caution: to some he revealed himself, but to others he did not, according as he deemed it useful for each. "Toward some," he wrote in a letter, "one must have the heart open and share the best with them; to others one must offer the mediocre, and not make oneself so very free with them; and again toward others one must keep oneself entirely closed and keep one's secret covered, because one sees in them no capacity to make a good use of it."

**22.** It is an excellent letter from which these words are drawn: therefore I cannot refrain from sharing something more of it, since the content is very fitting for the present subject: "You will allow me, honored Lady, to reveal to you the thoughts I have regarding the freedom we must use to freely communicate the gifts that God bestows upon us to those persons to whom such can bring some benefit, and not to keep that which comes from above as if stifled within ourselves; for in such a way we would [lose] the second fruit which God demands from His graces..."

## Part Three: The Life
<meta>catchword: „„Let</meta>

"...preventing them, namely, that after they have benefited us, they might also create benefit for others; and therefore He wills that we should communicate them <note>Refers to the spiritual gifts or insights mentioned in the preceding text.</note> lovingly and cautiously, so that they may be like a seed cast into good soil, bringing forth much fruit."

**23.** "I wish that we would regard ourselves in this world as a **crystal**, which, placed in the midst of this world, lets all lights shine through it that come down from above; and that through our good example, through the high esteem of **virtue**, through the disdain of **vice**, through the comforts and the interaction with people, and other **godly deeds**, we might communicate to all **creatures** the gifts we have received from **heaven**, without hypocrisy, or anything of our own, but behaving obediently toward them and letting them pass through, just as the crystal does with light."

"Furthermore, that all honor and all praise we receive from below should pass through us to **God**, without detaining it within ourselves; just as the crystal would let the lights of various torches, which might be beneath it, pass through, so that it might purify them and send them so much more brilliantly toward heaven. For in such a manner must we return the honor and praise given to us to **God**, who alone is worthy of honor and praise, and who has placed that within us for which we are praised—not so that the praise should remain in us, but that it should pass from us to Him, and He be praised and glorified."

"Further, one perceives that when nothing is placed opposite the crystal to catch the light shining through it, the light is not seen; the sun may shine from one side and the torches from the other; if you place nothing there that makes the brilliance reflect back, it is only in the crystal. In the same way, we can receive heavenly light and abundant **graces**; but if we do not approach **God** and our neighbor, to give to the one what we owe Him by right and to the other what we owe him out of love, then we will indeed have light, but only in ourselves, and as if hidden under a bushel <note>A reference to Matthew 5:15. A 'bushel' was a dry-goods measuring bowl; to hide a lamp under it was to stifle its purpose.</note>, where it is far too narrowly confined and cannot do its work, namely, to communicate itself, and might in time run the risk of being stifled and extinguished."

"Observe also that when the sun illuminates a crystal, no **body** <note>original: "Cörper"</note> is found that displays the sun's light so magnificently and communicates such great brilliance to its **rays** as the crystal; so also one sees no other light between it and the sun. But when the sun has penetrated the same crystal, it is a pure and lively brilliance that blinds one, indeed even burns, if it is so arranged <note>De Renty uses the optical properties of a crystal lens—which can focus light into a burning point—as a metaphor for the intensity of God's presence.</note>; to teach us that those things passing between **God** and us are secret matters, which must not appear until after they have passed through us."

<meta>This page continues the spiritual instructions of Gaston de Renty, specifically concluding his famous metaphor of the soul as a crystal. It then transitions into a biographical account of how he balanced his intense public service with his private spiritual life.</meta>

### of the Marquis of Renty. Chapter X.

"Let us therefore allow ourselves to be permeated by the graces of God, so that we may afterwards, with the radiance that proceeds from them, enlighten, warm, and ignite everything we can reach. Let us follow the example of this beautiful crystal, which is of a dense matter and allows itself to be permeated only by light: so let us also allow nothing to permeate us except that which comes from God, and that which returns again to God; and let us see to it that we do not give in to our senses (as happens only too often) and inordinately desire the things of the earth, which is the same as if we threw filth upon this crystal, which, though it is beautiful in itself, is yet no longer capable of the light because of the foulness with which it is surrounded."

"Let us therefore sacrifice ourselves to the Savior, so that we do not fail to use well the graces He communicates to us, neither for ourselves nor for others, and do not bury our talent <note>A reference to the Biblical Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30), where a servant is rebuked for burying his money rather than investing it.</note>. etc."

**24.** In a good zeal, this prudence is especially necessary: that one overloads neither the body nor the mind with too many or too difficult tasks, whereby inner devotion could be stifled; and that through care for the salvation of other people, one does not neglect one's own. In both respects, this zealous man was cautious. Concerning the first, he once wrote the following to a good priest, on the occasion of an illness that had befallen him due to excessively hard work in the service of his neighbor: "Allow me to tell you quite simply that, among other things, this is my greatest concern for you: that you might perhaps take too much upon yourself and make yourself useless because you give yourself away too much. The enemy sometimes, and commonly, knows how to gain his advantage in this way even in the best souls. You are no longer your own, but a man for everyone, and one who, with Paul, is a debtor to all men. Spare yourself then; not that you spare yourself entirely, but that you do not overload yourself with work and <term>fatigues</term> <note>original: *Fatiguen*; here referring to the physical and mental exhaustion resulting from over-exertion in spiritual duties</note>. I hear that God gives you much blessing; since I now take part in it, receive this reminder in love."

**25.** Concerning the observation of his soul's sanctification, he watched over it quite closely. He might have as much to do for his neighbor as he ever wished, yet he nevertheless strictly observed his devotional exercises. He spent much time, both by day and by night, in prayer and in communion with God; indeed, when he walked here and there through the streets during the day, he often <term>withdrew</term> <note>original: *retirirte*; from the French *se retirer*, meaning to seek solitude or a quiet place for reflection</note> into a church and remained there for entire hours in prayer. In this, he was (especially in the later years when he had the most business) incessantly in devotion to God, so that neither business nor external distractions hindered him any longer. Concerning which a certain close acquaintance once asked him whether, amidst a multitude of such occupations, he also always regularly kept his two usual hours of prayer? To which he gave the answer: "When I can, I keep three of them, yes, even four or five; but if an opportunity arises to serve my neighbor, I leave them without concern..."

# The Eleventh Chapter.

## Of the Fruit of His Zeal; Primarily in the Guidance of Some Chosen Souls in the Inner Way. His Great Light, Which He Possessed Therein.

->I.<-

God had placed such a powerful grace in this His servant that not only his works and his words, but even his mere presence, moved and edified others. Once, during Shrove Tuesday <note>The German "Fastnacht" refers to the Carnival season of feasting and revelry preceding the fast of Lent.</note> in Paris, while he was in the house of a needy person to perform his usual works of charity, he heard a great tumult of people singing and dancing in the house next door. He left his poor charge alone for a while, went there, and looked at these people, who were so taken aback by his mere presence that they immediately stopped their singing and dancing. Thereupon, he spoke to them against such a disorderly and wild life—which was especially prevalent in those days—with such great earnestness that they all began to weep; and several of these fellows went and confessed their sins.

2. At another time, when he went to visit a poor girl who had been seduced by a young man and left pregnant in the greatest poverty, he found her sunk in such deep melancholy that she was determined to do herself harm. However, he spoke to her, and God gave his words such grace and power that he raised up her dejected spirit and brought her to a state of peace. Afterward, he went to the young man, who at first treated him poorly and despised everything he said; but after Renty had repeatedly set before his eyes the danger to his soul and threatened him with the justice of God, he finally moved him so that he began to weep. The young man offered to do everything Renty told him; and so, through Renty's reminders, he was brought to a truly repentant mind, married the aforementioned girl, and they lived well together from then on.

3. Once, when he was in Pontoise with some good friends and they had searched for him in vain here and there for the midday meal, he was finally found in the prison, sitting at the table with the prisoners for whom he had ordered a meal to be prepared. He spoke with them very lovingly, comforted them, and exhorted them to a better life. He had his eye particularly on one among them who had been a very stubborn sinner for a long time, and who, even in prison, where to him

4. Behold the blessing with which Renty’s dedication to the service of his neighbor was accompanied. And this blessing—to touch hearts—accompanied him almost everywhere: which is not surprising, for he was an instrument united and joined with the **Lord** of hearts and the Savior of souls, seeking solely the glory of **God** and the salvation of his neighbor, sparing himself in nothing that was required for that purpose. For this reason, he had the habit, before dealing with anyone, of first surrendering himself to the Savior (as he expressed it), so that he might speak in His spirit and power. Since this Savior, who already seeks the salvation of men so fervently, found him so capable and fit in His hand, He made use of him to carry out great things, and granted him mighty graces to perform such wonders. These should rightly serve as a lesson and a cause for shame to those whose office it is to promote the salvation of men, yet who, through their own fault, achieve so little benefit in it.

<margin>Thus he traveled, for example</margin>
5. Sometimes he felt a special prompting to go here or there. Thus he was, for example, once powerfully urged to go to Pontoise <note>A town on the outskirts of Paris.</note>, although he knew no reason why, and he also had much to do in Paris that might have held him back. Yet, as he blindly followed this inspiration and went there, he found a very distinguished gentleman from a far-distant province, whom **God** had led there for the purpose of hearing from the mouth of our Renty how he might work out his salvation and attain the perfect service of **God**—something which that gentleman had neglected poorly until that time. Mr. Renty then instructed him in this, and said, when he returned to Paris, that he did not know how this gentleman had disappeared afterward.

6. [Now, although this faithful servant of **God**, as we have heard, had a great grace for helping and edifying all people, he had an even greater grace for advising and assisting certain chosen souls on the narrow path of perfection. We shall see an example of this in the following biography of Elisabeth of the Infant **Jesus** (a); we will therefore only mention a little of it here, so that room remains for other matters.]

7. A certain Countess of Châtre, who was very entangled in the love of the world and vanity, but was afterward drawn by **God** and reached a high degree of virtue and godliness through a rough path, and a few years later...

died; she was so touched and guided by the counsel and service of our *Renty* that he himself was amazed at her progress. She soon achieved a great **detachment** <note>The German word "Abgeschiedenheit" refers to a state of spiritual stillness and separation from worldly desires, a key concept in 17th-century mysticism.</note> from all the small comforts which people of such rank (especially when they are of such a delicate **disposition** <note>Original: "Complexion." On her part, she received and practiced everything he said with the greatest reverence, believing that the **Lord** himself had spoken to her through his mouth. And she had sufficient reason for this: for she sincerely testified that once, when she was in great distress and suffering of mind and heard him speak, she did not see *Mr. Renty*, but the Lord *Jesus* in him, with a great light and radiance, who spoke to her: "Do what my servant will tell you." 
By these words, she was instantly delivered from all her pain and remained filled with **God** and with a sweet peace, which was accompanied by a living sorrow for her sins and a true contempt for the world and for herself.

11. His experience in the ways of **GOD** then led people from all sides to seek his advice on such internal matters. And however reluctant he was, out of humility, to undertake these duties, **GOD** nevertheless sufficiently showed, through the wonderful blessing that followed, that this work of His servant was also according to His good pleasure.

## Chapter Twelve.
### Of his outward nature, interaction with people, and conduct in business affairs.

->I.<-

Of the nature of his outward conduct and interaction with others, we wish to cite a few witnesses one after another. “I was immensely pleased in Mr. Renty,” (says one,) “by his great recollectedness <term>Recollectedness: "Eingekehrtheit," a spiritual state of being focused inward on the presence of God even while engaged in worldly duties.</term> and his intimate union with **GOD**, which was accompanied by a deep peace and wonderful stillness of the soul that shone forth from his face, which one could not look upon without being moved to devotion. This union with **GOD** was, it seemed to me, unceasing; and he never appeared to be distracted. He also never did anything lightheartedly; nor did he say a word that was not necessary. The politeness <gloss>complaisance</gloss> that he showed in company did not cause him to pour himself out into external things; he remained directed with his devotion toward **GOD** in his interior, and stayed united with Him, regardless of the outward circumstances, without any regard for the opinions of men. Not as if he were not very courteous; but one noticed well that he paid more attention to what was happening within than to everything else.”

# Of the Marquis de Renty. Chapter XII.

2. This perpetual presence of **GOD**, (says another,) kept him so deeply occupied in his inner self that he never poured himself out into external matters, regardless of what might happen outwardly, no matter how strange or extraordinary it might seem to him. Never have I seen him admire anything of all that the world considers high and admirable; nor did he ever direct his eyes, even for a short while, toward anything out of curiosity <note>The original German "Fürwitz" implies a meddlesome or idle curiosity that distracts the soul from God.</note>. He walked the streets recollected <note>The term "eingesammlet" (recollected) refers to a state of inner focus where the soul stays gathered in God's presence despite external movement.</note> and modest, with a steady pace, without looking here and there; for **JESUS CHRIST** was so entirely his occupation and his All in all things, that except for Him, and except for that which concerned His honor, nothing moved him or hindered his devotion.

3. When he visited others, or received visitors, or when he otherwise found himself in a devout assembly wherein he had to speak, he spoke in his turn with a constantly devout spirit and a composed manner, using short but powerful expressions. Never was he seen to be hasty, neither to speak nor while speaking; nor was he heard to speak with a more vehement voice, regardless of how great a hurry he was in. If he happened to give information about a matter, or recounted something that had occurred, he did it briefly, without adding a single word that was not necessary; so much so, that someone said of him that one would hardly find a man who spoke better, and at the same time less, than he did.

4. In social interaction, he never spoke of vain, useless things, or of the latest news; but always of good things that concerned the Kingdom of **GOD**, following the example of the Savior; and when he saw that people were drifting into worldly or worthless topics, he took his leave of the company, or went away quietly without saying a word.

5. Even of good things he spoke moderately, and said that one must speak of **GOD** and Divine things with deliberation; for this reason, he could hardly endure it when pious people would sometimes talk with much circumlocution and without fruit for hours about godliness, only to return home afterward with an empty, dry, and distracted spirit.

6. All these, and many other excellent qualities, made his interaction with his neighbor very fruitful and useful; so that through his modesty, through his reputation, through his speaking, through his silence, and through his composed outward manner, a balm of devotion and virtue was, as it were, poured out into the spirits of others in every place he went. Moreover, through his humility, modesty, yielding nature, kindness, love, patience, and other virtues, he won the hearts of all those who knew him.

7. [But since there is certainly great danger in being so highly esteemed and praised by everyone, **GOD** ordained that he was slandered, condemned, and despised in an entirely unexpected and sensitive way, from the very side where he might have expected the most respect and approval—namely, from his own mother—so that his virtue would be kept safe by a useful counterweight; however, space in this extract will not permit speaking of this in particular.]

### Third Part: The Life

8. It is undeniable that Mr. **Renty** <note>The OCR spells the name "Rency," but historical records confirm this refers to Gaston de Renty (1611–1649), a French nobleman and mystic.</note>, concerning those things that aim at the service of **GOD**, had as many occupations as any single person in all of Paris, indeed, in all of France, could have. He had almost infinite such affairs. To this end, **GOD** had given him great strength, both of body and of spirit, along with a high skill in undertaking and carrying out matters, such that he—without rushing or being anxious, and without losing a moment of time—did this or that thing, then another soon after, and sometimes several at once, with a calm mind and steady, quiet attention. It was observed that he would often do three things at once without becoming unsettled or making a mistake. It was seen that he was pressed by various affairs that took him by surprise and had to be put into action immediately; and that at the same time, he read letters, gave audience to those who visited him, and gave clear and orderly answers to various persons on various matters.

9. In one of his letters he says himself: 
> "It is true, business comes running at me from 
> "all sides; I must read, I must write, I must work; 
> "a small <term>Second</term> <gloss>assistant or helper</gloss> would still find enough work to do, 
> "though I already take several to help: but do not worry about it; 
> "I do as much of it as I can right away, and the rest in its own time, without 
> "rushing. Our **LORD** does me the grace that He 
> "communicates His peace to me in all of this, and that I remain unconfused therein."

10. But see what order he maintained in his affairs. He weighed and considered a matter much before reaching a conclusion, yet without remaining so stiffly set in his own mind that he did not easily step back from it when he saw that another’s reasons were better than his own. Once the matter was decided, he showed himself ready, firm, and constant in carrying it out, and did not desist until he had brought it to an end. However, it sometimes happened that when he saw a matter was sufficiently established or already on its course, he would leave it to one of his friends who was capable of bringing it to completion; not because of any inconstancy of his mind, but so that he could begin another.

11. No matter how many and important his affairs were, he did not neglect his inner life because of them, as we have already touched upon above. His modesty and <term>recollection</term> <gloss>original German: "Eingezogenheit," referring to a state of being "drawn inward" or withdrawn from worldly distractions</gloss> showed very clearly that he was always devoutly attentive to his inner self and united with **GOD**, from whom he drew both light and strength to act, and to act all the more and all the better. 
> "I am," (he wrote once to his guide,) "now no less occupied with my <term>recollection</term> <gloss>original German: "Einsammlung," the practice of gathering the soul's faculties inward to focus on the presence of God</gloss>, but rather even more; I would well desire to do everything, and I work with a clear [insight and] manner in which I have no part, for it is our **LORD** who does everything."

### Of the Marquis of Renty. Chapter XII.

12. And another time he wrote to him <note>likely his spiritual director or "leader" mentioned later</note>: “When I must write or speak to those who desire information in this or that matter, it seems as though I possessed all knowledge; and I feel that I am ushered into everything I speak; but afterwards it is again cleared from the understanding, all gates are closed, and nothing more remains of it.”

13. And just as he well knew that the cause of **GOD** often finds the greatest opposition and contradiction, so he was patient in his affairs, and suffered with constant hope, without losing heart for the sake of any difficulty. If a good cause was entirely prevented, he nonetheless remained at peace after he had done his best in the matter. See what thoughts he had on such occasions: “We may well have a good and holy intention, which **GOD** Himself gives us: nonetheless, when He allows it to turn out quite differently than we wished, we must adore His hidden ways, which show us more mercy when they bring our intentions to nothing than when they succeed to our satisfaction. We must always fear that our own will does not fix itself upon any matter.”

14. In all his undertakings he was dependent on **God** and His providence, without over-thinking matters much in advance through his own reason. A close acquaintance once asked him whether he would do a certain thing at such and such a time; to which he replied: “Do you not know that I have no tomorrow?” Another time he said to the same person: “I see five or six matters which must necessarily be done; but I cannot say which among them I will do first, nor when, or how; for through the mercy of **GOD** I am entirely indifferent <note>original: "gleichgültig"; in this mystical context, it means "holy indifference" or being equally ready for any outcome God wills</note> to all.”

15. And to his leader he wrote: “At the end of September I hope to be in Paris. I shall expect your commands there, to go wherever you are staying, whenever it causes you the least inconvenience. When I am there, I will do whatever might please the **Lord** through you. I will consider nothing in advance, except only that I wish to obey Him, and follow His guidance through you, and indeed in everything, as well as it shall be in my power. I have experienced it several times, that when I thought most to do something in a place, I then accomplished nothing there; which has then taught me to walk entirely bare <note>original: "ganz bloß zu wandeln"; a term for spiritual poverty and simplicity, acting without preconceived attachments</note>. And then, when I think of it the least, and only abandon myself to **GOD**, then the most is accomplished: therefore I will let Him act, and you in Him.”

I heard the Gospel of Martha and Mary <note>Referencing Luke 10:38–42, where Martha is busy with service and Mary sits at Jesus' feet.</note>. Now, these words, *Martha, thou art troubled about many things*, had for a long time served me to withdraw myself from out-

### Third Part. The Life

"from external things, yes, even from internal, though good things, where they were not absolutely necessary—for example, visiting and instructing the poor, reading or writing something devotional, and the like. I recognized that it was useful at that time to omit these same things, so that in the **inaction of our own self** <note>original French: "dans l'inaction de nôtre propre"; a mystical term referring to the silencing of one's own ego and desires to let God act</note> I might be rightly formed and strengthened, and might arrive at the stripping away of my own will and my own liveliness, in order to await the command of **God**, and to follow the same in prudent simplicity, through the Spirit of **Jesus Christ**, who makes us alive, and truly lives in all those who give Him a hearing with reverence.

"Now, however, for three or four months that I have stayed here in **Lower Normandy**, I have been almost incessantly occupied with external things: speaking with everyone, helping the sick who came to seek me out, traveling, settling disputes, building, and so forth.

"Then it happened yesterday, as I had worked the entire morning, that I heard the aforementioned **Gospel** <note>This refers to the story of Martha and Mary in Luke 10:38–42</note>, and especially these words: *you are troubled about many things*, and an inner light came to me, and it was said to me: **'You are not troubled about many things.'** Then I recognized, and indeed in a very clear way, that all those things which one performs by **God's** decree, let them be whatever they may, do not trouble a person. And I saw, as it seems to me, clearly that Martha was not punished because she did a good work, but because she did it with [anxious] zeal. Through these words—*you are troubled about many things*—the Savior showed her that she performed her affairs with confusion and the disordered movement of her mind, even though she had a very laudable purpose as a pretext; and that the most necessary thing was to hear the **Eternal Word**. This is so that just as His humanity—whether it was acting, or preaching, or performing another work—received the movements of the **Godhead**, as He Himself said: *I do nothing of myself; what I have heard from my Father, that I speak*; so we likewise, through the **Lord Jesus**, who is this Eternal Word, should let ourselves be governed. Therefore, one must do nothing with confusion, but everything in peace and in this Spirit.

17. "At that time, I then received great support for all the lowly external services to which my duty bound me; and I found no difficulty in surrendering myself to this **sacredly disordered order** <note>original: "heiliglich unordentliche Ordnung"; Renty describes the chaotic demands of charity as a form of divine order that overrides his own planned schedule</note> in which I feel that **God** wants to have me, in order to do that which cannot happen without me. For three months now, I have likely not prayed on my knees for even three or four hours, except in church; and if one could only pray in such a manner, then I would truly have taken poor care of my duty.

"Indeed, it is certain that I have taken poor care of my duty; nonetheless, I am also not unaware that **God**, in those tasks which He gives us, well allows His presence and power to be felt, to bind the soul to Himself

Such a great opening the Lord gives to the soul, when He pleases, and as He pleases.

18. I had at that time such a sensitive impression of **GOD**, which nevertheless was so far above the senses (because this occurs in the most noble part of the soul, which is the Spirit), that one could have rolled me like a ball without me losing my **GOD** from sight. But here, everything is passing. Our Savior rolls the ball, when He sometimes wishes, in a strange way; and these various changes serve to help the soul, to accustom it to everything, and to ensure that it has nothing for itself, nor according to its own way, but everything for **GOD**, and according to His way.

19. Further, I also saw quite clearly that the soul which **GOD** uses for lowly things, and which applies itself to them with just as great faithfulness as if they were high things, and keeps to the order of **GOD** out of obedience, and to its own self-contempt, is no less pleasing to Him than the one who is occupied with glorious services. It does not depend on the works, but on the faithfulness with which one gives oneself to **GOD**, and does that which He wants to have. Who would not gladly convert a thousand worlds and lead all souls to **GOD**? Nevertheless, you shall only carry stones, or perhaps even, you shall do nothing. In patience there is much to sacrifice; but in other works, there is much pleasure. I believe, however, that it is much rarer to find a soul which is faithful in patience, and which does not want to do more than **GOD** wants of it, than such souls which are faithful in shining duties.

I know well that in everything **GOD** does all; but the sacrifice of patience and of standing still <gloss>original: "Einhaltens, cessation"; meaning a deliberate stopping or pausing of one's own activity</gloss> is far greater in such a heart which has love and zeal for **GOD’s** honor, and is therefore inclined to action, and thus needs more strength to restrain itself than to act.

20. Nothingness can serve as no nourishment; and the hunger <gloss>or the fiery desire to serve **GOD**</gloss> which would like to devour the four parts of the world, is forced to circulate <gloss>and run about</gloss> in its ever-reverberating flame <note>original: "dans son feu de réverbère"; a chemical or metallurgical term used here metaphorically to describe a desire that reflects back on itself when it finds no outward outlet</note> through I know not how many kinds of sacrifice, until it finally finds its end in this: that **GOD** is sufficient for Himself, that He has no need of us for His glorification, and that it is more honor for us that He uses us than that we should serve Him through our own efforts. For we are never so pure; we always mix something of our own <insert>from the self</insert> into it, and cause His work to lose something of its radiance, so that we are not only useless, but even harmful servants <note>A reference to Luke 17:10, "We are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty."</note>.

> 21. “I must also say one more word to you, to let you know what you must know of me, so that you may guide me aright once more: namely, that I am truly and deeply ashamed that I perform nothing for **GOD**: to such an extent that, when I consider His worthiness, His love, His gifts, and His communications through the union with **JESUS** Christ and His Spirit, I sometimes have such a strong oppression from it that it would be excessive and unbearable—since I see nothing in myself but misery, sins, and inability for anything good—were I not to quiet myself again through that which I have said of the all-sufficiency which **GOD** possesses in Himself, and that He makes of us what pleases Him, when on our part we remain obedient to Him and in <term>annihilation</term> <note>German: *Vernichtigung*. In 17th-century mysticism, this refers to "spiritual poverty" or the total surrender of the ego and self-will to allow God to act through the person.</note>.”

# The Thirteenth Chapter.
## On his devotion to the infancy of **JESUS**; and on his enlightenment in this mystery.

->I.<-

This holy man, in all his conduct and in all his devotions, as has already been noted several times, has always let his principal aim be to unite himself with our Lord **JESUS** Christ; because outside of **JESUS** Christ no salvation or blessedness is to be found, Acts 4:12 <note>Original: "Act. 4, 12." The verse states: "Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved."</note>. Among all the mysteries of the Savior, however, his devotion was drawn in a singular way to the mystery of His holy infancy, by means of the close acquaintance he gained with Sister Margaret of the Holy Sacrament, a holy Carmelite in Beaune (a), whom **GOD** kept entirely occupied in this mystery, and through this channel poured out such a great stream of grace and divine gifts into her heart, for herself and also for others.

2. That the dear Renty was led into this mystery not through a forced devotion, but through a special grace, he himself says in a letter as follows: 

> Previously I indeed had reverence for the devotion to the infancy of the Savior; but neither my station nor my spiritual foundation were found there; I placed myself into it from time to time; but it was not my primary nourishment: whereas now the holy Child **JESUS** has shown me the very great grace that He has made Himself known to me and has opened Himself. Now I find everything in the same, and in every concern I must only turn to Him.

3. After this, Renty offered himself up to this Divine Child in the following manner, which writing he sent to his guide:

### Part Three: The Life

“...life, so as not to use them except where it is necessary, and according to how they are given to us; which keeps us in great silence; and which finally brings forth a life that is dead to the world in its outward appearance, while inwardly the most holy soul of our Savior is constantly occupied with looking toward His Father, as well as with His love, with zeal for His honor, with the sacrifice of Himself, and with obedience, in order to enter into all states in total innocence, purity, and simplicity, through which He was to go according to the counsel of His Father.

6. “I saw then that, so we may behave well in all our states, as much on Mount Tabor <note>The mountain of the Transfiguration, representing spiritual peaks or moments of glory.</note> as on the Cross, to receive, preserve, and grow in grace therein, we must always begin with the childhood of our Savior, which teaches us the annihilation <term>Vernichtigung: a mystical term for the total setting aside of one's ego, will, and self-importance to be filled with God.</term> of ourselves, docility toward God, silence, and innocence, without regard for ourselves or our own benefit, but in the surrender of a child of grace—indeed, a child of the little child **JESUS**.

“This knowledge strengthened me more than ever before in my inner devotion to this mystery. In it, I felt my foundation, and in it I remained, in reverent expectation of what the following moments might require of me. For there the soul does not raise itself to anything through itself, but on the contrary, it annihilates itself and lets itself be led in a sense of smallness, and in grateful recognition in everything that happens, and in the simplicity of a pure and surrendered gaze. Oh, my Father, how guilty I shall be before God that I show so little faithfulness to His so great gifts! This causes me a very sensitive pain; He knows it.

7. “Thus, the childhood of **JESUS** is a state where one must die to everything, and where the soul, in faith, in silence, in reverence, in innocence, purity, and simplicity, expects and receives the commands of God, and lives [so to speak] from one dear day to the next, and sees, in a certain way, neither before nor behind itself, but unites itself with the holy child **JESUS**, who, annihilated in Himself, accepts all the decrees of His Father—for example, being visited by the shepherds and by the wise men, being circumcised, being carried to Jerusalem, being led to Egypt and staying there, being brought back from there, going to the Jordan, being baptized, being tempted, preaching, afterward dying on the Cross, and finally being exalted and perfected in glory. It seems to me, my dear Father, we must follow in these footsteps of **Jesus Christ**, our model, through the grace of His childhood.”

# of the Marquis de Renty. Chapter XIII.

9. Besides these profound and beautiful insights into the childhood of **JESUS** Christ, he had other beautiful insights into the three virtues of purity, innocence, and simplicity, in which the spirit of this mystery primarily consists. Renty composed a small writing about it, which began with these words:
> "I have seen my soul in a castle of peace, and upon the foundation of death, of nothingness, and of nakedness <note>original: "Blöße," referring to being spiritually stripped of all worldly attachments</note>, in order to live in Divine purity with the holy Child **JESUS**, <term>etc.</term>"
Because, however, this writing [says the author] is not easy to understand (a), we share here the explanation of it which he sent to his director.

10. > "I have seen my soul in the state [situation] of death, of nothingness, and of nakedness; that is, in purification, and empty of itself and of all created things. When the soul is suspended <note>original German: "aufgezogen," with the French "suspenduë" provided in the source</note> in a wilderness, where it no longer has a view of any thing, nor any support on anything, then (as was shown to me) **GOD** draws it high [or quite powerfully] to Himself, through the rope of pure love which He throws to it from heaven, as St. Catherine of Genoa <note>A 15th-century Italian mystic famous for her work with the sick and her writings on purgatory and divine love.</note> said; and this rope is the little child **JESUS**, in whose union we must offer our sacrifice to **GOD** in every way—that which in purity, in innocence, and in simplicity offers itself up and consumes itself for His glorification.
>
> "It has then been frequently shown to me (and this is also my foundation, as far as I can recognize it, despite all my unfaithfulness) that I must no longer act except through the guidance and governance of the Child **JESUS**; and His holy and Divine actions have been presented to me: His pure love for His Father, His sacrifice for His Father’s honor and for the eradication of sins, His submission to all His commands—which He saw clearly, which He waited for in patience, and which He carried out in their time: in the manger, in His stay in Egypt, in His hidden life, in His toil and labor even unto death. In all of this He did nothing through His own motion, but through the motion of **GOD**. It is shown to me that I must act in the very same way with this purity of spirit, for the preservation of which innocence and simplicity are given to me like two strong defensive walls to protect it.

Innocence then adapts itself to everything that I encounter, so that purity is not hindered in its effect—that is, in its focus on **God**.

13. "Simplicity is the other rampart <note>original: "Wehrmauer," literally a defensive wall or bulwark</note> of purity, and it concerns the past. It separates the soul from all duplicity and complexity, and takes away from it all sight of what one might have done or seen. In this way, the soul is enclosed as if between two ramparts, one of which protects it against the present and the future—namely, innocence; and the other—namely, simplicity—against the past.

They undoubtedly receive great gifts therein, and find there an inexpressible grace, along with a penetration and possession of the purity, innocence, and simplicity of this Divine child; just as the birth- or coronation-days of a king are the most opportune times to ask for and receive something from him."

# On his introduction into the mystery of the holy Trinity. 
# His Faith. His Hope.

->I.<-

Since we are now following the order of the experienced author of the biography of our Renty in this excerpt, and are to present more precisely the inner character of his mind and communion with **God**, we will mostly adhere to the own expressions of this inward soul, which have been poured out into the bosom of an enlightened guide <note>Referring to his spiritual director, Father Jean-Baptiste de Saint-Jure.</note> or other trusted friends; because otherwise no one can know what goes on in man, except the spirit of man that is in him. <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 2:11: "For what man knoweth the things of a man, save the spirit of man which is in him?"</note>
