### of the Marquis de Renty Chap. XIV.

[Wisdom] animated [him], he was, amidst his outward variety, at the same time unified within. Thus Renty himself said: "Nothing in the world is more secluded from the world than **GOD**; and the more the saints become saints, the more they are hidden <note>original: "retirez," French for withdrawn or secluded</note> in Him. This is what the Savior **JESUS** taught us by how He lived among men on earth, where He, despite all His visible duties, was always hidden <note>original: "retiré"</note> in devotion to **GOD** and in the bosom of His Father."

3. Several years before his death, his devotion was directed toward the adorable mystery of the most holy Trinity through a special inner pull. He wrote the following about it to his guide <note>original: "Führer," referring to his spiritual director, likely Father Jean-Baptiste Saint-Jure</note>: "All things fall away from my mind as soon as they have happened; nothing remains within but only **GOD**, through a pure faith. This faith allows me to abandon myself to the Lord **Jesus Christ**, thereby communicating to me strength and great confidence in **GOD**, the Trinity; for the operation of the three Divine Persons is shown to me there with distinction <note>In mystical theology, "distinction" refers to the ability to perceive the unique roles of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit within the unity of God.</note>. Faith shows me the love of the Father, who reconciles us through His Son; and the Father and Son, who communicate life to us through the Holy Spirit, who enables us to live in communion with **JESUS Christ**; and this works in us a wonderful union with the most holy Trinity, and at times produces indescribable effects."

4. To another trusted person, who also had great devotion to this mystery, he wrote one day "that the unique and peculiar nature of Christian grace consists in this: that it grants us to know **GOD** in Trinity, by uniting us with the Son, who enables us to act through His Spirit. To tell the truth, we are dedicated to the service of the most holy Trinity through baptism; we are consecrated for its glorification; we receive its seal and bear its mark, to make it known to all creatures that we belong to the Trinity.

5. "Let us dissolve in thanksgiving, and strengthen ourselves in the power of faith, so that we may be perfected through **Jesus Christ** in this adorable mystery. There are infinite things to say about what our heart experiences from the wide expansion of grace, but they cannot be said. Let us adore **GOD**; let us adore **Jesus Christ**; let us adore the Holy Spirit, who allows us to recognize the work of love and mercy of the Divine Persons within us; and let us apply the same to our benefit."

6. And that this was not merely a simple light <note>Here meaning an intellectual insight or inspiration.</note>, but a real enjoyment of this high mystery for him, is clear from these words, which he wrote to his guide in the year 1647: "The Divine goodness does in me what I cannot say. I possess the most holy Trinity, and I feel (or experience) with distinction the effects of the three Divine Persons."

# Third Part. The Life

7. He possessed faith to such a high degree that he was more convinced of the presence of **GOD** and the truth of the mysteries of faith than he was of the light of the sun. He lived in faith; he walked in faith; and he did everything in the spirit of faith. He looked upon all things with the eyes of faith, which do not stop at the outward appearance but penetrate into the interior; they do not consider a matter according to its present and soon-passing essence, but according to its future and abiding essence.

8. Thus, he also performed all his works with the hands of faith, which are entirely strong and charitable. These hands touch the pus and sores of the poor even more gladly—and with more love—than the most delicate people handle velvet and silk. 
> "The pure and lively faith of our first Christians," (said Renty) "ensured that, without all our 'skill' <note>original: "Geschicklichkeit," here implying a sort of human cleverness or over-refined spiritual technique</note> (which sometimes stems from a falling away from faith), they performed the heroic deeds we now admire in them; they certainly lived in faith, without forming and positioning their own spirit, but rather in great simplicity, power, and truth."

9. Strengthened by this faith, he said that it caused him no grief if the **Lord** left him in regard to "feeling" <note>original: "Empfindung," referring to the sensory or emotional awareness of God's presence</note> and placed him in dryness <note>A common term in mystical theology for a period where one feels no emotional comfort or "warmth" in prayer.</note>. He attributed the great restlessness and impatience felt in these states of deprivation to a lack of this virtue. 
> "One rarely finds," he writes in a letter, "people who practice prayer who receive or endure inner abandonment well, or who wait for some time at the gate of feeling and light without entering. They become weary; they look here and there and set to work by themselves to bring such things about, seeking some support alongside faith—which should, however, be enough for a spiritual person. The 'feeling' of **GOD** is a supplement <note>original: "un suplement," French for a substitute or addition</note> for our lack of faith; but the righteous must live by faith and lean upon this firm foundation, waiting for his **Lord** without becoming impatient."

10. To another person, he wrote the following regarding the faith of the Centurion at Capernaum: 
> "Where shall one find one who has the faith of this Centurion? Oh, how he would shame the spiritual people of today, who are indeed skilled enough to chatter about faith but have nothing of it but the sound! There are very few who possess the truth and the effects of faith. Oh, how few souls there are who are willing to bear the sufferings of the body or the spirit in the 'nakedness of faith' <note>This refers to "pure faith," which persists even when a person feels no spiritual joy or physical relief.</note>; and who seek remedies in simplicity from **GOD**, composing themselves in patience when relief does not follow as quickly as they desire! Almost everyone would like the Savior **JESUS** to be 'sensible' <note>In this context, "sensible" means something that can be felt or perceived by the senses.</note> to them—that He would come down into their house to heal their anxieties. If they do not have some sensible sign, the spirit runs to and fro, seeking its rest, which it nevertheless does not find; for this rest cannot be found in the activity of the spirit, but alone in its sacrifice <note>original: "Aufopferung," also meaning surrender or offering of oneself</note> in faith, which the spirit...

Renty critiques the spiritual practitioners of his day for seeking emotional comfort rather than the simple, heroic faith of the early Christians.</summary>

# The Marquis de Renty. Chapter XIV.

> "...draws to himself the power of Jesus Christ, who is our strength and life, in the midst of confusion and death."

11. This faith of our Renty was paired with a living hope and trust in **GOD**. In one of his letters, he wrote to his spiritual guide: 
> "Since I have trust, faith, and love, I fear neither devil, nor hell, nor all the cunning inventions of men; and I think of neither heaven nor earth, but only of doing the will of **GOD** in everything and everywhere."

12. Once, while he was overseeing a construction project, he climbed onto a scaffold which collapsed, falling with him and several other workmen. Some of the men were quite badly injured; however, he was seen to be not at all distressed or shaken by this fall. His spirit remained undisturbed, and he maintained his usual, unshakeable silence because he was fixed in **GOD**, who is immovable.

13. "Regarding my children," he wrote to someone, "I entrust them into the hands of the holy Child Jesus. I decide nothing beforehand; I do not know what shall happen tomorrow; but He gives me a great trust in His protection, which makes me blind <note>In this context, 'blind' refers to a holy indifference or 'blind trust,' where the believer does not need to see the path ahead because they trust the one leading them.</note>, and I desire nothing, and yet I am ready to desire everything."

14. When he considered himself, he said that he could not do even the very least thing; but if he turned his eyes toward **GOD**, he assured others that nothing would be impossible for him. To his guide he wrote: 
> "I have a powerful vision of how absolutely necessary Jesus Christ is to me. I see Him in His riches, and myself in my poverty; I see Him in His strength, and myself in my weaknesses; and my spirit, which is full of reverence because of the impression of these words: [Psalm 8, 5 <note>original: "Was ist der Mensch, daß Du sein gedenkest?" In most English Bibles, this is Psalm 8:4.</note>] *What is man, that You are mindful of him?* trusts itself to Him in total <term>surrender</term> <note>original: "Ueberlassung," a technical term in mystical theology referring to 'abandonment' or yielding one's will entirely to God's providence.</note> to His goodness. These words, *waiting patiently* <note>original: "langmüthig wartend"</note>, have frequently come to my mind for a long time now, without me remembering where they were taken from, nor what they meant in their original place—except that I must wait with long-suffering for the coming of our **Lord**, without anticipating **GOD** through my own searching or working, aside from the act of reverence and faithfulness in calling upon Him for His grace and hoping in Him. But a few days ago, as I took the New Testament in hand, my eyes fell upon the sixth chapter of the Epistle to the Hebrews as I opened it, where the Apostle speaks of faith in patience, through which we would inherit the promises of **GOD**, and cites the example of Abraham as proof, saying: *And so, after he had patiently endured, he obtained the promise.* This occurrence touched my heart, and I was comforted in my weakness. In this way, I am at peace upon the foundations of surrender in trust."

But should we then always lack the confidence to believe that Jesus Christ is a ghost? Should we not then go to Him in all our necessities, as to our only Savior? That we have so little faith, so little love, so little trust in the Savior—that is the cause of our weaknesses and our useless weariness of spirit; let us go straight to Jesus in trust."

# The Fifteenth Chapter.
## Concerning his love for God. His reverence toward God, and the resulting purity of his conscience.

->I.<-

How much the heart of this holy soul was occupied by the Pure Love of God—which is rightly called the queen of virtues—we shall now hear from some remaining testimonies. In the year 1648, he wrote the following among other things to his spiritual guide:

> "The Lord shines from time to time with His lights into my soul, which make it alive in Him. 3. “My spirit was enlightened this morning concerning these words: that we are in the world to know God, to love Him, and to serve Him... This Divine Lord creates a communion with our souls and establishes His kingdom within them, so that He may reign there in incomprehensible and eternal love.”

6. And he himself wrote to another person that he could not hide from her that he felt a fire in his heart which burned and consumed him without ceasing.

### Third Part. The Life ###

“...therefore not rest. Let us then burn, let us burn, yes, let us burn in everything and everywhere for God (and His glory): because we only exist through Him, why should we not live for Him? I say it freely, and would count it an honor to confirm this with my blood.” This burning zeal for the glory of God, which love worked within him, was precisely what kept him so occupied in outward affairs—to promote the glory of God in a thousand and yet a thousand ways.

8. In the year 1645, he wrote the following to his guide: “One day, as I was driven by a great longing to be entirely for God, and to be entirely consumed for His sake, I offered up to Him everything that one can and cannot [offer]. I would have gladly given Him heavens and worlds, if I had them; and on the other hand, I wished to be among all people, and in the most lowly state that might ever be found, yes, even (through the assistance of grace) to endure eternal pain with the devils, if He could thereby be more glorified. In this state of quiet zeal, there is no kind of martyrdom <note>original: *Marter*; referring here to intense physical or spiritual suffering</note>, no kind of high status nor lowliness, of adornment nor nakedness, which would not come to the soul’s mind, and which it would not accept, only to glorify God. One would wish to be a king to rule everything; and the lowest of the poor and miserable to suffer everything; and this indeed in 'unreason through an excess of reason' <note>original: *hors de raison par excez de raison*; a French mystical phrase describing a state where the soul's logic is overwhelmed by the "divine madness" of love</note>. One cannot comprehend how so many different things can be seen in such a short time; and one would need a very extensive discourse if one were to explain even a single circumstance of it. All I could do in this state was to give my freedom to God; I set such a gift down on paper and signed it with my blood.” See, what does love not say, wish, do, and what is it not capable of in those hearts that give room to its flames? Their unreason is greater wisdom than all the prudence of the worldly-wise.

9. Conformity <term>Gleichförmigkeit; the spiritual practice of aligning one's own will so perfectly with God's that they act as one</term> with God’s will, which is the infallible mark of love, was wonderful in this man. This was his true path and the lasting foundation of his state, namely the inward union of his will with the Divine, in which he was found in all sorts of circumstances, even the most adverse. He once wrote to his guide: “For three weeks, I have been overcome with a fever, with a flux <note>original: *Fluß*; a 17th-century term for an excessive discharge of bodily fluids, often dysentery</note>, and with exhaustion. In all this, my state has been nothing other than a simple following and clinging to that which God willed and did. I know of nothing special or remarkable that I could write to you, except that my heart is set upon the tribulations that will come upon me. I desire everything that God ordains, yes, I pray for it.”

Whoever wants nothing but what God wants is always satisfied, whatever may happen to him.”

13. One of the most excellent qualities of souls in the inward life is reverence before God’s presence. Mr. Renty was very much taken by this noble sentiment. He spoke of God with the deepest awe; and the sight of His highness kept him in an inexpressible humiliation <note>here meaning a state of profound humility or "lowliness" before the Divine, rather than shame</note>. When he was once asked by a close friend where this great reverence arose in him—which he held toward God at all times, in all places, and in whatever he had to do—his answer was that the sight of the majesty of God, which was present to him everywhere, also produced this effect in him everywhere, and kept him in awe and in the feeling of extreme smallness. I see myself so small, he said, so small, yes, as nothing at all, before this infinite majesty. A speck of dust <note>original: *Sonnenstäublein*; literally a "sun-dustling," referring to the tiny motes visible in a beam of sunlight</note> is indeed small in the sun; but I am even much less before God. I am nothing.

# Chapter Sixteen.
## Concerning his prayer, and the various types thereof.

->I.<-

As the author of this biography intends to continue speaking of our Renty’s prayer, he simultaneously describes in an orderly fashion the different types and stages of internal prayer, stating that there are primarily four, namely: (1) meditation, (2) prayer of the heart or of the affections, (3) active contemplation, and (4) passive contemplation.

2. In the prayer of meditation, the intellect is more active than the heart or the will, although the activities of the will must always follow and must never be neglected, lest it otherwise result in a mere empty speculation.

3. The usual subject matter that Mr. Renty took for his meditation at that time was the life, the suffering, and the death of our Savior, as these are indisputably the most useful meditations; for the Savior is given to us as our model, and our progress and entire salvation consist in His imitation and expression.

4. In the prayer of the heart, the will is more active than the intellect, the activities of which become increasingly fewer in this type of prayer until they eventually cease altogether; indeed, even the acts of affection, the heart, or the will are no longer so varied and manifold as progress is made, compared to how they may have been practiced at the beginning when the soul first enters this kind of prayer.

5. This prayer of the heart consists in a shared and cordial communion of the soul with the Lord, without—or at least with very little—reflection; in a sincere fellowship with GOD, as present and dwelling within the interior; where the soul strives to turn toward Him in the little chamber of its heart, firmly believing that He is present there; and accordingly (leaving behind inquiry and meditation), through the mere thought and simple remembrance of GOD, turns toward Him and awakens itself to deep reverence, adoration, self-annihilation <note>original: *Vernichtigung*; a mystical term referring to the total emptying of one's own ego and will to make room for God's presence</note>, to acts of praise, glorification, thanksgiving, sacrifice, petition, sorrow over sins, and primarily, the love of GOD.

6. The soul must hold itself in this manner before His presence, under this impression of reverence and humility; it may remain therein for a considerable time, so as to be all the more strengthened in it, for the time spent there is very usefully employed; and it should take even more time for this whenever it senses that the heart finds a greater opening for this exercise of faith and love.

### Third Part. The Life

7. In this, however, one must take care that in this type of prayer, it is not necessary to practice various types of such acts of faith <term>acts of faith: internal movements of the soul, such as expressing trust or devotion</term> at the same time; rather, a single one—perhaps of hope, of love, or another—is quite enough. This is especially true of one for which the soul finds itself capable and driven, and which it exercises with ease; for such ease is a clear sign that God wills for the soul to make use of it and be furthered by it. Now, as long as the assistance of God lasts in such an exercise, the soul must remain within it and continually carry on that same act, or gently repeat it; from which, without doubt, great benefit will spring forth for the soul.

8. "This prayer," says Renty, "does not happen through deliberation or reflection; but through a sincere love, which always prefers to give rather than to receive. This **darkness of faith** <note>original: "Dunkelheit des Glaubens." A common mystical concept where the soul trusts God without needing intellectual "light" or emotional "feelings."</note> is safer for the soul than all the lights it could possibly have; and the soul must make use of it with reverence and gratitude, but not with self-complacency or attachment. In this prayer, there is no straining of the intellect; it does no harm to the head; it is a state of **devout recollection** <term>recollection: a state of inward focus where the mind is gathered away from worldly distractions</term> in which one carries oneself before God, expecting from His Spirit whatever He may please to place within us; which we then receive in simplicity and trust, just as if He were speaking with us."

9. In **active or acquired contemplation**, the will holds even more dominance over the intellect and its activities than in the previous type of prayer, and it does so with greater simplicity. Furthermore, God works more here, and the human being works less; and His working in this prayer is also more spiritual, pure, and Divine. Therefore, the soul must await the working of God in peace and trust, without straining itself. Accordingly, this prayer is not so much distinguished from the previous one by its subject matter (for in this one too, the soul contemplates God and His perfections, and all truths of faith, especially the presence of God), but rather in this: that in the previous state of prayer, the soul kept itself active through its will or stirrings of the heart, and aroused itself to reverence, adoration, thanksgiving, sacrifice, and other acts of faith. Here, however, the soul merely looks upon its subject with simplicity, keeping itself otherwise quiet and still, and awaits the impressions and effects from the subject it contemplates in peaceful **serenity** <term>serenity: translated from "Gelassenheit," a central Pietist term meaning a state of yieldedness or letting go of the self to God</term>.

10. Thus, for example, one looks at a dear friend lying ill and full of pain; and this very sight moves the heart without further reflection or effort: in this way, one can contemplate the suffering Savior. Thus a bridegroom looks at his bride and, without further pondering, is kindled in her love: in this way, one can contemplate God and His perfections. Thus a subject looks at his king and is thereby moved, without effort or artifice, to stillness, devotion, and reverence: in this way, one can contemplate God’s presence. Thus an eager student looks at his teacher, waiting and noting his words; for he learns more through silence than another does through his own effort and chatter: in this way—

one seats oneself, with *Mary*, in spirit at *Jesus’* feet, and hears his words. And this is called contemplation.

11. Hence our *Renty* said: “It is a great imperfection that souls do not wait enough for God. That active *temperament* <term>temperament: the natural disposition or personality of a person, here referring to the human urge to always be "doing" something rather than being still</term>, which has not yet been overcome, moves about and thinks, under a fine pretext, that it is doing wonders; however, by this very means God is prevented from working in a soul, because He finds it in a state of movement and unrest, whereas, if it wishes to receive His influence, it must be in peace and silence.”

12. “One might indeed say” (he writes in one place) “I sometimes receive nothing in prayer; I fear that I might lose my time through idleness. But know that you by no means lose time when, in the losing of yourself, you place yourself before God in reverence and trust, so that you may wait upon Him. He cannot disapprove of such conduct.”

13. “Another will say: I have had distractions; I find myself in great dryness <note>original: "Dürre." In mystical tradition, this refers to a period where a person feels no emotional or spiritual "warmth" or "sweetness" during prayer.</note>, and am tormented with many other sufferings. I answer: Persevere with all these sufferings in your gaze of faith, of reverence, and in your expressions of love as much as you are able; keep yourself locked in the little chamber of your heart; let all these storms rage outside without worrying about them, following the example of *Noah*, who was calm in the middle of his little ship (just as his name indicates <note>The name Noah is traditionally associated with the Hebrew word for "rest" or "comfort."</note>), even though he was tossed by the waves on all sides and driven by the storm winds. This is necessary for the soul so that it may be purified and made capable of God's workings. Just as green wood, before it gives off a flame, sweats and drives out its moisture, and it is necessary that it suffer this purification so that it may be capable of catching fire; even so, all kinds of imaginations attack us, as it pleases God; but we must not be troubled by this, or withdraw ourselves from the holy exercise of prayer because of it. Let us only turn our sight away from this misery when we notice it, and continue calmly and without commotion in our offering, and be certain that we will not wait long for the Lord, and that He will not fail to come.”

14. He himself, *Mr. Renty*, when he was in this state, sometimes cried out loud when he was alone: “I am thine, O my God, despite all these distractions and all this dryness. I am thine; and I will remain thine forever and without reservation. Thou hast created me, and I will love Thee always.” Sometimes he wrote it with his finger on the earth; another time on his heart, and said: “I am content with everything that God wills and arranges for me; I want nothing more; I will not trouble myself either to have comfort or to come out of the dryness; my purpose is to praise God at all times.”

### Third Part. The Life

I suffer in the same way from dryness, distractions, and fatigue: but however it may be, I never cease, as if I did not wish to begin again well, and the longing for it is renewed within me. Sometimes physical fatigue disappears suddenly through an internal power shared with me, which enables me to continue the prayer, even outside the place and time of prayer, amidst my affairs and in conversation with people: and I can say to you in sincerity that, although I perform everything very poorly, as far as prayer is concerned, I have little distinction in all my time, because I find myself recollected <note>The term "recollected" (eingesammlet) refers to a state of being inwardly focused on the presence of God despite outward activities.</note> at all times and in everything." So much for active or acquired contemplation.

16. Regarding passive or infused contemplation <term>passive or infused contemplation: a state of prayer where the soul does not act by its own effort, but receives a direct, supernatural communication from God</term>, just as it depends entirely and solely on **God**, it also has no other rule than His good pleasure, according to which He is pleased to communicate Himself to a soul and lead it in this or another way. Just as Moses, when he ascended Mount Sinai, left behind the herds of animals, all the people, even his brother Aaron, and also his servant Joshua, and thus climbed entirely alone to the peak, and entered into the darkness <gloss>(a)</gloss> where **God** was, and spent forty days and forty nights in the contemplation and fellowship of this Divine Majesty: even so the soul, which is to be elevated to this contemplation, leaves behind the senses and reflections, together with all sensible and intelligible things, and is led into the darkness of faith, where **God** dwells, and gives Himself to the spirit to be contemplated and possessed.

17. This may be the aim of what our Renty wrote to his director in the year 1645:
> “For a long time, I have been able to make use of my intellect or memory neither in prayer nor almost at any other time. I see nothing; I feel nothing; I have neither taste nor attachment to anything; I only feel that my will is alive and ready for everything that might be shown to it that is for **God**.”

18. In another letter he wrote to him, he says:
> “I experience that for some time now my prayer is no longer governed by a rule. I possess the most holy Trinity with a fullness of truth and clarity, and indeed with such a simple <gloss>(b)</gloss> working, and one which proceeds even in the highest part of the spirit, that I am by no means drawn away from my outward occupations by it.”

19. In another he wrote:
> “**Jesus** Christ works the experience of His kingdom in my heart, and I feel well that He is **Lord** and Master in the same, and that I am entirely His. I currently have a greater opening, which

# The Seventeenth Chapter.
## Concerning his spiritual death and annihilation.

I.
Regarding spiritual death and annihilation <term>annihilation (Vernichtung): a mystical state where the soul's self-will and ego are perceived to vanish, leaving only the presence and will of God</term>, and the necessity thereof, Renty had the most beautiful insights <note>original: "Lichter und Züge" (literally "lights and features")</note>, of which we wish to cite some testimonies.

2. Thus he wrote the following about it to his guide: "As I had surrendered my free will to **God**, and had signed myself with my blood, just as I have reported to you, I was given to understand to what depth of annihilation a soul must reach if it is to become capable of **Divine Union**. I saw how my soul was brought, as it were, into a tiny point; I saw that it closed itself (or contracted), that it made itself small and brought itself into nothingness; and in that very moment I saw myself as if everything that the world loves and possesses were around me, and like a hand that removed all this from me and threw it into the abyss of nothingness.

Firstly, the external things: the kingdoms, the dominions, the magnificent buildings, precious furnishings, gold, silver, the delights, the lusts, etc., all of which so greatly hinder souls on the way to **God**, and of which He therefore wishes to see them stripped, so that they may reach the point of nakedness and death, which would translate them into fundamental riches and into true life.

# of the Marquis de Renty. Chapter XVII.

(3) He was dead and annihilated to honor, to esteem, and praise, as well as to all the scorns of men. When a trusted person asked him what thoughts he had when he heard others praising him, he replied:
> “I pay no attention or notice to it at all. It moves me just as 
> “little as if one were speaking to a block of wood. I am, through God’s grace, 
> “indifferent to praise and to contempt; neither the one nor the other 
> “makes any impression on my mind; and I do not even give it any 
> “reflection.”

(4) He was dead and annihilated regarding supernatural gifts, <note>In this context, "supernatural gifts" refers to spiritual experiences like visions or deep emotional feelings of God's presence, which Renty believed one should not cling to.</note> which are of incomparably greater value than those of which we have spoken. He desired neither virtue nor perfection, except within a detached and annihilated mind, without wishing to have this or that virtue, or this or another degree of perfection (by his own choice); rather, he desired it all just as God willed that he should have it, and said:
> “Self-love has such great

8. He was dead and annihilated to all illustrious and extraordinary things. Once, when promises of very great gifts were sent to him from God’s side, through a person who possessed a high state of grace, he wrote the following to his spiritual guide: "The things that have been sent and promised to me are what they are; I do not dwell upon them, nor can I rely upon them; one must live by faith."

9. He was dead and annihilated to the love of himself and to his natural disposition, which he had improved to such an extent that, whereas he was by nature lively and hasty, through grace he had become quiet and composed to such a high degree that all who knew him stood bewildered by it. Since he had by nature a high and proud spirit, he attained such a deep humility of heart <term>Herzensdemuth: a common 17th-century term for an inner state of lowliness before God</term> that he demonstrated this even in his outward appearance, at all times and in all places, through many singular actions. He was by nature inclined to joking, but he was nevertheless the most respectful man in the world toward everyone, even toward the very lowest. His emotions were so subject to him and in such good order that one would have said he no longer had any.

10. He was dead to all the higher faculties of his soul. <note>In traditional theology, these "higher faculties" are the Memory, Understanding, and Will.</note> He was dead to his memory, which was so empty of all things of this earth that not even a single image of them entered his mind that could have drawn him away from the remembrance of God. "Some time ago," (he writes to someone) "as I found myself in the midst of a crowd of great people, my mind was so enlightened and moved that I should not desire to know a single person, nor to be known by any. This produced in me a wonderful detachment <term>Abscheidung: a mystical term for the soul's separation from the world</term> from all things; and I recognized that one of the most excellent parts of the spiritual life depends upon this, which brings with it a great purity of mind, a great distance from the creaturely, and which makes the soul to be in the world as if it were not in it, in the forgetfulness and ignorance of everything that does not concern it, where it can endure nothing except only that which is necessary."

11. He was dead to his understanding, to his reason, and to his judgment; for he lived in faith, which properly causes the death of the former, as sufficient testimonies thereof have been cited in the preceding sections.

12. Finally, he was dead and annihilated to his own will, in that he made the same completely uniform to the will of God, so that in no way and in no thing did he want anything other than what God wanted. His own words regarding this sound as follows:

"I worship" (he writes) "the will of God in such a manner, in everything that He might please to assign to me, that hell would be a paradise to me if He gave me the command to endure the same."

### Of the Marquis de Renty. Chapter XVII.

12. Another time he wrote: "It is so far from the case that I should proceed in this matter through my reason, that I would much rather completely and utterly annihilate the same, so that it knows nothing else to speak of than nothing, and always nothing, in order to follow in everything the drawings of the Divine Will, in His measure and in His way."

13. To another person he writes: "For some time now I have found myself, both outwardly and inwardly, in such (circumstances and) affairs, that a poor small intellect, such as mine is, would soon have been stranded, if I had not surrendered everything to God. In Him, and through this way of surrender, I take all my support, adoring the decrees of His most holy and Divine Will, which has all things in His hand, to subject us to the same through justice, and to sanctify us therein through love, if only the trial shows that we have a childlike heart, namely the spirit of Jesus Christ, through which we sigh to our heavenly Father, Abba, Father!" <note>original: "Abba, Vater!" — "Abba" is an Aramaic word for "Father," used in the New Testament (Romans 8:15) to signify an intimate, filial relationship with God.</note>

14. (In such a way was the dear Renty completely dead to all things and to himself, in the conformity of the death of Jesus Christ, so that he might attain to the resurrection from the dead: and just this way we all must also enter, if we ever wish to become partakers of the pure *life* of God.) For just as our body can never become immortal, glorious, and perfect, unless it first dies and decays: just so our soul never attains to its perfection and bliss, which consists in union with God, and to its true life, unless it first dies to itself and to all created things in the power of Jesus.

15. This is the aim of what Mr. Renty wrote to his guide: "I see it quite clearly, that the only means to be united with God is to be <term>divested: "Entblössung" in the original; a mystical term for the process of "stripping" away all worldly attachments, desires, and self-will to stand "naked" before God</term> of all that God is not, and dead to all creatures and to oneself. Oh, how vividly I recognize the importance of this divestment and this death! And what shall I say? That which prevents this perpetual union of love, which we should have with His Divine Majesty, with this highest beauty, is perhaps an image, a slight attachment to something created; and should we suffer that such a small and unworthy thing should take us in God’s place? And that His Divine Spirit, which is an all-consuming fire of love, and surrounds us on all sides, should not be allowed the power to do with us as the external fire does with wood? <note>This metaphor of fire and wood is a classic mystic illustration, most famously used by St. John of the Cross, to describe how God's love transforms the soul by consuming its impurities.</note> And I, a sinful man, who on account of my wretched fullness (of myself and other things) am always discontented, and cannot be perfectly happy except through the possession of God—should I not allow myself to be occupied and filled with God? All that I am able to do through grace is this: that I gently separate myself from all things through a simple and loving turning toward Him."

16. To another person he wrote the following: "If we could grasp how very much the true divestment from everything makes the soul capable of receiving God; we would unceasingly ask this grace of Him, and without doubt we [ourselves]..."

placed him. On April 11, in the year 1649, after he had spent the entire day performing his usual works of charity, he was forced to take to his bed with illness, having already felt the malady for several days prior without saying a word about it. Immediately, he had to endure great pains throughout his entire body, of which his mind also became somewhat sensible. For he himself said that his delirious <note>original: "aberwißigen" — meaning nonsensical or irrational thoughts caused by fever.</note> notions were unheard of and so strange that, had grace not held him back, he would have said more absurd things than a madman; and that, for this reason, his illness was quite humbling: yet, a sinner must honor **God** in all states in which He places him.

2. In all these pains of his body, and in all these sufferings of his mind—and indeed through the entire duration of the illness—his foundation and his usual spiritual occupation consisted of heartfelt elevations of the soul to **God**, in acts and words of blessing, of praise, and of submission to everything the **Lord** did with him; in showing gentleness and obedience toward all those who served him, and he allowed himself to be handled so easily that everything done for him was called good, even when it often was not good at all.

3. He never complained, nor did he allow others to pity him, saying that he suffered nothing, even though his sufferings were great. And when a nursing sister <note>original: "Klosterschwester" — a nun dedicated to nursing the sick.</note>, who cared for him and with whom he had visited so many of the poor and sick, pressed him to tell her if he was not enduring a great deal? he answered:

> "O my sister, how much suffering the love of **God** endures! The servants of **God** suffer nothing."

When another person asked him if he did not have great pains? he said, no. But when the same person continued and said it certainly seemed so to her; he answered:

> "It is true, I feel myself heavily burdened with suffering; but I do not perceive it, because I do not pay attention to it."

When people urged him to take something sweet, he refused it and said:

> "That helps neither for living nor for dying, and is not necessary."

4. The medicines, though they were very bitter, he took with a joyful and contented face. And when one day, not long before his death, there was talk of an excellent medicinal remedy which, it was said, should have a great effect, he said:

> "**Patience** is a great medicine;"

and showed little inclination for that medicine: nevertheless, when they brought it to him, he took it without any resistance and without asking what it was, so much had he died to everything that concerned himself.

5. Although his illness always increased and weighed very heavily upon him, he nevertheless demanded nothing for his refreshment or relief. And when, on one occasion, white linens were placed on the bed and another pillow <term>Hauptküssen<note>An archaic German term for a bed pillow.</note></term> was given to him, he became quite ashamed, believing that this meant he was taking too much comfort, and said:

> "Look, **Monsieur** <note>Renty refers to himself in the third person as "Monsieur" to demonstrate his "annihilation" or detachment from his own identity.</note> has his comfort!"

to draw strength, he testified to him the love he bore for him; yet the words could not be so clearly understood: but afterward he said with a much clearer voice: "The perfection of the Christian life consists in this: that one is perfectly united with **God** in the faith of His Church; and one must not be confused by novelties <note>In the 17th-century context, "novelties" (Neuigkeiten) usually referred to theological innovations or heterodox movements like Jansenism, which Renty advised against.</note>. 15. Some time after this, shortly before his death, as he kept his eyes directed upward as if he had seen something, he said: "Where is the holy Child **JESUS**?" Thereupon he entered into the death struggle <note>original: "Todeskampf" — the final physical struggle before passing, often called the "agony."</note>, which lasted only about a quarter of an hour. For more than half of this time, he spoke the holy name of **JESUS** continually, and died thereafter quite gently, and entered into the place of his rest.

Thus lived, and thus died, the Marquis of Renty, one of the most magnificent lights that **God** has set up in His Church in our time, and an ornament of true godliness, as great as has been seen in a long time. He died in Paris, in the thirty-seventh year of his age, on the twenty-fourth of April, 1649.

# Preface.

->I.<-

The very same active and contemplative life which the Marquis de Renty led at court and amidst the bustle of men, this holy soul practiced within the solitude of a monastery. For as God has distributed to each, and as the Lord has called each, so should he walk; and in whatever state he is called, let him remain there with God. 1 Corinthians 7:17, 24. <note>The author uses this scripture to justify that holiness can be found both in public life (like de Renty) and in seclusion (like Elizabeth).</note>

2. More was said regarding the monastic life <term>Klosterleben; the communal life of monks or nuns</term> in the general preface to this work. If we look deeper into the true foundation and intention of those God-seeking souls (for we speak only of such) who properly enter the monastic life, no sensible person can deny that such individuals do so in order that they—in total renunciation of all transitory and deceptive treasures, honors, and pleasures of this world—might gladly devote their time, strength, and devotion solely to eternal things and the salvation of their immortal souls. To that end, they cast off all bonds, burdens, and worries of the things of this life; they offer themselves entirely to the Lord Jesus and his service, so that from then on they may only care for how they might please the Lord, their true Bridegroom, and be holy both in body and in spirit. Now, who could doubt that this mindset and inner disposition of their heart must be very pleasing to God? And who could doubt that God will accept and approve this entire sacrifice—yes, and even replace whatever else was renounced a hundredfold with spiritual blessings in heavenly goods? Indisputable examples of this are plain to see, one of which is the person whose life we have here before us.

3. Initially, this biography was prepared in the French language and brought to light in Paris in the year 1680 by the Dominican Sisters of the monastery there, in whose house this holy soul lived and had died shortly before. However, Elizabeth herself, through the guidance of the Good Spirit, was more the author of this little work than the persons who compiled it: for it does not consist of a dry and uncertain narrative; rather, the largest and most important part of it consists of vibrant testimonies from her own hand, wherein she reveals the lights and experiences communicated to her by God. The publishers have done little more than arrange these in a fitting order and accompany them with some outward circumstances of her conduct, of which they were eyewitnesses.

4. One would be able to share much more of these personal accounts of God’s guidance over her—which she set down at the express command of her spiritual director <term>Seelenführer; a priest or mentor providing personal spiritual guidance</term>—had this humble soul not burned everything she could find of such writings shortly before her departure. She did this out of a holy concern that the lights and graces, of which God made her so richly a partaker throughout her life, might be made known after her death. Therefore, we should all the more carefully preserve these few remaining pieces rescued from the fire.

5. This person and her biography are, without doubt, sufficiently confirmed and praised when we say that the well-known, pious Father Saint-Jure, the Marquis de Renty, and the dear Bernières were her most intimate soul-friends and spiritual directors; and that throughout this life story, the insights of these proven men and various pieces of their otherwise unpublished letters are to be found here and there. Mr. Poiret calls (a) this life entirely profound and inward, and judges it to be esteemed in no way less than the life of the Marquis de Renty. This is a judgment with which one may rightly agree.

6. This same man <note>referring to Pierre Poiret (1646–1719), a famous mystic philosopher and editor</note> had this little work printed in Amsterdam in the year 1702, following the aforementioned Parisian edition, and added it to the life of Mr. Renty as a second volume of the "Essential Christian"

---

(a) *Mystical Library*, pages 217, 247. <note>original: "Biblioth. Myst. pag. 217. 247." This refers to Pierre Poiret's *Bibliotheca Mysticorum*, a famous bibliography of mystical writings.</note>

# Preface.

...added to Christians, and also arranged several things better. This latter edition was used for this excerpt and translation, and (as with the other pieces in this collection) we have mostly reflected on God's <term>GOttes; the source text uses capitalization for the name of God to show deep reverence</term> inner guidance of this soul, and preferred to retain her own testimonies of it. If we look at her with clear eyes, we must confess that her words are quite profound and anointed, and that a truly brave, Evangelical, and pure spirit dwelt in this holy daughter.

7. Because Elizabeth of the Child Jesus <note>original: "Elisabeth vom Kinde JEsu"</note> held a singular devotion to the mystery of the infancy of Jesus until her death (as her name itself indicates), the editors of her biography wished to dedicate it to this Divine Child. We desire to do the same and conclude with the closing of that dedication <term>Dedication; the formal address or "giving" of a book to a patron or sacred figure</term>:

> "To You, O most holy Child Jesus, we offer up what we have left of this soul. Accept this fitting and most humble fulfillment of our duty, which we perform before You with the greatest possible reverence. And because You have moved our hearts to bring the life of Your faithful servant to light, grant that all those who read it may be so ignited in Your love that they may love and glorify You eternally! Amen."

# Chapter One.

## The Lineage, Childhood, Natural and Spiritual Gifts of Elizabeth of the Child Jesus; as well as her Desire for the Monastic Life.

-> I. <-

Elizabeth Baillou, otherwise known as Mother Elizabeth of the Child Jesus, was born in Paris on July 22, 1613, to very honorable, pious, and wealthy parents. Her father was Claude de Baillou, and her mother was Dionysia Picard. She possessed a greater strength and capacity of intellect than her gender usually carries with it <note>This reflects the 17th-century perspective on women's intellectual abilities, which the author intends as a high compliment to Elizabeth's exceptional mind</note>, a grounded judgment, a precise gift for discernment, and such a deeply penetrating insight that she could not easily have been caught or deceived by anyone. Along with this, she had a brave heart and a truly masculine courage <note>original: "männlichen Muth"; in this historical context, "masculine" was often used to describe spiritual fortitude and strength of character that was seen as transcending typical expectations</note>. Despite all this, she was friendly, pleasant, studious, and yielding toward everyone, so much so that she always believed her own light was much dimmer than that of others. She was well-formed in stature and also beautiful of face.

2. God preserved her soul in very great purity and innocence from childhood. When she was barely five years old, she already felt a tender devotion to the mysteries of the <term>Incarnation; the Christian doctrine of God becoming human in the person of Jesus</term>, the Birth, and the Childhood of the Son of God, so much so that she would even get out of bed at night to attend to her devotions; and her father had to grant her a private little chamber for her prayers. In such seclusion, she began to pour out her heart before God, occupying herself there with Him for entire hours without any childish behavior or the things children are usually inclined toward being noticed in her.

3. She was still young when she began to feel a great desire for the monastic life; she had even once truly agreed with another girl, without her parents' knowledge, to go to a Dominican <term>Dominican; a Catholic religious order focused on preaching and study</term> convent in Metz. But when they heard that such a convent was also in Paris, our young Elizabeth went there immediately and requested to be accepted into it, even though the thought of her parents caused her no small struggle, as she loved them heartily and was likewise very dear to them.

4. Meanwhile, the parents knew or suspected nothing of all this, until she once took the opportunity while her father was alone in his chamber to throw herself at his feet and make her intention known to him. However, the parents were not a little dismayed and sought to dissuade her from this mindset through all sorts of reasons. They even took two or three trips with her elsewhere, diverting her in various ways in the hope that the world—of which she had not yet had a taste—would drive the thoughts of entering the convent from her mind.

# Part Four. The Life of Elizabeth of [the Child Jesus], etc.

5. However, such delay, and the force which the young daughter exerted upon herself to obey her parents and to hide her distress, which she suffered in secret, caused her to fall into a serious illness during the third journey. Her father saw clearly that he himself was the cause of this evil, and it seemed to him as though it were said to him inwardly: "Speak only, and she will soon be healthy; it is currently within your power." Yet, he could not resolve to speak such a word, which was to cost him so dearly <note>The father is struggling with the "cost" of losing his daughter to the cloister, both emotionally and in terms of family legacy</note>. However, as the illness became ever more violent, and he feared God might take from him by force the one he would not give freely, he overcame his natural attachment and promised her that he would let her go into the monastery; whereupon an improvement soon followed, and she thus received the freedom to enter the monastery.

## The Second Chapter.
### Regarding her Entrance into the Monastery; her Self-Denial and State of Mind at that Time.

->I.<-

She was then received into our convent (says the spiritual daughter who composed her biography) with great joy, both on her own part and that of all the sisters, and one year later, which was the fifteenth year of her age, she was clothed <note>original: "eingekleidet"; this refers to the ceremony of receiving the religious habit, marking the start of the novitiate</note>.

2. In what manner our young nun practiced the mortification of her body in these first years, we shall pass over here for the sake of brevity, especially since it might not be suitable for everyone <note>The author likely refers to "bodily disciplines" or penances that were common in 17th-century asceticism but might seem extreme to a general reader</note>.

3. In obedience toward her superiors, she was incomparable. The blessed Margaretha of Jesus, who was the Prioress of the monastery at that time and took a singular pleasure in the earnest path of this daughter, wished once to test her virtue and commanded her to do something quite unusual, which, due to all the circumstances, required a very great self-denial. This noble-hearted daughter, however, accomplished it with the eyes of her reason closed <note>A metaphor for "blind obedience," or obeying without questioning the logic of the command</note>, and without making the slightest difficulty over it, even though she could easily have withdrawn from it. And when some of our sisters later reminded her of it, adding that they could not possibly have resolved to do it, she answered: "And I would be far more astonished if a devout religious soul <note>original: "Religieuse Seele"</note> were not faithful to her God in such a beautiful opportunity to overcome and annihilate herself. For a truly obedient person (a) must speak only of struggles and victories."

(a) Proverbs 21:28, according to the Vulgate <note>The original text cites verse 23, but in the Latin Vulgate, verse 28 contains the phrase "vir obediens loquetur victorias" — an obedient man shall speak of victory</note>.

# Part Four. The Life

4. The internal state of her soul, during these first years of her monastic life, can be somewhat understood from an old and nearly torn piece of paper, found somewhere in her own handwriting, wherein she prescribed some rules for herself during her years of probation <term>years of probation: also known as the novitiate, this is a testing period for a new member of a religious order before they take permanent vows</term>. Behold some of them:

> „I. As soon as I have awakened, I will lift my spirit to God, 
> „looking upon and adoring Him, just as I have His presence. I will 
> „awaken myself through one or another speech that the Child Jesus makes 
> „to me. Usually, I will imagine as if He lovingly said into the ear 
> „of my heart: 'My bride, my beloved, if you wish to follow me, 
> „then deny yourself, take up your cross, surrender yourself to Me, 
> „and follow Me.'
> 
> „II. I will dress myself quickly in the presence of God, etc.
> 
> „III. When I find myself in spiritual dryness <note>original: "Dürre"; in mystical theology, this refers to a period where a person feels no emotional or spiritual "warmth" or comfort during prayer</note>, I will ask 
> „the holy Child Jesus for permission to hide myself in the wound of 
> „His holy heart; so that, when I am united with this Divine Heart, 
> „I may take on its mind and inclinations, and bring forth not a 
> „single word from myself, nor through myself, but all in Him and for Him.
> 
> „IV. Especially I will strive to maintain devotion during eating; 
> „and to practice internal and external acts of self-denial as much 
> „as I am able.
> 
> „V. During work, I will look upon the kind God, who works more in 
> „that which I perform than I do myself: but who also works much 
> „more secretly and more lovingly within me, to restore His Divine 
> „image in me, and (if I do not resist Him) showers me with a 
> „thousand graces. Therefore I will enter into a sense of wonder, 
> „joy, thanksgiving, love, and submission to His Divine operations, 
> „giving Him more power over me than I have over those things 
> „which are at my service.
> 
> „VI. Concerning prayer, I will strive at its beginning to awaken 
> „all the powers of my soul to the presence of God with the greatest 
> „devotion I can; and in the course of the prayer take care that I 
> „do not dwell too much on intellectual reflection <note>original: "Ueberlegung"; she is prioritizing "affective prayer" (of the heart) over "discursive prayer" (of the analytical mind)</note>, but rather 
> „spend more time on the affections and movements of the heart.
> 
> „VII. I will strive never to lose the presence of God for a 
> „single moment by my own will.
> 
> „(1) I will yield myself to this kind God, that He may perform in 
> „me the work I have currently before me, and wherein I might 
> „otherwise best be able to glorify Him.

## Chapter Three.

->Vivid insight, which she then received, into her sins. Her<-
->earnestness even in the smallest matters. Resignation to all suffering.<-
->Crucifixion of her senses; and a vision of the<-
->riches in God.<-

->I.<-

After completing her years of probation <term>probation years: "Probjahre," the novitiate period where a candidate tests their suitability for monastic life</term>, she made her general confession and thereafter bound herself fully to the convent through a vow <term>vow: "Gelübde," a solemn religious promise, usually of poverty, chastity, and obedience</term>. At this time, God gave her a vivid insight into her sins and their loathsomeness, as can be seen from this writing found in her own hand.

> “I. After my general confession <term>general confession: "allgemeine Beichte," a confession covering all the sins of one's entire past life</term>, God gave me a clear insight into my unfaithfulness and sins; which insight I initially bore with much pain, as I could not understand how I could have committed so many sins and willfully gone against that which I owed to my God. But afterwards I saw that self-love <term>self-love: "Eigenliebe," a spiritual term for egoism or prioritizing one's own desires over God's will</term> stirred up such thoughts; wherefore I have since borne my failings with peace and with the annihilation <term>annihilation: "Vernichtigung," a mystical term for the total humbling or "emptying" of the self before God</term> of myself.
>
> “II. The hatred which God has made known that He bears against sin, and the ghastly contempt for all His Divine perfections caused by sins, make me feel such a great loathing for them that I would infinitely rather choose Hell and its torment <term>torment: "Quaal," intense physical or spiritual suffering</term> than to willfully commit a single, even minor, sin. Lord, my God, You know that I have no greater suffering in this life than that I have offended You; and I cannot understand how it is possible that I was ever so unhappy as to commit a willful sin. Oh, that I might not die of pain! And if I am to live longer, O Divine Love, let it at least be for this reason: that I may suffer in all parts of my body and my soul which have been rebellious toward You.
>
> “III. Let every evil that can be imagined storm upon me. Only preserve me from this evil: that nothing may be found in me that is contrary to You; then everything else will be sweet and pleasant to me. And before You would allow me ever to come to the point of offending You, I pray You, O You Life of my life, by all that You are, rather annihilate all that I am and destroy me completely, so that this loathsome monster <note>She refers here to sin as a "monster."</note> may never again have any existence within me. One of the two: Either take my life, or destroy my sins, etc.
>
> “IV. Since I have now, according to the justice of God <term>justice of God: "Gerechtigkeit GOttes," the theological concept that God's holiness requires a righteous response to sin</term>, deserved to be eternally separated from my God, who is my perfect happiness, and to suffer great torment for all eternity; it is entirely fitting that I, in this time <meta>The text continues on the next page, likely with the word "surrender" or "submit" (ergeben).</meta>

# Fourth Part. The Life of Elisabeth, etc.

> “[I] surrender to the sweet severity of love, which has preserved me so that I have not fallen into this terrible unblessedness; and that I, according to His adorable <term>adorable: "anbätungswürdig," meaning worthy of deep religious adoration or worship</term> guidance, endure in all stillness the separation from Him Himself, that is, from the sweet effects of enjoying His presence; and that I, instead of all delight and pleasure, have nothing else in this life than the deprivation of everything that could give me some refreshment. To this I surrender myself, and offer myself up to Him, to be for His sake (and according to His will) in a constant inward dryness <term>inward dryness: "inwendige Dürre," a mystical state where the soul feels no emotional warmth or spiritual "sweetness," testing one's faith</term> and desolation, and without accepting even any comfort from all the things of this earth, etc.”

2. Around this time, she entered into a new earnestness and said to herself: “Now then, now I will truly begin.”

In her brave resolution, nothing seemed too small to her; rather, she became entirely attentive, even in the most insignificant things. **God** has let me see, she said, through the light of His grace, how highly I must value those things which people are accustomed to call small; and what care I must apply to avoid an imperfection, or to practice some virtue, for the reason and with the intention that **God** is He who He is—namely, most perfect; because He has done so much for me, and I am in turn obligated to so much for His sake; and finally, because His love wants to work such things in me. She thus did not want to view and value works according to their outward appearance, but according to the ground and purpose from which they happen.

3. Just as she was faithful in little and small things, so has the **Lord** also set her over much and over great things, as we shall see hereafter; and it can also be seen from the following little letter, which was still found in her own hand and written at this time, that she was indeed called to something great. In it, she expresses herself in the following manner:

> “As I was about to go to reading, I suddenly found myself taken with the thought that I must prepare myself to suffer much; and that I must make myself ready for it, to have no single comfort in this life, because it would be very necessary for me to suffer much so that **God’s** purpose for me would be fulfilled. I saw this in such a way that I saw myself as separated and entirely removed from all things, and regarded myself as a stranger <note>original: "fremdes Mensch," used here to mean an outsider or alien to worldly concerns</note> here in the world, who must be exposed to all persecutions and contradictions; which initially startled my [human] nature; although according to my soul I felt very comforted, in that I was very glad to suffer something for the sake of the holy Child **Jesus**. Therefore, I surrendered myself to Him with tearful eyes and a willing heart, to do with me everything that might please His adorable goodness; wishing that not only no day or hour, but also no moment might pass by in which I would not have something to suffer, internally or externally.”

# Fourth Part. The Life

4. And this powerful insight made her intent only on how she might crucify her flesh and senses in every way. She restrained her eyes in such a way that she did not look up even once in three months; and it was noted that she knew those nuns who had been in the convent for quite a long time only by their voices, because she had never yet seen them in the face, no matter how often she had to be among them. And she would have always done so, had she not afterwards been commanded to proceed a little differently in this matter. She received permission to remove all the filth that she found in the convent; and this then often gave her opportunity to overcome herself, since she was by nature so very delicate and clean <note>original: "reinlich" - here implying a natural fastidiousness or daintiness that made physical filth repulsive to her</note>. Special examples of this I need not mention in this extract of her life: our present-day Christians are far too refined; it would be enough of an act of self-denial for them just to read it here, to say nothing of imitating what this or other holy souls have sometimes done at the impulse of grace.

5. Since our Elisabeth was very friendly and very edifying in her conduct, it was commonly assigned to her to be with the newly arrived daughters of the convent <note>the novices or new members of the religious community</note>, so that she might maintain their earnestness and strengthen them in their calling.

As these duties of love sometimes hindered her practice of prayer, she cut back much of her sleep to find the time for it again; thus she sometimes felt very exhausted, and she attributed this to her lack of earnestness. Around this time, it seems to have been that she wrote the following:

> “In my prayer I had an insight that in God there are infinite treasures for
> me; and that, if He wished to put only a single thought of them into my heart, 
> He could thereby work in me so great a fervor of love that I would be 
> fit to give my blood and life for my neighbor; so that it must be enough 
> for me that in God there is a great power that can make me go to 
> the service of love and actually perform it: thus I found myself much richer 
> in God than if I had possessed all kinds of gifts and goods in myself; 
> just like a child who has a very wealthy father, in whose hands the 
> riches are better preserved than in its own.”

### of Elisabeth of the Child Jesus. Chapter IV.

> “I. I will maintain silence as much as is ever possible for me: for this practice, as God has given me to recognize, is important and necessary for my perfection. And when the love of my neighbor compels me to speak, I will first lift my spirit to the Lord, as to the uncreated and incarnate Word <note>A theological term for Jesus Christ, referring to the belief that the eternal Son of God took on human flesh.</note>, that He may teach me to speak, or rather, that He may speak through me, and that I may be His mere instrument, or the **voice of one calling** (a), as John says; so that I only bring forth the words that He is pleased to put into my thoughts, which I will speak according to His will, in Him, and through Him.
> 
> “II. In the morning I will ask the holy Child Jesus to place a lock upon my lips, so that I do not open them except for His glory; and that it might please His goodness to purify them with the **glowing coal** (b) <note>A reference to the prophet Isaiah, whose lips were purified by an angel with a coal from the altar.</note> of His love.
> 
> “III. In the evening I will turn particularly to the Word made flesh, that He may give me the virtue of holy silence, both inwardly and outwardly; so that I may be able to hear what He wishes to speak to my heart.”

2. Her love for solitude brought her to the point that she even withdrew from the company of Mother Margaret of Jesus <note>Margaret of Jesus (1590–1660) was a prominent figure in the Carmelite order and a contemporary influence.</note>, who was not only affectionate but also deeply spiritual. In this, our zealous Elisabeth’s only purpose was that she might be known to no one but God alone, and that she might sacrifice everything for His sake. “What a cruel sacrificial priest love is,” she sometimes said to us, “which never says: It is enough.” For since love itself sacrifices those souls which are dearest to it, it also robs them of the most innocent delights and causes them to renounce even the most holy advantages.

3. This God, who in His love was so jealous for the heart of His bride, and who wanted her to have just as little confidence in herself as in any other creature, gave her one day the following insight, which she had to provide in writing to her spiritual director:

> “I have been very occupied with my noticeable faults and with my evil habits; so much so, that I did not know where to turn, as I saw nothing in myself but obstacles to grace, without finding any means to rid myself of them, because I am unfit for anything good. Then I remembered what you said to me: that one must not dwell on the sight of one’s own misery, but turn to God as soon as such thoughts enter our minds. Thereupon, in faith, I abandoned myself to God, wishing never to be anything else—whether in the **state of nature**, in the **state of grace**, or in the **state of glory** <note>These represent the three stages of the soul: human existence, life under God's favor on earth, and eternal life in heaven.</note>—except that which might please Him.

### Fourth Part. The Life

> “Then I had a vision of the presence of God within me, as the beginning and the cause of grace, which is infinitely effective and active; and I recognized that I could do more in Him than if I possessed all the virtues bestowed by nature, or even those acquired through my own diligence. In that same moment, as I recognized this, I heard this word quite clearly within me: **Do not fear**—as if someone had said to me: ‘Behold the treasures you possess within yourself; you have no cause to be afraid.’ This vision impressed upon me a great reverence and a total surrender to God, with a kind of certain confidence in the midst of my infirmities: that which I previously viewed as mountains now seemed to me only like motes of dust in the sunlight <note>original: "Sonnenstäublein." A common mystical metaphor for how human troubles vanish when compared to the magnitude of God’s light.</note>, in comparison with the power of the Spirit of God.”

These intelligible insights, or inward words, were indeed extraordinary gifts of grace; however, since everything aimed at the denial and annihilation of her self, there was not the slightest deception to be suspected in them.

4. Regarding the same matter, we have another beautiful insight, which she likewise recorded at the command of her guide:

> “I was occupied almost this entire day with the vision of my infirmities, which were given to me to see quite clearly. I could hardly lift myself up into God: for when I began to do so, I saw that this action, coming from myself, was so corrupted by self-love that I simply had to cease it; so that I remained before God like a beast (a) <note>original: "Thier." A reference to Psalm 73:22: "I was as a beast before thee," expressing a state of humble, wordless submission.</note>, which is useless for anything good, and I felt a poignant pain because of it. Afterwards, however, I had a penetrating vision of how I must seek all my comfort in the merits of Jesus Christ the Crucified; and that we are greatly indebted to God when He lets us see what we are. For when we find nothing in ourselves upon which we can lean, and yet cannot live without support, we are compelled to seek the same in God, in whom we find enough to hope for.”

5. All these insights only led her to take the most noble resolutions to run after her Bridegroom <note>In mystical tradition, the "Bridegroom" refers to Jesus Christ, symbolizing the soul's intimate union with the divine.</note> along the path of the most sublime virtues. See what she recorded for herself regarding this around that time:

> “I. So that I do not let the grace of God be in vain within me, I must:
>
> “(1) Withdraw from my senses everything that can serve to maintain their own life.
>
> “(2) Annihilate all seeing and deliberation of my own reason, looking at nothing and occupying myself with nothing but God alone, or that which points directly to Him.

In 17th-century German mysticism, this refers to the total "naughting" or emptying of the self-will to make room for God.</note>, to which He calls me. And to that end, I will keep myself, as much as is possible for me, in a state of the utmost lowliness toward God and toward all creatures; before whose eyes I wish to hide myself, and to be nothing in their thoughts, just as they shall be nothing in my thoughts: since I wish to recognize nothing but my God alone, and to be known by none but Him.

> 
> “(3) In my dealings with people, I will see to it that I say nothing that could in the least give offense to others. I will look upon the faults of others in a spirit of self-annihilation, which shall immediately draw me back from looking at that which might seem imperfect in others, in order to look only at my own failings.”

6. The violence that she constantly did to herself, and the severity which she exercised against her body, finally caused her no small amount of weakness. She had weakened her stomach to such an extent that she could hardly keep down the little she ate, and was seized by frequent and violent vomiting; which she kept secret as much as she could, and thereby increased her malady, because she had not used any remedy at the beginning. Consequently, she developed a certain kind of such dreadful hiccuping <note>original: "Schlucken." This likely refers to severe diaphragmatic spasms or "singultus," which in her weakened state would have been distressing to witness.</note> that one could not listen to it without shuddering. The most skillful <term>physicians</term> <note>original: "Medici."</note> who were summoned judged that her illness was very dangerous, and that she was unable to endure the rigors of cloistered life; they also assured her that she could not live another year if she did not keep strictly, and in all parts, to the diet ordered by them.

7. She did indeed plead most earnestly with the Superior <note>original: "Vorsteherin." The head of the convent.</note> that she might be dispensed from obedience to the physicians; however, she was compelled to be led into the infirmary. Here she found constant opportunity to deny herself,

## The Fifth Chapter.

->She becomes Mistress of the Novices. Her serious mind and purpose at that time. She teaches and leads others through her example and instructions, with all earnestness, wisdom, care, and love.<-

->I.<-

Since the Mistress of the Novices became ill around this time, eyes were cast upon Sister Elisabeth of the Child Jesus to fill such an important position, even though she had at most completed the twenty-third year of her age. However much her humility objected to this election by pleading her incompetence, she nevertheless had to submit to accepting this office out of obedience; for no one but she alone believed that she was unfit for it. And she held this position worthily for twenty-four or twenty-five years, though not consecutively, and ended her life therein.

2. All the novices submitted to her without any difficulty, although several of them were much older than she, and were also already very far advanced in godliness. One of them, Madame Daussone, who was counted among the most clever and virtuous women, once said secretly to a sister: "I sometimes see our Mother, the Mistress, looking as beautiful as a <term>cherub</term> <note>A type of high-ranking angel, often depicted in this period as reflecting divine light or wisdom.</note> during prayer. I told her that I could well recognize when our Lord had shown her a special grace; but she gave me quite a 'welcome' for it." <note>Likely meaning Elisabeth rebuked her or responded with such humility that it was a sharp "welcome" to the speaker's flattery.</note>

5. She began to practice herself what she wanted her novices <term>Probtöchter</term> <note>Literally "trial daughters," a term for young women in their probationary period before taking full vows.</note>

7. In her exhortations, she always adapted herself to the inclination and state of the

might encounter it: because, as an experienced warrior, she precisely recognized 
all its tricks and hiding places: so that one could never speak to her from an 
impulse of nature without her noticing it, no matter how much one sought to hide 
oneself; she also always used in her speech such precise and appropriate ways of 
speaking that she immediately won the heart, and led one, as it were against one's 
will, to work courageously toward one's own destruction <note>The spiritual "destruction" or dismantling of the self-centered ego.</note>.

8. She especially sought to awaken in her novices a great devotion
to the Incarnation, Birth, and Childhood of the Savior: and when she spoke of it—
namely, of the deep humiliation of the Godhead in the womb of a virgin, 
of the elevation of man to the Godhead, and of the various advantages 
and benefits that we must draw from this in the person of the eternal WORD—it 
was as if she had enraptured one's heart and mind, and she said such things 
about it that she could not have been taught except by the Holy Spirit Himself.

11. If some occasionally fell into temptations, oh, how she watched with them and supported them with strength in their sufferings; she made the yoke of the Lord as sweet for them as possible; she sometimes entered into their rational arguments only to better show them their falseness; she forbade them those things which she knew they were averse to, so that she might awaken in them a desire for them; and she herself did in their presence those things for which she knew they had a dislike, in order to make the practice of them easy through her example. She sometimes stayed whole nights with them where she deemed it necessary; she wept with those who wept, and gave them a thousand testimonies of her love and compassion; she devised all sorts of ways to at least weaken the power of the enemy <note>Refers to the Devil or spiritual temptation.</note> where the time had not yet come to destroy it; so much so that several such souls afterwards spent their lives in holiness and now enjoy the fruit of their constancy, which they (next to GOD) have to thank the care of this, their faithful mother.
