# Fourth Part. The Life

->of Elizabeth of the Child JESUS. Ch. V.<-

> “...the inner form of their spirit, always laying it at the feet of all the other sisters, and always regarding themselves as the most unworthy and imperfect.
>
> “VI. As for me, I will love them heartily, in GOD and before GOD; I will bear them patiently with the utmost love; I will serve them carefully; and I will punish them strictly, but also with gentleness.”

5. She began to practice exactly what she wanted her novices <note>original: "Probtöchter," literally "test-daughters," a term for young women in their probationary period or novitiate</note> to do. In everything that was to be done in the monastery, she herself was the first and the last. She observed the smallest rules of the house with great precision; she proved herself fervent in exercises of penance <term>Bußübungen: spiritual disciplines such as fasting or prayer intended to show repentance</term>, in works of humility, and in everything by which "nature" <note>In this spiritual context, "nature" refers to the ego, selfish desires, or human impulses that are seen as obstacles to divine grace.</note> is crucified. One would have said she had forgotten the loftiness of her own inner life in order to take up once more all the exercises of the beginning novices; thus she became "all things to all people," so that she might win all for Jesus Christ.

6. What she did herself, she also taught her novices, giving them excellent weekly lessons on obedience, poverty, exact faithfulness even in small things, the spirit of inwardness <term>Innigkeit: a deep, heartfelt sincerity and focus on the interior presence of God</term>, silence, the necessity of dying to everything in order to be entirely for GOD, and various other important points. These same points have indeed been written down many times by our sisters; however, since nothing is included here except what was found in her own hand, or at least a few short words that have remained unchanged—whereas the others might have been mixed or distorted—no attempt has been made to cite them here.

7. In her exhortations, she always adapted herself to the inclination and state of the novice. She never gave "nature" any quarter, wherever she might encounter it; being an experienced warrior, she recognized all its tricks and hiding places. Thus, one could never speak to her from a natural impulse <note>meaning a motivation coming from the ego rather than from God</note> without her noticing it, no matter how much one tried to hide; in her speech, she always used such precise and suitable expressions that she immediately won over the heart, and brought one, as if against one’s own will, to work courageously toward one's own destruction <note>A mystical term for the "death of the self" or the removal of the ego.</note>.

8. She especially sought to awaken in her novices a great devotion to the Incarnation, Birth, and Childhood of the Savior. When she spoke of it—namely, of the deep humiliation of the Deity in the womb of a Virgin, of the elevation of man to the Deity, and of the many advantages and benefits we must draw from the person of the Eternal Word—it was as if she had enraptured one’s heart and mind. She spoke of such things that she could not have been taught except by the Holy Spirit himself.

9. Furthermore, she instilled in the novices a peculiar horror of sin, and said to them, as if with a divine power: "I confess that I cannot..."

# Part Four. The Life

> "...takes it by nothing other than force. Therefore, do not believe that you will attain heaven if you lead a lukewarm life, if you do that which you desire according to the senses and according to nature. No, the kingdom of heaven is only open to those souls who do a constant violence <note>original: "Gewalt"; This is a reference to Matthew 11:12, suggesting that spiritual progress requires intense, forceful effort against one's own lower impulses.</note> to themselves.

> "I know well that you could say: What, must one then spend one’s whole life in a constant constraint, and always deny oneself the pleasure that one desires? Yes, it is the truth: the Christian life is a constant dying to self <note>original: "Absterbung," a common mystical term for mortification or the process of letting go of worldly desires to live for God.</note>: and if JESUS Christ could not enter into His kingdom except through suffering, what right do you pretend to have to His glory if you do not pass through the fire of tribulations, and if you do not wash your robe in the blood of the Lamb? On the other hand, however, when you consider that you shall have the eternal possession of God as your reward, should it then still be difficult for you to endure the tribulations which last for such a short time?

> "We always carry about in our body, says Paul, the dying of the Lord JESUS, so that His life may also be manifested in our body. For we who live are always delivered unto death for the sake of JESUS Christ, so that His life may also be manifested (a). I do not write this scripture passage in full, and would hardly be able to finish this letter if time did not fail me. Our Lord, who is the Word of Life (b), will tell you more of it in a moment, in the depths of your heart, than I could teach you of it in my whole life. Pray to this Divine Savior for me."

„IX. The words which have served as the basis and goal of this exercise are these (a): *For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God; but when Christ, who is your life, appears, etc.* In these words, I have found expressed the three ways of perfection: the <term>Purgative</term>, the <term>Illuminative</term>, and the <term>Unitive</term>.” <note>In Christian mysticism, these are the three stages of spiritual growth: purification from sin (Purgative), the enlightenment of the mind by divine truths (Illuminative), and the final stage of perfect union with God’s will (Unitive).</note>

2. That our Elizabeth must have occasionally possessed very extraordinary gifts of grace is also evident from some short letters that Father Saint-Jure <note>original: "Pater Jurius." Jean-Baptiste Saint-Jure was her spiritual advisor.</note> wrote to her. In one, it stated: „See to it that nothing appears externally of what is occurring in your interior. However, to prevent this, you must not turn away from those thoughts which give you a Divine impression. Only place yourself in such a location and in such a posture that it all happens within you without others becoming aware of it: and if someone then asks you—since one thing or another may break out against your will and despite your precautions—then say that you find yourself a little unwell (as this is indeed also true in regards to the body); but that it will surely pass, and that a little rest is the remedy for it.”

3. In another letter he says: „In the moments of great movement, see to it that you moderate them if they should go too far. Especially regarding the body, keep it as still as you possibly can. For indeed, the purer and more perfect the spiritual workings are, the less they enter into the senses; this is clearly seen in our Savior, who worked internally in the highest perfection, and yet was externally like other men.”

4. Nonetheless, these precautions could not prevent something of this nature from being recognized in her from time to time. Once, while she was with the <term>probationers</term> <note>original: "Probtöchter." These were likely young women or novices undergoing a period of testing before fully entering the religious community.</note>, she was suddenly seen as one who is entirely and completely occupied internally, and almost does not know what she is doing. She wished to say a vocal prayer; but it was suddenly impossible for her to speak it, so that she was forced to run away, and indeed with such an unusual speed that one could not follow her. She locked herself so tightly in her chamber that those who had followed her could see nothing more of these effects: until about half an hour later, when she came out again, appearing quite ashamed and completely <term>annihilated</term> <note>original: "vernichtiget." In mystical tradition, "annihilation" refers to the total humbling of the self and the ego before the presence of God.</note>.

5. Another time the matter became manifest. For in the church she even fell so far out of herself <note>This refers to a state of religious ecstasy or trance.</note> that it was believed she had become ill: indeed she was ill, but from love. She was then carried to the infirmary. But as they bothered and shook her greatly so that she might come to herself again—because they did not understand what might be wrong with her—there was one sister who pressed her more than the others to tell her what she lacked, and I know not how, coaxed these words from her mouth:

6. It may perhaps have been around this time that the Savior spoke these internal words to her expressly, which we found written in her own hand: *Be a throne of peace for me, and a peaceful dove.*

## The Seventh Chapter.

### Of her external sufferings. Of her internal heavy trials and purifications; in which she is supported by the Marquess of Renty and by her director.

->I.<-

Just as her graces were great and extraordinary, her sufferings—which she encountered both externally and internally around this time and thereafter—were no less so. God wished to make her somewhat prepared for this through His light and the impression He gave her beforehand of such impending sufferings.

2. Regarding the manner and way of suffering, these express words were spoken to her internally: *When one must suffer, one must do so without complaining, and in the silence of my love.*

3. Immediately after this, she was overcome by a long-lasting and tedious illness, which she initially tried to hide, but which finally revealed itself sufficiently so that she was forced to go to the infirmary. She had a violent fever, which continued to increase and lasted for more than three months in succession. Every day she had three violent attacks of it, which began either with heavy vomiting or with a dangerous <term>lethargy</term> <note>original: "Schlafsucht." In this period, it referred to an unnatural, heavy sleep or a state of semi-consciousness during illness.</note>.

### Fourth Part. The Life

...made the love that people had for her such that they left her no peace, but nudged and plagued her every moment to wake her up. She confessed that, if God had not supported her, she would have fallen into impatience a thousand times over; yet she suffered everything without complaining, except for her lack of spiritual mortification <term>unmortified nature; the state of not yet being completely dead to one's own self-will</term> and for the trouble she caused. The heat of the fever burned her tongue in such a way that it became as dry and as black as a coal; nevertheless, she would never have asked for a drop of water or any refreshment. And although she had uncommonly strong headaches, along with a heavy chest ailment and also a very strong swelling, she did not heed the needs of nature, but let her body lie there helpless; while she meanwhile was entirely lost in her God in perpetual prayer. Throughout the entire illness, she was as humble as a child, and allowed herself to be treated by those who attended her with such complete detachment <term>abgeschiedenheit; a state of being internally and externally surrendered to God's will</term> that one could never discover what she would have liked.

5. Finally, at one midnight, the whole evil suddenly shot into a leg, so that it swelled up as thick as the body of a two-year-old child, with such sharp, piercing pains that her head, which she could no longer move, and her entire body, which also lay there immovable, were somewhat shaken by it. The sisters who watched by her could not look at her without shedding tears; and the physician assured them in the morning, as he visited her in that state, that her pains were greater than those of a criminal being broken on the wheel <note>A brutal form of execution where a person's limbs were shattered with a heavy wheel</note>: Yet she was patient in everything. It did not last long, however, before the fever left her, the pains ceased, and she finally gradually regained her strength; only she kept a swelling in her legs, which caused her great discomfort for the remainder of her life.

6. However, this very painful illness of hers was not to be compared with the heavy inner sufferings and trials that followed, into which she was placed through Divine guidance. Her own words concerning this are, among others, as follows:

# Of Elizabeth of the Child Jesus. Chapter VII.

> "...as if You desired my destruction. You strike me with Your almighty hand, and You redouble Your blows in such a way that it seems You are my sworn enemy, and take Your pleasure in casting me to the ground.

> You came before me with blessings and raised me to Your Divine Contemplation <note>This refers to the state of "infused contemplation," a high form of wordless prayer where the soul feels directly united with God.</note>; but from this happy and pleasant sleep, You have cast me down into an abyss so much deeper and so much more terrifying, the greater my previous happiness had been. Finally, You have broken me through this fall, as if rejecting, condemning, and punishing my former way of life, in which I nonetheless sought to serve You in sincerity.

> I expected from Your goodness a constant increase of grace and light, a great stillness, and an unshakeable firmness in Your service, after I had bravely practiced various mortifications <term>Abtödtungen; spiritual exercises designed to subdue the ego and physical desires</term>; and I hoped to reach the point where I might enjoy Your Divine Presence, and have my way of life only in heaven: but now infinite evil and misery oppress me; thick darknesses have unexpectedly overtaken me, and have covered and oppressed my inner state, which was in peace and full of light. You have driven me into the wilderness, and brought me into the most extreme solitude, just as if I were of the kind of animals that stay in the most secluded places and do nothing but howl, moan, and sigh, as they die of hunger, thirst, and sadness."

7. Her experienced spiritual director <note>In the Catholic tradition, a director is a priest who guides a person's spiritual life and assesses the validity of their mystical experiences.</note>, who wanted to test her state and investigate closely whether there might be any deception in it, gave her to understand one day that he believed she was deceived. He placed her in a very lowly and common way of prayer, and intentionally gave her such exercises as were entirely contrary to that which is most sublime in the interior life <term>inwendiges Leben; the hidden, spiritual life of the soul</term>. She submitted herself indeed with much humility; but since on the one hand it was impossible for her to act against her inner pull, and on the other hand she feared displeasing her Bridegroom <note>A traditional mystical reference to Jesus Christ.</note> through disobedience to her director, she was severely tormented, until he eventually instructed her better again.

8. Now as her sufferings rose very high, and her director, Father Jurius, had no small compassion for her, he introduced her to the Marquis of Renty <note>Gaston de Renty (1611–1649), a famous French mystic and philanthropist known for his intense piety.</note>, and commanded her to open her state to him, so that she might thereby be all the more convinced and reassured of the correctness of her way: with whom she then, from that time on, entered into a very close and very holy union of the spirit.

9. He now sought in every way to take away from her the various terrifying thoughts she had created for herself without cause, and to that end once said to her: "I read in your interior as in a book: Fear nothing."

# Of Elizabeth of the Child Jesus. Chapter VII.

> “...alone, and that it be God alone, in whom you can find your rest and your perfection.”

12. (And certainly, this is how it happens; when God places someone in such sufferings, no one can comfort them until the hour of deliverance arrives.) One day, after she had spoken with Lord Renty <note>Gaston de Renty (1611–1649), a French nobleman and mystic mentioned on the previous page.</note> about her condition, a sister said to her upon her return: "Dear Mother, you must have received much comfort from the place you have just come." Whereupon, without thinking, she raised her oppressed eyes toward heaven and said with a sigh: "Oh, if only one knew what I suffer!" But she immediately fell silent and said nothing more.

13. However, grace pressed powerfully upon her, and she resolved to surrender herself with her full will to all these present and future sufferings, whether they came from without or within. This is evident from the following document, which was found written in her own hand and signed with her blood <note>In the 17th century, some mystics signed spiritual "contracts" or resolutions in their own blood to symbolize a total, life-and-death commitment to God.</note>:

14. 
> “The Lord Jesus Christ’s insatiable desire for suffering has made a most singular impression on me. it has moved me to sign this resolution—which I have made in His presence—with my blood: namely, that in all sufferings, from whatever side they may come and of whatever kind they may be, I will never say ‘it is enough,’ nor will I complain about them to any human being. And if I do speak of them, it shall only be to our Lord, to call upon Him for assistance, or to the worthy person He has given to lead me in His ways, so that I may be enlightened in my darkness and supported in my weaknesses—at least as far as I can judge that Divine Goodness wishes to grant me help through such means.
> 
> I have given myself to the Lord with a courageous heart, so that through love, and for the sake of His love, I may bear the deprivation of all that is dearest to me in His current providence. I also offer myself up, should it be the pleasure of my sovereign God, to be ‘crucified’ by the very person who currently lightens my small sufferings <note>She is likely referring to her spiritual director or a close confidant whose support she is willing to lose if God requires it.</note>. And because I view the sufferings that might come from that direction as the most sensitive <note>In this context, 'sensitive' means the most deeply felt or painful to the soul.</note> I could receive from any creature, I sacrifice myself with my whole will to endure it. I am willing to be regarded as a person who is entirely indifferent and utterly contemptible, without demanding any special treatment or any return of trust for my own total trust. Yes, even if my God wills it so, let people believe everything about me that the human mind can imagine or invent; let them have no certainty <gloss>original: "de mon secret"</gloss> <note>French for "of my secret."</note> regarding what happens within me in secret, nor of my faithfulness, nor of my constancy—which, in truth, I cannot possess without the singular assistance of grace. This grace I most fervently implore, so that I may say with truth that God is my everything and shall be so eternally. *Amen*.”

### of Elisabeth of the Child Jesus. Chapter VII.

„...alone, and that it is God alone in whom you can find your rest and your perfection.“

12. (And indeed, this is how it goes; when God places a soul into such suffering, no one can provide comfort until the hour of deliverance arrives.) 14. „The Lord Jesus Christ's insatiable desire for suffering has made a quite extraordinary impression upon me, and moved me to sign this resolution—which I have made before His face—with my blood: namely, that in all sufferings, from whatever side they may come and of whatever kind they may be, I will never say 'it is enough,' nor will I complain about them to any human being. This grace I most earnestly implore, so that I may say with truth that God is my everything and shall be so eternally. Amen.“

Not long after she had composed this, she already had the opportunity to practice it, upon the passing of Lord <term>Renty</term> <note>Gaston de Renty (1611–1649), a French nobleman and influential mystic who served as Elisabeth's spiritual advisor.</note>, who had hitherto supported her so faithfully. ## Chapter Eight.

### Her alternations between Heaven and Hell; in which Bernières supports her through his letters.

->I.<-

Just as the dear <term>Renty</term> had brought her into acquaintance and fellowship with the godly <term>Bernières</term> <note>Jean de Bernières-Louvigny (1602–1659), a French mystic and layman who provided spiritual guidance to many contemporary religious figures.</note>, she also took her special refuge and trust in him after GOD had taken the former from her; she also received no small support from him in her ongoing inner sufferings. Without regard to the specific subjects, we wish to include here several short letters he wrote to her.

> In one, he says: “The pillar and the first stone of your inner building must be faith, or trust in your JESUS, and mistrust of yourself and against your internal insights and light. Swallow these up into your JESUS. Confess and testify before Him that you are unfit to judge whether this light, this sweetness, or this feeling of love comes from Him or not. Ask Him to deal with it according to His will: and then walk with confidence; for surely, He will take care of you.
>
> “The second pillar and the second stone must be the good use of your sufferings, especially the internal ones, and everything that can bring tribulation to the soul. For according to whether one uses such sufferings well or poorly, progress in the spiritual life is promoted. They are the furnace in which the soul is melted; they are the fire in which it is purified to make it conformable to the source of infinite purity; finally, they are what lead the soul to death <note>Here referring to the "death of the self" or "mystical death," the total surrender of the ego to God.</note> in the shortest and surest way.”

The same, namely the understanding, receives without fear and embraces with joy this inner light which comes to it directly from God through an **infused grace**; because God so powerfully impresses the certainty of the truth He gives to it that the will does not stand a moment in doubt whether it should accept it or not. Everything that God works in such a way is supernatural, in that He does it through the operation of the Holy Spirit, without the senses. Now, the souls who walk by this **inner path** are subject to no deception because it is above the senses. And therefore, be entirely at peace.”

## Chapter Nine.

->Two exercises of solitude; wherein various glorious<-
->lights and graces are communicated to her.<-

->I.<-

(It has truly been a laudable and very useful habit among godly souls for
a long time, that those among them whose official duties or other circumstances
did not allow them to constantly attend to spiritual things, alongside
their daily hours of seclusion, occasionally took some six, eight, or more days
for seclusion and dedicated them to God. In complete freedom from all
external occupations, they would occupy themselves only with God, their inner self,
and with Divine things. Experience, and so many undeniable testimonies,
show clearly how God has confirmed these holy seclusions with a thousand-
fold light and blessing for sincere souls, so that godly Protestants should rightly
be stirred to emulation, without being in the least afraid of falling into a Papist
works-righteousness <note>In the 17th and 18th centuries, Protestants who adopted mystical or contemplative practices often faced criticism for "Papist" (Catholic) tendencies, specifically the idea that one could earn salvation through "works" like structured retreats.</note> thereby (a). Our Elisabeth can serve as an
example among others in this, as she not only had this good habit of
secluding herself now and then for such a purpose, but also sometimes had to
give her spiritual director a written report of how she spent these days of
seclusion and what God had communicated to her therein. From some such
reports, we wish to extract only a little here as a sample.)

<note>(a) See § 2 of the following Chapter 10.</note>

Afterward, I had an insight into the annihilation of Jesus Christ, which must be the rule for my own, etc.

> “Jesus Christ has been the sacrifice <term>Schlachtopfer: literally a 'slaughter-offering' or victim of sacrifice, common in 17th-century mystical language to describe Christ’s atonement.</term> for our sins: it is only right that we should be the sacrifice of His pains. Truly, our Savior applies Himself with as much care and love to lead you, to annihilate you, to work in you nakedness <gloss>nudité: nakedness or spiritual poverty</gloss>, divestment, and the eradication of your corrupted life, and to infuse you with His inner, supernatural, and Divine life, as if He had only to do with you alone. What a comfort this is for your soul! and what reason does it not have to entrust itself entirely to such great goodness! Then it is truly well with you. And see, this is the state in which I wish you to be.”

# The Ninth Chapter.
## Two Exercises of Solitude; in which various glorious lights and graces are communicated to her.

->1.<-

(It has truly been a laudable and very useful habit among godly souls for a long time that those among them whose official business or other circumstances did not allow them to constantly attend to spiritual matters, would—alongside their daily hours of seclusion—occasionally take some six, eight, or more days for seclusion <term>Absonderung: a period of spiritual retreat or withdrawal from worldly affairs.</term>, and consecrate them to God. In total freedom from all external occupations, they would occupy themselves only with God, their inner being, and Divine things. Experience and so many undeniable testimonies clearly show how God has confirmed these holy retreats for sincere souls with a thousandfold light and blessing. Therefore, godly Protestants should also be stirred to emulation, without fearing in the least that they might thereby fall into a Papist work-righteousness <note>original: *Papistische Werkheiligkeit*. A Protestant theological concern that outward religious acts might be viewed as "earning" salvation rather than receiving it by grace.</note> (a). Our Elisabeth can serve as an example in this, among others; she not only had this good habit of secluding herself now and then for such a purpose, but also had to give written reports to her spiritual director at times regarding how she spent these days of seclusion and what God had communicated to her therein. From some such reports, we wish to extract only a little here as a sample.)

### Fourth Part. The Life ###

„...only insofar as He sees us in His Son, through the conformity that we must have with Him.

„This gazing of my soul upon **God** must 1) be pure, without admixture of any self-seeking, seeking nothing in heaven or on earth but **God** alone. 2) It must be direct through a naked faith <note>original: "blossen Glauben"—in mystical theology, this refers to a faith stripped of intellectual images or emotional "sensations" of God</note>, which dispossesses the spirit of all its own workings, and causes it to look upon the light through the uncreated light, in a detachment from all inventions of my own spirit, which only darken this Divine beholding and are like a mist before the eyes of the soul, preventing it from clearly beholding the **Sun of Righteousness** <note>A common biblical metaphor for Christ (from Malachi 4:2), emphasizing His role as the source of spiritual light and healing</note>. 3) This contemplation must be simple, in the manner of a dove; that is, without paying heed (or reflecting) neither on the past, nor on the future, nor on the gifts of **God**, in order to take pleasure in them, nor even on the soul’s own gazing, which it must not look upon, so that everything may be for the Beloved. Of a soul that has arrived at this point, one can say that it is perfect, and that, because its eye (a) is simple, its whole body is also light.

„**Fourth Day.** I heard this Inner Word say to me: Because you surrender yourself to Me, I desire that you lie down in Me for rest. Afterward, I had an impression of peace that surpasses all sensation; and I received an inward confidence to find my rest in **God**, in the midst of all the confusion of this life, and despite everything that can torment the soul. There is no peace except in surrender, etc.

„**Sixth Day.** I recognized how very much the grace of the holy childhood of **Jesus** moves a holy soul to a great detachment from this world, and to a state of non-action <note>original: "Nichtwirkung"—a term used in Quietist and mystical traditions to describe a state where the soul ceases its own striving to allow God to act through it</note>, which, while it separates the creature from itself, makes it flexible and willing to follow the commands of its **God**.

„**Eighth Day.** I must have all the more reverence, and consider with so much greater devotion the occupations of the holy soul of **Jesus** with His Father, the less one thinks of it. The sight of this occupation of **Jesus** can serve me as a good means to collect myself again during external occupations, when I look upon the inner ground or spirit with which our Savior performed all these things. And after the work is completed, if perhaps the spirit has been scattered a little from its pure gazing upon **God**, I will seek to place myself back into it through union with the occupation of **Jesus** with His Father. I will then offer up to Him the perfection of this, His Divine occupation, and the purity of His gazing (upon **God**, His heavenly Father), as satisfaction for the impurity of my own gazing, by which I have turned away from this adorable object <note>original: "Vorwurf"—in archaic German, this refers to the object of one's attention or contemplation</note>. When I have brought a work to an end that **God** has commanded me, I will say to Him with our Savior (b): My Father, I have finished the work that You gave me to do,

# Fourth Part. The Life

> „to purify, to restore, to strip bare, to annihilate, to bring to life,
> „to unite, to transform, to deify. <note>These eight verbs describe the traditional stages of the "mystic way," where the soul is first purged of worldly desires and eventually "deified" or united with the Divine nature.</note>

> „In the morning prayer, I looked upon the great mercy which **God** shows to a sinful soul, such as mine is, in that He gives her the opportunity to converse freely and intimately with His Divine Majesty. And although it is the truth that this Divine Savior is always ready to communicate Himself to the soul through His Word and through the powerful draws of His love; yet it happens especially in solitude that He speaks to the heart, and there the soul, hearing Him, answers Him in return; so that this holy time can be called the Time of **God**. Which moved me to say to Him the words that our Savior spoke in the Garden of Gethsemane, though in a completely opposite sense: *This is Your hour, my Lord, this is properly Your time.* <note>Original: "Dies ist Deine Stunde." In the Gospel of Luke (22:53), Jesus says "this is your hour" to those arresting him, referring to the power of darkness. Elisabeth here turns the phrase around to dedicate a specific hour of light and prayer to God.</note> For although all other time is also Yours; yet this time is more especially dedicated to You by Your unworthy handmaid. It is Your time, wherein You wish to show me the great effect of Your power, which, through a beam of Your Divine clarity, can not only dispel the darkness of my understanding but also strengthen my will to surrender myself to You in Your following, and to bind myself to keep You company in all Your <term>states</term>, remaining faithful to You in all Your states into which it might please You to lead me. <note>In 17th-century mysticism, "states" (Stände) refers to the internal dispositions or specific mysteries of Christ’s life, such as His poverty, His hidden life, or His suffering.</note>

> „After I had spent the entire day in darkness and dryness, <note>Spiritual "dryness" refers to a state where a person feels no emotional or spiritual consolation during prayer.</note> the **Lord** placed me in the evening into a state of <term>annihilation</term> in His presence; and I remained in great peace, receiving a very great joy over my nothingness, and that **God** is absolutely Everything, etc. <note>"Annihilation" (Vernichtigung) is a technical term in mysticism for the total silencing of the ego so that God may act fully within the person.</note>

<margin>(a) Proverbs 8:31. (b) John 16:13.</margin>
> „Fourth Day. O **God**! what love, that You became flesh, not only to dwell among us, but to dwell in our innermost being; wherein You communicate Yourself in such a manner that the human spirit cannot grasp. O how powerful, piercing, and delightful are the arrows of Divine love, with which You pierce my heart, when You say to my soul that Your glory and Your love are enough for her; when You call her Your beloved; and when she answers You in return: *My Beloved!* O who can express the sweetness and loveliness of this language of love, which is but a single word in expression, but in sense and essence contains more than can be expressed? You continue also to give my soul testimonies of Your love; You assure her that Your (a) delights are to be with her; and ask her whether she also does not wish to find her pleasure in being with You? You give Yourself to her anew as the Word, and promise her that through Your Holy Spirit You wish to (b) teach her all truth.

<margin>(c) Matthew 8:20.</margin>

# Fourth Part. The Life

> „**Eighth Day.** I was occupied with the effects of unifying love, which always moves toward bringing everything into unity, and making of **GOD** and the soul (a) one and the same. But since there is now an infinite inequality between **GOD** and the creature, Divine love is always intent upon destroying the soul and annihilating it in all its workings, until it has brought the soul to a state of such perfect annihilation <note>original: *Vernichtigung*. In mystical theology, this refers to "self-annihilation"—the process of emptying oneself of all ego, desires, and self-will so that only God remains.</note> that nothing more stands in the way of its intent to bring the soul to unity and perfection in **GOD**; in which the loving soul, faithful to her heavenly Bridegroom, concurs with all her power, in that she consents and lets herself be destroyed and annihilated in perfect submission to the workings of this unifying love, which causes her to wish and seek with all her power for the separation from all things, even to the (b) complete loss of herself; which is necessary for her to reach that degree of unity where **Jesus Christ** wants us to be, and for which He prayed to His Father when He says (c): **I sanctify myself for them, so that they also may be sanctified in the truth: I in them, and You in me, so that they may be perfected into one**, etc.

> „**Ninth Day.** Just as love demands and works unity, so it also demands conformity, uniformity, and the over-forming <note>original: *Ueberformung*. This suggests a transformation where the soul's own form is superseded or "over-molded" by the form of Christ.</note> of the will, in such a way that a truly loving soul must have only one and the very same will with the beloved object <note>original: *Vorwurf*. In this archaic context, it means the "object" of one's attention or affection, specifically God.</note>. Whereby I have recognized that my soul, according to the Divine will, must accept everything with indifference, the darkness as well as the light, the bitter as well as the sweet, contempt as well as honor.

> „And even if the soul, in her highest indifference <note>original: *Gleichgültigkeit*. This is "holy indifference," a state where the soul is so surrendered to God's will that it has no personal preference for comfort or suffering, seeking only what God ordains.</note>—which must be her conduct—were permitted to choose something, she would have to choose what our **Lord Jesus Christ** chose for Himself; because the purpose of **GOD** the Father is that we should be entirely conformed to the image of the Son of His love.

> „**Tenth Day.** I perceived that the true happiness of the Saints in heaven consists in this: that **GOD** is everything in them, and that they are everything in **GOD**. In Him they are so completely lost that they can never reflect upon themselves. Therefore it happens that their joy is not caused by the sight of their own well-being and their eternal glory, but by the knowledge they have that **GOD** is; from this arises the love they have for this infinitely adorable and lovely **GOD**, in whom alone they have their pleasure, and in whom they will be eternally swallowed up, etc.

> „When the soul is perfectly purified, then **GOD** is to her a very clear mirror, in which she sees all things in an excellent manner.

> „Just as it is necessary, in order to maintain the life of the body, that one unceasingly draws breath and breathes it out again; even so, to maintain the true life of my soul—

### 2. Another excerpt from a six-day exercise of seclusion <note>original: *Absonderung*. This refers to a spiritual retreat where one is "set apart" from the world for prayer.</note>, written in the year 1655.

> „**First Day.** The **GOD** of infinite goodness has, from the morning of this first day, without looking at what I am, revealed Himself to my soul through a living touch, which has pierced even the innermost part of my heart; whereby an impression was given to me of these His words (a): **Go out from your country**, that is, go out from the fellowship of all creatures, and of everything that is created; separate your thoughts, desires, and inclinations from everything; go out from yourself, and abandon yourself entirely; enter into Me, who am your origin, your final end, and your perfect happiness.
>
> „Upon the insight of this truth, and upon the feeling that this loving and enchanting address caused in my soul, she received a vehement desire to enter into **GOD** through **Jesus Christ**, and also to let Him enter into her: to which she felt herself moved so much more powerfully as it was shown to her how almost all the world rejects this Divine Savior, who out of love for us annihilated Himself <note>original: *vernichtiget*. This refers to *kenosis*, the "self-emptying" of Christ described in the New Testament.</note>, etc.
>
> „**Second Day.** The most kind **GOD** has communicated and revealed Himself to my soul this morning in such a way that I find myself entirely unable to say almost the slightest thing of what I have experienced. I suddenly saw the unspeakable majesty to which the soul is elevated; and the incomprehensible goods which she enjoys when she is returned to and immersed, or rather swallowed up, in **GOD**; where she is as if in her element, as if in her center and perfect rest; where she acts without distraction, and suffers without any restlessness or movement. She is, she lives, and she acts in **GOD**, but in an entirely Divine way. She is not only conformed to **GOD** through the removal of all unlikeness, and she is not only transformed into Him through an annihilation of her thoughts, her desires, her inclinations, and her intentions; but she is made entirely Divine <note>original: *divinisée*</note>, to such an extent that she can say with truth that she (b) no longer lives, but that **GOD** alone lives in her through **Jesus Christ**. Yet one must rather keep silent here than speak poorly, because after all, all words are far too weak and imperfect to say anything becoming of such an exalted and Divine state.“

# Fourth Section. The Life

> „At the moment I partook of the <term>Lord's Supper</term> <note>original: *Abendmahl*. This refers to the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note>, God revealed His presence in the depths of my soul with a secret and tender touch; which was at the same time so powerful and penetrating, as God effectively showed me the infinite love He bears for me, so that one must greatly wonder how one can still remain in existence and not be destroyed by this effect, since the soul sees this infinitely majestic God entirely within itself, and itself entirely in God. At the same time, the vision the soul has of its unworthiness causes it to sink into shame; but it is also thereby ignited in fervent love, as it perceives the overflowing abundance of Divine Love, which so humbles this highest Majesty that He not only enters into a covenant with the soul, but also wills that the union should be so perfect and so intimate that the soul (a) should be one and the same with Him.

> „O God! who can say what happens in that soul to whom You have thus opened Yourself and united Yourself? Oh, what sweetnesses! what raptures! what <term>annihilations</term> <note>original: *Vernichtigungen*. A mystical term for the "nothingness" of the self in the presence of God.</note>! But what torment and pains does it also bring, that one cannot respond to this love of one's God according to one's duty and desire! What would the soul not want to do or suffer, if only this Divine Love might be increased within it! And how pleasant to it is everything that is most contrary to nature, since through the sacrifice (or <term>self-denial</term>) it practices therein, such things can be useful to it in reaching its ultimate goal! because it desires nothing so much as its own destruction, so that it may be entirely its God's, and entirely perfected in Him, and for Him, and that He may be everything in it that He wills to be there.

> „I look upon myself before God as a monster of pride and infidelity.

> „**Third Day.** Our Savior said to my soul: I have gone out from my Father to come to you: will you then not go out from yourself to come to Me?

> „Afterward, I found myself in a state wherein I had great joy that my God is everything and that I am nothing. In this nothingness, I saw that this God of Love took His pleasure and rejoiced in me, since I was, as it seemed to me, entirely surrendered to His power, so that He could freely do in me and with me whatever He willed; and I said with an expansion of my heart, and with a deep peace in all the powers of my soul, these words (b): **Love holds me in its free power; to Love I have surrendered myself forever.** So be it, O You Divine and pure Love; I implore You by Yourself, make these my words true!

# The Eleventh Chapter.
## How she was elected as the <term>Superior</term> <note>original: *Vorsteherin*. The head of the convent or religious community.</note> of the convent; and what virtues she practiced in this office.

->1.<-

Afterwards, our Elisabeth was elected as the superior of the house, against her will. However great her desire was for <term>self-denial</term> <note>original: *Verläugnungen*. The spiritual practice of setting aside one's own ego and desires.</note> and suffering, she initially could not bring herself at all to take this cross upon herself; instead, she did everything in her power to avert this blow; until finally, seeing that all was in vain, she threw herself down in solitude before God's face and, as a tool in the hand of the master craftsman, resignedly surrendered herself into the hands of Jesus Christ.

->2.<-

And so she now had to be mindful of how best to unite <term>Martha with Mary</term> <note>A common biblical reference to Luke 10:38–42, where Martha represents the active life of service and work, and Mary represents the contemplative life of prayer and listening.</note>; and she gave herself over to outward duties in such a way that she lost nothing of her inner devotion in the process. She left everything in God’s hands as if she had nothing to do; and yet she worked with such great diligence as if she expected everything to depend on her own industriousness.

->3.<-

At the beginning of this service, it happened that she wrote down the following:

> „I have given myself without reservation to the Lord Jesus, to be henceforth
> „entirely subject to His power and surrendered to His Divine Will, for
> „whatever He might please to do with me and in me, in time and eternity.
> „His infinite goodness has given me an inward assurance that He will,
> „though I am unworthy, accept me to be entirely His own, and to belong to Him
> „more than ever, and in a singular way.
> „I renounce forever the desire to be anything in myself, or in any single
> „creature; which I sign in the presence of the adorable <term>Trinity</term> <note>original: *Dreyeinheit*. The Christian doctrine of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note>,
> „the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.”

->4.<-

And in another place: „I have perceived with what persistence,
„faithfulness, earnestness, and perseverance I must give myself over to prayer, and
„take as much time as I possibly can to devote myself to it, and that constantly.

### Fourth Part. The Life

> „For I cannot doubt that God specifically demands of me that

5. In this office, which she held for nine years over three different terms, she showed more than ever that she possessed a firm intellect, a thorough judgment, a <term>manly courage</term> <note>original: *männlichen Muth*. In historical spiritual texts, this phrase refers to strength of character, fortitude, and rational resolve, qualities then considered "masculine" but highly praised in holy women.</note>, a loving heart, a burning zeal, and a beautiful and easy way of expressing herself; she was modest, sincere, charitable, watchful, precise, quiet, and always master of herself. And for all these virtues, as well as for the successful outcome of her undertakings, she gave honor to God alone.

<margin>(a) Psalm 119, 105.</margin>
The Divine Law was her earnest and constant meditation, and she regarded it as the safest rule of her life and conduct; so that she could well say, with David (a): **Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light on my path.**

6. She was wonderfully devout and precise in observing external <term>divine service</term> <note>original: *Gottesdienst*. This refers to the structured liturgical prayers and communal worship of the convent.</note>. Often she went to bed late in the evening due to necessary official business; yet early in the morning, she was without fail present again at the usual morning prayer, even though she was sometimes so burdened and weak that her body almost succumbed because of the force she exerted upon it to present it as a living sacrifice in the presence of God.

7. She was indeed uncommonly loving toward those under her authority; however, when yielding (regarding the <term>Rules of the Order</term> <note>The formal regulations and spiritual laws that govern the daily life of a monastic community.</note>) could lead to a bad habit or consequence, she was immovable against all the pleadings of "nature," which sometimes hides under the pretext of utility, necessity, convenience, or even love. For she instantly detected all the deceits of self-love, and generally answered all representations arising from nature with nothing other than a cold and serious silence, from which her mind could be sufficiently understood.

8. Just as she was convinced that her strength was the strength of her God, she saw herself as if all-powerful in those circumstances that concerned the general or specific welfare of our common dwelling; and when she was certain of the will of God in a matter, she became invincible; all difficulties, all opposition, and all human prestige did not affect her in the least. If one said to her: "How, dear Mother, people will say this or that about you," she looked at us with an eye of contempt and answered only with a sigh: "Yes, is that still stuck in your heart?" <note>original: *Ja, sitzt es euch auch noch da?* A rebuke suggesting the questioner is still too concerned with worldly reputation or "the self" rather than God's will.</note>

9. The delay of an undertaken matter did not weary her constancy; and a poor outcome did not make her discouraged, because she expected everything from God.

...[she] acted. She often said: Nothing proves the greatness of God and the uselessness of the creature as much as when He allows a matter to succeed when it seems entirely lost, and takes such paths toward it that (in our opinion) should only be fit to destroy it. For this was one of her main rules: that the works of God always meet with the most resistance; so much so, that in all her undertakings, the greatest obstacles were good signs to her that God had His hand in them.

## The Twelfth Chapter.

->Concerning her love for her neighbor, in regard to both the body and the soul.<-

->I.<-

How her love for her neighbor—both in physical and spiritual matters—was constituted, we can express briefly and powerfully enough with five words which we found recorded in her own hand. Love, she says, must be immeasurable, pure, heartfelt, generous <term>magnificent</term> <note>original: *magnifique*. In this context, it refers to a "magnanimity" or a noble-hearted, grand style of giving that reflects God's own abundance.</note>, and invincible.

2. Her compassion for the poor was beyond comprehension. She exhorted and moved everyone who interacted with her to show charity toward them. Various persons placed their charitable gifts into Mother Elisabeth’s hands to be distributed to the poor; which she then did with such great attentiveness, discernment, and zeal that the most wretched were always allotted the most.

3. She almost always inquired about their specific needs; she gave them clothes, linen, and shoes; she paid their house rent; she provided them with all necessities during their illnesses; she had them work and produce items that she herself did not need in the least, simply so they would not fall into the danger of sin through idleness; she even went so far as to seek out employment for them; yes, she herself brought them bread, broth, and whatever else was available.

4. She had her own box in which she deposited the money for the poor; and when there was not much left in it, she said: "If I could make <term>pistoles</term> <note>original: *Pistolen*. These were gold coins common in Europe; Elisabeth is poetically expressing her desire to sacrifice her own life-blood to provide for the needy.</note> from my own blood, the box would always be full." She also occasionally used the alms money on hand to purchase and distribute a large number of devotional books.

<margin>(a) 1 Corinthians 13:7.</margin>
5. Furthermore, she showed on all occasions that her love, according to the Apostle's description, was one that (a) bears all things, believes all things, and hopes all things.

### Fourth Part. The Life

She always defended those who were absent; she justified and excused everyone, unless the evil was entirely manifest; and she felt sorry when the guilty themselves revealed the faults she had wished to cover. She was always inclined to believe the good. And although she possessed much understanding and judgment, she nonetheless very easily believed the good of others. She was so convinced that God could change the hearts of His creatures in a moment that, however unlikely it might appear, she nevertheless believed without difficulty that a person today no longer possessed the fault in which they had been seen yesterday.

6. But her love for the soul of her neighbor was even greater than her love for what concerned their outward state. She placed herself truly in the breach between God and the sinner. Several people achieved conversion through her prayer. When someone spoke with her about a certain person who had previously lived in gross vices but afterwards, by means of her prayer, lived holily and died a blessed death, she said: "It is true that he cost me much." <note>This suggests that Mother Elisabeth viewed her intense intercessory prayer as a form of spiritual labor or "payment" offered for the souls of others.</note>

7. She spent much time with troubled souls; and it was enough to gain her favor simply to be numbered among them. She sought to comfort them, not only through her conversation but also through her letters. See here in what manner she wrote to certain persons who sought counsel from her in their sufferings:

8. In another letter she says: "I feel your condition, which not only nails you yourself to the cross, but keeps me nailed there with you. And because He (b) hears the prayer of the poor, present yourself as such before Him; then He will grant the desire of your heart for His glory much sooner than you can put together the words to present it to Him."

9. She even loved her enemies, according to the word of the Savior, and prayed for those who persecuted her. One day she said to a certain person who had caused her some vexation and injustice: "Today you were the first for whom I prayed." And it was her custom to offer her prayers to God for those, she said, who helped her get into heaven through the sufferings they caused her.

3. 4. Another young clergyman, who was by no means in a position to instruct Mother Elisabeth, once spoke to her in a very impetuous manner about various things in which he thought she was failing. She immediately threw herself at his feet, with the request that he might continue to tell her what **GOD** wanted from her; and, without trying to dissuade him from his conceived prejudice, she only promised that she would be intent on improving herself in those matters. This man himself later made this humiliation known, to her praise.

5. Another pious man, who had a certain soul under his guidance who claimed extraordinary holiness and revelations, came to her once and reported that **GOD** had revealed to this holy soul (as he esteemed her) that she, Mother Elisabeth, and the **Lord of Renty** <note>Gaston de Renty (1611–1649), a famous French nobleman and mystic known for his extreme piety and works of charity.</note>, were appointed by **GOD** for great things for His honor. Mother Elisabeth, however, gave this pious man no other answer than to look at him with a smiling face, giving him to understand that she only mocked this revelation, and that this person was certainly deceived. However poorly this man took such a reaction at the time—showing himself not a little offended that she mocked **Divine things** (as he viewed this revelation)—the outcome soon showed that the presumed saint had been miserably led astray by a foreign spirit <note>In the context of 18th-century spiritual discernment, a "foreign spirit" refers to a delusion or a demonic influence masquerading as divine inspiration.</note>.

6. We have found the following insight, which **GOD** gave to her, written in her own hand; it expresses very well the danger into which the praise of men brings us:

> Those, she says, who honor and praise us, do exactly as if someone took a person and placed them on the narrow edge of a very steep place, or on the summit of a high mountain, where they are in obvious danger of falling down.

In another place, she writes thus: When the soul remembers its imperfections and its natural inclinations toward evil, it is precisely then that our good **GOD** also remembers it, shows it His graces, and stands by it. But when the soul has forgotten its misery and its corruption, then the **LORD** our **GOD** forgets it as well, and turns the gaze of His grace away from it; for He does not wish to look upon lies, but only upon the truth, etc.

# Chapter Fourteen.
## Concerning her spiritual dying-away and annihilation. <note>In mystical theology, "annihilation" (Vernichtigung) refers to the total surrender of the individual will and ego, allowing the soul to be completely filled by God's presence.</note>

1. Concerning the spiritual death and annihilation of this precious soul, we can give almost no other report than through her own words, which we found recorded by her own hand, because she was otherwise very careful to keep hidden what was happening in her interior life. In one place, she writes thus:

> "Our **LORD** has given me an insight into that which I am; into that
> "which I am capable of; into that which I deserve; and into the ground of corruption that is
> "within me: which has given me a great desire to separate myself from these things
> "in all matters; and it makes me pray, with Saint Catherine of Genoa (a):
> "Quickly! quickly! draw me out of my being, and place me
> "into the fulfillment of my end, for which I was created."

2. In another writing, she says: "I have received many lights <note>In this context, "lights" (Lichter) refers to moments of sudden spiritual understanding or divine revelation.</note> which have moved me to earnestly desire and pray that I might be placed in the blessed state of death, for which my whole heart yearns; because **GOD** has testified to my heart that I shall never be that which He wants me to be in Him, so long as I am still something in myself. I have seen that this 'I myself' is such a terrifying and loathsome thing that I would wish to lie continually on my knees and beg the Savior **JESUS** that He might annihilate it forever.

3. “In annihilation, **God** builds the throne of His glory; there He exercises His power; and there He satisfies His love.

> “Through annihilation, this gracious **God** lives in us in the fullness of His love; and through the same, He causes us to live in Him, through the power and perfection of this very love: so much so that, when a soul has reached the point of complete annihilation, **God** truly speaks to her what He otherwise says to His beloved Son (a): *Today I have begotten you*; <note>original: "Heute habe ich Dich gezeuget." Is it not therefore a pity and a blindness that we do not love with a holy zeal and seek all means that can lead us to this blessed state?”

4. “**God** is the promised land toward which we must strive: but to arrive there, one must go through the wilderness of annihilation, which brings with it a strange nakedness and separation from all things.”

->of Elisabeth of the Child Jesus. Chapter XIV.<-

...sacrificial victim <note>original: "Schlachtopfer." In mystical theology, this refers to the "victim soul" who offers their suffering to God.</note> which must be offered to God by all creatures; as she also expresses this somewhere with these words:

> “Since I have given myself to God as a sacrificial victim, I must imagine that everyone has a right to help me carry out the total offering thereof to His Divine Majesty, in such a way that I must look with pleasure upon all adversities and mortifications <term>mortifications: the spiritual practice of "dying" to one's own desires and ego through self-denial</term> that I shall receive, from wherever they may come, as so many useful blows to completely kill that which might still live in me. I must also strive to inflict this blessed death upon myself, without which my burnt offering cannot be completed. For God expects this, so that He may consume it in the holy fire and in the ardent flames of His love.”

7. Regarding the respect of men, she cared so little for it that she used to say on such occasions: "If all creatures were for us, but God were against us, how miserable we would be! But if all creatures are against us, and God is only for us, what have we to fear?"
As a result, we have also found the following words, written in her own hand, which sufficiently show the desire she had to become more nothing in the eyes of creatures, so that God would be glorified through them:

> “All creatures,” says David <note>A reference to Psalm 19 or the general themes of the Psalms of David regarding God's glory in creation.</note>, “proclaim the glory of the Lord; and as for me, I say with all my heart—to contribute something to this glory—I wish with great inclination of my heart that all creatures may know and proclaim my lowliness and my miseries, and help me in every way to throw myself into the abyss of my nothingness, out of which I fear I might emerge through my pride.”

8. She sometimes said that those who are truly dead <note>original: "Abgestorbenen," referring to those who have achieved "mystical death" or total detachment from the world.</note> do not speak of themselves, neither for good nor for evil: and this was one of her wisdoms, that she never said anything about herself, just as if she had never existed. She never justified herself, no matter what might be thought of her; and in various such occurrences, which must have affected her quite sensitively, and in which she might have spoken only a single word to let it be known that she was right—indeed, to clearly prove that she had acted with good deliberation, without stubbornness or prejudice, and with no other intention than the glory of God—she did not even make a gesture <note>original: "Mine," meaning a facial expression or outward sign.</note> by which anyone could have arrived at other thoughts about her. And in this way, she remained in the greatest peace and silence, and let everyone think of her what they wished.

# The Fifteenth Chapter.
## More concerning her spiritual death and annihilation, in the imitation and union with the annihilation of Jesus Christ. The new life that follows this death.

->I.<-

We have also found in her own hand two decrees (or judicial sentences) of death which were given to her: one from Divine Love, and the other through the most adorable Trinity. Behold the first one here:

> 2. “So it shall then finally happen, and from this moment on, that I shall die without favor and without mercy. The final decree for this has been given by Divine Love, with this content: That nature shall be entirely destroyed in all its movements of the sensual life <term>sensual life: in this mystical context, it refers to the life of the physical senses and the egoic 'self' which seeks its own comfort</term>, which stands directly opposed to the life of grace through Jesus Christ and through His Divine Spirit. To that end, I must completely forget myself, as a thing that no longer is, and that no longer should be. And whenever I still perceive myself, it must always happen with an eye of contempt and of loathing, without ever keeping my eyes fixed on myself to seek myself. In such a way that I will hate everything that nature loves, and love everything that it hates, in a spirit of death, of annihilation <note>original: 'Vernichtigung'. A central concept in 17th and 18th-century mysticism, referring to the process of making the 'self' nothing so that God can be 'everything' within the soul.</note>, of joy, and of peace in the Holy Spirit; supporting myself, through simple and bare faith, upon the power and strength of our Lord Jesus Christ, in whom is all my hope and my total trust, as in my only All, who is given to me through the benevolence and through the unspeakable love of the Heavenly Father, to the end that He, as much as it may happen, may be entirely mine, just as He is entirely the Father’s; and that I, through a similar mutual love, may also be entirely His; which love, through the holiest bond of His Divine Spirit, makes me one with all these three adorable Persons. Amen.”

3. The second decree, on account of the most Holy Trinity, is of this content: “During my last exercises, the final decree of death, unto myself and all creatures, was given to me by the most holy and adorable Trinity.

> “The Eternal Father, as my Creator, wills that I acknowledge and honor His free sovereignty; sacrificing my life to Him, through the submission of the same to His power and to His purpose for me.

> “The Son, Jesus Christ, my Savior, demands, by virtue of justice, that I should die, because He has died for me, and I would be more ungrateful than can be expressed, if I refused to [offer] a human and... <meta>The text breaks off here; the catchword 'elen-' suggests the next page begins with a word like 'elendes' (wretched/miserable) or 'elendigen' (miserable/pathetic).</meta>

<summary>This page records two "decrees of death" written by Elisabeth, which are spiritual commitments to total self-annihilation and surrender to the Trinity. She describes the necessity of destroying the "sensual life" to allow for a life of grace and union with God.</summary>

### Part Four. The Life of Elisabeth, etc.

> “...to give this wretched life to Him who gave a completely perfect and Divine one for me.
> 
> “The Holy Spirit also commands absolutely that I should no longer have any life of my own; because I have nothing in me that is not entirely contrary to Him, and so long as I still live <note>referring to the 'ego' or 'natural life' rather than physical death</note>, He cannot work freely in my soul, where He wishes to find a vacancy and a total emptying <term>emptying: often called 'kenosis' in theology, the act of clearing out one's own desires to make room for God</term>, so that He may communicate to me the fullness of His grace through the perfection of His supernatural workings.

4. > “Since I have now heard this concerning these three most adorable Persons <note>The Holy Trinity</note>, I have accepted this just and adorable judicial decree with the highest willingness; and I offer myself from the innermost depths of my heart to take upon myself this death of grace, which is carried out by the hand of love, and for the sake of love.
> 
> “And in this way, considering that I am bound to die, I will from now on regard myself as a sacrificial victim dedicated to being offered up; and in all occurring events that are contrary to my natural feelings, I will rejoice, remembering that these are so many blows that take my life from me and help me toward this blessed death, which must precede the sacrifice. Therefore, I shall be grateful to all persons who will be helpful in assisting me to die to myself, in order to give myself to my God, to whom I desire to belong as much through love as I belong to Him through justice.”

5. > “And because there is or can be nothing in me that is not His, I irrevocably desire never to do anything except for Him, performing everything to that end in the spirit of humility, of mortification <term>mortification: the spiritual practice of 'dying to' worldly desires or the ego</term>, and of love. (1) Of **humility**; looking at what I am and what I can do; rejoicing that God is everything to me; recognizing His infinite majesty through my own lowliness. (2) Of **mortification**; through which I separate myself from myself and from all seeking of self-love, which must honor the holiness of God through its complete destruction. (3) Of **love**; voluntarily and fully submitting myself to the holy workings of the Spirit of God, to whose guidance I will abandon myself every moment, out of recognition and veneration of His free power and the might of His love. *I die daily* <note>original: 'Ich ſterbe täglich' from 1 Corinthians 15:31</note>, says Saint Paul; and I say even more: I will die without ceasing.”

6. We also add what the dear Bernières <note>Jean de Bernières-Louvigny (1602–1659), a French mystic and treasurer of France who was a spiritual father to many 'interior' souls</note> wrote to our Elisabeth regarding this same state; which also seems to be an answer to the preceding two Divine judicial decrees, which she undoubtedly sent to him:

> “As I see it, you have felt the stroke of death, that is, the stroke of love. I pray to God that He may be your perpetual reproach, and that you may be entirely His, in everything that can cause you suffering. Meanwhile, be untroubled; *in patience you shall possess your soul* <note>original Latin/Greek reference: Luke 21:19</note>, and you shall say to God that *it is in your hands* <note>original reference: Psalm 119:109</note>.”

# of Elisabeth of the Child Jesus. Chapter XV.

“...our Lord Jesus Christ, the God-man <note>original: "Gottmenschen"; a theological term referring to Christ being both fully God and fully human</note>, who has revealed Himself in my soul in various ways, as it has pleased His infinite goodness.”

12. In another [letter] she says: “It has been shown to me that when a soul wishes to struggle against a temptation or overcome certain difficulties through its own strength and through the workings of its natural understanding, it acts just like David when he tried to overcome Goliath in the armor of Saul. For all its natural cleverness is more of a hindrance than a help. If the soul wishes to carry away the victory, it must strip itself bare, like the young David, and take no other weapon than the living stone, which is the power of Jesus Christ. Through the merits of His five wounds, and through the power of His might—which was brought to nothing in the weakness of our flesh—He will make the soul victorious over the world, over the devil, and over the flesh.”

13. Once she asked the young daughters of the provost <note>original: "Probstöchter"; daughters of a high-ranking cleric or administrative official</note> by which path they desired to go to God? After each of them had answered according to her own inclination, she said: “And as for me, I will choose a tiny little path, namely, **Nothingness**; in this path, God does with His creature whatever He wills, without resistance.”

14. How faithfully she walked in this path can be seen from a letter that the pious Bernières <note>Jean de Bernières-Louvigny (1602–1659), a French mystic and influential lay spiritual director</note> wrote to her; [which we will not include in this extract, however, because it has already been printed separately in German, but we merely wish to mention it (a)].

15. (Through spiritual annihilation <note>original: "Vernichtigung"; a mystical term for the total surrender of the self/ego to God</note>, one is led into the wonders of the spiritual life, which consist in the renewal of the mysteries and states of the life of Jesus Christ. How deeply she understood this, she expresses with the following words:)

> “I have recognized the state in which my soul must stand so that it may fully agree with the purpose that the Son of God, my lovely Savior, has revealed to me; namely, that He wishes to be born in me, and thereafter, through the workings of grace and love, to renew in me all the mysteries or states of life which He passed through by this same love in the days of His flesh.”

16. It is likely that our Elisabeth sent this insight to Bernières; for he explains this truth to her thus:

> “When the soul is entirely annihilated, then Jesus Christ is and exists [therein]; and the creature (namely, the soul) is no more, lives no more, and acts no more. This is the highest degree of perfec—”

<note>(a) This can be found in *The Hidden Life*, Book IV, Letter XLIV.</note>

7. "You have done very well," he said: "I sent them all to you at once for that very reason, to see if your curiosity <note>original: "Fürwitz"; in this context, it refers to a restless intellectual desire to consume information rather than meditating deeply</note> was still so lively as to want to satisfy itself by reading them all one after another."

8. > „Just as You, o my Lord, she says somewhere to God, have let me know that one must, through a blessed necessity, die and separate oneself from all things, especially from oneself, so that one may unite with You, the fountain of all goodness; so I also will, whenever it pleases You, You my sole center, begin from this moment on to leave everything out of love, and live in this world as if I were not in it. 9. > „Lord, that is my purpose, to part forever from all creatures <term>creatures: in mystical writing, this refers to all created things—people, objects, or worldly comforts—as opposed to the Creator</term>, whom I deem unworthy to possess any part of my love, because they are (well understood) only a pure nothingness, and not suited to satisfy my heart, which is created for You. Should their false appearance, or their deceptive lure, seek to cheat me, I will take my refuge in You, You highest Truth, who will then, whenever it pleases You, let me know, in the light You have already shared with me, that everything which appears most beautiful to my senses in creatures is nothing other than a shadow and vapor, which in the very moment it appears, also passes away again.“

10. ### [The Life] of Elisabeth of the Child Jesus. Chapter 15.

Mm
<meta>Catchword: [perfection]</meta>

“...our Lord Jesus Christ, the **God-man**, who has revealed Himself in my soul in various ways, as it has pleased His infinite goodness.”

12. In another [letter] she says: “It has been shown to me that when a soul wants to fight against a temptation, or wants to overcome some difficulties through its own strengths and through the workings of its natural understanding, it then acts exactly like David, who wanted to overcome Goliath in the armor of Saul; for all its natural skill is more a hindrance than a help. If it wishes to carry away the victory, it must strip itself, like little David, and take no other weapons than the **living stone**, which is the power of Jesus Christ. Through the merits of His five wounds, and through the power of His might—which was annihilated into the weakness of our flesh <note>This refers to the "Kenosis" or the self-emptying of Christ to become human.</note>—He will make the soul victorious over the world, over the devil, and over the flesh.”

13. Once she asked the young postulants <note>original: "Probtöchter," referring to women testing their vocation before becoming novices.</note> by which paths they desired to go to God? After each of them had answered according to her own inclination, she said: “And as for me, I will choose a little pathway, namely, **Nothingness**; in this, God makes of His creature what He will, without resistance.”

14. How faithfully she walked in this path can be seen from a letter that the pious Bernières <note>Jean de Bernières-Louvigny (1602–1659), a prominent French mystic and layperson who influenced many spiritual writers of the era.</note> wrote to her; [which we, however, because it is already printed separately in German, will not include in this extract, but only make mention of (a)].

15. (Through spiritual **annihilation** <term>Vernichtigung: a mystical term for stripping away the ego and self-will to allow God to act entirely through the person</term> one is introduced into the wonders of the spiritual life, which consist in the renewal of the mysteries and states of the life of Jesus Christ. How thoroughly she perceived this, she expresses with the following words:)

> “I have recognized the form in which my soul must stand, so that it might fully agree with the purpose that the Son of God, my lovable Savior, has revealed to me; namely, that He wants to be born in me, and accordingly, through the workings of grace and love, to renew in me all the mysteries or states that He passed through by this same love in the days of His flesh.”

16. Our Elisabeth likely sent this insight to Bernières; for he explains this truth to her as follows:

> “When the soul is completely annihilated, then Jesus Christ is and remains; and the creature” (namely the soul) “is no more, lives no more, and acts no more. This is the last degree of perfection...”

### Fourth Part. The Life

-> „Let us be entirely for **GOD**; and may He also be entirely for us. I shall neglect nothing that is in my power to do for you, before His countenance, for His glory, for your comfort, and for my own salvation.“<-

7. The dear **Renty** <note>Gaston de Renty (1611–1649) was a French nobleman and famous mystic who, despite being a layman, provided spiritual direction to many, including Elisabeth.</note> once sent our **Elisabeth** a great number of very spiritual maxims. When he came to see her, he asked whether she had read them all? She answered: No; rather, she had taken only one each day. You have done very well, he said: I sent them all to you at once for that very reason, to see if your curiosity <note>original: "Fürwitz," meaning a meddling or over-eager desire for new information.</note> were still so lively that you would seek to satisfy yourself by reading them all one after another.

8. > „Just as You, O my **Lord**, she says somewhere to **GOD**, have let me recognize that one must, through a blissful necessity, die and depart from all things, especially from oneself, so that one may unite with You, the fountain of all goodness; so then I also will—whenever it pleases You, You my sole center—begin from this moment on to leave everything behind out of love, and live in this world as if I were not in it. From now on, I will set my heart and my affections in heaven, as it is the dwelling place of Your eternity and of my bliss in You; to such an extent that hereafter I will look upon my body as a shadow, or as a borrowed body, which shall dwell on earth for the sole purpose of doing there what You shall command it, and otherwise shall not move or act, except through the supernatural impulse of Your holy love.

9. > „**Lord**, this is my purpose: to separate myself forever from all creatures, whom I deem unworthy to possess any part of my love, because they are (rightly understood) only a pure nothingness, and not suited to satisfy my heart, which is created for You. Should their false appearance, or their deceptive allure, ever try to deceive me, I will take my refuge in You, You highest Truth; You will then, when it pleases You, let me recognize in the light that You have already shared with me, that everything in creatures which appears most beautiful to my senses is nothing other than a shadow and vapor, which vanishes again in the very moment it appears.“

10. Throughout her whole life, her primary devotion was directed toward the annihilations <note>The term "annihilation" (German: *Vernichtung*) in this mystical context refers to *Kenosis*, the self-emptying of Christ to become human and His ultimate humility.</note> of **Jesus Christ** in His incarnation and childhood:
> „I have perceived, she writes somewhere to her director, the height, the depth, the breadth, and the length of the annihilation in the infant **Jesus Christ**, to whom I must strive to make myself conformable, according to all the capacity He might please to impart to me for that purpose.“

11. In another writing she says:
> „It is shown quite clearly to me how necessary this annihilated Word <note>The "Word" (Logos) refers to Christ; the "annihilated Word" refers to the Word made flesh in a state of utter humility.</note> is for us; what inestimable treasures we find in Him; how highly we are obligated to keep ourselves united with the same through gratitude, through love, and through imitation. In all the insights that have been given to me, I have at all times had as my pattern, my guide, and my foundation
