8. „Just as You, O my Lord, she says somewhere to God, have let me recognize that one must, through a blessed necessity, die and depart from all things, especially from oneself, so that one may unite oneself with You, the fountain of all goodness; so then I also will; when it pleases You, You my sole center point <note>original: "Mittelpunct"</note>, begin from this moment on to leave everything out of love, and to live in this world as if I were not in it. ### -> Fourth Part. The Life <-

„...[union] <note>original: "sung"; likely the end of the word "Vereinigung" (union) or "Vollendung" (perfection) from the previous page.</note>, because JESUS Christ works the very same mysteries that He alone worked here on earth, as He suffers, works, walks, speaks, and" (in the annihilated soul) „leads exactly the same temporal life in which He lived on earth. And this is the greatest wonder: that while JESUS is in eternity, immersed in the **bosom of His Father**, where He lives in a completely glorious life, He nevertheless begins entirely anew to become Man, to be born, and to live in time, just as He lived during the days of His mortal life. These are the wonders of the **Mystical Life**; and this is the great masterpiece which God works in those souls who are faithful in annihilating themselves and renewing themselves in God."

17. Although we have no remaining testimony from Elisabeth from which we might see specifically how this was fulfilled in her, nevertheless, because God is a faithful God whose word never fails when the creature is faithful on its part, we have a certain kind of assurance: because God faithfully preserved this soul, He certainly worked great things within her.

18. However, among her writings we found a small note written on December 28, 1660, from which we see that the Lord, on that very day, made her a partaker of His **holy and Divine Childhood** in a special and quite extraordinary way, and permeated her with His Divine innocence, simplicity, and purity. Her soul was then placed in a contemplation of God that was so sincere, so pure, so detached from all things, and so swallowed up in Him, that she testified in that same writing: „she was in an **unapproachable light**; and she existed and worked in the grace, and through the grace, of the holy childhood.“

19. How great her innocence must have been is evident when she said: „One must not find it difficult to speak with me of sins and vices; for such things, thank God, make no impression on my mind, and nothing of them remains in my thoughts.“

20. She had attained such **simplicity** <note>original: "Einfalt"; a 17th-century spiritual term for a soul focused solely on God, free from self-reflection.</note> that her soul no longer paid attention to what she did or what she had to do; so much so that she could no longer even prepare herself when she had to lead the discourse at the sisters' gatherings, even though she always brought forth beautiful things. Neither could she think back on what she had spoken, but rather she let God act, surrendering herself to Him in the present moment to fulfill His holy will. She was pure and clear in her intention; she had only the glory of God as her motive in everything. „God alone,“ she said, „is that not enough? JESUS Christ, next to the glorification of His Father, set us as the goal of His human life, as He lived and died for our sake; and we, out of a terrible presumption, still refuse to [have] God for our...“

# Chapter Sixteen.
## Her Love for God.

->I.<-

How much the pure love of God took possession of the heart of this, His bride, and what wonders He worked therein, is fully and completely known only to Him and to this blessed woman. In the meantime, we wish to share the little that we have found remaining in writing, which she sent to her spiritual guide out of obedience (as the heading states).

->2. To obey.<-

> "On the last day of my **spiritual exercises** <term>Spiritual Exercises: Structured periods of prayer, silence, and meditation intended to deepen one's relationship with God.</term>, Divine Love, with which I had been occupied on this and the previous day, came and poured its Divine influences into my soul with such abundance that I suddenly found myself filled to the brim. It was so intense that it became difficult for me to remain at the service in the church and to recite it <note>This refers to the "Divine Office," the structured daily prayers chanted or recited by members of a religious order.</note>. For when these attacks come with such holy vehemence, though quite gently and in peace, the mouth and eyes soon close of their own accord, the senses are completely hindered, and the body becomes quite faint and bruised, so that I must use the greatest force to keep myself upright. And finally, if this lasts for even a short while, the body must cast itself down to the earth and let this Divine action pass over. I call it Divine because I do not believe that I add anything of myself; indeed, it seems to me to come all the more directly from God because He does it when I am not thinking of it at all.

> "But it is a very difficult, if not an impossible thing, for me to be able to tell you what actually occurs in this working of grace and love; for heart and soul, and everything that is in the soul, is so occupied with its God that it is almost in a **blessed inability** to reflect upon that which is occurring within it. The soul feels indeed with certainty that the Beloved is most inwardly present, and has greater certainty of this than if it saw Him with physical eyes; but it cannot express in what manner and way this happens."

# The Sixteenth Chapter.
## Her Love for God.

->1.<-

How much the pure love of God occupied the heart of this His bride, and what wonders He worked within it, is known fully and completely only to Him and to this blessed woman. In the meantime, we wish to share the little that we have found remaining of it in writing, which she sent to her spiritual director out of obedience (as the heading states).

->2. In order to obey.<-

> "On the last day of my spiritual exercises, Divine Love—with which I had been occupied both this day and the previous one—came and poured its divine influences into my soul with such abundance that I suddenly found myself filled to the brim, in such a way that it became difficult for me to remain at the service in the church and to recite it. For when these attacks come with such holy impetuosity <note>original: 'Ungestüm'; in mystical literature, this refers to a sudden, forceful rush of spiritual emotion that overwhelms the subject</note>, though entirely gentle and in peace, the mouth and eyes soon close of their own accord, the senses are completely inhibited, and the body is quite weary and exhausted <note>original: 'zerschlagen', literally 'beaten' or 'shattered', used here to describe the physical toll of an intense spiritual experience</note>, so that I must do myself the greatest violence to remain upright; and finally, when this lasts for a little while, the body must throw itself down to the ground and let this divine action pass over it. I call it 'divine' because I do not believe that I contribute anything of myself, and it seems to me to come all the more directly from God because He does it when I am not thinking of it at all.
> 
> "However, it is a very difficult, if not an impossible thing, for me to be able to tell you what actually occurs in this working of grace and love; for heart and soul, and everything within the soul, is so occupied with its God that it is almost in a blissful state of incapacity <note>original: 'Unvermögen'; a technical term in mysticism where the soul's natural faculties, like reason or speech, are suspended by the intensity of the experience</note> to reflect upon what is happening within it. It feels, indeed, with certainty that the Beloved is present in the most intimate way, and has a greater certainty of this than if it saw Him with physical eyes; but it cannot express in what manner or way this happens."

2. "My state is a ceasing of my own actions <note>original: 'Wirkungen'; refers to the operations of the soul's will and intellect</note>, a silent agreement to the actions of God; and in the true vision of my nothingness, my soul finds itself in the power of its God."

At another time she writes: "It seems at times to my soul as if a separation from myself and from all created things is taking place, whereby it is placed in the freedom to unite itself with its God."

3. Again she writes: "I have seen much more clearly than ever the almost infinite difference that exists between all that is said of God, and that which He lets my soul recognize and experience. I was astounded by how it was possible that the saints could still live after our Lord had fully shared Himself with them."

4. In another place she says: "When it pleases the Divine Lord of Heaven, He holds my soul in such a silence that it is not permitted to speak even a single word. With this it must be content: to know that it is dependent on the guidance of the great God."

5. At another time she expressed herself with these words: "My soul finds itself at times possessed with a burning desire for God alone, and feels entirely indifferent toward all His gifts, so much so that it cannot be satisfied with these little streams <note>The 'streams' represent spiritual consolations or secondary gifts, whereas the 'source' is God Himself.</note>, but wants the source itself entirely pure and complete: for in having God in such a way, it has everything, without perceiving anything with distinction. The sensation that the soul receives from this blissful possession places it in a state where it seems to be just like a person thrown into the sea, who sees themselves within it without seeing themselves fully flooded: thus the soul finds itself entirely sunken in God, and so powerfully permeated by His Divine Being that it no longer properly knows what it does, nor what becomes of it, because all the powers of its mind lose their own actions. Upon this grace follows a great fear of still finding oneself; and a fervent prayer to be preserved from it."

6. In the course of her life, God drew her entirely out of herself to immerse her completely in Himself. One day, while she was speaking with one of the convent sisters who had just withdrawn for spiritual exercises <note>Refers to a period of silent retreat and prayer common in religious life.</note>, these words escaped her, which she said with her eyes raised toward the heavens: "When one has gone out from God, one must enter into Him again; it eventually comes to the point that one enters so deeply into Him that one never comes out again."

7. To that place His goodness has drawn me, especially recently—I mean, into the possession of God, into God Himself. This grace is not an outflowing of God into the senses, or into the powers of the soul; but it is, as far as I understand it..."

# of Elisabeth of the Child Jesus. Chapter XVII.

> „your inclinations, your feelings, and your sufferings will not be so quickly changed and divinized <note>original: "vergöttert"; a mystical term meaning to be made god-like or united with the Divine nature.</note> as those which Jesus Christ has. You will still have to suffer many a death and many anxieties; and do not be terrified by this, for that is the usual guidance of Jesus Christ, that He transforms creatures into Himself in no other way than through many tribulations.

> „But be comforted; He has shown you far too much mercy that He should not wish to continue. Your understanding is undoubtedly correct in this, that you write it seems Saint Paul did not say enough when he speaks of his life having to be hidden in Christ Jesus, and that the same must be entirely lost in Him. And thus this Divine Apostle also understood it, because he says in another place that he <margin>(a) Galatians 2:20</margin> no longer lives, but Jesus Christ lives in him. We come again to the Divine fire which annihilates <term>annihilates (vernichtiget): the process of reducing the ego or self-will to 'nothingness' so that God can fill the soul.</term> you. The same will consume all things, and sometimes even the perceptible experience—that is, the sight and the feeling of your annihilation; in such a way that you will find yourself in such a lost state that you will recognize nothing within it; and the devil will make use of your natural rational spirit to persuade you that you are losing time and that you are useless. Then stand firm, and seek no light nor assurance. The more you are brought to this extreme degree, the more your losing of yourself in God will increase. Write us an occasional pleasant little letter from your hand, and never doubt our sincere love. Our greatest desire is that we all may one day be entirely submerged in Jesus Christ; that is the blessedness of this and the future life. Fare well in God, my dearest sister.”

9. Once more, our Elisabeth describes her state somewhere with these short words: „I am in very painful conditions. On the one hand, I am as if in a deep rest, in the bosom of the sovereign Lord, and follow only through silent consent: and on the other hand, I feel the weight of Divine Justice over me, which chastises me for my former and present infidelities. Oh! how terrible it is to anger God; and how sensible <note>Meaning "perceptible" or "painfully felt."</note> are the fruits of sin and infidelity shown against the drawing <note>original: "Zug"; the internal spiritual attraction or "pull" of God on the soul.</note> of God!”

# The Eighteenth Chapter.

->Concerning the last five years of her life, and the various and heavy sufferings she endured therein.<-

1. It pleased the Lord to lead Mother Elisabeth through very painful and rough paths, and to exercise her through all kinds of crosses and suffering, especially in her final years. In this way, He certainly kept His promises to her, for He once let her hear these express words in the depths of her soul: "I will tear you away from the earth and raise you upon the Cross. There you shall find no taste <note>In mystical literature, "taste" (Geschmack) refers to spiritual sweetness, consolation, or emotional comfort.</note> either in heaven or on earth; you shall taste nothing but the bitterness of the Cross."

2. To say nothing here of her internal sufferings, she also spent a good portion of her life in all kinds of illnesses, fevers, heavy hemorrhages <note>original: "Blutflüssen"</note>, and very violent headaches and toothaches. She bore all these sufferings with the greatest patience and silence in imitation of the Savior, of whom it is written in the Gospel: *Jesus remained silent.* And this silence of hers is the reason why we know only of those sufferings which she could not keep hidden.

3. When she was Superior <term>Superior (Vorsteherin): the elected head or leader of the religious community.</term> for the last time, it happened one night as she was going to morning prayer that another sister, who was also going there, struck the Superior's head violently in her eager pace because both were without light. Nevertheless, she still went to the prayer. Afterward, it was clearly seen that her eye had swollen completely black; but whatever anyone said, she would use no remedy, but considered it a trifle.

4. Three or four months later, while she was in the refectory <note>original: "Speisezimmer"; the communal dining hall of the convent.</note>, she suddenly felt a very powerful pain in the injured eye, such that she was forced to close the other eye; and in that moment, she realized that she could no longer see. Meanwhile, she remained in her usual tranquility without saying anything, until a sister came to find her to speak with a certain pious person in the parlor <note>original: "Sprachzimmer"; the room where cloistered nuns were permitted to receive and speak with visitors.</note>. She asked this sister: "Whether one might suddenly lose an eye all at once?" Now, as the sister answered in the affirmative—namely, that she believed such a thing could indeed happen—she said: "I have just now realized that I have lost an eye." The good sister then began to weep out of compassion; but Mother Elisabeth, who was dead to all that is dearest to nature <note>This implies she had reached a state of "holy indifference," where physical health or loss was secondary to the will of God.</note>, rebuked her for her sensitivity and forbade her to say anything about it to anyone. She then went to the parlor without showing the slightest sign of her distress and spoke of an entirely different matter with a wonderful devotion of spirit.

<summary>This page marks the beginning of the final chapter of Elisabeth’s life, detailing her physical illnesses and a specific injury that led to the sudden loss of her sight in one eye, which she bore with stoic spiritual detachment.</summary>

### Fourth Part. The Life of Elisabeth, etc.

4. She was indeed forced to take various medicines, but they had no effect. Following this, she was seized by a severe dizziness accompanied by almost constant vomiting, which lasted five or six days, so that she could not keep down even the slightest nourishment.

To refresh her and to stop the violent vomiting, it was ordered that she should be given some lemon syrup every hour; but the nurse, without tasting it first, gave her a syrup that was very poorly prepared and as bitter as gall. She never said a word, however, from which one might have suspected that it was of no use; and it would not have been discovered if another sister, who was feeling unwell and was also supposed to take some of it, had not said so. Mother Elisabeth was then asked why she had not mentioned this? But she simply smiled and said:
> It was not necessary.

5. In a short time, her eye became inflamed like a glowing coal. The pain was very piercing in three places of the head, with such violent attacks by day and by night that her body shook from them; and this lasted for nearly four months without any relief. For almost the entire time of her illness, she could not enjoy any kind of broth; and what little she did eat increased her ailment to such an extent that she said:
> If I found any pleasure in eating, I would soon erase such a fault through the great pain that it causes me.

6. She said to us once:
> At the moment I wake up, I look upon my pains as so many bailiffs <note>original: "Gerichtsdiener" – officers of the court who carry out a judge's orders; here used as a metaphor for divine discipline.</note> of Divine Justice, who seize me by the head in order to destroy sin within me.

7. When her nurse noticed one day that she was suffering more than usual, the nurse remembered that she had forgotten to apply a certain cooling water <note>A traditional liquid remedy or wash used to reduce inflammation.</note> to her eyes; she ran quickly and did so, whereupon the patient said:
> I have longed for that for a long time; however, one must suffer without refreshment as long as one can.

8. Her condition did not allow her to hear or speak much; nevertheless, from the few words that occasionally escaped her, one could sufficiently sense that she embraced her cross quite willingly, with love and pleasure. "O good cross!" she said;
> "O desired cross! O precious cross! O invaluable cross!"

9. But as her ailment grew worse daily, and the eye had completely turned out and protruded from her head the size of a small egg, being so black and misshapen that one could no longer tell what it had been, the doctors and surgeons resolved together to remove the eye entirely, because they feared that gangrene <term>gangrene (original: "kalte Brand"): the death of body tissue, which in the 17th century was often fatal if it spread.</term> might set in.

10. Accordingly, the 12th of June was appointed for this operation. That same morning, she was seen to be so collected <note>In mystical tradition, "eingesammlet" (recollection) describes a state of intense inward focus on God, withdrawing the senses from the world.</note> the entire time that it seemed as if she did

### Fourth Part. The Life

...no longer of this world, and her heart resided entirely where her treasure was. She awaited the physicians and surgeons <note>original: "Aerzte und Wundärzte" — In this period, "physicians" typically prescribed internal medicine, while "surgeons" or "wound-doctors" performed manual operations.</note> with a profound silence, and in such a state of self-forgetfulness that she never spoke a single word about it; and when they arrived, she received them with great politeness and without showing the slightest terror, without inquiring how long it might last nor how great the pains would be. Instead, she rose from her bed with the greatest devotion, like one who was completely immersed in God. In this great silence, full of reverence, love, adoration, and submission to the decree of her Lord, she lay down upon chairs placed together, where she was positioned quite flat, having only a single pillow beneath her head.

The surgeon then turned her eye with his fingers so that he might set the eyeball back into its previous position. Afterward, he took two long and slightly curved steel needles and pierced one from bottom to top through the eye-bone, and the other transversely beneath it in the shape of a cross; he then drew these four points toward himself and, with a pair of scissors, cut away all the veins and small membranes that held the eye fast, one after the other. During this bloody and protracted procedure, she did not let out a single sigh and seemed to be as insensitive as if she were already robbed of life; although one could perceive a terrible suffering in her face, and she lay entirely in blood, like a lamb that opens not its mouth even when it is being slaughtered <note>This is an allusion to the "Suffering Servant" in Isaiah 53:7, comparing Elisabeth's stoicism to that of Christ.</note>. The surgeons stood amazed at such wonderful composure <term>Gelaſſenheit: a central concept in German mysticism referring to a state of surrendered detachment and internal peace</term>; and a physician who was also present took her eye, gave it to the nurse, and said: "Behold, the eye of a saint."

As she was half-dead from pain in this manner, she was placed back into bed. And although her strength was exhausted by this violent operation, she still knew how to use it enough to thank these gentlemen with great politeness. Her nurse said to her that she had acted against obedience, because she had been commanded to complain if she could find relief through complaining. But she answered: "I would have had difficulty doing such a thing; for I was speaking with God and saying to Him a hundred times a day: My Lord!"

11. Just as such incidents commonly have very painful consequences, they had to begin again that very evening to cause her a new torment <note>original: "Marter" — can mean either physical torment or martyrdom.</note>, when they removed the first plaster, under which they found such a great quantity of clotted blood that the surgeon was forced to scrape it out with his nails as far as the wound reached, which was just as sensitive to her as the operation itself. At this, she became startled, because she did not expect such a violent action, so that she sighed once and afterward begged that they might show her the charity of warning her beforehand in such occurrences.

13. Five times a day she was bandaged. The dressing had to be moistened with egg white, which then soon dried and stuck so firmly that it always had to be pulled off with force. For the rest of her life, she had to have her bandages changed twice every day, and whenever it was even slightly cold, or the slightest wind touched her, it always caused her new suffering.

## The Nineteenth Chapter.
->Her final state, conduct, and blessed passing.<-

->I.<-

A certain man, very knowledgeable in spiritual matters, who used to read letters to the godly Bernieres <note>Jean de Bernières-Louvigny (1602–1659), a French mystic and influential layperson who acted as a spiritual director to many, including Mother Elisabeth.</note> during his blindness and write his responses, came to Paris around this time and visited Mother Elisabeth. To him, she spoke quite frankly and said, among other things, that since Bernieres’ death she had very rarely spoken of her sufferings and her inner joys; and as for her sufferings, she had borne them in silence as much as she could, without the help of creatures <note>In the spiritual vocabulary of the 17th century, "creatures" refers to any created being—people, friends, or worldly comforts—as opposed to the Creator.</note>, as she usually felt that when she wanted to speak of them, God held her tongue somewhat bound.

The same pious man then also asked her whether she had a certainty of the life of God within her; to which she answered: Yes. He asked her another question, from the answer to which he judged that she must have reached such an exalted state that she would not remain on earth much longer, because few attain such heights, and those who do reach them almost all die from it.

It is certainly to be presumed with good reason regarding this soul devoted to God that she must have reached a high degree of union with God, since almost everything we find expressed here was experienced while Bernieres was still living, after whose death our Elisabeth lived for eighteen more years; during which time, as mentioned, she kept herself secluded, and therefore her final and most noble state will likely remain hidden in God until she is made manifest with Christ in glory.

Nevertheless, the following, written in her own hand, was found with her after her death:

2. “Since your Divine Light, O my great God, You Divine Word, has allowed me to recognize and reach a little of your eternal love—that love which caused me to be Life in You from all eternity (a), and to which I must also sacrifice myself again eternally:

“I. So I take a firm resolution to give myself over to it without reserve, in order to seek your pure love in a devoted manner <note>The original German "verliebte Weise" implies the seeking of God with the passion and focus of a lover.</note>. This love allows for no division and requires at the very least that I show such exactness and such delicacy <note>original: "delicatesse"</note> toward it as created love has ever been able to work within my heart.

“II. I am willing, O Divine Love, to be more faithful than I have been; only to seek in everything, and above everything, your greatest glorification, and to delight your adorable heart with the most inward pleasure.

“III. Just as You, my divine Savior, have said: *If you love me, keep my commandments*: so I will hold myself unbreakably to the precise observation of all that I can recognize that You would have of me.

“IV. I will, as much as is possible for me, separate myself from the external, so that I may be more devoutly focused on the internal, and on that which my office <note>This refers to her duties or "Amt" within her religious community or station in life.</note> requires.

“V. I will strive in the spirit of love to show more heart-felt kindness to my neighbor, to bear with him and to excuse him as much as I am able.

“VI. Because I cannot love You, my lovely All, except in so much as I die to my self-love; so I will rejoice when something comes that can be helpful to the destruction of the same, and show myself grateful toward those people who are instrumental to me in attaining this great good.

“VII. I will never excuse myself, except where necessity and love require it. Through the grace that I expect from You, O my God, I will preserve the powerful impression that You have given me: namely, that You are All, and I am Nothing. Herein consists my joy, my pleasure, and all my good; and that I love the hidden life <note>The "hidden life" refers to a state of internal prayer and humility, living for God alone away from the notice or praise of the world.</note>, because my Divine Savior led such a life here on earth.”

3. She showed sufficiently through all her actions that the path of the righteous is like the sun in its rising, which ever increases in heat and light until the full midday <note>A reference to Proverbs 4:18: "But the path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day."</note>. Truly it was a wonder to look upon this soul in her age of sixty-four years; though she was so delicate by nature and worn out by long-lasting illnesses, living in constant, persistent weakness and fainting spells, she was nevertheless so courageous in practicing all outward rigors as she had ever done before. # Of Elisabeth of the Infant Jesus. Chapter XVIII.

<meta>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page’s catchword "te".</meta>...she felt herself to be nothing other than a breath of life: and when anyone wished to speak with her of this or that matter, she would say: "I am no longer of this earth."

4. Toward the end of the month of August, a sudden blindness struck her other eye, which lasted quite a long time that same day; the next morning, this occurrence returned, so that it was feared she would become entirely blind. She, however, remained unmoved and said: "If I become blind, then I shall see so much more clearly." <note>This reflects a common mystical theme where the loss of physical sight leads to the sharpening of "inner" or spiritual vision.</note>

5. Two months later, she was seized by a grievous affliction in her bowels, which was so violent that it nearly brought her to her end. Her countenance changed, and her entire body became as cold as the body of a dead person. The nurse did indeed compel her to take to her bed, but she wished to remain there only for a single day; and although she had to be permitted to attend the assembly again after three weeks, she was nevertheless like a light that is imperceptibly extinguished, so very weak and exhausted was her body.

6. On the 4th of December, she attended Holy Communion <note>original: "Abendmahl"</note> for the last time. Afterward, she retired for a time to prayer. When she had spent about half an hour in the holy embraces of her Bridegroom <note>A traditional mystical metaphor for the soul's intimate union with Christ.</note>, she had to interrupt such a joyful occupation, as she was called out so that she might also, like our Savior, become obedient unto death. She was, however, quite cold, because she had not been near the fire the entire morning. Shortly thereafter, she said to the Superior, who was with her at that moment: "I feel that my hand is completely numb; I shall likely become paralyzed in my limbs; but say nothing of this to our sisters; it would only trouble them." Scarcely had she spoken these words when she was struck by a stroke <term>Schlagsfluß: an older term for a sudden stroke or apoplectic fit</term>, whereupon she placed her hand upon her heart and said: "My God! I am dying." Immediately, she lost her speech and remained without any sensation until the following day, the 5th of December, 1677, when she surrendered her well-prepared soul into the hands of her Creator, in the sixty-fifth year of her age.

# Preface.

### I.

Maria Guyard entered the convent while her only son was still young. A few years later, she traveled to Canada, where she lived for approximately thirty-three more years, though she never saw her son’s face again during that time. This son of hers was indeed, through God’s grace and the persistent prayers of his holy mother, called and led away from the vanity of the world to the knowledge and service of God. However, since his mother was already in Canada by that time, the son did not cease to continually beseech her with letters, requesting that she share with him in writing the story of God’s guidance over her soul for his particular edification. To persuade her to do this, he complained to her that she had left him in the world so young that he hardly knew he had a mother at all. At that time, he said, he had not been in a state to receive her instructions; it would therefore be quite harsh and unjust if she were now to refuse him—at a time when he possessed a different understanding—that which could so greatly comfort and build him up. He testified that nothing served his progress in the spiritual life as much as what he had received in writing from her, his mother.

The mother answered these and other arguments with silence for several years, until she was finally commanded by her <term>spiritual director</term> <note>A priest or mentor who provides guidance on prayer and the inner life.</note> to grant her son’s request and send him the account of her life, which she was then obliged to do. Yet, at the same time, she used the most cautious safeguards to prevent it from ever falling into anyone’s hands except those of her son. And see, this is the plan of this biography, which has gained its detail through various letters to her son—wherein she explains herself more closely and further—as well as through several reports to her director. After the mother’s death, the son (who had become a Benedictine monk named Dom Claude Martin (a)) published all of this together in Paris in 1677, under the title: *The Life of the Venerable Mother Marie of the Incarnation, etc.* <note>original: "La Vie de la V. Mere Marie de l'Incarnation, &c."</note> Large quarto format <note>original: "Quart. form. maj."</note>, and he added many beautiful things of his own here and there. He intended to publish other writings by his mother, but to date, nothing further has been heard of them; only her letters have appeared in quarto in Paris. (b)

I have thanked God from my heart that I finally encountered this long-sought, rare, and magnificent life story in the library of the late Mr. Poiret <note>Pierre Poiret (1646–1719) was a prominent mystic, philosopher, and bibliographer who preserved many spiritual writings.</note>, and was thus able to include an excerpt of it in these *Assemblies of the Saints*. This excerpt has grown larger than some of the preceding ones; however, I can say in my defense that it cost me no small effort to keep it as short as it appears here, as I had to leave out so much that was beautiful. Therefore, for those who might have the book itself in hand, this excerpt will undoubtedly still be too short; in this, I fully agree with them, and I emphatically recommend this incomparable life to everyone who can obtain and understand it. But since it is so very rare, and moreover in a foreign language, and since not everyone can buy or read such large books, this excerpt will meanwhile be able to satisfy the hungry soul and eager heart through the faithful contemplation and acceptance of God’s most precious truths and the high wonders of His grace and love. He has, so to speak, poured these out with full hands into this purified vessel, and through her, allows them to be praised to our hearts so pleasingly from the ends of the earth. Throughout this text, one finds the very words of this soul who was perfected in God (if ever one has been on earth); and where I have had to insert a few things (for the sake of connection or to summarize historical details), such additions have been placed within brackets [ ] for distinction.

All those who knew this holy soul or have read her biography give magnificent testimony to her. One may consult the entire nineteenth chapter in the fourth book of her *Life* regarding this. Her director in Canada, Jerome Lalemant <note>Hieronymus Lallemand (1593–1673) was a Jesuit superior in New France.</note>, says:

> "The foundation of her union with God was un=
> "shakable, and both her life and her death were holy and beautiful; her memory will always
> "remain blessed. I have been (he continues) in all things and everywhere her useless servant;
> "and I have been content to be merely a spectator of the works of the Holy Spirit in her, without
> "interfering in anything (since I saw her in such good hands), for fear that I might defile everything."

(a) This man was known and dear to Madame Guyon: see her *Life*, Part I, Chapter 29, § 5, 10.
(b) After this was written, I see that a shortened version of the life of Marie of the Incarnation was also published in Paris in 1724, in octavo format.

# Preface.

### I.

Maria Guyard entered the convent while her only son was still young. A few years later, she traveled to Canada, where she lived for approximately thirty-three more years, though she never saw her son’s face again during that time. This son of hers was indeed, through God’s grace and the persistent prayers of his holy mother, called and led away from the vanity of the world to the knowledge and service of God. However, since his mother was already in Canada by that time, the son did not cease to continually beseech her with letters, requesting that she share with him in writing the story of God’s guidance over her soul for his particular edification. To persuade her to do this, he complained to her that she had left him in the world so young that he hardly knew he had a mother at all. At that time, he said, he had not been in a state to receive her instructions; it would therefore be quite harsh and unjust if she were now to refuse him—at a time when he possessed a different understanding—that which could so greatly comfort and build him up. He testified that nothing served his progress in the spiritual life as much as what he had received in writing from her, his mother.

The mother answered these and other arguments with silence for several years, until she was finally commanded by her <term>spiritual director</term> <note>A priest or mentor who provides guidance on prayer and the inner life.</note> to grant her son’s request and send him the account of her life, which she was then obliged to do. # Preface.

### I.

<margin>(a) This man was known and dear to Madame Guyon: see her *Life*, Part I, Chapter 29, § 5, 10.</margin>
Maria Guyard entered the convent while her only son was still young. A few years later, she traveled to Canada, where she lived for approximately thirty-three more years, though she never saw her son’s face again during that time. This son of hers was indeed, through God’s grace and by means of the Holy Mother’s persistent prayer, called and led away from the vanity of the world to the knowledge and service of God. However, since the mother was already in Canada by that time, the son did not cease to continually beseech her with letters, requesting that she might share with him in writing, and for his particular edification, the story of God’s guidance over her soul. To persuade her to do this, he complained to her that she had left him so young in the world that he hardly knew he had had a mother. At that time, he said, he had not been in a state to receive her instructions; and it would therefore be very hard and unjust if she now, when he had a different insight, also wanted to refuse him that which could so greatly comfort and edify him. He testified that nothing served his advancement in the spiritual life so much as what he had received from her, his mother, in writing. These and other arguments the mother answered with silence for several years, until finally she was commanded by her spiritual director to grant the son’s request and to send him the account of her life. She then had to comply, but at the same time she used the most careful precautions to prevent anyone but her son from ever getting it into their hands. And behold, this is the origin of this biography, which achieved its detail through various letters to her son—in which she explains herself more fully—as well as through several reports to her director. All this together was published in Paris in 1677, after the mother’s death, by the son (who had become a Benedictine monk named Dom Claude Martin (a)), under the—

I thanked God from my heart when I finally came across this long-sought, rare, and glorious life in the library of the late Mr. Poiret <note>Pierre Poiret (1646–1719) was a famous mystic, philosopher, and bibliographer who collected spiritual writings.</note>, and was thus able to include an excerpt of it in these *Collections of the Saints*. This excerpt has indeed become larger than some of the preceding ones; however, I can say in my defense that it cost me no small effort to keep it as short as it appears here, as I had to omit so much beauty. Therefore, for those who might have the book itself in their hands, this excerpt will no doubt still seem too short; I fully agree with them, and recommend this incomparable life with all emphasis to everyone who can obtain and understand it. But because it is so rare, and moreover in a foreign language <note>The original was in French.</note>, and because not everyone can buy or read such large books, this excerpt will meanwhile be able to satisfy the hungry soul and eager eye through faithful contemplation and acceptance of the most precious truths of God and the high wonders of His grace and love. He has, as it were, poured these out with full hands into this purified vessel, and through her, He allows them to be praised so tastily to our hearts from the ends of the earth. One finds here everywhere the own words of this soul perfected in God (if ever one has been on earth); and where I have had to insert some small thing (for the sake of connection or to grasp historical facts more briefly), such has been placed between brackets [ ] for distinction.

All those who knew this holy soul or read her biography give glorious testimonies of her. One can look up the entire 19th chapter in the fourth book of her life for this. Her director in Canada, Hieronymus [Jerome] Lallemant <note>Jérôme Lalemant (1593–1673) was a Jesuit missionary and superior of the missions in New France (Canada).</note>, says: "The foundation of her union with God is unshakeable, and both her life and her death have been holy and beautiful; her memory will always remain a blessing. I have been," he says further, "in everything and everywhere her useless servant; and I have been content to act only as a spectator of the works of the Holy Spirit in her, without interfering in anything (as I saw her in such good hands), for fear that I might defile everything."

<margin>(b) Since writing this, I see that a shortened version of the life of Marie de l’Incarnation was also published in Paris in 1724, in octavo <term>octavo: a book size where each sheet is folded into eight leaves</term>.</margin>

might. The dear Bernieres <note>Jean de Bernières-Louvigny (1602–1659), a French mystic and treasurer who supported the mission in Canada.</note> considered her, among others, to be a **Theresa of the New World**; and although he had held fellowship with so many holy souls, he nevertheless confessed, "that he had never seen a person who had been raised to such a degree as was the **Mother of the Incarnation**."

And in another place (a) he calls her a great and profoundly virtuous soul, who possessed a deep humility and an overflowing love, and who never lost her actual union with GOD; one to whom the name could have been given: **My (b) will is in her.** <note>original: "Mein Wille ist in ihr." This is a translation of the Hebrew name Hephzibah from Isaiah 62:4, which the Vulgate renders as "Voluntas mea in ea."</note> Of the life of this Saint, Poiret <note>Pierre Poiret (1646–1719), a French mystic and philosopher who edited many spiritual works.</note> says: (c) In the same are to be found incredible, but entirely Divine examples of **dying to the self**, and of the most sublime spiritual and **Mystical life**, as well as of the active life for the salvation of souls: to say nothing of others.

As an introduction to the following biography, I will add a few words from this holy soul, which she wrote to her son, among other things, when sending the account to him:

> "(d) Do (d) not think that this writing was composed with prior deliberation, so that one might perceive such an order in it as in regularly arranged books: such a thing would not have been possible for me in the state in which GOD holds me. The way by which His Divine Majesty leads me cannot allow me to pay attention to any method in what I write. As I took the pen in hand to make a beginning, I did not know a single word of what I wanted to write; but as I wrote, the **Spirit of Grace**, who governs me, caused me to produce that which pleased Him.

> "If, during the reading, it should perhaps come into your thoughts what might have moved the Divine Goodness to show me such great mercies, and to thus come before me with the blessings of His kindness: then I must tell you that I have sometimes reflected on this myself; but whenever I thought deeply about it, I could see nothing in myself but misery <note>original: "Elenzden," likely a typo for "Elenden" (wretchedness/misery).</note> and unworthiness. --- Therefore, if His mercies have been so great toward me in so many ways, it is an effect of His pure generosity.

> "Therefore, let us go purely to the Source, and together glorify and magnify our Benefactor for the excesses of His mercies over us, and for those which His most amiable goodness has shown to me in particular. Help me to sing His praise until the end of this life, so as to continue the same thereafter in eternity. --- As for me, I confess that at the time when this GOD of goodness called me, I was worthy of all rejection and contempt; and that even now, when He heaps His riches upon me, I do not see that I respond to His graces as I ought, nor that I am helpful to His purpose for me. Therefore, I shall never grow weary of saying that it is out of grace and by virtue of His pure goodness that He has shown me His favor and grace, and still shows it. Let us (e) then confess to the LORD and praise Him, for He is good, and His mercy endures forever! <note>original: "seine Barmherzigkeit währet ewiglich!" — a translation of the Latin "in aeternum misericordia eius" from Psalm 136.</note> Amen."

(e) Psalm 136:1.

## Chapter 1.

### The Origin of Marie of the Incarnation. Her first stirrings
### toward the Good in her childhood and youth.

->I.<-

**T**his excellent servant of **GOD**, Marie of the Incarnation <note>Born Marie Guyart (1599–1672), she was a French mystic and the foundress of the Ursuline monastery in Quebec.</note>, was born in Tours, France, on October 18, 1599, of a rather humble lineage. Her father, Florent Guyart, had nothing that could bring him much regard except for his honesty and piety. Her mother, Joan Michelet, had a more distinguished outward background. She descended from the old noble family of Babou <note>The Babou de la Bourdaisière family were prominent in the French court during the 16th century.</note>, from which many eminent persons in both the spiritual and worldly estates have sprung, although she herself no longer held the slightest prestige. This family has now received a brightly shining glory in this holy daughter, who, at the express command of her director <note>Her spiritual guide or confessor.</note>, described her own life as follows, just as we shall now hear in her own words.

2. From my childhood on, it pleased His Divine Majesty to prepare my soul to be His temple, and to deem it worthy of His mercies and favors. I was about seven years old when I once dreamed at night that I was in the courtyard of a certain country school, where I was engaged in something innocent with one of my companions. As I raised my eyes, I saw the heavens open, and our **Lord Jesus Christ** in human form coming down from there directly toward me. When I saw this, I cried out to my companion: "Oh, look there, our Savior: He is coming to me!" As this most adorable Majesty approached me, I felt my heart entirely ignited in His love, and I began to stretch out my arms to embrace Him. Thereupon, this most beautiful among the children of men <note>A reference to Psalm 45:2, "You are fairer than the children of men."</note> embraced me with a friendly and inexpressibly powerful, charming countenance. He kissed me very lovingly and said: "Do you want to be mine?" I answered: "Yes." And when He had my consent, we saw Him ascend back toward heaven.

When I awoke from sleep, I was so taken by this singular grace that I told it with simplicity to everyone who had the desire to hear me. In particular, the words of the Savior remained so impressed upon my mind that they never again left it; so greatly did they occupy all the devotion of my spirit through their sweetness.

3. This visit worked in me an inclination toward the good. And although, on account of my childhood, I did not consider that this draw toward the good originated from an internal cause, I nevertheless felt myself drawn on several occasions to deal with the Savior regarding my small matters. This I did with great simplicity, for I could not imagine that He should ever refuse a person anything.

<header>Fifth Section. The Life of Marie of the In[carnation].</header>

...[to know] why one should call upon Him humbly. I sometimes went alone to pray in secret; I was driven to this by (a) the **Spirit of Inwardness**, without knowing or thinking about what the Spirit of Inwardness was; I did not even know its name. But the goodness of **GOD** guided me in this: and as I was still a blind and ignorant child, I mixed my childish imitation of outward gestures—which I saw in others and in which I took delight—into my devotion.

4. However, when I was about sixteen years old, I began to be oppressed by the gnawing of my conscience, and I felt clearly how His Divine Majesty wanted me to confess such childhood trifles <note>Original: "Kindereyen." She refers to the small, innocent actions of a child that she later felt compelled to mention in the sacrament of confession.</note> quite precisely, and to disregard nothing in this matter. But I was ashamed of it and said to myself that I never would have believed I was offending **GOD** by them. And so I resisted the Spirit of **GOD**, who took hold of me inwardly through a secret and inward-working power, in order to have me entirely for Himself. Everything good that I happened to see performed, I did as well, and indeed without force; because the sweetness of this pull was incomparably more pleasant to me than anything else I might see elsewhere. Yet, because I still deliberated over this one matter—namely, confession—as to whether I should do it according to this impulse of the Spirit of **GOD** or not, it was a hindrance to me in obtaining the greatest graces.

5. Some time after I had received the first grace mentioned above, I was drawn by the feelings of the goodness of **GOD**, who hears those who call upon Him from the heart. I went into the church, sequestered myself in a remote place so as not to be seen by any person, and remained there for a good part of the day. My heart earnestly desired this Divine Communion; but I was so childish that I did not know that such a thing was "praying."

6. From my (b) fourteenth or fifteenth year onward, I had a great inclination toward the religious life <note>Original: "geistlichen Stande," referring to the desire to join a convent as a nun.</note>. I also presented this desire to my mother, who did not exactly refuse me, yet things remained as they were. And because I was very fearful <note>In 17th-century usage, this implies a mix of timidity, shyness, and a deep reverence that made her hesitant to push her own will.</note>, I did not dare to press the matter more firmly, but only simply stated my desire. It is clear to me, however, that the goodness of **GOD** did not yet want me in any religious order at that time, when I consider everything that happened to me in the following time through His Divine Providence. If you (she says to her son <note>Her son, Claude Martin, who later became a Benedictine monk and her biographer.</note>) were to know the particular circumstances of it—which you shall know in eternity—you would stand amazed by it; also by how I had to be entangled in the cross of the married state. I have always believed, and still believe, that I had to marry only so that I might serve the purpose which **GOD** had of bringing you into the world, and to bear various crosses <note>A common metaphor for spiritual trials or hardships.</note>; just as I had already offered you up to **GOD** before you were in this world.

# Chapter Two.

## Her Married State, Sufferings, Love for God’s Word, and Prayer in this State. The Death of her Husband.

1.
**GOD** then allowed (in the seventeenth year of my age) my parents to place me in a state (she speaks of the married state) in which, so it seemed, the freedoms and pastimes <term>Zeitkürzungen: Literally "shortening of time"; these were amusements or social distractions used to pass the time.</term> were permitted to me that had been denied me in their house. But **GOD** caused me to lose all inclination for such things entirely, and gave me a pull toward solitude <term>Abgeschiedenheit: A state of being retired from the world to focus on the internal spiritual life.</term>, which took hold of me inwardly through love for a good that I did not yet know; and He caused me to leave the company of those of my own age so that I might remain alone in the house and read godly books, since I had already completely given up vain books and those I had read merely for my own delight.

2. All our neighbors marveled at this and could not comprehend this seclusion <term>Absonderung: A deliberate withdrawal or separation from social norms and public life.</term>, nor the great inclination I had for the practice of virtue, and especially of patience; because they did not see what I experienced inwardly, nor how Divine Goodness was working there. I myself could not grasp it either, except that I followed His pull in prayer and was obedient to Him in the practice of those virtues for which He provided me the opportunity.

3. His Divine Goodness allowed me to endure great crosses for nearly two full years, for as long as my entanglement <note>The author uses "Verwickelung" (entanglement) to describe her marriage, suggesting it was a complex worldly state that complicated her spiritual path.</note> (in the married state) lasted. And in this very circumstance, **GOD** tested my soul: but He did not abandon it; because this inward support of which I have just spoken imparted strength to me, together with great patience and gentleness in all attacks, even the most sensitive <note>The "most sensitive attacks" likely refers to emotional trials or domestic conflicts that deeply affected her feelings.</note>. Prayer was my refuge.

[Her son says more regarding her great sufferings during the time of her marriage. Among other things he says: Throughout the entire duration of her marriage, she had to endure very heavy crosses; and if I were permitted to recount them piece by piece, there would be no one who would not cast their eyes toward heaven in astonishment that **GOD**, in such a short time, exposed a person whom He loved so tenderly to so many tribulations. For they were so heavy, and of such a strange and new kind, that I do not know if anything like them has ever been seen in the world. Lest I act against charity <note>Original: "Liebe." In this context, it refers to the Christian virtue of protecting the reputation of others, in this case, her husband.</note>, I will not name these sufferings specifically. I say only that her husband himself was the cause of them, although without intent and in an innocent manner; just as he often asked her for forgiveness with tears.]

4. I was at that time (she continues) approximately eighteen years old, and **GOD** gave me a great inclination for the frequent use of the Lord’s Supper <term>Abendmahl: The Sacrament of the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</term>, through which I

# Chapter Two.
## Her Married State, Sufferings, Love for God’s Word, and Prayer in this State. The Death of her Husband.

1. It then pleased God, (in the seventeenth year of my age,) that my parents placed me in a state <note>original: "Ehestand"; she is speaking of the married state</note> in which it appeared that I would be permitted the freedoms and pastimes that were denied to me in their house. But God brought it about that I entirely lost all inclination for such things, and He gave me a draw toward seclusion <note>original: "Abgeschiedenheit"; a state of being withdrawn from worldly society to focus on God</note> that took hold of me inwardly through the love for a Good that I did not yet know. He caused me to leave the company of those who were of the same age as I, so that I could remain alone in the house and read godly books, as I had already completely given up vain books and those I had read merely for my own amusement.

2. All our neighbors marveled at this and could not comprehend this withdrawal, nor the great inclination I had for the practice of virtue, and especially of patience; because they did not see what I experienced internally, nor how Divine Goodness was working there. I myself could not grasp it either, except that I followed His pull in prayer and was obedient to Him in the practice of those virtues for which He provided me the opportunities.

3. His Divine Goodness allowed that for almost two full years—precisely as long as my entanglement <term>Verwickelung</term> <note>The author uses "entanglement" to describe the complex social and worldly obligations of marriage that conflicted with her spiritual desires.</note> (in the married state) lasted—I had to bear great crosses. And in this very opportunity, God tested my soul: but He did not abandon her; because this internal support, of which I have just spoken, imparted strength to me, along with a great patience and gentleness in all attacks, even the most sensitive ones. Prayer was my refuge.

[Regarding her great sufferings during the time of her married state, her son says more. ### Section Five. The Life
<meta>catchword: awakened</meta>

...received a great courage and a great sweetness in my soul, along with a living faith. This living faith caused me to practice various good works, and worked in me a pull and grace of prayer, whereby that good, which I had in me through the previously received graces, was made perfect. My heart and mind were set only on the good.

5. I had read the Psalms in the French language; and because I had been told that the Spirit of GOD had dictated them, passages from them came to my memory every now and then, which I made use of as occasion arose; and I firmly believed that everything said through the Holy Spirit in them was true and infallible, and that everything that had essence would much sooner come to nothing than that these holy words should fail to have their power. Therefore I said that I placed my hope in GOD, and that He would give me everything for which I called upon Him because of this hope, and that, as I trusted entirely in His word, I would not be put to shame in my hope.

6. From my childhood on, I had heard that GOD spoke through the mouth of the preachers, which seemed excellent to me; and I had a great inclination to hear them, though I was still so young that I understood very little of it, except perhaps the stories <note>original: "Historie"; likely referring to biblical narratives or parables used in sermons</note>, which I then recounted when I came home.

7. As I grew older, the faith I had in my heart, together with what I heard of this Divine Word, always worked a greater desire in me to listen to it. I found nothing more glorious than the Word of GOD; and when I listened to it, it seemed to me my heart was like a vessel, into which this Divine Word flowed as a juice <note>original: "Saft"; in mystical literature, this refers to life-giving spiritual nourishment or grace</note>. This was no imagination, but an essential power of the Spirit of GOD, which was in this Word, and worked in such a way in my soul through an outpouring of His grace; which then, when it had received this overflowing fullness, could not contain it, but had to let it exhale, as it were, in prayer and in a conversation with GOD. Yes, I had to let myself out in speech through outward words, partly to GOD with a great fervor, partly to the people in the house with a great zeal.

As I heard a sermon one day on the holy name of JESUS, and the preacher had named this name frequently, this Divine Word, like a heavenly manna, so redundantly filled my soul that throughout the entire day my breathing said nothing else but, **JESUS, JESUS**, without my being able to stop.

8. In this diligent listening to His word, GOD gave me great light, and my heart was inflamed by it night and day, so that I began to speak to Him in an interior way, which was still new and unknown to me. I had indeed heard it said that one must perform meditations <term>Betrachtungen</term> <note>Formal, systematic mental prayer, often involving the imagination and intellect to reflect on religious truths.</note> in order to be able to practice the prayer of the heart; but I did not think that what my heart said to GOD was already such a thing: I only followed this inner pull; I also knew nothing further than that they were good feelings, which the Word of GOD [awakened] in my soul

Since then, God has always maintained in me this inclination to listen to His Divine Word, and has shown me great graces through this means. May He be praised for it in eternity!

9. I was nineteen years old when the Lord made a separation, and took to Himself that person to whom I had been joined (in the state of marriage) by His permission. Various dealings <note>original: "Händel"; referring here to legal or business disputes</note> which followed upon this separation caused me new sufferings, and indeed greater ones than a person of my sex, my age, and my little skill and experience could naturally have endured. But the overflowing goodness of God placed a strength and bravery in my heart which enabled me to endure everything.

<margin>(a) Psalm 91.</margin>
10. The foundation upon which I leaned were these holy words: *I am with those who are in tribulations* (a). I firmly believed that He was with me, because He had said it; so much so, that neither the loss of temporal goods, nor lawsuits, nor want, nor my son—who was only six months old and whom I saw, as well as myself, stripped of everything—caused me any unrest. My intellect had no human experience; but the Spirit of God, who possessed me inwardly, filled me with faith, hope, and trust, through which I successfully brought everything I undertook to a conclusion.

11. Although I loved your father very much (she writes to her son), and his loss was also painful to me at the beginning; nevertheless, as I now saw myself loosed and free, my soul melted in pure thanksgivings that I now had nothing more than God, to whom my heart and my loving inclinations could go out—and they did indeed go out in my solitude, where I had nothing to do but to think of Him inwardly and to raise you for His service. When your father’s mother saw that her only son had died, she had such a great fear that I would leave her that she died a month later; although I would certainly not have done so, but was rather determined to assist her as much as the Divine goodness would have permitted me during your upbringing. But this Goodness arranged it otherwise, for my benefit and yours; because otherwise I would have become entangled in <term>business dealings</term> <note>original: "Handthierung"; referring to the management of the family's commercial or trade affairs</note>, and in the youth in which I found myself, I would have run the danger of not following the path by which God wished to lead both you and me.

## The Third Chapter.

->A wonderful drawing toward a very deep repentance. The impression of the blood<-
->of Jesus Christ. She withdraws from worldly business;<-
->and lives for a year in solitude and<-
->communion with God.<-

->I.<-

After all those movements of God’s goodness to draw me to true inner purity—which I could not attain by myself—it finally pleased His Divine Majesty Himself to show me this grace, and to set me upon the path where He wished to have me. It happened, namely, on March 24, 1620. As I was going out to my business in the morning, I commended those affairs to God with my usual sigh: (a) *In thee, O Lord, have I hoped; let me never be put to shame* <note>original: "In dich, HErr, habe ich gehoffet, laß mich nimmermehr zu Schanden werden"; a citation of Psalm 31:1</note>; which words I had pressed into my soul with great certainty of faith. Then (I say) it happened that while walking I was suddenly brought to a halt, both inwardly and outwardly, and all thoughts regarding my business were taken out of my memory. Thereupon the eyes of my spirit were opened in an instant; and all the faults, sins, and imperfections that I had ever committed since the time I had been in the world were set before my eyes, both in general and in particular, with a much more certain distinction and clarity than any certainty that can be expressed through human diligence and art. At that very same moment, I saw myself completely immersed in blood, and my mind was fully convinced that this was the blood of the Son of God, for whose shedding I was guilty through the sins that had been set before my eyes, and which had been shed for my salvation.

2. Had the Divine Goodness not supported me in this, I believe I would have died of terror, so loathsome and terrifying did the sight of even the smallest sins appear to me. No human tongue can express this. To see that a God of infinite goodness and of an incomprehensible purity is offended by a poor earthworm <note>A common 17th-century metaphor used to emphasize human insignificance and humility before the Creator</note>—that exceeds terror itself. Yes, what is more, to see a God who became man and dies to atone for sin, and pours out all His precious blood to satisfy His Father and thereby reconcile sinners with Him again; it is unspeakable what the soul experiences upon seeing this unheard-of wonder. But finally, to also see therein that one is oneself responsible for it in one’s own person, and that even if one were the only person to have sinned, the Son of God would still have done exactly what He did for everyone; ah, then the soul can do no more, and it is annihilated.

---

(a) Psalm 31:1. <note>The German text cites Psalm 31:2 following the numbering of the Luther Bible.</note>

### Fifth Part. The Life of Maria of the etc.

Such effects are so piercing that they say everything in an instant and carry their power and effects with them, as also happened to me in this light.

3. In that very moment, my heart felt it was enraptured within itself, and completely transformed into love toward Him who had shown it this extraordinary mercy. This caused it—through the experience of this very love—to suffer such an overwhelming pain and sorrow for having offended Him that one cannot imagine it. No, it is impossible to imagine. This arrow of love was so piercing, and so relentless in refusing to ease the pain, that I would have gladly thrown myself into a fire to satisfy this love. And what is most incomprehensible: the severity of this love seemed sweet to me. It brought with it caresses and chains which bound and held the soul fast, leading it wherever love willed; and for its part, the soul considered itself blessed to be thus captured. In all these excesses, however, I saw myself always sunken in this precious blood, for whose shedding I was guilty; and that was the cause of my greatest pains, along with that arrow of love that had enraptured my soul and compelled me to confess my sins.

When I came to myself again, I found myself standing still right in front of a small chapel. I went inside and found a clergyman alone, just as if he were waiting for me. As I was then moved by the spirit that led me, I said to him: "My Father, I wish to confess, for I have committed such sins and such faults." I told him all the sins that had been shown to me, with the shedding of many tears which came from the pain I felt in my heart. A lady came in who could easily understand everything I was saying to the Father, for I spoke quite loudly; but I cared for nothing except how I might once again satisfy Him whom I had offended. When I had finished speaking, I noticed that the good Father <note>original: "Pater"; a common term for a priest or spiritual director</note> was very dismayed by the way I expressed myself; for, as he clearly saw, it was not natural but extraordinary. He said to me with great kindness: "Just go now, and come to me in my confessional tomorrow." I then left and returned to him early the following morning, repeated what I had said the previous day, and then he gave me <term>absolution</term> <note>the formal pronouncement of forgiveness of sins in the Catholic tradition</note>.

5. But to return to what happened to me: I did indeed return to our house, but changed into an entirely different creature—yes, so changed that I no longer knew myself. There I saw my ignorance revealed, which had caused me to imagine I was already quite perfect, and that my actions were very innocent and that I stood well with God. But after God had opened my eyes, I saw myself as I was, and I acknowledged that my "righteousness" was nothing but unrighteousness <note>The author uses the plural "Gerechtigkeiten" (righteousnesses), suggesting that her specific acts of self-perceived virtue were actually flawed or prideful</note>.

6. After this working of God in my soul, the impression of the blood of our Savior (which had been poured out over me) remained for over a year always in my

I felt my heart in great submission and obedience toward God, and followed all the inclinations He gave me: not as if I had <term>scruples</term> <note>In 17th-century spirituality, "scruples" refers to an obsessive or irrational fear that one is constantly sinning.</note>; rather, I possessed a great peace; but whenever something was shown to me as sin or imperfection, it happened with such great clarity that my spirit was convinced of it in an instant. 7. I still had some outward business to attend to; but the Lord granted me the grace to extricate myself from it. I had only one maidservant left, having already dismissed the other <term>household staff</term>, with the intention of entirely withdrawing from the confusing dealings of the world so that I might follow the inner pull calling me to solitude. I no longer troubled myself regarding temporal gain, although my relatives urged me toward it because God had given me skill in <term>trade</term>, and various persons offered to advance me funds for it. However, my heart felt something else, and my mind was occupied with other things. Therefore, without making any further delay, I put on <term>ridiculous clothing</term> <note>original: "lächerliche Kleidung". By dressing in a way that defied the fashion of her social class, Marie aimed to humiliate her ego and signal to society that she was no longer "on the market" for remarriage.</note> so that I might make it known to all my acquaintances that I no longer had any thought of entering into any social station in the world. I was then only twenty years old, and my son was not yet a year old.

8. My father then took me into his house, where my solitude was encouraged. For I stayed in the upper part of the house, where I performed various quiet tasks; and as my mind was always in its inner occupation, my heart spoke incessantly with God, so that I even wondered at it myself—that my heart spoke in such a way without me making it speak through my own effort. But I was driven to it by a higher power which, as I saw well, came from the impression of the precious blood and the sufferings of the Savior. Because it was something new to me, I wondered at it; and this wonder caused in me a singular esteem for the goodness and mercy of God: that His Majesty should humble Himself to communicate with me in such a way—me, whom I saw as the least of His creatures, for whom He had so lovingly shed His adorable blood. It was something incomprehensible to me that my heart spoke so familiarly and eloquently to Him. Nevertheless, without resisting, I surrendered myself to it and followed this inclination, which brought about in me more and more a hatred of myself, a forgetting of my own advantage, and a turning away from the world and its essence.

9. Ah, one must confess that the Spirit of God is a great teacher. I had never been instructed, neither in prayer nor in <term>self-denial</term>, so much...

# Part Five. The Life
<meta>catchword: my</meta>

"By me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go out and in, and find pasture" <note>This is a reference to John 10:9.</note>. I entered into Him and through Him. Into Him, I say, as I discovered His Divine Mysteries, which were to me like a rich pasture by which my soul was nourished. I went out from there without truly leaving, attending to the <term>affairs</term> <note>Referring to her external household or business duties</note> in which He had placed me; and I entered in again through a redoubling of love, by which my soul was moved never to cease taking its nourishment from the goods of this Divine Shepherd, who worked within her a perpetual communication of His life and His Spirit.

4. Around this same time, I received some books to read which taught the practice of <term>interior prayer</term> <note>A form of silent prayer focused on the internal presence of God rather than outward rituals or spoken words.</note> according to a certain method, with preparations, introductions, divisions, points, subjects, and colloquies <note>Structured conversations with God or saints.</note>. I understood all of this well and endeavored to put it into practice, because these books stated that if one did not do so, one ran the risk of being deceived by the Devil.

Through such activity of my imagination and my intellect, I resisted the inner pull of the Lord; and because I wanted so much to do it correctly, I did such violence to myself that I developed great headaches, from which I suffered much distress. Nevertheless, because I so desperately wanted to follow this book point by point, I did violence to myself anew every day, and thereby made my ailment even worse. In the meantime, I still possessed a great inner peace, coupled with the presence of God, to whose will mine remained sweetly subjected and united.

5. I was about twenty-one years old when God sent me Father Raymond as my guide, who was a very spiritual man and experienced in the direction of souls. He forbade me from <term>meditation</term> <note>In mystical tradition, "meditation" refers to structured, logical thinking about religious topics, whereas "contemplation" is a wordless resting in God. Her guide recognized she was being called to the latter.</note> during prayer, and said that I should abandon myself entirely to the leading of the Spirit of God and give him an account of everything that happened within me; which I then did with the greatest exactness.

6. As soon as I had found a guide to lead me in the ways of God, I felt greatly relieved: and if the Lord had not sent me this help through His servant, I would have rendered myself unfit for anything good. The headaches lasted for probably another two years after he had already had me stop the methodical meditation; yet the pains did not hinder me in the occupation in which His Divine Majesty held me. Hardly had I knelt down when this Divine Savior took possession of my mind, and I could do nothing else but say to Him: **"It is Love that has brought You to this state: if You were not Love itself, You would not have suffered in such a manner."** Thereupon my heart could do nothing more than endure the impressions of this Love. When it occasionally drew breath, it could say nothing but these words: **"No, if You were not Love, You would not have done such great things out of love for me."**

7. On such occasions, I sometimes had such a violent pounding of the heart that I was almost overcome. And if my heart had burst, I would [have found life] in death...
