# of Marie of the Incarnation. Chapter X.

> "...to have, and they are most blissful to be your prisoner, and to be held in your bonds: I say, in your bonds, which I would adore, for they are nothing else than your Holy Spirit, who fills them in a thousand ways with love and makes them drunk. O my adorable Love, a hundred times my love, a thousand times my love, an infinite number of times my love, one would have to see my heart laid bare and open if one wished to see the sweet negotiation of your love and its pleasant captivity. You know it, O my great God; that is enough for me: and I remain forever firmly attached to my great Love, the holy Word made flesh <note>original: "Fleisch gewordenen Wort"; refers to the Logos or Jesus Christ</note>, of whom I am the humblest slave, etc."

7. My spirit, however, became more and more simplified (afterwards), in order to exercise fewer and fewer inner and outer acts <note>original: "actes"; in mystical theology, these are specific, intentional movements of the will or mind toward God</note> which could have been sensory or perceptible to me; but in the depths of the soul, these words were unceasing: *Ah, my Love, my Beloved, be praised, O my God!* or even just these alone: *O my God! O my God.* These words in the depths filled me with a sweet nourishment, without any physical sensation. The Lord also took the violent emotional attacks away from me; and since that time my soul has remained in its center <note>original: "Mittelpunct"; a common mystical term for the deepest part of the soul where it meets the Divine</note>, which is God; and this center is within herself, where she is beyond all sensation. This is such a simple and such a delicate thing that the soul cannot express it. One can talk about everything, one can read, write, work, do what one will, and nevertheless this fundamental occupation remains always, and the soul does not cease to be united with God. Even the majesties of God do not draw her away from it; but, without standing still there, she remains attached to God in her simplicity, as she speaks to Him in the manner mentioned.

8. Now, when I saw that I remained so long in this state, I became fearful whether I might perhaps be deceived. But my Divine Bridegroom spoke these words to me inwardly: *Stay there; I will that you do here that which the blessed do in heaven.* I understood from these words that this is a very pure state, and that whoever knows how to keep themselves turned toward God, to praise His goodness, and to remain in constant attachment to Him through the union of love in the depths of their soul—where everything is in silence and separated from the senses—that person, I say, possesses the bliss of the saints in heaven. This way of staying with God continues with me perpetually.

9. At that time [when the Lord spoke those words to me], my soul sang in her wedding song: *Be praised, O my Love; be praised and glorified; O my sweet Love.* And this song lasted always, except during those intervals when perhaps new graces were given to me; but when these had passed, I began my song again. I was then twenty-eight or twenty-nine years old. God be praised eternally for His infinite mercies!

10. It seems to me that I have spoken before of the strong calling I had to the cloistered life <note>original: "Klosterleben"; life in a convent or monastery</note>, as soon as I was freed from those bonds which still held me in the world; and that the state of my business affairs did not permit me [to carry out] this intention...

### Part Five. The Life

had to carry out. This vocation followed me everywhere, and I spoke of it with my **Divine Bridegroom** <note>original: "Göttlichen Bräutigam"; a traditional mystical image for Jesus as the spouse of the soul</note> in the most intimate confidences I had with Him; He then gave me an assurance that this would yet come to pass, and this certainty gave me a confidence and a peace during the delay of this matter, which remained postponed only for the sake of my son. Nevertheless, I had such powerful stirrings from time to time that life in the world became unbearable to me.

11. Then it happened once that my **Divine Bridegroom**, seeing me in this suffering, united me with Himself in an unspeakable manner; and, just as if He wished to comfort me, He said to me quite clearly and with a very sweet love that I should have a little patience, for He would soon fulfill my desire. After these words, it seemed as if He wished to consume me in His divine and pure embraces, and He reaffirmed His promise to me once more.

12. I remained calm in this way until I was thirty years old, at which time an internal voice followed me everywhere, saying to me: *Hurry, it is time; there is nothing more for you to do in the world:* and yet, outwardly, I saw nothing that suggested this; rather, my brother involved me ever more deeply in business affairs.

<insert>[Here our Maria recounts in detail how, after many challenges and temptations, and not without a special divine providence, it was arranged that she became free and had the opportunity to enter the Ursuline Convent <note>an order of nuns focused on the education of girls</note>, leaving behind all that she had; we shall pass over this for the sake of brevity and only briefly describe her entry into the convent in her own words.]</insert>

13. The internal voice that followed me everywhere knocked constantly at the ears of my heart and opposed the voice of flesh and blood, saying: *Hurry, it is time; it is no longer good for you in the world;* until it finally gained the upper hand and caused me to leave my father and my son in the hands of God.

In the meantime, I said to my **Divine Bridegroom**: My chaste Love, I will not do this if You do not wish it; You must will for me, my Beloved, and everything shall be one and the same to me in Your divine will. Then He poured into my soul a divine nourishment and an internal strength, which made me feel as though I could have walked through fire and flames; and I received a courage that would have overcome everything.

14. And in this manner, I left everything that was dearest to me early in the morning, on **St. Paul’s Conversion Day, in the year 1631** <note>January 25, 1631</note>. As I went out of our house, my son [who was twelve years old] walked quite calmly at my side. He was not permitted to let me notice his sadness; but I saw clearly the tears running from his eyes, which gave me enough to know what he felt in his soul. I had such great compassion for him that, as I looked at him, it seemed to me

## Chapter Eleven.

Her delight in the convent life. Trials regarding her son, which nevertheless did not hinder her communion with God. Her profound peace following these temptations. The third revelation of the Trinity. The fruits of this high grace, especially an understanding of the Holy Scripture. The grace of "jubilation" <note>A state of wordless, ecstatic spiritual joy.</note>, of spiritual cheerfulness, and so forth.

->I.<-

1. It is impossible to express how sweet the convent life was to me after I had left the world and God had opened this earthly paradise to me—especially after such unrest as that which I had left behind. I saw myself received among the novices <note>original: "Probtöchter," literally "probationary daughters"; women in the initial testing period before taking permanent vows.</note>, where one need not worry about anything except observing the rules of the convent.

2. One of the first things imposed upon me was that I had to follow the common path of the others and give up my previous practices of penance. Although I loved **mortification** <term>the practice of spiritual self-denial or physical discipline to overcome worldly desires</term>, I felt in this situation neither a thought nor an impulse that would have been contrary to obedience. For the Lord gave me a great love for this "common life," which I have also maintained ever since, except for what obedience has allowed me or required of me on certain occasions.

3. God allowed me to face a great trial quite soon. A crowd of small children, who were my son’s schoolmates, gathered around him; they mocked him and cried out that he had been so foolish and simple-minded to let me go into the convent. They said: now he was without a father and without a mother, and would be utterly despised and abandoned. "Let us go," they said to him, "and fetch her back; we will make a fine noise so that they must give her back to you." At this, the child was so violently moved that he wept piteously. They then came in a great number before the gate of the convent and made such an unheard-of noise and shouting with the greatest vehemence—demanding that I should be given back—that it could be heard far and wide. At first, I did not know what it was; but among these confused voices, I heard the voice of my son, who called out with a loud cry: "Give me my mother! Give me my mother!" This cut through my

# Section Five. The Life

...treasures of Divine Glory <note>original: "magnificence"</note>. The eternal Father was my father; the most adorable Word <note>Refers to the *Logos* or Jesus Christ, the second person of the Trinity.</note> was my bridegroom; and the Holy Spirit was the one who, through His working, disposed and prepared my soul, and caused it to receive the Divine impressions.

9. In all this activity, I looked upon myself as nothing—indeed, as an entirely pure nothingness—which this great "All" chose so that I might receive the workings of His great mercies. I could say nothing else except: "O my great God, O most adorable abyss, I am pure nothingness." And the answer came to me: "And although you are indeed pure nothingness, you are nonetheless perfectly suited <note>original: "propre"</note> for me." This was repeated to me several times, as I humbled myself; and the more I humbled myself, the more I saw that I had grown greater; and my soul received such caresses as cannot be grasped by the senses, nor expressed in human words. Ah, who can express how highly God honors the soul which He has created in His image, when it pleases Him to lift it up into His Divine embraces.

10. After this extraordinary grace, which happened to me about two months after my entry into the convent <note>Marie entered the Ursuline convent in Tours in 1631.</note>, my spirit—which always retained the impression and the anointing of this great grace—became more withdrawn and distant than ever from the things of this world, and more moved toward the service of God. In this, God granted me an understanding of the Holy Scriptures with a nourishing sweetness. I understood in French what I was required to sing and recite in the Latin language; this so captivated my mind that, if I had not restrained my outward behavior, it would have broken out. Singing relieved me and gave my mind an outlet: my senses were so moved by it that I felt a strong urge to clap my hands and call upon the whole world to sing the praises of such a great God, who is so worthy that all should consume themselves in His love and service.

11. I sometimes found myself in a state of prayer where I feared I might fall into a kind of curiosity <note>original: "Vorwitz," referring here to an intellectual meddling or pride that interferes with pure devotion.</note>, which could prevent me from uniting with God purely in spirit, in the nakedness of the spirit <term>nakedness of spirit: a mystical state of stripping away all mental images, concepts, and self-will to be fully open to God's presence</term>. Certain words of the Holy Scriptures came to my memory, which I had perhaps read or heard. The meaning of such words was revealed to me, and I became aware that from them, a whole series of other scriptural passages emerged in my mind. I had such insight into these that it seemed as if someone were preaching to me and telling me the mysteries hidden within them; this gave me a sweet delight in the depths of my soul. I also saw therein all kinds of spiritual food for the nourishment of souls, and how differently they are nourished by it—for some use everything to their own ruin, while others receive a life of grace and love from it. There I discovered a great number of faults committed even by very spiritual persons, and the harm they suffer because they do not follow the counsels <note>original: "conseils"</note> given to us in the Holy Scripture;

When I walked, I did not feel that I was touching the earth. All of this did not consist of a mere sentimentality that poured into the senses, but in the power and vigor of the spirit that took possession of me.

### Part Five: The Life

...that which my neighbor did. I felt inclinations to throw myself down from somewhere; it seemed to me that I was deceived by the devil, and that I had been in error; and I believed now that everything which had happened within me, and which people had believed was from God, had been only pretenses and deceptions; for all the graces I had received came before my eyes, and I fell into great distress and suffering because of it.

2. Father Raymond (my spiritual director), who visited me, gave me all possible assistance; and as long as he was with me, the trust I had in him made me believe that he told me the truth; but as soon as he had gone away, I believed again that I had deceived him. My imagination <note>original: *Phantasie*</note> was in such motion through the mental images of the reproaches, which mingled together in a confused heap, that I got a violent headache from it, which lasted constantly; moreover, out of <term>obedience<note>In a religious order, "obedience" refers to the vow to follow the instructions of superiors as if they were from God.</note></term>, I had to perform such works that required diligence and attention, whereby my pains were further increased. But my imagination caused me more suffering than everything else; especially since its activity in me was quite extraordinary, as it had previously been held back by the occupations of the spirit, in which the imagination had no part but had to remain silent.

3. In the depths of my soul, I had a sense of <term>acquiescence<note>original French: *acquiescement*; a quiet surrender or acceptance of God's will.</note></term> regarding God, and it seemed to me that His Divine Majesty, who was exercising His justice over me, was within me in a place that seemed very distant to me, from which He looked upon me and took pleasure in seeing me suffer. But in this consent to the will of God, which I had in my sufferings, I did not know in which region of the spirit He might be; indeed, I could hardly see Him, because the darkness I endured was great; so that, in my opinion, I received no relief from Him, and I had to carry my cross alone; and all I could do was this: that I strove to compose myself in patience and not to fall into willful <term>imperfections<note>Marie distinguishes between "imperfections"—minor failings or human weaknesses—and deliberate, grave sins.</note></term>.

4. My sufferings lasted into the third year, except for some brief moments. I was in such an internal state that I thought I had fallen from a high mountain into an abyss of misery. Prayer was a torment to me because during it, I was attacked by all kinds of loathsome mental images. It seemed to me that I wanted evil and that I was an enemy to all good. What doubled my suffering was that I saw how I was becoming worse among holy souls than I had been among the godless people of the world. I believed that I was using God's graces only to my own harm; I saw myself constantly falling into very sensitive imperfections; it seemed to me that all the sisters had a burden in carrying me—indeed, that they had a loathing of seeing me because of my imperfections; when I was supposed to go into the <term>refectory<note>original: *Essaal*; the communal dining hall in a monastery or convent.</note></term>, it was even more difficult for me than if I had to perform a great <term>mortification<note>original: *Mortifikation*; a religious practice of self-denial or penance.</note></term>; I suffered day and night, and everywhere; and I did not believe that there was any grace left for me with God. The only thing that gave me some rest was the singing of the Psalms (in the community), through which, it seemed, all my sufferings were driven away, and which [filled] me with

5. Amidst all these sufferings, the <term>depths of the soul<note>original: *Grund der Seelen*. In mystical theology, this refers to the innermost essence of a person where they meet God, separate from emotions or intellect.</note></term> remained in peace, and would not have desired the diminishing of its cross for a single moment; and however much I suffered, I nonetheless had God constantly present. But to see God as an incomprehensible purity, and to see oneself in His presence as a collection of all such miseries which are contrary to this purity—that is a cruel martyrdom.

6. Despite all this, I still spoke with the Savior through words of love; but this very act increased my suffering as well, because I thought it only happened because I was accustomed to speaking in such a manner, and that such words did not proceed from a true love. One day, while I was in this distress, I offered up my entire cross to my Divine Bridegroom; and then He answered me inwardly: **"Upon whom will my spirit rest, if not upon the humble?"** <note>original: *Ueber wem wird mein Geist ruhen, als nur über den Demüthigen?* A reference to Isaiah 66:2.</note> I became quite ashamed at this and told Him I had no humility; just as I truly saw none in myself, though I did feel a great desire to become humble. These words of my Divine Love had something so lovely in them that they filled my inner being with an inexpressible consolation; I remained for a time in great stillness and inner simplicity.

7. Now, seeing myself for a little while at rest, I remained ashamed in His presence and said: "My dear Love, I am not weary of suffering; no, I am not weary." Consequently, my cross returned, to which I was then fastened more firmly than before. I became more darkened, more <term>dry<note>original: *dürre*. Spiritual "dryness" or aridity is a state where a person feels no emotional or sensible satisfaction in religious practice.</note></term>, more insensitive, and more besieged by various temptations than before. Terrible impurities were presented to my imagination which made me tremble; I hardly dared to open my eyes. Even the purest objects caused me evil thoughts against God, and so forth. My heart was so pierced with pain as I saw myself filled with such imperfections and evil stirrings that I spent my time in unheard-of anxieties; and I did not know whether God had entirely given me up because of my wickednesses.

8. Father Raymond, from whom alone I still received some comfort, was also taken from me and sent elsewhere; and my [new] confessor served no purpose other than to increase my sufferings. When I spoke with him of my trials and miseries, I received no other answer than that I had not "died" enough to myself; that my inner state had not been sufficiently guarded; and that I had no foundation in virtue—that this was the cause of my suffering. If the Lord gave me

9. My entire inner state then consisted of this: I held myself before God as a person already condemned to death. I was also too timid to perform inner <term>acts</term> <note>original: *actes*. In mystical tradition, "acts" are specific, intentional movements of the will or heart toward God, such as an act of contrition or an act of love.</note> on my own; only when I perhaps forgot what I was for a moment did I become aware that I was speaking tenderly to the Savior, and that I was complaining to Him that I did not love Him as I wished to—Him, who was my sweet love and who had shown me so much mercy.

10. This fear that I had been deceived disturbed me greatly, for I was not at all free or open with my confessor, and I feared him more than I can say. Sometimes three months would pass without him speaking to me, despite all my suffering. Among other instances, once when he had left me in extreme distress regarding my prayer, I remained in the greatest fear and thought he had given up on me because he judged my ailment to be beyond help. Surely, to leave a soul in such great mental suffering for three months—should that not give cause to increase the suspicion she had that she did not stand right with God? Therefore, I asked our Superior if I might be allowed to write to him. For although he often came to the house for the sake of the other sisters, I nonetheless did not dare to request that he come to see me. I then suggested to him that, if he deemed it useful, I would be willing to use a book during prayer to keep my imagination somewhat quiet, and to draw something good from it to occupy myself; I said I had no objection to behaving in this way, nor to the sisters discovering my ignorance; and that even if I had only lost time in prayer and given way to temptation until this hour, I still did not want to lose heart, but was ready to start entirely anew to serve the Lord better now. Nevertheless, he did not come to me, nor did he answer me; only three weeks later did he send a short note to our Superior with these words:

12. It seemed to me that the Divine Bridegroom <note>A central image in mystical theology, drawing from the Song of Solomon, where the soul is the bride and Christ is the bridegroom.</note> wished to use nothing but severity against me, and that I was imprisoned to endure an eternal torment. I united myself with His will out of love for Him, whose decrees I wished to love, no matter how much suffering they might cause me. Anyone who could see the soul in this state would have to weep out of compassion; especially since she always keeps her gaze fixed steadily upon her Divine Bridegroom, and yet He not only fails to ease her suffering in the slightest, but even increases it through an excessive bitterness. He does this by letting her see, on one hand, how pure and perfect He is, while on the other, she sees herself pursued by so many enemies from whom she cannot free herself.

To see that this Divine Bridegroom looks upon her, and yet meanwhile lets her sink into this abyss of suffering without wishing to help her—that causes her the most sensitive pain. Despite all this, however, she still sees that her Beloved lets her suffer so out of love; which then causes her to say to Him: I am content to be thus, O my worthy Love; I am content to be thus.

<margin>(a) Psalm 126:5.</margin>
13. Once, as I was completely sacrificing myself to His Divine will, I heard this word within my inner being, with as much clarity and distinctness as one can speak it (a): *You shall sow with tears, but reap with joy.* <note>original: "Du wirst mit Thränen säen, aber mit Freuden erndten." This is a German translation of Psalm 126:5.</note> Immediately following this, everything that had seemed difficult to me became sweet and easy. I certainly still felt my suffering; but the sweetness of these words increased the love of the cross within me to such an extent that I was willing to suffer until the Day of Judgment.

14. After this state, I fell into another which caused me far greater torment. The solitude that I had loved so much seemed to me to be a purgatory: it became unbearable for me to sit in a cell all day without seeing another human soul. I felt that I was clinging to creatures <note>In this context, "creatures" refers to any created beings, specifically other people, as opposed to God the Creator.</note>, yet I did not see a single one who might relieve me; instead, it seemed to me that they had all forgotten me. The work I performed, which I otherwise used to love, became so loathsome to me that I had to use great force upon myself to stick with it; my outward self became so weary from it that I could hardly bear myself. When I had to sing, I could not bring forth a single word, so great was the inward sorrow. In prayer, my first thoughts were of my various sufferings; and this meditation lasted from beginning to end, especially concerning what I had to suffer from my confessor and others who had caused me pain. On the other hand, I saw clearly that all of this was such an imperfection in me, which indeed constituted the greatest part of my suffering. My thoughts were constantly on the imperfections of other people; and when I looked at myself, I found that I was the most imperfect person in the whole world. All these impressions I had to [endure] like so many...

### Fifth Part. The Life of Maria of the Incarnation, etc.

[After our blessed Maria described several more remarkable changes and conditions of her heavy suffering, she relates in the following manner the means by which God finally delivered her from them.]

15. Around the same time, Father de la Haye, a Jesuit, occasionally came to our convent and gave an exhortation. Then I felt strongly moved to speak with him, but I did not let this be noticed at all, instead leaving it all to the Providence of God. This same Providence then arranged it so that my Superior asked me if I wished to speak with him and reveal my heart to him. I replied that I greatly desired to do so. Whereupon she then asked the Father to visit me often, as he was staying in Tours; which he then promised and also did with much love.

16. When I had told him orally the whole story of God’s guidance over me from my childhood onward, he wanted me to give him all of this in writing, so that he would have more time to examine it; my Superior also permitted it. However, I felt a great resistance to doing so unless I were also allowed to write down all my sins and imperfections, as far as I could remember them, so that he could judge my condition all the better. I then did this as faithfully as possible and gave it to the Father; who, after he had examined everything and received from me the explanations he believed necessary, assured me that it was the Spirit of God who had guided me, and that I would sin most deeply if I were to have a heart and love for any other thing but God alone. After these words, all my sufferings vanished, as if I had been released from a harsh imprisonment; and from the effects of this, I knew well enough that God had wanted this of me. I found myself as if in a new land, possessing once again my peace and intimate communion with the Divine Majesty as before, with the addition of a very great peace and quite extraordinary graces regarding the understanding of **Holy Scripture**, which the Father recommended I read instead of a <term>Rodriguez</term><note>A reference to Alonso Rodriguez, a Jesuit author whose manual "The Practice of Perfection and Christian Virtues" was standard reading in convents. Switching from a manual to direct Scripture was a significant shift in her spiritual formation.</note>. Afterward, I received such a great love and desire for inner suffering that, if I were given the choice either to enjoy all spiritual pleasures or to endure all the crosses and sufferings I have faced—which were certainly very diverse and so intense that I cannot describe even a thousandth part of them—I would nevertheless quite willingly take all my suffering upon myself: such an inclination the Lord gives me toward it, and He lets me recognize the great goods that are hidden within it when one bears it with due faithfulness.

# Chapter Thirteen.

Prophetic vision of *Canada*. She instructs the novices from the inner fullness of the Spirit. Her speeches were like ingenious proverbs. Her Apostolic state. Admirable effects of this state.

->I.<-

[Hereupon she relates a certain prophetic vision she had of her future journey to *Canada*, although she did not actually understand it at the time. Meanwhile, it seems that Divine Providence wished to prepare her for this important service through the instruction of the novices <note>original: "Probtöchter," literally "test-daughters," referring to women in their trial period before taking full vows.</note> of the monastery, an office which was assigned to her at this time.] In the second year of my profession, (she continues), I was made assistant mistress to the novices, of whom there were about thirty, and I was tasked with instructing them in Christian doctrine. I did this with a great zeal which **GOD** communicated to me; in which I also had an ease of expressing myself concerning the mysteries of the faith. I had much light regarding this and bore in my soul a grace of wisdom, which caused me to say things at times that I would not have dared to say without possessing this fullness of the Spirit.

2. Inwardly, I experienced that it was the Holy Spirit who had given me the key to the treasures of the holy incarnate **Word** <note>A theological term for Jesus Christ, derived from the "Logos" in the Gospel of John.</note> and had opened them to me in the understanding of the Holy Scripture. My spirit was more free and better able to endure the heavenly touches and Divine influences communicated to me, as one belonging to the kingdom of the holy incarnate **Word**, who nourished me and opened to me His riches and the sovereignty which His Father had given Him over hearts after He, through the shedding of His precious blood, had triumphed over the kingdom of hell and death.

3. In the inward union that I had enjoyed with His Divine Majesty, I recognized that my Divine Bridegroom was, as it were, the heart and the breast of the Eternal Father, from which a great stream of fire flowed—namely, the Holy Spirit—which flooded all the saints and nourished them with His Divine life. From this life and from this Spirit, my soul was now nourished, so that because of its fullness I could not prevent some small sparks from breaking out externally.

4. Whenever I was visited (which happened often), my words always carried something fiery with them, so that I also gained the reputation that all my speeches were like ingenious proverbs.

### Fifth Part. The Life

...but instead, they were brought forth through the fruitfulness of the Spirit which possessed me. When I then turned my eyes toward myself, I found myself in spirit in the midst of many throngs of souls who did not know my Bridegroom <note>A common mystical reference to Jesus Christ, particularly used by nuns to describe their spiritual relationship with the Divine.</note>, and therefore did not pay Him honors of submission. But I performed these honors in their stead; I embraced them and wished to immerse them in the precious blood of this adorable Lord and Master.

7. My spirit was constantly outside of myself; meanwhile, my body wasted away and became like a skeleton, so that my superior, who questioned me about my internal state, feared that this actual and prolonged withdrawal of the mind <note>original: "abstraction," referring to a state of being so focused on the divine that one is disconnected from the physical world.</note> might cause my death. For this reason, I was commanded to apply all my strength to break my thoughts away from it. I also did my best to obey, but it was not in my power to leave this state. When it was finally seen that it was impossible for me, they left me peacefully to the guidance of Him who moved my spirit so powerfully.

8. Father Dinet <note>Jacques Dinet (1584–1653), a Jesuit who served as a spiritual director and later became the provincial of the Jesuits in France.</note>, who had been given to me as a guide, and to whom I reported what was occurring within me regarding this Apostolic spirit, approved of my state. He said that what had been shown to me in the land (in the vision) might well come true through a mission to Canada. When he told me this, I had never even heard that a "Canada" existed in the world, and what I had seen in the spirit gave me no geographical knowledge of it. I, however, could not imagine that the Lord wanted to have me physically in a foreign land to perform some service for Him, as I lived enclosed in a monastery <note>As an Ursuline nun, Marie belonged to a cloistered order, making the prospect of international travel legally and practically extraordinary.</note>, even though my spirit was incessantly there.

9. As these states of my mind became more firmly established, it happened one day while I was in prayer that I was suddenly rapt in **GOD**. In that moment, the vast land that had been shown to me (in the vision) was placed before my eyes once again. Then the Adorable Majesty said to me:

> That is Canada, which I have let you see; there
> you must go.

These words, which brought spirit and life into my soul, placed me in that moment into an inexpressible annihilation <note>In mystical theology, "annihilation" (original: "Vernichtung") refers to the complete surrender and "melting away" of the individual self and its will into the Divine.</note> as this infinite and Adorable Majesty gave me this command. Yet, He granted me sufficient strength so that I could answer Him and say:

> O my great **GOD**, You can do everything, and I can do nothing; if it pleases You to help me,
> behold, so I am ready; I promise that I will be
> obedient to You; do in me and through me Your most adorable will.

I required no deliberation; the answer followed the command, and my will was united with the will of **GOD** from that moment on. A loving ecstasy followed, in which this infinite Goodness showed me such endearments as no human tongue can ever express, and there followed great inner fruits of virtue.

### I.

At this very time, while the Divine Majesty kept me so occupied, He also disposed the heart of Madame de la Peltrie <note>Marie-Madeleine de Chauvigny de la Peltrie (1603–1671), a wealthy widow who funded the Ursuline mission to Canada</note>, a very virtuous person of noble rank, to give herself and all her goods to the mission in Canada; she had been moved to this by reading a report <note>The "Jesuit Relations," annual reports sent from the missions in New France to Europe</note> in which Father le Jeune [a missionary in Canada] used these words among others: *Shall not a holy soul be found who has so much zeal that she might come and gather up the blood of the Son of God which is being lost in Canada, so that it may be applied to the salvation of the poor wild people?* By these heart-stirring words, this virtuous lady was won over, and she sought all possible means to put her good desires into action; she also prayed to the Lord that He might arrange her affairs in such a state as He deemed useful for the execution of this plan.

### Fifth Life. The Life of Marie of the Incarnation, etc.

firstly on the 4th of May of that same year they were able to embark. See with what disposition of mind she undertook this important journey:]

8. I threw myself [she writes] down before the Lord, and worshiped the Majesty of God for a long time, and offered myself to Him as a perpetual burnt offering <note>term: *Brandopfer* (burnt offering); in mystical tradition, this refers to a total self-sacrifice where the soul is "consumed" by divine love</note>. There I experienced that the Holy Spirit took possession of my soul, and imparted to it such movements as were suited to the undertaking I now wished to carry out in return for the love I wished to show to the most adorable Word made Flesh <note>original: *Fleisch gewordene Wort*; referring to Jesus Christ (the Logos)</note>, to whom I gave myself. O God! who can express what transpired during this giving and surrendering of my whole self. I cannot express it. On my part, I saw that the Spirit who led me gave witness to my conscience that I had never before done anything so much from the heart; and furthermore, I experienced that the holy Word made Flesh, the King and Monarch of all nations, loved and accepted my gift.

9. While I was in this communion with Him, we were led toward the shore of the sea, where we were surrounded on all sides by people who were watching. My spirit, meanwhile, was so occupied in its devotion and conversation with the most adorable Word made Flesh that it could hardly be drawn away from it. If one had looked at me outwardly, one would not have judged such things of me; for outwardly I did everything in a free and modest manner, as was fitting.

10. Finally we had to part, and leave our "Guardian Angel" [so she calls Bernières <note>Jean de Bernières-Louvigny (1602–1659), a wealthy layman and mystic who provided spiritual and practical support for the mission</note>, who had accompanied and protected them from Tours all the way to the ship for three months] forever, which did not happen without pain; but in his kindness, he took our affairs upon himself [thereafter as well] with more than fatherly care. In all the interaction we had with one another, from beginning to end, we recognized that this man of God was full of the Holy Spirit, and entirely an enemy of the spirit of the world.

11. As I set my foot into the boat which was to take us to the ship, it seemed to me as if I were entering Paradise; because I was taking the first step that enabled me to venture my life for the sake of the love of Him who had given it to me. I sang to myself the mercies of so good a God, who led me with so much love to the state for which I had longed for so long. Meanwhile, the anchor was weighed, the sails were raised, and the wind carried us away; and in this manner I left France, with the intention of never returning, and to dedicate my life to the service of the wild nations <note>historical term: *wilden Völker*; the 17th-century European term for the Indigenous peoples of North America</note>, so that I might make them tame <note>interpretive note: in this context, "tame" refers to the contemporary goal of Europeanization and conversion to Christianity</note>, and subject them to their rightful King, my heavenly and Divine Bridegroom.

# Chapter Fifteen.

*Their terrifying danger at sea; and her wonderful steadfastness and stillness of soul through it. Her great hardship on the land journey. The time of her arrival at Quebec. Modest, difficult, yet joyful beginnings there. She learns the languages of the heathens <note>term: "heathens" (*Heiden*); here referring to non-Christian Indigenous people from a 17th-century European perspective</note>; instructs the savages <note>term: "savages" (*Wilden*); the common, though now derogatory, historical term used by Europeans to describe the Indigenous peoples of North America</note>; and the difficulties therein.*

---

->1.<-

I continued my journey with the same pleasure and inward comfort with which I had begun it; especially as I saw myself constantly exposed to an unstable element, whereby I had to be in perpetual danger for my life. The entire time of my voyage was a real opportunity for a constant sacrifice; as I surrendered myself day and night as an offering to God in the unceasing dangers, but primarily in one occurrence of which I wish to speak more fully, and which will be no less unbelievable to those who hear of it than it was terrifying to those who saw it.

2. As it began to grow dark, an unheard-of and terrifyingly large mass of ice appeared, which bore down upon us with incredible power and violence, threatening us with nothing but inevitable shipwreck. It was as large as a city surrounded by walls and fortifications, and had jutting points like towers.

Everyone cried out: God have mercy! We are lost! So that at this sudden approach of death—which, by all human appearance, was inevitable—Father Vimond <note>Historical Note: Barthélemy Vimont was a Jesuit priest and superior of the missions in New France</note> gave the general absolution <note>term: *General Absolution*; a Catholic ritual where a priest grants forgiveness of sins to a group of people whose lives are in immediate danger</note>. During the time of all this shouting, my spirit was in as great a peace and stillness as one can ever be; I never felt the slightest stir of any terror, but found myself very well prepared to make a total sacrifice of myself, with a calm surrender of my will, never to see our dear natives again. In that very moment, I had before my eyes all the graces the Lord had granted me regarding Canada: His command, His promises, His guidance; and despite all this, my mind found itself in an indifference toward living or dying: my only desire was that God's will might be fulfilled, which by all appearances was now to happen through our death. Madame de la Peltrie <note>Historical Note: Madeleine de la Peltrie (1603–1671) was the wealthy patroness who funded the Ursulines' mission to Canada</note> held tight to me, so that we might die together. I took hold of my clothing so that, if the ship were to break apart, I could be seen in nothing but a decent posture <note>interpretive note: even in the face of death, Marie is concerned with maintaining the modesty and decorum required of her religious habit</note>.

### Fifth Life. The Life of Marie of the Incarnation, etc.

[...finally, on May 4th of that same year, they were able to embark. See with what state of mind she began this important journey:]

8. I cast myself down [she writes] before the Lord, and for a long time I adored the Majesty of God, offering myself to Him as a perpetual burnt offering <note>original: *Brandopfer*; a theological term for a "holocaust" or total sacrifice of oneself to God's will</note>. There I experienced how the Holy Spirit took possession of my soul, imparting to it such movements as were suited to the undertaking I now intended to carry out: a return for the love I wished to show to the most adorable Incarnate Word <note>original: *über-anbetungswürdige Fleisch gewordene Wort*</note>, to whom I gave myself. O God! who can express what transpired during this donation and surrender of my whole self? I cannot put it into words. Within myself, I saw that the Spirit who led me gave witness to my conscience that I had never before done anything so completely from the heart; and furthermore, I experienced that the holy Incarnate Word, the King and Monarch of all nations, loved and accepted my offering.

9. While I was in this communion with Him, we were led toward the seashore, where we were surrounded on all sides by people watching us. My spirit, meanwhile, was so occupied in its devotion and conversation with the most adorable Incarnate Word that it could hardly be withdrawn from Him. If one had looked at me outwardly, they would not have judged me to be so; for externally, I did everything in a free and modest manner, as was proper.

10. Finally, we had to part and leave our guardian angel [so she calls Monsieur de Bernières <note>Jean de Bernières-Louvigny (1602–1659), a French mystic and treasurer who sponsored and protected the missionaries</note>, who had accompanied and protected them from Tours until they reached the ship in the third month] forever, which did not happen without sorrow; but in his kindness, he took our affairs upon himself [even afterwards] with more than fatherly care. In all the interaction we had with one another, from beginning to end, we recognized that this man of God was full of the Holy Spirit, and was entirely an enemy of the spirit of the world.

11. As I set my foot into the boat which was to take us to the ship, it seemed to me as if I were entering Paradise; because I was taking the first step that would enable me to risk my life for the sake of the love of Him who had given it to me. I sang within myself the mercies of such a good God, who led me with so much love to the state for which I had long yearned. Meanwhile, the anchor was weighed, the sails were raised, and the wind carried us away; and in this manner, I left France with the intention of never returning, dedicating my life to the service of the wild peoples <note>term: "wild peoples" (*wilden Völker*); a common historical term for the Indigenous peoples of North America, reflecting the colonial perspective of the era</note>, so that I might make them tame <note>meaning: to convert them to Christianity and European customs</note> and subject them to their rightful King, my heavenly and Divine Bridegroom.

# Chapter Fifteen.

## Her terrifying danger at sea; and her wonderful constancy and peace of mind therein. Her great hardship on the journey by land. The time of her arrival at Quebec. Humble, difficult, but joyful beginnings there. She learns the languages of the heathens; instructs the savages <note>original: *Wilden*; the standard 17th-century European term for Indigenous peoples</note>; and the hardships thereof.

->I.<-

I continued my journey with the same pleasure and inward comfort with which I had begun it; especially since I saw myself incessantly exposed to an unstable element <note>The ocean</note>, through which I was in constant danger of my life. The entire time of my voyage was a true opportunity for a constant sacrifice; as I gave myself up to God as an offering night and day amidst the unceasing dangers, but primarily in one occurrence of which I will speak more fully, and which will be no less incredible to those who hear it than it was terrifying to those who witnessed it.

2. As it began to grow dark, an unheard-of and terrifyingly large piece of ice <note>An iceberg</note> appeared, which bore down upon us with incredible power and vehemence, threatening us with nothing less than an inevitable shipwreck. It was as large as a city surrounded by walls and fortifications, and had jutting peaks like towers.

Everyone cried out: "God have mercy! We are lost!" so that at this sudden approach of death, which to all human appearances was unavoidable, Father Vimond <note>Barthélemy Vimont (1594–1667), a Jesuit missionary who accompanied the nuns and later became the superior of the mission in Canada</note> gave the general absolution <note>A collective grant of forgiveness for sins, given by a priest when death is imminent and there is no time for individual confession</note>. During all this shouting, my spirit was in as much peace and stillness as one can possibly be; I never felt the slightest movement of any terror, but found myself very well prepared to make a complete sacrifice of myself, with a calm resignation of my will to the fact that I might never see our dear savages. In that same moment, I had before my eyes all the graces the Lord had granted me regarding Canada—His command, His promises, His guidance—and despite all this, my mind found itself in an indifference toward living or dying: my only desire was that God's will might be fulfilled, which according to all appearances was now to happen through our deaths. Madame de la Peltrie <note>The wealthy patroness who funded the Ursuline mission to Canada</note> held tight to me so that we might die together. I arranged my dress so that, if the ship were to shatter, I could be seen in nothing but a decent posture.

### Fifth Part. The Life

...turned to another side, whereby the ship made such a turn that this enormous ice, which at that time was only a spear's length from the ship, was now at the ship's side; and it was a visible miracle that it caused us no harm, as everyone cried out: Miracle, miracle! I saw this terrifying ice myself; but the darkness prevented me from being able to see its highest peak; it appeared astonishing to me, and I would never have believed that the sea could carry such an enormous mass without it sinking to the bottom. This happened on Trinity Sunday <note>original: *Sonntage Trinitatis*; the first Sunday after Pentecost</note>.

3. On two other occasions we thought we would perish, especially once when we were lost for about 60 miles among the cliffs without being able to get out. When we were back on the right course and drew near to the land, we encountered many savages <note>original: *Wilden*; the standard 17th-century European term for Indigenous peoples</note>, to our great joy. These poor people, who had never seen people shaped like us, stood quite dismayed: and when they were told that we were the Captain’s daughters <note>The travelers used simplified social categories familiar to the Indigenous people to explain their status</note> (for one had to speak according to the custom of their land), who out of love for them had left our country, our relatives, and all the splendors of France, they were as if enchanted with wonder; and even more so when they were told that we were minded to instruct their daughters, so that they would not have to burn in fire, but might be eternally blessed. They could not comprehend how such a thing could happen; and so that they might see what would come of it, they accompanied us by land (a) all the way to Quebec.

4. But to return to my previous narrative, I thought I would die of thirst on the ship; for the fresh water had been spoiled by the sea, and my stomach could not tolerate strong drink, which caused me an illness that tormented me greatly. I slept almost not at all throughout the entire journey; and this sleeplessness was accompanied by such a violent headache that, without causing my death, it could not have been more severe. In the meantime, however, my soul and heart possessed a very great peace, in the union of my highest and only Good. **GOD** be infinitely praised for His mercies which He has shown me during this time!

5. After so many accidents and storms, we arrived at Quebec on August 1, 1639. All the inhabitants were so happy to see us that, as a testimony of their joy, they ceased all their business that same day. The first thing we did after stepping off the ship was to kiss this land into which we had come to consume our lives in the service of **GOD** and our poor savages; and thereupon the *We Praise Thee, O God* <note>original: *Te Deum*; a traditional Latin hymn of praise and thanksgiving</note> was sung in the church.

6. The following day, we were led into the village of the savages, our dear brothers, where we received very great comfort and joy in hearing them sing the praise of **GOD** in their own language. Oh, how we were enchanted with joy that we saw ourselves among our good new converts! He who had first become a Christian gave us his daughter <insert>to instruct</insert>, and within a few days we were given more...

various others. We were given a small little house as our dwelling until a place to build the convent was chosen. This house consisted of only two small rooms, in which we considered ourselves better accommodated than if we had been in a royal palace, since we had our treasures with us, for which we had come: namely, our beloved new converts.

7. This small house was soon transformed into a hospital due to the smallpox <note>original: *Kinderpocken*</note>, from which three or four daughters of the savages <note>original: *Wilden*; the standard 17th-century European term for Indigenous peoples</note> died. In this poverty, the Divine Majesty gave my sisters such zeal and courage that not a single one felt any repulsion at the illness and uncleanness of the savages.

8. Then we also had to learn the language of the savages, to which I applied myself immediately, out of a desire to instruct them. However, since I had not been able to work with my head on any matter involving science or speculation for more than twenty years, this studying of such a completely foreign language caused me great headaches. When I considered the difficulty of this barbaric language, I believed that, by natural means, I would never be able to learn it. I dealt with this lovingly with our Lord, who, regardless of all difficulties, came to my aid in such a way that in a short time I understood and spoke it with very great ease, so that my inner devotion was neither hindered nor interrupted by it.

9. Around this time, the savages of both sexes came to us in crowds; I then instructed them in the duties of a Christian and in the mysteries of our faith, and conversed with them to the singular delight of my heart. Otherwise, the savages are very filthy and very hard to endure, partly because their [boucan] <term>boucan: meat dried or smoked over a fire, a term from which "buccaneer" is derived; here it refers to the smoky smell of the preserved food</term> dried meat, which they eat, causes a bad odor in them, and also because they use no linen. Nevertheless, none of this was disgusting to us; the Lord has also always preserved this mindset in us, so that we found our pleasure, and nothing but pure grace, among these souls purchased with the blood of Jesus Christ.

10. After I had come into this land and had observed everything I saw there a little more closely, I recognized that it was the same land that the Lord had shown me six years ago. These great mountains, these vast and wide forests, these almost immeasurable lands, the layout and the shape of the places that came into my sight, were exactly the same as those I had seen, and which were still as fresh in my mind as at the time when I saw them.

11. The uncleanness of the savage daughters meant that we sometimes found a shoe in our pot, and daily hair, coals, and similar filth, which nevertheless caused us no disgust. The people who came to visit us could not understand how we could accustom ourselves so, and that we [took] the little orphans—

We lived in this little house for more than three years, with many hardships for the body, but very content and comforted in the spirit.

## The Sixteenth Chapter.

### Change of her inner state. Her deep inner sufferings and purifications, which reached the point of despair. The purest act of abandonment to God. The ways of Divine Purity, for our necessary purification. The innermost ground remains free. Supreme abandonment. She accuses herself as guilty before God, both in general and in particular.

->I.<-

To come closer to my inner state and the guidance of God over me: after our embarkation <note>original: *Einschiffung*; referring to the 1639 voyage from France to Canada</note> I received the experience of what the Divine Majesty had shown me would happen. This began through a change in the peace I had initially felt into the kind of peace He gave me during our voyage. This was a fundamental and deep peace; however, although it dwelt within me, it felt distant from me, so that because of its subtlety, I saw it only as if in a far-off region. This was very painful to my nature and very distressing to the spirit <note>original: *l'esprit*</note>. And just as I have said of another state—that the powers of the soul no longer acted because God had made them as if lost and annihilated them in their very ground <note>original: *Grund*; a mystical term for the deepest center of the soul</note> as He took possession of it and mastered it—so they remained in this state as if dead, or rather as if crucified. In this state, the lower part experienced, both in its interior and its exterior, what it means to serve **GOD** at one's own expense; and in this point, one first recognizes whether one has any steadfastness in virtue. 2. From this state, I fell into one far more painful. I saw myself, according to my perception, stripped of all gifts of grace and nature that **GOD** had placed in me. I lost confidence in each and every person: and even the most holy, and those with whom I had held the most intimate friendship, were the ones who caused me the greatest cross and mortification <note>In this context, mortification refers to spiritual humiliation or the "dying" of the ego.</note>, in that **GOD** permitted them to have constant temptations of aversion toward me, as they afterward confessed to me. I saw myself as the very least and most contemptible person in the world; and in this impression, I could not sufficiently marvel at the goodness, the friendliness, and the humility of my sisters, that they were still willing to be subject to me and to bear with me. Because of this weight of humiliation, I hardly dared to lift my eyes; and in this lowliness of spirit, I applied myself to doing the very worst and meanest tasks, because I did not judge myself worthy to do others. During the hours of recreation, I hardly dared to open my mouth; but I listened to my sisters with reverence. Nevertheless, I forced myself at this time to avoid all peculiarity <note>original: *Sonderlichkeit*; meaning acting in a way that draws attention to her spiritual state</note> in this, as also in all other official duties, in which I conducted myself directly and as I was otherwise accustomed; I also had my mind free to learn the languages <note>likely the Indigenous languages, such as Algonquin or Huron, which Marie studied intensely to aid her mission</note>. I did not notice that a single person became aware of what I suffered, although at the time I believed that everyone saw my misery just as I did myself, seeing myself so filled with it that I could find nothing good within me: and this misery had, in my estimation, removed me from **GOD**, and deprived me of His grace and great mercies. There was only very little that I spoke of my condition with Father le Jeune <note>Paul Le Jeune (1591–1664), a prominent Jesuit missionary and superior in New France who served as a spiritual advisor.</note>, because I found myself unable to do so: yet he knew enough of it to have compassion for me and to fear what might follow from it.

This state arose from a temptation to despair, which was born, as it were, within these darknesses, without my recognizing the actual cause of it. I would have been plunged into ruin by this temptation had I not been supported by a hidden power of **GOD'S** goodness. For at times I was suddenly held still, and I saw myself truly on the edge of hell, where it seemed to me that flames came forth from the jaws of the abyss to swallow me up. Yes, I felt within me an inclination which pressed me to throw myself in, so as to cause a resentment toward **GOD**, against whom this inclination rose up, urging me to hate Him. 

But in that moment His goodness and mercy, through a certain hidden influence of His Spirit, awakened the higher part <note>In mystical theology, the "higher part" of the soul refers to the intellect and will that remains oriented toward God, even when the "lower part" or emotions are in turmoil.</note> of the soul, so that it truly wished to be cast into hell—not to be displeasing to Him, but so that His Divine Justice might be satisfied through the eternal punishment of my unworthiness. For I had robbed Him of a soul which **Jesus Christ**, through His infinite mercy, had purchased with His blood. This act was a simple vision of faith, through which I was delivered from this extreme danger: I saw that I deserved hell, and that the Justice of **GOD** did me no wrong if it plunged me into the abyss; and I was gladly satisfied with that, provided only that I was not deprived of **GOD'S** friendship.

4. At times I saw the various causes for the change in my state, and I also had the freedom to speak of it to the most adorable **Word made Flesh** <note>A title for Jesus Christ, referring to the incarnation.</note>. And as I once spoke with Him about it, with heart-stirring sighs and urgent cries of misery (*exclamations* <note>original: "exclamations"</note>), all the faults, imperfections, and impurities that I had committed in the spiritual life since His Divine Majesty called me to it were presented clearly to my mind. And what at another time had seemed like nothing to me now appeared terrible in the light of the immeasurable, infinite purity of **GOD**, which sought to demand from me an exact satisfaction <note term="satisfaction">The theological concept of "making amends" or atonement for sins through penance or suffering.</note> through all that I suffered under the guidance that His Justice held over me.

5. Oh, who can express the ways of this Divine Purity; and what a purity it requires from those souls who are called to a truly spiritual and inward life. This cannot be spoken; nor can one say how terrible, piercing, and inexorable Divine Love is in regard to this purity. This Love is an irreconcilable enemy to the spirit of nature <note>The "spirit of nature" refers to human ego, selfishness, or the fallen state of humanity that resists divine grace.</note>, even when one thinks it has been annihilated and that one has already overcome it and is entirely within the spirit of grace. Corrupt nature has hiding places, crooked paths, and wandering ways that are incomprehensible; and no one knows these ways except the Spirit of **GOD**, who alone can destroy them through His sharp-burning and most subtle fire, and through His omnipotence.

...performed such effects that matched His subtle sharpness. Nevertheless, my soul did not lose the sight of the holy <term>Incarnate Word</term> <note>original: "Fleisch gewordenen Worts." This refers to Jesus Christ as the Word of God made flesh.</note> in this <term>Purgatory</term>. But the very one who previously had appeared to her as only Love, and who consumed her in His Divine embraces, was the very one who crucified her and separated her spirit from her in all parts, except in her very ground—where the secret chamber and the seat of **GOD** was. To me, in this state, this ground appeared like an abyss in a secluded place. I cannot express it any other way; yet it is the truth that the state of which I speak possessed all of this.

7. Then this ground remained in a state of completely bare <term>Emptiness</term> <note>original: "Ledigkeit." In mystical theology, this refers to a state of being "void" or "stripped" of all created things and even spiritual consolations.</note>. Advanced souls can hardly endure this state; it is also the source from which despairs are born, which aim to plunge both soul and body into the abyss of hell.

8. Once, as I stood near the altar, I beheld a great flame which came out through a vent, and which appeared to me to be the flame of the abyss. Thereupon I felt moved in my whole being by a certain sudden **Sadness** and a vivid urge to throw myself into it out of contempt for **GOD**. However, His Divine mercy immediately held me back through a hidden power, and then this terrifying vision, along with its effect, ceased in a single moment. I believe that if I had not happened to find a piece of paneling (<term>wainscoting</term> <note>original: "lambris," a French term for wood paneling.</note>) at that place to hold onto, I would have fallen down, so exceedingly strong was this effect. This happened to me several times during the period of my great sufferings, but never with such violence as this time.

9. I have already reported that I carried my cross alone in regard to the creatures <note>In this context, "creatures" refers to all created things or people, as opposed to the Creator.</note>, who only served to make it heavier and more painful for me. Nothing supported me except this hidden power of **GOD**, and it enabled me to bear it with resignation to His Divine decrees and with submission to the effects of His Divine Justice, which I recognized to be entirely fair—except for those moments when I felt this **Emptiness**. For at that time, my soul was completely enveloped in darknesses which did not allow her to see anything else except what she suffered: namely, that she was entirely contrary to **GOD**. But when I came back to myself, I could not ask Him to be delivered from it, because it seemed to me that my sufferings must be eternal, and I myself condemned myself to this eternity.

### Part Five. The Life

...of darkness and painful obscurities, where I saw myself as if sunk into a hell, full of deadly sadness and bitterness, which arose from a temptation toward despair that was born, as it were, within these darknesses, without my recognizing the (actual) cause of it. I would have been plunged into ruin by this temptation if I had not been supported by a hidden power of God’s goodness. For at times I was suddenly held still and saw myself truly on the edge of hell, where it seemed to me that flames came forth from the jaws of the abyss to swallow me up. Yes, I felt within me an impulse which urged me to throw myself in, so as to spite **GOD**, against whom this impulse rose up and urged me to hate Him. But in an instant His goodness and mercy, through a certain hidden influence of His Spirit, awakened the <term>higher part</term> <note>In mystical theology, the "higher part" or "superior part" of the soul refers to the intellect and will, which can remain faithful to God even when the "lower" emotions and senses are in turmoil.</note>, so that it actually wished to be cast into hell—not to be displeasing to Him, but so that His Divine Justice might be satisfied through the eternal punishment of my unworthiness, which had robbed Him of a soul that **JESUS CHRIST** had purchased with His blood through His infinite mercies. This act was a simple vision of faith, through which I was delivered from this extreme danger: I saw that I deserved hell, and that the justice of **GOD** would do me no wrong if it cast me into the abyss; and with that I was gladly content, if only I were not deprived of the friendship of **GOD**.

4. At times I saw the various causes for the change in my state, and I also had the freedom to speak of them to the most adorable <term>Incarnate Word</term> <note>original: "Fleisch gewordenen Wort." This is a title for Jesus Christ, referring to God the Son taking on human flesh.</note>. And as I (once) spoke with Him about it, with heart-stirring sighs and urgent cries of misery (*exclamations*), all the faults, imperfections, and impurities that I had committed in the spiritual life since His Divine Majesty called me to it were presented clearly to my mind. And what at another time had seemed like nothing to me now appeared terrible in view of the immeasurable, infinite purity of **GOD**, which sought to demand an exact satisfaction from me through everything I suffered in the guidance that His justice held over me.

5. Ah, who can express the ways of this Divine Purity; and what a purity it requires from those souls who are called to a truly spiritual and inward life. That cannot be spoken; nor can it be said how terrible, piercing, and inexorable Divine Love is in view of this purity, which is an irreconcilable enemy to the <term>spirit of nature</term> <note>original: "Geist der Natur." This refers to "fallen" human nature or the ego, which resists spiritual transformation.</note>, even then when one thinks it has been annihilated and that one has already overcome it and is entirely in the spirit of grace. Corrupt nature has hiding places, crooked paths, and labyrinths that are incomprehensible; and no one knows these ways but the Spirit of **GOD**, who alone can destroy them through His sharp-burning and most subtle fire, and through His omnipotence.

6. When it pleases the Spirit of **GOD** to work on this, then this fire is a <term>purgatory</term> <note>original: "Fegfeuer." While often referring to the afterlife, mystics used this term to describe intense spiritual purification during life.</note> that is more piercing than lightning, a sword that divides, and such...

# Fifth Part. The Life

I accused myself before Him, out of an excessive inner pain which drove me to confess all my committed faults to Him, which had defiled His gifts and scorned the Spirit of Grace through which He had led me.

I testified to Him with the bitter pain of my heart that through my unfaithfulness—and because I had not behaved properly toward His graces—I had given the **Spirit of Nature** <note>In mystical theology, the "Spirit of Nature" refers to the unredeemed human ego and its natural impulses that resist the movement of divine grace.</note> cause and, to some extent, power, through which the utmost injustice and shame had been done to His adorable purpose. It is impossible to express how these insights, which came from Him who is appointed as the **Judge of the Living and the Dead**, were so powerful, piercing, and painful to the human spirit. And what is more, besides the dignity of a Judge which the soul saw in the holy **Word made flesh**, she also looked upon Him as her **Bridegroom**, who, regardless of the infirmities within her, had not taken from her the dignity of a bride. But He wished to test her without mercy, through the secret fire of His Divine Justice, without letting her see either what would follow this trial or how long it would last.

### Fifth Part. The Life

...conditions; yet in such a way that my understanding (*esprit*) <note>Original: *Verstand* (German), *esprit* (French). In 17th-century spiritual writing, this refers to the higher faculty of the soul capable of rational observation even during emotional turmoil.</note> was free, and it could clearly and precisely recognize my inner condition.

2. In this state, in my estimation, I was more prone to falling into sin than in the other, because I was freer. Ah, how many graces our good God has shown me in this regard, on countless occasions! I would have thrown myself into ruin during the violent attacks of this rebellion <note>Marie often uses "rebellion" or "uprising" to describe the natural human emotions and passions that seem to fight against the influence of Divine Grace.</note>, if his almighty hand had not supported me; especially in a bitterness that had become habitual to me, which moved me toward an aversion for my neighbor during certain contradictions where I was provoked. Nevertheless, the Lord supported me so that I never spoke a word contrary to the respect due to that person toward whom, for various reasons, I felt the greatest aversion.

3. I saw myself in this state as so poor and stripped of virtues that I could hardly bear myself; and truly, the virtue I practiced most was that of bearing with myself. Amidst these violent attacks of emotion, I had many affairs to manage; and people said that I was quite gentle and patient in them, as well as during the many contradictions that occurred; but I, seeing my misery, found myself quite imperfect.

4. Although our gracious God had restored me to his holy and intimate communion, this only humbled me all the more, because it was incomprehensible to me how such familiar access to his Divine Majesty could coexist with this rebellion of the emotions.

<margin>(a) Zephaniah 1:12.</margin>
5. I believed that I had strayed far from perfection; and this pressure was so heavy upon me that I could hardly endure it. As I once went into our cell, I received a sudden insight which confirmed me in this, and gave me to recognize that I was even much lesser and much poorer than I had ever grasped. And there it seemed that this verse of Scripture was fulfilled in me (a): 
> **I will search Jerusalem with lamps.** <note>Zephaniah 1:12. In a mystical context, this refers to God's meticulous scrutiny of the soul, using the "lamp" of divine light to find even the smallest hidden faults.</note>
For this rebuking and jealous spirit of pure love was relentless, and made it so that I had to obey Him without delay. Acts of contrition <term>contrition: sincere and painful remorse for sin</term> were governed by this same spirit and directed to the holy **Word** made flesh, with these words: 
> Mercy, my most chaste love; mercy, my chaste and Divine Bridegroom; I would not have offended You; mercy, my Divine Love; mercy, mercy!

6. This loving activity caused me to breathe out such doubled sighs incessantly, without being able to restrain them: 
> For mercy, my precious love, for mercy; I cannot will to have offended You. Ah, my Divine Love, send me a million punishments, and as many deaths as I take breaths, before You would permit me to offend You. 
I know well that I am nothing but filth and imperfection; but I will...

She experiences a profound mystical insight into her own poverty of spirit, prompted by a biblical verse about God's searching light.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the spiritual autobiography of Marie of the Incarnation. On the previous page, Marie described her struggles with her own temperament and the "rebellion" of her natural inclinations. Here, she explains how the Holy Spirit occupies the "ground" of the soul, protecting it from the devil and deceptive spiritual impurities, even while she still feels the sting of human emotion.</meta>

# Of Marie of the Incarnation. Chapter XVII.

...it could not be so. O Love, then destroy everything that is displeasing and repugnant to You, etc.

7. It is impossible to express what this Holy Spirit demands of a soul which He holds in an intimate, rooted (habitual) <note>Marie uses "habitual" in the classical theological sense: a permanent, settled state of being or a "habit" of the soul, rather than a recurring action.</note> and constant union with Himself: I say it once more, it is impossible to express. And this comes about because this immeasurable purity of God can suffer nothing that is contrary to it. For I have often experienced that nothing defiled can gain entry into this innermost part or ground of the soul <term>Ground of the soul (Seelengrund): a mystical term referring to the deepest, most essential part of a person where the soul meets God directly.</term>, which is the dwelling of God and, as it were, His heaven, as long as this Divine Spirit is its Lord and Master; and that the devil, although he is a very subtle and penetrating spirit, can find no access to it whatsoever.

8. There are nevertheless certain exhalations of imperfections and spiritual impurities which come from the spirit of corrupt nature, and are nothing other than these small malices, these small distortions, these small pretenses which, so that they might create a subtle mixture with that which belongs to the Holy Spirit, wish to sneak into this holy cabinet <note>In 17th-century spiritual writing, a "cabinet" refers to a private, inner chamber or a place for keeping treasures; here it is the most private space of the heart.</note>; and it seems that they are even more capable of doing so than the devils, because they cover themselves with a veneer of holiness, love, zeal, godliness, and the honor of God, so that they may all the more easily join themselves with the purity and uprightness of this Holy Spirit. In truth, they come very close to this sanctuary; but in vain: for in this rooted (habitual) state of intimate union, nothing counterfeit or impure can enter (into the ground of the soul).

9. In the rebellion of the emotions <note>Original: *Gemüthsbewegungen*. This refers to the "movements" of the soul, such as anger, pride, or sorrow, which Marie felt were "rebelling" against her spiritual will.</note> of which I spoke—and which, after those three years of my great inner suffering, lasted for more than four more years—it is so far from the case that one should hold fast to or strive after what the rebellious emotion demands (as might otherwise happen in weak beginnings), that one instead carries everything as a sensitive and very heavy scourge. All the evil that happens is not willful; rather, it is, as it were, a food by which humility and self-denial are nourished and maintained in those who feel such evil within themselves, and a weight which causes one to gain a great contempt for oneself. When one (in this state) perhaps acts too hastily in words or thoughts, it happens out of error (since one lacks light); when one is resisted or persecuted contrary to justice, one certainly feels a movement of anger or resentment, but nothing evil breaks forth from it; for one carries within the ground of the soul a fear of God, through which one has a hatred for revenge and resentment, and through which one is superior to this emotion. Nevertheless, one does indeed stumble at times out of weakness, so that when one is perhaps with a trusted person, one might speak some words of complaint—for example: this or that was done to me, such a word of insult was said to me, I was treated so unjustly, or the like. But in that very moment, the soul becomes so ashamed as it perceives its baseness, that it is led thereby to a great humiliation...

<meta>catchword: move:</meta>

<summary>Marie describes the Holy Spirit's absolute occupation of the "ground of the soul," which prevents even the devil from entering, though natural human "exhalations" of pride and emotion still attempt to mimic holiness. She explains that in her state of union, even when she feels anger or complains out of weakness, these "rebellions" only serve to deepen her humility and self-contempt.</summary>
