<meta>This page continues Marie of the Incarnation’s account of her internal spiritual struggle. Having established that the "ground of the soul" remains a sanctuary for God, she now describes the painful conflict between that inner peace and the turbulent emotions—bitterness, fear, and doubt—that still plague her "sensory" or lower self.</meta>

### Fifth Part. The Life

...is moved: and yet all this can coexist with this most intimate union in the ground of the soul, in a region (landscape) of peace, which seems to be separated from the soul itself.

10. That which further doubles her suffering is the bitterness in the sensory part <note>The "sensory" or "sensual" part of the soul (the *partie sensible*) refers to the faculty of feelings, emotions, and physical perceptions, which 17th-century mystics distinguished from the higher "spirit" or "will."</note>, which is stirred up as soon as anything adverse occurs, or against which she may feel an aversion: and I will never deny that such a thing is the most painful matter in the world for a soul that fears **God** and sin, and conversely loves the purity of the heart. Now I leave it to be considered whether this soul does not stand in fear, seeing in itself so many weaknesses and evil symptoms? It is unspeakable. She fears greatly that she is deceived: she believes that she never had any fundamental virtue; she is, as it were, convinced that her emotions were only dormant, and that the little she thought she possessed of the interior life was not from **God**, because it appears so clearly that neither the basis nor the essence of virtue is within her; she thinks that all her peace, and all her gifts, were false, or, if they were true graces—as they were held to be—that she has lost them through her own fault. Such reflections then torment the soul.

11. I took my refuge in **God**, spoke with Him in love, and in the shared access which His goodness granted me in the ground of my soul, so that He might take these conditions away from me, which were so contrary to the Divine fundamental teachings of His beloved Son, and even opposed to the pure love He demanded of me. I had other crosses and sufferings from which I could not desire to be delivered; but the Spirit who led me urged me that I should desire to be delivered from *this* one, always with the intention toward that true purity which is so little sought, so little found, and so little possessed in the spiritual life. After all my praying, it seemed to me that I was even more imprisoned and more tightly bound in certain matters than before, and that the holy Word made flesh <note>original: "Fleisch gewordene Wort" — a reference to Jesus Christ (John 1:14).</note> took pleasure in my bonds: then I abandoned myself to His ways, which were so unknown and hidden to me, to bear my suffering as long as He should find it good.

12. I still bore the rebellion of the emotions and the temptation toward adversity until August 15, 1647 <note>August 15 is the Feast of the Assumption of Mary, a significant date for a mystic named Marie.</note>, when in a moment I felt myself, as it were, unburdened of my heavy and painful garment, along with a sequence and influence of peace in the entire sensory part of the soul. That adversity was transformed into a heartfelt love toward those persons against whom I had felt some coldness, and for whom my natural inclination had felt the greatest bitterness; so much so, that I rendered them all possible services according to my calling and station when the opportunity arose. Indeed, because people did not know what was happening within me, nor the causes which moved me to behave in such a way externally (excepting those to whom I had to open the state of my soul), they could not comprehend how such a thing could happen, and they judged it variously, but did not hit upon the right mark.

<meta>catchword: 13. To</meta>

<summary>Marie describes a period of intense spiritual doubt and emotional bitterness that made her question the reality of her virtues, ending with a sudden, transformative experience of peace and charity on August 15, 1647.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the autobiographical account of Marie of the Incarnation. Having previously described the internal conflict between her soul's "ground of peace" and her sensory distress, she now recounts a specific external trial involving social humiliation and the grace of submitting her will to God.</meta>

### of Marie of the Incarnation. Chapter XVII. ###

->Z i<-

13. Around this time, something occurred which, both in view of its effect and its cause, could have caused me great humiliation; and indeed, it truly happened. This humiliation was all the more painful because, to all human appearances, it came from pious persons who were many times indebted to me. In short, **God** allowed such circumstances to arise that they could humble me more than anything that had happened to me before. When I learned what had occurred in the matter at hand, I did not say a single word in my defense; and our **Lord** granted me the grace that I felt no movement that could have stemmed from imperfection <note>original: "sentiments imparfaits" — a French term for flawed or unrefined emotional reactions</note> against a single one of these persons. I looked upon their conduct with a humbled spirit before **God**, and confessed that I was worthy of such thoughts and opinions being held of me because of my great imperfections, which could have been the true cause of it. Before this happened, our **Lord** had given me to understand that He wanted this specific matter from me <note>Marie is likely referring to a specific spiritual task or vocation she felt called to fulfill</note>, even though it was being opposed; yet I spoke of it to no one, but remained in my peace and stillness, just as if I had experienced every conceivable pleasure: for I did not doubt **God’s** will, nor that it would be fulfilled in its own time; as indeed it happened afterward, and in the very same way as the **Divine Majesty** had indicated to me.

14. I must say here to the glory of **God** that He has always granted me the grace not to stand stubbornly upon my own light and insights <term>light and insights: the internal spiritual understanding or "revelations" a person believes they have received from God</term>, whether they be natural or supernatural, but that I always feel inclined to submit my judgment. Just as I have this for myself, I would also like to see it practiced by all souls whom **God** calls to His service. Sometimes it pains me to see the opposite, though I bear it with patience.

15. The grace then, which was shown to me on the mentioned day, clearly gave me to understand the greatness of **God’s** mercy, and at the same time the state of the great internal sufferings and terrible temptations which I had borne for nearly eight years. From these two causes, I drew a conclusion as to how highly indebted I am to His **Divine Majesty**, that He helped and protected me so powerfully in all the various occurrences that took place during this time—which would be far too long to recount piece by piece—as would each and every one of His great graces and favors, despite my unfaithfulness. Ah! I am ashamed whenever I think of it, and I always find in it new reasons to humble myself and to sing the mercies of such a good **God** toward this nothingness and dust of the earth. May He be praised eternally!

## The Eighteenth Chapter.

The overflowing of peace and other graces after long-endured sufferings. She thanks the Lord for the humiliations. She is led into the practice of the fundamental teachings of the Gospel, through which the Lord has always guided her. The abundance of the graces of God shown to her, especially in regard to passages of Scripture. Introduction to the perfection of virtues.

->I.<-

It would not be possible for me to describe the overflowing of peace in which my soul found itself immersed, once it saw itself completely free from its bonds and restored to everything it believed it had lost: and not only did it recognize that it had lost nothing, but it also saw through experience that it had gathered a multitude of inexpressible treasures.

The soul recognized that what had taken away its sight of the goods it possessed in the innermost union with the Bridegroom <note>original: "Bräutigam" — a mystical reference to Christ as the spouse of the soul</note> had been only an ash that had hidden its fire and covered its light for its own good, and for its progress in the fundamental virtues, which it had not previously possessed to the degree that the **Divine Majesty** had granted it to possess thereafter.

2. These insights and experiences, however, which the soul had during this change of its state, were not lights attained through human reflection, but were impressions received that were more distinct and clearer than any light, and which occurred through the supremely adorable **Word made flesh** <note>The "Logos" or Jesus Christ</note> who dwelt within her: these were impressions that carried such effects as were fitting for the One who caused them, and were entirely uniform with the **Holy Gospel**, so that my soul could act in no other way than in this spirit and this insight. As I now looked upon this state, I could not cease praising **God** that He had allowed me to walk through so many narrow paths and thorns.

<margin>(a) Psalm 119:71.</margin>
3. I praise and glorify this holy and **Divine Savior** that it pleased Him to humble me in so many and various ways in His paths. I say to Him, with the Prophet (a): *Oh, how good it is for me that you have humbled me!* <note>original: "Ach, wie so gut ist es mir, daß du mich gedemüthiget hast!" — Marie quotes the Lutheran rendering of the Psalm</note> And I say this to Him in accordance with the truth. For I would not take all the treasures of the earth in exchange for not having gone through this state or humiliation, which I regard as infinitely precious—yes, more than I can say.

<summary>Marie describes the profound peace and spiritual "treasures" gained after a period of intense trial and humiliation, viewing her past suffering as a necessary "ash" that protected her inner fire. She expresses deep gratitude for these humiliations, citing them as the source of her growth in fundamental Christian virtues.</summary>

Fifth Part. The Life of Marie of the Incarnation.
Y 2

4. It seems to me that I have passed through those dens of lions and leopards of which the Bride speaks in the Song of Solomon <note>Song of Solomon 4:8: "Come with me from Lebanon, my bride... from the lions' dens, from the mountains of the leopards." Marie uses this as a metaphor for her spiritual and perhaps physical trials in the wilderness.</note>; and instead of being harmed by their bites, I have instead fortunately escaped into the dominion and into the hiding places of my heavenly Bridegroom, which are the holy fundamental teachings of the Gospel, which have flowed from His Divine mouth like streams of riches.

<margin>(a) Matthew 5:44.</margin>
5. When He said (a): **Do good to those who do you evil**; this is a law which seems to me to be written in my heart, with a power and with an impression of pure love, which I also experience when the occasion arises: not that I then have to force myself to deny my own will, but I am moved to it through an inclination and, as it were, a natural impulse, by virtue of the impression of the fundamental teaching of my Divine Bridegroom.

6. Just as I, since I have been in Canada <note>Marie of the Incarnation arrived in Quebec, New France (Canada), in 1639 to establish an Ursuline convent and school.</note>, have had very burdensome affairs at hand, and consequently have had to deal with people of various social ranks and of very different temperaments; thus these Divine fundamental teachings have been my strength and my support. People often took my conduct as something that came from my natural disposition, which, as they said, could suffer without effort and forget the vexations others might inflict on me; but they did not see that my spirit was possessed by this spirit of the teachings of the Son of God, which was the cause <term>principle <gloss>the underlying source or driving force</gloss></term> that impelled me to it. What I say of one of these fundamental teachings, I mean of the others as well.

[See here, which fundamental teachings this Evangelical <note>In this context, "Evangelical" refers to a life strictly modeled on the "Evangelium" or Gospel, a common term in 17th-century Catholic mysticism.</note> soul had written here in her heart, as she herself had prescribed them for her own practice at the time of her inner temptations (as mentioned in the previous chapter).]

1) When I am accused of a fault, not to excuse myself, even if I am innocent; and not to accuse those who have actually committed it, unless the honor of **God** depends upon it, according to the judgment of the one who is placed in authority.

2) When I think, or when it is a reality, that I am offended, insulted, rejected, and humbled, whether it be in words or in deed, then to watch over my heart, so that I do not let myself be carried away to complain or to make the matter greater than it is.

3) To say nothing to my own praise; nor to belittle another when they are praised, or when I, according to the rule of love, should praise them or say good things about them.

4) To flee envy and resentment regarding the external or internal gifts, or the pleasures, that another has; but rather to rejoice in them, and to deem myself unworthy to possess such things.

She provides a list of four spiritual rules for humility and charity that she practiced during times of trial.</summary>

### Fifth Part. The Life

5) To practice a heartfelt inclination toward those for whom I have a natural dislike; to accept their actions as innocent, and to judge their intentions according to the rule of love.

6) To practice a spirit of patience toward my neighbor, according to the fundamental teachings prescribed in the Gospel. <note>original: "Evangelio"</note>

7) To work at cutting off self-indulgences and unnecessary worrying about things that might cause some trouble.

8) To apply myself with all earnestness to inner and outer gentleness, to meekness, and to humility of heart, according to the Gospel.

9) Not to harbor suspicion or mistrust against anyone because of a slight appearance; nor to let myself be moved to any unrest because of it.

10) To suffer bodily pains and spiritual sufferings, as well as humiliations and mortifications, <term>mortifications</term> <note>original: "Abtödtungen". These are spiritual exercises intended to "kill off" one's selfish desires or ego to focus better on God.</note> whether they come from God or from one's neighbor, with love and with meekness.

11) To deny certain small desires and natural inclinations in everything, whatever it may be, without however harming either the spiritual or the physical.

12) To be obedient to the movements and inspirations of God; and in all of this, to follow the obedience and guidance of a spiritual father.

7. However, it is not my meaning that I have committed no imperfections through error (when I lacked light), or through haste—whether in the business of the house or outside the house—for I have always had to deal with neighbors. Furthermore, this land <note>Referring to New France/Canada.</note> is entirely filled with unrest and labor, especially since we settled here only a short time ago. ### of Marie of the Incarnation. Chapter XVIII.
Zz 3
<meta>catchword: away,</meta>

...this came into my mind in a single moment, without me having read it before; or if I had perhaps read it, I was not able to retain it. Thus, the fundamental doctrine which was brought forth in my mind by the Spirit who governed me, wiped away all other memories within me, even if they had been of holy things. That which occurred to my mind contained within it what was most useful for my advancement at that time, and simultaneously all kinds of blessings, remedies, and graces in the union of the holy Word made Flesh. <note>The "Word made Flesh" refers to the Incarnation of Christ, a central theme for Marie, who took the name "Marie de l'Incarnation."</note>

9. But after that time, and through the changing of my spiritual states, the workings of the Spirit of God also changed in their fruits, according to whatever state I found myself in. In this way, one and the same passage of Scripture had a completely different meaning and a completely different effect on me at one time than at another; yet always in a greater perfection: not indeed in respect to God, who is unchangeable, but in respect to the soul, which grows and increases in spiritual life and in sanctification. Whatever degree of union with God I have experienced, or still experience in this life, it is always something more than before; for God is infinite in His gifts.

10. Therefore, if I had described all the graces and favors which His Divine Majesty, according to His goodness, was pleased to communicate to me—since His great mercy called me to the spiritual life—both in respect to passages of the Holy Scripture and His inner workings in my soul, it would be a very large book. Indeed, it would be a book, as I said, showing ever higher and higher perfection and spiritual growth. But I have not described it: my unworthiness, and my lowly female sex, <note>In the 17th century, female religious writers often used "humility formulas," emphasizing their perceived weakness as women to deflect criticism and attribute all their wisdom solely to God.</note> held me back, as did the fear of spoiling the gifts of God and being numbered among the hypocrites; for by my writing, I would have given others cause to believe that I was something, when in truth I am nothing and in every way useless.

11. [Among the graces which the Lord communicated to her regarding passages of Holy Scripture, by all appearances the following is not the least, which she set down from the inner fullness of her heart around this time and shared in a letter to her son in the year 1647; <note>Marie's son was Claude Martin, a Benedictine monk who later edited and published her writings.</note> a portion of which is inserted here as a sample of such graces.]

Regarding the words (a), **You are the fairest in form among the children of men**, a light filled my spirit concerning the double beauty of the Son of God, so that my heart had to unburden itself through my pen, though without reflection and on a messy scrap of paper; for the Spirit allowed for no premeditation.

12. In the deep peace which Divine Goodness allowed to follow
my temptations, the union with my Divine Groom—through His holy
impressions—worked in me the foundational virtues of these Divine teachings of the

fruits or effects occurred with such extraordinary sweetness, and in such great
stripping away <note>Original: "Entblößung," a mystical term for the soul being stripped of all worldly attachments and ego.</note>, that what I had previously possessed of these virtues in the
states I had passed through seemed like nothing to me. And generally, in all
spiritual virtues, I experienced that I was an entirely different creature, and that God
held me in His possession through the fundamental teachings of His most-adorable Son,
where He led me in everything I had to do in my station, through the holy
influences and anointings of this saying (a): **Learn from me, for I am meek
and humble of heart**; as also the saying (b): **The Spirit of God
bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God.**

he told me that I must never refuse any service in temporal affairs,
because they did not distract me from the great communion which
the Divine Majesty was pleased to grant me with Himself.

## Chapter Nineteen.

### Persecution of the newly converted in Canada. The burning of their convent. Their conduct and astonishing peace during it, and their state of mind shortly thereafter. Outward poverty and hardship. The rebuilding of their convent.

->I.<-

In this very year, I experienced great suffering because of the persecution that the Christians suffered from the Iroquois <note>The Iroquois Confederacy (Haudenosaunee) was at war with the Hurons (Wendat) and their French allies during this period.</note>. Because I took the interests <note>Original: "Vortheile," meaning the spiritual advantages or the cause of God.</note> of my Divine Groom to heart, the destruction of His Church pained me deeply within, although my soul was entirely submissive to His decrees and the permissions of His Providence.

2. During this time (in the year 1649), the Fathers Brébeuf, Garnier, and Lalemant <note>Jean de Brébeuf, Noël Garnier, and Gabriel Lalemant were Jesuit missionaries martyred by the Iroquois. They were later canonized as part of the Canadian Martyrs.</note>, together with their flock, were burned and killed; and the Reverend Fathers of the mission among the Hurons, with the remaining Christians—of whom there were about four or five hundred—were forced to leave their place and take refuge here in Quebec. Oh, how deeply felt this blow was for me!

3. Those Fathers who remained alive had suffered more than those who died. One saw in them truly perfected souls in whom Jesus Christ lived more than they lived themselves; and their holiness was visible in the eyes of the whole world, so that everyone wondered at it. They were unrelenting and without mercy toward themselves, in order to kill within themselves all the inclinations of nature which are so obstructive to the followers of Jesus Christ. I have no words to express what I know of this; for what the creature cannot do by itself, grace does in them in such a way as one would never have thought possible.

4. At the end of the year 1650, our convent burned down in the following manner: A newly arrived lay sister, who had been appointed to bake bread, had secretly placed glowing coals into the kneading trough in the evening so that the dough might not freeze, but she had forgotten to take them out before lying down to sleep. In this way, at midnight, the kneading trough, the bakehouse, and the cellar caught fire; the cellar was not vaulted and was stocked with all sorts of provisions. Soon after, the floors—which were covered with double boards and filled with earth in between—also caught fire. Everything was made of pine wood. Had one of the teachers of the children <note>Original: "Meisterin der Kinder," referring to the Ursuline sister in charge of the boarding students.</note> not heard the noise of the fire, it would not have been half an hour before we all would have fallen into the flames. The sisters escaped half-naked and mostly barefoot.

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the account of the destruction of the Ursuline convent in Quebec by fire in December 1650. ### Part Five. The Life of Marie of the Incarnation, etc.

5. All I could do was throw the documents of the convent, which I had in my safekeeping, out through the window, along with some small boxes that were at hand. Whatever served for my own use I voluntarily abandoned to the fire, only throwing out my mattress for a poor sick woman. The short time I spent doing this saved my life, as it prevented me from going up to my administrative office <note>The office where she performed her duties as superior or treasurer.</note>, where I was just on my way to throw some belongings out the window. I could easily imagine that the sisters would have left all their clothes in their cells to save their lives. Had I gone there, it would have been the end of me, for all the paths leading there were immediately seized by the fire. When I saw that I could achieve nothing more, I bowed before the Savior as a sign of my surrender to His Providence and my consent to His dispensations. I was the last to remain in the house between two fires, and I had barely left my room—which was beneath the bell tower—when the bell fell down, and the fire followed after me with great fury.

6. In all the running back and forth, I possessed such great freedom of spirit and such quiet attention to everything I did, just as if nothing had happened to us. It seemed to me that I had an inner voice within me telling me what to do, where to go, what to throw out the window, and what to let the fire burn. In that moment, I saw the vanity of all things of this earth; and I was given a grace of such great stripping away <note>The term "Entblößung" refers to a mystical state of total detachment or spiritual poverty, where the soul is "stripped" of all earthly attachments.</note> that I can express its effects neither with words nor with the pen.

7. I found our poor convent community a little way off in the snow, so gentle and quiet in their manner as if nothing had happened; they only prayed to God as they watched this miserable spectacle. Some sat with bare feet in the snow. A certain honest man, seeing the sisters sitting there so calmly in devotion, said aloud that we must either be mad or have a great love for God to be so unmoved by this sudden loss of all our goods. But this honest man did not know the power of grace which our good Jesus poured into our hearts.

8. As soon as I saw that this accident was beyond remedy, I believed that my sins were the sole cause of it; and I was so strongly convinced of this that one could hardly have persuaded me otherwise. Therefore, my soul accepted this chastisement in that moment with great stillness, and cried to God for mercy because all my sisters had to suffer for it. I would have wished to endure the punishment alone, since I alone was the cause for Him to exercise His Divine Justice in such a way. Nevertheless, I looked upon this blow as the discipline of a good Father and a faithful Groom <note>Marie uses "Bräutigam" (Groom/Spouse) to refer to Jesus, reflecting her "mystical marriage" theology.</note> who—visiting us in such a manner during the Octave of His Holy Birth (that is, the 30th of December)—wished to place us in a state of total stripping away, which in some measure resembled His own stripping away in the manger.

# Fifth Part. The Life

9. My soul has never had a greater peace than on this occasion. I did not feel the slightest movement of any grief, any sadness, or any unrest; rather, I felt myself inwardly united with the spirit and with the hand that permitted and carried out this circumcision <note>Marie uses "circumcision" here as a mystical term for a painful spiritual "pruning" or sacrifice required by God.</note> upon us; so much so that, just as I was in God and in the completely willing acceptance of what was presently happening, it would not have been possible for me to do anything other than as I was urged and moved by His Divine Spirit, which, as I experienced, governed my steps and my deeds.

10. This thought was in my mind: that my sisters and I must accept this total loss of our convent, and everything inside it, in the spirit (and mind) of the Saints; for I had inwardly before my eyes the mind of all the Saints, both in the Old and New Testament, who possessed the spirit of contrition and accused themselves, and endured the temporal sufferings that God sent them, praising Him and singing His praise. As I was thus governed and urged by a loving activity, in the possession of a peace that I cannot express, my spirit and my heart said unceasingly:
-> You have done this, my chaste Bridegroom; may You be praised for it. It is my pleasure that You are pleased in that which You have done. <-
The thanksgivings that my soul brought to God in this misfortune occurred as often and as much as my breaths; and it was not in my power to cease this loving activity and this union of my whole soul with the Divine Will. The whole ground of my soul swam (so to speak) through a delight of love in the fulfillment of this holy and adorable Will of God, without examining anything, except only that I had a delight in it, that His purpose was fulfilled through our annihilation <note>The term "annihilation" (Vernichtung) refers to the total destruction of material things or the ego to allow for total union with God.</note>; especially in regard to my own person, because I had caused this house to be built and had endured great effort and labor, as well as many contradictions, to bring it into the state in which it had been until now.

11. Just as I was convinced, however, that I had committed many imperfections, I threw myself on the side of Divine Justice, thanked it, and testified to my inward delight because of all the events or accidents through which it wished to annihilate me, and especially because of this one. And so my inner activity could not cease praising Him; which indeed happened in a very intimate familiarity toward this most adorable Majesty, but it also came forth from a lovingly-humbled heart.

12. You urge me (she says in a letter) that I should tell you of our neediness. But, to tell the truth, it would be difficult for me to do so. It is indeed true, since we have lost everything through our fire, that we also lack everything; yet it seems to me that I need nothing. I believe the tranquility of mind that I experience makes me blind to my own needs, although I see the needs of others quite clearly. One must confess that

# Chapter Twenty.
## Her state of perpetual sacrifice and poverty of spirit. How she reached it step by step. State of extraordinary love. Unspeakable state in God.

->I.<-

After I have spoken of the building of our convent, I will now also speak of the building of my inner self, and of the state into which our Lord has led me since I took up the office of Superior <note>The "Superior" (Vorsteherin) is the head of the religious community.</note> for the second time (this happened in June 1651). This is a state of perpetual sacrifice (which, however, is much more spiritual and perfect than usual), by the spirit of which I am consumed in many ways. Although it is very difficult to speak of this, I will nevertheless cite some particular parts of it; and because obedience <note>In a monastic context, "obedience" refers to a formal command given by a spiritual director or religious superior which the nun is bound to follow as an act of faith.</note> has been laid upon me, I will do what is possible for me through the assistance of the Holy Spirit, who unceasingly overwhelms me with His graces.

2. # Chapter Twenty.

## Her state of perpetual sacrifice and poverty of spirit. How she arrived there by degrees. A state of extraordinary love. An inexpressible state in God.

### I.

After I have spoken of the rebuilding of our convent, I will now also speak of the building up of my interior <term>Interior: "Inwendiges" in German, referring to the "inner life" or the soul's private relationship with the divine.</term>, and of the state into which our **Lord** led me since I took up the office of a Superior <term>Superior: The head or administrator of a religious community.</term> for the second time (this occurred in June 1651). This is a state of perpetual sacrifice (which is, however, far more spiritual and perfect than usual), through the spirit of which I am consumed in many ways. Even though it is very difficult to speak of this, I will nonetheless mention some particular parts of it; and because obedience has been laid upon me <note>In religious life, "obedience" refers to the requirement to write or act under the direction of a spiritual confessor or superior.</note>, I will do what is possible for me through the assistance of the **Holy Spirit**, who unceasingly showers me with His graces.

2. Firstly, I may well say that the goodness and great generosity of my **Divine Bridegroom** granted me the grace that He communicated to me the effects of the **Divine Words** in the preaching of the Eight Beatitudes <note>The Eight Beatitudes are blessings listed by Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5).</note>.

Nonetheless, I do not imagine that this is in that degree of perfection as He has communicated to the great Saints; but only according to the measure as it has pleased Him to make my soul capable of it: for I expect everything from Him, and I have everything from Him; but of myself, I confess that I am nothingness and inability itself, and fit to hinder His singular graces in countless ways. It is wondrous that a **God**, who so many thou-

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Marie of the Incarnation’s reflection on her internal spiritual state following the rebuilding of her convent in Quebec (1651). ...thousands of millions of souls who love Him purely, He still chooses to turn His eyes toward the least of His creatures, granting her such a large share of His love and such an excellent place in His heart.

3. I have since learned that there are different degrees in true poverty of spirit <term>Poverty of spirit: A mystical state of total detachment from everything that is not God, including one's own spiritual consolations.</term>. When our **Lord** called me to the monastic life, His mercy allowed me to recognize its value and preciousness, as I mentioned briefly before. But at that time, I did not yet see what the **Spirit of God** intended to do in my soul and in my spirit to let me experience the essence of true spiritual poverty. He has done this from time to time since then, through the changes in internal states through which it has pleased His **Divine Majesty** to lead me. In order to bring these states into unity, He currently creates a true state of perpetual sacrifice and consumption <note>The German "Verzehrung" implies being "consumed" or "eaten up" by divine love, like a burnt offering.</note> which, because of its subtlety, is so terrifying to nature that one would have to experience it to believe where it brings the creature in its most noble part.

4. I may speak obscurely, yet I understand myself well; however, it is not possible for me to express even a thousandth part of the **Divine** impressions and holy effects which my **Divine Bridegroom** <note>Bridegroom: A traditional mystical image for Jesus Christ, representing the soul's intimate union with the Divine.</note> has worked in my soul. Furthermore, the many affairs and duties which I am required to attend to do not allow me to express myself at great length; therefore, I am content to say only the essentials of what the **Spirit** who governs me is working within me.

5. Nevertheless, I wish to set down a short discourse on this, to explain to some extent what I mean by the stripping of souls <term>Stripping: Often called "denudation" in mystical theology, referring to the process of being emptied of self-will and intellectual pride.</term>, by the state of sacrifice, and by true, spiritual, and essential poverty. <note>What follows is an excellent discourse, which could be called a brief summary of the **Mystical Way**. In it, she first indicates the various successive lights, delights, and graces that God communicates to faithful souls. According to her experience and description, the following state and a fifth purification and stage toward perfect poverty of spirit then follow. <meta>catchword: 14. The</meta>

is certain, that it is the Holy Spirit who binds me in such a way with the Father and with the Son. I also often find within myself that I say to Him: Divine Spirit, lead and govern me in the ways of my Divine Bridegroom <note>Marie uses the "Bridegroom" imagery common in Christian mysticism to describe the soul's intimate relationship with Christ.</note>.

11. I am unceasingly in this Divine communion, in such a delicate, simple, and enchanting way that it allows me no expressions. It is not an act <gloss>original: "acte"</gloss>, nor is it even a drawing of breath; it is such a gentle air <gloss>original: "air"</gloss> (a) in the ground of the soul, where **God’s** dwelling is, that I—as already stated—can find no words to explain myself.

12. My gazing upon this most adorable Majesty encompasses that which the Spirit urges me to speak to Him; and through the same Spirit, I speak. For in this language from spirit to spirit, in this communion with which His Divine Majesty deigns to honor my insignificance, I can do absolutely nothing except through His most simple movement. Since this movement is so simple, how then could my tongue or my pen say what it is? Even my own spirit can hardly distinguish it because of its great simplicity <term>Einfalt: A technical term in mysticism referring to a soul stripped of all complex thoughts and focused solely on God</term> and purity; which also continues to move more and more toward a greater simplicity.

13. There is yet another state in which I find myself, and which is, as it were, a consequence of the former. This happens to me most often when I am alone in our chamber. I undergo <gloss>original: "pâtis" - to suffer or experience passively</gloss> an impression in the soul; (I do not wish to say that it *is* an impression, I only use this word to express myself;) which is such a high, enchanting, and Divine thing—so simple, so pure, and so exalted above everything that can be perceived by the senses—that I cannot express it, except to say that I am in **God**, that I am possessed by **God**, and that **God** would soon have consumed me through His subtlety and through His lovely power <gloss>original: "efficacité" - inner working</gloss>, if I were not supported by another objective impression <gloss>original: "impression objective"</gloss> which follows the first. This second impression does not destroy the first, but rather tempers its greatness and excess, which would otherwise not be bearable in this life. For without the tempering of this other impression—which always has its relationship to the most adorable Word made flesh, my Divine Bridegroom—I would not be able to endure; because my soul has no strength nor life, except only in Him, who is my foundational state of objective love <note>Objective love refers to love focused entirely on God as the "object" of the soul, rather than on the self's own feelings.</note>, day and night, and every moment.

### of Marie of the Incarnation. Chapter XX.

14. The fruits which this state produces in my soul are these: A deep annihilation <note>In mystical theology, "annihilation" (Vernichtigung) refers to the soul's total surrender and the stripping away of the ego to make room for God.</note>, together with a true and thorough realization that she is nothingness and powerlessness itself; a disregard for herself and her own actions, which she sees are always mixed with imperfection, along with a complete conviction that this is so; which then places her in a state of great humility, however exalted she might otherwise be. This state also produces great patience in adversities; an inward and complete inclination toward peace and friendliness toward everyone; a gentle and inward diligence in showing goodwill toward those by whom she may have been offended; and a total turning away from any inclination toward resentment or ill-will. This state also gives her a great faithfulness in taking sufferings upon herself, in love and in union with the most adorable Word made flesh <term>Word made flesh: A reference to the Incarnation of Christ (the Logos), emphasizing his human nature and suffering.</term>, through affectionate outpourings into Him; a readiness to do everything and to take everything upon herself for **God’s** honor; and finally, a complete inclination to let herself be governed, and to subject her judgment to those whom **God** has placed over her.

15. It should further be noted that the Spirit, who has led me so affectionately, has always had the same purpose, and has moved my soul to the practice of these aforementioned virtues and many others of which I do not speak here: But He aimed always toward my following the Spirit of the Gospel <note>Marie refers to "Evangelischer Geist," meaning a life modeled strictly on the teachings and virtues found in the New Testament Gospels.</note>; for which my soul has had a perpetual pull from the beginning, as I unceasingly longed for the possession of the Spirit of Jesus Christ. He has given to all of this such perfection as pleased Him, through His holy workings, in all the states of prayer through which He led me as if by His hand, according to the abundance of His great, immeasurable mercy. Had I conducted myself toward it as I ought, I would have made far different progress on the path of holiness; however, my unfaithfulness makes me rightly fearful. I pray to the **God** of all goodness, my most adorable Bridegroom, that it may please Him to immerse my soul in His precious blood, and to be merciful to me. May He be eternally praised, lauded, and glorified by all angels and saints! I finished this writing on the 4th of August, 1654.

# Fifth Part. The Life

...been sufficiently ripe for a blessed eternity. Notwithstanding this, she continued to walk here on earth in this state for eighteen more years after that time. How she spent these years, both outwardly and inwardly, can be shared with the reader no more faithfully than once again through Maria’s own words, which we wish to cite with the greatest possible brevity from several existing letters.

->From July 12, 1663, to her son.<-

2. **God** has granted me the grace to remain faithful to Him in my state of sacrifice <note>Maria refers to her "state of sacrifice" (Stand des Opfers) as her total self-offering to God's will in the mission fields of New France.</note>, during an occasion where I saw myself almost every moment on the verge of completing my sacrifice—namely, during such great and terrifying earthquakes in this land that for a long time we believed the world was perishing. Within two months, there was not a single day when I did not have to keep myself prepared to be swallowed alive into the abyss of the earth, because one could not know when or where such a powerful earthquake would break out.

[On February 5th of this year, this terrifying earthquake began, and it lasted in its full strength until July. And although it was not continuous, the earth was moved several times every day and several times every night, and each shock lasted half a quarter of an hour, and sometimes even half an hour at a time. For more than six months afterward, the earth still moved now and then, and sometimes quite strongly, so that it can be said that its movement lasted for over a year.]

3. All day long, and at half past five in the evening, everything was still clear and quiet, when suddenly a horrific din and rushing was heard from afar, like a great multitude of coaches that seemed to roll over paving stones with unheard-of speed. This din had barely caught people's attention when one heard, beneath the earth and above the earth, something like a confusion of floods and water-waves which were terrifying, and like a hail of stones on the roofs of the houses, in the lofts <term>lofts: Translated from "Söllern," an archaic term for upper floors or attics.</term>, in the chambers, and everywhere else; and it seemed that the marble stones, of which the entire foundation of the land is made, along with our constructed houses, wanted to tear themselves to pieces and crush and shatter us under their devastated heaps. A thick dust flew from all sides; some doors opened by themselves, others slammed shut; the bells rang by themselves; and the towers of the churches as well as our houses were moved back and forth, just like trees when there is a strong wind; and all this with a terrifying overturning of the household furniture, which fell into a heap, the stones which tumbled down, the floors which split, the walls which cracked, and the livestock in the house, which behaved piteously, some running out of the house, others running in; in short, everyone was so frightened that they thought the Last Judgment <note>original: "jüngste Gericht"</note> was at the door.

4. This sudden occurrence was a thunderclap that struck consternation into all hearts. One took flight before the other, and everyone wanted to be the first...

of Maria of the Incarnation. Chapter XXI.
B b b
<meta>catchword: experienced.</meta>

...to run out; but one soon became aware, through the movement of the earth—which rose up under our feet just like a boat on a stormy sea—that it was a subterranean fire about to break forth. At the same time, some cried "Fire!"; others ran to the water to extinguish it; still others reached for their weapons, imagining that an army of the Iroquois <note>original: "Hiroquois", a historical spelling for the Haudenosaunee or Iroquois Confederacy, with whom the French colonists were often in conflict.</note> was arriving; some fell into faints; several clutched the trees, which were striking against one another and caused them no small terror; or they held onto the trunks, against which they were soundly battered by the violent movements. Most believed that the end of the world had come.

5. As for me personally, my state was as I have previously said. I have never experienced a condition that placed me in such a great stripping away of myself and of everything in the world. I had in my mind an impression of these words of the Son of God: *The Wisdom of God is justified by her children* <note>A reference to Matthew 11:19, suggesting that God's actions, however mysterious or frightening, are understood as righteous by those who truly follow Him.</note>; and at the same time I was moved in my soul to approve and love this providence of God. Indeed, in this very depth <note>original: "dans ce même fond", a French mystical term referring to the "ground" or deepest center of the soul where it communicates with God.</note> I felt compelled to sing something great, to laud and praise Him for this, His proceeding. I also felt an inclination of my whole heart and all my powers, which moved me to offer myself as a sacrifice to His Divine Majesty for all those sins of men that had necessitated Him to this chastisement. I could adopt no other disposition than to incessantly praise the high power of the Divine Majesty over all nature and over all hearts, whenever He wishes to shake them.

### From July 29, 1665.

6. In the year 1664, it pleased His Divine Goodness to visit me with a heavy illness. The malady took its beginning through an abundance and an outpouring of bile <term>bile: In the medical theory of the time, an excess of "yellow bile" was thought to cause fever and physical pain.</term> through all the limbs of the body, even into the marrow of the bones, in such a way that it seemed to me as if my whole body were being pierced through from head to foot. In addition to this, I had a persistent fever and a colic which lasted day and night, so that if God had not supported me, my patience would have failed me, and I would have called out with a loud cry.

7. Some time afterward, the illness made a new attack (so that it was thought once again that I would die). I suffered from pleurisy <note>original: "Seitenstechen", literally "stinging in the side," commonly referring to pleurisy or intense respiratory pain.</note>, along with kidney colic and violent vomiting, as well as a contraction of the nerves, through which the whole body, down to its furthest parts, was set into motion. And so that all pain should come together, it happened—because I could only lie in a single position in bed—that stones formed in the kidneys, which caused me unheard-of pains. Finally, a stone passed from me that was as large as a pigeon’s egg, and after it a great number of smaller stones.

This long-lasting illness was not at all vexing to me; and through the mercy of God, I did not feel a single movement of impatience.

Fifth Part. The Life

<meta>catchword: 16. Isaiah</meta>

O my GOD. My days and my nights pass in such a manner; and I hope that His goodness will, in these words, receive my soul in death, and that He will grant that I die even as He gives me to live. I have said, in these words; I say better, in this breathing, which allows me no power to perform any act <term>original: "acte" or "Wirksamkeit", referring here to a deliberate, conscious spiritual effort or exercise of the soul</term>: and I do not know how I should express myself when I must speak of matters so bare and so simple as these are, which complete my soul in its highest and sole Good, in its simple and universal All.

12. As I saw myself subjected to so many illnesses, I believed, according to the course of nature, that they would wear me down and would not come to an end except through death. Nevertheless, Love, which is stronger than death <note>A reference to Song of Solomon 8:6.</note>, has put an end to them; and see, I am, through the mercy of GOD, almost as healthy again as I was before this long-lasting illness, without knowing how long the same will last.

13. It also matters nothing to me, as long as only the most holy will of GOD is done. But I do not believe that my end will be very far off, as I am already in the seventieth year of my age. My moments and my days are in the hand of Him who gives me life; and everything is the same to me, as long as they all pass according to His pleasure, and according to His adorable purpose for me.

14. GOD has never led me through a path of fear; rather through a path of love and of trust: nevertheless, when I think that I am a sinner, and that for that reason I could fall into such a state where I would be deprived of the friendship of my GOD, then I am more humbled than one can imagine, and I am seized by a fear that this misfortune might perhaps happen to me. If this fear were to persist, I would be able neither to live nor to endure, because it concerns the separation from a GOD of love and of goodness, from whom I have received more graces and mercy than there are grains of sand in the sea. But trust, through a single glance, makes this fear disappear: and as I turn my sight away from such an unhappy object of thought, this trust causes me to abandon myself into the arms of my heavenly Bridegroom, to rest therein.

### September 25, 1670.

15. I see myself filled with so much unfaithfulness and misery, and I am so many times annihilated <note>original: "vernichtiget," related to the mystical concept of *anéantissement*, where the soul feels reduced to nothingness in the presence of God's majesty.</note> before GOD because of it, and so small in my own eyes (yet this latter state is always with me), that I do not know how I should remedy the matter, because I look upon my imperfections in such a darkness which has neither entrance nor exit. See here, I am at the end of my life, and I do (nonetheless) nothing that befits such a soul, which shall soon appear before her Judge.

->of Marie of the Incarnation. Chapter XXII.<-

<margin>(a) "By state," that is, it is not a fleeting grace, but an innate, profound, and abiding essence.</margin>

16. Nevertheless, however imperfect I am, and however annihilated <note>In mystical tradition, "annihilation" refers to the soul being brought to "nothing" so it can be filled entirely by God.</note> in His presence, I still see myself, through a certain state (a), lost in His Divine Majesty. For many years, He has held me close to Himself in a communion, in a connection, in a union, and in a shared intimacy that I cannot express. It is a certain kind of <term>poverty of spirit: a state of total inner emptiness where the soul relies entirely on God rather than its own thoughts or efforts</term>, which does not even allow me to converse with the angels, nor with the delights of the blessed, nor with the mysteries of our faith. At times, I wish to distract myself from my <term>inner ground: the deepest, most central part of the soul where God dwells</term>, in order to dwell upon these things and take pleasure in their beauties as things that please me; but I immediately forget them, and the Spirit that leads me places me once again even deeper into my ground, where I lose myself in the One who pleases me more than all things. There I see His loveliness, His majesty, His highness, and His power, without any act of reflection or searching <note>original French: "recherche"</note>, but in a **moment that lasts forever.** I wish to say something that I cannot express; and because I cannot express it, I do not know if I am saying it correctly. The soul has in this "ground" immeasurable treasures that have no limits; there is nothing coarse there, but an entirely bare and pure faith which encompasses infinite things.

17. The imagination, which has no part in this state, seeks to graze and flies here and there to find its nourishment; but this does nothing to the inner ground; the imagination cannot reach there, and its activity vanishes. These are nonetheless attacks that are weak and fleeting, yet they are also bothersome and provide an opportunity for patience and humility.

18. In this state, neither the inner nor the outer senses have any part, nor does the reflection of the intellect: all their activities are lost in this ground, where faith allows everything to be seen, independent of the powers of the soul. Everything, I say, is swallowed up in this ground, where God Himself and His Divine Spirit work. In this state of mind, one has no difficulty following the exercises of the community; temporal <note>Life's daily, worldly responsibilities.</note> business does no harm, because it is performed in peace and silence.

19. It has been nearly fifty years that God has kept me in this state; although at times, within this profound and abiding state, there have been simpler and more interior dispositions, where one is more freed from the senses and the purity of the spirit is greater. For now, it would be difficult for me to elaborate much or to give an account of my prayer and interior state; because what God gives me is so simple and so detached from the senses that I have said everything in two or three words.

20. Before this, I could do nothing else in my prayer except, like a drawing of breath in this inner ground, say: My God, my God...

### Part Five. The Life.

God, my great God, my life, my all, my love, my glory! Right now I say these very same things, or rather, I breathe them in this way; but moreover, when my soul produces these very simple words and this very inward breathing, she experiences the fullness of their meaning. And that which I do in my actual prayer, I also do the whole day long: when I lie down, when I rise, and in all other places. From this it follows that I cannot undertake any exercises according to a method <gloss>or prescribed order</gloss>, because everything returns again to the inner guidance of God over me. I only take a small quarter-hour in the evening to offer the heart of the Son of God to His Father for this **New Church** <note>This refers to the Catholic mission in "New France" (modern-day Canada), where Marie lived as an Ursuline nun.</note>, for the workers of the **Gospel** <note>original Latin: *Evangelii*</note>, and for my friends; which is done through short and simple "breathings." The singing of Psalms, which is a regulated exercise, does not burden me.

->From October 28, 1671.<-

21. My current state is of such a nature that, no matter what subject for prayer I might take—and even if I have just read one or heard one read with all possible devotion—I immediately forget it. It is not as if I cannot look upon a **mystery of the faith** at the beginning of my prayer, for I truly do so; but it happens with a most simple gaze, for I am in a state of inability to "meditate" <note>In this context, "meditate" refers to the intellectual process of thinking through a biblical scene or doctrine.</note> on anything. Instead, in a single moment, without reflecting on it, I find myself in my usual <term>ground: the deepest essence of the soul where God dwells</term>, where my soul contemplates God, in whom she exists.

22. I speak to Him according to the "movements" <note>inner spiritual nudges or inspirations</note> that He gives me for it; and this great intimacy does not allow me to contemplate Him without speaking to Him, and in this speaking, following His "pull" <gloss>or attraction</gloss>. If the pull is from His greatness, and I simultaneously see my "nothingness," then my soul speaks to Him accordingly. If it is from His sovereign dominion, it happens in the same way. If it is from His loveliness, and from the fact that in Himself He is nothing but Love, then my words are as if to my <term>Bridegroom: a traditional mystical term for Jesus, representing the soul’s intimate union with God</term>, and it is not in my power to speak any other words. This Love is never idle, and my heart can breathe nothing else but this.

23. I have said that the "breaths" by which I live are from my Bridegroom; these at times consume me in such a way that, if Mercy did not adapt His grace to suit my nature, I would have to succumb under it. This life would bring me death, even though none of this is apparent to the senses, nor does it prevent me from performing my regulated duties.

24. Sometimes I become aware—I do not know if others notice it too—that when I walk through the house, I walk unsteadily; this happens because my spirit suffers a certain "rapture" <note>a state of being "carried away" by intense spiritual joy or focus</note> that consumes me. On these occasions, I perform almost no <term>acts: deliberate, conscious mental efforts or specific prayers, as opposed to a state of passive contemplation</term>; for this consuming love does not permit me to do so.

<summary>Marie describes her transition from structured meditation to a state of "simple gaze" and "breathing" prayer, where she feels constantly united with God as her Bridegroom. She notes that this intense spiritual state is physically taxing, occasionally causing her to stagger while performing her daily duties in the convent.</summary>

<keywords>mysticism, simple gaze, inner ground, Bridegroom, New France, prayer methods, rapture, 1671</keywords>

### of Marie of the Incarnation. Ch. XXII.

25. At other times, my soul gains the upper hand, and she speaks to her **Bridegroom** <note>In mystical tradition, the "Bridegroom" refers to Jesus Christ, following the imagery of the Song of Solomon.</note> a language of love that He alone can give the soul the power to speak; but no matter how great the intimacy He grants me, I never for a moment forget my own "nothingness," and it is like one abyss inside another abyss that has no bottom. During these experiences, I cannot remain on my knees without being supported; for although my senses remain free, I am nevertheless weak, and my weakness hinders me. When I try to force myself not to sit or lean, my body—which is suffering and restless—causes a **distraction** <note>In the context of prayer, "distraction" (*Zerstreuung*) refers to anything that pulls the mind away from focus on the Divine.</note> that compels me to do one or the other, and only then do I return to stillness.

26. Now, although there is nothing coarse <gloss>material</gloss> in this inner occupation, my imagination does sometimes plague me with **trifles** <note>original: *Bagatellen*</note>; however, because they have no foundation, they vanish just as they came. This does nothing to the "ground" of the soul, which remains unchanging.

27. On other occasions, I endure a "crucifying state": my soul gazes upon GOD, who meanwhile seems to take pleasure in taking me prisoner. I would dearly love to embrace Him and converse with Him as I am accustomed to do; but He holds me like a bound person. In my bonds, I see that He loves me; yet I cannot embrace Him. Oh, what great torment this is! Nevertheless, my soul consents to it, because it is not possible for me to desire any other state than the one in which His Divine Majesty wishes to have me. I look upon this state as a state of purification, or as a **purgatory** <note>original: *Fegefeuer*</note>, for I can give it no other name; when this has passed, I find myself once again in my usual state.

# Fifth Part. The Life
<meta>Catchword: were,</meta>

2. The long-lasting and terrifying illness that she had suffered eight years prior left her with several persistent and significant weaknesses; primarily a weakness in both sides, which made it seem as though her body no longer had any support, and which was believed to stem from a **bilious humor** <term>bilious humor: in the medical theory of the four humors, an excess of bile was thought to cause heat, bitterness, and various physical ailments</term>. During the night between the fifteenth and sixteenth of January 1672, she was completely bedridden by an effusion of fluids from the brain to the chest, which made it seem as though she were suffocating. This was followed by extraordinary vomiting that lasted for twenty-four hours; afterward, a suffocating pressure arrived that allowed no relief, along with a persistent, violent headache and sleeplessness. Furthermore, this bile spread through her entire body and burned like a fire in her limbs, also making her body so heavy that three of the strongest people could hardly move it; and whenever this occurred, her pains were always doubled. All of this was also accompanied by a very violent fever which, it seemed, would have to consume her within a few hours.

<margin>(a) Galatians 2:19.</margin>
3. She suffered all her pains with a **meekness** and **serenity** <note>original: *Sanftmuth und Gelassenheit*. In mystical tradition, *Gelassenheit* refers to a state of perfect detachment and yielding to God's will.</note> which caused both devotion and dismay in all who visited her. Her words, her appearance, her gestures, and her entire being gave not a single sign of impatience or resentment; rather, the brightness of her countenance was a mark of the brightness of her heart, and an effect of that joy which she held in the **peak of her spirit** <term>peak of her spirit: the *apex mentis*, the highest point of the soul where the mystic experiences direct union with God</term> because she saw her nature lying entirely defeated and saw herself crucified with Jesus Christ. She rejoiced with Him in her usual union, and as a testimony to what an honor and happiness she considered this for herself, she took a particular pleasure in repeating these words of the Apostle (a): **I have been crucified with Christ.** <note>original: *Ich bin mit Christo gekreuziget*</note>

4. From the first day of her illness, she believed that she would die from it, and she said as much to those who visited her. One of the nuns, who was the only one remaining of those she had brought with her from France to Canada, and who felt great sorrow over this, said to her: "How, dear Mother, will you go away without me?" To which she replied with an enchanting kindness: "Do not be troubled, my child; GOD will always be your Father, and when I am before His Majesty, I will not forget you." All her words were like so many arrows that pierced the hearts of those who heard them, especially the nuns, as they saw that she was taking her leave of them.

->## of Marie of the Incarnation. Chapter XXIII.<-

5. [if it] were so, she would be just as content to remain in life as to die, or even to go to hell, if it could serve His greater glorification. "That is all well," said her spiritual leader, "but you must join us in prayer and do your utmost so that you may be preserved for this community, which believes it has need of you." Thereupon she prayed with the others and spoke these words: "My Lord and my God, if You believe that I am still necessary to this little community, then I do not withdraw myself from suffering and labor; let Your holy will be done!" God looked upon so many tears, so that in a short time (in a miraculous way) she became so much better that she could again walk through the house using two sticks; even the doctors often testified that she lived only by a miracle.

6. This lasted until **Good Friday**, when she made it known that she suffered extraordinary pains in both sides. A skilled surgeon was immediately called to examine her; he judged that there were mature **ulcers** <note>original: *Geschwüre*. In this context, these were likely deep internal abscesses caused by her long-term illness.</note> which necessarily had to be opened. This was done early the following morning, when two wounds were cut, four fingers wide and so deep they reached the bone; these had to be widened further that same evening.

7. In all these incredible pains, she allowed a great stillness of mind to be felt, without a single word of complaint or any movement of impatience, just as if her soul had been entirely separated from her body. Rather, all who were with her at that time perceived a new glow <gloss>of virtue</gloss> in her meekness, in her patience, in her humility, in her love, and in all her other virtues, in the same measure that the illness and pain increased within her. It only happened once, as the surgeon was dressing her wound—when he was cleaning it with an iron instrument and with his hand, and then placing into it thick wicks of scraped linen soaked in **sharp-biting water** <note>original: *scharf-beissendem Wasser*. This likely refers to a caustic or astringent antiseptic solution used to clean infected wounds.</note>—that she could not restrain herself from moving just a little because of the excessive pain. But she immediately noticed this movement, took it to be a sign of weakness and a fault, and said: "Ah, good God! How impatient I am!"

8. On the eighth day, the surgeon said that no improvement was to be expected for her. When she heard this, an extraordinary cheerfulness appeared on her face. From that moment on, the remainder of her life was a gentle and almost constant **ecstasy** <note>original: *Entzückung*. A state of being spiritually transported or "caught up" in God.</note>, and she went deeper into herself than ever before, so that she might die as she had previously said and hoped: namely, in the most intimate union with her **Bridegroom** <note>A common mystical reference to Jesus Christ.</note>. She spoke little, and only when necessary; and to whoever wished to speak with her, she likewise replied with few words, but with a truly **angelic friendliness** <note>original: *Englischen Freundlichkeit*. In 17th-century German, "Englisch" frequently means "angelic" (derived from *Engel*), rather than referring to the English nation.</note>.

9. Her Mother Superior, who was always with her and who so greatly lamented her loss, could not restrain herself from giving her a loving reproach: that she had brought herself to this state because she, regardless of her great weaknesses and advanced age, had always insisted on eating with the others without anything special for

to want to have for herself. Thereupon she replied: "When I am not sick, I must live like those who are healthy; my health and my life are of little importance; but it is of great importance to me, and it is my great business, that I be obedient to the Divine Majesty, and that I follow the laws of the station to which He has called me. When I came to Canada, GOD gave me to understand that it was His pleasure that I should live here in the Apostolic way, and eat what was set before me, and that I should also otherwise avoid any singularity <note>original: *Sonderlichkeit*; here meaning special treatment or behaviors that would set her apart from the communal life of the other sisters</note>, which law I have since then constantly kept before my eyes."

10. The little savages <note>original: *Wilden*. This historical term refers to the Indigenous children, likely of the Algonquin or Huron-Wendat nations, whom Marie educated in Quebec. On Saturday, the last of April, she entered into the death-struggle, if one may call it that, though there is no struggle, and life and death are the same to the soul. She lost her speech and hearing, but not her understanding; and one could see clearly from her outward appearance that her soul stood in a deep union with GOD. One hour before her departure, she shed three or four large tears. GOD alone, who was the master of her heart, knows from what source they came. A little later, she opened her eyes once more, but soon closed them again, never to open them again except in the blessed eternity. Finally, at six o’clock in the evening, she gave up her beautiful soul, without any violence <note>meaning she passed peacefully without a physical struggle</note>, into the arms of her heavenly bridegroom, the Eternal and Incarnate, most adorable Word <note>A theological reference to Christ as the *Logos* or "Word" from the Gospel of John</note>, to complete her marriage with the same in the most perfect way in heaven, on the last of April 1672, in the seventy-third year of her age.

11. The joyfulness with which she died remained depicted on her face, along with a certain majesty and such enchanting beauty, that it seemed her soul was already sharing a ray of its glory with the body.

# Preface.

Let us, by contemplating God’s guidance of His saints from the most distant Western lands, step back for a moment into our German Fatherland. For the Savior has His redeemed from every tribe, language, people, and nation, whom He makes kings and priests unto God. Hardly a land, station, or time can be found in which this eternal Good and Light of Life has not presented one or more witnesses of the truth and shining examples to humanity, to invite and entice them into His blessed fellowship.

We Germans must certainly lay our hands over our mouths <note>A biblical idiom (see Job 40:4) signifying humble silence or awe in the face of divine wisdom.</note> and justify the Lord, who has given us many such witnesses in more than one way, although they have at all times been recognized and accepted as such by only a few. The present example of this holy soul can convince us—if we are willing to open our eyes—that God has stretched out His hand in grace over our dear Germany since ancient times, and even in the darkest periods, He desired to visit it with some glimpses of light above other lands. Yes, He has done so, and He still does so in these our days; may we only walk while we have the light, before the darkness of His spiritual and physical judgments (deserved through sin and ingratitude) overtakes us. For who knows for what cause it occurred through Divine Providence that in the year 1342, twelve years after the death of this holy Gertrude, the monastery where she lived was most cruelly devastated, burned, and otherwise miserably treated during the war of that time? In any case, let this be recorded here for the reflection and warning of us all.

The life and the revelations of this soul were recorded partly by herself in the Latin language, and partly by a close friend of hers, namely (a) from the mouth of St. Gertrude, at the command of God and her superiors (as is noted therein). They have been printed often; for example, in German at Leipzig (b) in 1505, and at Cologne in 1657 and 1674. Furthermore, in Latin under the title *Intimations of Divine Piety* <note>original: "Insinuationes Divinæ pietatis." This is the Latin title of Gertrude's famous work, often translated as "The Herald of Divine Love."</note>, both in Cologne in 1579 and 1588, as well as in Salzburg in 1662, and in Paris likewise in 1662, etc.; also in Dutch, and several times in French. The last-mentioned Latin Paris edition is more accurate than the previous ones, and it has also been used for this short excerpt.

Even during Gertrude's lifetime, these writings were examined and confirmed by many reputable men known to the holy virgin, as Lanspergius <note>Johannes Lanspergius (1489–1539), a Carthusian monk who was a major proponent of Gertrude's writings.</note> mentions them by name; among whom a certain Master named Godfried Rex was powerfully converted through Gertrude's discourses. The judgment of another learned man, which he wrote after a diligent and precise reading of these books, sounds glorious: "I hold," he says, "in the true light of Divine Truth, that no one enlightened by God’s Spirit can either blaspheme or dispute those things written in this book; for they are holy matters, etc." The pious Ludov. Blosius (c) <note>Louis de Blois (1506–1566), a famous Flemish Benedictine mystic.</note> adds: "From this it is evident how far those still are from the Spirit of God who reject and laugh at these Divine revelations as women's dreams; may God forgive them this sin!" But since this person has been publicly declared a saint in the Roman Church, it is unnecessary to cite more testimonies from the same. Among Protestants, these matters are mostly unknown; however, they have praised it enough when they accept the judgment of Mr. Poiret <note>Pierre Poiret (1646–1719), a French mystic and philosopher whose "Bibliotheca Mysticorum" was a key resource for this author.</note>, since he titles the person "Enlightened, Angelic, and Heartfelt," but her life "Divine" (d). At least I know that this man read the books of Gertrude from beginning to end with attention, and could therefore judge them better than others.

Furthermore, the defense which the well-known and pious Lanspergius had placed before these books deserves to be read, in which he refuted the most common objections; since he

# Preface.

...wisely reminds those who show a distaste for revelations,
> “that even the Holy Scriptures are full of revelations; and therefore the name
> ‘revelation’ should not be so foreign, unless (he says) one would rather be counted among those
> from whom the Father has hidden His secrets—namely, the wise and clever of this world—than
> among the simple ones to whom He has revealed these things. But truly, (he says,) I fear that
> there will be few such simple ones in these days.”

That caution and the “testing of spirits” <note>A reference to 1 John 4:1, a common biblical warning to discern whether spiritual experiences are truly from God.</note> are necessary in such matters; that extraordinary gifts do not lead to an infallible conclusion about a person’s holiness, but rather the person’s holiness allows one to judge the correctness of their revelations; that one should desire neither these nor any other extraordinary things—this is acknowledged and has been warned of by all enlightened souls. However, who would dare to bind the hands of the Most High, preventing Him from stooping down to His wayward creatures in every possible way to reveal His manifold wisdom and love for mankind? Might not each person, according to their capacity and nature, be drawn, instructed, and led into fellowship with GOTT <note>The text uses the capitalized "GOTT" (God) throughout to emphasize divine majesty.</note>? Furthermore, there is even less reason for any doubt regarding the revelations presented here by this holy soul, as they do not deal with future or uncertain events, but with matters that glorify God, are beneficial to mankind, and are therefore worthy of all acceptance.

<margin>(a) *The Herald of Divine Love*, Book I, Chapter 16. <note>Original Latin: *Insinuat. L. I. Cap. 16.* This refers to Gertrude's primary work, *Insinuationes Divinae Pietatis*.</note></margin>
It is remarkably told how the holy Gertrude was compelled to make her books known; namely,
> “how it was indicated to her that it was the will of God that these
> writings should be made known to people, and she felt herself so powerfully driven in her spirit to do so.
> Yet she wondered at this and thought in her mind: what use could this possibly be? For she had
> firmly resolved to make them known to no one during her life; and after her death, she feared
> minds might only be confused by them, because she well knew that many would not only fail to find
> edification in them but would even despise and slander them. Then God answered her: ‘What do you
> think is the use when one reads that I visited John <note>Referring to the Apostle John and his Book of Revelation.</note> and spoke with him? It is only so that
> the devotion of those who hear it may be increased, and my love for the human race may be revealed.
> Thus, devotion can also be ignited in some when they read what you have received from Me, so that they
> too may become eager for it and improve their lives. I have placed My grace in you in such a way that
> I will demand much fruit from it. But if some, out of a malicious heart, wish to slander these things,
> let their sin be upon their own heads; but you shall remain innocent (a).’”

Every person is free to look upon these matters with the eye of a simple child, and thus he will find benefit, his soul will be nourished, and God will be praised. Or, he may look with a bitter, unbelieving heart, from which he will receive at the very least no benefit, nor will God receive any honor. For as that Teacher of the Church says: “The faithful always find something to doubt <note>This paradox suggests that faith is a choice made despite the possibility of doubt, whereas unbelief persists despite the presence of things worthy of belief.</note>, and the unbelievers find something they could believe.” Therefore, the crown is rightly given to the faithful for their faith, and judgment to the unbelievers for their unbelief.
