# Preface.

Let us, in our contemplation of God's guidance of His saints from the most distant Western lands, step back for a moment into our German Fatherland. For the Savior has His redeemed from every tribe, and language, and people, and nation, whom He makes kings and priests unto God. Hardly a land, station, or time can be found wherein this eternal Good and Light of Life has not presented one or more witnesses of the truth—shining examples—to mankind, to invite and allure them into His blessed fellowship.

We Germans must certainly lay our hands upon our mouths <note>A biblical expression (from Job 40:4) meaning to remain silent in humble awe or to admit one's own shortcomings before God's righteousness.</note> and justify the Lord, who has given us many such examples in more than one way, though they have almost always been recognized and accepted by only a few. The present example of this holy soul can convince us of this—if we are willing to open our eyes—that God has stretched out His hand in grace over our dear Germany since ancient times, and even in the darkest ages, willed to visit it with glimpses of light above other lands. Yes, He has done it, and He still does it in these our days; if only we would walk while we have the light, before the darkness (brought about by sin and ingratitude) of His spiritual and physical judgments falls upon us. For who knows for what reason it happened through Divine decree that in the year 1342—twelve years after the death of this holy Gertrude—the monastery in which she lived was most cruelly devastated, burned, and otherwise piteously treated during the wars of that time? In any case, let this be remembered here as a reflection and a warning to us all.

The life and revelations of this soul were recorded partly by herself in the Latin language, and partly by a close friend of hers, specifically (a) from the mouth of St. Gertrude, by the command of God and her superiors (as is stated therein). They have been printed often; for example, in German at Leipzig (b) in 1505, and at Cologne in 1657 and 1674. Furthermore, in Latin under the title *Insinuationes Divinæ pietatis* <note>Original: "Insinuationes Divinæ pietatis," usually translated into English as "The Herald of Divine Love."</note>, both at Cologne in 1579 and 1588, as well as at Salzburg in 1662, and at Paris also in 1662, etc.; also in Dutch, and several times in French. The last-mentioned Latin Paris edition is more accurate than the previous ones, and it was used for this short excerpt.

Even during Gertrude's lifetime, these writings were examined and confirmed by many proven men who were acquainted with the holy virgin, as *Lanspergius* <note>Johannes Lanspergius (1489–1539), a Carthusian monk who was a major promoter of Gertrude's writings.</note> cites them by name; among whom a certain Master named *Godfried Rex* was powerfully converted through Gertrude's discourses. The judgment of another learned man, which he wrote after a diligent and precise reading of these books, sounds magnificent:

> I hold, he says, in the true light of Divine Truth, that no one enlightened by God’s Spirit could either slander or dispute those things written in this book; for they are holy matters, etc.

The pious *Ludov. Blosius* (c) <note>François Louis Blosius (1506–1566), a Flemish Benedictine abbot and mystical writer.</note> adds:

> From this it is obvious how far those still are from the Spirit of God who reject and mock these Divine revelations as "women's dreams" <note>A dismissive term used by critics to diminish the spiritual authority of female mystics.</note>; may God forgive them this sin!

However, since this person has been publicly declared a Saint in the Roman Church, it is unnecessary to cite more testimonies from that source. Among Protestants, these matters are mostly unknown; nevertheless, they have praised her sufficiently when they accept the judgment of Mr. *Poiret* <note>Pierre Poiret (1646–1719), a French mystic and philosopher who, despite being a Protestant, highly valued Catholic mystical writings.</note>, as he titles the person *Enlightened*, *Angelic*, *Heartfelt*, and her life *Divine* (d). For once, I know that this man read the books of Gertrude from beginning to end with great attention, and could therefore judge them better than others.

Furthermore, the **Defense** <note>Original: "Schutzschrift," an apologetic text written to protect the work from critics.</note> which the well-known and pious *Lanspergius* had placed before these books deserves to be read, in which he refuted the most common objections; since he

# Preface.

—which especially gives those who show an aversion to revelations cause to wisely consider, "that even the Holy Scripture is full of revelations; and therefore the name of 'revelations' should not be so foreign to anyone, unless (he says) one would rather be counted among those from whom the Father has hidden His mysteries—namely, among the wise and clever of this world—rather than among the simple ones <note>The original German 'Unmündigen' refers to the 'babes' or 'little ones' mentioned in Matthew 11:25, implying those with a childlike, humble faith rather than intellectual pride.</note> to whom He has revealed these things. But truly (he says), I fear that few such simple ones will be found in these days."

That in such matters caution and the testing of spirits are necessary; that no infallible conclusion regarding the holiness of a person follows from extraordinary gifts, but rather that the correctness of their revelations is to be judged by the holiness of the person; that one must desire neither such things nor any other extraordinary matters—all this is admitted, and all enlightened souls have warned of it. However, who would nonetheless wish to bind the hands of the Most High, so that He might not, for the revelation of His manifold wisdom and love for mankind, descend in every way to His strayed creatures; so that each might be drawn and instructed according to their capacity and nature, and be led to fellowship with GOD? Moreover, there is even less room for any scruples <term>scruples: nagging doubts or hesitations based on moral or religious grounds</term> regarding the revelations which might be cited here from this holy soul, since they do not deal with future or doubtful things, but with such matters that glorify GOD and are salutary for mankind, and are therefore worthy of all acceptance.

<margin>(a) *The Herald of Divine Love* <note>Original: "Insinuat. L. I. Cap. 16." refers to Gertrude’s Latin work *Insinuationes Divinae Pietatis*.</note>, Book I, Chapter 16.</margin>
It is remarkably told how St. Gertrude was compelled to make her books known; namely, "how it was indicated to her that it was the will of God that these writings should become known to men, and she felt herself so powerfully driven to it in spirit; then she wondered at this, and thought in her mind, what use could such a thing be? For she had firmly intended to make them known to no one during her life; and after her death, minds might only be confused by them; because she well knew that many would not only draw no edification from them, but would even hold them in low esteem and blaspheme them. Then she was answered by God: 'What do you think then, what use is it when one reads that I visited John and spoke with him? It is only so that the devotion of those who hear it may be increased, and my love for the human race may be revealed: thus can devotion also be ignited in some when they read what you have received from Me, so that they also become eager for it and amend their lives. I have placed my grace in you in such a way that I will demand much fruit from it. But if some, out of a wicked heart, wish to blaspheme these things, let their sin be upon their own heads; but you shall remain innocent (a).'"

Every person is free to look upon these matters either with a simple, childlike eye—and thus he will have the benefit of his soul being nourished and God being praised—or with a wicked, unbelieving heart; and from that, he will at the very least receive no benefit, nor will God receive any honor. For, as a certain Teacher of the Church says: "The faithful always find something about which they could doubt; and the unfaithful something they could believe." Therefore, the crown is rightly given to the faithful for their faith, and judgment to the unfaithful for their unbelief.

[One may leave it undecided <note>The German phrase "an seinen Ort gestellet seyn" is an idiom meaning to set a question aside or leave it to be debated elsewhere.</note> whether all those prayers published under the name of Gertrude were really composed by this Saint; however, one finds in her books some beautiful little sighs <note>The original German "Seufzerlein" refers to short, spontaneous, and fervent aspirations or "breathings" of prayer common in 17th-century devotional literature.</note> which are worthy of being granted a small space here.]

### Offering of the Heart.

> "Behold, O Lord, with my whole will I withdraw my heart from all creatures, and offer it up to You; praying that You would wash it in the strengthening water of Your most holy side; and adorn it appropriately in the precious blood of Your sweetest heart; and prepare it fittingly for You in the lovely fragrance <note>Original: "Aufdünstung," implying a spiritual vapor or incense-like exhalation.</note> of Your Divine love."

### For the Grace of Dying to Self.

> "Behold, dearest Lord, in honor of Your most precious death, I lie completely cast to the ground, and ask You, for the sake of the love which compelled You to die—You who give life to all creatures—that You would kill in my soul everything that is displeasing to You within it."

### While Eating.

> "May the power of Your Divine love completely incorporate me into You, most lovable Jesus."

### While Drinking.

> "The effect of that love, which so vehemently held sway in Your innermost being, most dear Jesus, pour out and preserve within my own innermost being; so that, penetrating my whole essence, it may constantly trickle through all movements, powers, and senses of my body and my soul, to Your eternal praise."

### While Performing a Task.

> "Lord, I offer this work to You, through Your only Son, in the power of the Holy Spirit, to Your eternal praise."

### Humble Confession and Petition.

> "Behold, dear Lord, I, an unworthy sinner <note>The female form "Sinnerin" is used here, reflecting St. Gertrude's voice.</note>, confess with sorrow that I have, alas! out of human weakness, manifoldly transgressed against Your Divine omnipotence; and in many ways, out of ignorance, sinned against Your Divine wisdom; and in various ways have wickedly provoked Your inestimable goodness."

You artful Master Craftsman, most gentle Instructor, wisest Counselor, friendliest Helper, most faithful Friend. You flavorful union of the most intimate loveliness. O most tender Caresser, gentlest Mover of hearts, most fervent Lover, sweetest Bridegroom, most chaste Zealot. O most beloved Brother, blooming Youth, cheerful Companion, most charitable Host, most courteous Servant. I choose You before every creature; for Your sake I renounce all delight; for You I go to meet all adversity. In all of this, I desire to be praised by none but You. I testify with mouth and heart that You are the cause and the inner mover of this and all other good. In the power of Your zeal, I unite the intention of my devotion with the powerful effect of Your prayer, so that through the completeness of the Divine union, after all resisting movements are consumed, I may be led up to the summit of perfection.”

# Chapter Two.

->She is a special instrument of God; yet at the same time very humble, and in her heart detached from all things.<-

1.
If one looks generally, and indeed with an eye that knows how to recognize the traces of Divine Truth, at the little we still have left of this holy virgin, then one must confess that she truly was a friend of God, <note>The term "Friend of God" (Gottesfreund) was a common designation in medieval German mysticism for those who achieved a high level of spiritual intimacy with the Divine.</note> a humble and pure soul, a light of that same dark age, and an instrument for much awakening and conversion. The author of this book, who witnessed Gertrude’s conduct and shared in its blessing and power, often cannot find enough words to thank the Lord that He sent such an instrument to the world. In one place, she breaks out into these words:] To God the Lord, the Giver of all goods and all graces, must all that heaven contains, all that the circle of the earth and the abyss of the sea encompasses, give thanks and ascribe an infinite, eternal, unchangeable praise—such a praise, namely, that springs from Him and flows back into Him again—for His exceeding goodness, through which He has directed the stream of His mercies to the valley of our misery, and has found this soul, looked upon her, and chosen her for Himself. Witnesses are present to prove that He chose her and drew her to Himself as His own, so that He might work the mysteries of His goodness within her as His own instrument and make them known to the world, etc. [Now, after the author has extensively presented the testimonies of this, both from God’s side and from the side of other people, and finally from the inner nature of St. Gertrude, she proceeds to report on one or two of her virtues, which had as their foundation only the indwelling of Christ within her. She begins this with these words:]

2. St. Gertrude was one of those blessed souls whom the Lord chose to dwell within in a far more excellent way than in an external temple. For His praise, I wish to reveal what I have perceived of this holy virgin through a secret intimacy over many years: and therefore to explain briefly the manner in which she shone, as if with rays of virtue. For by this, as I hope, it will be placed beyond all doubt for everyone that this soul was inhabited by the Lord of Virtues, who adorned her both inwardly and outwardly with such a shining light of grace.

3. ### Sixth Part. The Life of Saint Gertrude. Chapter II.

[...account,] that she was only a channel through which God’s gifts and graces flowed to His chosen ones. Because she was (in her own opinion) the most ungrateful and unworthy, she felt she would receive both the great and the lesser gifts of God in vain and without benefit, unless she applied herself to scattering these gifts of God, both in writing and by word of mouth, for the salvation of her neighbor. And she did this with such great faithfulness—that is, with such great zeal for the glory of God, and with such low estimation of herself—that she sometimes said:

> “Even if I were to be tormented in hell immediately after my death, I would still rejoice that God the Lord is honored by other people through my work, or through whatever else it might be.”

4. She esteemed no one so lowly that she did not believe God’s grace was more fruitfully invested in them than in herself. She believed that the gifts of God which she received were given more for the sake of her neighbor than for herself; she felt she had no further part in them other than making them known; and only then did they first produce fruit in others, for which God would be praised.

5. If she happened to be at prayer, or was doing something else good, and a thought of vain-glory <note>The term "eitlen Ehre" refers to "vanity" or seeking the "empty praise" of others rather than the glory of God.</note> tried to rise within her, she paid it little heed and would sometimes say:

> “If someone sees this good thing and is thereby stirred to imitation, only then will God the Lord receive the fruit of praise from you through someone else, because you of yourself bring forth no fruit.”

For this reason, she believed she was like a scarecrow-mask <note>original: "Larve" – literally a mask or effigy. In this context, she compares herself to a hollow figure placed in a garden to protect the real fruit.</note> in the Father’s house, which is useful for nothing except perhaps to be tied to a stake or a tree in the summertime, so that the birds might be frightened away by it and the fruits thereby preserved.

6. She considered all people whom she saw to be better than herself. Once, while she was on a journey, she said out of extreme self-contempt:

> “Ah, my Lord, among the most distinguished wonders that You work, I consider this a singular miracle: that the earth still carries me, an unworthy sinner.”

To which words the Lord gave this answer:

> “The earth bears you willingly and justly, for heaven awaits with unspeakable longing the pleasant hour when it shall carry you.”

O wonderful sweetness of Divine Goodness, which exalts those who humble themselves!

7. When this humble virgin once requested another pious soul to pray to God for her, it happened that God said to that soul: “The faults that one sees in this my chosen one should more rightly be called a growth and advantage for her soul; for the fullness of graces which I constantly work within her could, due to human frailty, hardly remain protected from the wind of vain-glory if her virtues were not hidden from her own eyes beneath such faults. For, just as a field yields a richer harvest the more it is fertilized with manure <note>original: "Mist" – dung or manure. A common medieval metaphor where the 'filth' of one's perceived sins or lowliness provides the nutrients for spiritual growth.</note>, so too does she bring Me more abundant fruit of thanks from the recognition of her own weakness...” Nevertheless...

9. From this freedom of heart it also followed that she wished to keep nothing for herself in external matters that she did not need, but would give it away immediately. 10. She loved nothing except for the sake of the Lord; and she was so accustomed to directing everything to God’s praise and honor that whenever she attended to her necessities—whether she slept, or ate, or otherwise gave her body some refreshment or rest—she rejoiced greatly in it, just as if she had done it for the Lord. For she saw God in herself, and herself in God; therefore she wished to serve and do good to Him in her, and to herself for His sake, so that she might fulfill His word: *What you have done for the least of my little ones, that you have done for Me.* <note>A reference to the Gospel of Matthew 25:40.</note> Nevertheless, this Saint rejoiced incomparably more when she had done something of the kind for her neighbor.

11. She took great care not to draw any person’s heart to herself, or to ingratiate herself into any friendship. Indeed, she detested all human friendship whose cause and foundation was not God, viewing it as a deadly poison. Therefore, she was so zealous for the love of God that she could not endure a single word that tasted of human or sensual love; and she preferred to lack everyone’s service and benefits rather than allow anyone’s heart to be occupied with any personal affection toward her.

For just as when a person thinks in their heart, "do this," the hands immediately move to carry it out because they agree with and obey the heart; and when they think, "look at this," the eyes, which are in harmony with them, immediately open: in this way, she is also incessantly with me, and performs at every hour what I desire. For I have chosen her for myself in a special way, and above others, to dwell within her; therefore her will, and thus also the work of her good will, clings to my heart just like my right hand, with which I work whatever I will. ... Therefore it happens that, following the strong impulse of my spirit, she is compelled to hasten at all times, so that when one thing is done, she is found ready to take up another according to my impulse. Her conscience, however, is entirely satisfied; nor is she anxious if she has missed something of her usual exercises <note>Spiritual exercises or scheduled prayers (the Divine Office) which were strictly timed in monastic life.</note> because of this: for even though such things seem to be omitted (and missed) in favor of obedience to my will, they are nonetheless recovered elsewhere with double benefit, where my will has been fulfilled through her.]

# Chapter Three.
## Of her Love and Union with God. Of her extraordinary communion with Him. And of her childlike confidence.

-> I. <-

<margin>(a) Deuteronomy 6:5; Mark 12:30.</margin>
<margin>(b) See similar examples in Genesis 18:17ff; Exodus 32:14; Numbers 14:20.</margin>
It once happened, when Gertrude was required to read aloud in the convent according to the rule, and these words occurred (a): *You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength*; that out of the deepest devotion, she repeated them once more. When another devout soul <note>Likely referring to her confidante Mechthild of Hackeborn, who often recorded Gertrude's visions.</note> heard this, she said to God: "O Lord, how greatly must You be loved by this soul, who teaches You with such a fervent heart!" To which the Lord, among other things, replied: "I have carried this woman from her childhood, and I have nurtured her in my embraces, and I have preserved her stainless until this hour, so that she has united herself with Me with a perfect will... The sweetness of my Divine Heart <note>Gertrude was one of the earliest visionaries to focus on the 'Sacred Heart' of Jesus as a source of divine love.</note> is so softened and melted by the fervent love of her heart that it does not cease to let fervent drops of love, with wonderful loveliness, trickle into her soul." And He added further: "I have such great pleasure in walking with this soul that often, when I am offended by other people, I sink into her for rest, and let her feel either some constriction of the heart or a burden of the body. Since she is then accustomed to take this upon herself with such great thanksgiving, and to bear it with such great humility and patience, and to offer it up to Me with such great devotion of union with my sufferings; I am then completely reconciled again, and for the sake of her love, she causes Me to frequently spare countless people" (b).

2. [At another time the Lord said:] "I am entirely her own: I have given Myself into her embraces as a prisoner with full affection. For the love of the Divinity has so inseparably united her with Me, as gold and silver are melted by fire into a single metal."

3. [It is remarkable what is testified here and there in her writings concerning the intimate communion of love of this holy soul with her heavenly Bridegroom. To cite but a little from a great deal,] it once happened that, weighing her own inconstancy, she turned to the Lord and said: "My Beloved, it is good for me that I cling to You alone." Then the Lord embraced her intimately and replied: "And to Me it is always delightful that I cling to you, my beloved." ### Sixth Part. The Life of Saint Gertrude. Chapter III.

4. When she heard from the Gospel that it was said to the Savior: *You have a demon* <note>original: "Du hast den Teufel"; a reference to John 10:20 or 8:48, where critics of Jesus accuse Him of being possessed.</note>; it was as if she could not bear such words. Therefore, she said to her Beloved: "Greetings to You, life-giving gemstone of Divine Nobility! Greetings to You, unfading flower of human dignity, dearest Jesus, You my highest and only salvation!" To which her most gracious Lover, affectionately caressing her, gave as an answer: I, your Creator, your Redeemer, and your Lover—I have, by forsaking all my bliss, acquired you for Myself through the agonies of death.

5. Once the Savior said to her: What do you command, commanding Lady Queen? <note>This title reflects the "Mystic Marriage" tradition, where the visionary soul is treated as a royal spouse of Christ.</note> She answered: "Lord, I desire with all my heart that Your most praiseworthy will, according to Your very best pleasure, be fulfilled in me." Then the Lord named to her specifically all those persons who had recommended themselves to her prayers that same day, and said: What do you ask for this one, and for that one, and for the others? She answered: "Lord, I desire to ask nothing else for them, except only that Your most pleasing will be accomplished in them all." Thereupon the Lord said again: What do you want then, that I should do for you? She gave as an answer: "I wish only, in place of all delights, that both in me and in every creature, Your most pleasing and most praiseworthy will be accomplished, and that, for the accomplishment of the same, every one of my limbs be found entirely ready to surrender itself to all suffering." Upon this the Lord spoke: Behold, now I will make it so that you appear as pleasing before my eyes as if you had never in the slightest transgressed my will.

6. Another time the Savior caressed her and said: Behold, here I am, what do you want to give me? She answered: "Be most welcome, my only salvation; my entire, yes, my only true good! Alas, dearest Lord, I, unworthy as I am, have prepared nothing that would be befitting of Your Divine Glory; but I offer to Your goodness my whole being, wishing and praying that You Yourself would prepare in me everything that Your Divine Friendliness might delight in to the highest degree." Upon this the Lord said: If you will grant Me this authority within you, then give me the key, so that I may take and place everything that pleases me in freedom. She asked: "Which is the key?" and received as an answer: Your own will.

She answered: "Alas, dear Lord, I have nothing that corresponds to Your dignity; I have only this will: that if I had everything that You have, I would renounce it all and give it all to You so generously that You could give it to whomever You wanted." # Chapter Three.
## On her love and union with God. On her extraordinary communion with Him. And on her childlike trust.

->I.<-

It happened once, when Gertrude had to read aloud in the convent as part of her duties, and these words occurred (a): *You shall love the Lord your God, with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength*; that she repeated these same words once more out of the most inward devotion. Now, when another devout soul <note>Likely a reference to one of Gertrude's sisters at the Helfta monastery, possibly Mechthild of Hackeborn.</note> heard this, she said to God: "O Lord, how greatly must You be loved by this soul, who teaches others to love You with such a burning heart!" To which the Lord replied, among other things: "This one I have carried from her childhood, and I have nurtured her in my embraces, and I have kept her undefiled until this hour, so that she has united herself with Me with a perfect will... The sweetness of my Divine Heart is so softened and melted by the burning love of her heart that it does not cease to let fervent drops of love trickle into her soul with wonderful loveliness." And He added further: "I have such great pleasure in walking with this soul that often, when I am offended by other people, I sink into her for rest, letting her feel either some constriction of the heart or an ailment of the body. Since she is then accustomed to taking this upon herself with such great thanksgiving, and to bearing it with such great humility and patience, and to offering it up to Me with such great devotion of union with my sufferings; thus I am completely satisfied again, and because of her love, I often spare countless people (b)."

2. [Another time the Lord said:] "I am entirely her own: I have given Myself into her embraces as a prisoner with complete affection. For the love of the Godhead has so inseparably united her with Me, as gold and silver are melted into a single metal through fire."

3. [It is remarkable what is testified here and there in her writings regarding the intimate communion of love <note>original: "vertraulichen Liebesgemeinschaft"</note> between this holy soul and her heavenly Bridegroom. To cite just a little from so much,] it happened once that she, considering her own instability, turned to the Lord and said: "My Beloved, it is good for me that I cling to You alone." Then the Lord embraced her inwardly and answered: "And to Me it is always lovely that I cling to you, my beloved." Soon after, she said: "I, a lowly child of man, greet You, dearest Lord." To which it was answered: "And I greet you in return, my beloved."

She asked: “**Lord**, how should I meet You, since You wish to come to me so very gently?” and received the answer: I demand nothing from you, except only that you come entirely empty, in order to receive.

8. Once, when she was enraptured and had become so <term>unfit for outward things</term> <note>original: "ungeschickt zum Aeussern." This refers to a state of deep ecstasy where the mystic is physically unable to perform daily tasks or focus on the material world.</note>, the Savior said: Leave your love with Me; let it take your place with Me; and you, take care to govern your body.

9. Another time He said: Give heed only to Me, and enjoy the sweetness of My grace.

10. Again, the Savior once said to her: Which of these two do you choose, O daughter: that I serve you, or that you serve Me? For she enjoyed **God** in two ways: one way was being so enraptured in **God** that she could tell very little of this enjoyment for the benefit of her neighbor; in the other way, however, she could apply this enjoyment to the benefit of others. Therefore the **Lord** asked her this. But she, because she sought only what was the **Lord’s**, chose the latter <note>Gertrude chooses the "active" fruit of contemplation—being able to help others—over the purely private joy of ecstasy.</note>.

11. Another time, when Gertrude heard that a certain person, for whose soul’s salvation she had applied a great deal of diligence and faithfulness, did not respond with the faithfulness they owed—indeed, even disdainfully twisted some of the kindness she had shown them—she took refuge in her distress with the **Lord**. He then spoke to her with kind comfort: Do not be distressed, dear daughter, for I have permitted this for your own good. For just as a mother who has a dearly beloved little son wants to have him with her at all times, but when he wants to run about to play with his companions, she places a mask <note>original: "Larve." A common theatrical or carnival mask used here as a metaphor for a frightening deterrent.</note> or something else frightening here and there, so that the little son becomes afraid of it and runs back into her lap: so too, because I wish to have you always near Me, I allow your friends to be contrary to you in some things; so that, when you find no complete faithfulness in any creature, you may run to Me all the more fervently.

12. ...is witnessed.] She had at all times such a secure trust in **God** that neither tribulations, nor harm, nor any obstacles—indeed, not even her own failings nor sins—could darken it. It caused her no distress when the **Lord** had withdrawn His <term>sensible grace</term> <note>original: "empfindliche Gnade." In mystical theology, this refers to the emotional or physical feeling of God's presence, as opposed to a "dry" faith where God's presence is believed but not felt.</note> from her; rather, to have it or not to have it was much the same to her. Only, in times of adversity, she sometimes became even stronger in hope, through which she knew for certain that both the adverse and the pleasant, the internal no less than the external, all things together, must work for her best. In adversity, she expected the Divine comfort all the more abundantly, through which she wished to allow herself to be prepared by the present tribulation.

14. [For she had been taught by the Lord Himself:] I would wish, He once said to her, that my chosen ones did not regard Me as so cruel; but rather that they believed, and esteemed it as something good—yes, for the very best—when they can do some service for Me at their own cost <gloss>that is, without comfort or spiritual taste</gloss>. And another time: I find more pleasure in you when you have longing with suffering, than when you have devotion with joy.

15. If she had stained herself anywhere with the spots of sin, she took her refuge at the feet of **Jesus**, so that she might be washed clean of all spots in His blood. But when she perceived that the influence of Divine grace met her in abundance, then she did not give herself over to any penitential exercises, but voluntarily surrendered herself to the Divine pleasure and His drawing, with which He anticipated her; and she conducted herself in such a way as a skillful instrument for every work of love which was to be accomplished in her and with her.

16. All the gifts that she had received from **God**, she attributed to trust alone; and she valued them all the more as gifts of grace because she had truly received this noble gift of trust from **God** out of grace and without any merit. Through this trust she was so strengthened that she often desired to die; yet, because she was always united with the Divine will, life and death were almost one and the same to her.

17. It happened once that she fell down a hill while walking. At this, she was rejoiced in spirit and said to the **Lord**: “Dearest **Jesus**, how well it would have gone for me if this fall had been a means for me to come to You so much more quickly!” When we then wondered at this speech and asked her whether she did not fear dying without having previously received the <term>sacraments</term> <note>In the Catholic tradition, dying without the Last Rites (Confession, Eucharist, and Anointing of the Sick) was a common source of anxiety, as these were seen as the essential final preparations for the soul.</note>, her answer was: “I do indeed desire from my heart to use the holy sacraments before my death; but I prefer the Providence and the will of the **Lord** my **God** to them with total confidence; for I do not doubt in the least that this is a healthy preparation for death. Therefore, I wish and long to come to Him, whether it happens through a sudden or a slow death, as it is pleasing to Him. For whether I depart from here through this or through another death, I hope that **God’s** mercy will not—”

18. [Because of this childlike trust of hers, it happened that our Gertrude, according to the Savior’s word, asked for whatever she wanted, and it was given to her. We may well confirm this here by citing a single miracle, which an eye- and ear-witness <note>This witness is likely one of the sisters of the Helfta monastery, possibly the primary author of Gertrude’s biography, the *Herald of Divine Love*.</note> recounts as follows:] It happened one evening, after supper had been held, as the sisters had gone into the courtyard to perform some task; and, while the sun was still shining, dark clouds hung in the air, threatening a heavy rain, that our Gertrude, from the depths of her heart, so that I heard it, said sighing to the **Lord**: “O **Lord God**, Creator of all things, I surely do not hope that You would be as if forced to obey my unworthy will: if Your bountiful goodness, contrary to what befits Your justice, is pleased to hold back this rain only for my sake; then I much rather desire that Your well-pleasing will be done, and the rain pour down.” She said this out of the surrender of her will to **God**. But see what happened? She had not yet finished her speech when it began to flash with great violence, to thunder, and to rain. But because she was very frightened out of compassion for the sisters, she said once more to the **Lord**: “Ah, most gracious **God**, if it pleases You, let Your goodness refrain yet a little while, only so long until we have performed the work laid upon us.” Upon which prayer the most kind **Lord**, so that He might show how He heard her in everything, held back the rain until the work was brought to an end. But no sooner had this occurred, and we had barely stepped inside the door of the monastery, than a violent tempest of rain, thunder, and lightning fell down. Thus, thus is the **Lord** (as it were) obedient to the prayers of His chosen ones, who for the sake of His love have denied all their desires!

3. We have often seen that, for this very reason, she neglected eating and sleeping so that she might serve souls—indeed, Christ Himself—by leading those souls back to Him. And she did all this with such alacrity of spirit that it seemed she felt no burden in it, but only pure joy. Indeed, when necessity required it, she sometimes even deprived herself of the sweetness of <term>contemplation</term> <note>Contemplation refers to the quiet, meditative prayer where a mystic feels the presence of God; Gertrude was known to sacrifice these private moments to help others.</note> so that she might either stand by tempted souls, comfort the faint-hearted, or otherwise kindle someone in the love of **God**.

4. Truly, at the time when this holy soul lived, no one was found from whom the streams of holy doctrine flowed more abundantly, more usefully, or more powerfully than from our Gertrude. For she had received from the **Lord** a wise tongue, which was pleasing to people and full of all comfort and power, so that it penetrated into the innermost parts of the heart; many who experienced this themselves have testified to it, asserting that the Holy Spirit dwelt and spoke within her. Some were healthfully converted from vanity through her; others she brought to the knowledge of **God** and of themselves; at times she comforted some, and at others she kindled those who already stood in the love of **God** even more fervently: for hardly anyone could speak with her (even if they were not at first well-prepared within) without having to confess that they had drawn great comfort from her words.

5. Yet one must not think that she had previously planned what she would say through human cleverness, or how she might persuade people through art or wit: such things were far from her. Rather, one must believe without doubt that everything she did or said for the comfort and salvation of mankind was given to her by the Holy Spirit, who works and speaks as He wills, according to the requirements of the time and the edification of souls.

6. Many have testified that they were often more moved and softened by a single one of her words than by a long speech from the most proven preachers; and

### Part Six. The Life

were forced to shed overflowing tears whenever she spoke. We have often seen hard and stubborn people come to her, who previously could be softened or brought to **humility** by no one; yet, when they had listened to her words for only a short while, they were so transformed that they immediately promised to believe her and be obedient in all things.

7. This grace, however, is not to be attributed to her words alone, but primarily to her powerful prayers. For many who were heavily burdened with severe temptations or other sufferings were so completely liberated as soon as they had commended themselves to her prayer, that they often sent word through friends to give thanks first to **God**, and then also to this, His chosen one, for their deliverance.

At another time, as she prayed for some who had commended themselves to her prayer, she received this answer from the **Lord**:

> Just as in former times under the Law, <note>The "Law" refers to the Old Testament period.</note> everyone who took hold of the horns of the altar <note>original: "Hörner des Altars"; a biblical reference to seeking sanctuary or making a solemn appeal for mercy (see Exodus 27:2 or 1 Kings 1:50).</note> rejoiced that he had obtained peace and freedom; so also now, because I have chosen out of grace to dwell in you, everyone who commends himself to your prayers with confidence shall be preserved through My grace.

It happened once, after she had prayed for someone and felt ashamed that the person had not possessed greater faith to obtain more than they had received, that the **Lord** said kindly to her:

> As much as anyone hopes to obtain through you, so much shall he without doubt receive from Me; and whatever else you promise someone in My name, that I will certainly give to him. For even if the one for whom you pray, hindered by human weakness, might not feel My working within himself: I will nevertheless, according to My promise, work in his soul that which serves for his advancement.

8. Another time, when Gertrude feared the **Lord** might accuse her of some presumption—that she had perhaps answered someone too readily regarding their doubts and had assumed too great an authority for herself—the **Lord** comforted her with these words:

> Fear no more from now on; be comforted, and strengthen yourself, and be secure. I, the **Lord**, your **God**, your Lover, have created you out of free grace. I have chosen you so that I might dwell in you through My grace and enjoy you for My delight: therefore, I also answer through you all those who ask Me through you humbly and devoutly.

After some days, as she meditated with wonder upon this Divine promise and simultaneously remembered her own lowliness, she asked the **Lord** how it was possible that He could deem her, such a completely unworthy person, worthy of this grace, and work such wondrous things in her? Then the **Lord** touched her tongue and spoke:

> Behold, I have put My words in your mouth; <note>A reference to the calling of the prophet Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:9).</note> and all that which you shall say to others from My impulse and in My name, that

# of Saint Gertrude. Chapter IV.

...I establish in truth. And whatever you promise to anyone on earth, for the sake of my goodness, I shall confirm and hold as powerful in heaven." She replied: "Lord, it would cause me grief if someone were to be damned because I, speaking by the prompting of the Spirit, said something like: 'no fault shall go unpunished,' or something of that nature." To which the Lord said: "When you speak such things out of zeal for justice, or for the salvation of souls, my goodness will go before the person to whom you have spoken, and warn them to perform **penance** <term>Penance: An act of devotion or repentance performed to express sorrow for sin and a commitment to spiritual improvement.</term> for their guilt, so that they do not bring judgment upon themselves by despising your words."

9. "But, my dear Lord," (she said,) "if it is as You Yourself admit, that Your goodness speaks through my mouth; why is it then that my words have so little effect in some, whom I would so gladly lead to Your praise and their own salvation?" To which the Lord answered: "Do not be surprised that your words sometimes remain without fruit; for in former times, when I preached in my **humanity** <note>original: "Menschheit"; referring to the period of Christ's life on earth as a human being.</note> with divine zeal and power, my words did not produce the fruit of salvation in the hearts of all people. For through my Divine Providence, all things are ordered and accomplished at the right and appointed time."

10. Whenever Saint Gertrude was compelled by circumstance to reprove someone harshly, she overcame her natural bashfulness and set aside all human fear, doing so purely through trust in Him alone, with whose service she wished to fill the whole world. If she had to remind and convince someone, she knew how to bring forth her words with such great friendliness, wisdom, and modesty, that no one had a heart so hard—provided there was still a spark of the **fear of God** <term>Fear of God: In this historical and religious context, this refers to a profound sense of awe, respect, and accountability toward the Divine rather than simple terror.</term> in them—that they were not moved to improvement by her words.

If she noticed that someone was softened by her exhortation and awakened to penance, she turned to them with great love and compassion; then her heart was melted, and she gave herself over to comforting them as much as she could. Yet, she did not show this so much before people with many rambling words; instead, it happened mostly through the desires of her heart and diligent prayer to **God**.

However, if it happened that she could not bring her neighbor to improvement through her reminders, it weighed upon her heart so heavily that she would not allow herself to be comforted at all until she had brought it to the point where she sensed at least some improvement, either through persistent prayer for that person or through her and others' spiritual exhortations. If anyone tried to comfort her in such a case, saying she should not worry about one who did not wish to improve himself, and that she suffered no harm from it as he would have to bear his own damnation, it was like a sword through her soul; she said she would rather suffer death than allow herself to be comforted in such a way regarding someone's misfortune.

### Here begins the *Memorial* <note>original: "Memorial"; here referring to a spiritual memoir or record of divine favors.</note> of the Abundance of Divine Goodness, as it was so named by the Lord of Majesty.

1. May the abyss of uncreated wisdom call unto the abyss of wondrous omnipotence, to the praise and exaltation of the astonishing favor which, through the abundance of Your infinite mercy, O all-sweetest God of my life, You only Beloved of my soul, has flowed down into the valley of my misery through desert, pathless, and dry places—that is, through the manifold hindrances I placed against Your grace. For in the twenty-sixth year of my age, on that day so blessed for me, namely the 24th of February <note>original: "Februarii"</note>, in a truly desired hour as the dawn began, You, O Truth, O God, who are brighter than all light but also more secret than all hidden things, You who had resolved to drive away my thick darkness, began my conversion lovingly and gently. You began by stilling a restlessness which You had stirred in my heart a month prior; through which restlessness, as I believe, You wished to tear down the tower of my vanity and curiosity which my pride had built up within me. Although I had hitherto, in name and dress, vainly professed the **religious state** <term>Religious state: Life lived under monastic vows, such as those of a nun.</term>, You did this so that You might find a way to show me Your salvation.

2. When You had said this, although I knew that I was physically in the place I just mentioned, it nevertheless seemed to me that I was in our **choir** <term>Choir: The part of the church where the nuns gathered to sing the Divine Office.</term>, specifically in the corner where I was accustomed to offer my lukewarm prayers; and there I heard these words: "You have licked the earth with my enemies, and sucked honey from among the thorns; return at last to Me, and I will receive you, and make you drunk with the stream of my **Divine Delight** <note>original: "Göttlichen Wollust"; in this mystical context, it refers to spiritual ecstasy or the "torrent of pleasure" mentioned in Psalm 36.</note>." ## of Saint Gertrude. Chapter VII.

I thought: if only a skillful, trusted friend were present to keep me company and cheer me in my solitude, or to make it fruitful for others. Then You, Lord my God, the source of inestimable delight <note>original: "Wollust"; in this historical context, the term refers to spiritual ecstasy or intense divine joy rather than carnal desire.</note>, put a thought into my mind. 2. Although, if I am to confess the truth, the most diligent improvement I could have achieved for even a moment—even if it had lasted my whole life—would in no way have been worthy to earn a single instance of Your grace, even the strictest one, which I have ever received after so many vices and, alas, such heavy sins.

And so that You may be pleased to preserve this excellent gift of Your soul-saving presence within me, I offer You that excellent prayer of Yours, which You, with the shedding of Your bloody sweat, poured out devoutly in Your agony of death <note>A reference to Christ's prayer in the Garden of Gethsemane.</note>; praying that, through the power of such a most perfect prayer, You might complete me entirely in Your union, and draw me intimately to Yourself. Thus, as often as I must be of service in external affairs for the salvation of my neighbor, I may remain undivided and unchanged among them, and, after I have fulfilled the same in the most perfect way to Your praise, I may immediately return entirely to You in my innermost being—just like water moved by a storm wind, which, when the wind subsides, immediately returns to its stillness. May You find me at all times as devoutly turned toward You as You show Yourself present to me, and thereby bring me to such perfection as Your justice has ever allowed Your mercy to bring such a soul, who is burdened by the weight of the flesh and who so greatly resists You. Likewise, may You receive my last breath with Your most intimate embraces and most powerful kiss, in such a way that my soul may find itself without delay where You, **GOD**, beyond place and undivided, in blooming eternity, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, live and reign for all eternity. # The Eighth Chapter.

## The wounding of her heart through love. The gift of the Child Jesus; and the most intimate union with Him.

->I.<-

After this, in the seventh year, it happened before Advent that, through Your prompting, I asked a certain person to include the following words for me daily in her prayer: “For the sake of Your wounded heart, most beloved Lord, pierce her heart with the arrows of Your love; in such a way that she may no longer retain anything earthly, but that she alone be held by the power of Your Divinity.” Through the prayers of this person, You were moved, as I trust, on the Sunday before Christmas—when Your mercy, from the rich abundance of Your kindness, permitted me to go to Communion <note>The reception of the Eucharist; in the 13th century, frequent communion was less common, making this a significant spiritual event.</note>—to put a longing into my soul. By this I was compelled to break out into the following words: “Lord, I confess that according to my merits I am not worthy to receive the smallest crumb of Your gifts; but I unite myself with the desire of all who stand present here, and implore Your goodness that You pierce my heart with the arrow of Your love.” and immediately I felt, both through an inward pouring of Your grace and through yet another manifest sign, that the power of this word had approached Your Divine Heart.

2. However, my desire was not yet fully stilled by this, until Wednesday, when You were there as if suddenly, and wounded my heart, while adding these words: “Here must come together the entire company of all your affections <term>Gemüthsneigungen: refers to the various inclinations, feelings, or dispositions of the soul</term>; namely, the whole sum of your pleasure, your hope, your joy, your sorrow, your fear, and all your other emotions <term>Gemüthsbewegungen: literally "movements of the soul," or passions</term>, must be made firm in My love.”

3. Whatever I might have spoiled in this through my own malice, let that be replaced by the power of love, whose fullness dwells in Him who sits at Your right hand, and who has become bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh. <note>original: "Bein von meinen Gebeinen, und Fleisch von meinem Fleisch"; a reference to Genesis 2:23, used here to describe Christ's shared humanity with Gertrude.</note> Through Him, I offer to You, in the power of the Holy Spirit, the complaints over my far too many misfortunes by which I am oppressed; especially in that I have dealt so unfaithfully, so negligently, and so irreverently with Your aforementioned gifts. Truly, if You had reached out even a simple piece of thread to me, unworthy as I am, as a remembrance of You, I should rightly have held it in higher honor than I have regarded Your gifts.

4. You know it, O my God, You searcher of my secrets, that this very thing is the cause which forces me—even against my will—to put these things into writ- <note>This word is interrupted by the page break; "schrift-" is a catchword for the following page, likely intended to be "schriftlich," meaning "in writing."</note>

O truly invincible power of the Right Hand of the Most High, that such an earthly vessel, cast down to dishonor through its own fault, has contained within itself this so precious juice! O indeed a most clear testimony to the superabundance of Divine Goodness, that it has not withdrawn from me—who strayed so far in the wrong paths of vice—but, according to the measure of my capacity, has impressed upon me this sweet, blessed union!

# Chapter Nine.

## She is pressed upon the Lord's breast as a seal, and most inwardly united with Him.

### I.

On the day of the Purification of Mary <note>Also known as Candlemas (February 2nd), celebrating the presentation of the infant Jesus in the Temple.</note>, as I was keeping watch over God and over myself; I saw my soul in the form of wax well-melted by the fire, how it was to be pressed upon the Lord's breast as a seal; and suddenly it seemed as if it were placed upon the same, even in part drawn into the treasury itself, [into the Heart of Jesus,] in which dwells the fullness of the Godhead bodily. Colossians 2:9.

2. O consuming coal, my God, You who have within Yourself, bring forth, and impress a living ardor, in that You have so unquenchably taken the upper hand in the moist [soil] of my slippery soul, since You first dried up in her the stream of worldly pleasure, and thereafter also softened her from the hardness of self-will, in which she was for some time so very much hardened! O You truly consuming fire, who exercise Your power against vice in such a way that You simultaneously cause a lovely ointment in the soul! In You, and in no way in another, do we receive the power that we may be transformed again into Your image and likeness of our origin. O powerfully burning furnace, in the lovely vision of true peace, through whose effect the dross is changed into tested and choice gold! namely, when the soul, weary from many kinds of deceit, finally desires with the whole longing of the mind to seek the Highest Good, which is in her, and which You Yourself are, in the truth of Your eternity.

<margin>(a) Genesis 13:15.</margin>
3. Thereafter, on the Sunday before Lent <note>Quinquagesima Sunday, the final Sunday before the start of the Lenten fast.</note>, You showed me what kind of land it is that Your ever-welling mildness promises, when it is said: (a) *To you and to your seed I will give this land;* as You touched Your most blessed breast with Your venerable hand. O blessed land, making one blessed through the inflows of beatitudes! Field of delights, whose smallest grain can superabundantly satisfy the desire of all the chosen—whatever else can ever be imagined by the human heart as desirable, lovely, delightful, beautiful, and sweet!

4. As I now gave heed to that which I must give heed, if not as I should, yet as I could; behold, there appeared the kindness and love <note>The German *Leutseligkeit* here translates the Greek *philanthropia* used in Titus 3:4.</note> of God our Savior, not because of the works of righteousness by which I, unworthy as I am, would have deserved such, but according to His unspeakable mercy, and made me—unworthy because of my extreme lowliness, indeed justly deserving of a curse—

<summary>Saint Gertrude describes a mystical vision where her soul, softened like wax, is sealed onto the Heart of Jesus, symbolizing a transformative union with the Divine. She reflects on God as a purifying fire that turns the soul's "dross" into gold and envisions His breast as the promised land of spiritual delight.</summary>

Abominable as I am, yet through rebirth into adopted childship, I am made strong and capable of receiving within me the adorable, super-heavenly, beyond-invaluable, most inward
->**Union with You.**<-
But how, my God, could such a thing be consistent with my merits and Your judgment, that You could accomplish this gift within me? Truly, love—which looks upon no worthiness but is rich in grace, that [as it were] unreflective and headlong love, I say, which waits for no judgment nor is grasped by reason—has brought You, my sweetest God (if I may say it reverently), like a drunkard to the point of folly <note>The "folly" or "intoxication" of God is a common theme in mystical theology (the *ebrietas spiritualis*), suggesting a love so vast it seems to defy human logic or justice.</note>, so that You have united such utterly unequal things. Or, to put it more becomingly: Your own natural, lovely kindness, inwardly moved by the sweetness of Your love (according to which You are not only loving, but are Love itself), has moved You to call the most distant child of man—who is in every way needy and contemptible in both life and morals—from the ends of the uttermost lowliness to join with Your Royal, indeed, Divine Dignity. You do this so that everyone may draw a great confidence toward You; just as I believe and wish for every Christian person, in the fear of my Lord, that in the corruption of God's gifts and in the offending of one’s neighbor, no one may be found who has done worse than I.

But because the invisible things of God can be somewhat prefigured to the dull understanding through that which is made; so the Lord appeared to me (as far as I can express an inexpressible thing), as if He were, at the side of His breast—where He had, as said above, received my soul like well-melted wax—as if He were wet with frequently breaking drops of sweat, just as if the wax had been melted by the greatness of the heat hidden within. These appearing drops nevertheless drew this divine treasury into itself with such wonderful, but also unspeakable, indeed, unthinkable power, that it was clearly to be seen what an overmastering power love (which cannot contain itself) achieves there, where Your so great and so unfathomable, most inward mystery, [the treasury of Your heart,] is unlocked.

5. O eternal summer, secure dwelling, place that holds within itself everything that can delight, paradise of perpetual enjoyments, overflowing stream of inestimable pleasures <note>original: "Wollüste." In this context, it refers to spiritual bliss or "delights," rather than carnal lust.</note>; You who entice through a blooming spring of all kinds of loveliness; who coax with a pleasant sound, indeed, the lovely, charming melody of an intelligible *music*; who refresh through a glorious-smelling breeze of heart-strengthening *spices*; who intoxicate through a joy-making sweetness of manifold inward taste; and who ravish through a wonderful caress of secret embraces! O blessed and again blessed, and so to speak, hundredfold holy is he who, moved by the guidance of grace, is deemed worthy to approach with innocent hands, pure heart and lips, to where he can be most inwardly united and incorporated with his beloved God! Oh, what does that person see, what do they hear, what do they smell, what do they taste, what do they feel! Yet why does my unskilled tongue try to stammer about it? Which (although I am admitted there by Divine favor), nevertheless [as it were] with a callus of my own infirmities or negligence...

# The Tenth Chapter.

## The High Dignity of a Soul Raised to Union with God. How Gertrude was compelled and brought by God to write.

-> 1. <-

<margin>(a) Psalm 91:15</margin>
Not long after that time, when I was once again forced to keep to my bed by a severe illness, and the other sisters had other tasks to attend to so that I lay alone one morning, the Lord—who cannot abandon those who are forsaken by human comfort—came to me, according to the word of the Prophet: (a) *I am with him in trouble.* For He showed me how from His left side, and as if from the innermost part of His blessed heart, a certain stream of crystalline purity and solidity issued forth. Flowing over His venerable breast, it covered it like a precious necklace; it was transparent with the colors of gold and rose, arranged in alternating patterns. Whereupon the Lord said: "The illness from which you lie prostrate sanctifies your soul in such a way that, if for my sake you should stoop to other thoughts, words, or actions—just as if you were going far out from me, as is shown to you in that same stream—then, just as the golden and rose colors shine through the crystalline purity, so also the cooperation of my golden Divinity and the perfection of the rose-colored <note>In medieval mysticism, rose often symbolizes the Passion and the humanity of Christ, while gold signifies His divine nature.</note> patience of my Humanity will cause all your works to please me through the purity of your intention."

2. O high dignity of the tiniest speck of dust, which the most high and heavenly noble Gem takes up from the filth of the streets to set upon His head! O excellence of this humble little flower, which the sun’s ray itself draws up from swampy places, as if it should shine together with the sun! O bliss of the blessed and holy soul, which the Majestic Lord esteems so highly that, although He Himself is almighty and able to create all things, He nevertheless draws her so sweetly and unites her with Himself for her salvation with Him; of the soul, I say, which, although adorned with His image and likeness, is yet as far removed from Him as a creature is from the Creator! And for this reason, a thousand times blessed is that soul to whom it is given to remain in such a state—to which I, alas, as I fear, have never yet attained for even a single moment!

# Part Six. The Life

3. O gift, which is above all gifts: namely, to be so abundantly satisfied in this apothecary <note>The "apothecary" or storehouse of spices was a common medieval metaphor for the healing and aromatic properties of the divine nature.</note> by the spices of the Godhead, and to be made so abundantly drunk—yea, filled—in this joyful wine cellar <note>A reference to the "Cellar of Wine" in the Song of Solomon 2:4, a central image in medieval bridal mysticism representing the soul's intoxication with divine love.</note> full of Divine Love, that one cannot move a foot in the slightest [elsewhere or] toward any place where one suspects the power of such a strong scent might vanish. Moreover, wherever one is required to go by the guidance of love, one carries the surges of such an abundance around, so that one can share the wealth of the Divine overflow and the sweetness of the scent with others! That You can give this gift, Lord, my God, according to Your great omnipotence, to Your chosen ones—this I fully trust You to do. Indeed, that You would also wish to give the same to me, according to Your loving kindness, I do not doubt in the least. But how You are able to give me such a thing, given my unworthiness, in that I cannot fathom Your inscrutable wisdom at all. But now I bless and give thanks to Your almighty and wise goodness, my God; for everything of Your mildness that could ever be applied to me, I have always received inexpressibly far beyond my merit.

4. However, as I judged it so entirely absurd to publish this writing, and for that reason had stopped writing and decided to apply myself to other exercises, I heard these words from the Lord: "Know for truth, that you shall not depart from the prison of the flesh <note>A common philosophical and theological term for the mortal body.</note> until you have paid even the last farthing <term>Heller: a small copper coin of very little value, here referencing Matthew 5:26</term> that you are holding back." But as I thought to myself that I had applied the aforementioned gifts of God for the benefit of my neighbor through speech, even if not in writing, the Lord replied with this word: "If the Lord had only spoken His teaching to those present, it would have been spoken and not written. But now it is written for the salvation of many." And the Lord added: "I wish to have, without any contradiction, a certain testimony of my Divine goodness in your writings for these last times, in which I am minded to do good to many."

5. Therefore I was burdened within myself, and I considered how difficult, or even impossible, it would be for me to find such sense or words by which I might present these things to human understanding without causing offense. This downpour poured over my soul, and under its impetuous falling-down I, a poor little human, a young and delicate plant, had to succumb and lie suppressed; I could drink in nothing of it for my advancement, except for a few very important words which I could by no means reach through my sensory understanding.

6. For which reason, even more burdened, I asked what use this could possibly be? But Your friendly goodness, my God, according to Your usual favor, lightened this burden and refreshed my soul with these words: "Since the overflowing of these water-waves seems useless to you, see, I lay you against my Divine Heart, so that I may infuse these words into you gently and lovely, from time to time, according to the measure of your capacity." Lord God, I confess

## The Eleventh Chapter.

->How kindly God endures our weaknesses. How useful tribulation is; and how eager service is so pleasing to God. How the Christ Child Jesus was given to Gertrude.<-

->I.<-

When I allowed myself to be moved to anger on a certain evening, and there was a convenient opportunity for prayer <note>original: "Bäten," an archaic spelling of "Beten" (to pray). Gertrude often reflects on how her human temper conflicts with her spiritual aspirations.</note> before dawn the next morning, You presented Yourself to me in such a strange form that I judged from Your appearance that You must be quite destitute and weak. Then my conscience punished me because of the preceding incident, and I began to consider with lamentation how unseemly it was to disturb the Author of the highest purity and stillness within myself through the thorns of evil confusion; and I deemed it more fitting—indeed, I resolved—that I would rather wish You to be absent than present, namely, only at that hour in which I was negligent in resisting the enemy when he incited me to such things that are so contrary to You.

Whereupon I received Your answer in the following manner: "Just as a sick person, who has barely reached the point where he could let himself be led by others into the pleasant sunshine, if a sudden thunderstorm should occur, can be comforted by nothing except the hope that the previous brightness and serenity will return; so it is also with Me, who have come to love you and have chosen to dwell with you, amidst all the storm-winds of overflowing weaknesses <term>Gebrechen: refers to human moral and physical frailties</term>, that I wait for the serenity of your improvement and humility." Since You have shown me this even more abundantly in this manifestation, these three days in succession, because the tongue is too weak to explain such things, let it, I pray You, be carried out through love.

2. Often You have revealed to me, through Your gracious enlightenment, how the soul, as long as it dwells in the frail human body, becomes darkened, like one who, standing in the middle of a narrow chamber, from all sides, around...

...around him, from above and below, as if he were inhaling a thick fog which this chamber <note>Gertrude often uses the "chamber" or "cell" as a metaphor for the human heart or the physical body.</note> exhaled onto him, just as a boiling pot emits a steam from itself. If it then happens that the body encounters some suffering, the soul receives—through the suffering which a member of the body feels—an air mixed with sunlight, as it were, and is thereby transfigured in a wonderful manner. And the more general or heavy the suffering is, the purer the transfiguration it brings about for the soul: especially the tribulation of the heart, or practice in humility, patience, and the like, which make the soul so much brighter and purer the closer and harder they strike it.

3. At another time, when I was to go to the Lord’s Supper <note>The "Abendmahl" or Holy Communion.</note> and You had shared Yourself with me most abundantly, I reflected within myself what I might possibly be able to do whereby I might, in some small measure, return a minor service to You for such great grace. Then You, wise Teacher, presented to me that word of the Apostle: <note>original: "Ich habe gewünschet ein Fluch zu seyn für meine Brüder" — a translation of Romans 9:3.</note> *I have wished to be a curse for my brothers*; and You said therewith: "it is a great thing when a soul leaves the sweetness of internal enjoyment and, for Your sake, pays heed to the external senses to govern them and to use them in works of love for the salvation of the neighbor."

4. On the day of Your most holy Birth, I received You, You tender little Boy, wrapped in swaddling clothes from the manger and pressed to my heart; so that from all the bitterness of the necessities of Your childhood, I might bind together for myself a bundle of myrrh <note>A reference to Song of Solomon 1:13, a common medieval metaphor for the suffering of Christ held close to the believer's heart.</note> that would remain between my breasts, so that from the same, the grape of Your Divine sweetness might be offered closer to my inward being. As I then presumed that I would never be able to receive a greater gift than this was; You, who often grant an even more glorious gift to the one whom You have already favored, deigned to exchange the abundance of Your healing grace toward me in such a manner [with yet another].

5. Then, on the very same day of the following year, I received You in the form of a most tender Child from the lap of the Virginal Mother, whom I carried for a time against my breast. I confess, however, that I did not honor this gift, while I had it, with sufficient devotion. But whether this happened to me because of Your justice, or because of my own negligence, is unknown to me. Because I nevertheless hope on the one hand that Your justice, with the cooperation of Your mercy, ordained it so that my unworthiness would be known to me so much more clearly; and yet on the other hand fear it happened to me because of my negligence, namely that I did not turn myself earnestly enough away from useless thoughts: so You answer for me, **Lord, my God**, which of the two was the cause. But as I wished to do my best to collect myself somewhat and to embrace You with loving caresses, I perceived that I gained little [thereby], until I began to pray for sinners and other suffering souls; then I immediately felt the fruit of such prayer, and it seemed that You delighted Yourself therein.

# Chapter Twelve.

## God’s Wisdom in Leading His Own. The Benefit of Humility. God’s Condescension toward His Creatures.

->I.<-

One day, as I was about to go to the table and beheld the brilliance of the sun in its full power, I said in my mind: "If the Lord, who created this sun—and whose beauty, as it is said, even the sun and moon admire, and who is also a consuming fire <note>A reference to Hebrews 12:29: "For our God is a consuming fire."</note>—if He, [I say,] were as truly present with me as He has often presented Himself to me, how would it be possible that I could live among men with such a cold heart and so wickedly?" And behold, suddenly You brought this to my mind and spoke: "In what should my omnipotence be exalted, if it were not in this: that I, wherever I may be, can so hold myself within myself that I am neither perceived nor appear, except only insofar as it is useful, according to the requirements of the place, the time, and the person? For from the beginning of creation until now, in the entire work of redemption, I have made more use of my kind wisdom than of my majestic power. And the kindness of this wisdom shines forth most in this: that I bear with the imperfect until such a time as I lead them through their free will to the way of perfection."

2. On a certain feast day, as I saw that many who had recommended themselves to my prayers went to the Lord’s Supper <note>The "Abendmahl," referring to the Sacrament of Holy Communion.</note>; but I was prevented by bodily weakness or—as I fear—turned away by God because of my unworthiness; and as I remembered various benefits shown to me by God: then I began to fear the wind of vain glory <note>A translation of *eiteln Ehre*, referring to the spiritual pride of taking personal credit for divine graces.</note>, which might perhaps dry up the streams of Divine grace, wishing that such a mind might be given to me through which I might remain shielded in the future. Thereupon, I was instructed by Your fatherly friendliness in the following manner:

> ,,that I should indeed look upon Your love for me
,,like the love of a father of a household, who rejoiced because of the pleasing beauty of his many
,,children, who were also praised as blessed by the great multitude of the household and the
,,neighbors; but among them he had a small little son,
,,who was not yet equal in beauty to the others, over whom
,,he nevertheless had compassion with fatherly love, took him often upon his lap,
,,and with both words and through small gifts, caressed him more sweetly than the others.,,

And You added this as well: ,,that, if I thus esteemed myself more imperfect than others with inward ,,conviction, then ,,the stream of Your honey-sweet Godhead would never cease ,,to flow down into my soul.,,

### Part Six. The Life of Saint Gertrude. Chapter XII.

3. I bring You praise and thanks, my dearest God, You lover of humanity, for these and many other healing lessons through which You, most beloved Teacher, have often instructed my ignorance. In the fellowship of the bitter passion of **Jesus Christ**, Your Son, I bring You my lamentations and offer up to You all His pains and tears for all my negligences, by which I have extinguished Your sweet-flowing Spirit within me. I pray, in union with the most powerful prayer of this Your beloved Son, and in the power of the Holy Spirit, for the correction of all my sins and for the restoration of all my failings.

4. I give thanks to Your kind mercy and Your merciful kindness, dearest God, for the revealed testimony of Your most worthy goodness, through which You have strengthened my wavering mind. This happened as I once, according to my custom, prayed with impetuous desire that I might be delivered from the prison of this miserable flesh; not so that I might no longer feel its manifold misery, but rather so that Your goodness might be relieved of the debt of grace <note>original: "Gnadenschuld." A theological term suggesting that God, out of His infinite love, has "obligated" Himself to provide the grace necessary for a soul's salvation.</note> which You had committed Yourself to pay for the salvation of my soul—a commitment to which the most ardent love of Your own Divinity compelled You.

As I was thus desiring to be delivered, it seemed to me as if You, who are the ornament and crown of heavenly glory, lowered Yourself from the throne of Your majesty with a lovely and gentle inclination, and leaned toward sinners. From this condescension, certain outpourings of an exceedingly sweet essence <note>original: "süßen Saftes" (sweet juice/nectar). In mystical literature, this often refers to the "liquefaction" of divine grace or the sweetness of the Holy Spirit.</note> were poured out through the entire expanse of heaven. All the saints bowed down to these with joy, and after they had been quenched from this stream with sweet delight, as it were, they broke out into lovely-sounding songs of praise to God, because He holds sinners in such high esteem. As this happened, I heard these words at the same time:

> Consider how lovely this praise penetrates the ears of My majesty and reaches the melted depths of My loving heart; and guard yourself that you no longer desire so impetuously to be dissolved <note>A reference to the Pauline expression in Philippians 1:23: "I desire to depart (be dissolved) and be with Christ."</note> for the purpose of no longer being such a one in the flesh to whom I, as to such a one [still living in the flesh], grant the gift of My gracious goodness. For the more unworthy the person is to whom I graciously lean down, with all the greater reverence shall I be justly exalted by all creatures.
