# The Thirteenth Chapter.

## A Grateful Account of Various Special Graces which God Bestowed upon Gertrude; and the Confirmation of the Same.

->1.<-

My heart and my soul, and the whole essence of my flesh, together with all the senses and powers of my body and my spirit—indeed, all creatures together—must give You praise and thanks, sweetest God, most faithful lover of human salvation, for Your most precious mercy, because You have deigned to clothe me, Your least and most useless instrument, with Your gift.

Firstly, that You have assured me through Your grace, “that anyone who desired to go to the Lord’s Supper <term>Lord's Supper: refers to the Eucharist or Holy Communion</term>, but was held back by the fear of a wavering conscience, should they, driven by humility, request to be strengthened by me, Your least handmaid, then Your ever-flowing goodness would deem them worthy because of this humility, so that they would receive this Sacrament with benefit for their eternal salvation.” To this You then added, “that if Justice should perhaps not wish for someone to be judged worthy by me, You would never allow such a person to see fit to ask me for counsel.” O You most exalted Sovereign, You who dwell on high and look upon the lowly, what did Your Divine mercy say when You saw that I so often approached unworthily, and therefore deserved judgment according to Your Justice? And since You wish to make others worthy through the virtue of humility—even though You could certainly do this better without me—You have nevertheless, in Your goodness, looked upon me in my misery and wished to perform this through me, so that I might at least in such a way share in the blessing of those who received the fruit of salvation through my exhortations.

2. Secondly, since my misery requires not only this (but even more), Your mercy, O kind God, did not stop at this one remedy <note>original: "Arzneymittel." Gertrude frequently uses medical metaphors for spiritual healing.</note>. Therefore, You have also assured me, most unworthy as I am, “that whoever, with a contrite heart and a humbled spirit, should complain of and reveal any faults to me, You, most merciful God, would judge them more or less guilty according to whether they heard from me that the fault was great or small; and that they should, through Your grace, from that very hour always have such relief that they should never again be oppressed by that same fault as dangerously as before.” And in this, too, You have looked upon my wretched poverty: that since I have been so negligent all the days of my life that I—alas!—have probably never properly overcome even the smallest fault, I might at least share in the victory of others, in that You, my good God, deign to use me, Your very least instrument, so that through the words of my mouth You may communicate the grace of victory to others among Your friends who are better than I.

<summary>Gertrude describes two specific spiritual privileges granted to her: the authority to encourage the fearful to receive Communion and the power to provide relief to those confessing their faults to her.</summary>

### Part Six. The Life

<margin>(a) Mark 4:24.</margin>

3. Thirdly, the overflowing generosity of Your grace wished to enrich my deficiency with this assurance:
> “that namely, whomever I should promise any benefit, or the forgiveness of a crime, trusting in Your Divine goodness, Your kind love would hold to that promise as firmly according to my word as if You Yourself had sworn it with Your blessed mouth in truth, and it would certainly come to pass: for You added further that if this healing fruit should seem to be delayed longer than one wished, that person must only persistently remind You how I had promised them salvation in Your name.”

And in this very thing You provided for my salvation, according to the word in the Gospel <note>original: "Evangelio"</note> (a): *With the measure you use, it will be measured to you*; so that namely, since I—alas!—often commit great faults without ceasing, You might at least have the opportunity in this way to speak a more merciful judgment over my own debts.

4. Fourthly, so that You might do good to my poverty, You also added this and assured me,
> “that everyone who, with a humble and devout intention, would commend themselves to my prayer, should without any doubt obtain all the benefit through it that he could ever believe a human could receive through the prayer of another.”

And therein You also wished to come to the aid of my negligence, since I am so sluggish in offering my prayers for the Church, that You allowed me a share in the benefit of Your elect—who desire some blessings through me, unworthy as I am—to make up for my own deficiency.

5. Fifthly, You did not fail to increase my salvation in this as well, by granting me as a special grace,
> “that everyone who, with good will, upright intention, and humble trust, spoke with me regarding the progress of their soul, should never depart from me without spiritual comfort or edification;”

since You, as it were, foresaw that this very thing would be useful for my poverty; because I often—alas!—indulge in useless words and spill the gift of eloquence, which You have generously entrusted to me, an unworthy person, as if upon the ground, I might at least gather some fruit of spiritual benefit from the good that You would entrust to others.

6. [Thereafter Saint Gertrude recounts several more special benefits that God showed her, with a humble desire that others might give thanks to the Source of all good in her stead.]

> Firstly, (she says,) for the love with which Your free grace and goodness chose me from eternity; which is to be called the greatest gift of grace above all others: and since You well foresaw the entire course of my evil life, and Your gifts despite my perversity and ungratefulness—even so much that, if I lived among the heathens, You could have rightfully denied me the use of human reason—nonetheless Your goodness, which far exceeds all our evil, chose me for the monastic life <term>monastic life: living as a nun in a cloistered community, specifically the convent at Helfta</term> even before other Christians.

# Of Saint Gertrude. Chapter XIII.

7. Second, that You have drawn me to Yourself so healingly. And this very thing, I confess, is a work of Your gentleness and goodness, which is naturally Your own; for You have drawn my unruly heart—which rightly deserved iron chains—to Yourself with such lovely enticements; just as if You had found in me a gentle spirit like Your own, and as if it were delightful to You above all else to unite Yourself with me.

8. Third, that You have united me so intimately with Yourself. And I rightly attribute this to the overflowing abundance of Your generosity, which pours out beyond all measure; as if the multitude of the righteous were not enough to receive the abundance of Your goodness, and You therefore deigned to call me—who deserved it least of all—to come forward: not so that You might more easily justify one who was already fit for it, but so that in one who was least fit, the miracle of Your grace might shine forth all the more clearly.

9. Fourth, that You have deigned to dwell lovably in my soul and to take Your pleasure in me. And this I attribute (if I may speak thus) to Your enchanting love, according to which it pleased You to testify to this even with words, saying:
> "that it is Your delight that Your almighty wisdom, out of such 
> "wonderful grace, can unite itself with such a one who is 
> "entirely unlike You and quite ungrateful."

10. Fifth, that You deign to bring me to a blissful completion <note>This refers to a "happy death" or the final perfection of the soul in heaven.</note>. According to the faithful testimony of Your truth, I humbly and firmly hope to receive this benefit from the sweetest friendliness of Your most kind love, and I gratefully embrace it with a love free of worry, relying not at all on any of my own merits, but solely on the free grace and friendliness of Your soul, O You my highest, indeed, only true and eternal Good.

11. Beyond all this, the inestimable virtue of Your love, my God, has added this: that the aforementioned gifts have also been confirmed to me through the following covenant. For as I was once weighing these things, and by comparing my wickedness and Your goodness (which is infinitely abundant to my joy), I was brought to the presumption of objecting that You had not confirmed such gifts to me with a handshake <note>original: "Handschlag"; a traditional gesture used to seal a legal or formal agreement.</note>, as is otherwise done with promises. Then Your friendliness, which allows itself to be so easily dealt with, promised that it would graciously satisfy my objections, and said: "Do not object to such things; come here, and receive the confirmation of My covenant." And immediately my lowliness saw You, as if You were opening the treasure chest of Divine Faithfulness and unerring truth to me with both hands—namely, Your Divine Heart—commanding me, perverse as I am (who, like the Jews, demanded signs <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 1:22: "For Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom."</note>), that I should stretch out my right hand. Thereupon You drew back Your most holy Heart, which You had opened to me, after my hand was enclosed within it, and said: "See, I promise that I will preserve the gifts I have bestowed upon you undamaged for you..."

## Chapter Fourteen.

### The Lord shows her His face. She also partakes of His kiss and His embraces.

1. I also considered it quite unseemly that I, as an ungrateful person, should pass over the following benefit received from You in silence. It happened once on the second Sunday in Lent <note>Historically called *Reminiscere* Sunday from the first word of the Introit.</note>, that as these words were being sung: *I have seen the Lord face to face* <note>original: "Vidi Dominum facie ad faciem." This refers to the story of Jacob in Genesis 32:30.</note>, etc., my soul was illuminated by a wonderful and inestimable radiance with the light of Divine Revelation; and a certain Face appeared to me, which was turned toward mine, a Face which, as Bernard <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian monk and mystic whose writings on the "Face of God" and the Song of Songs were central to Gertrude's spirituality.</note> says, "is not formed <note>meaning: not created or shaped by another</note>, but forming <note>meaning: the active power that gives form to all life</note>; which does not blind the bodily eyes, but gladdens the face of the heart; pleasant, not because of color, but because of the gift of love." Now, since Your brightly shining eyes appeared placed directly opposite my eyes, You alone know how You, my loving Sweetness, then gladdened not only my soul but also my heart and all my powers through this honey-sweet vision. Grant me, therefore, that I may pay You a devout service throughout my whole life.

# The Fifteenth Chapter.

## A renewed confession of the singular graces and gifts of God, and of her own failings. The conclusion of this writing.

->1.<-

Let my soul praise You, Lord God, my Creator; let my soul praise You, and confess to You from the innermost depths of my heart Your mercies, with which Your ever-flowing goodness has so undeservedly preceded me. O my sweetest lover <note>original: "Liebhaber"; in the tradition of bridal mysticism, this refers to Christ as the Bridegroom of the soul</note>, I give thanks, as much as I ever can, to Your immeasurable mercy, alongside which I praise and glorify Your long-suffering patience, with which You have looked through Your fingers at me <note>an idiom meaning to "overlook" or "turn a blind eye" to faults</note> while I spent all the years of my childhood and youth—almost until the end of my twenty-fifth year—in such a blinded folly. During that time, in thought, word, and deed, without any gnawing of my conscience (as it now seems to me), I would have committed whatever came into my mind, wherever I was free to do so. This would have been the case had You not prevented it, either through a natural horror of evil and a desire for good—which is naturally my own—or through the external correction of my neighbor, or through other means, and had You not preserved me through Your free grace and mercy. I lived just as if I were a heathen among the heathens, and had never heard that You, my God, would either reward the good or punish the evil, even though You chose me from my childhood—namely, from the fifth year of my age—to dwell among Your devout friends in the monastery <note>Gertrude was offered to the monastery at Helfta as an oblate at age five</note>, and to be made ready for You. Now, although Your blessedness can neither increase nor decrease, since You have no need of our goods: nevertheless, my so sinful and negligent life has (if I may say so in some measure) served to diminish Your praise, whereas my whole being, along with all creatures, should rightly praise You incessantly at every moment. What my heart feels about this, or could feel, since it is moved even to its depths by Your most gracious condescension, You alone know.

->2.<-

Therefore, O dearest Father, I offer up to You in this movement of my heart, for the atonement of all my sins, all the suffering of Your most beloved Son, which He endured from the hour He cried while lying on the hay in the manger, and suffered thereafter through all ages <note>referring to the stages of Christ's life</note>, until He bowed His head on the beam of the Cross and gave up His spirit with a loud voice.

# Of Saint Gertrude. Chapter XV.

Furthermore, most beloved Father, to compensate for all my negligence, I offer up to You the entire and most holy life of Your Son, which was most perfect from the hour when Your Only-Begotten, sent down from the throne, entered into our world, until the moment He presented the glory of His victorious flesh <note>The "victorious flesh" refers to the resurrected and glorified body of Christ ascended into Heaven.</note> before Your fatherly countenance.

3. No less do I sink myself, in thanksgiving, into the deepest abyss of humility; I praise and adore Your most excellent mercy and sweetest kindness, through which You, Father of Mercies, held thoughts of peace and not of affliction toward me—who led such a corrupt life. Indeed, You chose to exalt me through the multitude and greatness of Your benefits, as if I had led an angelic life <note>original: "Englisches Leben"; in this context, "englisch" means "angelic" (from the Latin *angelicus*), referring to a life of pure devotion, rather than the English nationality.</note> on earth above all other children of men.

[4. Thereupon, this humble soul continues and recounts once again, with grateful confession, the multitude of graces shown to her by God; namely, her conversion, the unwavering presence of Christ within her, the imprinting of His wounds in her heart <note>This refers to the "stigmata" or the mystical experience of sharing in the wounds of Christ’s passion.</note>, that He gave her His heart and exchanged it with her own, that He so wisely uncovered her faults, granted such great promises and privileges, appointed the highest angels for her protection, and united Himself with her in such an inexpressible manner, etc. However, because these same graces are touched upon here and there above, we wish only to cite the register of her miseries and frailties, with which she gracefully concludes the chapter on her most excellent gifts of grace in the following words:]

5. Now, just as gold shines so much more golden when other distinct colors are placed beside it, and among all others the color black creates the greatest contrast because of its lack of resemblance to gold; so do I also add what is mine—namely, the blackness of my ungrateful life—against the divinely shining multitude of benefits shown to me. For just as You, according to Your innate royal, even Divine gentleness, could give no other gifts than those becoming of You; I, on the other hand, according to my innate coarseness and awkwardness, have received them no differently than is characteristic of the most contemptible of destroyers. And yet Your naturally inherent royal gentleness overlooked this very thing, so that You never seemed to do me any less good because of it.

6. When You then (You who have Your sweet rest in the super-celestial palace of fatherly goodness) chose to enter into my miserable dwelling as Your abode, I, a naughty and impolite hostess, took such poor care to attend to Your pleasure. Out of simple human decency, I surely would have attended with more diligent care to a leper who, driven by necessity, had come to stay with me after causing me much injustice and trouble.

7. Likewise, against this benefit which You, who clothe the stars, have shown me in the lovely and orderly arrangement of my interior, in the imprinting...

### Sixth Part. The Life

...touching of Your most holy wounds, and most friendly caresses (in which You allowed me to experience more delightful spiritual pleasures than I would have found in physical things even if I had traveled the whole world from sunrise to sunset), yet I, most ungrateful, have committed this shame against You and held this in low esteem; and, by seeking outward pleasures, I have all too irreverently preferred "onions and garlic" to Your heavenly manna <note>A biblical reference to Numbers 11:5-6, where the Israelites grew tired of God's miraculous manna and longed for the pungent foods of their former captivity in Egypt; here it represents choosing base, worldly desires over spiritual gifts.</note>, and have mistrusted Your most faithful promises, O You truthful **GOD**, and turned my hope away from them, just as if You were a lying man who had never kept His promise.

8. Likewise, against this grace—that You so kindly heard my unworthy prayers—I have, alas, often hardened my heart against Your will, even to the point (which I say with rightful tears) that I sometimes acted as if I had not understood Your will, so that I might not be compelled by my conscience to fulfill it.

9. Likewise, since it would be right that I should be so much more grateful because Your sweetness preserved Your gifts for me unharmed despite all my negligence, and that I should guard myself so much more against all negligence; I have, on the contrary, in a tyrannical, indeed, devilish way, repaid good with evil, by becoming only more emboldened to live without caution.

10. Above all this, my greatest guilt lies in the fact that, after such an incredible union with You—known to You alone <note>Gertrude is referring to the "Mystical Marriage" or "Unitive Way," a state of deep, direct spiritual intimacy with the Divine.</note>—I did not shy away from staining my soul again with those failings <term>Gebrechen: translated here as failings, it refers to the inherent moral or physical weaknesses of human nature</term> which, by Your permission, should only still cling to me so that I might fight and overcome them with Your help, and therefore possess a so much greater glory with You eternally in heaven.

11. And now, O You most kind Creator of my heart, because of these and other things which may come to my memory, let the sighing of my heart ascend to You, and accept these lamentations over my all-too-many unhappy behaviors toward Your so divinely noble goodness; which (lamentations) I offer up to You in the communion of that noble compassion and reverence which we, through Your gift, can offer to You through Your most beloved Son, in the Holy Spirit, on behalf of all those who are in heaven, on the earth, and under the earth.

12. Because I am then entirely unfit to bring forth any worthy fruits for improvement, I flee to Your goodness, You my sweetest lover, that You would inspire those whose hearts are bound to You with devout faithfulness to compensate with their prayers for my exceedingly great deficiency, which [prayers] serve only for Your due praise. For You know it best, You who look into my heart, that nothing else but pure love for Your praise compelled me to write these things, so that after my death many who read this may (so to speak) marvel at Your so kind grace—that Your love, for the sake of man's salvation, ever had to stoop so very low, and permit...

<meta>catchword: that</meta>

13. Behold, most beloved Lord, this is the talent <note>original: "Pfund" - referring to the biblical 'talent' or 'pound' from the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25), symbolizing the spiritual gifts Gertrude feels she must account for.</note> of your most precious intimacy, which You have entrusted to me, the most contemptible and unworthy creature, and which I recount, out of love for Your love and for the benefit and advantage of Your praise, both in what has preceded and in what follows. You are my witness that I most deeply desire that You be praised and thanked for the fact that Your so very profound goodness has not withdrawn itself from my unworthiness. I also desire that You may be praised through this: namely, that some who read these things may delight in the sweetness of Your goodness, and being drawn by it, may experience greater things than these in their inner being; and thus, through these representations painted as if before their eyes, they may be enticed to taste within themselves the hidden manna, which cannot be communicated through any pictorial representation of physical things, but for which only he who eats it hungers even more. With which You, O God, Almighty Giver of all gifts, wish to pasture us according to our need on the whole path of our pilgrimage <note>original: "Fremdlingschaft" - a common pietist term for earthly life, viewed as a temporary exile from the heavenly home.</note>, until we, beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled faces <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:18, describing the direct experience of God's presence.</note>, are transformed into that very same image, from one glory to another, as if by Your lovely Spirit. Amen.

# The Sixteenth Chapter.
## The Final Spiritual Disposition of St. Gertrude. Her Last
## Illness and Blessed Departure.

->I.<-

(To conclude this history, let us hear a little more about the final spiritual disposition of this soul, as much as has been reported to us, and how she finally died a blessed death.)

1. As St. Gertrude had not been visited by the Lord for a time—though without it being difficult for her to bear—it happened once, on a certain occasion, that she asked the Lord where this came from? Whereupon she was answered: "Too close a presence sometimes makes it so that good friends cannot fully look at one another. When, for example, someone embraces his friend who comes to him, he cannot, during this all-too-close connection [and embrace], delight in gazing upon his lovely countenance." From this she understood that the withdrawal of [perceptible] grace sometimes provides a person with manifold benefits and greatly increases their virtue; provided that they are not otherwise found negligent in the exercise of good and in self-denial, even if they perform everything with difficulty at that time.

2. Afterwards, as she once considered how it might be that she was now visited by the Lord in a different way than in previous years, it was

it was answered to her: In the earlier years, I gave you many kinds of answers and instructed you through them, so that you could make my pleasing will known to other people as well. But now, I let you feel and understand my inspiration <note>original: "Eingebung" — a term for internal divine prompting or revelation</note> only in your spirit, which I enlighten; this is something that one could only with great difficulty express with words. For I have chosen you for this, and I use you for this: that you should be, as it were, my treasury <note>original: "Schatzkammer"</note>, in which I deposit the riches of my graces. I take care that everyone finds what they seek in you, as in a bride who knows all the secrets of her bridegroom and who, because of her long dwelling with him, recognizes his pleasing will in everything. For she must reveal to others this will of the bridegroom, which she has recognized by virtue of her singular intimacy with him.

3. That this holy soul was afterwards enlightened in a singular way, as described, and how she experienced this within herself, she also made known to others. For even when she prayed fervently regarding a matter, she could by no means receive any answer from the Lord as she otherwise used to; but whenever she found grace to pray for someone, she knew it—both through experience and through Divine Inspiration—with total certainty that it should happen. This was just as clear as during the time when God gave her assurance of it through his spoken answer.

When anyone else sought counsel or comfort from her, she immediately felt that she was given what she should resolve or advise. She felt this with such great faith and certainty that she would have dared to suffer death for the truth of what was thus inspired in her—even though she previously knew nothing of such a matter or how she should answer it, and had been instructed in it neither by men nor through reading (books), indeed, without having thought about it in the slightest beforehand.

4. If it happened that she prayed for a matter and God revealed nothing certain to her therein, she comforted and rejoiced herself greatly that God's unsearchable wisdom remained hidden even from her. She was well aware that this same wisdom ruled over everyone without respect of persons, since Divine Wisdom is most closely bound with His love. Therefore, she believed it was safest—and advised others of the same—that one should simply leave everything to Divine Providence <note>original: "Göttliche Vorsehung"</note>. And she did this with more joy, and much more willingly, than if she had searched out all the hidden secrets of God.

5. [Only a few things can be touched upon regarding the passing of Gertrude; especially since the nature of her final illness left her unable to speak. The most prominent things left to us in writing are told as follows:]

This venerable woman Gertrude, beloved by God, administered the office of Abbess <note>The head of a community of nuns; Gertrude of Hackeborn (often confused in early texts with Gertrude the Great) led the convent at Helfta.</note> for 40 years and 11 days wisely, gently, and with wonderful modesty: in regard to God, with fervent love and devotion; in regard to her neighbor, with the greatest love and care; in regard to herself, with deep humility and much hardship. ### of St. Gertrude. Chapter XVI.

providing them with what was necessary, serving them with her own hands, both in what contributed to their refreshment and to their rest, and in everything else they needed; unless her subordinates <note>The sisters under her care as Abbess</note>, out of love for her, absolutely would not allow it. And not only in this, but also in other things—for example, sweeping the monastery, making the beds, carrying out the refuse <note>original: "Unflat" — filth or waste</note>, and putting back in its place whatever lay in disorder—in these things she was the first, and indeed, often occupied quite alone; whereby she then encouraged her subordinates to follow her, partly by her example and partly by kind words.

6. Now, as this soul, beloved and dear to both God and man, flourished like a rose in these and all other virtues, it finally happened that at the end of forty years and eleven days, alas! she was stricken by a stroke <note>original: "Schlag" — likely a paralytic stroke or apoplexy</note>, which pierced the hearts of her subordinates like an arrow, as all those know who have known this most noble soul. For we by no means believe that in the whole wide world a person could be found whom God has preceded with such gentle blessing as this soul. She received more than a hundred persons into the monastery and raised them with motherly care: of all this, and of her virtues, as well as what others outside the house thought of her—those who saw her and heard her wisdom-filled words—it would be too lengthy to tell. For this reason, we pour all of this back into the abyss of Divine Goodness with praise and thanksgiving.

7. For twenty-two weeks she was deprived of speech by this stroke <note>original: "Schlagfluß" — apoplexy or paralysis</note> until the end of her life; she could only speak these two words: "my spirit" <note>original: "mein Geist, [spiritus meus]"</note>. Because those who were around her did not know what she meant by them, it often happened that they did otherwise than she desired. When our blessed mother had repeated the words "my spirit" for a long time and achieved nothing by it, she finally remained silent, like a gentle little lamb, and looked on with a quiet nature at what was being done against her will. Indeed, she sometimes smiled quite amiably at it, without ever letting the slightest sign of impatience be perceived. And what was noted in her previous lifetime was also clearly seen in her during this illness: namely, that she was never so unwell that she did not immediately become lively again as soon as she heard a conversation or a word about God, just as if she had nothing to suffer.

8. She also showed in this illness that she was perfect in the love of Christ. If someone came to her, she welcomed them with her usual words, "my spirit"; she took them affectionately with her one hand, which she could barely move; she spoke to them through signs, as well as could be done, with such heartiness that being with her was not tedious to anyone, but more pleasant than if one had carried on an agreeable discourse with another. From those who left, she took her leave with those same words, "my spirit," and lifted her weak hand so gracefully to bless them that it was refreshing to behold.

# Preface.

-> Our salvation in the name of Jesus! <-

1. 
With the publication of this Second Volume of the *Biographies of Holy Souls* <note>original: "Lebensbeschreibungen Heiliger Seelen." This refers to the collection of spiritual biographies compiled by Gerhard Tersteegen, a famous 18th-century German pietist and hymn writer.</note>, I once more hand over this work to the Lord Jesus Christ, for His pleasure and honor, and to His community for their edification in true sanctification! He, the Prince of Salvation <term>Herzog der Seligkeit: A title for Christ used in the Luther Bible (Hebrews 2:10), implying a leader or captain who brings his followers to spiritual wholeness</term>, who has also led these children into glory, will surely know how to justify His ways—by which He brought them there and of which a small sketch is shared here—before all people. I only wish with all my heart that, since we now have so great a cloud of witnesses around us, the Lord would bless and strengthen their testimony in our hearts. May we be encouraged by this to lay aside every weight, and the sin which so easily ensnares us, and to run with patience the race <note>original: "Kampf" (struggle/fight). The author is paraphrasing the imagery of a race or athletic contest from the New Testament.</note> that is ordained for us—each according to his own kind, calling, and circumstances—looking away from ourselves and all creatures to Jesus, the Author and Finisher of faith! Hebrews 12:1–2.

2. Furthermore, I find nothing special to mention in this place. I do not wish to take up space answering all the objections and contradictions that have occurred, or might still occur, against this work and its subject matter. I will not rob myself or the dear reader of time and devotion; among the wise and godly such a defense would be superfluous, and among the unwise it would be in vain. The latter do not even look at what is answered to them; they are not concerned with being set at ease regarding their grievances and doubts. If they were, they could already find such answers in other widely available writings, as well as partly in the preface that was placed before the First Volume of these biographies. For my part, I am not so foolish as to want to force anything upon a single person. It is better to be useful than to please thousands.

<summary>In this preface, the author dedicates the second volume of his biographical collection to Jesus Christ and the spiritual growth of the Christian community. He frames the lives of the saints as a "cloud of witnesses" (referencing Hebrews 12) intended to inspire readers to pursue their own path of sanctification while dismissing potential critics of his work.</summary>
<keywords>Preface, Gerhard Tersteegen, Biographies of Holy Souls, Jesus Christ, sanctification, Hebrews 12, cloud of witnesses, spiritual race, religious edification</keywords>

<page-num>IV</page-num>
<header>IV. Preface.</header>

3. If one looks only at the foundation from which most, if not all, objections against such matters arise: it is either blind **sectarianism**. These are Catholics <note>original: "Papisten" (Papists). A common 18th-century Protestant term for Roman Catholics, used here to illustrate sectarian prejudice.</note>, and what good can come from *Nazareth*? <note>A reference to John 1:46: "Can anything good come out of Nazareth?"</note> etc. Such people will listen to no counter-arguments. One must have patience with them until they learn to understand, as *Peter* (a) did, that God is no respecter of persons. Or, there is a deception of the flesh hidden beneath it, through which one has a concealed dread of any presentation of the pure truth, and even more of any model of holiness; so that one might not be disturbed in one’s hypocrisy and laziness. Or, finally, atheistic reason lurks behind it, which has a secret aversion toward everything that radiates a singular mark of an Invisible, Present, Almighty, All-Wise, and All-Good Being. Where such a state exists in a person, no *disputing* helps; he always seeks something to criticize and has many plausible objections as to why he cannot approve or accept this or that; however, the ground from which such doubts and contradictions spring remains mostly hidden from himself and others. Even if his words are refuted by counter-arguments, one still reaches no end; that wicked ground is fertile enough to continually bring forth new contradictions.

4. Therefore, I will content myself with this one reminder: namely, that everyone, in judging even these holy matters, should recognize their own foundation and intention before GOD, so that they do not sin against God’s beloved ones, indeed against the Spirit of Glory, (b) which is God’s Spirit who rested upon them, just as they themselves now rest in the bosom of God’s infinite glory. Nevertheless, if some have their mockery regarding what is done or written by God’s saints, we should not be moved by it: What do worldly <note>original: "thierische Menschen" (animalistic men). In a biblical context, this refers to the "natural man" who lacks spiritual perception (1 Cor 2:14).</note> men know of how to judge spiritual and divine things? Only a little more patience! Soon we shall hear them speak in another tone when they—alas!—shall sigh out of anguish (c) of spirit and say: "This is he whom we once held in derision and as a proverb of reproach. We fools accounted his life as madness and his end to be without honor; how is he now numbered among the children of God, and his lot is among the saints!" *That day will come!* <note>original: "Illa Dies veniet!"</note>

5. Since it has also been suggested by good friends that these stories might be condensed somewhat more briefly: this could not yet happen because most of the biographies were already prepared before such a suggestion was heard. Not to mention that others—who do not have, or could not or would not read, the many books from which these matters were gathered—suggested the opposite, and preferred to have a brief but sufficient excerpt in one book. Moreover, those with experience know how, in order to give a proper concept of a history or an inner experience, one often cannot avoid including one or another circumstance that seems superfluous.

(b) 1 Peter 4:14. \
(c) Wisdom of Solomon 5:3.

He also explains that the length of the entries is necessary to properly convey the "inner experience" of the saints.</summary>

...lead. Meanwhile, the author was still minded to satisfy those readers as much as possible in a following third volume, and to keep the biographies about half as short, so that twelve of them could be included. However, because I have since encountered such circumstances that it seems uncertain whether I will have the remaining time, strength, and freedom for such laborious work: I will at least take this opportunity to provide a brief guide on how these matters should be continued, should someone else after me (in the event I cannot do it myself) wish to take this task upon themselves.

I wish, therefore, to briefly touch upon the persons and their histories, and at the same time name the necessary books (as far as they are known to me): in doing so, I will follow no other order than simply listing the persons as they occur to my thoughts and sight, one after another.

### 1. J. M. B. de la Mothe Guyon.
<note>Jeanne-Marie Bouvier de la Mothe-Guyon (1648–1717), a famous French mystic and leading figure of the Quietist movement.</note>

->Proverbs 31:26<-

> **She opens her mouth with wisdom, and on her tongue is**
> **the law of kindness.**

6. Just as this French lady was, in these our days, a refined vessel of the pure love of GOD, a mirror of bare faith, and a chosen instrument of the Holy Spirit, regardless of all the heavy persecutions and slanders she had to endure; so too has a great light and weight been given to the inward life through her writings. She was born on April 13, 1648, and died on June 9, 1717, at Blois. Her life—which she herself described in three parts—as well as the rest of her writings in their entirety, were published, as is well known, by Mr. *P. Poiret*. <note>Pierre Poiret (1646–1719) was a French mystic and philosopher who edited and promoted Guyon’s works.</note> Nearly all of these were printed before his death at Amsterdam from 1713 to 1722 (although "at Cologne" <note>original: "à Cologne"</note> is printed on the front) in 39 small volumes in octavo. <note>original: "Tomis in 8." Octavo refers to the size of the book, roughly 5 by 8 inches.</note> Both her life and her *Discourses*, letters, and other small works can now also be seen printed in the German language at Leipzig. After the works of *Madame Guyon* had all been printed in the French language, another 20 or 21 of her letters were found and added to the end of the fourth part of the works of *M. Bertot*, called *the Mystic Director*; <note>original: "le Directeur Mystique"</note> this fact does not seem to have been known to the German translator.

7. To publish a pithy extract of her life would, in my opinion, be all the less superfluous; for those who, in these days, bypass the practice of dying to self <note>term: "Absterbung" (mortification). The spiritual practice of denying one's ego and worldly desires to make room for God.</note> and the like, and imagine themselves into a premature and immoderate composure, <note>term: "Gelassenheit" (yieldedness or serenity). A central concept in German mysticism referring to the state of letting go of one's will to God.</note> could be convinced of their error through the guidance of this holy person. This is despite the fact that in her writings she uniquely promoted true passivity <note>original: "Passiveté." A state of soul where one is receptive to God's action rather than initiating one's own religious activity.</note> and yieldedness to God, and for that reason was also numbered among the *Quietists*. <note>Quietism was a 17th-century movement within the Catholic Church that emphasized internal stillness and passive contemplation, often criticized for supposedly neglecting outward religious duties.</note>

### VI. Preface.

8. Because so little news remains of the final years of Madame Guyon’s life, but I have the pleasure of being acquainted with friends who corresponded with her or even had personal contact with her: I will undoubtedly do the reader a favor by saying at least a word about how this holy soul lived and eventually died after her imprisonment, in which she was held for ten years.

Not long after Madame Guyon <note>Jeanne-Marie Bouvier de la Mothe-Guyon</note> was released from her heavy imprisonment, she received permission to retire from Paris to Blois; where she led a common and quiet life for many years in a row. Her household consisted of a chambermaid, two housemaids, and a manservant. She was visited there from time to time by the Bishop of Blois, as well as by her eldest son, who lived on an estate not far away; no less was she also visited by good friends, even from Germany and England. In her house she had a chapel, where divine service was performed daily; because she had to lie sick in bed most of the time and the chapel was next to her chamber, she often attended from her bed; she also usually received Holy Communion <term>Holy Communion (German: *H. Abendmahl*)</term> every other day.

9. Her quite impartial spirit <note>Tersteegen uses "impartial" to describe her ecumenical openness to those outside the Catholic Church.</note> is also sufficiently evident from the fact that at such a time she maintained a strong and close correspondence with various foreign friends from among the Protestants. Among such, the late Mr. Poiret <note>Pierre Poiret (1646–1719), a French mystic and philosopher who edited Guyon’s works.</note> was not the least, whom she always mentioned with high esteem and wrote to as a very (a) dear brother, and always testified that she stood in a special and intimate union of heart with him. It is deemed unnecessary to report more on this.

10. Regarding the illness and passing of Madame Guyon, I also wish to share the excerpt of a small letter written by a gentleman from Scotland who was an eyewitness to her death.

## 11. Margaretha von Beaune.

->Life of Margaret, Book X, Chapter 6. <note>original: "Vie de Margar. Liv. X. Cap. 6."</note><-

->Everything is sweet, wherever only the little JESUS is found.<-

11. Margaretha von Beaune, known as *of the Holy Sacrament* <note>Marguerite du Saint-Sacrement (1619–1648)</note>, was born in Beaune in Burgundy on February 7, 1619, and died in that same place as a Carmelite nun on May 26, 1648, in the 28th year of her age. Her biography was published in Paris in 1654 and dedicated to the Queen of France by Father Amelote <note>Denis Amelote, a prominent French Oratorian priest and theologian.</note>, although his name does not appear on the frontispiece; it is true that the author employs a bit too much rhetorical flourish, yet this is easily distinguished from the actual facts of the matter.

12. Margaretha was and remained a little child from her birth until her death; for this was her true state and most singular character: namely, the innocence, the purity, and the simplicity of a small child. She was as if submerged and transformed into the Infancy of JESUS, and into the unceasing devotion and veneration of this Divine Infancy, its qualities and mysteries; through this channel, infinitely many and wonderful graces were communicated to her for herself and for others. This soul revived the particular devotion to the Infancy of JESUS and gave many pious and holy souls cause to enter, as it were, into this "Order of the Companions of the Infancy of JESUS." Otherwise, through all kinds of heavy suffering and illness, Margaretha also bore on her body the marks <term>marks (*Mahlzeichen*): often used to refer to the stigmata or physical manifestations of Christ's suffering.</term> of the crucified JESUS until her death, no less than the state of His infancy in her inner being.

13. I cannot break away from this dear child without sharing some of her own words with the reader, so that they may have a small taste of them. First, I set down a few words that the Infant JESUS spoke to her; once He said: *In you I will make known the wonders of my childhood.* Another time: *I wash you with my blood, I wash you with purity.* Another time: *Just draw from my heart; nothing shall be refused you.* There follow some short sayings of her own:

> “Ah! that many hearts, ah, that many hearts would be subjected at the feet of the
> “Infant JESUS! All creatures must recognize His supremacy! All spirits must
> “become dependent on Him.
> “God and your soul, that is enough.
> “Peace with God, and not so much activity <note>Tersteegen uses "activity" (*Wirksamkeit*) here in the mystical sense, referring to the restless striving of the human will as opposed to quiet rest in God.</note>.

> “As soon as one begins to speak (of indifferent things), my brothers—the angels and the saints—cause me to glorify God with them, and nothing remains in my mind <note>original: "Gemüthe," referring to the inner soul or disposition</note> but these words: God alone is holy, and great, and worthy of adoration.

> “She could not hear the noise of the world at all, even when the cannons were fired in the city and all the bells rang; but instead, she heard a sound of God, as she called it, which always echoed around her: God is great, God is holy, God is just, God is love, God is life, God is light, God is worthy of adoration.

> “One must not think of the pains, but let the body be what it is: there are other things that are far more worthy of occupying us.

> “It is better that we think of God and His perfections than of ourselves, our infirmities, and our miseries.

> “We are useless servants <note>A reference to Luke 17:10</note>; all our deeds—if the holy Child Jesus does not elevate them with His gaze and set His seal upon them—are neither worthy before God nor deserving of any reward.

> “Purity consists in having nothing in the heart but the love of the little Jesus.

“During her final illness, she said among other things:

> “The pains I endure in my brain would be enough to rob me of my reason: but the holy Child Jesus holds me with His divine hand and gives me the grace that I do not think of it.

> “I have cause enough, on account of my great sins, to fear death; but I trust in the mercy of Christ.

> “I am in a perfect peace; I die quite content and in perfect joy. It seems to me the holy Child Jesus calls me, in His friendly way, that I should come to Him.”

### III. Mr. Pierre de Queriolet. <note>Historical records identify him as Pierre de Kériolet (1602–1660), a French penitent often called the "Bandit of Brittany."</note>

->**JESUS receives sinners!**<-

14. **Mr.** Queriolet was a French nobleman, born at Auray, in the province of Brittany, on July 14, 1602. Even in his childhood, he was devoted to all kinds of vanities, foolish antics, perversities, and an unrestrained life, which only increased with his years. While he was studying, he committed reckless escapades; he could be held back from his wicked conduct and criminal acts neither by the fear of God nor by the fear or shame of men. Upon leaving school, he took approximately 2,000 livres <note>A significant sum of French currency at the time.</note> in money from his father and fled France in his desperate state of mind. He intended to go to Turkey so that he might become a Turk <note>meaning a convert to Islam</note> and fight against the Christians. When his money was spent, he turned to the Evil Foe and also sought out sorcerers with all diligence, so that they might help him achieve his goal through dark arts and admit him into their society. His poisonous and cruel nature meant that he was always thirsty to quarrel, fight, and murder; he would intentionally walk through the narrowest alleys so that he might bump into those he met, thereby finding an excuse to fight. He could put seven or eight men fighting against him to flight; everyone feared him like a lion. To cite one example: In the city of Vannes, he had started a quarrel with a prominent gentleman; the gentleman met him in a street with four or five of his servants, all armed, intending to attack Queriolet. He, who could have easily escaped, fell upon them like a lion, murdered the gentleman, and chased the others away; the following day, he went out among the people again without fear, just as if he had only killed an ant. He fought countless times, yet it was not enough for his cruelty; he went to war, where he killed more people in both Italy and Germany <note>original: "Teutschland"</note> than the writer dares to say, etc. etc. He was entirely given over to fornication, adultery, and all sorts of similar abominations; and the more evil he could practice and instigate, the better he liked it, etc. He hated God and everything good, and mocked it as much as he possibly could; he hated the name of God and could not bear it when the poor asked him for alms for God’s sake—he would rather give to them if they cursed. He later recounted himself that if he heard others praising God, he would blaspheme Him. After he finally received a powerful impression of Hell, he felt some stirrings of repentance, began a different life, and even entered a Carthusian monastery <note>A Catholic religious order known for its extreme silence and austerity.</note>. However, it did not last long before he returned to his old ways:

> And then I became (he says himself) worse than I had ever been before, and there was no godlessness that I did not practice; previously I had indeed been wicked, but now I was an atheist, believed in neither heaven nor hell, and cared for nothing.

He mocked his previous change of heart and even laughed at God’s threats and judgments, etc. etc.

15. This epitome of all godlessness, who in his extreme malice was like a hardened brand from the fires of hell, was nevertheless snatched as if from the very pits of hell by the mighty hand of God. He was truly converted during the occasion of the (a) infamous possessed ones of Loudun <note>The Loudun possessions (1632–1634) were a famous case of mass hysteria and alleged demonic possession among Ursuline nuns in France.</note>, through whom the most hidden secrets of his heart were revealed to him—things which no other human being could have known. This conversion began on January 3, 1636. From that time forward, he led a penitent, extraordinarily austere, secluded, and godly life. He showed exceptional devotion in serving the poor and possessed great steadfastness for nearly 25 years, namely until his death, which occurred on October 8, 1660.

16. The dear Bernières <note>Jean de Bernières-Louvigny (1602–1659), a French mystic and influential layman.</note>, who was acquainted with Kériolet, reports that in a conversation he had with him, Kériolet recounted how in the first three years of his conversion, he received much light, spiritual sweetness, and sensible graces from God. However, all of this was afterwards darkened, followed by fierce temptations, listlessness, confusion, and all manner of internal and external suffering. Kériolet remarked, however, that no soul should be dismayed when this happens, but should instead compose itself in patience and love the Cross, through which the soul is more and more purified and the faithfulness of its love is tested. The life of this man, who before his conversion had been a Councilor in the Parliament of Rennes, was printed in Lyon in 1670 under the title: *Le Grand Pecheur converty*, or *The Great Sinner Converted*.

## IV. John of the Cross.
<note>Latin: Johannes à Cruce.</note>

->Compendium of his Life, Chapter 9.<-

> Lord, to suffer and be despised for your sake!

17. John of the Cross, a pure and deeply enlightened soul, was the son of a lowly weaver in Spain. He lived a holy life there during the time of the Reformation and, as a faithful assistant to St. Teresa, helped to reform the Carmelite Order. He died blessedly at Úbeda on December 14, 1591, in the 49th—or as others claim, the 56th—year of his age. The brief biography of him, such as the one placed at the beginning of his books and which G. Arnold <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714), a radical Pietist historian known for his sympathetic accounts of "heretics" and mystics.</note> incorporated into his *Lives of the Faithful*, cannot give us sufficient knowledge of his person and spiritual foundations. The version published in Lyon in 1676, though somewhat expanded, is also insufficient; a more extensive life of this man was edited in Paris in 1638. If one wished to produce a truly adequate and edifying description of his life and teaching, one would need not only to extract the most essential parts from the last-named book but also, above all, to include various passages from his excellent writings. These are full of Divine Unction <note>A term used to describe the "anointing" or spiritual power perceived in a text.</note> and give us the most beautiful understanding of his inner life—upon which most historians, alas, are accustomed to reflect the very least! This would be all the more necessary, because no

<margin>(a) See <note>Latin: "Vid."</note> Arnold's History of Mystical Theology <note>Latin: "Hist. Theol. Myst."</note> Chapter 23. P. Poiret’s Mystical Library <note>Latin: "Biblioth. Mystic."</note> page 118 sequence & 272.</margin>

19. One or two people (a) have already described the character and content of his teaching, which certainly gives little comfort to self-love and nature, because his principle was: The less you wish to be something, the more you will truly be something. The purpose of his doctrine is to direct the soul toward full union with God, where Divine Wisdom, Divine Silence, and a perpetual banquet might be experienced; on this mountain of perfection, the soul ascends through love. He says that one arrives there through the following straight path of perfection: “In nothing must you wish to know anything, in nothing must you wish to taste anything, in nothing must you wish to possess anything, in nothing must you wish to be anything, but only the Whole (namely, God). For whenever you rest in any one thing, you cease to cast yourself into the Whole itself; and therefore, so that you may go from the whole to the Whole, you must leave the whole for the sake of the Whole. And when you have reached the point that you possess the Whole, you must possess it while wanting nothing. For if you wish to have something within the Whole itself, you do not have your treasure purely in God. In this nakedness <note>The spiritual state of "dispossession" or "detachment" from worldly desires.</note>, the spirit finds rest and refreshment; for because it desires nothing, nothing drives it upward. Nothing presses it down either, for it remains in the center point of humility. For whenever it desires something, it is in that very thing that it becomes weary.”

### VI. Johannes Rusbroch.

->Life of Rusbroch Chapter 11.<-

> ->**Each is only so holy as they cling from the heart to goodness.**<-

23. Johannes Rusbroch <note>more commonly known today as John Ruusbroec</note>, or Ruisebroek, lived in the fourteenth century in Brabant. He lived first as a secular priest <note>a priest who serves in a parish rather than a monastery</note> until the 60th year of his age, when he entered the Augustinian monastery of Groenendaal <note>original: "Grünenthal"</note> near Brussels. There, he blessedly concluded his holy life in 1387, when he was already 88 years old. The "good odor" <note>a reference to the "odor of sanctity," or the reputation for holiness</note> of his godly life and deep enlightenment also moved Tauler to visit him and to learn much from him. Geert Groote <note>original: "Gerhardus Magnus," the founder of the Brethren of the Common Life</note> did the same, about which more can be read in the report by Thomas à Kempis in the *Life of Geert*, Chapter 10. Almost from his childhood, Rusbroch was enlightened by God, so that one can easily conclude that this man, by such a great age, must have attained a deep experience and a mature light.

<margin>(a) See Arnold, History of Mystical Theology <note>original: "Hist. Theol. Myst."</note> Chapter 21. Poiret, Library of Mystics <note>original: "Biblioth. Mystic."</note> pages 11 and 268 following.</margin>

24. Not long after his death, his life was briefly described, as it stands placed before his writings. The industrious Surius translated these precious writings into Latin and thus preserved them; for only one of his books (namely: *The Spiritual Marriage* <note>original: "das von der Geistlichen Hochzeit"</note>) is found remaining in the Old Dutch language. In Latin, these works were printed several times in Cologne in 1552, 1609, and 1692, and were also made common and highly recommended in the German language (1701 Quarto in Offenbach) by Gottfried Arnold, as is well known. I do not see on what basis the Dutch editor of Tauler’s sermons (Antwerp, 1593) attributed the fifth Christmas sermon on Colossians 3:2-4 to Rusbroch. For one thing, Rusbroch was never a preacher, much less a "Doctor" <note>a formal scholar or teacher of the Church</note> as he is commonly called, but rather an unlearned Augustinian monk who had hardly begun to learn grammar. The anointing <term>Salbung: the direct teaching of the Holy Spirit upon the soul</term> alone made him learned, and from this divine fountain his teachings flowed unmixed. However, the small tract on *How a person may become earnest, inward, etc.*, which was first printed with Tauler's German works by the order of Dr. Spener, is undoubtedly the same one found among Rusbroch’s books under the title *On the Perfection of the Children of God*. Similarly, Rusbroch’s tract on the *Four Subtle Temptations* is inserted into Tauler's sermon for the first Sunday in Lent. # VI. Johannes Rusbroch
->Life of Rusbroch, Chapter 11.<-

->**Every person is holy only so far as they cling to goodness with their heart.**<-

23. Johannes Rusbroch, or Ruisebroek <note>John Ruusbroec (1293–1381), one of the most important Flemish mystics.</note>, lived in Brabant during the fourteenth century, first as a secular priest <note>A priest who lives in the world rather than in a religious order.</note> until, in the 60th year of his age, he entered the Augustinian monastery of Grünenthal <note>Groenendaal, near Brussels.</note> near Brussels. There he blessedly concluded his holy life in 1387, when he was already 88 years old. The "good scent" of his godly conduct and deep enlightenment also moved Tauler <note>Johannes Tauler, a famous German mystic and preacher.</note> to visit him and learn much from him. Gerhardus Magnus <note>Geert Groote (1340–1384), founder of the Brethren of the Common Life.</note> did the same, regarding which more can be seen in Thomas à Kempis’s report in the *Life of Gerhard*, Chapter 10. From his childhood onward, Rusbroch was enlightened by God, so that one can easily conclude that this man, at such a high age, must have attained a deep experience and mature light.

<margin>(a) See Arnold, *History of Mystic Theology*, Chapter 21. Poiret, *Mystic Library*, pages 11 and 268 following.</margin>
24. Not long after his death, his life was briefly described, as it stands placed before his writings. The industrious Surius <note>Laurentius Surius (1522–1578), a Carthusian hagiographer who translated many mystical works into Latin.</note> translated these precious writings into Latin and thus preserved them; for only one of his books (namely: *The Spiritual Espousals*) is found remaining in the Old Dutch language. In Latin, these works were printed several times at Cologne in 1552, 1609, and 1692; they were also made common and highly recommended in the German language by G. Arnold <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714), a Pietist historian who sought to revive interest in "true" mystical Christianity.</note> (1701 Quarto edition at Offenbach). I do not see on what basis the Dutch editor of Tauler's sermons (Antwerp 1593) attributed the fifth Christmas sermon on Colossians 3:2–4 to Rusbroch; for one thing, Rusbroch was no preacher, much less a "Doctor" <note>A title indicating a high degree of formal academic theological training.</note> as he is commonly called, but rather an unlearned Augustinian monk who had barely begun to learn grammar. The anointing <note>A biblical term referring to the Holy Spirit's direct teaching of a believer.</note> alone made him learned, and from this divine fountain his teachings flowed unmixed. However, the little tractate on how a person may become earnest, inward, etc., which was first printed with Tauler's German works at the direction of Dr. Spener <note>Philipp Jakob Spener (1635–1705), the "Father of Pietism."</note>, is undoubtedly the very same one found among Rusbroch’s books under the title *Of the Perfection of the Children of God*. Likewise, Rusbroch’s tractate on the *Four Subtle Temptations* is inserted into Tauler’s sermon for the first Sunday of Lent. Lovers of such works prefer Rusbroch above almost all other mystical writers; (a) therefore, one could add to his biography a short summary of his wholesome teaching, as...

There is something remarkable about this dear man: when he humbles himself to those of low estate, no one is clearer or more common <note>In this context, "common" means accessible or plain-spoken for the ordinary person.</note> than he; but when he speaks wisdom to the perfect <note>The "perfect" refers to those advanced in the spiritual life.</note>, one must have eagle eyes to follow him, and yet he always retains a lovely, captivating power. I will repeat only a single passage here, which can already give us a small concept of his thorough knowledge and experience:

25. “If you,” he says, <margin>Seven Safeguards, Chapter 3. <note>original: "Sieben Bewahr. Cap. 3."; likely referring to Ruusbroec's *The Seven Steps of the Ladder of Spiritual Love*.</note></margin> “wish to practice and possess love and holiness in the highest degree, you must strip and make your intellectual faculty bare of all images, and raise yourself through faith above reason, to where the rays of the eternal sun shine. These rays will enlighten you with their brilliance and teach you all truth; the truth, however, will set you free, and will ground and establish your bare contemplation in an image-free nakedness <note>A mystical term referring to a state of soul stripped of worldly perceptions to better receive God.</note>. Blessed are the eyes that attain the sight of this! For the power of love always follows this vision with pure love, and in that following, the stream of Divine Grace constantly flows, leading such a soul to the fountain of the Holy Spirit. There, the veins of eternal sweetness flow lovably, making the soul drunk and lifting it above reason—as if into a wandering or onto trackless paths, namely into the very wilderness of eternal bliss; and this is the root and essence of true holiness, from which root the inward practice of virtues constantly grows, for love cannot be idle.”

But that this, and what else he has written, were his own experiences, is shown by the following words, from which we can simultaneously perceive his humility and childlike trust: <margin>Contemplation, Chapter 80. <note>original: "Beſchaulicht. Cap. 80."; likely *The Mirror of Eternal Blessedness*.</note></margin> “I renounce myself, and submit myself and my writings to the eternal truth, to the faith of the Holy Universal Church, and to those teachers who have explained the Holy Scripture through the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, what I feel and experience within me remains with me, and I cannot drive it from my spirit; indeed, even if I could win the whole world, I could not doubt or despair in the Lord Jesus, that He would want to damn me. But if I hear something else, I will gladly remain silent.”

XV.
**Preface.**

...a Dominican well-practiced in the Way of the Cross. In the 18th year of his age, he was powerfully converted to God and drawn toward the love of Eternal Wisdom. On one hand, he enjoyed many spiritual consolations; on the other, he disciplined himself severely through a strictly regulated life until he reached forty years of age. At that time, he was led into a "higher school" <note>A metaphorical "higher school" of spiritual testing where the believer moves from self-imposed discipline to trials sent directly by God.</note> and, like a brave knight, was tested through all manner of strange external and deep internal sufferings, which led him to true *Gottgelassenheit* <term>Gottgelassenheit: A central theme in German mysticism meaning "divine surrender" or "serene abandonment" to God's will.</term>. He also wrote several small books filled with Divine Wisdom. Through these writings, as well as his holy life and powerful sermons, many people were pulled from the snares of the devil toward God. Most of the details of his life and guidance were coaxed from Suso’s own mouth and secretly recorded by one of his spiritual daughters, Elsbeth Stägel <note>original: "Elisabet Staglin"</note>, a holy and sensible Dominican nun in the convent at Töss. Although he burned some of these records when he discovered them, he was eventually commanded by God to preserve the remainder and even add a few sections himself after the daughter’s death.

27. His life story and complete writings are available in German, as translated from the Latin by Anshelm Hoffman (Cologne, 1661). However, that translation is not the best, so many prefer the Latin version by Laurentius Surius (Cologne, 1615, in octavo). These writings of Suso deserve a new translation from the original Swabian <note>Swabian is the High German dialect of southwestern Germany where Suso lived.</note> language, which has a particular emphasis and power. I have that version at hand, printed in Augsburg in 1512, though it is rarely seen otherwise. One finds only four of Suso's sermons among his works, though the last of these is also found in Tauler’s *Postill* <note>A "postill" is a collection of sermons or commentaries on the Gospel lessons.</note> for the Sunday of *Vocem Jocunditatis* <note>original: "Sonntage Voc. The sermon is based on John 10:11.</note> and the sermon for the first Sunday after Trinity (Luke 16:19) are likewise said to be by Suso. These three are not found in the old editions of Tauler’s sermons.

# **Preface.**

Tauler, just as Daniel Sudermann <note>Sudermann (1550–1631) was a teacher and writer who collected and preserved many medieval mystical texts.</note> has also preserved in his *Emblems* a little song by Tauler, which begins:

> “I must flee from all creatures, <note>In mystical writing, "creatures" refers to all created, worldly things as opposed to the Creator.</note>
> “And seek inwardness of heart;
> “If I am to draw my spirit to God,
> “So that it may remain in purity, etc.”

In the old editions of Tauler’s works, one finds in his life story the following teachings, which I do not remember seeing in other German books; for this reason, and because Tauler’s fundamental principles are contained therein to a considerable degree, I wish to set them down here:

### Here follow three good teachings.

> (a) “O dear child! If you wish to come to God and to your own best state,
> “you should diligently observe these three points. First, you should intend God
> “barely and purely; seeking the honor of God in all things, and not
> “your own; especially His will, and not yours. Second, that in
> “all your works and outward dealings you diligently observe yourself; look into your bottomless
> “nothingness, <note>A central concept in German mysticism: the realization that the self, apart from God, has no independent existence.</note> and with a constant presence, observe what you are dealing with, what may be within you,
> “and observe your inner ground with all diligence. Third, do not take
> “upon yourself what is not commanded of you; let all things stand as they are; what is good,
> “let remain good; what is evil, do not judge; turn instead into your inner ground,
> “and remain there, and take heed of the Fatherly voice that calls to you to remain
> “steadfast in Him.

> (b) “O dear child! Keep these two points, and you shall attain great things:
> “First, be truly small outwardly and inwardly from the ground of your heart, not with words,
> “but in truth. In your entire understanding, down to your very ground,
> “and in your own eyes, be small and nothing, without any pretense. Second, have
> “true Divine love—not what we call love in a sensory way, but in an
> “essential way, in the most inward intention of the heart.

> (c) “Therefore, O man! you should be bare <note>Original: *bloß*. This refers to being "stripped" or "unencumbered" by worldly thoughts or the ego.</note> of all notice, understanding, and
> “sensuality, because God the Lord is unencumbered and bare; thus the spirit may be
> “joined to that bare, pure Being. For the soul must necessarily be unencumbered and bare
> “if it is to understand the hiddenness of His secrets. Therefore, a person
> “must cut away all things in which they might find something of their own self.”

year of her life, until her death, which occurred on May 25, 1607, as she was entering her 42nd year. She was a virtuous, holy soul, a fervent lover of Jesus Christ, the Eternal Word, and of His Holy Cross. When she was approximately 19 years old, she was placed into a state of heavy inner suffering, in which she was besieged and tested for five whole years by all kinds of terrifying temptations and distresses, including extraordinary assaults by evil spirits. Before this time, and especially thereafter, she walked in great communion with the Lord. Ecstasies <note>Original: *Entzückungen*. These are states of mystical trance where the person is perceived to be caught up in divine communication.</note> were very common for her, during which it was remarkable that she spoke many Divine discourses and secrets, which were carefully recorded by those who were around her.

33. Aside from these many ecstasies, this holy soul also frequently experienced such overflows of Divine Love that she seemed to be entirely outside of herself; she would run through the entire house, crying out: "Love, Love, Love! Oh my Lord! No more love, no more love! It is too much, Oh my Jesus! This love that You bear toward the creatures. <note>In this context, "creatures" refers to all created human beings.</note> It is not too much for Your Highness, but it is too much for their lowliness." At another time she cried out: "Oh God of Love! Oh God of Love! Oh God of Love! Oh God! You who love Your creatures with pure love." At another time she said: "Do you not know, dear sisters, that my Jesus is nothing but Love? Yes, Oh my Jesus! You are entirely lovely and joyful, delightful and refreshing, satisfying and uniting; You are pain and solace, labor and rest, death and life all at once! Yes, what are You not? You are white and sufficient, high and immeasurable, wonderful and inexpressible!" Once, while running through the monastery, she took one of her fellow sisters by the hand and said: "Come, you also, and run with me, so that we may call out 'Love,' so that we may strike up a song of Love." Meeting another, she pressed her hand firmly and said: "Oh soul! Do you also love Love?" She even ran once and seized the rope of the bells, began to ring them, and cried out: "Come, souls, and love: come, souls, and love the Love by which you are loved!" etc.

34. For the last five years of her life, she was led through all kinds of torment and heavy illnesses of the body. Three years before her end, her ecstasies also ceased, as was made known to her internally; in her final ecstasy, in which she commended the Cross of Christ to everyone, she spoke these words among others: "Oh my Jesus! You want me to become like a little daughter; yes, You want me to be born anew; alas! how small must I become again? Because of such smallness and humiliation, these souls will no longer know me." From then on, she became like a different person, partly through the illnesses and sufferings of the body, and partly because of the manifold nakedness of her mind; <note>Original: *Bloßheit ihres Gemüths*. A mystical term for "poverty of spirit" or a state where the mind is stripped of all worldly images and intellectual consolations.</note> nonetheless, she overcame everything with bravery and patience, and completed her sacrifice upon the Cross.

->Life of Cath[erine], Chapter 18, Verse 1.<-

## Remember me, and I will remember you.

36. Catherine of Siena was born in the year 1347 in Siena, to a citizen and cloth-dyer of that same city, Giacomo Benincasa; she died in Rome in 1380, having reached only 33 years of age. She was a virgin of the Dominican Order, although the women of that order at that time still lived each for herself in her own house and little room, and did not yet take vows. <note>Catherine belonged to the "Mantellate," a group of laywomen (Third Order) who followed Dominican spirituality while living at home rather than in a cloistered convent.</note>

<margin>(a) H. Warthen. Appendix to the Literary History of William Cave.</margin>
Even the Protestants (a) must admit that her godliness was unfeigned, her chastity and purity of life unstained, and her love for the poor, as well as her zeal for the Church, was very great. In her writings, she comes quite close to the character of St. Teresa.

37. Her life was recorded by her confessor, Raymond <note>Raymond of Capua (c. 1330–1399), who was Catherine’s spiritual advisor and later Master General of the Dominican Order.</note>, and is also available in the German language, published in Augsburg in 1619. However, anyone wishing to have a sufficient understanding of the life and spiritual foundation of this holy soul must immediately examine her other writings. Her dialogues on the Passion were likewise published by her confessor. She herself dictated her six dialogues <note>Often known today as *The Dialogue of Divine Providence*.</note>, and they were printed in Latin at Ingolstadt in 1583, and partly in Dutch at Ghent in 1717. Also published are 375 of her letters to people of all ranks and stations.

38. Whoever looks upon the writings and deeds of this person must marvel at her earnestness in godliness and her tenderest love for **JESUS** Christ, and especially at her manly courage <note>In the 18th century, "manly courage" (*männlichen Muth*) was a high compliment used to describe a woman who showed exceptional strength of character or spiritual fortitude.</note> and the divine simplicity and power of her speeches, through which she could silence all worldly wisdom, move hearts, and ignite their desires through the fire of heavenly love; for this reason, she was held in great esteem by everyone, even by Popes and Kings, although she was such a young and unlearned maiden.

39. Once, she came from Tuscany to Avignon and delivered a sharp sermon of rebuke to the Pope concerning the abominations of his court. When he objected, asking how she could know the state of his court since she had arrived only a few days prior, she answered with majestic gestures: “To the praise and honor of Almighty God, I may well say that I [perceive] the stench of the abominable sins committed at this court...”

# Preface.

“...the court <note>This likely refers to the papal court at Avignon or Rome, whose corruption Catherine frequently criticized.</note> commits, I have already felt in my fatherland, far more so than the sinners themselves who daily commit such grave sins.” Just as she vividly saw the ruin of the Church, she also prophesied much regarding an improvement of the Church, when it would once again return to its first poor, gentle, and humble state. To this end belong the following expressions with which she concludes one of her letters: “O sweet love of God, fulfill soon the longing of your servants! I wish to say nothing more than that I am dying of longing in this desire. Therefore, be compassionate toward me as well, and pray to the Divine Goodness that the good and lovely time may come soon. Abide in the holy, sweet loveliness of God; immerse yourselves in the blood of the crucified Christ; and do not grow weary for any reason, but be all the more brave and comforted. Rejoice! Rejoice! And let all effort be sweet to you. Love, love, love one another. O Jesus, sweetness! O Jesus!” The following short instruction on how to attain perfection was once presented to her by God: “If you wish to do my will after the example of your Savior—in which all your happiness and salvation lies—then you must fundamentally abandon your own will in all things, deny it, and annihilate it. For the more you die to yourself, the more you will live in me; and the more thoroughly you root out what is yours from within you, the more abundantly I shall put what is mine in its place.”

## XI. Francis of Assisi.

->My God and my All!<-
<note>Original Latin: *Deus meus & omnia!* This was the famous aspirated prayer of St. Francis.</note>

<margin>40.</margin> St. Francis was born in Italy, specifically in Assisi in the Duchy of Spoleto, in the year 1181. Not far from this city, on October 4, 1126, he departed this temporal life in the 45th year of his age. He was the son of a prominent merchant and was himself devoted to the mercantile trade. He spent the years of his youth in vanity, indulgence, and ambition, until the grace of God powerfully enlightened him when he was in his twenties and turned him into a completely different person; thereafter, he became the founder of the entire Franciscan Order.

<margin>41.</margin> The fact that some monks have exalted him excessively and invented many fables <note>A reference to the "Little Flowers of St. Francis" or other legendary hagiographies that the author, writing from a later perspective, views with some skepticism.</note> about him does not diminish the singular holiness of this man in the least; it is only a pity that his person and history have become all the more contemptible to the world because of it. The pious Bonaventura <note>St. Bonaventure (1221–1274), a major scholastic theologian and biographer of Francis.</note> and others have recorded his life; these biographies can be found collected in a Brabantian book, *The Vineyard of St. Francis*, printed in Antwerp in 1518. If one had this book at hand, along with Bosquierus’s *Franciscan Antiquities* <note>Original: *Antiquitates Franciscanæ* by Philippe Bosquier.</note>, as well as the *Minor Works of Francis* <note>Original: *Opuscula Francisci*.</note> printed in Antwerp in 1623 and Lyon in 1636, a simple eye would encounter truly excellent things from this man; though some of it might not please everyone. Outwardly, he led a poor, strict life, and was a fool before the world for Christ’s sake; before God and in the...
