# Preface.

...but in truth, he was a man of God, a heart entirely filled with humility and love; through his exemplary conduct and unadorned preaching, countless people of that time were moved and converted to a life of earnestness and the love of God.

42. His humble and pure mind is already evident from his following discourses, which he once delivered to his disciples:

> “Blessed is the servant of God, who does not exalt himself any more because of the good that God speaks or works through him, than because of that which God works or speaks through another!
>
> “Blessed is the servant who gives all good to the Lord! For whoever keeps anything for himself hides his Lord’s money, <note>A reference to the Parable of the Talents in Matthew 25.</note> and what he thought he had shall be taken from him.
>
> “Blessed is the servant who receives punishment and discipline as gladly from another as from himself!
>
> “Blessed is the servant who is found as humble among his inferiors as among his superiors!
>
> “Blessed is the servant who hides the secrets of God in his heart!” etc.

He also gave them this further reminder: “They should by no means neglect holy prayer because of their preaching or their office of leadership; for subordinates are built up when the preachers practice much prayer and do not shy away from small, lowly works; otherwise, they could not teach such things to others without shame.”

Therefore he also said: “Those who allow themselves to be driven by art and <term>idle curiosity<note>The original German *Fürwitz* refers to a meddlesome or intellectual prying that seeks knowledge for vanity rather than for spiritual growth.</note></term> will find their hands empty on the day of tribulations.”

“They should not be so eager to possess much art and many books, but rather ground themselves in holy humility, in pure simplicity, in fervent prayer, and in **holy poverty**. The brothers (he said) must, after the example of Jesus Christ, pray more than they read, so that they may be true disciples of the Holy Gospel.”

And what he taught in this regard, he also practiced himself. Once, someone heard him frequently repeating these words during the night:

> O dear Lord! Who are You? O my sweetest God! And what am I, a poor little worm <note>St. Francis frequently referred to himself as a "worm," echoing Psalm 22:6 to express his humility before the Divine.</note> and Your small servant?

This and nothing else did he speak to God. At another time he prayed:

> Sweetest Father, since You desire my salvation, deliver me from myself, for I am my own true enemy; and bring me through Yourself to Yourself, otherwise I shall never be certain of my salvation! etc.

### XII. Bernard, Giles, Masseus, Leo, Rufino, etc.

->The Life of Giles. Chapter IX.<-

->One for the One. <note>original: "Una Uni." A common mystical phrase implying the total devotion of the individual soul to the one God.</note><-

43. These and several other early followers and companions of St. Francis walked with him in that very same spirit. In all of them, there shines forth an extreme contempt for all worldly honors, possessions, and comforts, together with great simplicity, humility, and a fervent love for God and their neighbor. In these and other virtues, they shone as heavenly lights during the dark times of that age. Their biographies can also be found in brief in the aforementioned Dutch book; <note>Likely a reference to a 17th-century compilation of Franciscan lives popular in Pietist circles.</note> whoever has received the spirit of discernment from the Father will already know how to keep the best from it all. Here and there in their histories, one finds something truly Divine, from which one can sufficiently see that they were truly friends of God. Would to God that the Franciscan cloisters were still filled with such souls today!

44. Bernard said as he was dying: 
> “Never has a man angered me whom I did not afterwards love far more, with a singular love, than I did before.”

Giles <note>Brother Giles (Aegidius), the third companion of St. Francis, known for his short, proverbs-like spiritual wisdom.</note> spoke: 
> “Holy sorrow, holy humility, holy love, holy joy, holy inwardness: these make a holy and good soul.”

Masseus said: 
> “It is better that one visits the living saints than the dead; the living saints will teach you many things—how they passed through all kinds of external and internal trials and temptations, and how you must overcome the same; and such will benefit your soul more than if you travel through the lands to view dead bodies <note>A critique of the medieval practice of making long pilgrimages to view the relics of deceased saints.</note>.”

Juniper (of whom Francis used to say: “Would to God that we had a whole forest full of such juniper trees!”), when he was mocked or slandered, would say: 
> “O, my dear friend, throw these precious pearls into my lap: just keep throwing them with confidence!”

John of La Verna <note>original: "Jan von Alvernen." A later but significant Franciscan mystic associated with Mount La Verna.</note> said these words as he was dying: 
> “Whoever wishes to attain eternal bliss must cling alone, and with great fervor, to the crucified Jesus.”

45. Behold there, a group of twelve pious and holy souls briefly touched upon; they would provide a writer with abundant material to produce a third volume of these biographies. ...of many people and books; indeed, it is not intended to give anyone cause to distract their heart from the **one thing necessary** <note>original: "Einzignöthigen." A reference to Luke 10:42, a central concept in Pietist and mystical thought emphasizing internal devotion over outward activity.</note> through excessive reading of books. Rather, through such excerpts, the goal was to consolidate diverse readings, to shorten the lengthy as much as possible, and thus spare devout hearts the effort of reading and searching through so much; since it is known all too well that even the holiest readings and contemplations do more harm than good where one exceeds moderation, and the eye does not remain carefully fixed on **GOD** and our own heart. Everything should point us and draw us to this One. To be with **GOD** alone, and in communion with **GOD**, is the ultimate and unfailing goal in which one finds salvation and life eternally; this is what makes us holy. The glorious and uniquely blessed **GOD** of love is inexpressibly near to us in the lovely **JESUS-name**; let us then heartily accustom ourselves to walking in the light of His sweet presence, until through knowing Him and being in fellowship with Him, we lose sight of all creatures, and finally even ourselves. For **GOD** alone is enough!

> <note>original: "Ehre sey dem Vater, und dem Sohn, und dem H. Geist..." This is a translation of the "Gloria Patri," a traditional Christian doxology (a short hymn of praise) used to conclude prayers and hymns.</note>

--- Page 556 ---
<meta>The catchword from the previous page, "The," flows into the title on this page. This page serves as the "Vorbericht" or Preface to the biography of Saint Teresa of Jesus, contextualizing her life within the broader movement of church reform and explaining the sources used for this specific German edition.</meta>

## The Life
# of Saint Teresa of Jesus.

### Preface.

It is highly remarkable, and did not happen without the prompting of a higher hand, that around the time this holy soul lived, such a powerful drive and labor toward a renewal and improvement of the churches manifested in all places and in nearly all spirits. Whether and to what extent each person took hold of this at the right end and led it to the desired goal, we leave for the Lord of the House himself to decide; however, it is certain that *Saint Teresa* and her helper *John of the Cross* <note>Saint John of the Cross (1542–1591) was a Spanish mystic and Carmelite friar who, along with Teresa, founded the Discalced Carmelites.</note> are not to be counted among the least of those who contributed something toward a thorough reformation of the churches through their lives, actions, and writings; whoever can view the whole state of affairs with a free and enlightened spirit will gladly give their assent to this.

They applied the axe to the root, as it were, leading souls by word and example into a real renunciation of the world and of themselves, and into a heartfelt, pure love for God through the path of **Interior Prayer**, <term>Interior Prayer: A form of silent, contemplative prayer focused on an internal dialogue with God rather than recited formulas.</term> whereby all corruption was checked, a real improvement was effected in souls, and a light was set up for the entire corrupt generation. Through the lives and writings of both aforementioned saints, the light on the internal paths of Christianity especially broke through again, and the practice of constant prayer of the heart—primarily in the monasteries—came into vogue once more.

Although since that time (as has happened with other improvements) almost everything has settled back into the old ruts, countless hungry spirits have nonetheless sought and found healthy nourishment in these writings: as can be seen from the multitude of editions and translations and the high regard for these matters among so many nations. *Teresa's* writings have been printed multiple times in Spanish, as well as in Latin, Italian, Polish, Dutch, French, and German; most recently in 1730, the third German edition was published in Cologne.

At the express command of her spiritual director, *Teresa* described the greatest part of her life herself; in which her simplicity and honesty shine forth everywhere to such a degree that one could be sufficiently convinced of the truth of the content by that alone, even if no other abundant testimonies were present. She in no way embellishes her affairs, but relates what happened or was experienced accurately and in detail; yet in such a way that any distaste for the lengthiness is easily dispelled by the heartiness of her style of writing. It is not a mere and dry history; rather, one finds therein the most moving depictions of the vanity of the world, of true humility, of the love of God, and especially of the different types of **Interior Prayer** and the unspeakable graces which His Divine Majesty is accustomed to communicate to a soul on this path: all of which she explains candidly from her own experience.

<margin>(a) Lyon 1620.</margin>
This extract was indeed taken from the newest German edition; however, others were also kept at hand—namely the Latin and Dutch versions—so that the sense of the author might be given more accurately and emphatically. To be sure, an extract of this life was also incorporated into the *Lives of the Faithful* under the name of Mr. *G. Arnold*; <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714) was a famous German Pietist historian known for his sympathetic accounts of "heretics" and mystics.</note> but we could not follow that version, because we believed it would be more pleasant for the reader if this Saint herself were introduced speaking in her own unaltered words, rather than if one had tried to express her meaning, however faithfully. Not to mention that that previous extract only reaches until the year 1562; this one, however, is carried out until her death (which occurred in the year 1582), using *Teresa's* book on the foundations of her convents and *Francisco Ribera's* *Life of Teresa* (a). <note>Francisco de Ribera (1537–1591) was a Jesuit who became Teresa's biographer shortly after her death.</note> Additionally, various details have been inserted here and there from *Ribera*, who was a well-known friend of *Teresa*.

<summary>This preface introduces Saint Teresa of Jesus and John of the Cross as key figures of spiritual reform through "Interior Prayer." It explains that this edition is based on Teresa's own autobiographical writings and reliable historical biographies like that of Francisco Ribera.</summary>
<keywords>Saint Teresa of Jesus, John of the Cross, Interior Prayer, Church Reformation, biography, mysticism, Francisco Ribera, Gottfried Arnold</keywords>

--- Page 557 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Vorbericht" or Preface. The previous page established Saint Teresa and Saint John of the Cross as pivotal figures in church reform who emphasized interior prayer. This page focuses on how Teresa’s reputation transitioned from one of suspicion to widespread acclaim, even among Protestant scholars, and concludes with Teresa’s own humble introduction to her life story.</meta>

<page-num>Preface. 3</page-num>

Although this holy soul suffered many contradictions and heavy persecutions from her dear ones, both during her life (a) and to some extent after her death (b); it nonetheless soon changed to such a degree that even many who held the greatest suspicion of her, after they had most precisely tested her spirit and conduct, became her greatest defenders. Thus, one could cite an incredible multitude of unimpeachable eyewitnesses and testimonies regarding her life and extraordinary holiness—indeed, one could fill an entire book with them. However, since these are largely to be read at the beginning of her works, and because *Teresa* has also been publicly declared a Saint, it would be quite superfluous to provide any *approvals* <note>original: "Approbationes"; formal ecclesiastical endorsements of a text's orthodoxy.</note> from the Roman Catholic Church here.

To point out just a few testimonies from the Protestants: a recent (c) author defends *Teresa* and calls her a soul very sensible according to both nature and grace, and thoroughly practiced in the spiritual life, etc. Dr. Anton <note>Paul Anton (1661–1730), a prominent German Pietist theologian and professor at Halle.</note>, a professor at Halle, speaks of the works of *Teresa* in a public *lecture* <note>original: "Collegio"; a university course or lecture series.</note> as follows (d): 
> “These *works* <note>original: "Opera"</note> are not free from all sorts of *particular devotions of the Roman Church* <note>original: "Devotionibus particularibus Rom, Ecclesiæ"</note>; on the other hand, however, there are also many glorious truths—indeed, principal truths—therein. She pressed straight toward God and flew right over the other *particulars* <note>original: "Particularia"</note> of superstition; for this, one cannot thank God enough. Meanwhile, she wrote lamentably of us, *based on the premise* <note>original: "ex hypothesi"</note> of what she knew and heard; yet her Christian heart is well-recognized, because she always prayed for us, etc.”

*Gottfried Arnold* <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714) was a radical Pietist historian whose "Non-Partisan History of the Church and Heretics" shifted how "heretics" and mystics were viewed.</note> has not only (as mentioned) published an extract of her life, but he also recognizes (e) in her a precious foundation of humility and heartfelt simplicity. He notes that she spread herself in her time like a sweet savor of Christ and led many a soul to the Lord. He recommends for imitation the example of humility, which dwelt in such a rich measure in this person, together with her world-scorning conduct. From her writings, one can more clearly perceive the purity of her mind in the service of God, as well as her remaining experience in the ways of the Lord. After this same man, in another book (f), cited a multitude of *approvals* from others, he briefly indicates the *summary* and the *character* of her discourse in the following manner: 
> “She presented that mystical doctrine in an intimate way of love and prayer, which by others is mostly taught according to a scholastic method. For although she describes her subjects not without good order, she nevertheless affects no art therein, but speaks out of the pure movement of the heart, through the experience of fervent love. In particular, however, she urges toward constant internal prayer, and even more toward such supernatural longing and groaning for God, through which the soul is united with Him; so that one may thus be deemed worthy of infinite and inexpressible graces and be established in love. Toward this end, the author seeks everywhere to powerfully awaken the heart and to soften it from its natural hardness toward a constant love of God, and deep adoration and veneration of His infinite power, etc.” 

*Pierre Poiret* <note>Pierre Poiret (1646–1719) was a French mystic and philosopher who edited the works of many spiritual writers.</note> praises and recommends *Teresa* here and there in his writings (g), and in the latter place indicated below, has defended her as a holy and pure soul against the impudent lies of a poor slanderer.

Let each of us call upon the Father Himself for the spirit of discernment; and then read this history with a humble and obedient heart, and it will by no means pass without the refreshment and edification of one's soul.

As an introduction to this biography, *Teresa* writes the following:

> “I ask for God’s sake, all those who shall read through this my life, that they would set before their eyes that the same was such an evil life, that among all the Saints who have converted to God, I have found not a single one whose example I could take comfort in. For I see in them that from the time they were called by the Lord, they did not turn back again to offend Him further with sins; but I have not only become worse again, but it also appeared as if I diligently resisted those graces which I received from the Divine Majesty. May He be blessed into eternity, that He has waited for me so long! I also ask Him with all my heart, that He would grant me the grace that I may bring forth this my life story with all clarity and truth, and that such may redound to His glory and praise. Who shall be praised and blessed without ceasing by all creatures! Amen.”

(a) See here Chapter 20.
(b) *See: Elucidation of the Mystical Theology of Saint John of the Cross. Chapter 1.*
(c) *Alethophilus* <note>A pseudonym meaning "Lover of Truth."</note> Defense of *Mystical Theology, Part II,* Section 70. *Holland Edition.*
(d) *Collections for the Building of the Kingdom of God.* no. 18.
(e) *Lives of the Faithful,* p. 206.
(f) *History of Mystical Theology, Chapter* 23.
(g) *See: Library of Mystical Theology, p. 129, 345. Posthumous Works, p. 252, 667. following.*

# Chapter One.
## Teresa’s Lineage. The first stirrings of devotion in her childhood. The vanity of youth. From which she is rescued and once again touched anew by God.

->1.<-

Saint Teresa of Jesus, who was called Teresa of Ahumada until the founding of her first convent, was born on March 28, 1515, in Avila <note>original: "Abula"; the Latin name for the city of Avila in Spain.</note>, Spain. Her father was Alonso Sánchez <note>original: "Aloysius Sauches"; a Latinized version of his Spanish name.</note> of Cepeda, and her mother Beatriz of Ahumada, both of noble descent, and—what is most important—at once virtuous and God-fearing. This holy daughter, who became a mother of many children in the spirit <note>A reference to her role as the foundress of the Discalced Carmelite Order.</note>, described her life extensively at the command of her spiritual guide. From this, and from others of her writings, we intend, with Divine assistance, to prepare this concise yet sufficient biography using her own words.

> 2. My father (these are Teresa’s words) was very devoted to reading good books; therefore, he also kept such books, written in the Spanish language, at home so that his children might also become accustomed to them. This, as well as the care our mother took to ensure we prayed diligently, began to encourage me toward the good when I was (in my estimation) six or seven years old. There were three sisters and nine brothers of us, all of whom, through God’s grace, imitated their parents in virtue, except for me alone, even though I was the favorite of my father.
>
> One of my brothers was approximately my age, and him I loved the most; we two often read the lives of the Saints together. But when I saw the pain and martyrdom that the Saints endured for God’s sake, it seemed to me that they had purchased heaven and the enjoyment of God very cheaply, and I desired greatly to die in such a manner: not indeed out of love for God, but so that I might in this way soon enjoy the great goods which, as I read, are kept in heaven.
>
> I often conversed with this little brother of mine about the means and ways by which we might achieve this; we finally resolved together that we would travel to the land of the Moors <note>original: "Mohrenland"; referring to Muslim-controlled territories where they hoped to be martyred.</note> and beg our way there so that they might strike off our heads. And it seems to me that the Lord granted us enough courage for it, if only we could have found a means, and the greatest obstacle seemed to be that we had our parents at home.

(a) *Life of Teresa* <note>original: "Vie de Theres."</note>, Book I, Chapter 4.

# Seventh Part. The Life of Saint Teresa etc. Chapter I.

<sig>A 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: nicht</meta>

[...until their uncle encountered them and took them back home to their mother, who had been very distressed. The boy, however, excused himself by saying that his sister, *Teresa*, had persuaded him to do it.]

4. We were greatly astonished to read that hellish torment and heavenly joy should last forever, and we felt a particular desire to repeat often: *For eternity! For eternity! For eternity!* Through the frequent repetition of these words, it pleased the Lord that the way of truth remained impressed upon me even in that childhood age.

We also resolved to become hermits, and began to build little hermit-huts in a garden that was by the house, though they collapsed again immediately; I gave alms as much as I could; I sought solitude to perform my little prayers, of which there were many; when I played with other children, I took special delight in building convents, as if we were nuns. It pains me greatly now when I think of what the reason must have been that I did not persevere in the good desire and resolution I had begun.

5. Although my mother was very virtuous, she was nonetheless inclined to read the old books of chivalry and heroes <note>These "Ritter- und Helden-Bücher" refers to chivalric romances, like those that famously drove Don Quixote mad; they were popular adventure stories of the era.</note>, and she also gave us children time and permission to read the same; this displeased my father to such an extent that we had to take care that he did not see it. I began to grow entirely accustomed to these books, and I even held that I did no wrong in it, even though I spent many hours of the day and night in this vain exercise; thereupon I also began to adorn myself, desiring to please others with my appearance, and took extraordinary care to have beautiful hands and hair, to wear fragrant things, and other such vanities, as many of them as I could have. And this diligence toward excessive finery clung to me for many years.

6. I had several cousins (for otherwise no one was allowed into my father's house); we were almost always together with them, and loved them very much. With them, I also liked to chatter about everything I knew that was pleasant to them, and listened to their childish nonsense, which was not always of the best sort. I also had a female relative <term>Baase: an archaic term for a female cousin or aunt</term> who was very frivolous in her conduct; I associated with her constantly and had conversations with her, because she helped and encouraged me in all vanities and delights. My father and my sisters greatly disliked this friendship and often punished me for it. However, because they could not find a proper reason to end the association, their efforts were in vain, as I was very cunning in all things worldly. This companionship has now changed me to such an extent that it left almost no sign of a virtuous nature and soul in me, just as if they had impressed their own habits and qualities upon me.

7. And although I was never inclined toward heavy sins and vices, because I naturally had an abhorrence for all dishonorable behavior and took my pleasure only in chatter and time-wasting company, nonetheless, because I had the opportunity...

# Seventh Part. The Life

<meta>catchword: 11. Whether</meta>

not avoid them, then the danger was already at hand; from which God nevertheless rescued me in such a way that it is clearly seen how He cared for me even against my will, so that I might not completely ruin myself. This could not happen so secretly that a suspicion did not arise with my father; for as it seems to me, not even three months had passed since I had pursued these vanities, when I was placed in a convent in this city, where they are accustomed to educate such persons <note>Teresa was sent to the Augustinian Convent of Our Lady of Grace in Avila in 1531.</note>.

8. The first eight days, the convent seemed very difficult to me, but more because I feared my vanity might have become known than because I was enclosed there, for I was already tired of that same vanity. But within eight days I was more satisfied there than in my father's house. And although at that time it was still very contrary to me to enter religious life <note>original: "geistlich zu werden"; this refers to the process of becoming a nun</note>, I was yet delighted to see such pious nuns; and my soul began again to accustom itself to the good exercises of my early years; and I saw well what a great grace God shows to those whom He brings into the company of pious people. Blessed be You, O Lord! that You have endured me so long.

9. One of these nuns slept with us <note>In the shared dormitory for the young students</note>, in whose holy company I began to find pleasure; she told me in what way she had come to the convent, solely because she had read the words in the Gospel: *Many are called, but few are chosen* <note>original Latin: "Multi sunt vocati, pauci vero electi" from Matthew 22:14</note>. She also told me of the reward that God prepares for those who leave everything for His sake. This good company now began gradually to root out those habits in me which the evil company had planted, and to impress back into my mind the desire for eternal things, and also to diminish somewhat the great distaste for the life of a nun. When I saw that one wept during prayer, or had some other virtue, I was envious of her for it, because my heart was quite hard in this regard. I began to say many vocal prayers, and to commend myself to everyone in the house, that they should ask God to place me in such a state in which I could serve Him.

10. For a year and a half I was in this convent, then I fell into a severe illness, so that I had to return to my father. When I improved, I was taken to my sister, who lived on a farm <term>Meyerhof|A steward’s farm or country estate</term>. On the way, there lived one of my father’s brothers, a very virtuous man and a widower; he spent his time reading spiritual books, and his conversation was usually about God and the vanity of the world: I had to read aloud to him from those same books. Although I had no particular desire for it, I nevertheless acted as if it pleased me; for I was always most diligent in trying to please others, even when it was otherwise contrary to me, so that what would have been a virtue in others was a great fault in me. O gracious God! in what way and manner did His Majesty not gradually prepare me for the state in which He wished to use me, while I (even against my will) did violence to myself and overcame myself; may He be blessed for it for eternity, Amen.

<meta>This page continues Teresa’s account of her internal struggle regarding her vocation. This page concludes her first chapter and begins the second, detailing her final decision to enter the convent and the physical and emotional toll of that choice.</meta>

# of St. Teresa of Jesus. Ch. II.

11. Although I stayed there for only a few days, the Divine words which I both read and heard there, as well as the good company, had such power over my heart that I began to recognize once more the truth I had grasped in my childhood: namely, how everything is so futile, how vain the world is, and how quickly everything vanishes. I also began to fear that if I were to die, I might perhaps be damned. And although my will was not yet entirely inclined to enter religious life <note>original: "geistlich zu werden"; this refers to the process of becoming a nun</note>, I saw nevertheless that this state would be better and safer; therefore I gradually resolved to force myself into it.

I spent about three months in this conflict: the evil enemy suggested to me that I would not be able to endure the burden and hardship of the Order because I had been raised so delicately; but I countered this with the toil and pain that Jesus had suffered for us, and that it would therefore not be much for me to suffer something for His sake as well; He would surely help me bear everything.

---

## The Second Chapter.

->She enters the convent. And lives there quite contentedly, yet sickly. Her practice of prayer. Unfortunate cure and consequences of her illness. Fruits of her prayer.<-

1. During these days, while I was preoccupied with such thoughts, I also persuaded one of my brothers to enter a monastery by pointing out the vanity of this world; we therefore both resolved to go to the monastery very early on a certain day [the 2nd of November, 1535].

As far as I can remember, it truly seems to me that when I left my father's house, I was in such a state that I do not believe I will feel greater pain on my deathbed; for it felt to me as if all my bones were being disjointed <note>original: "alle meine Gebeine verrücket würden"; an idiom describing extreme internal agony</note>. Since I did not yet have a love of God that could make me forget the love for my father and friends, I had to use great force against myself in all this. However, the Lord granted me such courage against myself that I nevertheless carried it out.

2. As soon as I had taken the habit <note>term: Habit; the distinctive clothing worn by members of a religious order</note>, the Lord immediately let me know how faithfully He stands by those who do violence to themselves to serve Him; for from that hour such a great joy came over me regarding my chosen state that it has never left me to this day; and God transformed the dryness <note>original: "Truckenheit"; a term used in mystical theology to describe a period where one feels no emotional or spiritual consolation during prayer</note> with which my soul was afflicted into a great tenderness of heart, so that everything practiced in the convent was pleasant and lovely to me.

# Seventh Part. The Life

7. ...did not avoid it, the danger was already at hand; from which GOD nevertheless rescued me in such a way that it is clear to see how He cared for me even against my will, so that I might not completely ruin myself. This could not happen so secretly that my father did not suspect something; for it seems to me, not even three months had passed since I followed these vanities when I was placed in a convent in this city, where such persons are usually raised <note>This refers to the Augustinian Convent of Our Lady of Grace in Avila, which took in young women from noble families to prepare them for marriage or religious life</note>.

8. The first eight days, the convent life seemed very difficult to me, but more because I feared my vanity had somehow become known than because I was enclosed there, for I was already weary of those same vanities. But within eight days, I was more content there than in my father’s house. And although it was then still very repugnant to me to enter the religious life <note>original: "geistlich zu werden"; the process of becoming a nun</note>, I was nevertheless happy to see such pious nuns; and my soul began again to accustom itself to the good exercises of my early years; and I saw well what a great grace GOD shows to those whom He brings into the company of pious people. Blessed be You, O Lord! that You have tolerated me so long.

9. One of these nuns slept near us, in whose holy company I began to find pleasure; she told me in what manner she had come to the convent, solely because she had read the words in the **Gospel** <note>original: "Evangelio"</note>: *Many are called, but few are chosen.* She also told me of the reward that GOD prepares for those who leave everything for His sake. This good company now began to gradually root out in me those habits which the bad company had planted, and to impress back into my mind the desire for eternal things, and also to lessen somewhat the great dislike for convent life. When I saw that one sister wept while praying, or possessed some other virtue, I was envious of her for it, since my heart was quite hard in this regard. I began to say many vocal prayers and to commend myself to everyone in the house, that they should ask GOD to place me in such a state in which I could serve Him.

10. I was in this convent for a year and a half, when I fell into a serious illness, so that I had to return to my father. As I improved, I was taken to my sister, who lived on a **farm estate** <term>Meyerhof; a large manor farm or steward's property</term>. Along the way lived one of my father’s brothers, a very virtuous man and a widower; he spent his time reading spiritual books, and his conversation was usually of GOD and the vanity of the world: I had to read to him from these same books. Although I had no particular desire for it, I nonetheless pretended as if it pleased me; for I always endeavored to the highest degree to please others, even when it was otherwise repugnant to me, so that what would have been a virtue in others was a great fault in me. O gracious GOD! in what ways and manners has His Majesty not gradually prepared me for the state in which He wished to use me, while I (even against my will) did violence to myself and overcame myself; may He be blessed <note>original: "gebenedeyet"</note> for it for all eternity, Amen.

# of St. Teresa of Jesus. Chapter II.

11. Although I stayed there only a few days, the Divine words that I read and heard there, as well as the good company, had such a power over my heart that I began to recognize again the truth I had understood in my childhood: namely, how everything is so fleeting, how vain the world is, and how quickly everything vanishes. I also began to fear that if I were to die, I might perhaps be damned. And although my will was not yet entirely inclined toward entering religious life <note>original: "geistlich werden"; the process of becoming a nun or monk</note>, I saw that this state was better and safer; therefore, I gradually resolved to force myself to enter it.

During this struggle, I spent about three months: the evil enemy <note>The devil</note> suggested to me that I would not be able to endure the burden and difficulty of the Order because I had been raised so delicately; but I countered this with the toil and pain that **Jesus** had suffered for us, and that it would not be much for me to suffer something for His sake as well; He would surely help me endure everything.

## The Second Chapter.

->She enters the monastery. She lives there very contentedly, yet in poor health. Her practice of prayer. An unfortunate medical treatment and the consequences of her illness. The fruits of her prayer.<-

### 1.

During those days, while I was occupied with such thoughts, I also persuaded one of my brothers to enter a monastery by pointing out the vanity of this world. We both decided to go to the monastery very early on a certain day [November 2, 1535] <note>November 2nd is All Souls' Day, a significant day for reflecting on mortality and the souls of the departed</note>.

As far as I can remember, it seems to me truly that when I left my father's house, I was in such a state that I do not believe I will feel greater pain on my deathbed; for it felt as if all my bones were being pulled apart. Because I did not yet have the love of **God** that would make me forget the love for my father and friends, I had to do great violence to myself in all of this. However, the **Lord** granted me such courage against myself that I carried it out anyway.

### 2.

As soon as I had taken the habit <term>Habit: The distinctive clothing worn by members of a religious order, representing their commitment to a consecrated life</term>, the **Lord** immediately let me know how faithfully He stands by those who do violence to themselves to serve Him. From that hour, such a great joy came over me because of the life I had chosen that it has never left me to this day. **God** transformed the dryness <term>Dryness: A technical term in Christian mysticism (original: "Trockenheit") referring to a period where a person feels no emotional or spiritual "warmth" or satisfaction in their prayers</term> with which my soul was afflicted into a great tenderness of heart, so that everything practiced in the monastery was pleasant and lovely to me.

# Seventh Section. The Life

<meta>catchword: 11. Whether</meta>

...did not avoid it, the danger was already at hand; from which God nevertheless rescued me in such a way that it is clear to see how He cared for me even against my own will, so that I might not entirely ruin myself. This could not happen so secretly that a suspicion did not arise in my father; for as it seems to me, not even three months had passed since I had pursued these vanities <note>original: "Eitelkeiten"; refers to her interest in worldly fashion, romance novels, and social status</note> when I was placed in a convent in this city where persons of that kind are usually raised.

8. During the first eight days, the convent seemed very difficult to me, but more because I worried that my vanity might have become known than because I was enclosed there, for I was already weary of those same vanities. But within eight days, I was more content there than in my father's house. And although it was then still very much against my will to become a religious <note>original: "geistlich zu werden"; to enter a religious order as a nun</note>, I was nonetheless gladdened to see such pious nuns; and my soul began to accustom itself again to the good exercises of my earliest years; and I saw well what a great grace God shows to those whom He brings into the company of pious people. Blessed be You, O Lord! that You have tolerated me so long.

9. One of these nuns slept near us, and I began to find pleasure in her holy company; she told me in what manner she had come into the convent, solely because she had read the words in the Gospel: *Many are called, but few are chosen.* <note>Matthew 22:14</note> She also told me of the reward that God prepares for those who leave everything for His sake. This good company now began to gradually root out of me those habits which the evil company had planted, and to impress back into my mind the longing for eternal things, and also to somewhat lessen my great dislike for the convent life. When I saw one nun weeping during prayer, or another who possessed some virtue, I was envious of them, for my heart in this regard was quite hard. I began to say many vocal prayers and to recommend myself to everyone in the house, asking that they should pray to God to put me in such a state in which I could serve Him.

10. I was in this convent for a year and a half when I fell into a severe illness, so that I had to return to my father. As I improved, I was taken to my sister's house, who lived on a farmstead <term>Meyerhof: a managed farm or manor estate</term>. Along the way lived one of my father's brothers, a very virtuous man and a widower; he spent his time reading spiritual books, and his conversation was commonly of God and the vanity of the world: I had to read to him from these same books. Although I truly had no particular desire for it, I nonetheless pretended as if it pleased me; for I always strove to the utmost to please others, even when it was otherwise contrary to my own will, so that what would have been a virtue in others was a great fault in me. O gracious God! in what ways and manners has His Majesty <note>A term Teresa frequently uses for God</note> gradually prepared me for the state in which He wished to use me, while I (even against my will) did violence to myself and overcame myself; may He be blessed for this in eternity, Amen.

### Seventh Piece. The Life

<meta>catchword: cher</meta>

3. I confess that I often spent those same hours, which I previously used to pamper and adorn my body, in sweeping the house; and when I remembered that I was now freed from those former vanities, a new joy arose in my heart. This surprised me, and I could not understand from where it came. When I think of it, there is nothing in the world so difficult that I would not trust myself to endure it. For I have now learned in many things that if I help myself in the beginning through a serious resolution, His Majesty <note>original: "seine Majestät"; Teresa frequently refers to God as "His Majesty."</note> repays it even in this life in such a way that only those who experience it can understand. For when something is done out of pure intention for God, He wills that the soul initially be terrified by it; and the greater this fear is, the greater is the reward when she overcomes it, feeling thereafter all the greater comfort and delight.

4. O You my God and my only rest! Here I do not know how to continue; for when I remember the manner in which I made my profession <note>The formal act of taking permanent religious vows as a nun.</note>, with what resolution and comfort I performed it, and how I have been wedded to You, I cannot speak of it without tears. They should rightly be tears of blood; indeed, my heart itself should burst, and even that would be too little when I see how I have offended Your Divine Majesty again.

5. The first year I spent in poor health, and therefore my father exerted himself to see how I might be helped. Because I found no relief from the doctors of this city, he arranged for me to be taken to another place which was famous for the healing of many kinds of illnesses.

6. My cure was supposed to begin at the start of the summer, but I had already set out at the beginning of winter. In the meantime, I stayed at my sister’s house because the place was nearby. During the journey, my father gave me a book <term>The Third Spiritual Alphabet <note>original: "Abcedarium tertium"; a famous work by the Franciscan Francisco de Osuna that taught the "method of recollection."</note></term> which teaches how one should collect oneself in prayer. I rejoiced greatly over this book and resolved to follow its guidance with all seriousness; I also began to spend certain hours in solitude.

7. Along this path, the Lord has so anticipated me with His favor that He granted me the gift of the **Prayer of Quiet**; at times I even reached **Union**, although at that time I did not understand what either one was, or how highly such a gift was to be valued. It is true that this Union did not last long; however, it left such great effects in me that although I was not yet twenty years old, I felt as if the entire world were beneath my feet. I felt pity for those who followed the world, even in permissible things.

8. I applied myself, according to my ability, to have Jesus Christ our Lord and highest good internally present within me everywhere. And this was my way of praying. Whenever I contemplated any mystery of His life, I would imagine it as present within me, although I spent most of my time reading spiri—

8. ...reading <note>The text continues from the previous page: "...spent my time reading spiritual books."</note> spiritual books, because the Lord had not given me the skill to reflect much with my understanding. For eighteen years, I spent my time in such a laborious way and in such dryness <note>Spiritual "dryness" or aridity is a term used by mystics to describe a period where prayer feels empty, difficult, and devoid of emotional consolation.</note> (namely, that I could not meditate). Throughout all those years, I did not dare to begin my prayers without having a book in my hand; my soul feared entering into prayer without a book as much as if it had to fight against a great multitude of people. However, by means of the book—which served as a companion and a shield with which I had to catch the blows of my many distracting thoughts—I comforted myself. Otherwise, I was not always in such dryness, but as often as I did not have a book with me, my soul would immediately become confused and my thoughts scattered. Often, it was enough for me simply to open the book; sometimes I read a little, sometimes a lot, according to the grace the Lord granted me.

9. When the time had finally come, they led me with great care to the place where I was to be cured. I remained there for three months and endured great pain, because the cure was far too violent for my nature. Within two months, I was almost completely ruined by the medicines, and the pain in my heart (for which I had traveled there) was much greater; it felt at times as if my heart were being torn and mangled by sharp teeth, so much so that they feared I would lose my mind. Due to a great lack of strength—since I could eat nothing out of revulsion except for perhaps a little broth—and having a constant fever, I was completely exhausted. Because they had given me <term>purgatives</term> <note>Strong laxatives or emetics used in early medicine to "cleanse" the body of ill humors, often causing severe dehydration.</note> every day for an entire month, I was so withered that my tendons began to contract and pull at one another. This caused such unbearable pain that I could find no rest day or night, and a great sadness of spirit also fell upon me. With such "profit," my father led me home again, where I was visited by doctors once more; they all completely despaired for my life and said that, on top of everything else, I had <term>consumption</term> <note>original: "Dörrsucht"; a wasting disease, often referring to tuberculosis or similar terminal conditions.</note>.

10. Now I marvel at it myself and consider it a great grace from God that His Majesty <note>Teresa’s preferred title for God, reflecting her view of Him as a Great King.</note> granted me such patience, so that one could clearly perceive that it came from Him. What helped me greatly toward this patience was that I had read the life and history of Saint **Job**, as Saint **Gregory** describes it in his ***Moralia*** <note>original: "Moralibus"; referring to Pope Gregory the Great's *Moralia in Iob*, a famous medieval commentary on the Book of Job.</note>. I had also begun to practice prayer, as if the Lord had wanted to arm and prepare me beforehand so that I could endure it all with such conformity of my will to His. All my conversation was only with God, and I commonly had these words of Saint **Job** in my thoughts and on my lips: *Shall we receive good at the hand of the Lord, and shall we not also accept the evil?* <note>original: "Haben wir Gutes von der Hand des HErrn empfangen, warum sollten wir das Böse nicht auch annehmen?"; a quote from Job 2:10.</note> And I believe this strengthened me.

### of Saint Teresa of JESUS. Chap. III.

...spent [time] with books, because the Lord had not given me the skill to reflect much with my understanding. I spent eighteen years in such a laborious way and in dryness (namely, that I could not meditate). Throughout all these years, I did not dare to go to prayer <note>In this context, "prayer" refers to "mental prayer" or quiet contemplation, rather than recited vocal prayers.</note> without having a book at hand; so much did my soul fear going to prayer without a book, as if it had to fight against a great multitude of people. However, by means of the book—which served as my company and as a shield with which I had to parry the blows of my manifold thoughts—I comforted myself. For otherwise I was not always in such dryness; but whenever I did not have a book with me, my soul would immediately become confused and my thoughts scattered. Through the book, I gradually gathered them again and brought the soul back to its senses, as if by coaxing it with kindness. Often it was enough for me just to open the book; sometimes I read a little, sometimes much, according as the Lord granted me grace.

9. Now when the time had come, they led me with great care to the place where I was to be cured. I remained there for three months and endured great pain, because the cure was far too violent for my nature. Within two months, I was almost completely destroyed by the medicines, and the pain in my heart (on account of which I had gone there) was much greater; so much so that at times it felt as if my heart were being torn and mangled with sharp teeth, so that people even feared I would go mad. Because of a great lack of strength—since I could eat nothing else for the horror of it except perhaps a little broth—and having a constant fever and being completely exhausted, and because they had given me purgatives every day for a whole month, I was so withered and dried out that even my tendons <note>The original German "Spannadern" refers to tendons or nerves that felt as though they were shrinking or contracting painfully.</note> began to pull together. This caused such unbearable pain that I could have no rest day or night; added to this, a great sadness of spirit fell upon me. With such "profit," my father led me home again, where I was visited by doctors once more; they all despaired of me entirely and said that, on top of everything else, I had consumption <term>The original term is "Dörrsucht," an old word for a wasting disease or phthisis, where the body appears to dry up and wither away.</term>.

10. Now I marvel at it myself and consider it a great grace from God that His Majesty granted me such patience, so that one could clearly perceive it came from Him. What helped me much toward such patience was that I had read the life and history of Saint Job, as Saint Gregory describes it in his <term>Moralia</term> <note>Original: "Moralibus." This refers to the "Moralia in Job," an extensive commentary on the Book of Job by Pope Gregory the Great.</note>; and also that I had begun to practice prayer, as if the Lord had wanted to arm me and make me ready beforehand, so that I could endure it all with such conformity of my will. ### Seventh Part. The Life

...at any hour and moment, I would give up the ghost; indeed, they sometimes even held me for dead, and there was much calling upon and praying to God for me. Blessed be He who was willing to hear such pleading! For after the grave had already been open in my cloister for a day and a half <note>Historical accounts of Saint Teresa’s life note that her sisters had already prepared her grave and performed funeral rites, believing her deceased during this profound coma.</note>, it pleased the Lord to let me come to myself again, whereupon I immediately desired to confess. Yet had I died at that time, it would, in my opinion, have been doubtful for my salvation. And this is certain: when I consider within myself how the Lord has, as it were, raised me again from the dead, I am still so terrified by it that I tremble all over.

12. From this four-day fainting spell <note>original: "Ohnmacht"</note>, I remained so badly damaged that God alone can know what unbearable pains I felt within me. My tongue was shredded and bitten; my throat was as if I were to suffocate, because I had swallowed nothing for a long time; and from great exhaustion—as if I must die—I could not even get water down. All the limbs of my body were as if they were dislocated, with a great weakness of the head, and my whole body was contracted and drawn together like a ball; for this was the outcome of the pains of those days, that I could move neither arm, hand, foot, nor head, any more than if I were dead, unless others moved me. Only one finger (it seems to me) on my right hand could I move. Thus, I could not be touched in any way, because everything about me was so ill-disposed and painful that I could not endure it. In a linen sheet, which one person held on one side and another on the other, they had to lift and lay me, which lasted until Easter.

13. But soon I hastened to return to my cloister, so that I had myself carried there in such a poor state, even though I was nothing but skin and bone; and I remained in this miserable condition for over eight months. I was deprived of the use of my limbs for almost three years, though it gradually became better.

14. # The Third Chapter.

->After regaining her health and neglecting inner prayer, **Teresa** becomes distracted by vanity. Ruin and danger in most convents. She guides her father toward prayer and recounts his godly life and death. She also returns to prayer herself and recommends associating with the devout.<-

->I.<-

Thou faithful **God**, behold, I desired health so that I might serve Thee better, and that very health was a cause of my harm. I did indeed think at times that if I were to reach damnation through health, it would be far better for me to remain in such a state [of illness]; but nonetheless, I also thought that I would be able to serve **God** much better with a healthy body. And this is how we deceive ourselves, in that we do not entirely surrender ourselves to **God** in everything **He** wishes to do with us, who yet knows better what is useful for us. For who would have thought that I should fall again so soon after receiving so many graces from **God**? After His Divine Majesty had begun to give me the virtues?

**O Lord**! Must we then hover in such a dangerous life? I, however, **O Lord**! often would not accept the same, and would not notice when **You** called me back, as I will now relate.

# Seventh Section. The Life

from one vanity to another, from one opportunity to another, I moved in such a way that I ventured into great opportunities for sin. I had entangled my soul in so many vanities that I was already ashamed to return to **God** and to draw near to Him again through such a special friendship and fellowship (as is the act of conversing with **God** through prayer). And this was the most harmful deceit the evil enemy <note>original: "böser Feind" — a common term for Satan.</note> could have inflicted upon me: namely, that I began to fear practicing inner prayer <term>innerliches Gebät: also known as mental prayer or contemplation, involving a silent, personal conversation with God rather than reciting set formulas.</term> under the guise of humility, because I saw myself as so wicked. It seemed better to me to live according to the common course of others—since I was one of the worst among the wicked—and that I was only obligated to pray vocally <note>Reciting standard prayers like the Our Father or Hail Mary aloud, as opposed to the silent "inner prayer" she felt unworthy of.</note>, rather than practicing inner prayer and having such great fellowship with **God**, I who was worthy only of dwelling among the hellish spirits. I felt that I was merely deceiving people by maintaining a good outward appearance.

3. Therefore, I believe it harmed me greatly that I was not in an enclosed convent <note>A "closed" or "enclosed" convent (clausura) practiced strict separation from the world. Teresa’s current convent, the Incarnation in Ávila, was quite relaxed at the time, allowing many visitors and social visits.</note>; for the freedom which the pious could use rightly and well would surely have dragged me—being malicious as I am—straight to hell, had the **Lord** not rescued me from such dangers through so many means and ways. If parents were to follow my advice, I would counsel them not to look toward or consider placing their children in such places or convents where their salvation is in greater danger than in the world itself. They should at least take care of their honor, and would do much better to allow them even the humblest marriage than to put them into such convents, unless the children are very much inclined toward the good of their own accord—and may **God** grant that even this inclination helps—otherwise, let them keep the children at home. It is a pity that many desire to separate themselves from the world, thinking they are entering the service of **God** and avoiding worldly dangers, yet find themselves in a tenfold world, such that they do not know what to do or how to help themselves.

4. The path of true spirituality, however, is so little practiced that a clergyman or nun who wants to begin living up to their calling uprightly and seriously, as is fitting, has more to fear from their own fellow members of the order than from all the devils themselves. They must act with more vigilance and dissemble <note>original: "dissimuliren" — to hide one's true feelings or intentions.</note> more when they speak of the friendship and fellowship one should have with **God**, than when they gossip about other disorderly friendships and affections <note>original: "unordentlichen Freundschaften" — attachments or "particular friendships" that distracted from religious devotion.</note> which the evil enemy is accustomed to weave in the convents. I do not know why we wonder that such many and great evils are found in the Christian churches today, since those who should be an example to others, from whom all others should learn virtue, so poorly soil the work and the labor, and so dissipate the spirit that the first holy Fathers left behind in the convents; He knows how necessary it is [to restore it], Amen.

### Of St. Teresa of Jesus. Chapter III.

...that it would bring such great harm to my soul and distraction of the mind, because I commonly saw others doing the same. However, once when I was with a certain person <note>Teresa frequently received visitors in the convent parlor, a practice she later realized hindered her spiritual progress.</note>, the Lord wished to give me to understand that such acquaintances were not fitting for me. **Christ the Lord** appeared before me with a very stern countenance and made me understand that such things were not pleasing to Him. I saw Him with the eyes of the soul much more clearly than I could have ever seen Him with the eyes of the body; and His form remained so impressed upon me that, although more than twenty-six years have passed since then, it is as if I were seeing Him present right now. I was violently terrified and confused by this, and I no longer wished to see that same person with whom I was then dealing. It harmed me greatly that I did not know it was possible to see something in a way other than with physical eyes; the evil enemy <note>original: "böser Feind" — referring to the Devil.</note> urged me to believe it was impossible, and that it was perhaps a delusion or a work of the devil, and other such things.

6. I also had a friend among the sisters who was now old, a zealous servant of **God**, and very devout. She also warned me from time to time; but not only did I not believe her, I even became at odds with her, believing she was offended by me without cause. I have wanted to recount this so that one may see my own wickedness and, on the other hand, the great goodness of **God**, and how I would have well deserved hell for such great ingratitude.

7. During my illness, when at first I could not yet help myself, I had an intense longing to help others toward virtue. This is a common temptation for beginners, though it turned out quite well for me. Because I loved my father very much, I wished for him to possess that same good which (in my opinion) I enjoyed through the practice of inner prayer <term>innerliches Gebät: also known as mental prayer; a form of silent, personal conversation with God that goes beyond reciting set prayers.</term>. Since I believed no higher good could exist in this life, I sought to bring him to the point where he would give himself to this practice. To that end, I gave him books; and this practice took such a hold in him that within about five or six years he had improved so remarkably that I greatly praised **God the Lord** for it.

8. Very great adversities met him in many ways, and he survived them all with great conformity of his will to the Divine. He came often to visit me, as it was a comfort to him to speak of divine things. Later, however, when I had given way to distractions <note>original: "Ausschweifungen" — here meaning spiritual "wanderings" or diversities of interest rather than moral debauchery.</note> and had abandoned prayer—and because I saw that he still believed I was as I had been before—I could not restrain myself but had to reveal the truth to him. For I had abandoned the practice of prayer for a whole year and more, believing that such a course was more consistent with humility. But because he had by then already reached a high degree of perfection <note>original: "Staffel der Vollkommenheit" — a common mystical term for spiritual maturity.</note>, he no longer stayed with me as much as before; instead, when he had seen me, he would leave again, for he said it was only a waste of time. Not only him, but several other persons I brought to give themselves to prayer, even while I was still stuck in these vanities.

### Section Seven. The Life

9. Around this time, my father fell into the illness from which he eventually died. He made a beautiful end <note>A "beautiful end" in this context refers to a "good death," a significant concept in 16th-century spirituality where the dying person remained conscious, repentant, and received the last rites with devotion.</note>, and died so willingly that it gave us cause to praise **God**; as also for the salutary teachings he gave us. He earnestly commanded us to pray for him, that we should serve **God** at all times, and well consider that all things are transitory. With tears, he told us how much he regretted that he had not served **God** more diligently, and he wished that he had been one of the strictest members of a religious order that could be found.

10. Very laborious was the life that I led then, because through prayer I recognized my faults better. On one side, **God** called me; on the other, I followed the world. Divine things were indeed very pleasant to me, but worldly things still held me bound. It seemed as if I wanted to reconcile these two opposing things, which are yet so entirely contrary to one another: that is, the spiritual life and spiritual comfort, and sensual joys and delights. In prayer, I suffered much toil and labor, since the spirit was not master but servant; therefore, I could not <term>interiorly collect or enclose myself<note>This refers to "Recollection," a specific stage of Teresian prayer where the soul withdraws from external sensations to find God within.</note></term> (which was my only way of praying) without simultaneously enclosing a thousand kinds of vanities. In this way, I spent many years, so that I now wonder how I was able to endure it without ceasing one or the other. This much I know well: that it was never in my power to cease my prayer, because He who loved me held me with His hand, so that He might later grant me greater graces.

11. You faithful **God**! If I were to recount all the opportunities that **God** turned away from me during these years, and how I cast myself back into them again, as well as all the dangers from which He rescued me! O **Lord** of my soul! How shall I ever be able to sufficiently weigh the graces that You granted me through those same years? Also, how at the time when I offended You most, You prepared me in a short time through a very great repentance, so that I might taste and enjoy Your sweet refreshments and graces. Truly, You, O my King! have used such a means in this that was for me at once the sweetest and most painful punishment that could be found: namely, You chastised my misdeeds with great and sweet consolations.

12. It is a great misery when a soul finds itself alone among so many dangers; for (as it seems to me) if I had had someone with whom I could have discussed all of this, it would have helped me so that I did not fall back again—at the very least out of shame, since I felt no shame before **God**. Therefore, I advise those who practice prayer, especially in the beginning, that they strive to have fellowship with persons who also practice the same. Much

# The Fourth Chapter <note>In the standard editions of St. Teresa's *Life*, this marks the beginning of Chapter 8.</note>

## The Utility and Safety of Interior Prayer. How Teresa was finally more encouraged and graced with the presence of **God** in prayer. ->I.<-

Not without reason have I considered this time of my life so diligently, for I see clearly that no one could take pleasure in such a wretched thing; I also wish that those who read this might feel a horror of me, as of such a stubborn and ungrateful soul toward Him who has shown her so much grace. I also wish that I had permission to recount how many different times I was unfaithful during this period, for lack of leaning upon this strong and firm pillar of prayer. I sailed upon this stormy sea for nearly twenty years, falling and rising again, though not as I should have, since I sank back down afterward. It is true that during these years I sometimes took care for many months, and once even for an entire year, not to offend **God**; I also practiced prayer diligently and applied great effort so that I might not offend Him. I recount this so that everything I write here may be according to the highest truth; however, I remember few such good days, so they must have been few, while the bad days were many. <meta>This page continues Chapter 8 of the autobiography of St. Teresa of Avila (labeled here as the Fourth Chapter of the section on "The Life"). ### Seventh Part. The Life

...spent in **prayer**, unless I was very ill or otherwise prevented. When I was unwell, I was better off with **God**; I also took care that those people who associated with me were of a similar disposition. I prayed to **God** for this and often spoke of Him. Thus—excluding only that one year of which I have spoken—out of the twenty-eight years that have passed since I first began to practice **prayer**, I spent over eighteen years in this struggle and battle, trying to reconcile **God** and the world at the same time.

2. This I can say from my own experience: whoever has once begun to practice **prayer**, even if they still commit many wrongs, should nevertheless not abandon it. For this is the means by which they can be set right again; without it, however, things will be very difficult. And let no one be persuaded by the evil enemy <note>The "evil enemy" is a common historical term for the Devil.</note>—as happened to me—to abandon it out of a sense of humility. Instead, let them believe that **God’s** words cannot fail: namely, that if we have true repentance and firmly resolve never to offend **God** again, He will receive us back into His former friendship. But as for those who have not yet begun this practice, I beg them for the love of **God** not to deprive themselves of such a great good. There is nothing to fear here, but rather much to be desired. Interior prayer <note>original: "innerliche Gebät" — refers to mental prayer or contemplation, where one speaks to God from the heart rather than just reciting set formulas.</note> is nothing else than making friendship with **God**, and frequently keeping company in private with Him whom we know loves us. And if you perhaps do not love Him yet—because for it to be a true love and lasting friendship, the condition and nature of the persons must be equal and in harmony on both sides; and while there is no lack on the **Lord's** side, we on our side are flawed, sensual, and ungrateful—if you therefore cannot bring yourself to love Him so fervently because He is not like you, nevertheless, because it is so important for you to be in His friendship and because He loves you so much, bear this discomfort <note>original: "Pein" — refers to the boredom or spiritual "dryness" one feels when beginning a prayer practice.</note> willingly when you remain for a long time with the **Lord**, who is so unlike you.

3. O, the infinite goodness of my **God**! See, it seems to me that I now see both You and myself in this way. O You joy of the angels, how I wish, when I consider this, to melt away entirely in love for You! O how true it is that You gladly endure the one who cannot endure You and Your presence! O what a faithful friend You show Yourself to be, my **Lord**! How kindly You deal with him, how You suffer him and wait until he becomes like You, and meanwhile, how gladly You endure his ways! You, O **Lord**, hold it in high regard when he occasionally desires to love You; and for the sake of a tiny speck of true repentance, You forgive everything with which he has offended You. This I have clearly experienced in myself, and I do not see, my **Lord** and Creator, why the whole world does not strive to draw near to You through this extraordinary friendship.

5. Therefore, my soul was now tired and exhausted; though it wished to rest, the bad habits I had formed did not allow it. ### Seventh Part. The Life.

...spent in prayer, unless I was very ill or was otherwise prevented. When I was ill, I was better off with God; I also took care that those people who associated with me were of a similar disposition, and I asked this of God and often spoke of Him. Thus (excepting only this past year, of which I have spoken), out of the twenty-eight years that have passed since I began to practice prayer, I spent over eighteen years in this struggle and battle, trying to manage both God and the world at the same time.

2. This I can say from my own experience: that whoever has once begun to practice prayer, even if they still do much that is evil, should nevertheless not abandon it. For prayer is the means by which one can be set right again; without it, however, things will go very hardly. And let no one be persuaded by the Evil Foe <note>The "Evil Foe" or "böser Feind" is a common period term for the Devil.</note> (as happened to me) to give up prayer out of a false sense of humility. Instead, let one believe that the words of God cannot fail: namely, that if we have true repentance and firmly resolve never to offend God again, He will receive us back into His former friendship. But to those who have not yet begun this practice, I beg them for the love of God not to deprive themselves of such a great good. There is nothing to fear here, but rather much to desire. For interior prayer <note>original: "innerliche Gebåt" — also known as mental prayer; a contemplative, heart-to-heart conversation with God rather than the recitation of set formulas.</note> is nothing other than making friendship with God, and often spending time in private with Him whom we know loves us. And if you perhaps do not yet love Him—since for it to be a true love and lasting friendship, the conditions and dispositions of the persons must be equal and in harmony with each other; and while on the Lord's side there is no lack, as is well known, we on our side are at fault, sensual, and ungrateful—if, therefore, you cannot bring yourself to love Him so fervently because He is not your equal, nevertheless, because it is so important for you to be in His friendship and because He loves you so much, gladly endure the discomfort <note>original: "Pein" — refers here to the mental strain or "pain" of staying focused in prayer when one feels spiritually dry or distracted.</note> you feel when you stay a long time with the Lord, who is so unlike you.

3. O, the infinite goodness of my God! Behold, it seems to me that I see both You and myself in this state. O You joy of the angels, how I wish, when I consider this, that I could melt away entirely in love for You! O how true it is that You gladly tolerate the one who cannot tolerate You and Your presence! O what a faithful friend You show Yourself to be, my Lord! How kindly You deal with him, how You endure him and wait until he conforms to Your way, while in the meantime You gladly bear with his ways! You, O Lord, value it highly when he occasionally desires to love You, and for the sake of one tiny speck of true repentance, You forget everything with which he has offended You. This I have clearly experienced in myself, and I do not see, my Lord and Creator, why the whole world does not strive to draw near to You through this extraordinary friendship.

# Seventh Section. The Life #

...what others have striven with the greatest effort and labor to obtain, merely by being willing to accept it, the Lord has overwhelmed me, throughout these last years, with comfort and sweetness <note>original: "Süssigkeit" — a technical term in mystical theology referring to an intense, spiritual pleasure or "sensible devotion" felt during prayer.</note>.

But that I should have asked Him to grant me such comfort, or any kind of tender, sensible devotion, I have never been so bold; this alone I asked Him: that He would grant me grace so that I might not offend Him, and that He would forgive my great sins. And because I saw that these sins were so great, I did not even dare to intentionally desire such sweetness and comfort. Indeed, it seemed to me His goodness was doing a great deal simply by permitting me to be in His presence; for I saw clearly that, had He Himself not drawn me to it, I would never have come. Only once in my entire life do I remember asking for such sweetness from Him, when I found myself in great dryness of spirit <note>original: "Truckenheit des Geistes" — a state where a person feels no emotional or spiritual "warmth" in their religious practice, often described as a desert experience.</note>; but as soon as I realized what I was doing, I was filled with shame, seeing how little humility I possessed.

8. At times, I unexpectedly felt such a sensation of the presence of God within me that I could in no way doubt that God was inside me, or that I was completely submerged and absorbed in Him. This was not like a vision or apparition <note>Teresa distinguishes here between "intellectual" or "infused" presence and "imaginary" visions where one actually "sees" a figure.</note>; rather, it lifts the soul so far above itself that it seems as if it were entirely outside of itself. The will then loves, the memory seems almost lost, and the understanding does not reflect (so it seems to me), yet it does not lose itself; rather (as I have said), it does not act, but is as if stunned with wonder at the many things it understands there; for God wills that it should realize it can grasp nothing of all that His Divine Majesty presents to it.

9. I beg him to whom I am sending this, for God's sake, that he would make known what I have said so far regarding my evil life and sins; from this moment on, I give him permission to do so, and if it pleases him, even now while I am still living; so that I may no longer deceive the world, which imagines there is something good in me. And this I can say for certain and in all truth (at least as much as I feel in myself now), that this would be a great comfort to me. However, regarding what I shall say from here on, I give him no such permission; nor do I wish, if he should show it to anyone, that he say who it is who experienced these things, or who wrote them. For this reason, I do not name myself or anyone else, but will write it as much as possible so that I may not be recognized; and this I ask of you for the sake of God.

If the Lord should grant me the grace to say something good, it will be His and not mine, since I am without learning or a pious life, and have been instructed in this by no scholar, nor by anyone else. For only those who command me to write know that I am writing this—and they are not here at present. I write it so that I must almost steal the time for it, and with great effort, for it hinders me from spinning <note>Teresa was a cloistered nun; her "work" for the community involved manual labor like spinning wool to help support the poor convent.</note>, and I live now in a poor convent and am burdened with many duties. # The Fifth Chapter.

## Teresa begins to describe her various experiences and states of prayer. And treats first of meditation.

-> I. <-

Accordingly, St. Teresa begins to describe the different types of interior prayer; since all of this has flowed from her own experience, it must necessarily be included here as a small depiction of her inner guidance and the best part of her biography, as much as this short summary will allow.

Our Saint presents our interior to us under the image of a garden, which the soul, as a gardener, must tend; so that she may present the four main stages of prayer in a somewhat graspable way, she says this garden can be watered in four ways: (1) Either that one draws the water as if from a well, or (2) pulls it up by a well-sweep <term>well-sweep: a long pivoted pole used to raise a bucket from a well, requiring less effort than hand-drawing but more than irrigation.</term> or wheel; or (3) that one conducts the water from a river or stream into the garden. Or finally (4) that God the Lord Himself waters the garden through abundant rain.

### Seventh Part. The Life

...very difficult for them; they must also gradually accustom themselves to wanting to see or hear nothing, and actually putting this into practice at the hour of prayer, surrendering themselves to solitude; and thus separated, reflecting on their former life. Thus one also contemplates a mystery of the Passion of Jesus Christ, as for example, when He was bound to the pillar; so it is now good to reflect for a while and consider the pain He endured there, for whom He suffered it, and who He is that suffered it; yet one must not always weary oneself with such reflection, but rather remain there with Christ, keeping the intellect in peace and silence. When the soul is able, let her fix the eyes of the intellect on Him who sees her, and keep Him company; let her desire this or that from Him, humble herself before Him, and delight in Him, etc.

3. This is an excellent way to grow much in a very short time; indeed, whoever applies themselves to keeping this precious company with them, using it diligently, and seeking from the heart the love of this Lord to whom we are so deeply indebted, of them I say that they have already progressed much.
