# Seventh Piece. The Life

a disregard for honor, and not to be bound to worldly goods. We have such small-minded and narrow hearts that we imagine we would immediately lack for earthly things if we were to cast off concern for the body and devote ourselves to the spirit. From that moment on, it seems to us that it would help toward a better *recollection* <note>original: "Versammlung des Gemüths" — a technical term in mysticism for gathering one's internal thoughts and focusing them entirely on God, rather than letting them wander.</note> of the mind if there were plenty of everything the body requires, because such worries cause unrest in prayer. It pains me that we have so little trust in GOD and so much self-love that this worry can make us restless, and yet we still think we are spiritual in our mindset.

Those who walk in such a way want (it seems to me) to balance the body with the soul in such a manner that they do not lose their comfort and yet still enjoy God in the hereafter; but these are merely **rooster-steps** <note>original: "Hahnen-Schritte" — an idiom referring to very small, hesitant, or insignificant progress that covers little ground.</note> with which one will never arrive at the freedom of the spirit. And yet, one can indeed follow the saints in this: by practicing solitude, silence, and many other virtues that will not immediately kill our miserable bodies—though they certainly want to be so properly tended to that the soul is thrown into disorder.

I too am of such a weak nature; as long as I had not fully resolved that I would not care for the body or my health, I was always bound so that I could accomplish nothing; though even now I do little enough. But I understood this trick of the devil: whenever he would suggest to me that I would lose my health, I said: "It matters little if I die." When he suggested I should rest, I said: "I need rest no longer, but rather the Cross," and so forth. Since I have no longer paid so much attention to myself and ceased pampering myself, I have been in much better health.

c) [Teresa gives a third warning against the **untimely urge to convert others**, and says:] Whoever would do any good in this case must first be well-strengthened in virtue, so that they do not become a temptation to others. Another disadvantage follows from this: namely, that the soul neglects its own progress; for what we should most diligently strive for in the beginning is to take care of our soul alone, and to think as if there were no one else on earth but GOD and our soul. And much depends upon this.

d) Another [and fourth] temptation is a pain that such souls feel over the sins and faults they see in others; the evil enemy <note>The "evil enemy" is a common historical reference to the Devil.</note> suggests to them that this pain comes solely from a good desire that God not be offended, and from a sense of the dishonor shown to Him. And immediately they want to remedy this evil; which then makes them so restless that it prevents prayer. However, for a soul that wishes to practice prayer, it is safest to trouble oneself about no one, and to pay attention only to oneself, how one may please God. # The Sixth Chapter.
## II. Concerning the Prayer of Quiet.

->I.<-

It seems to me a great help that, while I am writing this, I am actually in this state of prayer <insert>of which I am writing</insert>. For I see clearly then that it is not I who says this, or who has organized it with her understanding; nor do I know afterward how I was able to write it, and this happens to me frequently.

We shall now say something of the second way of drawing water <insert>to irrigate our garden</insert>, where the gardener, by means of the mechanical wheel and the well-crank <note>original: "Brunnen Wag" — a water-hoisting device, such as a shaduf or a pulley system, which requires less effort than pulling buckets by hand.</note>, brings out much more water and with less effort, being able to rest at times rather than working constantly. This method is assigned to that prayer which is called the Prayer of Quiet <term>Prayer of Quiet: "Gebät der Ruhe," a state of contemplative prayer where the soul experiences a supernatural peace and stillness.</term>. Here the soul begins to collect itself; it already reaches something supernatural, because it can by no means reach this state on its own, no matter how much it might strive for it. It is indeed true that it appears she has labored for a while by turning the wheel or exercising the understanding; nevertheless, the water stands much higher here, and thus there is much less work than when it had to be drawn from the well.

2. This prayer is thus nothing other than a gathering of the soul's powers <term>soul's powers: "Seelen-Kräften," the traditional faculties of the soul—memory, understanding, and will.</term> within itself, so that it may enjoy that same comfort with greater delight and pleasure. Yet the aforementioned powers are not lost here, nor do they fall asleep; the will alone acts here in such a way that it is captured without knowing how.

...a disregard for honor, and not being bound to worldly goods. We have such faint-hearted and narrow hearts that we imagine we would immediately lack for earthly things if we were to cast off care for the body and devote ourselves to the spirit. From that moment on, it seems to us that it helps to better collect the soul if there is a sufficient supply of everything the body needs, because worries cause unrest in prayer. This pains me: that we have so little trust in **God** and so much self-love that this worry can make us restless, and yet we think in our minds that we are spiritual.

Those who walk in such a way want (as it seems to me) to balance the body with the soul in such a way that they do not lose their rest here and also enjoy **God** there; but these are only *cock-steps* <note>original: "Hahnen-Schritte" — a metaphor for small, tentative, or prideful steps that do not cover much ground.</note>, with which one will never arrive at the freedom of the spirit. And so one can indeed follow the saints in practicing solitude, silence, and many other virtues that will not immediately kill our miserable bodies—even though they want to be so orderly attended to that the soul is thrown into disorder.

I am also of such a weak nature; as long as I had not yet entirely resolved that I would not regard the body or health, I was always so bound that I could accomplish nothing; although even now I do little enough. But I understood this trick of the devil: whenever he would suggest to me that I would lose my health, I said: it matters little if I die. When he suggested to me that I should rest, I said: I need no more rest, but rather the cross, and so on. Since I have not paid so much attention to myself and pampered myself, I have been in much better health.

c) <insert>Teresa gives a third warning against the premature urge to convert others, and says:</insert> Whoever should be of some use in this case must first be well-strengthened in virtue, so that they are not a temptation to others. And much depends upon this.

d) Another [ and fourth ] temptation is a pain <note>original: "Pein" — an intense spiritual or mental suffering or distress.</note> that such souls feel over the sins and faults they see in others; the evil enemy suggests to them that this pain comes solely from a good desire that **God** should not be offended, and from a feeling of the dishonor done to Him. And from that moment on, they want to remedy this evil; which then makes them so restless that it hinders prayer. However, for a soul that wants to practice prayer, it is safest to trouble oneself about no one, and only to take heed of oneself, how one may please **God**. Much depends on this; for if I were to recount all the faults I have seen committed by relying on this "good intention," I would never reach an end. Therefore, let us always use diligence...

# The Sixth Chapter.

## II. Of the Prayer of Quiet.

->I.<-

It seems to me a great help that, as I am writing this, I find myself actually in this state of prayer [of which I write]. For I see clearly then that it is not I who says this, nor have I arranged it with my intellect; nor do I know afterwards how I was able to write it. This happens to me frequently.

We shall now say something of the second way of drawing water [to irrigate our garden]. This is when the gardener, by means of a mechanical wheel and a bucket-pump <note>Teresa uses the metaphor of a *noria* (a water wheel with buckets) to describe a stage where spiritual refreshment comes with much less human effort than drawing water by hand from a well.</note>, brings up much more water with less effort, and can sometimes rest during the process rather than working continuously. This method is applied to that state of prayer which is called the **Prayer of Quiet**. Here, the soul begins to collect itself; it reaches toward something supernatural, because it can by no means reach this state on its own, no matter how hard it might strive for it. It is true that it seems as if the soul has labored for a while in turning the wheel—that is, the exercise of the intellect—yet here the water stands much higher, and thus the work is much less than when it had to be drawn manually from the well.

2. This prayer is, therefore, nothing other than a gathering of the soul's powers <note>These "powers" or faculties usually refer to the Memory, Intellect, and Will.</note> within itself, so that it may enjoy that same consolation with more delight and pleasure. Nevertheless, these powers are not lost here, nor do they fall asleep; the **Will** alone acts here in such a way that it is captured <note>or "captivated"</note> without knowing how.

For this love holds our own love so bound that it leaves it no freedom at that time to love anything other than You alone.

The other two faculties <note>Teresa refers to the Scholastic concept of the "three powers of the soul": the Will, the Intellect (Verstand), and the Memory (Gedächtniß).</note> [the intellect and the memory] help the will so that it may make itself fit to enjoy so great a good, although it sometimes happens that they are very much a hindrance to the will, even when it is already united [with God]. For although the will is not yet entirely swallowed up in God here, it is nevertheless so well occupied (without even knowing how) that no matter how much the other faculties exert themselves, they cannot rob it of its rest and joy; rather, without any effort, it gently helps itself so that this tiny spark of divine love <note>The "spark" (Fünklein) is a common mystical term for the deepest part of the soul where the human meets the divine.</note> does not go out.

All that occurs here is full of the highest comfort, and with so little effort that this prayer does not tire one, even if it lasts a long time. The tears that God gives here now flow only with joy; and though one feels them, they are not caused with diligence, nor forced out.

3. 4. No earthly wealth, no power, no honor nor pleasure is sufficient to share with us this joy or comfort for even a single moment, since it is a true joy—indeed, such a joy that satisfies and suffices for the heart. In those earthly things, there is always a "No" or a lack to be found alongside the "Yes"; here, however, at the same time, everything is a pure "Yes," and the "No" only comes afterward, when one sees that it is over and one cannot have it again, nor knows how one might have it again. # The Seventh Chapter.

## III. Concerning the Sleep of the Soul’s Powers.

->1.<-

Now we wish to speak of the third water with which this garden is watered, which is flowing water; here, one waters with much less effort, though one must still labor a little to direct the water. Here the Lord is, as it were, the gardener Himself, and performs everything Himself. This is, in a sense, a sleep of the soul’s powers <term>Seelen-Kräften: In the psychology of Teresa's time, these were the Intellect, Memory, and Will.</term>, where they do not lose themselves entirely, yet they do not understand how they are operating. The sweetness, delight, and enjoyment here are incomparably greater than in the preceding stage.

->2.<-

The powers of the soul are fit for nothing else here than to occupy themselves with God; not one of them dares to stir, nor can we make them move, unless we were to turn away from them with great diligence—though it seems to me that even this could not easily happen at such a time. Many words are spoken here in praise of God, yet without order, unless the Lord Himself puts them in order; at the very least, the intellect can contribute nothing to it. The soul would like to cry out loud to praise God, but it is so situated that it cannot remain within itself, experiencing a sweet and pleasant restlessness. Now, now the flowers open; now they begin to give off their scent. Here the soul would wish that everyone could see her and recognize her glory, so that they might praise God for it, and so that they might help her praise Him and share in her joy, for she cannot bear such great joy alone. It reminds me of that woman in the Gospel who called her neighbors together. <note>original: "jenem Weib im Evangelio"; referring to the Parable of the Lost Coin in Luke 15:9, where the woman rejoices with her friends.</note>

->3.<-

Gracious God, what a glorious state of the soul this is! She should wish to be nothing but tongues to praise the Lord; she speaks a thousand kinds of holy follies <note>original: "heilige Thorheiten"; a mystical concept where the soul's intense love for God appears as madness or irrationality to the world.</note>, only so that she might please Him who treats her in this manner. I know a person <note>Teresa is almost certainly referring to herself here, as was her custom to speak in the third person out of humility.</note> who, although she was no poet, nevertheless composed well-ordered verses without prior thought, in which she clearly expressed her pain.

> Grant, O my King! I pray, that just as I now, while I am writing this, am possessed by this holy folly through Your great goodness and mercy (for without any merit of mine You show me this grace), that all others with whom I associate may also become foolish in Your love; or grant that I...

She characterizes this state as one of "holy folly," where the soul is overwhelmed by a joy it wishes to share with the whole world.</summary>

Behold, your handmaid, O Lord! can no longer endure so much misery <note>German: *Mühseligkeit*. O You, my true Lord, and my highest glory! What a delicate and yet exceedingly heavy cross have You prepared for those who reach this state? Delicate, because it is lovely; heavy, because times come when no patience is so great that it might endure it; and yet, she would never wish to be freed from it, unless it were so that she might come to You. But when she remembers that she has served You so very little, yet could still serve You if she were to live longer, she wishes for an even heavier burden, and would willingly live until the end of the world.

4. Nothing can restrain me from stepping out of [the proper] order in my writing when the Lord ravishes me outside of myself. 5. Thus, here God Himself performs the Gardener’s office; the will of the soul alone consents to those same graces that it enjoys, and it shall offer itself willingly to everything that the true Wisdom wishes to work within it, for which truly a great heart is necessary. For the joy is so great that it sometimes seems very little or nothing is missing for the soul to depart entirely from the body; and what a blessed death would this be? To this, it seems to me, it fits quite well what was said to Your Reverence: that one should lay oneself and surrender oneself entirely into the arms of God. If God wants to raise the soul up to heaven, let Him do so; if He wants to lead it down to hell, it does not grieve her, as long as her highest Good is with her; if He wants to make an end of her life, she wants it too; if He wants her to live a thousand years, that also pleases her. His Majesty may now deal with her as with His own property; the soul is no longer her own, but entirely given over to the Lord; therefore, she cares for nothing. Only, all this happens without any effort of the intellect, for the intellect simply stands there full of wonder.

6. That which the poor soul perhaps could not have attained in twenty years with toil and labor and exhaustion of the intellect, this heavenly [Gardener] accomplishes...

However, He does not yet allow the soul to distribute these fruits to others until she herself has first eaten so much of them that she has now increased [in strength] and become strong, and has not merely tasted of them here and there; this is so that she does not nourish others without her own benefit, and before she pays [as it were] the fruit to Him who gave it to her, while perhaps she herself might meanwhile die of hunger.

7. Here, too, <term>Humility: In Teresa’s writings, humility is "walking in truth"—recognizing one's total dependence on God.</term> is much greater and deeper than in the preceding state; for she sees that she has done neither little nor much in the matter, but has only consented to it. The memory remains free there, and perhaps also the <term>Power of Imagination: The "Einbildungs-Kraft," which Teresa often called "the fool of the house" because it wanders during prayer.</term>; and because it finds itself alone, one must marvel at what a conflict it causes, and how it seeks to throw everything into unrest; it wearies me, and I hate it for that reason, and often say to the Lord: "When, O my God, will my soul at last be entirely united to praise You, and not divided into pieces without being able to help herself?" Here I see what an evil sin has caused us, because it has oppressed us in such a way that we cannot do what we would gladly do: namely, to constantly converse with God. It happened to me again this very day, that I see how my soul melts with longing to be entirely united there, where her best and greatest part is, and yet it is impossible for her, and the memory and the power of imagination cause her such a conflict. ## Chapter Eight.
### IV. Regarding the Union of All the Soul’s Faculties.
<term>Soul’s Faculties: In the psychology of St. Teresa’s time, the soul was understood to have three powers or "faculties": the Understanding (intellect), the Will (desire/love), and the Memory (including imagination).</term>

->I.<-

I will say nothing that I have not experienced myself. To confess the truth, when I began to write about this last water, it seemed as impossible to me as if I were expected to speak Greek; <note>original: "Griechisch reden." Teresa often used the inability to speak Greek as a metaphor for a task that was intellectually impossible or beyond her natural education.</note> I desisted for that reason and went to Holy Communion. Blessed be the Lord, who thus assists the ignorant! See, then God enlightened my understanding as to how I should describe it, so that just as His Divine Majesty has done in the preceding prayer, so He will also speak here what I myself neither can do nor know. And what I say is the fundamental truth; therefore, whatever is good will be His teaching; the evil, however—it is well understood beforehand—comes from the abyss of all evil, which is I myself.

2. Now to speak of this water that comes from heaven, which with its abundance fills and refreshes this entire garden; <note>This "Fourth Water" represents the Prayer of Union, where the "rain" of God's grace falls without any effort from the gardener (the soul).</note> this same water sometimes comes when the gardener is least concerned about it. Nevertheless, it is the truth that this almost always happens at the beginning after long-sustained internal prayer, for the Lord raises this little bird from one step to another until He sets it in the little nest, so that it may find its rest therein, after it has flown long and exerted itself to seek and please God.

3. While the soul seeks God in such a manner, she feels with such exceedingly great and sweet delight <note>original: "Wollust." In this context, it refers to spiritual bliss or "delight," not carnal lust.</note> that she almost entirely dissolves, with such a fainting away <term>Ohnmacht: A spiritual swoon or "ecstasy" where the soul is so overwhelmed by God's presence that the physical body loses its strength.</term> that her breath begins to fail, along with all the strengths of the body, so that she cannot even move her hands except with great difficulty; the eyes close without her desiring to close them, and if she keeps them open, she sees almost nothing. She sees well [if she wants to read] that letters are there, but because the understanding does not help, she cannot read them even if she wanted to; she hears, but does not know what she hears. ### of St. Teresa of JESUS. Chapter VIII.
<meta>catchword: -ness</meta>

...to express; for all external strength is lost, and the internal strength is increased, so that she <note>In the original German and Spanish, the "soul" (die Seele/la alma) is grammatically feminine; Teresa consistently refers to the soul as "she."</note> may better enjoy her glory. This prayer does not injure one’s health, even if it lasts a long time; and what harm could such a great good inflict? The external effects are so noticeable that one cannot doubt it must have been something great, because it even takes away all physical powers with such great delight, and yet leaves them strengthened afterward.

4. One cannot easily notice how long the soul remains in this union of all the soul's faculties, because while one is [within it], one perceives nothing; yet I say that it lasts a very short time, at the longest half an hour, without one of the soul's faculties returning to itself. The will holds its ground here the longest; the other two immediately begin to become burdensome again; but because the will remains calm, it draws them back to itself again, where they stay for a little while once more, then return to themselves and become active. In this way, several hours can pass; for when the two faculties have begun to become intoxicated and to taste of this Divine wine, they lose themselves again very easily, and all three enjoy the joy together.

5. Now we wish to come to the internal aspect—what the soul feels here. I thought to myself, as I was about to write this and had just been in this state of prayer, what the soul actually does at that time. Then the **Lord** said these words to me: 
> Daughter, she annihilates herself entirely so that she may better enter into me; it is now no longer she who lives, but I. 
<note>This is a reference to Galatians 2:20: "It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me."</note>
And because she cannot comprehend what she understands, she understands in an incomprehensible way. Whoever experiences this will understand it to some extent, for it cannot be said more clearly, because everything that happens here is so obscure. This alone I can say: that the soul finds herself close to **God**, and such a certainty of this remains in her that she cannot help but believe it.

All the soul's faculties fail her here and are suspended in such a way that one can in no way perceive that they are working. When the soul contemplates any mystery, she even loses it from her memory, as if she had never thought of it; the will is undoubtedly kept occupied in love, but does not understand how it loves; when the understanding understands, one still does not understand how it understands—it seems to me it understands nothing.

6. In the beginning, I was in ignorance because unlearned men <note>original: "Ungelehrten." Teresa often struggled with confessors who lacked the theological training to understand her mystical experiences.</note> told me the **Lord** was only present through His grace; but I could not believe it, for this seemed so clear to me that I understood [as it were] that His very own presence was there. A very learned man later removed this doubt for me, telling me how **God** is present and has communion with us, which greatly comforted me.

### Seventh Part. The Life
<meta>catchword: the</meta>

...surrounded by goodness; so much so that she <note>In the original German and Spanish, the "soul" (die Seele/la alma) is grammatically feminine; Teresa consistently refers to the soul as "she."</note> would like to dissolve into nothingness, not out of pain, but out of sweet tears, with which she finds herself imperceptibly bathed. She does not even know when or how she shed them, yet it delights her greatly when she sees that the power of this fire is extinguished by such water, which nevertheless [at the same time] causes the fire to prevail all the more. This may seem like speaking Hebrew <note>original: "Hebräisch geredet." A common historical idiom meaning to speak in riddles or in a way that is difficult to understand.</note>, yet it happens exactly this way. It has happened to me at times that I was so far out of myself that I did not know whether it had been a dream, or whether the glory I felt within me had truly happened to me; but because I saw myself so full of tears, which flowed so powerfully and without effort that it seemed as if they rained down from these heavenly clouds, I realized from this that it had not been a dream.

8. This happened in the beginning, when such moments still lasted only a short time; the soul remains powerfully encouraged and magnanimous from this, so that, if she were to be hacked to pieces for God's sake in that very moment, it would be a great comfort to her. There, the most noble promises and resolutions are made; there are the most vivid, burning desires; there, one begins to feel a loathing for the world and to clearly recognize one's vanity, and indeed in a higher way than in the previous <term>stages of prayer: Gebäts-Staffeln; refers to Teresa’s famous classification of the four degrees of prayer</term>; so too has humility grown more here, for the soul sees clearly that she did nothing to achieve or keep such a state; she sees that she is completely unworthy of it, because she has come to such a place where the sun shines very clearly, and no spiderwebs <note>Teresa often uses the metaphor of sunlight revealing dust or spiderwebs to describe how God's presence reveals even the smallest hidden faults in a person.</note> remain hidden.

She recognizes that she is indeed worthy of hell, yet is instead punished with glory; she would like to melt away from the desire to praise God; and even now I feel this within myself. Blessed be you, my Lord, who from such a hideous puddle as I am, makes such pure water that it may be set upon your table! O you joy of the angels, that you would thus exalt such a contemptible little earthworm!

9. Now the soul, because she clearly recognizes that the fruits are not her own, can also begin to share them with others, and this causes her no lack. She begins to be useful to her neighbor, so much so that she hardly notices it herself or adds anything of her own accord; others notice it well, for the flowers have now increased so much in scent that others feel a desire to approach them. They recognize that she has virtues, and they see that these fruits are very good and desirable, and therefore they would like to help her eat them. When this soil is well-cultivated and surrounded by the cross and persecutions, by gossip and illnesses; (for I believe few reach this point without such things) and when it is also well-softened through total renunciation of all self-interest, then this water sinks so deep into it that it almost never dries out again.

10. Once I thought: O Lord! how could it be consistent with your justice that you allowed so many who served you zealously to [not receive] that grace...

of Saint Teresa of Jesus. Ch. IX.

...did you not receive it, you who bestowed it upon me, though I am so evil? There you, O Lord, answered me: “Serve me, and do not meddle in this.”

O infinite liberality! How great and glorious are your works! That you should show such high graces even to souls who have offended you so greatly—this surpasses all my wit and understanding. When I begin to think of it, I sometimes help myself with all sorts of absurd speeches. Often I say: “Lord, see what you are doing; do not forget my great sins so quickly. And since you have forgotten them for the sake of my forgiveness, I pray you, remember them so that you might keep some measure in showing your graces! O my Creator, do not pour such precious oil into such a broken vessel; for you have already seen many times that I spill it again. Do not let your love take such complete upper hand, O eternal King, that you put such precious jewels at risk,” and so forth.

# Chapter Nine.
## Concerning Raptures and Other Graces.

->I.<-

<margin>(a) Way of Perfection, Ch. 6. <note>Original: "Klosterst." (Klosterstiftung). This refers to Teresa’s manual of instruction for her nuns.</note></margin>
This rapture [of which we are speaking here] far surpasses union, and its effects are much greater and more varied. [It is therefore quite distinct from other so-called ecstasies, by which unpracticed or sensitive natures are sometimes overcome, and against which Teresa warns in another place (a), describing the matter as follows:] It often happens that someone begins to experience a certain **Prayer of Quiet**, like a spiritual sleep, which so possesses the soul that if we do not know how to conduct ourselves in it, much time can be spent in vain, and the strength of the body can be exhausted through one’s own fault. I know some who remained thus absorbed for seven or eight hours and thought it was all a pure rapture; indeed, every virtuous exercise so possessed them that they were immediately outside themselves.

2. 3. [True rapture is quite a different matter, which is now further described by our Saint <note>St. Teresa of Avila (1515–1582), the Spanish mystic and reformer of the Carmelite Order.</note> from her own experience as a very high gift of God’s grace:] The Lord, so to speak, seizes the soul, just as the clouds seize the vapors of the earth, and the cloud soars toward heaven and lifts the soul with it, and begins to show it the things of the Kingdom of Heaven which He has prepared for it.

4. Often it seems to me as if the body becomes so light that it takes away all its weight; when one is in rapture, the body remains as if dead, without being able to act or do anything; and it remains in the same position in which the rapture overtook it; whether one is sitting, or has the hands open or closed, so it remains. For although one rarely loses the senses, it has happened to me at times, though seldom, and not for long. Usually, however, they are confused; and even if the body can do nothing regarding external things, it still understands and hears, as if from a distance. Mostly the eyes also remain closed, even though we do not intend to close them; and if they are sometimes open, one still distinguishes nothing.

5. But I do not say that one perceives or hears when the rapture is at its height, that is, when the powers of the soul <note>In classical theology, these are the three faculties: memory, understanding, and will.</note> are lost because they are united with God; for at that time, it seems to me, the soul neither sees, hears, nor feels. But this complete transformation of the soul into God does not last long; as long as it lasts, however, one perceives nothing from the powers of the soul and does not know what is happening. But you will object: how then does it happen that sometimes the rapture lasts for several hours? To this I answer from what often happens to me: that this grace is enjoyed with distinct intervals; sometimes the soul deepens and sinks into God, or better said, it is deepened by the Lord, and when He has kept it with Him for a while, He lets it go again, and keeps only the will with Him.

6. Here there is no means or way to offer resistance; instead, often without any preceding thoughts or cooperation, such a sudden and powerful impulse comes that you see and feel that this cloud or this mighty eagle <note>A traditional metaphor for the overwhelming power of the Divine, often associated with St. John the Evangelist or the Holy Spirit.</note> soars upward and seizes you under its wings, and you see that you are being led away, and you do not know where; for even if it happens with delight, the weakness of our nature still causes us to be afraid at first, and it requires a brave and courageous spirit that dares to risk everything, no matter what may come, and that places itself entirely in the hands of God and follows willingly wherever it is led; for you are led there even if you do not want to go, and indeed so violently that I often wanted to offer resistance and used all my strength for that purpose, out of fear of some deception; sometimes I was able to achieve something with great...

->### Of St. Teresa of Jesus. Chapter IX.<-

->C 2<-

...exhaustion of my strength; at other times it was quite impossible for me <note>That is, to resist the onset of the ecstasy.</note>, but the soul was lifted up, yes, at times even the whole body from the earth. This has happened only rarely; for because it occurred once while we were gathered together, it pained me greatly, as it seems to be a very unusual thing; therefore I then commanded the sisters that they should not speak of it. At another time it happened during a sermon, when I lay down at full length upon the ground, and the others came and held my body; nonetheless, it was clearly perceived. Therefore I begged **the Lord** that He would no longer grant me such graces as were outwardly visible. Now it appears that it has pleased **the Lord** to hear me, since from that time on nothing of the sort has happened to me; though it is true that this was not very long ago.

7. The effects, however, which the rapture causes, are great: here one can see how great the majesty of Him is who can work such things, so that one’s hair stands on end; it also leaves behind a great fear of offending so great a **God**. But this fear is paired with an exceedingly great love, which arises anew from seeing that He bears such great love toward a foul little earthworm <note>original: "faules Erdenwürmlein." A common expression of humility in 16th-century mysticism, emphasizing the distance between the human and the divine.</note>; so much so that it seems as if He were not satisfied with drawing the soul so powerfully to Himself alone, but that He also wants to have the body, which is still so mortal and made of such unclean earth. It also leaves in us a wonderful estrangement and detachment from all things, so that I could not easily describe how it is. Such persons are indeed already completely detached from all things regarding the spirit; but here **the Lord** wills, as I believe, that the body itself should put this into practice, and here arises a new distaste for all things of this world.

Often the body remains entirely healthy from this, which previously was very ill and full of great pain, and is even more nimble and capable than before; for what is given here is a great thing. When one afterwards comes back to oneself, and the rapture has been great, it happens that the powers of the soul remain so bewildered and absorbed for two to three days that it seems as if they were not themselves. This is where one feels the highest pain, because one must return again to living <note>Teresa refers to the "pain" of returning to the mundane world after the beauty of the vision.</note>.

<margin>a) She treats this more extensively in *The Interior Castle* <note>original: "Seelenburg." Teresa’s masterpiece describing the journey of the soul through seven "mansions."</note>, Mansion VI, Chapter 5.</margin>

8. [The types of rapture are, according to Teresa’s experience, distinct, and are called by her sometimes simply a rapture, sometimes an elevation, and sometimes a "flight of the spirit," as each is always higher than the other. Rapture, properly so called, has been treated thus far in this chapter; of "elevation," nothing special shall be mentioned in this extract to save time and space. ### Seventh Piece. The Life

it seems to be nothing else than that the commander of this fortress <note>A recurring metaphor in Teresa’s writing, where the soul is a castle or fortress.</note> ascends or is raised 
up to its highest tower, so that he may plant the banner for **God** there. 
From there, he looks upon those who are down below, as one who finds himself 
in safety; he fears no danger anymore—indeed, he even longs for it, as one 
who is now somewhat assured of victory. Here one sees clearly how 
utterly nothing all things on earth are to be valued. One who stands high can 
survey many things. Such a person desires and wants nothing else than 
what the **Lord** wants; therefore, he also humbly prays to the **Lord** and 
hands over the keys of his will to Him. See, here the gardener <note>Teresa previously used a metaphor comparing stages of prayer to different ways of watering a garden; here, the humble gardener has become a commander.</note> is now 
made the commander of the fortress. I am of the opinion that a soul that 
reaches this state henceforth neither speaks nor acts for itself; instead, 
this highest King takes care of everything it should do or leave undone.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;10. O kind **God**! How clearly one sees here what the meaning of that 
verse of David <note>Refers to Psalm 55:6: "Oh, that I had wings like a dove! I would fly away and be at rest."</note> is, and how rightly he prayed for wings of a dove, and how 
rightly all people should also plead for them. One recognizes clearly 
enough that this is a flight with which the spirit soars, so that it may 
rise above everything that is created, and especially above itself; but 
it is a gentle flight, a delightful flight, a flight without any noise.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;11. O how sovereign and commanding is a soul that the **Lord** raises 
to this height, so that it can see all things before it without being 
entangled in them! And how ashamed it is of those times when it was 
entangled in them! How it marvels at its former blindness! What 
compassion it has for those who are still ensnared therein, especially 
when they are persons devoted to prayer whom **God** visits with 
consolation! It would like to cry out loud to show them how greatly they 
are deceived; indeed, sometimes it even does so, although a thousand 
kinds of persecutions fall upon it like a downpour. People consider such a 
soul to be lacking in humility and think it wants to instruct others, 
from whom it should rather learn itself. Especially when it is a woman 
<note>Teresa often comments on the specific difficulties women faced in the 16th century when claiming spiritual authority or mystical experiences.</note>, then a condemnation begins, and indeed rightly so, for they do 
not know how powerful the impulse is that compels her, so that she 
cannot refrain from revealing their error to those she wishes well.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;12. The sun shines very brightly here, and therefore, no matter 
how much a soul strives to make itself perfect, once it is touched by 
the rays of this sun, it sees itself as cloudy and full of dust. Before 
the soul was in this rapture, it seemed to itself that it was careful 
not to offend **God**; but when it reaches this point where this Sun of 
Righteousness <note>original: "Sonne der Gerechtigkeit." A biblical title for Christ from Malachi 4:2.</note> shines upon it, making its eyes open, then it sees 
so many specks of dust that it would like to close its eyes again; for 
it is not yet a right-natured chick of this mighty eagle, that it 
should be able to look upon this sun with unmoving eyes.

# Of St. Teresa of Jesus. Chapter IX.

...only blinded. Therefore it often happens that the soul remains entirely blind, immersed, and bewildered with wonder at the great things it sees. Here true humility is attained, so that one cares little about saying good things of oneself, or having them said by others. The Lord of the garden distributes the fruit here, and not the soul; therefore, nothing sticks to its fingers <note>An idiom meaning the soul takes no personal credit or selfish profit from God's gifts.</note>. All the good that it possesses is directed toward **God**; if it speaks anything of itself, it is done for His honor, and the soul knows well that it has nothing of its own in the matter. And even if it did not wish to know this, it could not remain unknown to it; for the soul sees it clearly with its own eyes. Whether it wishes to or not, its eyes are closed to earthly things, and it must keep them open to behold the Truth.

13. So I have now spoken of the effects caused by the raptures <note>German: *Verzückungen*; often translated as ecstasies.</note> that come from the Spirit of **God**. Yet, to confess the truth, more or less of this occurs. And it is true that the **Lord** can work so powerfully in a soul in a single rapture that it may afterwards have little trouble in attaining perfection <note>German: *Vollkommenheit*; the state of complete union with God’s will.</note>; for no one can believe, unless they have experienced it, what the **Lord** grants to a soul here.

Why His Divine Majesty does such a thing is only because it so pleases Him; and as it pleases Him, so He does it. And even if the soul were not yet ready for it, He prepares it Himself to receive this good which His Majesty gives to it. In this way, it even seems to some extent as if it were no longer in the soul's power to turn back and live in the sins in which it once lived.

14. Its understanding is now so accustomed to recognizing the truthful Truth that everything else seems like mere child's play. Sometimes the soul laughs within itself when it sees that distinguished [so-called] spiritual persons and individuals devoted to prayer make such a great matter of a tiny point of honor, which this soul has now trodden under its feet. They say, indeed, that this is done out of discretion <term>Discretion: Here used as a critical term for a worldly or overly-cautious "prudence" that prioritizes social standing over spiritual abandon.</term> to maintain their reputation so that they might be more useful to their neighbor; but such a soul knows very well that they would be more useful in a single day if they set aside this reputation for the love of **God** than they would be with it in ten years.

15. Therefore, this soul leads a laborious life and lives in a constant cross; but meanwhile, it increases very much. And when those who lead such souls believe that they have now reached the highest step, it is seen that they are improved much more shortly thereafter, because the **Lord** constantly shows them more graces. For **God** is their soul; He is the one who now takes care of it, and thus He shines before it at all times; for He stands by it as if constantly present and preserves it so that it does not offend Him; He caresses and encourages it to serve Him.

16. When my soul had reached the point where **God** shared such great grace with it, all my evil and my faults came to an end, and the **Lord** gave me...

## The Tenth Chapter.

->She resumes the narrative of her life and recounts how **God** granted her a supernatural gift of prayer. Her fear regarding this. She is further confused by the inexperienced, but finally calmed and encouraged by those with more experience.<-

->I.<-

Now I will turn back again to the narrative of my life. What follows hereafter is another new book, and another new life; the life I led before was *my* life, but the life I have led since I began to explain these matters of prayer is the life which **God** has lived in me, so it seems to me. Blessed be the **Lord**, who has delivered me from myself.

2. As soon as I began to clear the occasions [of distraction] out of the way and to devote myself more to prayer, the **Lord** also began to bestow His grace upon me, appearing to desire nothing more than that I should be willing to receive it. His **Divine Majesty** therefore began very often and habitually to grant me the **prayer of quiet** <term>prayer of quiet: a state of contemplative prayer where the soul is captivated by God's presence, leading to deep inner stillness</term>, and indeed often the **union** <term>union: a state of prayer where the soul’s faculties—will, memory, and understanding—are completely joined with God</term>, which lasted for a good while. I, however, began on one hand to be afraid, because the sweetness I felt was so great, and often happened without my being able to prevent it. On the other hand, I also felt within myself a very great assurance that it was from **God**, especially when I was in prayer; I also saw that I was greatly improved by it and received greater strength. But when I became a little distracted again, I began to fear once more whether the **evil enemy** <note>The Devil</note> might not perhaps, under a good appearance, occupy my understanding in this way so that he might rob me of **internal prayer** [meditation] <note>The German text uses *Betrachtung*, referring to discursive mental prayer or reflecting on mysteries.</note>, which seemed to me to be a great loss because I did not understand it.

3. When I saw that fear was thus gaining the upper hand in me because the prayer was increasing, it occurred to me that there must be a very great good or a very great evil hidden herein. For I now understood well that what I experienced was a supernatural thing; because at times I could offer no resistance to it, just as it was not in my power to have it when I myself wished. Therefore, I thought to myself, there was no other remedy for me than to strive to have a pure conscience and to [keep myself] from all occasions to sin...

### Page 40

...withdraw, even if they were only venial sins <term>venial sins: in Catholic teaching, lesser sins that do not break a person's relationship with God but weaken it</term>; for if it were from the Spirit of **God**, the benefit would be certain in itself; but if it were from the evil spirit, since I was striving to please the **Lord** and not to offend Him, it could do me little harm, but rather result in the enemy’s loss. When I had thus resolved and unceasingly begged the **Lord** that He would assist me, after I had continued this for several days, I saw that my soul did not have enough strength to reach such high perfection by itself, on account of certain inclinations I had toward things which, though not very evil in themselves, were yet sufficient to ruin the whole matter.

4. Now I had been told of a priest who was learned and lived in this place, whose piety the **Lord** began to make known among the people; a noble and holy person made an introduction for me to him. When she brought him to me so that he might speak with me, and I was full of shame at having to be seen in the presence of such a holy man, I told him how things stood with my soul and my prayer; thereupon he began with a holy and brave resolution to lead me as if I were one of the strongest (as might well have been the case in view of my prayer) and wanted me to no longer offend **God** in any way. As I saw his swift resolution even regarding small things, for which I did not have sufficient strength to fulfill perfectly at once, I became distressed; and because I saw that he took up the state of my soul as something that should be finished all at once, I well noticed that I was in need of a much longer cure. In short, I recognized that the means he prescribed for me were not those by which I should be helped; for although I had come far in receiving great graces from **God**, I was still quite young in the virtues and in self-denial <term>self-denial: the spiritual practice of setting aside one's own desires and ego to better serve God</term>. The sadness I felt because I could not, in my opinion, do what he told me, was enough to make me despair and give everything up altogether.

5. But this was my misery, that I knew neither little nor much how to say what my prayer was like. As I looked around in various books to see if I might find anything to explain my way of prayer, I found in a book called *The Ascent of Mount Sion* <note>original: "Aufsteigung zum Berge Sion"; this refers to a work by Bernardino de Laredo, which was influential for Teresa in explaining the "prayer of quiet."</note> all those signs that I felt in myself when I was thus without any thoughts in prayer; I marked this place and gave the book to that nobleman so that he and that other priest might tell me what I should do.

6. When I had delivered the book and at the same time opened my life along with my sins as well as I could, these two servants of **God** considered it with great love. I awaited their answer with great fear, and had also requested many persons to commend me to **God**; finally the nobleman came to me and said that, in both their opinions, this came from the evil spirit; they therefore held it advisable that I should deal with one from the **Society of Jesus** <term>Society of Jesus: the Jesuit order, then a relatively new religious order known for their expertise in spiritual direction and discernment</term> and discover my whole life to him, and not overstep anything of all that he would say to me. This answer caused me such anxiety that I did not know what to do, and I did nothing but weep constantly.

-># Of St. Teresa of Jesus. Chapter X.<-

7. As I then found myself very distressed in a small prayer-closet <term>prayer-closet: a private space or oratory used for personal devotion</term>, not knowing how things would yet go for me, I happened to read in a book (and it seems God placed it into my hands) how St. Paul says that God is very faithful, and that He never allows those who love Him to be deceived by the evil enemy; this caused me very great comfort. 8. Thus I would also take a great guilt upon myself if I did not make room for the graces that God bestows upon me. 9. In this manner I spent almost two whole months, applying all possible diligence to resist the Divine comforts. Through this resistance, I achieved that His Divine Majesty instructed me; for previously I thought I necessarily had to keep myself very solitary if such comforts were to be shared with me in prayer, and I hardly dared to move. But afterward I saw how little this mattered; for the more I exerted myself to turn away from them, the more the Lord overwhelmed me with that same sweetness and glory, so that it seemed to me I was entirely surrounded by them and could not escape on any side, and indeed it was not otherwise. I also began to bear a new love for the most holy humanity of Christ; my prayer also began to be better grounded; I also received a better desire for works of penance.

# The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus. Chapter X.

7. When I was in a small prayer-chamber <note>Likely an "oratory" or "closet," a private space for prayer.</note> feeling very distressed, not knowing how things would go for me, I happened to read in a book (and it seems God placed it in my hands) how Saint Paul says that God is very faithful, and that He never allows those who love Him to be deceived by the evil enemy. 8. When I then discussed my soul with this servant of God <gloss>a Jesuit</gloss>, he said that he understood my language <note>The "language" refers to her specific way of describing interior spiritual states, which many others found confusing.</note> well, and he encouraged me <note>The original German "machte mir ein grosses Herz" literally means "made me a big heart," a phrase meaning to give someone courage.</note>, saying that the Spirit of God was evidently working there. "For who knows," he said, "whether God wants to help many people through you," and other things besides. He told me I would also take a great debt upon myself if I did not make room for the graces that God was bestowing upon me. In everything, it seemed to me as if the Holy Spirit were speaking through him to heal my soul, so powerfully were his words impressed upon me, through which he also made me feel very ashamed. He also told me that I should daily direct my prayer toward a mystery of the Passion of Christ; I was to resist the inner gatherings <term>Versammlungen</term> <note>This refers to "recollection," a state where the soul's faculties are gathered inward toward God.</note> and "sweetnesses" <note>Spiritual "sweetness" or "consolations" are feelings of joy or peace experienced during prayer.</note> as much as I was able, until he should tell me otherwise.

9. Through this confession, I found my soul so softened and calm that it seemed to me no task would be so difficult that I would not undertake it. I began, therefore, to change myself in many respects, even though my confessor did not drive me to it; for he guided me in such a way that I did everything out of free will and out of love for God. In this manner, I spent almost two whole months applying all possible diligence to resisting the divine comforts. Through this resistance, I achieved a state where His Divine Majesty instructed me; for previously, I thought I had to keep myself strictly solitary if such comforts were to be imparted to me in prayer, and I hardly dared to move. Afterward, however, I saw how little this mattered; for the more I exerted myself to turn away from them, the more the Lord overwhelmed me with that same sweetness and glory, so that it seemed to me I was entirely surrounded by them and could not escape on any side—nor was it any different. I also began to carry a new love for the most holy humanity of Christ <note>A central theme for Teresa: focusing on the person of Jesus rather than just abstract divinity.</note>; my prayer also began to be better grounded, and I felt a greater desire for works of penance.

10. It was around this time that Francis Borgia <note>Francisco de Borja (1510–1572), formerly the Duke of Gandia and a high-ranking nobleman, who gave up his titles to join the Society of Jesus.</note> came to this city (he who had previously been the Duke of Gandia, but afterward left everything and entered the Society of Jesus). My confessor arranged for me to speak with him. After he had heard me, he said it was the Spirit of God, and that he held it not advisable to resist Him further, although I had done so until now—

### Seventh Section. The Life

...had done right within. He told me that I should always begin my prayer with a point or mystery of the Passion of Christ; then, if the Lord wished to raise my spirit, I should not resist Him, but allow His Divine Majesty <note>A favorite title Teresa used for God, reflecting both His sovereignty and His closeness.</note> to lift it, without seeking or promoting it on my own part. Thus, he prescribed advice and means for me as one who was very mature in the spirit; for in this case, experience is of great use. He also told me that it would be an error to resist this any further. Because of this, I remained very comforted, as did the aforementioned nobleman <note>Referring to Francisco de Salcedo, a pious layman who had previously been skeptical of her.</note>, who rejoiced greatly that he had told me it was the Spirit of God.

11. [Afterward, I became acquainted with another pious Jesuit] <note>This was Father Juan de Pradanos.</note>; he began to urge me toward a greater perfection and told me that I should omit nothing whatsoever that I might do to please God entirely. And this he did with great discretion, because my soul was not yet strong, but very tender—especially regarding the leaving behind of certain friendships. Although I did not offend God in these, the affection I had for them was great. I said to him, therefore, that since there was no offense against God in this, why should I show myself ungrateful to them? To this he answered: I should commend this to God the Lord for several days in a row, asking that He might grant me light as to what would be best in this matter. When I had remained in prayer for a long time one day, asking the Lord to help me so that I might please Him entirely, I began to speak the commanded prayer. As I was praying it, I was overcome by such a sudden <term>rapture</term> <note>original: "Verzückung"; a state of spiritual ecstasy where the soul feels suspended or carried away from the physical senses.</note> that it took me, as it were, completely out of myself. I could not doubt it at all, for it was an altogether too recognizable thing. This was the first time that God granted me the grace of rapture; in it, I heard these words:

> I do not wish for you to have your fellowship with humans hereafter, but with angels.

This caused me great terror, as the movement of the soul was great, and these words were spoken very deeply into my spirit. I was afraid because of it, though on the other hand, it also caused a great comfort—which remained with me after the fear had passed (which, in my opinion, arose because it was something new).

12. This, however, has been truly fulfilled in my deeds; for never afterward have I been able to enter into any particular friendship <note>A term for exclusive emotional attachments that might distract from a total devotion to God.</note> or seek comfort therein. I can have no special love except for those persons whom I know love God and apply themselves to serving Him. It has not been in my power to do otherwise; I now pay little heed to whether they are friends or relatives if I do not perceive this in them. If they are not persons devoted to prayer, it is a heavy <term>cross</term> <note>original: "Creuz"; used here to mean a spiritual burden or a source of suffering.</note> for me to associate with anyone. And this is the truth, as far as I am aware, without any exception. From this day on, I have remained so heartened and courageous as to leave everything for God’s sake, since it pleased Him to transform His servant in a single moment (for it seemed no longer than that to me) into a completely different person, so that it was no longer necessary to command me to do so. Blessed be the Lord, who in one moment has granted me this freedom, which I could not force through with all my effort and labor over many years!

# Chapter Eleven.

## How God addresses the soul. The signs and effects of such speeches, and the harmful fear that can accompany them. How the soul is reassured and emboldened by the Lord. Examples of such powerful locutions <note>In mystical theology, "locutions" are a form of private revelation where a person receives a clear message internally.</note>.

->I.<-

In my opinion, it would be well for me to explain how this happens when God addresses someone in their soul, and what the soul feels at that time. For since then, such a thing happens to me quite often. These are very distinct and well-formed words; yet they are not heard with the physical ears, but are nevertheless heard and understood much more clearly. It is impossible not to perceive them, even if one goes to great trouble to resist. In this address that God makes to the soul, I must hear it even if it displeases me; and the intellect <note>Teresa uses "Verstand" (intellect/understanding) to describe the faculty of the mind that processes these messages.</note> must pay attention so that it perceives it. For God wills that one hears it, and here, willing or not willing does no good. He who is all-powerful shows herein that He is Lord over us.

2. I would like to explain what kind of deception could creep in here (though I believe that for someone who has great experience in this, little or no deception can occur). It may well happen that someone who commends something to God in prayer with great zeal and strong imagination might think they have heard something. However, someone who has previously heard something in the first manner <note>Referring to genuine divine locution.</note> will clearly recognize what it is, because there is a great difference between the two. When it is a matter that the intellect itself has fashioned—no matter how subtly it happens—one will notice that it is the self that has arranged or spoken it. The intellect will also clearly notice that it is not "listening" in that moment, since it is actively working; the words it forms for itself are, as it were, muffled and fantastic <note>Meaning "of the imagination" or "illusory" in the older sense of the word.</note>, and one can turn away from them.

3. Another and even more certain sign is that this speech [of the intellect] produces no effect. In that other speech, however, which comes from the Lord, both Word and Work are joined together. Even when it happens that the Lord’s words are not intended for devotion but for a rebuke <note>original: "Strafe" - while it can mean punishment, in this context it refers to a divine correction or reprimand.</note>, they immediately prepare the soul for all that is good, producing a tender devotion, enlightening, refreshing, and quieting it. Even if the soul has been afflicted by dryness <note>A term for "spiritual dryness" (Ariditas), a state where a person feels no emotional or spiritual comfort in prayer.</note>, sorrow, or unrest, such things are wiped and taken away as if by a hand—or even better. It is also such a clear voice that not a single syllable of it is missed. It is just as if one were hearing a very holy or learned person of great authority speaking; yet even this comparison is too poor, because these words sometimes possess such majesty in themselves that even without remembering who it is who speaks them, they make a person tremble if they are words of rebuke, and make one melt with pure love if they are words of love. These are things that were far from the memory. Furthermore, such profound sayings are suddenly spoken that much time would otherwise be needed to put them in order, and it seems to me that one cannot possibly believe it to be a thing we have devised ourselves.

# Seventh Part. The Life

<meta>catchword: 8. It</meta>

4. It is therefore not necessary for me to dwell on this any longer; for it would be almost a miracle if someone experienced in these matters were to be deceived, unless they deliberately wished to deceive themselves. It has often happened to me that I had doubts and wondered whether I might have been blinded in some way (though this only happens after everything is over; for while the experience lasts, it is impossible to doubt). Later, after a long time, I nevertheless saw the words fulfilled. For the Lord ensures that such things remain in the memory, and one cannot forget them.

5. The intellect and the soul itself remain full of wonder at the things they perceive. It is exactly as I have said, and anyone who has experience of it will recognize it; it is not different by a single letter <note>original: "keinen Buchstaben anders"—meaning precisely or exactly as described</note>, and I thank God that I have been able to express it in this way.

6. It is, however, important to know that whenever one sees a vision or hears such words, it never happens at the time when the soul is united in the ecstasy <term>Verzückung: a mystical state where the soul is "carried away" or "rapt," often involving a loss of outward consciousness</term> itself. For at that time (as I explained above), all the powers of the soul <note>In the theology of the time, the "soul-powers" (Seelenkräften) referred to the intellect, memory, and will.</note> are entirely lost. But when this short time has passed, and while the soul is still in a state of ecstasy, then these things of which I have spoken occur.

7. When such things come from the evil enemy <note>The "evil enemy" is a traditional term for the Devil.</note>, they leave behind not only no good effects, but even evil ones. This has happened to me no more than two or three times, and I was immediately warned by the Lord that it was from the evil enemy—to say nothing of the great dryness it leaves behind, it also creates a great unrest in the soul. The sweetness and the "taste" that the evil enemy gives is, in my opinion, very different from the others. He might perhaps deceive someone with this sweetness who has not had, or does not have, any other sweetness from God—I mean the true sweetnesses that consist of a lovely, powerful, deeply impressed, delightful, and quiet refreshment. For certain brief moments of devotion in the soul, and other minor movements which are blown away by the first little breeze of persecution, I do not call true devotions, even though they are good and holy feelings at the start; they are not enough for one to distinguish the effects of the evil spirit. <insert>When such things originate from the evil enemy,</insert> no softening remains in the soul, but rather it leaves the soul as if frightened and full of gloom. And so, such things are only given credit insofar as they agree with Holy Scripture; if it deviated from this in the slightest, I would believe much more firmly that it came from the evil enemy than I now believe it comes from God, however strongly I believe that. In such a case, it is not necessary to seek many signs or ask from what spirit it comes, since this is such a clear sign of the evil enemy that even if the whole world tried to assure me it came from God, I would not believe it. In summary <note>original: "In Summa"</note>, when it is from the evil enemy, almost everything good vanishes and flees from the soul, and it remains listless, confused, and without any good effect. For even if it appears as though it awakens good desires, these are not powerful, and the humility it leaves behind is false, restless, and unpleasant.

8. Great harm came to me from the excessive fear that several people had regarding this matter. It happened particularly once that many of them had gathered—people to whom I rightfully gave great credence. They discussed among themselves how I might be helped, because they loved me dearly. I believe there were five or six of them, all zealous servants of God. They all concluded that what was spoken to me inwardly <insert>what was spoken to me inwardly</insert> came from the evil spirit. They told me I should not receive Communion <note>original: "communiciren"—at the time, frequent reception of the Eucharist was often viewed with suspicion in women claiming mystical experiences.</note> so often, that I should distract myself with other business, and avoid solitude. Since I was naturally very fearful outside of prayer, and seeing that so many of them confirmed this—even though I still could not believe it—it caused me great distress of conscience, for I considered my doubt to be a lack of humility. After all, these were all people of incomparably more pious lives than mine, and learned men besides.

I directed all my prayer toward this end, and whenever I knew of another servant of God, I begged him to ask His Divine Majesty to lead me by a different path. This lasted for nearly two years, during which I constantly petitioned the Lord. Nothing could comfort me when I thought about whether it were possible that the evil enemy should speak to me so often. Since I no longer went into solitude at certain hours to pray, the Lord saw to it that I was recollected <term>versammlet: a state of "recollection" where the soul's attention is drawn inward to God</term> even in the midst of conversation and while I was dealing with others. Without my being able to choose it, He would then say to me whatever He pleased, and I had to listen, however unwillingly I might be. When I was thus alone, without a single human being to comfort me, unable to pray vocally or read, and completely distraught by such great tribulation and fear that the evil enemy might be deceiving me, full of unrest and grief and not knowing what to do, I remained in this state for four or five hours. No comfort came to me from either heaven or earth; rather, the Lord let me suffer, surrounded by a thousand kinds of fear of danger.

While I was in this great distress, these words alone were enough to take away all anxiety and place me in complete peace: **Fear not, my daughter, for it is I, and I will not leave you; fear not.** Behold, with these words alone I was completely stilled, filled with strength and courage, and so assured with such peace, light, and knowledge, that I saw my soul entirely changed in an instant. In my estimation, I would have been willing to argue with the whole world that this was from God.

6. But when this short time has passed, and the soul is nevertheless still in rapture, then those things occur of which I have spoken.

7. When such a thing comes from the evil enemy <note>original: "bösen Feind" — a common term for the Devil</note>, it leaves behind not only no good effects, but even evil ones. This has only happened to me two or three times, and I was immediately warned by the Lord that it was from the evil enemy; to say nothing of the great dryness <term>Dürre: a technical term for spiritual desolation or a lack of emotional warmth in prayer</term> it leaves behind, it also causes great unrest in the soul. He might perhaps deceive one who has not, or has never had, other sweetness from God—by those true sweetnesses, I mean those which consist in a lovely, powerful, deeply impressed, delightful, and calm refreshment. For certain brief devotions <term>Andachten: here meaning fleeting moments of religious sentiment or "pious feelings"</term> of the soul, and other slight movements that are blown away by the first little wind of persecution—such small flowers, I say, I do not call devotions, even though they are good and holy feelings in the beginning; they are not sufficient to allow one to distinguish the workings of the evil spirit. <insert>When such a thing stems from the evil enemy,</insert> no softening remains in the soul, but it leaves it as if terrified and full of ill-humor. And so, credit is only given to such things insofar as they agree with Holy Scripture; if it deviated from this in the slightest, I would believe much more firmly that it came from the evil enemy than I now believe it comes from God, however strongly I may believe it. For then it is not necessary to look for many signs or to ask what kind of spirit it comes from, since this is such a clear sign that it comes from the evil enemy, that even if the whole world wanted to assure me it came from God, I still would not believe it. In short, when it is from the evil enemy, all good as it were disappears and flees from the soul; it remains displeased and confused, and without any good effect. For even if it looks as though it awakens good desires, they are not powerful, and the humility <term>Demuth: the central virtue of recognizing one's own nothingness before the majesty of God</term> it leaves behind is false, restless, and unpleasant.

# Section Seven. The Life
**Page 46**

[If only I] had the fitness, and new words to praise and exalt Your works, as my soul understands them. Let everything leave me, oh **Lord**! as long as You do not leave me, then I will not leave You either. Even if all the scholars set themselves against me, and all creatures persecute me, and all devils torment me, as long as You, oh **Lord**! do not leave me; for I have indeed experienced with what great gain You help those who trust in You alone.

Oh, what a kind **God**! Oh, what a good and mighty **Lord**! His words are deeds. Who else do my powers obey like this? Who else, in such great darkness, illuminates everything in a moment and softens a heart that previously seemed entirely made of stone? Who bestows such sweet <term>tears: original "Zähren"—an archaic term for tears, often specifically referring to those shed in spiritual ecstasy or repentance</term> where one expected nothing but a long-lasting drought? Who is it that instills such good desires? Who is it that creates such a heart? What was I thinking, that I was so afraid? What is this? I desire to serve this **Lord**, I want nothing else but to please Him; I desire no joy, no rest, nor any other good than solely to do His will. Since this **Lord** is so powerful—as I see and know He is—and since all devils are His slaves (and there is no doubt about this, for faith teaches it), if I am also a servant of this **Lord** and King, what harm can they do to me? Why should I not be strong enough to fight the whole hellish host? "Now come on, all of you," [I said], "I want to see what you can do to me." And there remained in me such a sovereign power over them that I no longer regarded them as more than gnats.

10. Would to **God**! If only we feared what we ought to fear, and recognized that more harm comes to us from a minor sin than from the entire hellish army combined.

I cannot understand the fear of those who say, "Devil, devil!" when one could say, "**God, God!**" and make the devil tremble in such a way. We know well that he cannot move without the **Lord’s** permission: what then does this [fear] mean? I am now much more afraid of those who fear the devil so much than I am of the devil himself; for he can do nothing to me. But those others—especially when they are <term>confessors: priests authorized to hear confessions and provide spiritual direction</term>—cause great unrest, and I spent several years so miserably that I now wonder how I was able to endure it. Blessed be the **Lord**, who has so faithfully helped me! Amen.

11. Another time I found myself in great <term>tribulation: original "Trübsal"—a state of deep distress or suffering</term> over a matter where almost the whole city and the <term>order: the religious order to which Teresa belonged, the Carmelites</term> murmured against me. I was also otherwise very distressed when the **Lord** said to me: **"What do you fear? Do you not know that I am almighty? I will fulfill what I have promised you."** This was indeed fulfilled afterward. This happens so often that I cannot tell the number. Often they have also been words of correction (which still happens when I commit an imperfection) which are so sharp that the soul might melt away; at the very least, they are so powerful that they bring about improvement.

of **Saint Teresa of Jesus**. Chapter XII.

12. When many books were once forbidden to be read <note>This refers to the 1559 "Valdés Index," a list of prohibited books issued by the Spanish Inquisition, which included many popular spiritual works in the vernacular Spanish.</note>, I felt this very deeply because I read some of them with great pleasure; now, however, they were only permitted in the Latin language. Then the **Lord** said to me: "Do not be troubled; I will give you a living book." His **Divine Majesty** has been the true book in which I have read the truths. Blessed be this book, which so impresses upon the heart what one should read and do that it can never be forgotten.

# Chapter Twelve

## Intellectual appearance or presence of the holy humanity of Jesus Christ. Divine manner of instruction. Excessive modesty of men. Imaginary appearance or vision of the holy humanity of Christ. Glory and utility of the same. Which graces make the ignorant suspicious and lead them to attribute things to the evil enemy. God reassures them through inner, powerful impulses and piercings <note>original: "Verwundungen"—refers to the mystical 'wounding' of the soul by divine love</note>.

->I.<-

But to return to the story of my life: it happened after the passing of two years, during which both I and other persons had prayed so diligently—specifically, that the **Lord** would either lead me by another way or reveal the truth, since these addresses from the **Lord** occurred so frequently—it happened on a feast day while I was in prayer that I saw beside me, or better said, I sensed (for I saw nothing, neither with the eyes of the body nor with the eyes of the soul) that Christ stood beside me, and I saw <note>In mystical theology, "seeing" often refers to an intuitive intellectual certainty rather than visual perception</note> that it was He who spoke with me. I, who was completely ignorant that such appearances could happen, was overcome with great fear at the beginning and did nothing but weep; although, as soon as He spoke even a word to me to reassure me, I remained from that moment full of peace, full of comfort, and without any fear, as I otherwise used to be.

2. It seemed to me as if the **Lord** **Jesus** were always walking at my side; and because it was not a vision of the kind that occurs through the imagination <term>imagination: original "Einbildung"—in this context, it refers to 'imaginary visions,' which are mental images presented to the mind's eye. Teresa is distinguishing this from an 'intellectual vision' which has no image at all</term>, I could not see in what form He was; however, I felt very clearly that He was always at my right side and was a witness to everything I did or left undone. And whenever I only slightly gathered my spirit <term>gathered my spirit: original "mein Gemüth versammlete"—the practice of 'recollection,' or drawing one's attention away from the world to focus on the presence of God within</term>, or was not very distracted elsewhere, I could never be ignorant of the fact that He stood beside me. From that hour, I went to my confessor, full of anxieties, [to tell] him this...
