Seventh Section. The Life
<meta>catchword: 12. When</meta>

...would have the aptness, and new words to praise and exalt Your works, just as my soul understands them. Though everything should abandon me, O Lord! if only You do not abandon me, then I will not abandon You either. Let all the learned men rise up against me, and all created beings <note>original: "Creaturen"—refers to all living things or worldly entities</note> persecute me, and all the devils torment me, if only You, O Lord, do not abandon me; for I have experienced in truth with what great profit You help those who trust in You alone.

O, what a kind God! O, what a good and mighty Lord! His words are deeds. Who else is there whose commands my powers thus obey, and who, in such great darkness, illuminates everything in a single moment, and softens a heart that previously seemed entirely made of stone? Who grants such sweet tears <note>original: "Zähren"—an archaic term for tears, often used in a spiritual context of "the gift of tears"</note> where one expected nothing but a long-lasting dryness <note>original: "Dürre"—refers to "spiritual aridity," a state where a person feels no emotional or spiritual connection during prayer</note>? Who is it that gives such good desires? Who is it that makes such a heart? What was I thinking, that I was so afraid? What is this? I desire to serve this Lord; I long for nothing else but to please Him; I desire no joy, no rest, nor any other good, but only to do His will alone. Since this Lord is so powerful—as I see and know that He is—and since all devils are His slaves (and of this there is no doubt at all, for our faith teaches it), and since I am a servant of this Lord and King, what harm can they then do to me? Why should I not be strong enough to fight against the whole hellish host? "Now, come one and all," [I said], "I want to see what you will be able to do to me." And there remained in me such a reigning power over them that I no longer regarded them as more than flies.

10. Would to God we feared what we ought to fear, and recognized that more harm comes to us from a single slight sin than from the entire hellish army combined.

I cannot comprehend what kind of fear it is that makes people say, "the devil, the devil," when one can say, "God, God," and make the devil tremble so. For we know well that he cannot stir without the Lord’s permission. What, then, does this mean? I am now much more afraid of those who are so greatly afraid of the devil than I am of the devil himself; for he can do nothing to me. But those others—especially when they are confessors <note>priests authorized to hear confessions and provide spiritual direction</note>—cause great unrest, and I spent several years in such misery that I now wonder how I was able to endure it. Blessed be the Lord, who has so faithfully helped me! Amen.

11. Another time, I found myself in great tribulation concerning a matter where almost the entire town and my Order murmured against me, and I was otherwise very distressed; then the Lord said to me: "What do you fear? Do you not know that I am almighty? I will accomplish what I have promised you." And it was indeed fulfilled afterward. This happens so often that I cannot tell the number. Frequently, these have also been words of correction (which still happens when I commit an imperfection), which are so sharp that the soul might dissolve over them; at the very least, they are so powerful that they bring about improvement.

12. When once many books were forbidden to be read <note>This likely refers to the Spanish Inquisition's Index of Prohibited Books issued by Inquisitor General Valdés in 1559, which banned many popular spiritual works in the common tongue (Spanish) that Teresa enjoyed.</note>, I felt it very much, because I read several of them with great pleasure; now, however, only those in the Latin language were permitted. Then the Lord said to me: **"Do not be troubled, I will give you a living book."** His Divine Majesty has been that true book in which I have read the truths. Blessed be this book, which impresses upon the heart what one should read and do in such a way that it can never be forgotten.

## The Twelfth Chapter.

**Intellectual appearance or presence of the holy humanity of Jesus Christ. Divine way of instruction. Exceeding modesty of men. Imaginary appearance or vision of the Holy Humanity of Christ. Its glory and usefulness. Which graces make the ignorant suspicious and lead them to attribute them to the evil enemy. God reassures them through internal powerful impulses and piercings.**

### I.

But so that I may return again to the history of my life, it happened after the course of two years—during which both I and other persons had prayed so diligently that the Lord would either lead me by another way or reveal the truth, since these addresses from the Lord occurred very frequently—it happened on a feast day, while I was at prayer, that I saw beside me, or better said, I perceived (for I saw nothing, neither with the eyes of the body nor with the eyes of the soul) that Christ stood beside me, and I saw that it was He who spoke with me. I, who was entirely ignorant that such appearances could happen, was overcome with great fear in the beginning, and did nothing else but weep; although, as soon as He spoke even a word to me to reassure me, I remained from that moment full of peace, full of comfort, and without any fear, as I otherwise used to be.

2. It seemed to me as if the Lord Jesus were always walking at my side; and because it was not a vision of those that occur through the imagination <term>imaginary vision: in mystical theology, this refers to a vision perceived by the internal senses (the mind's eye) rather than the physical eyes</term>, I could not see in what form He was; yet I felt very clearly that He always stood on my right side and was a witness to all my doing and leaving. And whenever I only slightly gathered my mind <note>original: "Gemüth versammlete"—referring to the practice of "recollection," a focused state of prayer</note>, or was not very distracted elsewhere, I could never be ignorant of the fact that He stood beside me. From that moment I went to my confessor, full of anxieties, to tell him such—

### Seventh Part. The Life
<meta>catchword: to look</meta>

to indicate such a thing. He <note>Teresa’s confessor.</note> asked me in what form I saw Him? I answered him that I did not see Him. At this he said: How then did I know that it was Christ the Lord? I answered that I did not know how, yet I could not fail to notice that He stood beside me, and that I clearly saw and felt Him; also that the internal gathering of the soul was much greater, and I was constantly in the **prayer of quiet** <note>A state of contemplative prayer where the soul experiences a deep sense of peace and God’s presence.</note>; that the effects it caused were of a much different nature than usual, and that all of this was very clear and pure. I do not say that one sees a specific clarity, but rather such a light which, without one seeing any physical light, illuminates the intellect so that the soul may enjoy such a great good. This brings great benefit with it. However, it is not the same as when one experiences the presence of God in the **prayer of union** or of quiet; there, one only becomes aware of certain influences of His divinity; but here, one sees that the **most holy humanity** <note>term: Most Holy Humanity. Refers to the physical, human nature of Jesus Christ as part of his divine person.</term> of Christ keeps us company at the same time. So the confessor then asked me: Who said that this was the Lord Christ? I answered: He has often told me so Himself; but before He told me, it was already impressed upon my intellect that it was He.

4. It also happens in the same way with another manner by which God instructs the soul and speaks to it without words, in the way I have mentioned. And this is such a heavenly language that it can be very poorly explained here on earth. God instills in the innermost part of the soul what He wants it to understand, and presents it there without any image or form of words. Here, it seems to me, the evil enemy can interfere the least.

[The soul is there] just like someone who had never learned to read, much less studied, but nevertheless became aware within himself that all arts and sciences were already known to him, without knowing how or from where, because he had never applied any diligence even to learn the alphabet; so too the soul finds itself in a moment gifted with **wisdom**, and the mystery of the **Holy Trinity** and other high matters are given to it to understand so clearly that there can be no theologian so learned against whom the soul would not dare to engage to defend the truth of these high things; it remains so astonished by this that a single one of these graces is sufficient to completely transform a soul.

4. It seems to me the Lord entirely desires that the soul have some knowledge of what happens in Heaven; and that just as they understand each other there without any speaking, so it happens here, and God and the soul understand each other, purely and alone when His Majesty wills that it understand, without any other effort, revealing to each other the love that these two friends have for one another. Just as here on earth, when two persons love each other, they understand each other if they only look at one another; so it happens here, without us knowing how, these two lovers gaze kindly upon each other, as the Bridegroom says to His Bride in the **Song of Solomon** <note>original: "Hohen Lied". Also known as the Song of Songs, a book of the Bible often interpreted by mystics as an allegory for the love between God and the soul.</note>.

5. Oh, the wonderful goodness of God! Do You then, O Lord, allow Yourself to be looked upon in this way...

### Of Saint Teresa of Jesus. Ch. XII.

...look from those eyes which previously saw so poorly, namely the eyes of my soul? Grant that through this sight they may henceforth be accustomed to looking upon nothing low or earthly, and that nothing outside of You may satisfy them. O, the ingratitude of men! It seems that by now the number of those whom the world holds as fools has entirely decreased—those who performed brave, heroic deeds as true lovers of Christ <note>Teresa refers to the saints who embraced "holy folly" or radical poverty, which the secular world rejects as madness.</note>.

O world! O world! How much your prestige grows because there are so few who truly know you. Perhaps we imagine that God is better served if we are held to be wise and modest people? From that moment on, we worry about causing offense if we do not appear grave and with great authority, each according to their status. Even monks, priests, and nuns imagine it to be something strange if we were to wear something old or patched, and that it would give a bad example to the weak; just as if one were to diligently attend to solitude or prayer. Indeed, the points of perfection and the great zeal that the saints had are now forgotten; this truly causes more harm than anyone being offended if the clergy clearly demonstrated in deed what they teach with words.

6. To return to my purpose: I spent several days while this vision remained very constant within me, and it brought me such benefit that I was never without prayer. Also, in everything I did, I strove to perform it in such a way that I did not offend Him whom I clearly saw beside me as a witness and overseer. And although I was sometimes afraid, because I was told so many [contrary] things, this fear did not last long because the Lord immediately reassured me again. One day while I was in prayer, the Lord wished to show me His hands alone, with such exceedingly great beauty that it is impossible for me to praise them enough. This caused great fear in me; for anything that is still new creates a great fear in me at the beginning.

7. A few days later, I also saw this Divine Face, which left me quite ecstatic. I could not grasp why the Lord allowed Himself to be seen by me so gradually, until I later understood that the Lord led me according to what my natural weakness required—may He be blessed for eternity! For such a great glory, had it shown itself all at once, could not have been endured by such a vain and base creature.

8. On a feast day, this **Holy Humanity** <term>Holy Humanity: The physical human nature of Jesus Christ, which Teresa began to see in her visions as glorified and beautiful.</term> revealed itself to me entirely, with such beauty and majesty as I wrote to Your Reverence <note>E. E. abbreviates 'Euer Ehrwürden,' referring to her confessor, to whom she was required to submit her writings.</note> at that time by express command. And I must say that even if there were nothing else in heaven to delight the eyes but the beauty of glorified bodies, it would still be an exceedingly great glory—above all to behold the humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ, even in such a manner as our weakness is able to endure here. What will it be like then, where one enjoys this good entirely? This vision,

### Seventh Part. The Life

Even though this happens through the imagination <term>Imagination: in this context, Teresa refers to the "imaginary vision," which is not "made up" but is a vivid image presented by God directly to the mind's eye</term>, I have never seen this or anything else with my physical eyes, but only with the eyes of the soul. Those who know better than I say that the kind of appearance I spoke of before <gloss>[at the beginning of the chapter, called an "intellectual vision"]</gloss> is more perfect than this present one; but this one is much more perfect than anything one sees with physical eyes.

8. Even if I labored for many years with my own imagination to try and picture such a beautiful thing, I would not be able or know how to do it, because it surpasses everything one can imagine here on earth—even just the snow-white radiance and light of it alone.

9. This is not a radiance that blinds the eyes; rather, it is a bodily appearance and an infused brilliance <note>original: "eingegossener Glanz" refers to light that is poured into the soul by God rather than originating from a natural source</note> that gives the sight a great delight and does not burden it. It is accompanied by a clarity through which this Divine beauty may be seen. It is a light so distinct from what one sees on earth that even the brightness of the sun itself, if compared with the clarity and light presented to the sight there, would appear so dark that one would be reluctant to even open one's eyes afterward.

It is ultimately such that, no matter how highly intelligent a person may be, they could never in all the days of their life imagine what this is like in itself. God presents it so quickly that one does not even have time to open one's eyes, even if it were necessary to do so; but it matters little whether they are open or closed when the Lord wants us to see such things, even if we did not want to. Here, no turning away of the mind helps, nor is any force sufficient to resist it, nor is any diligence or care so great that one could prevent it; this I have experienced very well.

10. This appearance has such exceedingly great power that I consider it impossible for a human to endure it if the Lord did not choose to help the soul in a supernatural way through an ecstasy <gloss>[in which the appearance of this Divine presence is lost through spiritual enjoyment]</gloss>. It is true that the soul afterwards forgets the specifics, yet this majesty and glory remain so impressed upon her that it is impossible to forget the experience itself.

11. These two kinds of appearance <gloss>[namely this "imaginary" one and then the "intellectual" one]</gloss> have always come to me at the same time. For with the eyes of the soul, one sees the excellence, beauty, and glory of the most holy humanity <note>Teresa refers to the physical form of the resurrected Christ</note>; but through that other way—the intellectual vision—it is given to us to understand that He is God, that He is almighty, that He commands everything, rules all things, and fills all things with His love.

12. This appearance is to be held in very high esteem, and in my opinion, it is without any danger; for from the effects it produces, one can clearly see that the <image-desc>small heart-shaped ornament</image-desc> enemy <note>The devil or tempter</note> has no power here.

13. It cannot be sufficiently expressed how the soul is enriched by this, and how even the body becomes healthier and stronger because of it. I put forward these and other reasons when people told me it was from the evil enemy <note>the devil</note> and pure delusion; and I brought forth parables as best I could, but it all helped very little. For because there were very holy persons in this city—compared to whom I was a mere wretch—whom God did not lead by this path, they were immediately filled with fear. And it seems that my affairs, because of my sins, were carried about from one person to another, even though I told no one but my confessor and those he commanded me to reveal it to.

14. They told my confessor <term>Beichtvater: a priest who hears confessions and provides spiritual guidance</term> that he should be on guard against me, so that he would not be deceived by the evil enemy, which distressed me greatly. I feared that there would no longer be anyone who would want to hear my confession, but that everyone would flee from me; therefore I did nothing but weep. But he always comforted and calmed me, and commanded me that I should hide nothing from him, which I also did; saying that if I did this, even if it were from the evil enemy, it should not harm me, but the Lord would bring good out of the evil. For three years and more, he endured much with me amidst such anxieties; for during the great persecutions against me, and in many things where by God's providence people judged ill of me, they came to him with all these matters and accused him on my account. Partly he had to answer those who thought I was being led astray; partly he had to work to quiet me and take away the fear—which he himself often only made greater. He also had to calm me because with every appearance (whenever it was something new), God allowed a great fear to overcome me. All this arose from the fact that I was such a great sinner and had sinned so much before.

15. Those servants of God who were suspicious of me dealt with me much, and when I said something to them somewhat carelessly, they thought it came from a lack of humility and that I wanted to teach them; and when they saw a fault in me (as they surely saw many), then everything was immediately condemned together.

16. This lasted for a considerable time, and I was troubled from many sides; but by means of the grace that the Lord showed me, I endured it all. I say this so that one may understand from it how difficult it is when one has no one who is experienced on this path; and there were so many things that they could have driven me out of my mind, and I did not know what else to do in these anxieties than to lift my eyes to God.

### Seventh Piece. The Life

...with which He spoke the words with His gracious and Divine mouth, or sometimes also His stern earnestness. And though I desired most intensely to notice the color or shape of His eyes so that I might describe it afterward, I have never been worthy to see them, nor have I been able to manage it; instead, the vision vanishes entirely. I do sometimes see that He looks at me kindly and friendly, but this gaze is so powerful that the soul cannot endure it, and there follows such a sudden <term>rapture: a state of intense spiritual ecstasy (Verzückung) where the soul feels suspended or caught up in God</term> that the beautiful form is lost, so that the soul may all the better enjoy Him. Thus, here there is no place for one’s own will, whether one wants to or not, and it is clear enough that the **Lord** here desires nothing else but humility and the despising of ourselves, and that we accept what is given to us and praise Him who gives it.

18. Almost always the **Lord** appeared to me in the form He had after He was risen, except when I was sometimes in tribulation; then He showed me His wounds on the tree of the Cross or in the garden several times; with the crown of thorns also a few times; sometimes even as He carried the Cross, yet always with a glorified body. I had to endure much shame and hardship when I spoke of these things. People held it so certainly that I had the evil spirit <note>original: "bösen Geist," referring to the devil or demonic influence</note> that some even wanted to pressure me. Yet I shall never regret having seen these heavenly visions, and I would not exchange a single one of them for all the goods and pleasures of the world. I saw that I increased greatly in the love of **God**. To Him I turned and lamented my concerns, and I always rose from prayer comforted and with new strength.

20. I found within me powerful impulses of this love, which, although they were not as unbearable as those I have spoken of elsewhere, I still did not know what to do; for no thing could satisfy me, and I could not contain myself, but it truly seemed to me as if my soul were being torn out of my body. ### # of St. Teresa of Jesus. Chapter XII.

...what a feat of **God**! What a subtle discovery you have used with your wretched handmaid! You hid yourself from me, and meanwhile you enticed me with your love, and inflicted on me such a sweet death, which my soul would never have wanted to do without.

21. He who has not experienced these powerful impulses cannot understand this; for it is not some unrest of the heart, or a devotion that, as it were, chokes the spirit so that it cannot remain within itself; this is much lower, and one must gradually and gently restrain the sudden sighs and quiet the soul. I had things of this kind in the beginning, and my head was weakened by them, and my spirit so exhausted that I was not fit to attend to prayer again the next day or even longer. Thus, in the beginning, great moderation <term>Bescheidenheit: in this context, it refers to spiritual discretion or the tempering of emotional outbursts to preserve physical health</term> is necessary.

22. But these other powerful impulses are entirely different from those, and it is not we ourselves who lay the wood under the fire; rather, it is as if we, after the fire is already lit, were suddenly thrown into it to burn there. The soul does not strive for this pain with which it is wounded because of the **Lord's** absence; rather, sometimes such an arrow is shot into the innermost and most vital part of the heart that it does not know what is happening to it or what it desires; yet it recognizes well that its longing is for **God**, and it seems that the arrow is prepared with such a poison that it causes her to deny herself for love of this **Lord**, and she would even gladly lose her life for His sake.

23. It cannot be sufficiently expressed how **God** visits the soul here, nor the great pain it suffers, so that it knows nothing of itself; yet this pain is so sweet that there is no pleasure in the world that brings such delight. At times, these impulses take over the entire body, so that one can move neither hands nor feet; indeed, even if one had been standing upright before, one sinks down like someone falling into a faint, and cannot even catch one's breath, but only lets out several sighs, which are not very large (because the soul can do no more) but are very deeply felt.

24. But it has pleased the **Lord** that I have seen such a vision here several times. I saw an angel beside me on the left side in physical form (which I am rarely accustomed to seeing, although an angel has often appeared to me, it usually happens without me seeing them, but like the other visions of which I spoke before). In this vision, however, the **Lord** willed that I see him thus: he was not tall, but small, very beautiful, his face was so inflamed that he seemed to be one of the highest angels, who are as if entirely burning, and these are, I believe, those whom they call **Seraphim** <note>original: "Seraphim"; in Christian theology, the highest rank of angels, whose name is derived from the Hebrew word for "burning ones"</note>; they do not tell me their names, yet I see well that in heaven there is such a great difference between one angel and another that I could not express it. In his hand I saw a long, glowing arrow, and at the tip of the iron, it seemed to me there was a little fire; he thrust this through my heart several times, and it penetrated to the innermost part of the same;

So great was the pain that I was forced to utter such moans of lamentation; yet so overflowing was the sweetness that this exceedingly great pain caused me, that it is impossible to desire to be without it; the soul cannot be satisfied with anything less than **God**. This is not a physical pain, but a spiritual one, although the body also participates in it, and not a little.

24. So sweet is this attraction of love <note>original: "Liebesanmuthung" — an 18th-century term for a spiritual impulse or affection</note> between the soul and **God**, that I pray to the goodness of **God** that He might grant a taste of it to anyone who might perhaps think that I am lying about this. Throughout those days, as long as it lasted, I walked about as if I were outside of myself; I wished neither to see nor to speak, but only to delight in my pain, which for me was a greater glory than can otherwise be found in all creatures. This happened to me from time to time until it pleased the **Lord** that those great ecstasies <term>Verzückungen: rapturous trances where the soul feels suspended or caught up in the divine</term> came to me; since then, I do not feel this pain as much, but rather another, which is to be prized far higher.

25. I could not prevent these great impulses now, yet I also feared having them, because I could not grasp how such an overflowing spiritual pain could exist together with such exceedingly great pleasure; and although I did not cease to apply diligence in resisting them, I could accomplish so little that I sometimes became weary of it. I saw quite clearly that no one understood me, yet I did not dare to say so. However, it pleased the **Lord** to diminish a great part of my suffering at that time by bringing the blessed man Peter of Alcantara <note>Saint Peter of Alcantara (1499–1562) was a Spanish Franciscan friar known for his extreme asceticism; he became a crucial supporter of Teresa's reforms</note> to this city. This holy man enlightened me in everything, saying that I should not be troubled, but rather praise **God**, and be completely certain that it was the Spirit of **God**; he rejoiced greatly with me. Although he had now comforted and quieted me, I could not reach that complete certainty that would leave me without any fear—especially when the **Lord** left me stuck in agonies of the soul, of which I shall speak now; nevertheless, I remained very comforted.

sicknesses; but because I did not have the anxieties of the soul along with them, I endured everything with a very joyful spirit. However, whenever both were present together, the pain was so great that I was very much distressed by it. At such times, I forgot all the graces that the **Lord** had previously bestowed upon me, and I remembered them only as if they were a dream, which served to increase my torment; for the intellect then became so sluggish and sleepy that it entangled me in a thousand kinds of doubt and suspicion. It seemed to me as if I had not known how to understand things correctly, or perhaps it had been a delusion; it would have been enough that I alone was deceived by it, but I feared that I might also lead other godly people into deception along with me. I also appeared so wicked to myself that it seemed to me that all the evil and all the heresies that had arisen were coming about because of my sins. This is a false humility <note>Teresa often warns that the devil uses a distorted sense of "unworthiness" to make a soul stop praying or lose hope.</note> which the evil enemy <term>the devil</term> devised so that he might make me restless and try to see if he could bring the soul to despair. This is clearly felt from the unrest with which it begins, as well as from the confusion of the soul, and from the darkness and anxiety, from the dryness <term>aridity: a state where a person feels no emotional or spiritual "warmth" in prayer</term> and unfitness for prayer and all good things; it seems as if the soul would suffocate and make the body clumsy in all things.

2. It seems as if the **Lord** would destroy everything with fire and sword; the justice of **God** is presented to one, and although one already believes that there is also mercy, this brings no comfort; rather, when the soul sees such great mercy, it only torments her more grievously. This sometimes lasted for eight or fourteen days, or even three weeks or longer. As it seems to me, it suddenly takes possession of the intellect, sometimes with such trivial things that I would otherwise only laugh at; the soul is also as if bound with chains, so that she can think of nothing else but the absurd things that the enemy suggests to her.

3. It is impossible to express what the soul suffers in this; she seeks help here and there, but **God** allows her to find none. Faith is then as if dead and slumbering, as are all other virtues; it is as if she speaks everything only outwardly with the mouth. The knowledge of **God** appears to her like something she has heard from afar. Love is also lukewarm. If she wants to go and pray, or to remain in solitude, it only happens with vexation. If she wants to help herself by reading, it is just as if she cannot do it. When I had read several lines four or five times, I understood less of it the last time than the first. But to associate or speak with someone at such a time is even worse; for the evil enemy puts such a spirit of anger <note>original: "Zorngeist"</note> into one that it seemed to me I could have devoured everyone, without being able to do otherwise. Going to the confessor also does not help, and it often happened to me that they scolded me <note>original: "ausputzten" — a vivid 18th-century term for giving someone a "dressing down" or a stern lecture</note> so badly that when I later pointed it out to them, they themselves wondered and said it had not been in their power to do otherwise; and even when they set out to comfort me kindly, they could not do it. They spoke the most vexing words to me, and although I usually rejoiced over such things, at that time it was a great martyrdom to me. Moreover, it also tormented me because it seemed to me that I was deceiving them; I even went to them and warned them quite earnestly that they should be on their guard against me, as I might perhaps be deceiving them.

### Seventh Part. The Life
<meta>catchword: out</meta>

4. But whenever the **Lord** spoke just a single little word to me, such as: "Do not be troubled," or "fear not," or when I saw some vision, I would suddenly become healthy, as if nothing had ever been wrong with me. Then I would delight in **God** and complain to Him about how He could allow me to suffer such pain and martyrdom; but it was well repaid, for usually a great abundance of heavenly graces followed afterward. It seems to me as if the soul, like gold, comes out of the furnace much purer and clearer to behold the **Lord** within itself. Therefore, all these adversities seem insignificant afterward, even though they previously seemed unbearable, and one even longs to suffer them anew if it would serve the **Lord** more.

5. At other times, I find myself in such a state that I cannot have a single right thought of **God**, nor think of good things with any strength or permanence. I cannot even pray, though I am in solitude; yet, I notice that I still recognize Him. Here I realize that the understanding <note>original: "Verstand"; refers to the analytical mind or intellect</note> and the imagination are to blame; for the will, it seems to me, is good and ready for all good things, but the understanding is so confused that it is like nothing else but a madman whom no one can bind. I do not have enough power over it to keep it still and quiet for even as long as it takes to recite the Creed. Sometimes I laugh at myself and recognize my misery; I watch the understanding and give it room to see what it will do and where it wants to go. Then—praise **God**!—it very rarely attaches itself to anything evil, but rather to things that are neither good nor evil, such as whether there is something to do here or there. And then I recognize better what an exceedingly great grace the **Lord** does for me when He keeps this fool <note>The "fool" refers to her wandering intellect.</note> bound in perfect contemplation <term>Beschaulichkeit: a state of quiet, focused prayer where the mind rests in God</term>. I consider within myself what it would be like if those people who consider me pious saw me in this madness. I feel great pity that my soul must be seen surrounded by such bad company <note>The "bad company" is her own distracted thoughts.</note>; I would gladly see it in complete freedom and then say to the **Lord**: "O You my **God**! When will the time finally come that I shall see my soul entirely united in Your praise, and enjoy all my powers in You? Do not allow, O **Lord**, that I be so divided and torn apart any longer."

6. At other times, my soul becomes quite simple and childlike, and it seems to me that I do neither good nor evil, but only follow (as they say) the common crowd. I feel neither torment nor joy; I regard neither life nor death. It seems to me as if the soul goes about like a little donkey <note>original: "Eselein"; Teresa often used the image of a humble beast of burden to describe the soul's simple endurance.</note> in the pasture, which feeds itself without even noticing it. For without doubt, the soul in this state is not without food, and enjoys several of **God’s** great graces, because it does not find this miserable life difficult to live and bears it with equanimity.

7. Since I have previously mentioned certain confusions, I will speak of some others that the enemy <term>the devil</term> openly inflicted upon me. Once he appeared to me on the left side in a cruel shape; I particularly looked at his mouth, which was terrifying. It seemed as if a great flame of fire came out from his body

8. Another time he tormented me for five hours with such cruel pains, and both internal and external anxieties, that it seemed to me it was no longer bearable; he caused me to move and thrash my body, head, and arms violently without being able to stop myself; those who were with me stood full of terror and did not know what to do. I helped myself (as is my usual custom) with internal exercises <note>St. Teresa often refers to "mental prayer" or focused internal acts of faith</note> and asked the **Lord** that if this served Him, His Majesty might grant me patience and then leave me in such a state until the end of the world. Then I saw beside me a small, hideous Moor <note>original: "Mohren." In the 16th century, this term was commonly used in Europe to describe people of North African or African descent; in this religious context, it is used as a symbolic, though derogatory, representation of a demon</note>, who gnashed his teeth like a desperate man. When I saw him, I laughed and was no longer afraid. This happened to me again quite recently, though it did not last as long.

9. Another time I saw a great number of devils around me, and it seemed to me as if a great clarity completely surrounded me and did not allow them to approach me. And I understood from this that **God** protected me so that they did not come too close, lest I should offend **God** in some way.

10. At other times it torments me greatly when I see that people respect me and say much good of me, and in this I have suffered much. When I consider the life of the **Lord JESUS** and other saints, it seems to me that I am walking a completely different path than they; since they walked through nothing but contempt and shame, this made me walk in such fear that I hardly dared to lift my head and wished to be seen nowhere; however, I do not feel this when I suffer persecution, but rather the soul finds itself so sovereign, and it feels as if it were in its own kingdom and had everything under its feet.

11. These fears have greatly hindered the freedom of my spirit, and the **Lord** afterward gave me to recognize this truth: that this was not a good humility, because it made me so restless. For if I believe for certain within myself that nothing of all the good is mine, but belongs to **God**—and just as it was not difficult for me to hear that others were praised, but rather I rejoiced that **God** showed Himself glorious in them—then it should also not be difficult for me that He showed His works in me.

12. As I was once distressed over this, the **Lord** said to me: why did I fear? For nothing else could follow from this but that they would either murmur against me [those who did not believe it] or praise Him; both of which would be a gain for me; therefore I should not worry. This quieted me very much and still comforts me when I remember it.

13. Truly, I see nothing else in the world that pleases me, "except that it will tolerate no faults in the devout which it does not seek to improve through its grumbling and draw toward perfection." <note>Teresa observes that the world's harsh criticism of religious people actually serves to refine their souls, even if the world's intent is unkind.</note> When the world sees someone begin <note>This refers to someone beginning a dedicated spiritual or monastic life.</note>, it immediately expects them to be perfect, and it can scent a fault from a thousand miles away—which may, in fact, be a virtue. In such a state, one is expected neither to eat nor sleep, nor (as the saying goes) to even draw breath; therefore, a great heart is needed for this.

14. When the **Lord** had already granted me many of those graces of which I have spoken, it happened one day while I was in prayer that I suddenly found myself, in an instant and without knowing how, entirely in Hell. I understood immediately that the **Lord** wanted me to see the place which the devils had prepared for me there, and which I had deserved through my sins. This all happened in a very short time, yet even if I were to live for many years, it seems to me impossible that I could ever forget it. The entrance appeared to me like a long and narrow alleyway, much like a low, dark, and cramped oven; on the ground were putrid puddles of water with a pestilential <note>meaning plague-like or foul-smelling</note> stench, which were also full of worms and vermin. At the end, there was something like a deep hole in the wall, resembling a chest, into which I was pressed. All of this, however, was still pleasant to look upon compared to what I felt therein; as for describing the sensation as it truly is, it is impossible for me to even begin, nor can it be fully understood. I felt such a fire in my soul that I do not know how to describe it, and such incomparably great bodily pains that, although I have endured the greatest pains a person can suffer on earth according to the doctors' testimony, all of that is nothing compared to what I felt there—especially when I saw that they would last without end. And yet, all this is still nothing compared to the death-struggle of the soul; it was such an anxiety, a confinement, a painful torment with such despairing grief that I do not know how to express it sufficiently. For if I say it is as if one's soul were being torn out of the body, it is saying very little; because in that case, life is taken away by another, but here the soul tears itself apart. In short, I do not know how to describe it. In this pestilential place, where there was absolutely no comfort, one can neither sit nor lie, and there is no room, even though I had been pressed into this narrow hole in the wall; for these walls are terrible to behold, and everything there causes one anguish; there is no light, but rather nothing but the uttermost darkness, and yet one sees everything that can be painful to the eyes. Thus the **Lord** willed me to see with my own eyes what He had delivered me from through His mercy. I have remained full of terror because of this, and even now, as I write this (though almost six years have passed), the natural heat almost leaves me for fear right where I am. Consequently, whenever I am in all kinds of adversities and pains, I never think of it without everything that a person can suffer here appearing to me as mere nothing; it seems to me that we complain without cause. ## The Fourteenth Chapter

How she was prompted and called to found a new convent. Preparations, difficulties, and persecutions in this endeavor. Teresa must travel to visit a noble lady. The miserable life of such persons of rank. She resolves to found her convent in poverty.

->I.<-

After I had now seen these and other great and secret things, which the Lord in His goodness wished to show me—both of the glory that will be given to the devout and of the pain of the wicked—I desired to withdraw myself from people and to separate myself entirely and all at once from the world. My spirit found no rest, though it was a sweet and pleasant unrest. I saw clearly that it was God, and that His Majesty had granted the soul a heat <note>a spiritual fervor or intensity</note> to be able to digest other and coarser foods than it had eaten before; so I thought to myself what I might do to honor God, and it occurred to me that the best thing would be if I kept my monastic rule as perfectly as was possible for me. However, although God the Lord was diligently served in the convent where I lived, the sisters went out from time to time; also, it was not founded according to the original strictness <note>Teresa refers to the "Primitive Rule" of the Carmelites, which was much more austere than the mitigated rule practiced in her current convent, the Incarnation</note>; there were also other inconveniences, so that it seemed to me I was kept there far too softly, because the house was large and pleasantly built. The going out was particularly inconvenient for me, because certain persons, whom my superiors <term>Obristen; the religious authorities in charge of her convent</term> could not refuse, liked to have me with them; therefore, it happened little by little that I could now remain very little in the convent: although, because I gave good teachings to certain persons—which I had learned from those who instructed me—great benefit was achieved.

2. Then it happened once that a certain person said to me and several others: If we had the desire to live in the manner of the Discalced <note>original: "Barfüsser" — literally "barefoot," referring to the reformed friars and nuns who wore sandals instead of shoes as a sign of poverty</note> nuns, it might perhaps be possible for a new convent to be built for that purpose. I, who was already occupied with such desires, began to negotiate with that widow <note>Teresa refers to her friend, Doña Guiomar de Ulloa</note> who also had this longing; she also began to propose means by which one might have an endowment <note>original: "Einkommen" — the financial means or property income required to support a religious foundation</note>.

3. One day after Communion, His Majesty strictly commanded me that I should continue this work with all my power; He also made great promises to me, that this convent would by no means be abandoned, and that He would be very much [honored] in it.

4. [ As I was now further urged by God to do this—although for my part I foresaw and dreaded the great unrest—I finally recognized that it was God's will. Thereupon I made my intention known to my confessor <note>a priest who provides spiritual guidance and hears confessions</note>. And so much of this came that my companion <note>Doña Guiomar de Ulloa, a wealthy widow who supported Teresa's project</note> grew weary of the matter.

5. When I was thus troubled, His Majesty <note>Teresa’s respectful way of referring to God</note> began to comfort me and to give me such courage, saying to me: from this I would be able to gather what the saints suffered who initially founded convents, and that I would have yet more persecutions to endure, but we should not heed them. Both of us then found ourselves comforted, with a great courage to resist all opposition and to meet it. And certainly, among all those devoted to prayer—indeed, in the entire city—there was almost no one who was not against us at that time. In my own convent there was also much tumult because of it. They even refused to absolve my companion <note>The clergy refused to grant her the sacrament of confession, a severe form of social and spiritual pressure</note>.

6. He requested eight days' time to answer us; but although he had previously fully intended to dissuade us with all diligence, and was even warned by others, nevertheless as he began to think upon it, his mind was changed, and he advised us that we should quickly take up the matter and carry it out, and told us in what manner this must happen. ]

7. Under such circumstances and with the help of much prayer, we had already bought a house, though it was small; the income was also meager, yet I trusted that the Lord would be helpful.

As the matter was now brought so near to its end, the Provincial changed his mind and would not permit it; thus my confessor commanded me to desist from it, although it had cost me so much trouble and adversity—as God knows—until I had brought it thus far. As it now came to a standstill, the murmuring against me increased, saying that it had been pure women's vanity <note>original: "Weibertand," implying trivial feminine nonsense or a foolish whim</note>. In my entire convent I was very ill-regarded because I wanted to found a convent that was to be more strictly enclosed <note>The "Discalced" reform emphasized "enclosure," meaning the nuns would have very little contact with the outside world</note>; they said I was bringing shame upon them thereby, and that they could serve the Lord just as well there. Some said I should be put in prison; a few others defended me to some extent; because I was not allowed to say the most important thing—namely, that the Lord had commanded it of me—I kept silent about it.

At times the Lord granted me such great grace that none of this burdened me, and I could easily let the matter rest; however, no one could believe this of me, not even my confessor <note>a priest who provides spiritual guidance and hears confessions</note>. But I (because it seemed to me that I had done my utmost in the matter) believed I was no longer obligated to do more regarding what the Lord had commanded me, and so I remained at home, believing for certain that it would one day still be brought to a conclusion. What distressed me most was that my confessor wrote to me one day: I should surely see now that what had happened was a pure dream; I should therefore improve myself from now on and speak of it no more; I could well see what a scandal <note>original: "Aergerniß," referring to the public outcry in Avila</note> had arisen from it, and other things besides, to grieve me. This pained me more than everything else combined, because it occurred to me whether I might have perhaps given occasion for God to be offended, and whether these appearances might have been nothing but delusion, and my whole prayer a pure deception.

9. This distressed me so violently that I was quite distraught. But the Lord comforted me frequently and strengthened me again—all of which it is unnecessary to recount; He also said then that I should not worry, for I had done Him a great service. Here the Lord taught me at the same time what a great good it is to endure adversities and persecutions for His sake; for the increase of the love of God in my soul was so great that I wondered at it. Around the same time, those (a) powerful impulses of the love of God began to increase more, as did greater raptures <term>raptures: intense states of mystical ecstasy where the soul feels "caught up" or transported by divine love</term>, although I said nothing of this gain.

10. For five or six months I thus remained silent about this work: [at the end of this time a new Rector <note>original: "Rector," the superior of a Jesuit house</note> of the Society of Jesus <note>the Jesuit order</note> came to the city, a very spiritual man of a brave spirit]. As I began to deal with him, the Lord also began to urge me again that I should take up the work of the convent once more; and I was to present many matters and reasons to him and to my confessor so that they would not hinder me, some of which struck them with awe. Finally, my confessor gave me permission again to apply all possible diligence.

11. Thus we became one with another, agreeing that the matter should be pursued with the utmost secrecy; therefore I brought it about that one of my sisters bought the house and prepared it as if it were for herself. However, I endured a great deal of trouble in obtaining the money to buy and prepare the house. Once, when I was in great need and did not have a single heller <note>original: "Heller," a small coin of very low value, used here to mean "a single penny"</note> with which to pay the workers, the Lord provided me with money in such a way that all who heard of it were amazed.

12. The house seemed to me to be far too small, but the Lord said to me: **I have told you before that you should move in however you could.** And as if He were crying out to me, He said further: **Oh, the greed—**

She lived more than seventy miles away from this city, and while traveling, she had gone several miles out of her way to speak with me because she had heard of me. The **Lord** had moved her in that very same year and month, just as He had moved me, to establish another convent of our Order. <insert>[She had come from Rome with the official letters of authority for this purpose]</insert>. She was a woman of strict life, devoted to prayer, and one to whom the **Lord** granted many graces. She stayed with me for fourteen days, and we consulted with one another.

17. This woman made it known to me that our original Rule commands that one should possess nothing of one’s own; this was something I had not initially considered, because I was focused on how we might be free from the worry of basic necessities. Meanwhile, I had not noticed how much worry it brings when one actually possesses property. I had seen several poor convents that were not very recollected <term>recollected [German: *eingezogen*; referring to a state of strict monastic discipline and focus on God]</term>; however, I did not realize then that they were poor *because* they were not recollected, and not that they were dissipated because they were poor—for poverty did not make them any richer. When she told me this, I was well pleased, for His Majesty <note>A term Teresa frequently uses to refer to God.</note> had granted me a great desire for poverty.

18. I found, however, almost no one who shared this opinion—neither my confessor nor the learned men with whom I dealt. That Dominican <note>Likely Fray Pedro Ibáñez, a prominent theologian.</note> wrote me two full sheets of refutations, arguing that I should not do it. But I replied that I did not wish to make use of his theology if it meant failing my calling, or failing to keep the counsel of Christ with the greatest possible perfection; I told him that in this case, his learning was of little service to me. I saw so many difficulties in having a yearly income, and saw that it caused so much unrest and distraction, that I did almost nothing but argue with the scholars about it. Even when they occasionally persuaded me, as soon as I returned to prayer and saw **Jesus** so poor and naked on the Cross, I could not endure the thought of being rich.

was known, a great tumult arose because of it. 6. When I arrived and gave my account to the Prioress, she was somewhat calmed. They all sent at the same time for the Provincial <term>Provincial: The regional superior who oversees all houses of a religious order in a specific province.</term>. After the Provincial had sternly rebuked me with words, I did not desire to excuse myself, but rather asked for forgiveness, and that he should punish me and only bear no grudge against me.

7. After two or three days, several of the city officials, together with the town judge and some from the chapter <term>Chapter: A council of high-ranking clergy who assist in the administration of a cathedral or diocese.</term>, came together and unanimously decided that this convent should by no means be permitted. One alone, a Dominican (a), said: This was not a thing that could be abolished so quickly; one should weigh it well, there was still time enough for that, and such things belonged before the Bishop, and other similar things. And the uprising was so great that it was a miracle it was not abolished immediately.

8. The tumult of the common people was so great that nothing else was talked about; everyone criticized me and went to the Provincial and to my convent. What was said about me hurt me just as little as if it had not been said; I only feared that the convent might perhaps be overturned <note>Meaning "suppressed" or "dissolved."</note> again; this tormented me greatly. And so I was very distressed during these two days in which these two meetings were held. In such great distress, the Lord said to me: 
> Do you not know then that I am powerful? Why then do you fear?
He also assured me at the same time that it would not be overturned, and I remained very comforted by this.

9. In the meantime, they sent a report of the matter to the Royal Council, and a command came that the course of events should be presented in order. See, it had now become a great lawsuit. For in the name of the city, several of them traveled to Court <note>The Royal Court of King Philip II of Spain.</note>, and several were also to go there in the name of the convent, but there was no money available, and I did not know what I should do. Those four pious servants of God <insert>[in the newly established convent]</insert> were there alone, and accomplished more with their prayer than I did with all my business, although very great diligence was also necessary there. However, he could never bring them so far that they did not immediately insist again that the foundation should be overturned. This conflict and unrest lasted for about half a year, and I wondered how the Evil Foe <note>German: "der böse Feind," a common reference to the Devil.</note> could rebel so violently against a few weak women; and how it could occur to everyone that twelve women, along with their Prioress (for there were to be no more than that), could be so harmful to the city, especially since they led such a secluded life.

11. To put it briefly, it cannot be explained enough how much we had to suffer in these two years spent from the beginning of the convent until it was finished. When the city was finally quieted a little, the aforementioned Dominican <note>This refers to Father Pedro Ibáñez, a learned theologian who provided the legal and spiritual defense for Teresa’s reform.</note> who stood by us was brought back here at an opportune time; he approached the matter so skillfully that through certain ways and means, he managed to get the Provincial to give permission for me, along with several others, to come to this convent. Before this, it had seemed almost impossible that he would allow it. Exceedingly great was my joy on the day we finally entered.

12. Now, when we began to hold divine services, the people also began to have a great devotion to this convent, and more nuns received the habit <term>Received the habit: The ceremony where a novice formally enters the religious life and begins wearing the order's specific clothing.</term>; and the Lord began to move those who had persecuted us most, so that they became very favorable toward us and shared alms with us. They now considered good what they had so long rejected, and said they now clearly recognized that it was a work of God. And without us asking for it, the Lord moves them to provide us with alms, so that we live without any lack of what is necessary.

13. It is a very great comfort to me that I find myself among such souls, who are so utterly stripped of all things and detached. Solitude is a comfort to them, and it is a pain to them even to think that they should see anyone or have dealings with anyone, unless it be so that they might further ignite someone in the love of their Bridegroom <note>The "Bridegroom" is a traditional mystical term for Jesus Christ, to whom the nuns are spiritually wed.</note>. Therefore, no one comes to this convent unless they wish to speak of such matters; others please neither us, nor we them.

14. Oh, the great power of our God! I often marvel at it when I consider how His Majesty specifically willed to stand by me so that the founding of this little corner of God might finally be brought to an end; for that is what I consider it...

### Seventh Part. The Life ###

<note>original: "Siebendes Stück. Das Leben"</note>

...[since it] had occurred, a great tumult arose because of it. The Prioress <note>The superior of the Monastery of the Incarnation, where Teresa was formally a member.</note> immediately sent for me, with the command that I should come there at once. 6. When I arrived there and answered to the Prioress, she was calmed to some extent; and they all sent at once for the Provincial <note>The regional superior of the Carmelite Order.</note>. When he arrived, I went before the court <note>A formal disciplinary hearing within the religious order.</note>, and indeed with great joy; I reminded myself then of the judgment that was held over Christ. I confessed my guilt as if I were very worthy of punishment, and I was also regarded as such. # Chapter Sixteen.
## Extraordinary effects of the graces which God showed her. Her boldness in her dealings with God. The folly of worldly courtesies. She is shown the things of the kingdom of heaven. Sees the Son of God in the bosom of the Father.

->I.<-

I am reluctant to continue recounting even more graces beyond those already told; for these are already too many to believe that such things have happened to so wicked a person. However, so that I may obey the Lord, who commanded me, and Your Reverence, I will say a few more things to His honor; may His Majesty grant that it may serve for the benefit of your souls!

2. It is to be noted that from every grace the Lord granted me, my soul always drew a great profit. For example, from the contemplation of Christ <note>original: "Beschauung Christi"—referring to a specific type of meditative or visionary prayer where the practitioner "sees" the humanity of Christ.</note>, His exceedingly great beauty remained imprinted on my soul, and the same is still impressed upon me today. For it is enough to have seen Him once, how much more so since the Lord has shown me this grace so often? From this, a great benefit has remained with me. For after I beheld this great beauty, I have never since seen anyone who pleased me when compared to Him; for if I merely cast the eyes of devotion upon the image I have in my soul, I am so free in that respect that everything I see since then disgusts me compared to the excellence and adornment I see in this Lord. Thus, I also regard no science nor any pleasure as anything compared to the hearing of a

### of St. Teresa. Chapter XVI.

...of a single word that is spoken by this Divine Mouth. How much more so since I have heard so many of them? I believe it would be impossible for anything else to occupy my memory; or rather, I am immediately liberated from other thoughts whenever I merely remember this Lord a little.

3. There also grew within me a much greater love and confidence toward this Lord when I beheld Him. For I saw that although He is God, He was also at the same time Man, who is not appalled by human weaknesses, and who well knows of what a **weak vessel** <note>original: "Gemächte," a reference to Psalm 103:14, "For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust."</note> we are made, being inclined to fall because of the first sin, to heal which He came into the world. I can deal with Him as with a friend, even though He is a Lord; for I recognize that He is not like those whom we have as lords here on earth, who found all their glory upon fictional and assumed authority. With such earthly lords, one must speak only at a certain hour, and only special persons are permitted to speak; if it is some poor man who has some business, he must use much circumlocution, and much more favor, effort, and labor are required for him to accomplish anything.

But if one has business with the King himself—oh, that is not for poor people at all, or those who are not noble! In that case, one must inquire who the King’s secret servants are; and these must, above all things, not be among those people who have already despised the world and trampled it under their feet. For such people speak the truth and fear or respect no one; they are of no use at court, and one must not employ them there. Instead, one must remain silent there when something seems wrong; indeed, one must not even think of it, lest one become hated.

4. O King of Glory and Lord of all kings! How Your kingdom is not at all armed with such feeble splinters <note>original: "Spänlein." Teresa uses this metaphor to describe the fragile, temporary supports of earthly power compared to God's eternal strength.</note>, since it is without end and eternal! How little one needs an intermediary with You! Whoever merely looks upon Your person sees at once that You alone are the one who is worthy to be called a Lord; You manifest such majesty and glory that You need no attendants or guards for one to recognize that You are the King. For here on earth, one would hardly recognize a king by himself and alone, even if he dearly wished to be recognized as such; one would not believe him, because he has no more than others. One must see external signs in order to believe it. Thus, it is necessary that he has this external, fictional appearance; for if he did not have this, no one would respect him. The fact that he appears powerful to others does not come from himself, but this authority or appearance must come to him from others.

O my Lord! O my King! Oh, if only one knew how to represent the Majesty that You possess! It is impossible not to see and perceive that You are, from and in Yourself, a most mighty Emperor; whoever looks upon this Majesty is struck with awe. But even more, O Lord, is one struck with awe who sees Your humility alongside that Majesty, and the love that You show to such a one as I am. In everything, one can deal and speak with You just as it pleases us, once the first shock and fear of seeing Your great Majesty has passed.

# Seventh Piece. The Life

5. In the world today, however, things are so arranged that a person's life should rightly be much longer, if only so that one could finish learning all the new fashions, courtesies, and ceremonies. I cross myself <note>original: "Ich segne mich." This reflects a gesture of surprise or wonder, similar to saying "God bless me."</note> when I see how things are going in the world now, for I would never know how I ought to live if I had to deal with the Great <note>High-ranking nobility or those in power.</note>; since they do not take it as a joke when someone forgets themselves and does not show people much more honor than they deserve; instead, they take it so seriously that you must excuse yourself, saying it was not ill-intended, and even then they will hardly believe you.

6. I say once again, I truly would not know how I should live, so weary does a poor soul find itself in such matters. For how someone—who should rightly always be thinking of how he might please GOD and hate the world—can at the same time so diligently take heed of how he may satisfy those who live in the world, I simply do not know how that can be. Indeed, if one could learn it all at once, it might be tolerable; but now one must even have a special school for the mere titles and headings of letters, for there one must leave space now on one side, now on the other; and the person one previously barely addressed as "Your Respectability," one must now call "Your Grace." <note>Teresa is satirizing the increasingly complex and rigid social etiquette of 16th-century Spain, which moved from the simpler "Your Worship" (Vuestra Merced) to more inflated titles.</note> I do not know where it will all end. I am not yet fifty years old, and I have already seen so many changes that I do not know how one is supposed to live. What then will those do who are only now coming into the world?

7. But look, in what trifles <note>original: "Lappereyen" (nonsense/silliness).</note> have I involved myself. I ought to be treating the great wonders of GOD, and I have stumbled upon the contemptible things of the world. But because the Lord has granted me the grace to leave them behind, I will stop speaking of them. However, those who protect and observe these vanities with so much effort may settle it among themselves; and God grant that we do not have to pay for them in that life which is without change! Amen.

8. It happened once that such a powerful rapture <term>Entzückung: a state of mystical ecstasy where the soul is "carried away" from the senses.</term> fell upon me that I could not resist it; and it was to me exactly as if I were in heaven. There I saw great things in a short time. Afterwards, the Lord showed me even greater mysteries; and there were so many of them that even the least among them was enough to fill the soul with wonder and to value all things of this temporal life as nothing. I wish indeed that I could explain even a little of the very least that I understood there, but I find that it is impossible. Once, I had been in this state for longer than an hour, where the Lord showed me wonderful things, and He, as it seemed to me, did not leave my side, and said to me: "See, O daughter! what those lose who are against me; do not fail to point this out to them." Oh Lord! how little my saying helps with those who are blinded by their evil works, unless Your Divine Majesty enlightens them. Some persons to whom You granted the light have been improved by hearing of Your great wonders; but they also see, O Lord! that such things were shown to such an evil and miserable creature, so that I also consider it a great thing that anyone was found who believed me. ### of St. Teresa of Jesus. Ch. XVI.

...blessed be your holy Name and your mercy, because I have sensed, at the very least, a visible improvement in my soul from it. After this, my soul would have wished to remain there forever and not return again to life, since the contempt for all earthly things that remained within me was great; everything seemed to me to be refuse and filth <note>original: "Mist und Koth." This vivid language is typical of Teresa's "contemptus mundi" (contempt for the world), viewing secular vanities as worthless compared to God.</note>, and I see clearly how carelessly we employ our time when we occupy ourselves in them.

9. This is an excellent dominion of the soul over all things, which is so great that I do not know if anyone will understand it except the one who possesses it themselves; for this is the true, proper, and natural detachment <term>Entschlagung: A total renunciation or letting go of worldly attachments.</term> from all things, and it happens without any effort of our own, because God does it all. For His Majesty <note>Teresa frequently uses the title "His Majesty" (Seine Majestät) to refer to God, reflecting the courtly language of 16th-century Spain.</note> discovers these truths in such a manner that they are so impressed upon a person that one sees clearly that we could not have acquired them ourselves in such a way and in such a short time. This has also caused me to fear death very little—whereas before I always feared it greatly—but now it seems to me a very easy thing for one who serves God; for in a moment the soul finds itself delivered from this prison and set in its rest. For when God thus elevates the spirit and shows it such excellent things in these ecstasies <note>original: "Verzückungen." These are the raptures or "flights of the spirit" Teresa describes throughout her life.</note>, it seems to me to have a great likeness to the departure of the soul from the body; for in a moment it finds itself in possession of all this good.

10. I set aside the pains that one feels in the departure, because they are of little account; and it is indeed believable that those who love God uprightly and have renounced all temporal things have a much slighter and sweeter death. It also seems to me that it has helped me much toward the knowledge of our true Fatherland <note>original: "Vaterland." In this context, it refers to Heaven as the soul's true home.</note>, and to understand that we are pilgrims here; and it is a great thing for one to recognize what is above and to know where he shall live. For if someone wishes to travel to a land where he shall live forever, it helps him much in enduring the toil of the journey that he has previously seen that it is a land where he will sit in great peace.

11. It also helps much in the contemplation of heavenly things to strive to have one’s fellowship above, which then happens quite easily. This is a great gain, since even a single glimpse of heaven collects the soul; for because the Lord has wished to show it something of those things that are above, it thinks upon them thereafter. And it happens to me at times that I have my company and my comfort with those whom I know live above, and it seems to me that they are the ones who truly live; by contrast, however, those who live on earth seem to me to be so dead that it feels as if the whole world offers me no company, especially when I feel those powerful impulses.

12. Everything seems to me to be a pure dream, and everything I see with bodily eyes a mere child’s play; but what I have seen with the eyes of the soul is that which it longs for, and because it still sees itself so far from it, that is a bitter death to it. Through the precious blood that his Son shed for me,

### Seventh Part. The Life of St. Teresa, etc. Chapter XVI.

...may His Majesty <note>Teresa’s standard title for God, reflecting the royal etiquette of her time.</note> prevent—since it has pleased Him that I should recognize something of this and begin to enjoy it to some extent—that what happened to Lucifer should happen to me, who through his own fault lost everything!

13. One night while I was in prayer, the Lord began to speak several words to me, and thereby brought to my mind how evil my life had been before, which greatly ashamed and pained me. For although such words are not harsh, they awaken such a sensitive pain that they almost annihilate a person; and one gains more in the knowledge of oneself through one of these words than if we were otherwise to contemplate our own misery for many days. He placed before my eyes what a great will and inclination I had previously had toward great vanities, and said that I should consider it a great thing that He allowed this will, which before was so poorly applied, to now be directed toward Him, and that He accepted it.

14. When the Lord began to bring my evil life to my mind, I started to think with many tears whether the Lord might perhaps show me some grace; for this usually happens when I receive some special grace from the Lord, that I have first been completely reduced to nothing within myself, so that I clearly see how it is so far above all my merits, and I realize that it comes from the Lord alone. After a little while, my spirit was taken up in such a way that it seemed to me it was entirely outside the body. There I saw the most glorious humanity of Jesus Christ <note>A central theme in Teresian mysticism is the "Sacred Humanity"—the belief that one should meditate on Jesus as a human even at high levels of prayer, rather than seeking a purely formless or abstract God.</note>, with much greater glory than ever before, and through a wonderful and clear understanding it was presented to me how He was in the bosom of His Heavenly Father—though how this could be, I would not know how to say, for unexpectedly I found myself present before the Godhead. I remained so stunned and affected by this that several days passed before I could come to myself again; and it was always as if I had the Majesty of the Son of God present before me.

This same vision I have also seen on three other distinct occasions, and it is, in my opinion, the highest of all the visions the Lord has let me see, and it brings very glorious and great fruits with it, for it purifies the soul excellently and withdraws from our sensuality <term>Sinnlichkeit: In this context, it refers to the physical senses and worldly appetites that distract the soul from God.</term> almost all its powers; it is a violent flame which, as it were, consumes all the desires of this life; there also remains from this such a reverence toward God impressed upon the soul that I do not know how to describe it.

# Chapter Seventeen.

## Various other graces shown to Teresa.

2. But many more have been helped in their souls than in their bodies, as is a well-known matter. And it has often happened that the Lord released souls from heavy sins because I prayed for them, as well as others whom He has drawn to greater perfection. These graces which the Lord has granted me are so many that I would weary myself and others who read it if I were to recount them all.

3. But what wonders me more is that when the Lord sees that something is not fitting or useful, I cannot pray to Him for it even if I wanted to; instead, I would pray quite negligently, without spirit or earnestness. Other things, however, which His Majesty <note>original: "Majestät" — Teresa’s respectful title for God.</note> wishes to do, I feel that I can ask for often and urgently, even when I am not otherwise so careful about them; it seems to me that they place themselves before my eyes. In the other case, however, it is as if one is speaking loudly and cheerfully with someone, for one sees that He listens gladly.

# Seventh Part. The Life of St. Teresa, etc. Chapter XVI.

...may His Majesty prevent—since it has pleased Him that I should recognize something of this and begin to enjoy it in some measure—that what happened to Lucifer should happen to me, who through his own fault lost everything!

13. Once, when I was at prayer during the night, the **Lord** began to speak some words to me, and through them He brought to my mind how evil my life had been before, which greatly shamed and pained me. For although such words are not harsh, they nonetheless awaken such a sensitive pain that they virtually annihilate a person; and one grows more in the knowledge of oneself through a single one of these words than if we were to contemplate our own misery for many days. He placed before my eyes what a great will and inclination I previously had toward great vanities, and said that I should consider it a great thing that He permitted this will, which had previously been so poorly applied, to now be directed toward Him, and that He accepted it. <note>In her writings, Teresa emphasizes "self-knowledge" not as a source of despair, but as a necessary foundation for humility before receiving divine grace.</note>

14. When the **Lord** began to bring my evil life to my mind, I started to think with many tears whether the **Lord** might perhaps wish to show me some grace; for this commonly happens when I receive some singular grace from the **Lord**, that I have previously been entirely reduced to nothing within myself, so that I may clearly see how that grace is so far beyond all my merits, and I realize that it comes from the **Lord** alone. After a little while, my spirit was so carried away that it seemed to me to be entirely outside the body. Then I saw the most glorious **Humanity** of **Jesus Christ**, with much greater glory than ever before, and through a wonderful and clear understanding, it was presented to me how He was in the bosom of His heavenly Father; but how this was, I would not know how to say, for unexpectedly I found myself present before the Godhead. From this I remained so confounded and affected that several days passed before I could come to myself again; and it was always as if I had the Majesty of the Son of **God** present before me. <note>The "Humanity of Christ" is a central theme for Teresa; she argued against contemporary mystics who suggested that one should move beyond the physical image of Jesus to reach God, insisting instead that Christ’s humanity is the only door to the divine.</note>

I have also seen this same vision on three other distinct occasions, and it is, in my opinion, the highest of all the visions that the **Lord** has allowed me to see, and it brings with it very glorious and great fruits; for it purifies the soul excellently and withdraws almost all strength from our physical senses. It is a violent flame that, as it were, consumes all the desires of this life; there also remains from this such a reverence toward **God** impressed upon the soul that I do not know how to describe it.

# Chapter Seventeen.

## Various other graces shown to Teresa.

->I.<-

Once, when I was earnestly entreating the Lord to restore the sight of a certain person to whom I was indebted, as she had almost entirely lost it and I felt great pity for her; yet I was simultaneously worried that the Lord might not hear me because of my sins. Then He appeared to me as He had on other occasions and began to show me the wound in His left hand; with the other hand, He pulled out a large nail. It seemed to me as though He were pulling out the flesh along with the nail, so that one could easily perceive the great pain involved, which awakened in me a deep compassion. And He said, “that I should not doubt that He who had been willing to endure this for my sake would much rather do that which I asked of Him; and He promised me that there would be nothing I might ask of Him that He would not do, because He well knew that I would ask for nothing except what would be for His honor; thus, He would also do this thing which I now asked of Him.” Furthermore, “I should only remember that even at the time when I did not yet serve Him, I had never desired anything from Him that He had not done, and indeed better than I had known how to ask; how much more would He do it now, since He knew that I loved Him, and of this I should not doubt.” I do not believe eight days had passed before the Lord restored that person’s sight. <note>original: "Gesicht wieder erstattet" – refers here to the restoration of physical vision.</note>
