### Part Seven. The Life

...not live as I am bound to live; with how many imperfections do I see myself burdened? It is true that I sometimes wish to be without feeling, so that I might not see so much evil in myself. May He who is all-powerful be pleased to improve it!

5. I remember how difficult it is for those to whom God has granted the knowledge of the Truth to deal with the people of this world—to act in the affairs of this world where the Truth is so deeply hidden, as the Lord once told me. For many of the things I write here do not come from my own head, but rather my heavenly Master tells them to me; and because I have a great **scruple** <note>In this context, "scruple" refers to a persistent worry or religious doubt about committing a small sin or being inaccurate.</note> about adding or taking away even a single syllable in those matters where I explicitly add: **"This I have understood,"** or, **"The Lord told me this,"** I therefore record it as if I were saying it of myself if I do not remember it quite perfectly, or perhaps because some of my own thoughts have been mixed in with it. However, I do not call what is good "mine" here, for I well know that there is nothing of the kind in me except what the Lord has given me entirely without any merit of my own; rather, I call "mine," or said by me, that which has not been revealed to me through any revelation.

6. Once, when I was very restless and confused, such that I could not collect my spirit <note>original: "Gemüth nicht versammlen" — referring to the practice of 'recollection' or centering one's thoughts on God.</note> and was caught in a great struggle because my thoughts turned to things that were not perfect—and it seemed to me that I lacked the complete detachment from all things that I usually possessed—seeing myself thus in a bad state, I feared that perhaps the graces the Lord had shown me were a deception and a delusion. In short, I found myself in great darkness of the soul. While I was in this tribulation, the Lord began to speak to me and said:

> "That I should not be troubled, for from this state I could understand how miserable I would be if He chose to withdraw Himself from me, and that there is no security as long as we live here in this flesh."

It was also given to me to understand,

> "how this strife and battle was well worth it because such a great reward follows it; it also seemed to me as if the Lord had compassion for us who are here in the world; but I should not think that He had forgotten me, for He would never leave me, though it was necessary that I should do my part in it."

7. The Lord said this to me with great friendliness and loveliness, along with other words in which He showed me a great grace, which are not necessary to recount here. Often His Divine Majesty said these following words to me, showing great love: **"You are mine now, and I am yours."** The words, however, which I am always in the habit of saying, and which I believe I say with truth, are these: **"Lord, what do I care for myself? I care only for You."** Such words and comforts make me very ashamed.

# Of St. Teresa of Jesus. Ch. XVII.

8. At another time, when I stood in this same doubt—namely, whether these visions <note>original: "Erscheinungen" — supernatural appearances or revelations</note> were from God—the Lord appeared to me, spoke to me sternly, and said: "O children of men! How long will you be of a hard heart?" He told me I should examine myself well in one thing: whether I had surrendered myself entirely to Him. If that were the case, then I should believe that He would not allow me to be lost.

9. I was greatly distressed by this stern rebuke; then He spoke to me again with great kindness and sweetness, saying that I should not be troubled. He said He well knew that, for my part, I would not fail to devote myself to everything that might serve Him, and that everything I desired should come to pass (as indeed that which I then requested has since happened). He told me I should pay heed to love, and how it increased toward Him from day to day; from this, I would see that it was not from the evil enemy. <note>original: "böse Feind" — a common term for the Devil or Satan.</note> Furthermore, I should not think that God would allow the evil enemy to have so much room in the souls of His servants, nor could the enemy give me such clarity of mind and such inner peace as I possessed.

10. Once, while I was at prayer, I felt within myself such a great delight <note>original: "Wollust" — in this mystical context, it refers to an intense spiritual joy or ecstasy, rather than worldly pleasure.</note> that (because I judged myself unworthy of such a great good) I began to think how much more I deserved to be in that place which I had seen prepared for myself in Hell; for, as I have said, I never forget the manner in which I found myself there. <note>Teresa refers to a famous vision described earlier in her autobiography where she experienced the specific place in Hell she felt her sins had earned her.</note> Through this reflection, my soul began to catch fire even more, and a rapture of the spirit <note>original: "Verzückung des Geistes"</note> overcame me in such a way that I cannot describe it. It seemed to me as if my spirit were filled with and in the midst of that Majesty which I have understood at other times. In this Majesty, a Truth was given to me to understand, which is a fulfillment and perfection of all truths; yet I cannot say how this is, for I saw nothing. Then it was said to me—though I did not see by whom, yet I understood well that it was Truth itself: "This is no small thing that I do for your sake, but is one of those things for which you are deeply indebted to me; for all the harm that comes to the world arises because people do not recognize the truths of Scripture in clear truth; not a single dot <note>original: "Pünktlein" — a reference to the 'jot and tittle' of Matthew 5:18, meaning the smallest detail of the law or scripture.</note> of them shall be left behind." It seemed to me that I had always believed this, and that all the faithful believed it. Then He said to me: "Ah, daughter! Few are those who love me with truth; if they loved me, I would not withhold my secrets from them. Do you know what it means to love me with truth? It means to recognize that everything is a pure lie that is not pleasing to me. What you now understand, you shall see clearly from the benefit it creates in your soul." And so, God be praised, I have experienced it; for since then, everything I see that is not directed toward the service of God appears to me as such vanity and pure lies that I would not know how to say how I understand it, or how I pity those whom I see surrounded by such darkness regarding this truth. It has also brought me other gains and benefits, which I will recount here, although I will not know how to describe much of it.

# Seventh Part. The Life

### Page 76

11. From this experience, there has remained in me a great desire to speak of nothing but very truthful things, which far surpass the matters dealt with here on earth; because of this, it has begun to vex me to live any longer in the world. It left within me a great tenderness of heart, comfort, and humility. Much, it seems to me, the Lord has shared with me without my understanding in what manner, yet there remained in me not a single suspicion that this might be a deception or an illusion. Though I saw nothing, I well understood what a great good it is to regard nothing that does not help toward a greater union with God; thus, I have recognized what it means for a soul to walk in truth before the Highest Truth Himself. What I understood there, the Lord gave me to understand, who is Truth itself. All that I have said, I have understood, sometimes through words He spoke to me, sometimes without words, and some things much more clearly than others which were told to me with words. I understood very great truths regarding this Truth, far better than if many scholars had instructed me; for in no way could they have impressed the vanities of this world so deeply upon me, nor could they have given me such a clear understanding. This Truth is in itself the Truth, without beginning and end, and all other truths hang upon this Truth, just as all other love hangs upon this Love, and all other glories upon this Glory—although all of this is spoken darkly compared to the clarity with which the Lord wished to give me to understand these things. And how well the power and might of this Majesty shines forth here, since in so short a time such a great gain remains in the soul, and such great things are impressed upon it.

12. O! my Glory and Majesty! What are You doing? O my almighty Lord! Look and see to whom You grant such glorious graces; do You then not remember that this soul has been an abyss of lies and a sea of vanities, and all this by her own fault? For even though You had already given me a nature that had an abhorrence of lies, I myself have nevertheless acted so that I dealt in lies <insert>or vanities</insert> in many things. How does it fit, O my God! Or how is such great grace and favor suited to one who has deserved so poorly from You?

13. Once when I was with the others in the choir <note>The "choir" refers to the area of the convent chapel where the nuns gathered for communal prayer and the Divine Office.</note>, my soul was suddenly gathered together, and it seemed to me as if it were entirely like a clear mirror, which was completely clear on the back and sides, as well as top and bottom; in the center of it, Christ the Lord showed Himself to me, as I was accustomed to seeing Him. It seemed to me that I saw Him clearly on all sides of my soul, as if in a mirror, but the mirror was also entirely engraved into the Lord Himself through a loving communion <note>original: "Gemeinschaft"</note> that I would not know how to express.

14. This appearance seems to me to be useful for those persons who practice <term>recollection</term> <note>original: "Gemüths-Versammlung" — a mystical practice of gathering the wandering thoughts and focusing the spirit entirely inward toward God.</note>, so that they may learn to look upon the Lord as being in the very innermost part of their souls; for this meditation takes better hold and is also far more useful than if one considers Him outside of oneself. It is therefore not necessary for us <insert>to seek God</insert> by climbing into the heavens, or going further than into our own selves, for

## of Saint Teresa of Jesus. Chapter XVII.

...this only serves to weary the spirit and distract the soul, and it also brings less benefit.

15. Once, while I was at prayer, it was suddenly shown to me (without my seeing any physical form, although it happened in the clearest possible way) how all things are seen in **GOD**, and how He contains them all within Himself. I do not know how to describe this, but it has remained deeply impressed upon my soul. It is one of the greatest graces the Lord has shown me, and one that has made me blush with the most shame whenever I remembered my committed sins. It seemed to me—though I cannot say for certain that I saw anything—(yet it must have been something, because I wish to use this comparison for it, but it happens in such a subtle way that the understanding cannot grasp it). Let us say, then, that the **Godhead** <term>Godhead: the essential nature of God</term> is like a very bright diamond stone <note>original: "Diamant-Stein"</note>, much larger than the entire world, and that everything we do is seen in this diamond; and indeed, in such a way that this stone contains everything within itself, because there is nothing that is not enclosed within this jewel. It was truly a great wonder for me that I saw so many things at once in this clear diamond in such a short time; and whenever I think of it, it is still very painful for me to see what foul and abominable things appear in this most pure clarity—right there were my sins, and at that time I did not know where to hide myself for shame.

16. Oh, if only one could make those understand who commit the most unchaste and foul sins, so that they might remember how these things are not hidden, because they are committed even in the very presence of such a **Majesty**; and how rightly a single sin deserves hell; for it cannot be sufficiently understood what an exceedingly heavy thing it is to do such a thing before such a Majesty, and how much such things are contrary to His Divine nature. But one also perceives from this His great mercy, in that He still endures us, we who know all of this.

17. Once the **Lord** comforted me and said to me with great love:
> “I 
> “should not trouble myself, for in this life we could not always remain in the same 
> “state; sometimes I would be zealous, at other times not; sometimes restless, 
> “at other times calm, and soon again tempted. But I should trust in Him, and 
> “not be afraid.”

18. Since I resolved to serve this my **Lord** and Comforter with all my strength, I have, it seems to me, felt no more torment; for even if He allowed me to suffer a little, He comforted me again in such a way that I long for the cross and tribulation without any difficulty. Therefore, I live, in my opinion, for no other reason than only to suffer, and I sometimes say to Him from my whole heart:
> **Lord, either suffering or death,** <note>original: "HErr, entweder Leyden oder Sterben." This is a German translation of Teresa's famous Latin motto: "Aut pati aut mori."</note>
> **otherwise I desire nothing from you.**
It gives me comfort whenever I hear the clock strike, because it seems to me that I am then once again a little closer to seeing **GOD**.

### Seventh Part. The Life

19. As I thought to myself one day <note>original: "eines (a) Tages"</note> how much more purely one lives when one is separated from all business and worldly affairs, and how imperfect and burdened with many faults I must be when I deal with such things, I heard this: Daughter, it cannot be otherwise; strive always in everything to have a good intention <note>original: "eine gute Meynung"</note>, and see that your soul clings to nothing, and that you look to me, so that everything you do is conformed to what I have done.

20. As I was full of fear one day whether I was in the grace of God or not, He said to me: Daughter, there is a great difference between light and darkness; I am faithful; no one will be lost without knowing and recognizing it. Whoever promises themselves security because of spiritual comfort and sweetness <term>sweetness: "Süssigkeit," a term for pleasant emotional or sensory feelings experienced during prayer</term> will be deceived. True security is the testimony of a good conscience. But let no one think that they can remain in the light by their own power, just as no one can prevent the natural night from coming; for such things rest upon my grace. The best means that can be found to preserve the light is for the soul to recognize that it can do nothing of itself and that it comes from me; for even if the soul were in the light, the moment I turned away from it, the night would overtake it. In this consists true humility: that the soul recognizes how much it is capable of, and what I am capable of. The instructions I give you, do not fail to write them down, so that you do not forget them, since you are also happy to write down the exhortations of men.

21. At another time, the **Lord** <note>original: "HErr"</note> stood quite clearly beside me and began to comfort me with great friendliness, and said among other things to me: Do you see me here, my daughter, that it is I? Show me your hands. And it seemed as if He took them and pressed them to His side, and said: See my wounds; you are not without me; endure the short course of this life.

22. While I was in the monastery at Malagon <note>Teresa founded this monastery in Spain in 1568</note>, the **Lord Jesus Christ** showed Himself to me through an imaginary vision <term>imaginary vision: a vision where the mind perceives an image, distinct from a physical sight or a purely wordless understanding</term>, and I saw that instead of the crown of thorns, and around His whole head where He had perhaps been wounded before, He had a very shining crown. Then I began to think what a great pain this must have been, because He received so many wounds from it, and this pained me. Then the Lord said to me: "I should not have compassion for Him because of these wounds, but because of the many wounds that were being struck against Him now." Then I said to Him: What then could I do for this, since I was determined and ready for anything? Then He answered me: "It was now no time to rest, but I should hurry to establish these monasteries; for in the souls of these monasteries He has His rest; I should accept as many of them as were offered to me, because there were many who did not serve Him because they had no place or opportunity."

### Of Saint Teresa. Chapter XVII.

23. One day as I commended one of my brothers to the Lord and said: "Why is my brother in such a place where he is in danger of his salvation? If I, O Lord, were to see one of your brothers in such danger, what would I not do to help him? It seems to me I would omit nothing that was possible for me." Then the Lord said: "O daughter! Daughter! My sisters are those who are in the convent, and you hesitate? So, take heart." <note>Teresa is being reminded that her spiritual family—the nuns in her reformed convents—must be her primary concern over her biological siblings.</note>

24. When I was the Prioress in the Convent of the Incarnation <note>original: "Kloster der Menschwerdung," the convent in Avila where Teresa first took her vows</term>, His Majesty said this to me on a certain occasion: "Fear not, my daughter, that anything shall be able to separate you from me."

25. Another time, when I thought to myself what a heavy thing this life is, because it prevents us from being able to stay constantly in the wonderful company of the Holy Trinity <note>original: "heil. Dreyeinheit"</note>, I said to myself: "Lord, provide the means so that I may endure this life." Then He said: "Consider, O daughter! that after the end of this life you will no longer be able to serve me as you do now. Eat for my sake, and sleep for my sake, and everything that you do, do it for my sake, just as if you yourself no longer lived, but I lived in you." <note>This echoes the Pauline sentiment in Galatians 2:20: "It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me."</note>

26. <header>Seventh Part. The Life</header>

...which the Lord has bestowed upon me. May He be blessed forever for having taken such care of me!

28. Since I am now out of the world and find myself in a small and holy company, I look down as if from a height and from above, and care very little what people say or know of me. I would care more if a soul were to increase even a little in virtue than for everything that might be said of me; for since I have been in this place <note>Teresa refers to the first reformed convent of St. Joseph in Avila</note>, it has pleased the Lord that all my desires aim toward this. And the Lord has granted my life such a way of sleeping that it almost always seems to me as if I were dreaming what I see, nor do I feel any particular joy or sorrow within myself. But if something of the kind is caused in me, it passes away so quickly that I wonder at it, and it produces no other sensation in me than if I had otherwise dreamt something.

29. In this manner I live now, Reverend Father; may Your Reverence <note>original: "E. E." – abbreviation for "Eure Ehrwürden," a formal address to her spiritual director</note> pray to God that He either take me to Himself or grant means and ways so that I may serve Him. May His Divine Majesty grant that what is written here may be of use to you; it has cost me much effort because of the lack of time. The effort would be blessed if I had written something so that the Lord might be praised through it only a single time; I would consider myself sufficiently rewarded by this, even if Your Reverence were to burn it immediately. I can say with truth that it has been much harder for me, and I have felt it more, to describe the graces that the Lord has shown me than the transgressions I have committed against His Majesty. From what is written here, you will see how well all effort is invested when one gives oneself entirely to Him who communicates Himself to us so far beyond all measure. May He be blessed forever!

# Of Saint Teresa of Jesus. Chapter XVIII.

[...be cited under the most edifying circumstances. Thus, once again, these are *Teresa’s* own words:]

2. For five whole years after the founding of the *Convent of St. Joseph* in *Abula* <note>original: "Abula," the Latin name for the city of Ávila</note>, I remained there; those years (so it seems to me) will be the most peaceful of my entire life. During that same time, several young maidens entered the Order, young in years, whom the world had already tried to claim for its vanity, but whom He has led into His house, endowed with such perfection that it put me to great shame. When we were thirteen in number, which was the limit we had resolved not to exceed, I delighted in these holy and pure souls, whose only care was to serve and praise God the Lord. There His Majesty sent us whatever we needed without us even asking; and whenever we lacked something, their joy was only greater. I praised the Lord that I saw so many high virtues in them; but especially that they discarded and forgot all things, except for serving Him.

3. I, who was their superior <term>Vorsteherin: the mother superior or woman in charge of the convent community</term>, cannot remember ever having worried about such things; I also held it for certain that the Lord would not let those suffer want who had no other care than how they might please Him. And when at times there was not enough food for everyone, and I said to them that the food belonged to those who were in most need of it, each one thought that she was not among them, and so the food remained untouched until God the Lord sent more, so that there was enough for all.

4. As for the virtue of obedience (to which I am very inclined, although I did not know how to practice it until these servants of God taught me), I could tell many things about what I have seen in them in this regard, etc.

5. While I was among these angelic souls <note>original: "englischen Seelen," meaning souls like angels (Engel) rather than the nationality</note> (for they seemed no different to me, as they did not hide a single fault from me, even internal ones; likewise, the graces and generous desires, and the complete detachment from all things which the Lord granted them, were exceedingly great; their greatest comfort was their solitude, and it was pure pain to them when someone came to visit them, even if it were their own biological siblings)—when I, I say, considered the excellence of these souls and the great courage that God shared with them for suffering and for His service, which was certainly nothing feminine <note>Teresa uses this phrase to describe a spiritual strength and resolve that she felt transcended the social and cultural expectations for women in the 16th century</note>, I often felt that God was gathering such a rich treasure in them for some other great purpose and end; although it did not enter my mind what would later follow from it, which at the time seemed quite impossible.

For who is more willing to give than You? If only there is someone who is willing to accept it. Or who is he, who would so gladly let one serve him at his own expense, as You?

# The Nineteenth Chapter.
## Detailed account of the convent foundation in the city of Toledo. Love of poverty and the earnest way of faith of the first daughters there. Example of the joyful passing of one of them.

->I.<-

In the city of Toledo (these are the own words of our Saint), there lived a distinguished merchant, a pious servant of God named Martin Ramirez, who had never wished to marry but lived as a devout Christian. After he had gathered his wealth through honest trade and with the intention of establishing a work pleasing to God the Lord, he became terminally ill; he died with the thought of founding such a convent, but since his time had already passed, he left the matter to his brother Alphonso. I was in Valladolid at the time when they reported to me that if I wished to accept this foundation, I should hasten to go there; therefore, I traveled there shortly thereafter, having with me two sisters from the convent in Avila, great servants of God. We were immediately given a room where we could stay in seclusion, as if in a convent.

Then I remembered the youth whom Father Martin of the Cross <note>original: "Pater Martin von Creuz"</note> had sent to me, and I spoke of it to my companions; they, however, laughed at me greatly and said I should certainly not do it, as it would serve no purpose other than to make the matter public. But I would not follow their advice, for because he had been sent to me by this servant of God, I had the confidence in him that he would accomplish something, and that this had not happened without some mystery. I therefore had him called and entrusted to him, in the highest secrecy, the state of our affairs, with the request that he look about for a house for this purpose; I would then provide a guarantor for the rent. This guarantor was the good Alfonso de Avila <note>original: "Alphonsus d' Avila"</note>, of whom I have said that he had fallen ill. To the youth, this seemed quite easy, and he said he would find a house for me. The very next morning, he came to me and said: he had already inquired about a house and already had the keys with him; it was also very close by, and we should therefore go and inspect it. This we did, and the house was good and suitable.

7. Often when I think of this foundation, I wonder at the marvelous arrangements of God; nearly three months had passed during which wealthy people throughout the city of Toledo <note>original: "Tolet"</note> had searched here and there for a dwelling and had been unable to find one, just as if there were no house in the whole city; and this poor youth comes along and finds one immediately. Also, while this convent could have been founded without any trouble had we come to terms with Alfonso Alvarez <note>the wealthy benefactor mentioned in the previous chapter</note>, the Lord arranged that this agreement could not be reached, so that this foundation might be established through poverty and much toil.

8. Since the house pleased us, I immediately ordered that we should take <term>possession</term> <note>original: "Possession" — the formal legal act of occupying the building to establish the convent's existence</note> of it before anything was prepared inside, so that no hindrance might come between us. Not long after, the youth Andradus <note>The young man sent by Father Martin</note> came and informed me that the house would be cleared that same day, and we should therefore bring our household goods into it. I answered that there was not much to do there, as we had nothing with us except the straw mattresses and a blanket; no doubt he must have wondered at this. My companions were annoyed and said, why had I told him such things? If he saw us so poor, he would no longer want to help us; but I had paid no attention to that, and he likewise seems to have cared little, for he was so diligent in preparing the house and hiring the workmen that he was second to none of us in his efforts.

9. Just before nightfall, we went into the house with a <term>notary</term> <note>original: "Notario"</note> to take possession of it, and spent the night in great fear, cleaning and prepar—

...passed, [and the divine service <note>original: "Gottesdienst"</note> was performed the very next morning.] But when the woman who owned the house learned that it had been turned into a church, she first gave us much trouble, thinking that we would not buy the house from her at a high enough price; yet God arranged it so that she was finally quieted. However, after the City Council became aware that the monastery had already begun—something for which they had never wanted to give permission—they became very indignant about it. They went to the house of a prominent clergyman and told him of their astonishment at the presumption of a woman who dared to set up a monastery against their will, saying they intended to do this and that. (The Governor, however, had departed immediately after he had given me the permission.) This clergyman then quieted them as best he could, saying that I had done the same in other places and would undoubtedly not have done it without sufficient permission. A few days later, they sent us an excommunication order <note>a formal ecclesiastical censure forbidding the sisters from taking part in sacraments</note>, stating that no further divine service should be held there until I could present sufficient letters of authority <note>original: "Gewaltbriefe," referring to legal mandates or patents</note>. This I then did; whereupon, because it had already been accomplished, they finally allowed themselves to be pacified.

10. For several days, we made do with our straw mattresses and a few blankets, without any other household furniture. On that first day, we did not even have enough wood to roast a single herring; and I do not know who it was that God inspired to lay a small bundle of wood in the church for us, which helped us a little. At night, we had to endure considerable frost, even though we covered ourselves with the blankets and our coarse cloaks, which often serve us well. The inner comfort and the joy we felt in this poverty <note>original: "Armuth"</note> were so great that even now I often think to myself what glorious treasures the Lord keeps locked within the virtues. This lack we suffered caused a sweet contemplation <note>original: "Beschaulichkeit," a term for mystical prayer</note> within us; yet it did not last long, for immediately afterward we were abundantly provided for, even more than we desired. And it is the certain truth that I became so saddened by this that it seemed to me as if I had possessed many golden jewels that had been taken from me, leaving me entirely poor. My companions felt the same; for when I saw them looking somewhat sad, I asked them what was the matter? To which they replied: "What should be the matter, dear Mother? It simply seems to us that we are no longer poor." From that time on, I have always longed more to be very poor, and there has remained in me such a prevailing spirit by which I esteemed all temporal things lightly, because through the lack and absence of them, the inner good is increased, which truly brings much other pleasure and rest with it.

11. The first sister who entered this house was named Anne of the Mother of God <note>original: "Anna von der Mutter GOttes"</note>. She was about forty years old and had spent her whole life in the service of God; and although she did not lack for good days at home, being an only child and well-to-do, she much preferred to choose poverty and submission <note>original: "Unterthänigkeit"</note>. She came then and spoke to me. She had, indeed, little health; but because I saw that she possessed such a...

# Page 87
## of Saint Teresa of Jesus. Chapter XIX.

...[since she was a] good pious soul and was so well-resolved, I held her to be suitable to make a beginning for this foundation; and I have therefore received her. Now God has been pleased to grant her much better health within the strictness and submission of the Order than she had previously had during her freedom and comfortable days. But what moved me particularly to devotion is that before her **profession** <term>the formal act of taking permanent religious vows</term> she gave her belongings and property (as she was quite wealthy) to the convent. This seemed burdensome to me, and I did not want to agree to it, but told her it might be that she would perhaps not be satisfied, or that we might not want to admit her to profession, and this would indeed be a hard thing. Although, had such a thing occurred, we would not have kept what she had given us, I nevertheless wanted to emphasize this to her with great diligence so that it might not cause her any **temptation** <term>original: "Anfechtung," referring here to a spiritual trial or doubt</term>, and so that I might also better test her spirit. But she answered that if such a thing happened, she would gladly lose it for God's sake, and I could never persuade her otherwise; and she lived very well-satisfied and in good health.

12. The practice of **mortification** <term>self-denial or discipline intended to overcome sin</term> and obedience was very great in this convent; so much so that during the time I stayed there, the superior sometimes had to be very careful with her words; for even if she said something by chance, it was carried out immediately. And this happens not only in this convent, but in all the others many such things occur which one could relate, so that God might be praised in His servants.

13. It also happened, while I was still there, that a sister became sick unto death; after she had received the **Holy Sacrament**, she was so full of joy that we spoke to her without hesitation, asking her to pray to God for us, just as if she were already in the other world. Shortly before she passed away, I went in to stay with her; as soon as I entered, I saw **His Majesty** <note>Teresa's habitual way of referring to Jesus Christ</note> at her head, in the middle of the upper part of the bedstead, with His arms somewhat outstretched, as if He wanted to protect her; and He said to me: *I should be assured that all the virgins who would die in this convent, He would protect in such a manner; and that they should fear no temptation in the hour of death.*

14. I remained powerfully comforted by this, and gathered in my spirit. After a little while, I drew near to speak with her, and she said to me: *O Mother, what great things I am about to see!* and so she passed away like an angel. In several others also who have died, I have noticed that they passed away with great calm and peace, just as if they were in an ecstasy or in the **prayer of quiet** <term>a state of contemplative prayer characterized by the soul's peaceful awareness of God</term>, without any sign of temptation. I also hope in the goodness of God that He will preserve this grace for us through the merits of His dear Son. Therefore, my daughters, let us apply diligence that we may be true **Carmelites**, for our day's journey will soon come to an end.

# Chapter Twenty.

**Theresa founds several convents. Her arduous journeys, obstacles, and God's assistance therein. The earnestness and virtues of the first sisters. Harsh slanders and heavy persecution of Theresa and her convents. Her state of mind during these trials.**

1. In this same year of 1569, Theresa founded both a monastery for men and a convent for women in Pastrana, and in the following year, one in Salmantica <note>the city of Salamanca</note>. In the description of these, we again observe the earnest walk of faith of these daughters of the convent. I have truly, says Saint Theresa, often felt a great consolation when I have seen these such pure souls praise God; for that they are such can be gathered from many things, as much from their obedience as from the fact that one sees them so well-content despite such strict enclosure and solitude, and from their joy whenever an opportunity for **mortification** <term>original: "Abtödtung"; the practice of self-denial or discipline to overcome the impulses of the flesh</term> arises. And where the Lord perhaps gives a superior more grace to exercise them in such things, there I see them even better satisfied.

2. But this I know: that the sisters in no convent that the Lord has founded until now have suffered as much, in many ways [through external unrest and hardship], as in this one. However, by the grace of God, there are pious sisters within it who endure it all with joy. May His Majesty grant them that they may continue in this; for whether one has a good house or not, little depends on it; indeed, we find much more joy in being in a house from which we can be driven out, when we remember that the Lord of all the world also had none; I have never seen a sister who was troubled by this. May His Divine Majesty grant us, through His infinite grace and mercy, that we may only not be excluded from the eternal dwellings, Amen.

3. [In the following years, Theresa continued with the founding of various convents, as she was called here and there for such purposes. During her many difficult journeys through the desolate and hot land, she had to endure great hardship, which she, along with her manifold bodily illnesses, bore willingly and with joy for the love and honor of God. Of these arduous journeys, her trip to Sevilla <note>Seville</note> can give us an idea, where in the year 1575 she founded her eleventh convent; her own words regarding it are as follows:]

I can say with truth that when we climbed into the carriage, because the sun shone upon it throughout the entire day, it was exactly as if we were entering into a **purgatory**; nevertheless, the sisters spent the journey with delight and joy.

For those six whom I had with me were such souls that it seems to me I would have dared to travel with them even into Turkey, and they would have had heart and courage enough (or better said, the **Lord** will grant it to them) to suffer for His sake, for this was their constant conversation and only desire; thus they were also very well practiced in prayer and in **mortification** <term>original: "Abtödtung"; the spiritual practice of self-denial or "dying" to one's worldly desires</term>.

5. One day before Pentecost, **God** sent these sisters a heavy cross, namely that a very high fever seized me, and I thought it was a lethargy <note>original: "Schlafsucht"; a state of drowsiness or stupor often associated with severe illness</note>, so far was I out of myself; they, however, constantly sprinkled me with water, which was nevertheless so warm from the sun that it could provide little cooling. I must also recount what a poor inn we had in such distress, because they had given us a tiny little chamber under the roof in which there was no window; but when the door was opened, the sun shone fully into it. They saw to it that I lay down in a bed, which was so soft that I would much rather have lain on the ground; for it was high on one side and low on the other, so that I did not know how I should lie in it; for it was no different than if it were filled with sharp stones. What a miserable thing it is when a person is sick! For with a healthy body, everything is easy to endure. Finally, I thought it would be better for me to get up again and for us to travel onward, as it seemed to me that I would more easily endure the sun in the open field than the heat of that same chamber. How will it then go for the poor damned in Hell, where in eternity there will be no change? For even when one only exchanges one pain for another, it nonetheless seems to be a relief, as happened to me; when I sometimes had a great pain on one side and turned to the other, even though I felt just as great a pain there, it still seemed to me to be a relief; so it was for me at that time. I myself was not troubled that I was sick, but my sisters suffered much more than I. and so forth.

6. It is remarkable what Ribera <note>Francisco Ribera (1537–1591), a Jesuit priest and the first biographer of Saint Teresa</note> recounts: how Theresa, having come upon a large field not far from the inn at Alvina <note>likely referring to a stop on the road to Seville</note>, encountered there several malicious soldiers and other fellows who, due to a dispute, were attacking one another with bare swords; all of Theresa's companions were in the greatest fear; she herself, however, said only to the soldiers: "Dear brothers, remember that **God** is present here, who will judge you." And instantly they fled away.

# Of Saint Teresa. Chapter XX.

...that one fears neither death nor any condition of this life, and always maintains such a joyful spirit as you all have now, and floats in such happiness, compared to which no greater can be found—namely, that you fear no poverty, but rather desire it. God will not deny you His mercy if you do not trust in yourselves, but place your confidence in Him and have a courageous spirit, for such is very pleasing to His Majesty <note>Teresa’s standard way of referring to God, reflecting the courtly etiquette of her time.</note>. You need not fear that anything will be lacking to you.

11. You have now surely seen that it has cost effort and labor, although I have described only the least of the hardships; for to tell of it in detail would be tedious—both regarding the difficult travels and the rain and snow, where we often lost our way; and above all this, that I was often so sick during it. Besides this, it was no small effort to deal with so many different people and adapt to their customs, as had to be done in every city. Also, that I had to leave my children and dear sisters when I traveled from one place to another; which, as I can assure you, was no small cross <note>original: "Creutz"; used here to mean a heavy spiritual or emotional burden.</note> for me, especially when I thought that I would never see them again, and at the same time saw how painfully they felt it and wept over it. For although they are otherwise completely detached from all love and affection for creatures <note>In spiritual writing, "creatures" refers to any created being (people, animals, objects) as opposed to the Creator.</note>, God did not give them the grace to be able to discard this inclination—perhaps only for my greater pain, because I also love them so; although I did violence to myself as much as possible so they would not notice it, and even scolded and punished them, it helped little, because the love they bear for me is great, as can be seen from many things that prove it is a true love.

12. But it happened, either because His Majesty wished to grant me a little rest, or because it vexed the Devil that so many convents were being founded in which God was served, that <insert>[ at this time ]</insert> an order was brought to me that I should not only found no more convents, but that I should also no longer leave the convent I chose for my dwelling—which was almost the same as putting me in prison. In addition to this, they laid two false testimonies against me in very important matters.

13. But so that you, my sisters, may see the mercy of God and how His Majesty does not forsake those who desire to serve Him, I tell you that this not only did not vex me, but also caused such a sudden joy in me that I could not contain myself; to the extent that I do not wonder what David did when he danced before the Ark <note>A biblical reference to King David dancing with abandon to celebrate the return of the Ark of the Covenant.</note>, for I would have wanted to do no less at that time, out of pure joy, so that I did not know how to hide it. As for the fact that I was to found no more convents, that was for me a desired rest and a thing I had often longed for—namely, to end my life in peace—although those who had brought this about did not intend it so, but rather thought to cause me the greatest heartache, even if they may otherwise have had a good intention.

# Seventh Part. The Life

14. I have often found joy in the heavy opposition of people regarding these foundations; however, I do not remember having felt such great joy in any adversity as I did here [when I was slandered in such difficult matters and consequently confined to a cloister]. My chief joy (in my opinion) came from the thought that, because I earned such poor thanks from creatures <note>In spiritual writing of this period, "creatures" refers to any created being—people, animals, or objects—as distinguished from the Creator (God).</note>, I would be all the more pleasing to the highest Creator. For I recognize this well: whoever does something for the sake of earthly things, or to earn the praise of men, is greatly deceived; today they like one thing, tomorrow another, and what they once speak well of, they will soon speak ill of again. Blessed be You, O my Lord and my God! You who are always and eternally unchanging, Amen; whoever serves You faithfully until the end shall live without any end in eternity.

15. [Following this, Teresa recounts how, through the envy of the mitigated Carmelites <note>The "mitigated" Carmelites were those who followed a relaxed version of the religious rule, as opposed to Teresa’s "Discalced" or reformed branch which sought a return to strict poverty.</note> (who thought their honor and profit were being diminished), a very heavy persecution was stirred up against her convents, so that for four years no further foundation could be undertaken. This continued until finally, by means of the King of Spain, the oppressed were helped; otherwise, they would have been destroyed by the fury of the Papal Nuncio <note>A Papal Nuncio is a high-ranking diplomatic representative of the Pope.</note>. We shall briefly examine her state of mind during this storm through a few words from a letter written by Teresa around this time, and then return to the history of her convent foundations:]

16. ->JESUS be in the soul of my Father!<-

I have received your letter in this prison <note>Though Teresa uses the word "prison," she was actually under a form of house arrest or forced confinement within one of her convents by order of Church authorities.</note>, in which I find myself with the highest delight, because I endure all these hardships for my God's sake. It only pains me that the Reverend Fathers concern themselves on my account; let them not worry, for I, like another Paul (though not with such holiness), can say that the prisons, hardships, persecutions, torments, mockery, and disgrace for the sake of my Lord Christ and my Order are to me pure refreshment <note>original: "Labsale"; a word for something that provides deep comfort or cooling relief.</note>. Never have I found myself better freed from all burdens than just now. It is God's own way to stand by the troubled and the imprisoned with His grace and help. I thank my God a thousand times, and it is right that we all thank Him for the grace He shows me in this prison.

17. Oh, my dear Father! Can there be any greater comfort, joy, and sweetness than to suffer something for the sake of our most kind God? When have the saints ever found themselves better in their center <note>original: "Centro"; referring to a state of spiritual rest or being aligned with God's will.</note> and in greater joy than when they suffered for the sake of their Lord Christ and God? This is the surest way to God, and the most certain of all; therefore, the cross should be our comfort and our joy. So let us, my Father, seek the cross, long for the cross, embrace adversities—and woe to the Order of the Discalced <note>The "Discalced" (meaning "shoeless") Carmelites were the members of Teresa's reformed order who went barefoot or wore simple sandals as a sign of humility.</note> on the day when it shall lack the cross, and woe to us all. Your Reverence reports...

...in the letter, [it said] how the Lord Nuncio <note>The Papal Nuncio was the Pope's diplomatic representative. At this time, the Nuncio Sega was particularly hostile toward Teresa's reforms.</note> had requested that no more Discalced <note>The "Discalced" (shoeless) Carmelites were the reformed branch of the order that followed a stricter, more primitive rule.</note> convents should be founded, and that those already established should be dissolved again at the Father General’s request and insistence; and that the Nuncio was very incensed against me, calling me a restless woman and a gadabout <note>original: "Landstürmerin," likely translating the famous Spanish insult "fémina inquieta y andariega," implying she was a woman who unacceptably wandered the country instead of staying in a cell.</note>; and that the world was, so to speak, in arms against me and against my sons <note>She refers to the friars of her reformed order as her "sons."</note>, who are now hiding in the high clefts of the mountains and in the most remote monasteries so that they might not be found and imprisoned.

This is what I weep for; this is what I feel; this is what pains me: that my sons must suffer so many persecutions and adversities because of a sinner and a wicked nun; abandoned by everyone, yet not by God. For of this I am certain: that He will not leave us, nor will He forsake those who love Him so dearly.

# Chapter Twenty-One.

## The remarkable foundation of a convent at Villa-Nova with nine pious virgins. Several foundations, and especially the final one at Burgos, under many hardships.

->I.<-

([In the year 1580, after the unrest of the aforementioned persecution had subsided, Teresa founded the convent at Villa-Nova <note>Today known as Villanueva de la Jara in Spain.</note>, a foundation for which she had previously encountered so many difficulties that for several years she could not resolve to do it. Already in the year 1576, she had received letters from the Magistrate of that same city, in which it was requested that she might accept into a convent nine young women who had enclosed themselves in a small house there some years prior, living in such seclusion and holiness that the entire city was moved by it.]

But I [so Teresa continues further] could not at all bring myself to allow it. After a month and a half, a messenger came again with a letter from the Magistrate, in which they pledged to let them suffer no want; I, however, was afraid to accept so many together, and it seemed to me there might perhaps be a clique among them against any others who might come there. Since I also saw nothing certain regarding their maintenance (for what they offered moved me little), I found myself quite confused by it. But afterward, I recognized that it had been the evil enemy who made me so faint-hearted at that time (even though the Lord had otherwise granted me courage enough), as if I had no trust in God. In the end, however, the prayers of these pious souls were more powerful.

2. For once, as I was commending the matter to the Lord, He gave me a sharp rebuke and said: With what treasures I had [provided for] the other convents...

# Seventh Part. The Life

<meta>catchword: 6. Journey</meta>

...would have well established it? And He commanded me that I should permit this house; for then He would be greatly served therein, and it would also result in the benefit of souls. Because such words of God are so powerful, I not only gladly permitted it, but it also seemed to me that I had done wrong by delaying so long and by paying so much heed to human considerations.

3. When I had decided within myself to permit this foundation, I considered it necessary that I travel there myself with the sisters who were to remain there, even though it was very difficult and contrary to my nature, because I had arrived in Malagon <note>Malagón was the site of Teresa's third foundation (1568); she often suffered from chronic illness during her travels.</note> in a very poor state and was still constantly sick. We thus departed on February 13, and it felt to me as if I had never been ill; I wondered at this myself and reflected on how much depends on us not paying attention to our own weakness when we see that we can perform some service for God. Let whatever adversities may follow happen as they will, since He can give strength to the weak and health to the sick; and even if He did not do so, nothing would be more useful to our souls than to suffer somewhat. And for what else is our life and health useful, except that we may lose it for the sake of such a great King and Lord, and that we attend only to His honor and forget ourselves? Believe me, therefore, my sisters, that in such a way you will never meet with an ill result; the Lord desires nothing more from us than the resolution, so that He may afterwards do everything.

4. On the first Sunday of Lent we arrived at Villa-Nova <note>Villanueva de la Jara, located in the province of Cuenca, Spain.</note>, and the convent was established. When we entered the small house, the nine virgins were all standing inside the door in their accustomed clothing, just as they had first entered; their clothing, however, was very modest, from which one could sufficiently perceive that they cared little for themselves, so poorly were they adorned; also, nearly all were so plain of feature that one could well see they had led a rigorous life. There they received us with the shedding of many tears out of great joy, and one noticed well that it came from their hearts; their virtue was also evident from the cheerfulness they possessed, as well as their humility and obedience toward their Prioress and all the others who had come there to establish the convent; they did not know how to show them enough love and kindness. Their only fear was that we might perhaps depart again on account of their poverty and narrow dwelling.

5. They had endured enough hardship during the six years since they had moved into this house; they lived in great poverty, to say nothing of the effort they had to apply to sustain themselves; for they had never wanted to accept alms, lest people think they were doing it so that they might be fed—just as they managed with little food, hard beds, and very narrow quarters. I see now, after having dealt with them and seen their piety, that their prayers and tears have accomplished so much that they have been received into the Order <note>The Discalced Carmelite Order.</note>. Therefore, I consider it a greater treasure that such souls dwell therein than if they possessed great estates.

6. None among them had been superior over the others, but each worked with great humility as much as she could. The two older ones among them managed the business both inside and outside the house, while the others never spoke to any people, nor did they desire to do so. They had no key for the door, but only a latch; no one was allowed to go to it, for only the eldest gave an account and answer. They slept very little so that they might earn their sustenance and not miss their hours of prayer, of which they had many; on feast days, however, they spent the entire day in prayer. They guided themselves according to the books of Louis of Granada <note>Luis de Granada (1504–1588) was a Dominican friar and a famous mystic whose spiritual writings were immensely popular.</note> and Peter of Alcántara <note>St. Peter of Alcántara (1499–1562) was a Franciscan ascetic and a close mentor and supporter of Teresa's reforms.</note>, although only one among them could read properly.

7. They had an oven in the house and managed everything as orderly as if they had an appointed authority among them. This moved me to praise God, and the more I associated with them, the more I rejoiced that I had come there. And it seemed to me that even if I had to endure much more hardship, I should not have regretted it, so that these souls might be comforted. My companions who remained there told me that it had been somewhat unpleasant for them during the first few days, but once they got to know them and saw their virtue, they were very happy to stay with them and loved them dearly.

8. Virtue and holiness are a powerful thing. It is quite true that my companions were of such a nature that, even if they had to endure much difficulty and hardship, they would have gladly borne it with God's help; for they were eager to suffer for His honor. And whichever of our sisters does not feel this desire within her should not consider herself a true Discalced Nun <note>The "Discalced" (barefoot) Carmelites were the reformed branch of the order founded by Teresa, emphasizing poverty and austerity.</note>, since our desire should not be to rest, but rather to suffer, so that we may in some measure follow our Bridegroom, to which His Divine Majesty may deign to grant us grace!

9. [After Teresa had described the foundation of the two convents at Palencia and Soria, which we pass over here for the sake of brevity, there follows finally the foundation of her last convent in the city of Burgos in the year 1582, where she also completed her life's journey not long after its completion, and was received into the heavenly fortress <note>The original German text makes a play on words between the city "Burgos" and "Burg," meaning a fortress or castle.</note>.]

10. [Initially, when the foundation of both this convent in Burgos and that in Palencia was discussed, Teresa had little desire to found convents, because she had survived a deadly illness and had not yet regained her strength at that time] although [she says] this does not usually discourage me so much when I see that something serves God's service and honor; I do not know what the cause of this reluctance must have been. For if it had arisen from having few means and help for it, then I certainly had much less for other foundations. [All my friends urged me and strengthened me, yet it helped little, and I could not resolve to do it.]

# Part Seven: The Life

but should the right heat once come to me, then we shall see that often I am not the one doing anything, but He who is capable of all things.

For the Lord said to me, as if with a rebuke: "Why do you fear? When have I ever forsaken you? I am the same as I have always been; do not neglect to establish these two foundations." <note>The "two foundations" likely refer to the late-stage projects in Soria and Burgos.</note> O Almighty God! How great a difference there is between Your words and those of men? From this I remained so determined and courageous that the whole world could not have turned me away from it.

11. [Nevertheless, *Theresa* had reservations about traveling to Burgos in person because she was quite sickly and the cold was very great; but God strengthened her inwardly, saying she should not let this cold trouble her, for He was the true heat, and thereupon she changed her mind. For although, she says, nature sometimes resists in difficult and adverse things, the will does not, and the resolution to suffer something for the sake of this great God remains constant; therefore I am accustomed to say to the Lord that He should not heed such movements of weak nature, but only command me what pleases Him, for I would not fail to do it through His grace. At that time it had snowed and was cold; and my poor health made me most timid. But the cold was so tolerable to me that the Lord, in this case, truly kept His word.

12. (The hardships of the journey were extraordinarily great; but because such things, though perhaps not so great, have already been mentioned in other foundations, let them remain untouched here. When she arrived in Burgos with her sisters, she unexpectedly found the greatest adversities in her undertaking, about which she exclaims:) O Lord God! How certain and true it is that when someone performs a service for You, You immediately reward them with a greater cross? <note>In this context, a "cross" refers to a spiritual or physical burden or hardship meant to test and refine the believer's faith.</note> And what a precious reward is this for those who truly love You?

13. During the foundation itself, so many strange, successive adversities and difficulties arose that it often appeared she would have to depart again with her sisters without having accomplished anything; and the Lord said to her once on such an occasion: "Now hold fast, *Theresa*!"

14. As great as the longing of the daughters of the convent <term>Klostertöchter: the nuns of the Discalced Carmelite reform</term> had been to obtain an enclosed house; <note>An "enclosed house" refers to the practice of "clausura," where nuns live entirely separated from the outside world to focus on contemplative prayer.</note> so great also was their joy when the Lord, after long delay, finally provided one for them; so that even our Saint herself was moved by it and said to God:) Lord, what else do these Your handmaidens seek but to serve You, and to be enclosed for Your sake, from whence they shall never come out? No one can believe what joy is felt during these foundations unless he has experienced it himself, when we now see ourselves enclosed, where no worldly person can enter in to us; for as dear as they may ever be to us, they cannot bring us such great comfort and joy as we have when we see ourselves enclosed.

15. It reminds me exactly as if one pulls many fish out of the water in a net, which cannot live unless they are put back in; so too are those souls disposed who are accustomed to the flowing water of their Bridegroom <note>original: "Bräutigam"—a mystical reference to Jesus Christ</note>; when they are pulled out from there and must look upon the nets of the world, they truly do not know how to live until they find themselves back in that water again. I sense this in all these sisters, and recognize it from experience: that those nuns who still feel a desire in themselves to go out into the world have not yet found the living water.

16. I fear, however, that this comes from two things: namely, because they either did not enter this state purely for His sake, or after they entered it, they do not recognize the great grace that God has shown them by choosing them for Himself. He has freed them so that they do not have to be subject to a husband <note>Teresa frequently wrote about the "honorable slavery" of marriage in 16th-century Spain, viewing the convent as a place of greater personal and spiritual autonomy</note> who often shortens their life and, alas, also often costs them their soul. Oh, You true God and man! You, my Bridegroom, is this then to be considered a meager grace? Let us praise Him, my sisters, that He has bestowed this upon us, and let us never grow weary or tired of praising this so great King and Lord, who has prepared for us a kingdom that has no end, in exchange for such a small, slight labor which is yet mixed with much comfort and will end tomorrow. May He be blessed in eternity! Amen.

## The Twenty-Second Chapter.
### Teresa’s Final Journey, Illness, and Blessed Passing.

->I.<-

<margin>(a) Chapters 14 and 15.</margin>
<margin>(b) Book III, Chapter 15.</margin>
Finally, let us also hear in brief of the final illness and passing of St. Teresa, as her companion, Anna of St. Bartholomew, described it in her own *Life* (a), and as Francisco Ribera described it in the *Life of Teresa* (b). From Burgos our Saint came to Palencia, and from there she was called to Alba <note>Alba de Tormes</note>. During this time, she suffered many setbacks and hardships, especially on the road to Alba, which was to be the final journey of her life; the illness that would end her pilgrimage had already made its first attack. On this journey, she once had to remain for an entire day without anyone being able to find the slightest thing to give her for some refreshment. And when we were in a small peasant’s hut overnight another time, a great weakness overcame her, so that she said to me: "My daughter, if you only had something to give me; I feel that I am going to faint." ...than but a few dried figs. I gave the people in the house money, with the request that they might search for a few eggs for me. But when I saw that the people brought the money back, because nothing could be obtained even for money, I turned to Theresa; and when I saw her half-dead countenance, I could no longer restrain myself from weeping. It felt to me as if my heart had been crushed and cut through, because I had to watch our holy mother <note>The narrator is likely Anna of Saint Bartholomew, Teresa's close companion and nurse</note> essentially dying without being able to offer her any refreshment. She, however, spoke to me with angelic <note>original: "englischen," which in this archaic context means "angelic" rather than "English"</note> patience and a joyful face: "Do not weep, dear daughter, God wills it to be so."

2. The hour of her passing—truly blessed for her, but exceedingly painful for us—drew near. She accepted her sufferings now, as always, with joy; but I, because I was less dead to the world <note>term: "abgestorben" (dead to the world)—a mystical term for the state of having completely renounced earthly attachments and self-will</note>, grieved so deeply for her sake that our mother had to comfort me, saying: I should not be troubled, for she was well satisfied with the figs she had eaten.

3. The following day we arrived at Alba <note>Alba de Tormes</note>, completely exhausted and weak, and at her request she went to bed immediately, saying: "O my God! How weary I am; in twenty years I have not gone to bed as early as I do now." In the morning she stood up once more, but had to lie down again, and the doctors immediately gave up hope for her. This was in truth a very hard blow for me.

4. Two days before she departed, while I was alone with her in the chamber, she said these words to me: "Dear daughter, the hour of my departure has already come." These words pierced my heart. She said that she no longer had need to live in this world, and she gave the fellow sisters many good and exceptionally emphatic reminders, accompanied by great demonstrations of love. Upon receiving the Holy Sacrament, she spoke many sublime, sweet, and loving things, which awakened a great devotion in all those present. Among other things, she said: 
> O my Lord and my Bridegroom! Now the hour has come for which I have long yearned. Now it is finally time that we see one another. Now it is time, my Lord, for me to go; blessings upon the hour, let Your will be done. The hour has come for me to depart from this land of misery <note>original: "Exilio," Latin for exile</note> and for my soul to enjoy together with You what she has so greatly desired.
With great devotion, she begged for the forgiveness of her sins and said that she hoped for salvation through the merits of our Lord Jesus Christ. She frequently repeated several verses from the 51st Psalm: 
> Cast me not away from Thy presence; and take not Thy holy Spirit from me.
But especially this other one: 
> A broken and a contrite heart, O God, Thou wilt not despise. 
This she had in her mouth until her speech failed her.

5. Father Anthony of Jesus, one of the first two Discalced <note>term: "Barfüsser" (barefoot)—referring to the Discalced Carmelite reform which practiced greater austerity, including going without shoes</note> Carmelites, asked her whether she wished for her body to be taken to Avila <note>original: "Abula," the Latin name for Avila</note> or if it should remain at Alba? To this, she gave sufficient indication with her face that such a question displeased her, and said: 
> "Shall I then have anything of my own?" <note>A reference to her strict vow of poverty; she believed that even her dead body should not be treated as her "property" or "belonging" to a specific place</note>

### of Saint Teresa of Jesus. Chapter XXII.

Will no one give me a little earth here? <note>This likely refers to the narrator’s extreme exhaustion and perhaps a humble desire to be buried where she stands.</note> I did not leave her side for a single moment, and everything I needed for my own necessities, I had brought to me so that I would not have to go away from her, for it was also a comfort to her to have me with her. On the same day she gave up her spirit, Father Anthony <note>Pater Antonius; likely Antonio de Jesús (1510–1601), one of the first friars of the Discalced Carmelite reform</note> was with her. When he saw how exhausted I was in the morning, he commanded me to go and eat something. But as soon as I was out of the chamber, our holy mother began to look from one side to the other (for she had already lost her speech). The Father asked her if she desired for me to be called? She immediately indicated by nodding that this would be very dear to her. As soon as I entered and she saw me, she began to smile at me kindly and showed me such signs of love that she took me by the hand and laid herself in my arms. I held her thus embraced in my arms, and she remained so in a state of high contemplation <term>Beschauung (contemplation): In Catholic mysticism, this refers to a wordless, loving focus on God</term> for fourteen hours, immersed in God and completely motionless, until she gave up her spirit.

6. I remained, on my part, more dead than she herself. She was so ignited by the love of her heavenly Bridegroom <note>A traditional metaphor in mystical literature for Jesus Christ</note> that her heart had to surrender to it and succumb to its power. Now, because the Most High is infinitely good and lays no more upon anyone than they can bear, it happened that, as He saw me lying almost prostrate with grief, He appeared to me at the foot of our holy mother’s bed with unspeakable glory, majesty, and brilliance. This glorious vision lasted long enough for me to have time to change my painful sorrow into a total surrender to His will, and with these words to ask the Lord for forgiveness: "My Lord, if Your Divine Majesty still wished to leave me the desired company of our mother for my comfort, I would nevertheless desire of You with heartfelt humility that You would not leave her in this life for one moment longer, because I have now seen her glory!" During the time that I was speaking thus to the Lord, she gave up her spirit into His hands; this occurred on the fourth of October, 1582, at the age of sixty-seven years and six months. <note>Teresa died on the night between October 4 and 15, 1582—the very night Spain transitioned from the Julian to the Gregorian calendar.</note>

# The Life

## Foreword.

As we, in the continuation of these godly life-stories, once again bring a simple female person to the fore, and shall hereafter let several more such examples follow: it might almost be deemed necessary to encounter the objection of those who, out of an indiscreet contempt for this sex, are so ready to cry out suspicion and push away with disgust whatever may come before them regarding their godliness or testimonies; whereby timid souls <note>original: "blöde Gemüther." In this context, "blöde" refers to souls that are simple, shy, or easily discouraged, rather than its modern German meaning of "stupid."</note> may be led astray in their edification. But because this objection and scruple has already been weighed and refuted with the balance of the sanctuary <note>A biblical metaphor (Leviticus 27:25) meaning to judge things by a divine or holy standard of truth.</note> by many (a) godly and learned men, it is considered superfluous to take up space with it here. In Christ there is neither man nor woman, but they are all one in Him. He wished to make Himself more closely known and familiar to a Samaritan woman and a Mary Magdalene than to the scribes and other men. In the stories of the martyrs, the bravery of women has manifoldly equaled the fame and constancy of the most courageous warriors of Christ. At all times and in all places, female persons have made up no small part of the assemblies of the devout. Not to mention those extraordinary instruments of God whom He has equipped from this weaker sex even in these days.

If one asks for the cause, the answer lies open to the day from the words of the Apostle (b): What is weak before the world, that **GOD** has chosen, so that He might put to shame what is strong, etc. In this regard, the thoughts of a recent and thorough author (c) do not displease me when he says:

> "**GOD** will never cease to avenge the shame which the Devil has inflicted upon the female sex; and He will, as long as the world stands, make use of this sex to carry out great works of grace; and at every time raise up one or another female person to a singular holiness and godliness, so that He might not cease through her to put the Devil to shame."

But one will hopefully encounter, in the examples which occur in these biographies, so much ground of unfeigned truth and godliness that it will not be necessary to dwell upon this matter. See here, in this present example, a simple peasant girl <note>original: "schlechte Baurendirne." At the time, "schlecht" meant plain or humble, and "Dirne" meant girl or maiden.</note> by birth, whose deeds and words it will be neither a harm nor a shame for us to hear, since the King of Heaven has deemed her worthy of His familiar intercourse and fellowship. See, the image of **Jesus** in her: her fervent love for **GOD** and for her neighbor, her faith, her patience, her humility, innocence, self-denial, readiness to serve, and other virtues which she practiced on every occasion; and of which she tells us her lessons here so childlike. One thing more, see how **GOD** chooses and exalts the despised; in her childhood she tends the sheep in her father's house; in her youth she lives as a lowly lay sister in a poor, hated monastery in Spain; she is called to France, and from there into the neighboring Low-

<margin>(a) 2 Samuel 7:8-9. <note>The original margin cites 2 Samuel 6, but the text quotes 2 Samuel 7:8-9.</note></margin>
lands: everywhere she establishes monasteries and becomes a mother to many children whom she wins for Christ; she flees all prestige, yet becomes famous in all places against her own seeking, so that even kings, dukes, and princes considered themselves fortunate to know her and to have recommended themselves to her prayers. Thus, God was able to say to her according to the letter what He formerly spoke to David: (a) I took you from the sheepfolds, that you should be a leader over my people. I have been with you wherever you have gone, and have cut off all your enemies before you, and have made you a great name, like the name of the great ones on earth.

This life was written in Spanish by Anna herself, along with several discourses, by order of her spiritual director; and it was published several times in both the French and Dutch languages until it was also printed in the German language in Cologne in 1669, in Quarto <note>A book size where each sheet of paper is folded twice to create four leaves.</note>, and indeed expanded with a special treatise on the excellent virtues and graces of Mother Anna, which another had described in French, and then also with a description of the life and virtues of twenty of her spiritual daughters, in which much good is still to be found.

This latter piece has been left entirely untouched in this extract, and only the most important parts from the rest have been inserted here, as much as space allowed. Thus, almost until the end, one will find only the own unadorned narrative of this pious soul herself; wherein the humble sincerity of the author shines through everywhere, giving a pleasant testimony both of the loving-kindness of God and of her innocent, faithful walk in communion with Him. May the Lord grant that it may fall deep into our hearts and take root!

Saint Teresa used to say often of our Anna: *I have the name of a saint, but she has the deeds of a saint.*

The famous Jerome Gratian <note>Hieronymus Gratianus (1545–1614), a key figure in the Discalced Carmelite reform and a close collaborator of Teresa of Avila.</note>, renowned for his wisdom and godliness—of whose praise Teresa tells much in her "Monastery Foundations" (b)—investigated the spirit, guidance, and supernatural gifts of this Anna and found them to be proven; he then composed a special treatise (c) consisting of five dialogues about them. However, he shows in the preface of such dialogues, among other things with the following words, that he undertook this investigation deliberately and with proper caution:

> "Our office is that we, like goldsmiths, have the
> touchstone of Holy Scripture at hand. And therefore it is very well done when, in a
> soul who gives herself to prayer, there is perhaps a small piece of gold of a supernatural experience or
> spirit, that she brings such to our hands; so that we may examine whether it be true
> or false gold, and how heavy it is in weight; so that she may not be deceived by him who
> is accustomed to disguise himself as an angel of light, and take for pure gold what is only a false
> metal; and also so that we may make vessels from that which they tell us, which also may be of use
> to others. ... For these reasons, I have seen fit to earnestly desire and strongly
> insist that Mother Anna might discover to me some matters of her spirit; for although
> I know many things, because it has been more than 48 years since I heard her and Saint Teresa's
> confession, I have nevertheless deemed it useful to examine her anew, etc."

Several more testimonies and approvals are to be found in the editions of her small works.
