# Chapter One.
## Mother Anna’s Origins and Extraordinary, Godly Childhood.

In the name of JESUS I begin to write what follows, as it has been imposed and commanded of me through holy obedience <note>In a religious context, "holy obedience" refers to the duty of a nun or monk to follow the instructions of their superiors or confessors, often as a spiritual exercise.</note>.

->I.<-

I was born in Spain, in the year 1549, on the first of October, in a market town half a mile from the city of Ubalda <note>Likely Úbeda</note> in Old Castile <note>A historic region in central-northern Spain.</note>, where my parents had their fields, meadows, and livestock, and were abundantly blessed by God with temporal goods according to the circumstances of their station. My father Ferdinandus Garçias <note>original: "Ferdinandus Garçias," the Latinized form of Ferdinand Garcia</note> and my mother Maria Mançanas <note>original: "Maria Mançanas," the Latinized form of Maria Manzanas</note> were both very devoted to the fear of God and to virtue.

[They were very diligent in outward Divine Service]. Every Sunday they gave a loaf of bread and approximately a quarter of wine <note>A "Viertel" was a common historical liquid measure, roughly equivalent to a quart or a liter depending on the region.</note> to the poor of that place; they cared particularly for the sick, having them diligently visited by their people, and purchasing and paying for medicine and other necessities for their needs. Whenever my mother heard a child crying in the street, she immediately had inquiries made as to whether its father and mother were still living. If not, she took it into our house and had it cared for and raised with great love and kindness.

There were seven of us siblings, namely three brothers and four sisters; so that my brothers would not be led astray or learn bad habits, my father kept an honorable clergyman in the house to instruct them in reading and writing, and all of us in the teaching of the Catechism <note>A summary of Christian doctrine used for instruction.</note> and in the mysteries of our Christian faith.

2. When I was still very small, about three years old, and could not yet speak fully, they wanted to let me walk alone in a room where my sisters were doing their needlework; meanwhile, my mother happened to pass by and said to them: "Take care of the child so that she does not fall; how easily it could happen that she might hurt herself or even fall dead." To this, one of my sisters replied: "Oh! what a great grace our Lord would show her if she died at this age, for she would go straight to heaven." The other sister said in return: "Let us take diligent care of her, for who knows—if she remains alive, she might yet become a great saint." The first one then repeated: "What you say is still very uncertain, but now there is no danger, and you know well that when children get older, they already begin to sin."

I listened well to this conversation of my sisters and understood their words; and because they spoke of sinning, I lifted my eyes upward, without my—

### Of Anna Garcia. Chapter I.

...an ecstasy would come, in which I would sometimes remain for several hours. The Child JESUS also came often to me; He was exceedingly beautiful. Especially powerful were His divine eyes, which had the strength to draw my soul out of itself and toward Him, so that I could not look upon Him without losing myself. His hair was like that of the Nazirites <note>The Nazirites were individuals in the Bible who took a vow of holiness, which included never cutting their hair.</note>; His height was equal to my own. What my spirit felt in such company is impossible for me to express; I would have gladly remained night and day without eating or drinking. It seemed to me that I was in a paradise of glory and would never wish to be without these joys, but rather wished to seclude myself in a far-distant place to possess this comfort forever. Because of this, I said one day to the Child Jesus: "My Lord, since You keep me company, let us go onto a mountain far removed from the society of men; for when You are with me, I shall lack nothing." Our Lord smiled at this simple suggestion of mine and gave me to understand without speaking that this was not what He desired of me. In this blessed company, I loved solitude so much that it was like a deathly pain and torture to even look upon the world.

7. I was so deeply immersed in the enjoyment of such inner delight <note>original: "Wollust" — in this 17th-century context, this refers to spiritual bliss or rapture rather than carnal desire.</note> that night would sometimes fall while I was out in the middle of a field, perhaps half a mile from our market town, so that my brothers wondered greatly that I came home so late. This was not without reason, for since they knew nothing of the company I kept, they could have had many different thoughts about my absence.

8. I practiced such a form of prayer (though I did not know what it was called) that I found myself completely occupied most of the time by the love of the sweetest JESUS. Therefore, I began to think of ways and means to go to another place where I might be unknown and despised by everyone; to this end, I found it most convenient to hide my female gender and put on men's clothes. I did not fear any hardship that might befall me in carrying out this plan. I spoke to no one of this plan except for one of my cousins <note>The original "Baase" refers to a female relative or close companion.</note> who was the same age as I, and who was very virtuous and full of godly desires. When we both went to church, we had the opportunity to speak with one another, and we believed our hearts were entirely ignited with the love of God. Therefore, I said to her once: "We will put on men's clothing and go into a wilderness away from people." My companion, however, who was more prudent than I, answered: "The times are no longer such that one can carry out such an undertaking." She said further: "Believe me, my sister, there are a thousand and a thousand dangers and hardships in carrying out such a plan." Nevertheless, I stuck to my first opinion and pressed her so strongly and constantly that I finally persuaded her to give in. We then decided to make ourselves hermits' clothes and steal away at night. To which end we chose a certain night, namely when

## Chapter Two.

->Her youth: how she rejected the allurements of marriage. How she received an inclination and occasion for the monastic life, and on that account was tested with various hardships.<-

->1.<-

Now that I had grown up, my siblings intended to marry me off; but my thoughts and my heart were far removed from such a purpose; for that reason, I prayed very diligently and kept my body even more strictly than before; also, at that time, I was vehemently attacked with a thousand kinds of temptations against my purpose, which caused me great pain and distress; the devil was also not idle in oppressing and frightening me through his usual cunning tricks; but I fought against them, disciplined my body, often lay on the bare ground—even though it was in a very damp place—and remained there until the power of the temptation was stilled. Once, however, I was also greatly comforted by God, at which time my desires to serve Him were newly ignited and increased.

2. This implies they appeared physically or spiritually deformed or lacking in grace compared to her visions</note> to me. In such a manner I kept myself finely withdrawn and felt myself very courageous in my constant resolution not to marry; for I considered the especially great graces that Almighty God showed me, which also required a very great faithfulness and purity, and made me very highly bound to His Divine Majesty.

I became completely faint and fell to the ground, but at the same time I said these words: The Most Holy Trinity be with me! My companion held me and sought with all diligence to drive away my terror; but because I was very weak and battered, she led me back home under her arms. All along the way, we saw three persons dressed in white, of an equal height and size, walking before us; and when I asked who they were, my cousin answered: "They must be shepherds who might be coming from their flocks." But as we came into the village, they vanished before our eyes.

### The Third Chapter.

->Her entrance into the convent. Her initial inner suffering. The subsequent inflammation in the love of God and zeal for the salvation of souls. Her mortification. Devotion to the suffering of Christ. Is comforted externally by Theresa, and internally by God.<-

->I.<-

1. [After I had now endured one or two more difficult trials and the displeasure of my siblings, and the nuns at Ávila <note>original: "Abula," the Latin name for the city of Ávila</note> had written at least twice that I should come there, I was finally led there after a long delay by one of my brothers and by my sister.] I, for my part, went there very well satisfied; however, on the other hand, I was so afflicted with all kinds of temptations as if all of hell had conspired together to wage war against me. And yet, I did not dare to open my mouth about this inner struggle and anxiety, for they would have rightly said I was foolish to enter the convent in such a state. But when I arrived at Ávila and was received into the convent, all the storm of temptations that had previously tormented me so harshly vanished in a moment; it felt to me just as if a hat had been taken from my head <note>A German idiom for a sudden sense of relief or the lifting of a burden</note>, and I remained so well satisfied and so full of joy as if I had been placed in a paradise of delights; and it felt no different to me than if I had spent the whole time of my life in this place and had been raised in the company of these pious souls.

2. But a few days after my entry, the Lord withdrew Himself from me and left me very desolate, for which reason I complained to Him in the following manner: 
> My Lord, what is this supposed to mean? Have You then now entirely forsaken me? If I did not know You so well, I would believe You had deceived me, and if I had thought that You would withdraw Yourself from me, I would not have entered into this state.

3. Such pain and dryness of mine lasted the entire time of my year of probation <note>The "probjahr" or novitiate is the testing period before a nun takes her final vows</note>. He said earnestly to me that He wanted to give me an answer to a desire I had to know whether the thirst He suffered on the Cross had been natural? Thereupon He said to me: 
> My thirst was for souls (by which, however, it is not denied that His thirst was also natural); this you shall now take to heart, and walk a different path than you have done until now.

4. As far as the external mortifications <term>mortifications: Physical acts of self-denial, such as fasting or other penances, intended to discipline the body and strengthen the spirit.</term> are concerned, which I practiced during that time—when the impetuous and powerful flames of the love of God, and also the fervent zeal for the salvation of souls, had so thoroughly inflamed me (which in my estimation lasted at least fifteen years)—I would have, as it seems to me, done so much therein that I would have exceeded the limits of natural strength, if only I could have had permission for it. Otherwise, I also did many things with deliberation so that I might be regarded as foolish; and, O my God! I had no need for great art in this, because I am indeed as clumsy and awkward as I am.

5. From my childhood, my soul has been filled with special devotion and love for the bitter suffering of our Redeemer and Savior, so that whenever I saw only a painting of this mystery, tears would immediately overcome me, and I wished from my heart to be poor and despised, and to be treated poorly for the sake of this my Lord. When I still lived with my brothers, I gave all of my clothes to the poor that I could manage to take away unnoticed; I also gave them everything else that was in my power; indeed, I even hid the food that I was given to eat and distributed most of it among the poor.

6. When I was still very small, it happened on a Good Friday <note>original: "Charfreytag"</note> that a distinguished preacher came to preach in the place where we lived, and I went with my sisters to hear him. I had a great longing and hope that he would say wonderful things about the love of the Lord Jesus, with which He had endured so many sufferings. But the good gentleman brought forth almost nothing according to my desire, but instead occupied himself only with I know not what points of theology, which pained me beyond measure, so that throughout the whole sermon I did nothing but weep. And when my sisters asked me why I was weeping, I gave them the answer: "Because the pastor did not preach well." But they countered: "How could you know such a thing? What do you understand of it?" Then I said to them: "Oh, dear sisters! If I might preach according to what I feel, it seems to me I would do it much better."

Therefore, our Mother Teresa said to me one day: "My daughter, when in the future the bell is rung for bedtime, you shall then cease your prayer and go to sleep like the others." When I now wished to be obedient in this and retire to rest, I said to our Lord: "My Lord, I have no permission to stay with You any longer; You must allow me to sleep." And it is a thing to be wondered at, how much it pleases God that we are obedient to our superiors; for the entire time ordained for sleep, He let me sleep with the others, and when I awoke, I found Him in my soul, just as if He had been waiting for me. My body was then so light, as if it were endowed with a supernatural agility <note>original: "Fertigkeit"; here meaning a physical lightness or ease of movement often reported in mystical literature</note>, so that I feared whether some deception might lie behind it; for when I walked, it seemed as if I weighed hardly as much as a straw; and everywhere I was, I felt myself ignited and filled with this strong love of God.

## The Fourth Chapter.

### The power of divine love, from which her body falls ill. Her wonderful care for the sick, and persistent zeal of love.

->I.<-

By the aforementioned strong vehemence of the love of God, my nature was altered, and my strength decreased in such a way that I gradually seemed to approach death; the physicians were called for this reason to help me; but because the origin of my illness was unknown to them, they spoke of it in different ways; some said I had <term>consumption</term> <note>original: "Dörrsucht"; literally a "drying-up sickness," referring to a wasting disease or atrophy, often used in this period to describe the physical decline of mystics.</note>, and prescribed many kinds of remedies for it, which made me even sicker and weakened me so much that I could no longer lift my feet from the earth or take a single step; my body was in a very pitiable state, and whatever remedies they used, they were not able to help me in the slightest.

2. At that same time, Mother Theresa moved to Seville, but because I was in such a state, she could not take me with her. And because I had such strong desires to suffer something, I said to the Lord: My God! I have indeed desired suffering from You, but because I now see that I am too burdensome to the convent because of it, I wish that You would send me suffering in such a way that the others do not have to have any inconvenience with me, but rather that I may serve and attend to my dear sisters without them troubling themselves on my account—only that if something to be suffered occurs, it should fall upon me alone. Thereupon His Divine Majesty said to me: I will do what you [ask] of me...

### Eighth Part. The Life

...desire of me, you will have to suffer in the company of my friend Teresa; you will both have much to suffer on your travels.

3. After this, I remained in that same outward condition until Mother Teresa returned from Seville, which lasted for a full year; when she arrived back at Avila <note>original: "Abula"; the Latinized name for the city of Avila in Spain.</note>, she found me still very sick and miserable, so that I could hardly stir or move. But on the very evening of her arrival, she said to me: "My daughter, although you are sick, come nevertheless to my cell." In appearance, I was certainly not fit to obey her, but I went nonetheless without any hindrance from my illness, as if nothing had been wrong with me. At that same time, five sisters were sick with fever, and among them one named Isabella, who could take almost no nourishment. On the following morning, however, the Mother said to me again: "My daughter, although you are sick and weak, I still want you to be the attendant <term>Aufwärterin</term> <note>The sister assigned to wait upon and care for the sick in the infirmary.</note> for all the sick sisters of our house; for there is no one else who can do this." Upon this I remained silent, not wishing to contradict holy obedience, but I thought to myself: how will I be able to do this, since I can hardly lift my feet from the ground? Nevertheless, dragging my body halfway along, I went into the kitchen to prepare something for the sickest of all, whose little chamber was reached by a staircase of fourteen steps. As I reached the bottom of these stairs, I said to our Lord: "Help me, my God, for I cannot take a single step further"; then our Lord appeared to me standing at the top of the stairs, in the form in which He walked here on earth, surrounded by a wonderful beauty, and spoke to me: "Come up, my daughter." And as He said this, I found myself above at His blessed feet without any effort, and He went with me into the chamber of the sick sister, sat down there by the bed, and leaned upon the pillow like a nurse <term>Krankenwärter</term> <note>A caregiver; Anna uses the masculine form here to describe Christ’s direct, tender actions as a physical healer.</note> who wants to comfort his patient, and spoke to me: "Set down here what you are bringing, and go hence to carry to the others what they need; I will care for this one myself." I went away with great speed, just as if I had not been sick, with an inward longing to return soon and further enjoy the sweetest presence of the Lord. I hurried as much as I could; but when I came back, He was no longer there. I found, however, the sick sister very joyful, and she asked me with a laughing mouth: "My dear sister, what have you brought me? In all my life I have never eaten anything more lovely or pleasant." At this time I told her nothing of what I had seen, although we loved each other very much; but some time afterward I asked her whether anyone had been with her while she was eating? She answered me: "No," but said she had never felt such comfort in her soul, and had been so strengthened that it seemed to her she was healthy; and indeed, from that time on she remained quite fresh and healthy. I remained silent once more, and let nothing be noticed, and the other sick sisters also became healthy immediately.

4. Now when the sick were all healthy, and I found myself in rest once more, the vehemence of the love of God and the strong zeal for souls <term>Seeleneifer</term> <note>A burning desire for the spiritual salvation of others, often described by mystics as an agonizing thirst.</note> began again within me...

### of Anna Garcia, Chapter IV.

...began to grow, and increased to such an extent that I had to begin practicing other outward tasks so that I might turn away from it <note>Anna is likely referring to an intense mystical fervor or internal "fire" that made normal functioning difficult.</note> somewhat. It was like a hungry, gluttonous man presented with various foods for which he has such an insatiable desire that it seems he must die of longing; but he sees that if he follows his appetite, it will cause his death, which holds him back; yet the more he is held back, the more his hunger for it grows; so it was with my desires. I strove to practice works of love according to the opportunities that arose, and I thanked Almighty God that He had restored my health and thus given me the chance to satisfy my desires somewhat, though I was not worthy of it; rather, His Divine Majesty gave me such grace.

5. Our sisters wondered greatly that Mother Teresa had commanded me to be the infirmarian <term>Krankenwärterin</term> <note>The nun in a convent responsible for nursing and overseeing the care of the sick.</note>, since I was so ill myself; but so that one might see the extraordinary grace our holy mother had in discerning what she should command, His Divine Majesty allowed me to be made well in an instant through the power of holy obedience. This filled everyone with great wonder, and me more than all, because I was unworthy of such grace and benefit.

6. As I then strove to perform the office of infirmarian as best as I could, and had a very sick sister to care for, I once let her sleep a little and meanwhile hid myself in a cellar to pray for a while. During this time, I fell into an interior recollection <term>innerliche Versammlung</term> <note>A term used in Carmelite spirituality to describe a state where the soul withdraws from the senses to focus entirely on the presence of God.</note> and heard a voice speaking to me: "Rise up, my friend." I recognized immediately that it was the Lord's voice and replied at once: "My Lord, what do you command?" But He gave me no further answer. I went upstairs immediately to see what was required of me; and I saw that they had been searching for me everywhere because the sick sister was longing for me. When I came into her chamber, I found her very weak due to a severe fainting spell that had overcome her in the meantime.

7. These and similar graces the Most High God has bestowed on me, of which I am entirely unworthy; not because there is anything good in me, but to reveal His infinite goodness through them. He sought me without my knowing it, so that I would not be lost entirely, and His mercy would become all the more known. The outward works commanded of me by obedience I performed with great comfort, though they were mixed with many imperfections; I found no burden in them, but rather joy and a peculiar delight, and it seemed to me to be pure love of God.

# Chapter Five.

Through a vision, she is encouraged to embrace suffering. She also recounts some of the sufferings she endured while with *Teresa* during her travels, illnesses, and death; as well as the detachment of her soul after *Teresa's* death.

---

->I.<-

One day while I was in the church, I was gathered inwardly in prayer by means of some suffering, when our Lord appeared to me in the form in which *Pilate* presented Him to the people <note>This is the "Ecce Homo" scene from the Passion, where Jesus is shown to the crowd before His crucifixion.</note>, with bound hands, crowned with thorns, with a rope around His neck, and covered in wounds. At the same time, I heard the cry of the *Jews*: "Crucify Him, crucify Him!" <note>original: "Creuzige Ihn, creuzige Ihn"</note>, which pierced my soul to the very marrow. Then His Divine Majesty approached me and said in a very friendly and loving manner: "See, my daughter, the state I am in; do you truly think that your suffering is worthy to be compared with Mine?" These words pierced my heart like arrows and left me completely inflamed with His love, and encouraged to suffer much more than had happened to me until then.

2. This vision disappeared immediately; however, whenever I now feel any sensitivity or irritation over some small thing, I remember this sight in order to overcome my weakness. I also remembered how His Divine Majesty had previously told me that I would have much to suffer in the company of Mother *Teresa*, who was ill. And although she suffered much more on our travels than I did, nevertheless her sufferings affected my heart more than I can express; I was also very distressed because there was so little to be found in the inns <note>The inns or "ventas" in 16th-century Spain were notoriously poorly supplied and uncomfortable for the traveling nuns.</note> with which she might have refreshed herself in her exhaustion, weakness, and the hardships of the journey.

3. When she was at the foundation in *Villanueva de la Jara* <note>original: "Villa - Nova de la Xara"</note>, and there was no other water available in that convent except a deep draw-well, she had a wheel built to draw the water with less effort. As she went out one day to inspect the work, one of the workmen carelessly let go of the wheel, which fell with great force directly onto the arm that she had previously broken once before, whereby it was severely injured again. She accepted this, according to her custom, with great patience and peace. A few days later, an abscess <term>Apostem</term> <note>An old medical term for a localized collection of pus or a deep boil, often life-threatening before modern medicine.</note> formed in her side, which caused her great pain and became so severe that we expected nothing but her death. At last, however, the abscess broke, and she was thus delivered from the danger, and we all from our great fear.

4. When I [think of] all that which she [suffered] in these years, which I spent with her...

### Eighth Part. The Life of Anna Garcias. Chapter V.

[brought] and endured, I would find no end, since everything found in the books regarding this is hardly the smallest part of it. And what is told about the foundation <note>A "foundation" refers to the establishment of a new convent.</note> in Burgos—which was her last—is to be regarded as almost nothing compared to what she had to endure there, both in poverty and in other matters, where we sometimes did not have even a single morsel of bread to eat.

5. I remember that one day *Teresa* found herself in a state of great weakness, and we had nothing to refresh or sustain her but a small piece of bread dipped in water; that was our entire supply. Because the river <note>The Arlanzón River in Burgos, which flooded severely in 1582.</note>, on whose bank our house stood, had risen so high, the people from the city could not come to us to help. The water had already filled the lower rooms of our house to the top; and because the house was old and dilapidated, it shook whenever a wave struck it, as if it were about to collapse, so that we were in the greatest danger of being flooded at any moment, from six o'clock in the morning until the following night. The room where our Mother *Teresa* lay was so poor that one could see the stars in the sky through the roof, and the walls were so cracked that the cold, which was very sharp at that time, had free entry. We were very distressed that we had nothing to give our holy Mother to eat, and since it was already late, she said to me:

> My daughter, see if a little bread is left over, and give me a piece of it, for I feel very weak.

These words broke my heart. But we had a novice <term>Probtochter: a woman in her probationary period before taking her final vows as a nun</term> who was of a very strong nature; we had her wade into the water up to her waist to fetch some bread, which we gave to our holy Mother to eat, having nothing else in the entire house to refresh her.

6. Finally, some men came to us, wading and swimming through the water; if they had not come, however, it would have been the end for all of us and we would all have perished. I had two poor blankets on our bed, one of which I used at night to cover our Mother *Teresa*; the other I placed around the bed (because the wind whistled through everywhere) without her noticing; for if she had noticed, she would not have allowed it. When she began to sleep a little, I sat down by her bed; then when she woke and called me, I acted as if I were coming from my own bed; hence she once said to me:

> How is it possible, my daughter, that you are here so quickly?

7. Otherwise, when she slept, I went to wash her linens and cloths, and I had a singular comfort in providing her with clean linen during her illness; in this way, I remained many nights without sleep, to see with due care if and what she needed; for if I could do even the slightest thing to please her, I let nothing hinder me. Sleep did not trouble me much either, but I stayed awake without effort—indeed, I found myself as well and comforted as if I had slept through entire nights and had pampered my body tenderly.

### Eighth Part. The Life of Anna Garcias. Chapter V.

8. **GOD** the **Lord** was the one who did this for the comfort of our Mother Theresa; for if she had noticed that the slight effort and labor I applied on her behalf caused me any inconvenience or difficulty, she would not have allowed it and would have suffered great pain because of it; the goodness of **GOD** worked these and other miracles in me, a poor sinner, who was not worthy to serve such a saint.

9. From my childhood on, I had a longing to be in the company of a holy soul; but now our Lord has granted me this grace, not because of my desire or my merits, but out of pure mercy; for such a desire did not come from me, but from Him, who ordained everything thus and moved me to have a longing for such grace; therefore I must rightly feel ashamed, because I find myself in such holy company (of which I am entirely unworthy) and because of my <term>pride</term><note>The original term "Hoffart" implies a spiritual vanity or an inability to fully grasp the grace offered.</note> do not make as much use of it as others would have done, if they could have enjoyed such a great good.

I have been with her and around her for about fourteen years, and it seemed to me that this time was not even a single day long, and our Holy Mother was so well satisfied with my meager services that she was never without me. [Here Mother Anna further recounts the sufferings and hardships she endured in the company of Holy Theresa, before and during her final illness, until she peacefully passed away while lying in her arms, as can be read at the end of the preceding biography of Theresa, and continues in the following manner].

10. I was by nature inclined to love, especially I bore an exceedingly great love for Mother Theresa, as well as for other <term>nuns</term><note>original: "Klosterfrauen"</note> who walked sincerely and were also loved by her. Mother Theresa, however, sometimes said to me during her life that this attachment to the friends of my soul was not useful, and that for my progress and greater perfection I should strive to desist from it; but I remained bound, until finally our Lord broke the bond. For from the hour that Holy Theresa gave up her soul into the hands of her Creator, I have remained completely free and loosed from this. And it seems to me that I am now more inclined to love those from whom I expect no benefit or personal comfort of <term>self-love</term><note>original: "Eigenliebe"; in a monastic context, this refers to the ego or the desire for emotional satisfaction from others.</note> than all others. Otherwise, I am as if I were alone in the world, and love all in **GOD**, and for **GOD'S** sake.

# Chapter Six.

## Her Peacefulness, Peace of Mind, and the Many Graces and Miracles that GOD Worked in, with, and through Her.

->I.<-

When I was in the convent in Madrid, some discontent arose between the Superior, Mary of Saint Jerome, and the sisters, during which time I had my practice in the three years of her <term>government</term><note>The original German "Regierung" refers to the term of office or administration of a monastic superior.</note>. For my part, I had a great desire to see everything in perfect peace and constant unity; I served them all to the best of my ability, with great love and a joyful spirit. Therefore, they all had great confidence in me, though I always took diligent care and made it my concern not to offend the required sincerity toward my Superior. Whenever the sisters came to me to complain and to indicate to me that they had some hardship because of what they considered the strict government of the Superior, I said to them: "Know, my dear sisters, that our Reverend Mother Prioress loves you each and every one from her heart, and seeks nothing but your benefit; therefore, give no place or entrance in your hearts to adverse thoughts; try it once, and deal with her in simplicity and sincerity; for I know for certain that she desires to serve you in everything that is permissible and possible for her." To the Mother Prioress, however, without revealing any complaints of the sisters, I said: "My dear Mother, the sisters love Your Reverence very much, therefore I pray you would comfort them when they come to you; for although they are all pious and virtuous, they are yet somewhat timid and withdrawn; therefore I pray you would receive them kindly when they come, listen to them, and comfort them."

2. In such a way I spent the three years, in all circumstances, to promote the inner peace and unity of minds; and although I had to suffer quite a lot in doing so, I nonetheless bore it with joy and special comfort to my soul, because it all happened to the honor of the most sweet **JESUS**; I also felt no hardship or bitterness in it. Meanwhile, the love and confidence that the sisters bore toward me reached such a point that, out of great humility, they persisted with the Superior until she permitted them to begin the exercises of the <term>novices</term><note>Original: "Prob-Töchter," literally "probationary daughters," referring to those in their trial period before taking full vows.</note> anew under my guidance, regardless of the fact that I was only a <term>lay sister</term><note>Original: "Lay-Schwester." Lay sisters were typically tasked with manual labor and domestic duties, such as kitchen work, rather than the liturgical leadership roles of choir sisters.</note> who belonged to the kitchen service and other manual labor.

3. During those three years, I found myself most of the time so occupied with and in **GOD** and gathered in prayer, that I felt no differently than one who is in a strong fortress and rests and sleeps therein without worry. Such a person, even when a strong wind or storm arises, does not heed it much because he is well-protected and secured in the fortress; indeed, the whistling of the

### Eighth Part. The Life

...of the wind only makes him sleep that much more peacefully. It often seemed to me that the Lord held me up just like a piece of <term>sponge-wood</term><note>The original "Schwamm-Holz" likely refers to cork or a light, porous wood like balsa that cannot be sunk.</note> that floats upon the water, which is never submerged by any storm or waves, but always floats upward. His <term>Divine Majesty</term><note>A formal, respectful way of referring to God, common in 17th-century spiritual writing.</note> dealt with me inwardly with such intimate familiarity that it seemed as if He never left me alone. It would not be possible for me to recount all the particular graces and tokens of love which His Divine Majesty showed me during that time; but because He endowed me so richly with them, and compensated me for everything I had to suffer for His sake, I will mention only a few that particularly come to mind.

4. One day I went to bring food to a sick sister; she then spoke some words to me that might have caused me *mortification*<note>In this context, "mortification" refers to a feeling of humiliation or a blow to one's pride intended to discipline the soul.</note> and sensitivity; however, I did not say a word in response, nor did I let the slightest sign be noticed that it bothered me. Because I found myself in the presence of God, and He was present in my heart, I felt instead great compassion for the good sister and did not think that she had offended me. After I had served her at her meal and waited upon her, she went into the garden, while I withdrew to a separate place. I felt myself so filled with God that as soon as I knelt down upon the earth, I was immediately taken by a great <term>recollection</term><note>The original German "Versammlung" refers to a mystical state where the soul's powers are "gathered" or "collected" inward to focus entirely on God.</note>. Then I saw Christ the Lord, in the form of a gardener, standing at my side; He laid His arm under my head, and so I rested upon this most holy and heavenly support. His Divine Majesty said these words to me: "Through this you shall see what it is to live without complaining, and what love is." From these words I understood—just as if it had been told to me with a living voice—what *John* says: <note>original: "GOtt ist die Liebe, und wer in der Liebe bleibet, der bleibet in GOtt, und GOtt in Ihm."</note> "God is love, and he who remains in love remains in God, and God in him." And His Divine Majesty likewise gave me to understand how pleasing it had been to Him that I had behaved in such a way on the aforementioned occasion. It is something that one can neither express nor easily believe, what my soul felt during this; my strength could not have endured it if God the Lord had not restrained the power of love, through which I was, so to speak, melting away.

Although in the aforementioned and other occasions things sometimes occurred that could have distressed or disturbed me (because they were in themselves quite bitter and harsh), they reached the ears of my spirit no differently than if they had been the most beautiful music and the loveliest song of the noblest birds.

5. At the time when I was living in Madrid, a great need and lack of rain arose; because it had not rained for such a long time, all the grain and plants in that region were drying up. Public prayers were ordered in all places, but no rain would come, and the heavens seemed to be made of brass. When my <term>confessor</term><note>A priest who hears confessions and provides spiritual direction.</note> saw such distress, he came to the convent and asked me if I would not call upon our Lord to send a rain and [serve] the common [good]...

### of Anna Garcia. Chapter VI.

...[if anyone] wanted to come to the aid of my need? I answered: No, my father, there are enough pious people who take care of it. Thereupon he commanded me that I should betake myself to prayer and persist strongly to obtain rain. Meanwhile, however, it happened that several persons of high rank came to the <term>grille</term><note>The "Gitter" or grille was a barred window in the convent parlor that allowed cloistered nuns to speak with outsiders while remaining separated from the world.</note> and requested to speak with a sister, and I was then commanded to go along as a companion; but I said nothing of what the confessor had commanded me, because I had resolved to perform my prayer during the time that the others would be talking to one another. And so we both went into the parlor, where I betook myself to prayer while the others spoke, which lasted about half an hour; meanwhile, the heavens began to rain so abundantly as if they wanted to flood the entire earth. I had betaken myself to prayer with the intention of fulfilling my obedience, and the same obtained the desired rain, whereas previously there had not been the slightest appearance of rain; but **GOD** the **Lord** taught me through His mercy how powerful obedience is.

6. Once, after having received Holy Communion, I remained in a singular peace and great <term>recollection</term><note>The German "Versammlung des Gemüths" refers to a state of deep interior focus where the soul's faculties are gathered away from worldly distractions to be present with God.</note> of my spirit, and there I saw on both sides four beautiful little white animals, just like little lambs, who lay with their mouths upon the earth and worshipped the **Lord**; and I heard a voice therewith, which spoke: Your reverence is like unto these. My soul remained constantly gathered in the presence of this my **Lord**, with a true knowledge of my own nothingness or non-being, whereby I was held in an inward silence, which is impossible for me to explain or to express with words; but it was something exceedingly excellent and of very great value; it remained everywhere in me and with me, wherever I went, without any hindrance or confusion from any people, no differently than if I had been alone in the monastery.

7. At the time when I was in the monastery foundation at <term>Ocaña</term><note>Original: "Ocagnia," a town in Spain where a Reformed Carmelite convent was founded.</note>, I fell into a sickness and remained for nearly three whole days without being able to enjoy a single morsel; after three days had passed, I still remained in such a lack of appetite for food that I had no desire for anything in the world except for sweet <term>bitter oranges</term><note>The text uses "Pomeranzen" (Seville/bitter oranges) and "Oranienäpfel" (sweet oranges). In the 17th century, citrus was often used medicinally for the sick.</note> or oranges, which nevertheless do not grow in that region and were also difficult to find at that time. I nonetheless let nothing be noticed of it, fearing I might cause the sisters concern; otherwise, I would have gladly forced something down, but it would not go. Now, as I wanted to try something again once more, the bell rang at the grille; and when the portress came there, an unknown poor man was there, who said to her: Take these three oranges and carry them to a sick woman. As soon as I had seen them, I began to praise **GOD**, not only for the gift (although I had never seen such beautiful oranges) but also most of all for His goodness, which takes such great care for those who hope in Him. Oh, what a great thing it is to leave something for the sake of His love! Be it ever so little and so small as it may. Oh, how well and how richly He knows how to repay it.

# Eighth Part. The Life
<meta>catchword: my</meta>

[The violence] of the wind only causes one to sleep all the more peacefully. Often it seemed to me that the Lord held me up just like a piece of <term>sponge-wood</term><note>The German "Schwamm-Holz" likely refers to cork or a very light, buoyant wood. This is a metaphor for the soul staying "above water" through divine grace despite the "waves" of worldly or spiritual trouble.</note> that floats upon the water, which cannot be sunk by any storm or waves, but always floats upward. His Divine Majesty dealt with me inwardly with such intimate familiarity that it seemed as if He never left me alone. It would not be possible for me to recount all the particular graces and testimonies of love which His Divine Majesty showed me during that time; but because He endowed me so richly with them, and compensated me for everything that I had to suffer for His sake, I will make mention only of a few that occur to me in particular.

4. From these words I understood, just as if it had been said to me with a living voice, what John says: <note>original: "GOtt ist die Liebe, und wer in der Liebe bleibet, der bleibet in GOtt, und GOtt in Ihm."</note> *God is love, and he who remains in love remains in God, and God in him.* And His Divine Majesty likewise gave me to understand how pleasing it had been to Him that I had behaved so in the aforementioned situation. It is something that can neither be spoken nor easily believed—what my soul felt during this; my strengths could not have endured it if God the Lord had not restrained the power of love, from which I was, as it were, melting away.

Although in the aforementioned and other occasions things sometimes occurred to me that could have distressed or disturbed me (since they were in themselves quite bitter and harsh), they reached the ears of my spirit no differently than if they had been the most beautiful music and the loveliest song of the noblest birds.

5. At the time when I lived in Madrid, there arose a great need and lack of rain, because it had not rained for so long a time that all the grain and plants in that region were drying up. # of Anna Garçias. Chapter VI.

would come to the aid of my distress? I answered: No, my father, there are enough pious people who will take care of it. Thereupon he commanded me that I should betake myself to prayer and persist strongly in obtaining rain. Meanwhile, however, it happened that several persons of high rank came to the <term>grille</term><note>The "grille" was a metal screen in the convent parlor that separated the cloistered nuns from visitors, allowing them to speak without physical contact.</note> and desired to speak with a sister, and I was then commanded to go along as a companion; but I said nothing of what the confessor had commanded me, because I had resolved to perform my prayer during the time that the others would be speaking with one another. And so we both went into the <term>parlor</term><note>Also known as a locutory, this was the room where nuns could speak to visitors through the grille.</note>, where I betook myself to prayer while the others spoke. This lasted about half an hour, and meanwhile the sky began to rain so abundantly as if it wanted to flood the entire earth. I had betaken myself to prayer with the intention of fulfilling my obedience, and that same obedience obtained the desired rain, whereas previously there had not been the slightest appearance of rain; but God the Lord taught me through His mercy how powerful obedience is.

6. Once, after receiving the <term>Holy Supper</term><note>Refers to the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note>, I remained in a singular peace and a great <term>recollection</term><note>In mystical theology, "recollection" is a state where the soul withdraws from external distractions to focus entirely on the presence of God within.</note> of my soul, and there I saw on both sides four beautiful little white animals, like little lambs; they lay with their mouths upon the earth and worshipped the Lord; and I heard a voice therewith, which spoke: Your reverence is like unto these. My soul remained constantly gathered in the presence of this my Lord, with a true realization of my own nothingness or <term>non-being</term>, whereby I was held in an internal silence which is impossible for me to explain or express in words; it was, however, something exceedingly excellent and of very great value. It remained everywhere in me and with me, wherever I went, without any hindrance or confusion from any people, just as if I had been alone in the monastery.

7. At the time when I was at the monastery foundation in <note>original: "Ocagnia"</note> Ocaña, I fell into a sickness and remained for almost three whole days without being able to enjoy a single morsel; after three days had passed, I still had such a distaste for food that I had no appetite for anything in the world except for <term>sweet oranges</term><note>The original text uses "Pomeranzen" and "Oranienäpfel." While "Pomeranzen" usually refers to bitter Seville oranges, Anna specifically asks for "sweet" ones.</note>, which do not grow in that region and were also difficult to find at that time. I nevertheless let nothing be noticed of this, fearing that I might cause the sisters worry; otherwise, I would have gladly forced something down, but it would not go. As I was about to try something again once more, someone rang the bell at the grille; and when the <term>portress</term><note>The sister in charge of the monastery entrance and receiving messages or gifts.</note> went there, an unknown poor man was there, who said to her: Take these three oranges and carry them to a sick woman. As soon as I saw them, I began to praise God, not only for the gift (although I had never seen such beautiful oranges), but most of all for His goodness, which takes such great care for those who hope in Him. Oh, what a great thing it is to leave something for the sake of His love! Be it ever so little and so small as it may. Oh, how well and how richly He knows how to repay it.

8. Something of the same kind happened to me another time in that same place; I lay sick in bed and found myself quite weak and faint on account of a medicine I had taken. No one could ever find out where these things had come from; one could only believe that it must have happened through a special providence of God.

...as if I had served the Lord Jesus <note>original: "HErrn JEsυ"</note> in His own person; nevertheless, she showed no such kindness as she did toward others. I, however, showed in return that it was a great pleasure and joy for me to serve her. When I brought her food or otherwise came to her, I was not surprised that she did not receive me kindly, because I attributed it to the power of her pains and illness; meanwhile, the inner love with which I served her caused me to find a delight and joy in this <term>self-denial</term> <note>original: *Verläugnung*; the spiritual practice of suppressing one's own desires or ego to serve God or others.</note>.

It happened one day that I brought her food, and I had used special diligence to prepare the dishes so that they might taste well to her, and I said to her: "I most kindly ask Your Reverence to please try a little of it; perhaps it will taste well to you." But she not only refused to taste it, but also commanded me to go away, which I then did, and I was filled with great joy that a good opportunity for self-denial had come my way. When I was alone and <term>recollected</term> <note>original: *versammlete*; a state of deep, focused inward prayer or meditation common in Carmelite mysticism.</note>, the Lord approached me and spoke: "Do you think that I pay you as the people of this world do?" With this, He allowed my soul to be showered with such inward joy as if I had been in Paradise.

6. Once, when I was in our convent in <note>Abula is the Latinized name for Avila, Spain, where St. Teresa of Avila founded the first convent of the Discalced Carmelite Reform.</note> Avila, and was in contemplation of the bitter suffering of our Lord, I became somewhat inwardly gathered. In this recollection, our Lord appeared to me in the form of a fleeing man who wishes to hide himself because people are pursuing him to take him prisoner, for which reason he perhaps slips into the door of a friend to stay and hide there for a little while; in just such a manner our Lord came to me, and yet spoke not a single word. It caused me such great sorrow to see Him in such a state that I said to Him: "My Lord, what do you want? Behold, here is my heart; let Your Majesty just enter therein." He, however, turned back again without saying a single word to me, but left my soul completely pierced with extreme pain because I had seen His sorrow.

7. So that one may recognize the goodness of God, I will here recount what occurred in our convent in Avila: Our Lord allowed a nun there to be afflicted with <term>leprosy</term> <note>original: *Aussatz*.</note> to test her virtues, for she was a very pious soul. The physicians said that one was bound in conscience to let her leave the convent to be cured, otherwise all the others would be infected with the disease. God, however, gave me and another sister the desire to serve and wait upon this sick woman so that she might not be cast out of the convent. Therefore, we both went to the <term>Prioress</term> <note>original: *Vorsteherin*; the head of the convent.</note>, who was very troubled and distressed because she did not know how to handle this matter; we both begged her now that she would entrust the care of this sick woman to us, offering to take all the trouble and danger upon ourselves. By this the Prioress was greatly comforted, and

The doctors had her sweat and prescribed very strong medicines for her, but the monastery was so poor that there were few means available for what her illness required. When the sweating began intensely, I washed her bedsheets and cloths at night, which she had used during the day, so that I could return them to her the following day; these were so full of pus and gave off such a foul odor—as did the body of the poor sick woman itself, like a dead corpse—that it would have been impossible to endure such a stench if one had not fixed one's eyes on GOD and resolved to suffer something for the sake of His love. During the day, I served her in everything she needed with the greatest possible diligence, and at night I let her rest to gain time to wash her linens. In this practice, I persevered for forty days, but in the meantime, I did not neglect to fulfill the office of the <term>portress</term> <note>original: "Pförtnerin"; the nun responsible for guarding the convent entrance and greeting visitors.</note>, because at that time there were few nuns in that monastery. I also performed all the toil and hardship, indeed with such delight that I could have wished for no greater pleasure. The foul odor was so strong that the other sisters could not pass by the chamber of the sick woman. But (as has been said) this sick sister was an exceedingly pious and virtuous soul, and His divine Majesty held her very dear and precious; there is also no doubt that it was very pleasing to Him that we both served her in this repulsive illness, since neither the labor nor the lack of sleep or food caused me any inconvenience. From this, it clearly appeared that GOD was with us, for my companion spoke in the same way. (a)

After forty days had passed, the sick sister attained her perfect health, as if she had never had this illness; but during the illness, she had suffered very much. One day I felt a great compassion for her, because I saw her in great suffering, and therefore prayed to our Lord <note>original: "HErrn"</note> that He might please alleviate her pain and suffering somewhat; then He showed me the sick woman as exceedingly beautiful and in a high degree of perfection and glory which He had prepared for her, and said to me: **"It is not yet all won; it is not yet time to free her from suffering."** Because of such graces that I received from GOD in such occurrences, I am especially indebted to His goodness; for if other people had received the like from GOD, I would have thought they had deserved them; but I have neither deserved nor even been able to recognize them. May His holy name be blessed for eternity! Amen.

***

(a) This sick woman was named Anna of Saint Peter <note>original: "Anna à St. Petro"</note>, by birth a high-born noble lady from the Netherlands. Afterward, she suffered not only these and similar external hardships but also much internal distress and abandonment, with which she was pierced as if by a two-edged sword, and her spirit was separated from nature. Our Mother Anna, whose life we have here before us, used to say often afterward that the mere sight of this sister moved her soul to devotion, because she had an <term>angelic appearance</term> <note>original: "Englisches Ansehen"; in this period, "englisch" was often used interchangeably with "engelisch" (angelic) to describe a person of radiant or holy countenance.</note>.

### Section Eight. The Life of Anna Garcia. Chapter VII. ###

8. The evil spirits appeared to me on various occasions; but I feared them no more than if they were merely flies. One day, while I was at prayer <note>original: "Gebät"; an archaic spelling of *Gebet*</note>, I saw a devil before me performing very strange and foolish antics, and as he did so he said: "Cursed be he who does you so much good!" and immediately afterward I heard a voice cry out: "Leave her in peace, for she has great need of these consolations."

9. One day, when I lay sick in bed and began to sleep a little, I heard a commotion in my sleep, as if someone were running through the chamber, which caused me to wake up and become alert. I then saw a whole heap of devils who, as I lifted my head, all took flight and hid themselves in a small hole that was in the chamber. This caused me to laugh when I saw them fleeing so, and how each among them struggled to be the first to escape; they appeared as nothing other than thick heads and large claws.

10. Another time, when our holy Mother Teresa <note>St. Teresa of Avila (1515–1582), the founder of the Discalced Carmelites and Anna’s mentor.</note> was ill and I had something to do for her service during the night, I went there with a small lamp in my hand to perform the task. Then the devil met me in the shape of a cat, jumped upon the lamp, and extinguished it. I grew so angry at this that, had I not been in the dark, I would have thrown the lamp at his head. When I returned to Teresa, I found her laughing, and she asked me: "My daughter! what has happened to you?" I then told her everything that had occurred and how I had grown angry against the evil enemy; she, however, said that such a thing was not well done, and she was not pleased that I had allowed myself to be overcome by anger. This happened at Burgos, in the house of a rich man who had died a godless death, in which we were living at the time; we were greatly plagued with ghosts there, so much so that no other person wanted to rent that house.

11. Once in the evening, I went to perform my prayer in our garden, where there were some stone slabs upon which the sisters sometimes used to pray. As soon as I arrived there, I found myself so filled with the love of God that, after I had knelt down upon the stones—and it happened to be freezing very hard—I nevertheless remained there in contemplation without feeling the slightest discomfort from the cold. When I finally wished to stand up again, I found that my clothes were frozen fast to the stones, from which it clearly appears what the grace of God is capable of when He endows a soul with it, which I experienced quite well on this occasion.

# Chapter Eight.
## Preparations for her journey to France. The happy state of her soul, and the various dangers along the way.

->I.<-

Some time before, God had shown me that I would yet travel to France upon a dark sea; this had remained always imprinted upon my mind. But because my human nature was somewhat terrified by it, our Lord appeared to me one day in an <term>intellectual vision<note>A type of mystical experience where the person perceives a spiritual truth or divine presence clearly without any visual image or audible sound.</note></term>, in which I felt His presence very clearly without any visible form, and He asked me with these words:
> Must not the olives and the grapes give up their juice through the press and the torture of the winepress? All my friends have walked this path.

Afterward, I heard these further words:
> Even so do I wish to have you.

These words awakened in me a new courage and an offering of myself to everything that God would desire of me, and I resigned my heart most earnestly into His hands; I also felt tangibly that this resolution I had made was dear and pleasing to Him.

2. This occurred at the time when several noble persons [namely <note>The brackets in the original indicate an explanatory insert identifying the French delegation: Jean de Brétigny, Monsieur Gaultier, and Pierre de Bérulle (later a Cardinal), who were instrumental in bringing the Carmelite reform to France.</note> Monsieur de Brétigny, Gaultier, and Bérulle, in order to establish our convents in France as well] arrived from France in Spain to petition the authorities so that several nuns of our Order might be sent there. The request of these persons was handed over to several men who were very learned and, at the same time, great servants of God; however, after long deliberation, they remained in doubt as to whether it would be beneficial to send any to France, and through this, I also became wavering and fell into great doubt as to whether it was truly God who had spoken to me. But as my heart hovered in such thoughts, God gave several other souls to understand that it was His divine will that I should depart.

3. In our convent, however, and throughout almost the entire city, I was commended most earnestly to our Lord, for it was difficult for them to see me depart for a foreign land, and all the sisters were full of sorrow because of it; for this convent in <note>original: "Abula"; the Latin name for Ávila, Spain.</note> Ávila is truly a house of God, in which everyone loved one another dearly. And although I was not worthy of it, they nevertheless loved me beyond measure, just as I also loved them inwardly, for they were very pious and holy souls.

4. In the meantime, the aforementioned French gentlemen had to spend nearly an entire year before they could obtain permission, and meanwhile, they had to suffer much scorn and adversity, as they were by no means recognized as being such great servants of God as they were in truth. For my part, as already mentioned, I was also at that time so confused, oppressed, and seized with such fear for the reasons stated, that I did not know where I should turn or go, because I

# Part Eight. The Life of Anna Garcia. Chapter VIII.

I feared it might be the evil enemy <note>original: "der böse Feind"; a common term for the Devil</note> who wanted to deceive me; for this reason, I did nothing but weep day and night and could not stop my crying. Meanwhile, I called upon our Lord most earnestly, praying that He would not let me be deceived by the evil enemy. On the other hand, I was inwardly encouraged and driven, and our Lord said to me: I should be faithful to Him and now fulfill that which I had offered and promised Him at another time.

It cannot be believed how the Devil and the flesh <note>Refers to "the flesh" as the source of human weakness and worldly desires, contrasting with the spirit.</note> assaulted and oppressed my spirit. They argued to me that I should think carefully; that I had already reached my later years <note>Anna was approximately 54 years old at this time, which was considered quite elderly for such a grueling journey in the 17th century.</note>; that I would not be able to endure such a long journey but would likely die from it without achieving any benefit; and that I did not understand the language. Therefore, they argued, I should not thoughtlessly put myself in such great danger of body and soul. They reminded me that I was loved and held in high esteem in my own convent, where I had all the comfort and peace of my soul; I should just leave the business alone, as others more suitable would surely be found for it. In a word: they said I would utterly lose myself. Beyond all this, they suggested that I would be hated, persecuted, and despised by everyone; my own good friends would not approve, and in their absence, I would have to suffer many adversities and have no one at hand to whom I could complain of my concerns or reveal the state of my soul. All these thoughts drove my mind back and forth and put me in great worry. Oh, what a wretched thing it is when a poor, weak woman is so terrified!

5. While I was floating back and forth between the stormy waves of such thoughts, our Lord drove me on with power, as did my other good friends. One day the Lord said to me:
> Do not delay, and do not neglect to go there; for if you do not go, nothing will happen; all the others, after they have arrived there, will return. <note>This was a prophetic statement; historically, several of the Spanish nuns who went to France found the conditions too difficult and eventually returned to Spain, while Anna remained to establish multiple convents.</note>

At another time, when I was in the midst of the struggle before our departure, our Lord said to me:
> Pay attention: just as sparrows are caught with birdlime <note>A sticky substance smeared on branches to catch small birds; here used as a metaphor for spiritual attraction.</note>, so shall souls stick to you and be won for Me for all eternity.

6. At that time, the final resolution was made, so that the four of us truly set out on the journey on August 29, 1603. Our Right Reverend Father General Franciscus <note>Francisco de la Madre de Dios, the superior of the Discalced Carmelites.</note> went with us for a part of the way on the first day, but then took his leave and gave us his blessing at our request. He did this with great sorrow, just as we were also saddened by such a parting; for he loved us like a father. It was therefore no wonder that tears were shed at this parting, since those souls united in God suffered a great blow, as they were not only leaving their fatherland for their entire lives but were also being separated so far from their spiritual father, who was such a godly man. However, although we found ourselves weak according to our nature—

# Of Anna Garcia. Chapter VIII.

found, we were nonetheless strong in spirit, courageous, and steadfastly determined to proceed, and ready to suffer for GOD and the salvation of souls even unto death.

6. Before we arrived at Bayonne <note>A city in the French Basque Country, a major stopping point for travelers crossing from Spain into France.</note>, such a downpour came upon us that it was almost impossible to continue. This, however, must be attributed to the goodness of GOD, who wished to test the patience of His servants; for night overtook us on a high mountain, and it was so dark that we could not see our own hands. We were finally forced to spend the night there under the open sky; we had neither bread, nor wine, nor water with us, except for what fell in abundance from heaven. The air was so tempestuous that it seemed as if the whole sky would fall down upon the earth at once. Along with this, the roaring of the sea, which was close by, was exceedingly great and terrifying, which at any other time would have struck enough fear into me alone. But during this entire journey, my soul for the most part felt great tranquility, the singular assistance and presence of her **Heavenly Bridegroom** <note>A traditional mystical title for Jesus Christ, signifying the soul's intimate union with the Divine.</note>, along with great comforts of grace and a heavenly peace. Only once did I become very distressed, because I could well imagine that it was burdensome to my sisters that they had taken me with them, as I was so very inconvenient and of no use for such a work. But as I had been very troubled and ashamed within myself that day because of these thoughts, the LORD appeared to me in the evening at the inn; He showed Himself most lovingly to my soul, comforted me and spoke:

> Take heart, my daughter, I will help you, and be with you.

8. After this vision, I remained entirely free from all the distress that had previously tormented me. It seemed to me as if I were a mistress and ruler of the whole world, so great was the freedom of my spirit. It was also a great and singular comfort to me to be despised for the sake of the love of GOD. Throughout the way, I also had such a vivid presence of the **Most Holy Trinity** that neither the dangers—of which there were not few—nor anything else could turn me away from it or rob me of it; everything served to aid my <term>inner recollection<note>German: *innerliche Versammlung*; a meditative state where the senses are withdrawn from the world to focus entirely on the internal presence of God.</note></term>. One day, as I was at prayer, we were crossing a bridge over a large river. When we were in the middle of the bridge, the Devil played one of his little tricks and would have gladly thrown us into the depths of the water, if only it had been in his power. The horses leapt about in terror and lifted our carriage up on one side, so that two wheels remained on the bridge while the other two were already hanging out over the water in mid-air. My companions were completely terrified and called upon GOD the LORD to come to their aid in this danger. The coachman, however, continued across the bridge in such confusion that one could plainly see the Devil was the author of this calamity and danger; for once we were across, the carriage fell into a valley full of thorns and stones. I was sitting in the boot <note>German: *Aushang*; likely a projecting seat or exterior part of the carriage.</note> of the carriage, which fell over on my side, so that everyone cried out that I was dead. But as I fell, I called upon the Holy Trinity and felt neither thorns, nor stones, nor any injury, nor even the slightest pain; it felt to me as if I had been held up by hands and protected from all harm.

## Chapter Nine.

->Her arrival in Paris. Her foundation of a monastery and office of superior at Pontoise, from whence she is placed back in Paris in the same office. Her great zeal for souls. GOD puts His words into her mouth. And shows her many other graces. Her humility through it all.<-

My soul indeed sees nothing, but it feels such a reverence toward the Most Holy Trinity as if it saw the same.

It seemed to me that I was a contemptible little earthworm—as indeed I am in truth—but I had never before recognized this with such clear light as upon this occasion. As I then one day pleaded with God that He might look after His own honor and stand by me, since I found myself entirely alone and forsaken, He spoke to me: **I am here; I guard you like the apple of my eye.**

3. During the time that I was Prioress in Pontoise, the death of one of our nuns was reported to me from Spain, who had died with a common reputation for holiness. As I felt a great longing and zeal for her virtues within me, because she had worked much, our Lord said to me: **For those who are bound to a higher calling, it is not best to do much in outward works, but rather to die to themselves, and to bring all their desires, passions of the soul, and inclinations into the service of virtue and to kill them.** The Lord spoke these words to me very quickly, but they left in me a singular zeal for the denial of myself, and a great light to recognize the infinite goodness of God; and I found myself bound anew to be faithful to His Divine Majesty in everything, as much as was possible for me.

4. The manner of my internal prayer and communion with God was at that time the presence or assistance of a light which was in my soul, and I felt inwardly such a reverence toward it that it seemed to me all the powers of my soul had lost their essence and effect, and had no other essence or effect than that which they received from this light; it was not as if I saw the Lord Jesus (as I am otherwise accustomed to) or another Divine Person, but as if the entire Most Holy Trinity were with me. My soul sees nothing, it is true, but it feels such a reverence toward the Most Holy Trinity as if it saw the same.

5. Another time, I saw my soul fashioned like a little silkworm <note>The silkworm is a famous metaphor used by St. Teresa of Avila in 'The Interior Castle' to describe the transformation of the soul in prayer.</note>, which is industriously fed and carefully guarded by those who raise it; but when it is grown, it begins to spin a delicate little silk thread with its mouth and to make itself a little hut, in which it enjoys such sweetness that it does not notice its own dying, until it is robbed of all its strength, remains enclosed in its shell, and dies. Now my soul saw something similar within itself, for with just such sweetness and stillness, it gave to God the Almighty everything it had, all of which it had nonetheless received from Him; and it enclosed itself, just like the silkworm, in its nothingness and the knowledge of its

# Section Eight. The Life

...of their nothingness <note>In the mystical tradition, "nothingness" (Nichtigkeit) refers to the soul's recognition of its own insignificance compared to the vastness of God.</note>, with a sweet love that always spins in my heart, which no longer wishes to be or to live: for dying is the true life of souls. I wished that I had a thousand lives to lose; I would give them away with joy, so that only God the Almighty would be exalted and glorified, and there is nothing on earth that can satisfy me, except alone to give up and lose my life for my Beloved.

6. Another time, I complained to our Lord and asked Him with great confidence how He could permit me to be held back in these offices <note>The "offices" refer to her administrative duties as Prioress, which she felt distracted her from a life of humble service.</note>? I also presented my poverty and nothingness to Him, saying: I am indeed only a hollow straw. To this He gave me the answer: **With straws, I light the fire.**

7. I have also never lacked Divine help and assistance, even though so many and heavy adversities occurred to me that they seemed, as it appeared, enough to completely suppress the spirit and make me unfit for all things. What otherwise humbled me the most were the occasions where people wanted to show me the most honor; to this also much was contributed by the thoughts of those who were given to us in place of authority, who intended to make use of me for their own purposes. In this, they undoubtedly had their eye on the glory of God, yet I experienced thereby how inconstant creatures are. For as soon as these superiors noticed that I would not agree with their opinion in everything, all the love and inclination they previously had for me vanished at once. For although I am otherwise imperfect and very unfaithful to the Lord, He has never let me deviate so far from Him that I should have departed in the slightest piece from what I believed in my conscience was my duty. In this, I also had no regard for the status of men, whoever they might be; nor the slightest fear of any harm that might arise from it; rather, it was dear to my soul, yes, a delight and joy, to be like a stranger and without friends, because I sought, as it seemed to me, nothing else but God alone.

8. While I was still at Pontoise, I felt a strong desire rise up in my soul one day to do something to please God the Almighty, if only I were fit for anything; but I saw alongside this that I was nothing else but a worthless little earthworm, that I had nothing in myself, knew nothing, nor was I in the least useful for anything before God or men. Nevertheless, I also saw that my heart was ignited with burning desires to perform my works so that God might be glorified and praised thereby; I also thought no further of any other reward for my toil and labor. Then I was taken up by a great tenderness of the love of God and by an inner recollection <term>innern Versammlung: A state of "recollection" or "gathering" where the soul withdraws from external distractions to focus entirely on the internal presence of God.</term>, and I felt that the Lord was with me, who said to me: **Just so do I wish to have you, without you being anything or knowing anything, so that I may do with you what I will; for the wise of the world with their human cleverness do not hear Me, but think they know everything themselves.**

9. At Pontoise now I was very content, and my daughters <note>The "daughters" are the nuns under her care.</note> walked with great precision. In the meantime, however, I heard that our superiors were negotiating among themselves to call me back to Paris and to burden me with the office of Superior <term>Vorsteherin: The Prioress or head of the convent.</term> there, which distressed me greatly because there is such great pride in that place. As I found myself one day inwardly gathered in the aforementioned pain, and yet was very ashamed before the Lord that I was not better resigned to the will of the superiors—since I also saw clearly that God wanted me to travel to Paris—I made a great new resolution and said: "Do with me, O Lord, what You will! I see well that I am not fit for it, and for that reason I am in great fear; and it is moreover a great shame and pain to me to be honored. My God! Why will You let this suffering come upon me?" Thereupon the Lord came to me in great clarity and said: **In such a manner must those walk who perform the works of God, as I also walked upon earth: sorrowful in honor, and joyful in shame and suffering.** By these words of the Lord I was greatly comforted, felt within me a great joy and love for God, remained also very ashamed within myself, and once more took heart to go wherever they wanted me.

In the meantime, it was nevertheless very painful for me to leave those pious souls, who seemed to be more like angels than humans, for our Lord carried them in His hands through manifold comforts and joys which He shared with them; moreover, the inhabitants of the city were so well-disposed toward me that they wanted to prevent my departure by force, and one was therefore necessitated to lead me away secretly at midnight.

10. When I arrived again in Paris, I was received with joy by all the sisters; and I have given the profession <note>The formal act of taking permanent religious vows.</note> to twenty-eight novices <term>Probtöchter: Literally "trial-daughters," referring to women in their probationary period before becoming full nuns.</term> in this city. There, our Lord renewed in me an exceedingly great desire and fervent longing for the salvation of souls, which graces increased in me with a new excellence. It was like a violently burning fire of love, which seems to overpower everything and pull it toward itself like a magnet, so that even tribulation and adversity, cross and suffering, have no power against this love; rather, the spirit is made even more courageous and strengthened thereby. In this thirst for the salvation of souls, one does not fear in the least any dangers, nor any suffering or effort; rather, one has a desire to involve oneself in such things. For the pain that one suffers in such a kind of inner prayer is greater than other pain and suffering. Therefore, I advise all fearful ones, when they find themselves in such states, that they strive to be faithful to God the Almighty and not easily let themselves be confused or frightened; that they also do not become weary or verdant in laboring for the edification and the best interests of souls.

11. It is to be lamented that those who have the opportunity to create great benefit for the salvation of souls sometimes do not let it concern them much
