And although I traveled alone from our convent, and indeed with poor health, and little prospect of enjoying better health because old age was at the door, I nevertheless always found the comfort I could have wished for, if I had sought any comfort or begun it for that reason. For it seems as if God showed Himself to be, as it were, bound to me, just as a father is obligated and bound to assist his child in everything; and in whatever need or distress my soul finds itself, He does not abandon it, but comes to my aid at once.

12. The first year of my office as Superior in Paris passed with great comfort for me; for the sisters, who were all postulants <note>original: "Probtöchter" - these were the first French women to join the new foundation on a trial basis.</note>, walked with great diligence and zeal on the path of discipline. Our Lord also showed them many signs of His love; and notwithstanding that the majority were from distinguished, high-noble families, they yet seemed to be completely simple children who had returned to the state of innocence—so great was their simplicity. They dealt with me with great sincerity and familiarity, as if I had raised them. Although I therefore had cause to comfort myself when I saw that these souls walked so well, on the other hand I did not lack internal suffering because of my office and what was connected with it; for whenever I had to perform only those things that the office brings with it, and saw thereby that I was so unsuited, it distressed me greatly and gave me much to suffer. For it seemed to me to be the greatest contempt and humiliation for me that could have happened to me in this world, <note>that I had to administer such an office.</note>

Now, as my heart was occupied with these aforementioned desires, I saw quite clearly that this was granted and given to me with such well-being that it cannot be explained in any way; and I saw myself, as it were, completely transformed into another spirit. I felt that our Lord drew near to me and gave me strength and gentleness to speak the truth in a good manner, so that it could not be taken ill by anyone; instead, everyone recognized and believed the truth, and they were moved and driven toward virtue. I spoke it as our Lord had inwardly inspired me, and the words coming out of my mouth produced such effects as if our Lord had spoken with them. In a word: my speeches were from His Divine Majesty, as my Lord and the Master of my soul, in whom He had His delight and joy.

15. During the **Christmas holidays** of this year, I received many graces from the Lord, which I certainly needed, for many sorrowful days also passed when He left me very much alone; but during the aforementioned holidays, God poured such grace into me that it seemed as if He possessed me entirely, and as if I had been in heaven; the body no longer gave me any trouble, as if I had none; I found myself as peaceful as if I were in pure delights, and I enjoyed the presence of God in a very sublime way.

## On Obedience.

We see what we owe to God the Lord, and what the love He bears for us is worth; so let us then show Him such a reciprocal love as He requires of us, and as much as we are ever able. To Him we must give our will, and faithfully pray that He may accept it, be its master, leader, and Lord, without any ownership or anything remaining to us of it, so that we may be in deed and in truth His bondslaves.

We must rather die than not be obedient; and blessed is she who dies in such a manner!

Ah! I beg you, my dear daughters, let us fear no toil nor labor, for the people of the world suffer more in the fulfillment of their own will than the religious <note>original: "Geistliche" — here referring specifically to those living under religious vows in a convent.</note> do in the denial of it.

The sisters must be humble and sincerely open their hearts to the Superior <note>original: "Vorsteherin" — the Prioress or head of the house.</note>, since she bears the burden of her subordinates and must give an account to God the Lord for their souls. If the subordinates are well-pleased with God and truly submitted to His most holy will, His Divine Majesty will instruct them and also give light to the Superior to lead them, and they will enjoy the sweet fruits of obedience to the great benefit of their souls.

All our progress on the path of perfection consists in submission and obedience; for this is very contrary to self-love, which always fights against us and creeps in almost everywhere. Self-love is very subtle, crafty, and deceptive; it knows how to disguise itself in a thousand ways and appears to us on all sorts of occasions; for before good thoughts even enter the mind, self-love is already there to deceive us, as can be clearly seen in many persons who appear holy on the outside but are only hypocrites <note>original: "Gleißnerinnen" — a term for female hypocrites or those putting on a "shining" but false front of piety.</note>, who deceive the servants of God with feigned devotion and false appearances.

Those who deny themselves and their own will, who wish for nothing else than to submit to the Divine pleasure and to subject themselves to the judgment of another for God’s sake—ah! how justly and rightly will such people be able to say with Saint Paul: *I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me.* <note>A translation of the Latin Vulgate phrase from Galatians 2:20: "Vivo autem, iam non ego: vivit vero in me Christus."</note>

## 2. On Purity.

You know well, my daughters, from the time when you were still in the world, that you were accustomed to making use of a mirror to see if you were beautifully adorned, and whether your finery might be pleasing to those who would see you; we have exactly this now in our Lord Christ, who is the true mirror in which His brides should behold themselves. In Him, we should see what is agreeable and pleasing to the eyes of our heavenly Bridegroom; His eyes are entirely simple, pure, and chaste, and He likewise demands from us a simple obedience and an angelic <note>original: "Englische" — in this period of German, this is an archaism for "angelic" (derived from 'Engel'), rather than referring to the nation of England.</note> purity.

When we have entirely given and actually surrendered our will to Him (our Bridegroom), then we can believe that He now looks upon us in all our works and loving inclinations as something that belongs to Him; therefore, our outward conduct should also be modest, as befits a religious <note>original: "Geistlichen" — meaning a person living under religious vows.</note> person. Our speech should be very moderate, simple, and thoughtful; our eyes mortified <note>original: "mortificiret" — a term for spiritual discipline, meaning to restrain one's senses or desires to focus on the divine.</note> and withdrawn; our ears deaf to everything that is not God, etc.

All the virtues of our Lord Jesus Christ are, as it were, fragrant flowers of diverse colors which are planted in the garden of His most holy life, so that each soul may gather those that are particularly useful to her in her calling and for perfect harmony with the divine pleasure. O truly blessed and again blessed are the souls whom this heavenly Bridegroom invites into His so exquisitely and beautifully planted garden! His voice penetrates their innermost marrow, illuminating them with the radiance of His countenance and drawing them powerfully to Himself with the ropes of His love! "Come, my brides," He says, "into my garden, which I have planted for you and watered with my blood; come and knock at the door, and I will open to you; learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart." <note>A reference to the Gospel of Matthew 11:29.</note>

## 3. On Poverty.

There is no surer sign that someone is poor in spirit than when they are truly obedient; for obedience is the true touchstone of the other virtues.

Those who possess the virtue of poverty find it a joy and delight that in everything—in clothing as well as food—they always receive for themselves the worst, the poorest, and that which others most reject. This they do not even do out of self-denial, but because everything superfluous burdens and weighs upon them, just as if they had never known anything else but holy poverty and the detachment of their minds from all things of this world. The truly poor do not love themselves, nor do they love honor, favor, reputation, or the esteem of men; rather, their greatest desire is to deny themselves in everything and to die to the comforts of the body, so that they may thus become more conformed to the poor Christ, our Redeemer and Bridegroom, and [fully]...

# Eighth Part. The Life

may follow after. O blessed soul, who recognizes the value and beauty of this virtue <note>referring to Poverty, the subject of the preceding section</note>!

Even if there were no other good in it than the enjoyment of freedom and peace, which the truly poor possess—since they gain dominion over all their enemies and passions <term>original: "Gemüthsbewegungen" — the stirrings of the mind or soul, often translated as passions or emotions</term>—it should nonetheless rightly give everyone a heart to strive after it.

Let us be diligent to do what the Lord says: *Be perfect, even as your heavenly Father is perfect.* This is to be understood of the inner man: namely, that he should always be bound and united with God through the bond of love; and that he should so exercise himself in that same love that all our works may be perfect—namely, as such that come from God and are directed back to God. This can and must happen through the inner strength of the spirit of the children of God, who have their will free and released from all temporal things, from self-love, and from the passions, and who always choose the best and what is most useful for their souls.

I remember that I often saw how we lacked all things and had nothing to eat; yet, in the midst of this poverty, there was such an abundance of the spirit that the sisters did not feel this lack, so great was the inner comfort and joy.

### 4. On Detachment. <note>original: "Abgeschiedenheit" — a central concept in German mysticism referring to the state of being "set apart" from worldly desires to focus entirely on God.</note>

Mortification <term>original: "Abtödtung" — the spiritual practice of "dying" to worldly desires or the ego to grow closer to the divine</term> must be both internal and external; for the external helps little if it is not ordered by and does not proceed from inner humility and total self-denial.

Not everything depends on being enclosed within four walls and observing external exercises; that is not yet the end of it. More is required; the interior must be present. In everything, one must have a perfect intention—namely, to do and suffer everything for the love of God—otherwise, we would find ourselves greatly deceived and fall short. One has seen the outward appearance in former times even in many [so-called] religious <note>original: "Geistlichen" — meaning those living under religious vows, such as monks or nuns.</note> who seemed so holy outwardly that one might have wished to canonize them; but under that false appearance, they nurtured such vanity that it serves nothing but to bring souls to ruin, as has been seen in many who perished in this way.

Much depends on one detaching and divesting oneself from the world, from friends and relatives, and also committing vain riches to oblivion; and not this alone, but that one should also forget oneself.

Remember what a miserable state you were in when you were, as it were, sunken in the vanities of the world.

Friendship with all, says Saint Bonaventure, but intimacy <note>original: "Gemeinschaft"—closeness or fellowship</note> with few. As Saint Bernard also says: A pious person should observe three things: speak little, have little [worldly] joy, and pray much.

### 5. On Gentleness and Humility.

Let us, dear sisters, love one another, labor in love, increase in zeal and true humility, and walk in the spirit of gentleness; of this we have a beautiful example in Christ **Jesus** our **Lord**, Redeemer, and Master. I remember that He is called a Lamb in the *Scriptures*; Saint John does not give Him the name of a Wise Man, though He is indeed Divine Wisdom itself; nor does he call Him a Strong One, though He is strength itself; nor a brave hero, though He triumphs so gloriously over all His enemies; rather, he calls Him only a gentle little Lamb, which allowed itself to be dragged to the death of the Cross without any resistance; there He overcame His enemies, not with the sword, but with the wood of the Cross. Let us, my dearly beloved sisters, consider this model well and follow it in gentleness and humility. Let us leave all bitterness, resentment, melancholy, and adversity to the people of the world; such things would suit us very poorly, for we ought to have the nature of a simple little sheep, following the example of our Bridegroom.

### 6. On the Observance of Their Calling.

Pay attention to the voice of your calling <term>original: "Berufs"—in this context, the religious vocation or "summons" to the monastic life</term> and of your heavenly Bridegroom, by which He has called you into His pleasure garden <note>original: "Lustgarten"—a common mystical metaphor for the cloister or the soul's interior life where God dwells</note>; follow Him with joy. He is Himself the way by which we should go; let us therefore not listen to the weakness and timidity of our flesh.

Take your refuge at all times in prayer, for this is the nearest and surest way; because the **Lord** Christ says: Ask, and it shall be given to you. Be then comforted and of good courage, my dear daughters; the word of **God** cannot fail nor deceive. Remember always what I have said: that His Divine Majesty has called you out of the world, where every hour and moment you were in a thousand dangers of losing yourselves, and has placed you in His pleasure garden, of which He Himself says that He delights therein.

# The Eleventh Chapter.

## Continuation of her spiritual discourses: On Silence.

### On the duties of a Superior <term>original: "Vorsteherin"—the mother superior or prioress of the convent</term>. On the signs of a true vocation.

### I. On Silence.

Above all, dear sisters, it is of great importance that silence be kept inviolably. For not without cause does the Apostle exhort us that we should work in silence <note>referring to 2 Thessalonians 3:12: "with quietness they work"</note>; if we intend to triumph over ourselves, we must learn to keep our tongue in check, so that no one may recognize the inward virtue with which we work; indeed, if our heart is truly humble, the evil enemy himself will be deceived and will not be able to recognize the profit with which we labor. I beg you, my dear sisters, listen a little to what the Holy Scripture says: *In silence and hope shall be your strength* <note>Isaiah 30:15</note>; therefore we should work in silence; for although we are indeed bound to manual labor, yet this must happen in such a way that one is not hindered or turned away from the interior life by it; for we are much more bound to the interior life, because we must contemplate the law of God day and night and keep watch in prayer.

2. Let us always have before our eyes the clear mirror of the life of our **Lord Jesus Christ**, who, although He was who He is, nevertheless did not cease to pray without ceasing; and what we should consider most of all is the great silence which His Divine Majesty kept while He worked and carried out the task of our redemption on earth, for from the twelfth year of His age until the thirtieth, nothing is reported of Him. By no means was it a vain use of time that He kept His wisdom and Divine nature hidden for so many years and walked among men as one of them; He went into the Temple to say His prayers like the others, He walked up and down among them like a poor man, and seemed in their eyes to be an ignorant person; but I do not doubt that during the time of this silence and hidden life, He spoke with His heavenly Father, addressing Him often and much, saying what He later spoke on the wood of the Cross: *Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.*

3. O infinitely incomprehensible love, which burned inwardly in His heart! You speak, O Lord! without words, and although You did nothing according to outward appearance, yet You did not cease to work the miraculous mysteries for which You came into this world: namely, to instruct ignorant people in the exercise of virtues. Ah! where would we have found patience, humility, poverty, and other virtues? Where would we have learned to bear one another's burdens, to suffer one for the other? If the Son of God [did not teach] us

...would not have taught such a thing, in that He gave and presented Himself to us as a living example of all perfection. O blessed silence! wherein You, my sweetest JESUS, cry out and preach to the whole world through Your example. My Lord! one could write countless books about Your silence, and Your friends can learn more wisdom from it than from all books.

4. When we turn the eyes of our soul to the night of His holy Passion <note>the period of Christ's suffering leading up to the crucifixion</note>, what wonderful lessons of silence do we see there? How is it possible that the manifold and terrible ignominy, mockery, and unjust treatments did not have so much power over You that You would have broken Your holy silence on their account and brought Your innocence to light? When we look upon how You, O innocent little Lamb! are led from one judgment seat to another, pitiably scourged, crowned with thorns, spat upon and defiled in Your face; when we look upon how You carry the heavy wood of the Cross, how finally on Mount Calvary Your most holy limbs are stretched apart, and You are nailed to the Cross; and how You nevertheless did not open Your Divine mouth: how should it be possible that we, seeing all this, should not be ignited and moved to love holy silence?

5. O how blissful is the silence which makes a soul especially capable of intimate fellowship and communion with God! In silence one becomes wise and hears what the Lord speaks inwardly; but when one listens to Him, one learns His wisdom. A soul cannot be truly spiritual where it does not, as much as it is able, withdraw itself from its activities and outward affairs, and keep itself gathered in a deep silence; there it finds what it seeks, namely, union and intimate fellowship with God. Silence makes the soul enter into the blissful darkness of which Saint **Dionysius** <note>likely Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century mystic who wrote about "Divine Darkness" as a way to know God beyond human understanding</note> speaks, in which darkness it enjoys such a clear and wonderful light or **vision of God** <term>original: "Anschauen GOttes"—the intuitive, contemplative sight of the Divine</term> that it cannot be expressed or explained.

6. One may indeed safely believe that such a soul would always remain in the bliss of silence if it were permitted, because its whole walk and commerce is in heaven. Saint **Bonaventure** <note>a major 13th-century Franciscan theologian known for his writings on the soul's journey to God</note> says that the reason why there are so few spiritual persons is because they do not know how to prepare themselves to hear the voice of God; instead, when they come to prayer and do not immediately find a "taste" or sweetness in it, they go away at once and seek their comfort elsewhere. These are like the negligent householders who do not ensure that their wine barrel is well closed; because the wine is not well protected, it loses its strength and turns sour. Others, on the contrary, provide well for their wine, so that when the merchants come, they find in it a lovely scent, beautiful color, and a pleasant taste according to their desire; thus, my dear sisters, it is with the virtues: they are preserved and maintained through silence and deep humility.

### Continuation of her spiritual discourses: On Silence. On the duties of a Mother Superior <note>German: Vorsteherin; referring to the head of the convent, often called a Prioress in the Carmelite tradition</note>. On the signs of a true vocation.

## On the Duties of a Mother Superior.

7. The Mother Superior of the novices <note>original: "Probtöchter," literally "test-daughters" or "probationary daughters"</note> must conduct herself in such a way that the novices can read in her deeds what she tells them with words.

8. She should use discernment to govern each according to her ability; she must not overload them with more physical austerities than they can bear; she should occasionally reveal some of her own weaknesses to the daughters, so that they may reveal their own more freely and without hesitation; there is great benefit in this practice.

9. When a soul is in the darkness of temptation, the Superior must make everything easier for her and encourage her; yet she should not, for that reason, cease to keep her practiced. For the devil doubles his secret malice when he finds a soul idle and without the exercise of mortification <note>original: "Abtödtung," the practice of "dying" to one's worldly desires</note>.

10. From the very beginning, a newcomer should be practiced in those things she must do for the rest of her life. If one assists them at the right time, supporting and encouraging the good desires with which they left the world, then the Lord for His part does not fail to enlighten them more and more. In this way, they finally learn to understand clearly that they have entered the spiritual (or Christian) life only to do penance, to surrender their own will, to die to themselves, and to live in the constant crucifixion of their flesh—thereby following the cross-bearing Christ—rather than to be treated tenderly and to live according to their own pleasure.

11. The Superior should instill in the novices a love for poverty, for solitude, and for detachment from all creatures; she should teach them to look at nothing else and concern themselves with nothing else but to fasten themselves entirely to the Cross with Christ their Bridegroom, to die to themselves in Christ, and to seek nothing but the imitation of Christ.

12. She should also give them to understand that God the Lord, the true Bridegroom of souls, is occasionally accustomed to hide Himself to test His handmaidens through inner dryness <note>original: "innerliche Dürre," a state of spiritual desolation where one feels no comfort in prayer</note> and suffering; that He sometimes behaves as if He had completely abandoned and forgotten them, so that He may see if they will be faithful to Him; and that the Lord maintains them in true humility and submission through this means. Such a conversation ensures that they walk in the fear of God and give no ear to the temptations that might disturb them in their calling.

13. The Superior should take care that her teachings, and what she gives the daughters to meditate upon, are always seasoned with the life and merits of Jesus Christ, especially with His most holy and bitter Passion and death; for through this, she will accustom them to drink the living water from His holy wounds. If they then continue to drink from this fountain of life, they will often see and experience the treasures that are to be found therein. This is

14. When one accepts daughters <insert>[into the convent]</insert>, one must take great care to see whether they are simple and candid, for this is a virtue which is most conducive to humility and inner peace. Those, however, who do not possess this candor suffer, and in time, they also cause others to suffer. Not being simple and candid is a hidden trial <note>original: "Anfechtung," referring to a spiritual struggle or assault from the devil</note>, which is usually unknown to those afflicted by it; for they believe themselves to be quite discreet, cautious, and wise when they keep secret that which occurs within their souls, yet they ultimately find themselves deceived by the enemy.

15. The novices <note>original: "Probtöchter," literally "probationary daughters"</note> must be simple in all things, upright, and, as it were, blind and ignorant; they must develop a delight and love for those things that seem bitter and difficult to them, and entirely forget all the pleasures and joys of all earthly things.

## On the Signs of a True Vocation.

16. Whether the novices' spirit and vocation <note>original: "Beruf," the spiritual calling to the religious life</note> be from God, and whether they possess a good spirit, is seen from this: If they do not make excuses, even when they are punished without cause or fault. If they gladly confess their shortcomings. One should not judge them based on whether they have more or fewer trials; for those who are tried more frequently and more intensely usually have the surest and best vocation; rather, judge by whether they accept these trials with humility. They should reveal these trials to their superiors with simple candor, and carefully observe and follow their teachings.

These souls, who are humble of heart (even when the Divine light that drew them out of the world hides itself from them), nevertheless wait with patience for the time when the storm of trials has passed and both the mind and nature are humbled; for they well know that God's light and the strength of His grace will soon appear again to reveal to them the good they must seek.

For those truly called by God, although they endure many hardships and are often and repeatedly humbled and tested, everything is nevertheless right with them. They are well satisfied and always seek to be lowered and humbled; they do not even deem themselves worthy to dwell in the house of God among His handmaidens. They are always ready and willing to cast themselves under the feet of all others and to be the least of all.

17. But the others, who have no true vocation, never reveal their failings and faults; instead, they seek to cover, gloss over, and excuse them. But the more they wish to hide their faults, the more they are seen; for their actions, manners, and conduct are frivolous, bold, and inquisitive; they wish to...

# Section Eight. The Life

...know everything that happens in the world. Thus, they always want to learn, and yet they never arrive at a true knowledge of themselves, much less at perfection. Consequently, they never experience true virtue and find no taste in its practice, because they do not seek it rightly.

## Chapter Twelve.
### Her two-year internal and external trials. Mystical Death; with brief alternations of pure graces and illuminations, aimed toward that end.
<note>Mystical Death refers to a profound spiritual state where the soul's self-will and sensory attachments are "stripped away" to allow for a deeper union with God.</note>

->1.<-

Towards the end of the first year of my office as Superior <note>original: "Vorsteheramt"</note> in Paris, God allowed all my joys, comforts, and pleasures to be greatly diminished—indeed, to be changed into a very vivid, great suffering and affliction. <margin>From the outside</margin> our superiors began to imagine many things about me that I had never even thought of. <margin>From the inside</margin> the Lord also hid Himself at that same time, in such a way that it was to me as if I had lost my very faith; moreover, I had no living person to whom I could reveal my suffering. It is known to God alone in what pain and distress my soul was then. And because I could well believe that everything came from the hand of God, and that I was unfaithful to His Divine Majesty, this also caused me a great fear.

->2.<-

Oh, what does a soul not resolve to do, and how does it not offer itself up to God the Almighty, and offer itself for everything that might be dear and pleasing to Him, as long as it has His Divine Majesty with it? How strong and immovable does it then believe itself to be! But as soon as the Lord hides Himself only a little from it, it immediately seems to the soul that it must soon sink entirely; it believes itself to be with Saint Peter <note>A reference to the biblical story of Peter trying to walk on water but sinking when his faith wavered.</note> in the midst of the sea of tribulations and adversities. Its courage fails entirely, and it lets its heart and faith sink. I was not simple <note>original: "einfältig," here meaning "spiritually childlike" or "single-hearted"</note> enough to be able to make good use of these trials, although I felt clearly enough that our Lord stood by me and helped me carry the cross; I also noted well that it must be useful to me. Nonetheless, I felt the cross very much, and I entreated our Lord earnestly that He would teach me to perfectly fulfill His will.

Afterward, I noticed that the Lord Jesus in His most holy humanity approached me, and although I did not see Him, I nevertheless knew Him, just as if I had seen Him with bodily eyes; He said to me, with a show of great love and sweetness: He would take upon Himself all my concerns and self-abasement <note>original: "Vernichtigung" — a mystical term for the total reduction of the ego to "nothingness" before God.</note>. I felt such a great and overflowing love of God, and such strength of spirit, that if I had been commanded to throw myself into the sea or walk among lions, I would have done so without delay; I feared nothing, as if I were already in glory; for the Lord God had left His power in my soul, so that all these attacks of adversity could not disturb my inner peace in the slightest, much less suppress it. This grace was very singular, as was the condition that remained within my soul because of it.

As much as it seems to me, I desire nothing else but the glorification of God, nor do I seek any other pleasure, comfort, or delight than this.

And from that time on, the [inner] unrest, suffering, and adversity also increased greatly; the evil enemy <note>The "evil enemy" is a common historical reference to the Devil or demonic temptation.</note> did his best to augment it, and it may well be that because I have been such a great sinner, and am so sluggish and negligent in doing good, the Lord was perhaps angry with me for that reason.

# Eighth Part. The Life

...down at His feet, and pleaded with Him urgently for grace and mercy; and if I had perhaps erred in coming to France, He should not let it turn to my ruin. I promised our Lord anew the improvement of my life, to serve Him faithfully from my whole heart henceforth, in love and sorrow, in affliction and prosperity, in praise and contempt, in health and sickness, in life and death, in the cross and suffering, or however else it might please His Divine Majesty. During this time of my affliction and anxiety, our Lord came to me at times and comforted me with sweet words, but immediately withdrew again, leaving me once more in my solitude and abandonment.

6. One day, a person was sent to me who had previously loved me very much. This person came to me with great freedom and boldness and began to rebuke me severely, giving me, among other things, this reprimand: that I lived without any outward severity or self-denial <note>original: "Verläugnung" — often referring to "abnegation" or the setting aside of one's own will</note>, and the like. Now, at that very time, I was afflicted with a fever, and I had been bled <note>Bloodletting was a common medical practice of the time, often leaving the patient physically exhausted.</note>. Weak nature felt this blow intensely, and the devil placed all sorts of things before my eyes, suggesting that I should give her a sharp answer so that she would not come back the next day. But I only said to her: she should go for now. Afterward, I went to prayer and commended the matter to God; then He said to me: "Why are you sad? Should you not be comforted and rejoice that people say what they want of you, and that you are held to be a poor and useless person? Such things and much worse were said of me. The laws of the world are far different from my laws. Afflictions, sufferings, self-denial, and patience—these please Me."

7. After I had once not felt the company of our Lord for several days, it happened that His Divine Majesty returned into my soul, and through His presence, I was internally recollected <term>Recollection: A state of prayer where the soul gathers its faculties inward to focus entirely on the presence of God.</term>. A linen cloth <note>original: "Leylach" — a sheet or shroud-like cloth.</note> was shown to me, full of small crosses, as if they were pinned to the linen, and I was invited to accept them. Because I now had God present, I consented to it; and with such consent, I immediately felt them enter my soul and unite and, as it were, incorporate themselves with me, so that they became one thing with me. My soul was thereby granted such an inward joy that cannot be expressed in any way, for it brings with it an excellent ornament of perfection that far exceeds the natural capacity of my understanding. And then God gave me to know what a grace this is; and how the perfection and excellence of virtues consist in the cross and suffering; and how all true virtues must be incorporated into the cross and united with it, because outside of it they are not perfect and do not have their beauty. These crosses, together with the sweetness they revealed to my soul and with which my soul received them, have united themselves with me in such a way that both my soul and body have nothing else, and the soul desires nothing else but the cross, nor does it find elsewhere that which it sees and finds in the cross: namely, strength, wisdom, patience, and humility. The cross is all its refuge.

<meta>This page continues Chapter XII of the life of Anna Garcia (Ana de San Bartolomé). ### of Anna Garcia. Chapter XII.

For love desires to be put to use in and for the service of the Beloved, but finds no better means for this than suffering for the Beloved. And although this suffering consists in the denial and death of oneself, and in everything that is conducive to that end, it is nevertheless very dear and precious to the soul: indeed, I hold that the soul of the righteous runs and strives after the Cross as a greedy man after gold and silver.

8. Therefore, O Bride! O Christ-loving soul! if you truly love Christ, you must climb upon the Cross with Him, deny yourself entirely, and die a complete death; you must turn away from the earth and from all temporal things, letting go of your own will and opinions altogether, and [ when He calls out on the Cross: "I thirst" <note>original: "Mich dürstet"</note> ] reach Him the drink for which He so inwardly longs, which is nothing other than that you recognize Him as the King, Bridegroom, and Lord of your heart. You must draw near to Him, make yourself conformable to Him, and surrender yourself entirely; and then your request will not be considered presumptuous when you offer yourself to be fastened to the Cross with Him and to die.

9. Now, however, it is to be known that there is a difference between the death one suffers at the time of the Cross, and that which one suffers at the time of heavenly consolations. As for the death of the Cross, [ it happens first actively <note>original: "activè"</note>, when namely ] the Lord binds and compels us to work and labor for it with great courage day and night. And [ second, it happens passively <note>original: "passivè"</note>, when namely ] God permits our enemies to attack us on all sides and exercise us upon the battlefield of the Cross, of tribulations, persecutions, and the like. Alongside this, [ which creates the greatest distress ] His Divine Majesty places the soul in a very **dark night** <term>Dark Night: A term popularized by St. John of the Cross describing a phase of spiritual purgation where the soul feels abandoned by God</term>, letting it sink as if into its own solitude, dryness, and abandonment, where it is tormented with great fear and anxiety as to whether it might perhaps offend Him. And all of this is so vivid, and so very much to the extreme, that the soul suffers constantly without any rest or security, and watches in "prayer without prayer," stripped of all consolations; there, everything and anything that happens to it brings it into doubt and a thousand worries. Finally, it comes into a state of forgetfulness [ like the dead ] and loses the memory of all help and all comfort that might come from heaven or from the earth; and there it accepts death.

10. In the other state, in which our Lord caresses the soul and ignites it with the fire of His love, it also longs to die. For the presence and the sight of her Beloved, the love she bears for Him, and the contemplation of His glories and perfections cause her death, because she sees that she is still bound to flesh and blood and cannot fly up to where she might possess without hindrance that which is communicated to her here. And thus she dies in truth the **death of love** <term>Death of Love: A mystical state where the soul's desire for God becomes so intense that the physical body can hardly sustain it</term>; but it is a very sweet death. Food is reached to her already "pre-chewed" <note>This metaphor suggests that God does all the spiritual work for the soul, like a mother bird feeding a chick</note>; she gives nothing of her own and is completely rich. In short, her Bridegroom is with her everywhere; He surrounds and accompanies her and says she should only be still, and He commands all things to keep silent so that the soul may sleep securely.

# Eighth Part. The Life

11. But in the other death [of the Cross] <note>original: "des Creutzes"</note> our Lord invites the beloved soul to the Cross, to become one with Him among the thorns and nails, and to give Him to drink, because He dies of thirst for the salvation of souls; He also commands her to help Him and follow Him. Here He is entirely surrounded with flowers and apples, and gives His beloved to drink from the wine of His wine cellar. O blessed death! O blessed conversation! O most blessed soul, who has attained such a state!

12. Once when I was alone and happened to have the broom in my hand to sweep, I knelt down on the ground (for it seemed as if I were compelled to remain there) and then I saw a light go out from my heart in the form of a pillar, which came out from the dark depth of my soul and rose up to the Holy Spirit; this happened in such a brief recollection <term>recollection: a state of intense interior focus or mystical prayer</term> that I do not know if I already had one knee on the ground or not. The aforementioned pillar of light had such clarity that from my heart up to heaven, nothing else seemed to be but a clear sky. This vision left my soul, together with all my bones and limbs, refreshed and strengthened with such a sweet anointing <term>anointing: a spiritual sensation of being blessed or healed, often described as a soothing oil</term>, as if I had been anointed with the most precious ointments, so that even my body became quite light from it, because this grace was also communicated to the body as well. It all happened in a very brief silence, and my soul remained entirely changed and renewed by it. A joy was shown to me here, which came forth from the sadness that lay in the depth and ground of my soul, just like the scent of nard <note>original: "Narden"</note> <term>nard: an expensive, fragrant oil used in antiquity, often symbolizing devotion and sacrifice</term> which rises high when it is pressed; thus I saw that this joy held the upper hand over all pain and sadness, and also ruled over them. I also saw clearly that it was from God. I saw it all with the eyes of the soul as clearly, and more clearly, than if I had seen it with physical eyes. My soul was now further enlightened in the knowledge of the great truth: how she is bound to die in everything that God might desire from her.

13. For the Lord is accustomed, when the soul is in the midst of the Cross and suffering, in tribulation, fear, and anxiety—sometimes over several days, and then again after several days—to come to her, to strengthen and comfort her, even without letting Himself be seen or speaking anything with her; and this sometimes happens when she is abandoned by all help and comfort from creatures <note>original: "Creaturen"</note> <term>creatures: in this historical-religious context, this refers to other human beings or worldly things</term>. The soul indeed senses that He is present, and His shadow alone makes her alive again and gives her joy and comfort in the midst of the Cross and suffering.

14. All these appearances did not last long, but passed by quickly; but the weight and the effects of the Cross remained in me for two whole years. I spent entire nights sleepless, inwardly begging the Lord that He would help me and instruct me, so that I might recognize His Divine pleasure <note>original: "Wohlgefallen"</note>. In the morning I woke the sisters for prayer, and God granted me the grace and strength that with all my distress, anxiety, and suffering, I could follow the community everywhere and perform whatever tasks might arise, although my heart often—

15. Once, when I was burdened with great anxiety and sadness, I leaned against the wall and fell into a faint, for I then thought my life was coming to an end. 16. And provided they do not offend Almighty God in this, I pray His Divine Majesty that He would allow them and incline them to do against me whatever they please. However, I understand this only on the condition that our Lord remains with me and I do not lose Him; for without Him I desire nothing of the kind, since I am well aware that alone I have no more power than a tiny ant <note>original: "Ameißlein"</note> and would be unfaithful to Him. But where the abandonment by creatures is greatest, there the Lord God strengthens the soul with His help and assistance.

## The Thirteenth Chapter.

### Various high graces which God shared with her. Transformation. Inner Simplicity. Wonders of the Divine Essence. Communication of her graces to others. The soul’s state of being untouched amidst her external hardships in Paris and Tours. The fullness of the love of God.

->I.<-

One day when I was in prayer, our **Lord** granted me the grace to visit my soul and to transform it into Himself with great union. Although this did not last long, the effects flowing from it persisted for a considerable time; for I remained as if I had become Divine through it, both in body and in soul, to such an extent that it seemed as if I had no natural functions at all—indeed, not even the slightest movement. On the following day, after receiving **Communion** <note>The sacrament of the Eucharist</note>, the same thing happened to me; it also passed very quickly, just as on the previous day, but the effects remained for more than fourteen days. For although I saw nothing, I felt such majesty in the depths of my soul as if I had seen the **Most Holy Trinity**. It was not that I saw anything, but what I felt was much more powerful than if I had seen it. And although during these days some occasions arose through which I could have been saddened or anxious, my soul was not moved or confused in the least, nor did it lose its **simplicity** <note>In mystical theology, "simplicity" (Einfalt) refers to a state where the soul is focused entirely on God, free from complex thoughts or distractions</note>; rather, it remained in a state of **Simple Contemplation** <note>term: "Simple Contemplation" (Einfältige Beschaulichkeit); a form of wordless prayer where the soul rests in God's presence</note> throughout all occurring events, without any multiplicity of effects.

2. But now, as I am writing this, it does not happen in that way; for although the aforementioned grace has not entirely passed, it is nevertheless not as it was before. Now the spirit is more courageous, the zeal and the desire to see **God** are greater, and the longing to devote myself entirely to the service and honor of **God** is also much stronger. This now causes a greater activity of the intellect and less simplicity;

### Of Anna Garcias. Chapter XLIII.

[...detachment] from the senses; for where there is more of nature, the effects are more lively and sensitive, and one must then keep a watchful eye so as not to stumble or go astray—from which, however, the weight of the previously mentioned prayer is freed.

3. With the first grace, one finds oneself like someone who has all kinds of food that one might wish for right in front of them, without the effort of having to strive for it, so much so that they do not even need to sit at the table to enjoy it. With the other grace, however [where the soul is left more to its own activities], it is just like someone who is very hungry for a food which they cannot obtain without great effort and labor, and when they have finally obtained it, they must still apply great diligence to enjoy it. Thus, the soul here must also labor to maintain itself in the knowledge of **God** and of itself, which is of such importance that whoever does not practice this will always remain poor in virtues. And this knowledge of the truth brings a rest and peace, making the soul calm and willing in all things and in all occurring circumstances, for everything that **God** desires from her.

These and other supernatural things are difficult to describe or explain; I also find and confess that my understanding is far too weak and poor for it. Therefore, I have wanted to indicate here that I do this purely and alone to fulfill <term>Holy Obedience</term> <note>original: "H. Gehorsam"; the vow to follow the instructions of religious superiors as if they were the voice of God</note>, otherwise I would not have dared to do so in the slightest.

4. A year ago on <term>Whitsunday</term> <note>Pentecost; a feast celebrating the descent of the Holy Spirit</note>, I received a particularly great supernatural grace and consolation, along with a supernatural, unusual light. For our **Lord** showed me some wonders of His Divine Being which I had not recognized until then; and this knowledge was not of such a nature that I could name it or make it understood, but my soul felt an inward, great love of **God**, and a new knowledge of His mercy, with such reverence as if all her senses and powers had become pure tongues to praise **God**—though this passed very quickly.

5. Several days later, I found myself very troubled because I did not know how I should behave regarding several matters that were weighing on me. In that moment, I received a strong impulse to desire a grace and light of the **Holy Spirit** from our **Lord**, so that He might be pleased to teach me His Divine Will. With such longing, I went and gathered myself [in prayer] a little, and saw that the radiance of a small light entered into my soul and ignited it, just as fire is accustomed to ignite dry wood. Now, as my soul was thus burning, I asked our **Lord** that this grace might also be shared with all our sisters, and it happened according to my request.

6. [Regarding external matters], Mother **Anna of Jesus** <note>Ana de Jesús (1545–1621), a close companion of St. Teresa who led the expansion of the order into France and the Netherlands</note> had meanwhile arrived in the Netherlands and had left me stuck in the aforementioned distress; however, at that time, she sent a letter to ask whether I also wanted to come there? # Eighth Part. The Life

152

...but I excused myself; for although I had to suffer much at that time, I was nevertheless entirely determined not to choose a change of country unless **God** the **Lord** had beforehand made such a thing known to me.

7. I performed my office as <term>Prioress</term> <note>original: "Vorsteherin"; the leader of a convent</note> with the highest diligence in every way; otherwise, I was no more in the house than the least among all. Especially I practiced patience, of which I had great need. The time remaining to me after the <term>Choir</term> <note>the communal singing of the Divine Office</note>, I spent mostly in the humblest duties, as the poorest and least among all, as I was indeed in truth; this I did with great joy and singular delight.

8. After I had now spent three years in my office as Superior in Paris, I had to travel to Tours to found a new convent there, [as indeed occurred under much toil and disgrace]. Meanwhile, from that time on, I enjoyed more joy and rest, so that said disgrace and gossip appeared to me no differently than distant thorns that could not touch me. Although we were spoken of so ill, the convent nevertheless gave off such a good scent of virtue that people of all kinds—including very noble persons—came to us from distant places to be received; so much so that once as many as twenty applied on a single day for that purpose, which was then no small cause to praise **God**.

9. His Divine Majesty granted me very great graces in this convent; notwithstanding that I was so completely alone that I had no <term>confessor</term> <note>a priest who hears confessions and provides spiritual guidance</note> nor any other person with whom I could discuss my spirit and prayer. But none of this troubled me; I was greatly comforted there by **God** the **Lord** and visited with His graces, of which He had deprived me at another time. Through this, the practice of virtues and <term>mortifications</term> <note>original: "Abtödtungen"; spiritual exercises such as fasting or self-denial used to overcome worldly desires</note> were made very easy for me; it seemed to me that my strengths were doubled, and I often found myself unexpectedly gathered in the presence of **God** in such a way that His Divine Majesty allowed me to feel the spirit of St. Paul within me, so that I said: 

> Who shall separate me from Christ? Neither suffering nor the lack of any necessities shall be able to part me from Him. <note>original: "Wer wird mich von Christo absondern?"; a paraphrase of Romans 8:35</note>

I was quite intoxicated with the love of **God**, to such an extent that if Almighty **God**, who thus graced me, had not strengthened my nature, I could not have endured it. And what the Apostle says in another place, I also said on this occasion, namely: 

> I wish to be banished for my brothers and to die for Christ. <note>original: "Ich wünsche verbannet zu seyn..."; a paraphrase of Romans 9:3</note>

While my soul here, with burning love and strong submission and <term>resignation</term> <note>original: "Gelassenheit"; a central mystical concept of letting go of one's own will to accept God's will</note> to the will of **God**, without any condition or reservation, offered itself up to the Lord, He spoke to me: 

> In this consists the glory of the righteous, that they fulfill my will. 

He also said to me, besides this, several other loving words, through which my heart was so struck and softened that I remained as if in <term>rapture</term> <note>original: "Verzückung"; a state of intense spiritual ecstasy</note> over it.

# Chapter Fourteen.

### She travels from Paris to Mons in Hainaut. A year later she founds the convent in Antwerp. Her constant presence and company of GOD. Fundamental virtue. And other graces that she experienced there.

->I.<-

After the three years of my office as <term>Prioress</term> <note>original: "Vorsteheramt"; the head of a convent</note>, I returned to Paris, and not long after that I was commanded to travel to the Netherlands, for which we set out on our journey on October 6, 1611; I set out on the way with great joy and was very much comforted by our **Lord**. Upon my first arrival in the Netherlands and in the city of <term>Mons in Hainaut</term> <note>original: "Bergen in Hennegau"</note>, I was received there with great love, together with the <term>Fathers</term> <note>the male priests of the Discalced Carmelite order</note> who accompanied me, and I remained there for a whole year. Meanwhile, there were negotiations regarding a foundation in the city of <term>Antwerp</term> <note>original: "Anthorf"</note>; however, I did not think that I would be the one commissioned to go there, for I thought they would surely choose others for such a work who were more suitable than I.

2. One day, after I had understood that it was the will of our superiors that I should travel there, I commended the whole matter to **God** the Almighty, earnestly praying that He would give me the grace to fulfill His divine pleasure; but if it were not His divine will that the work should be done through me, that He would change the minds of the superiors. Then I was comforted by our **Lord**, for I was very troubled and sorrowful; and after I had received <term>Holy Communion</term> <note>original: "das heil. Abendmahl"; literally "the Holy Supper"</note>, He spoke to me: "Take heart, and know that this foundation shall be a torch that will illuminate this entire land." Whereupon I then resolved within myself to take up the cross with good courage, not doubting that it would happen as I had been told. And right at the beginning of this foundation, **God** the Almighty also brought several noble young women, gifted with great spirit, zeal, and understanding, to the highest wonder of the entire city. In the beginning, we were in such poverty that we had no more than fifty <term>Brabant guilders</term> <note>original: "Brabändische Gulden"; the local currency</note> with us (which were even borrowed); furthermore, there were no church vessels or other such necessities available; also, the City Council was opposed to us, although the Almighty changed their minds in a short time. Now the **Lord** gives me such comfort and inner peace that no person will be able to believe it; I attend to prayer much more and more constantly than before, and it goes better for me; sometimes the spirit [in this my advanced age] is just as strong as it was at the beginning of my entry into the convent.

### Eighth Part. The Life

<meta>catchword: 7. The</meta>

...feels no burden; just as if nature itself felt no more weight in the practice of virtue. I find myself very ashamed because of this, for I do not rightly make use of such help, nor do I practice the virtues properly, but rather live on with such great heedlessness and negligence that it is a shame. As for what concerns the help and assistance of the **Lord**, I have experienced it in all occurring circumstances desde my childhood, and from the time I began to serve **God the Lord**. Only in **Paris** did our **Lord** leave me in such darkness that it truly seemed to be a "dark night" <note>This refers to the "Dark Night of the Soul," a period of spiritual desolation described by many mystics like St. John of the Cross</note>; for the visions and graces He showed me passed so quickly that the comfort I received from them was likewise soon gone, and besides this, I was burdened with physical illness most of the time. But from the time I arrived here in **Antwerp** <note>original: "Anthorff"</note>, I cannot say that our **Lord** has left me without His strength and help, as He has ignited and deepened me in His love in a singular way, because I find myself in His presence at all times.

4. Once during the **Easter holidays**, it seemed to me that I held **Christ the Lord**, as He rose from the dead, in my heart at all times; this lasted until the **Feast of the Ascension**, when it seemed as if He separated Himself from me. This happened in such a way, however, that it seemed to me as if His Divine Majesty had torn the heart out of my body, so great were the pains that such a separation caused me, and it seemed to me that He had taken my heart with Him. With these and similar graces, my soul remained in <term>internal recollection; innerliche Versammlung, a meditative state where the senses are gathered inward to focus on God</term>, and one day I saw that a flame went out from the fire I had within me, which soared upward with a great brilliance.

5. Another time it happened on **St. Catherine’s Eve** <note>The evening before November 25th</note> that a letter was handed to me which set before my eyes how inconvenient and of little use I was, and what a poor rule I maintained. I remained quite calm and was not moved in the least to resentment or anger; instead, I said to our **Lord** that I desired nothing else but to serve Him alone and to promote His honor. Thereupon He appeared to me in the form in which He walked upon this world, with a peaceful and friendly countenance and great majesty; He remained at my side for some time, after which He disappeared again, and my soul, through such an excellent majesty, entered into an **internal recollection** which lasted for several days.

6. It cannot well be believed with how great a love the **Lord** treats and deals with my poor soul, which is yet, alas, so ungrateful! Often I feel that our **Lord** is united with my soul in the same way as, perhaps, **two sisters** might be. Once I awoke from sleep, and as I became alert, I found myself so burning with His love that I could not endure its impetuous violence; and the **Lord** united Himself with my soul more and more; He opened His heart to me, placed me within it, and my soul settled a little into rest.

### Of Ana de San Bartolomé, Ch. XIV.

7. Love is not always within me in such a manner, but rather like something that comes and goes; but as for what concerns the presence and company of **God** on my part, it is felt by me in such a way that, although I do not see Him with bodily eyes, it nevertheless seems to me that I am more certain of it than if I saw Him. And when I feel this divine company, it does not seem to me that I am practicing the virtues, but rather that a certain simplicity is found in the soul. This simplicity is of such a nature that, even when occasions arise that would otherwise usually cause me pain, resentment, or difficulty, I do not feel them at that time; instead, it is to me as if water falls upon a hard stone and flows off without penetrating or doing any harm to the stone.

8. Sometimes when I pray to **God** that He might have mercy on sinners, forgive them, and still His gathered anger, He then shows me such great love that I cannot express how my soul perceives it. It is to me as if I were outside the body in a land of delights <note>original: "Wollüsten" – in this mystical context, it refers to spiritual raptures or heavenly pleasures rather than worldly ones</note>, where the soul finds everything it can wish for in its **Lord** and Friend, yet for itself it desires nothing, but only the honor and glory of its Beloved. Therefore, this is its sole prayer and desire:
> O **Lord**! make Yourself known to all people, so that everyone may love You; do not allow souls to fail to recognize who You are; I know, O **Lord**! that when You reveal Yourself to them, they will all love You;
this the soul says with fervent love, and His Divine Majesty takes such great pleasure in such a conversation that He communicates His love to her more and more.

9. Ah, my **God**! how ashamed I find myself when I consider that Your infinite goodness takes no heed of my wickedness, and only aims to make Yourself known to me, so that I may love Him in return, who is Love itself. He begins with a little light and sweetness, just as one lights a little fire with a few straws; but afterward, when wood is placed upon it, such a conflagration arises from it that one cannot endure it.

10. During the time that our **Lord** dealt with me in such a lovely way and revealed Himself to me, He nevertheless hid Himself for several days, and then my soul remained as if in a wilderness, all alone, so darkened and obscured as if it had never had any knowledge of **God**. Furthermore, it was seized with great fear and worry that perhaps the previous graces and revelations had been a deception of the Enemy. I did indeed submit myself in everything to the will of God, but alongside this I felt such a great anguish of my heart, as if it were being squeezed and tormented in a winepress <note>The "winepress" (Kelter) is a traditional biblical and mystical image for intense spiritual suffering or purgation</note>.

11. Only on **Epiphany** <note>original: "drey Königen Tag" (Three Kings Day), celebrated January 6th</note> a great impetuousness of love overcame me, along with a very intimate recollection, and His Divine Majesty said to me: *I will be your companion, and stay with you, until I lead you with me.* With this, my soul remained entirely ignited in His love, full of reverence and gratitude toward His Majesty, who showed me so many and such great graces, without

...some of my own merits. <note>The author, Ana de San Bartolomé, frequently uses self-deprecating language to emphasize that her spiritual gifts come from God's grace rather than her own worthiness.</note> This vision, as well as the feeling it produced in me, did not last long; however, after it had passed, I remained for several days in a very vivid presence of **God**, with inward peace and the usual comfort of the virtues, in which I have, until now, practiced myself very little or not yet rightly.

12. After this, at another time, I fell again for several days into an inner affliction <note>original: "innerlichen Betrübniß" — this refers to a state of spiritual desolation or "heaviness of heart" often described by mystics</note>, which was no less than the previous one. While my soul was thus gathered in such bitterness, I betook myself to prayer and began to contemplate the poverty and solitude, as well as the pains and contempt, which the **Lord Jesus** suffered in this world. There, He gave me to recognize the great wonders of His pains and His abandonment much better than I had ever heard until then. I would gladly indicate and explain them here, but it is impossible for me, for He showed me such things regarding this that, even if I were to think upon them my whole life long, I would [by my own power] be able neither to understand nor to feel what our **Lord** let me taste and experience in that same moment. Thus, my soul remained in such affliction that my strengths were too few to endure that which I felt, had not **Almighty God** especially helped me. Afterward, however, I saw our **Lord** in the form of a man crowned with thorns, who said to me: "See! everything I suffered is for you." When I heard these words, I almost went out of myself, without being able to speak a single word, and the words came to my mind which are attributed to St. Augustine, namely: *If I were God, and You were Augustine, I would want to make myself Augustine in order to make you God, so deeply do I love you.* <note>This is a famous mystical paraphrase often attributed to St. Augustine, emphasizing the "wonderful exchange" (admirabile commercium) where God takes on humanity so man can share in divinity.</note> I can say that I felt that very same sensation of love in my soul.

***

# The Fifteenth Chapter.

## Tenderness and Power of Divine Love in her. Her later inward trials; along with other graces. And final Gelassenheit. <term>Gelassenheit: a central concept in German mysticism meaning "releasement," "equanimity," or "yielding to God's will."</term>

### 1.

Once, our **Lord** showed me that man, outside the presence of **God**, is like a fish out of water; for just as the fish must live and be nourished in the water, and die when one pulls them out; so also, when man separates himself from the presence of **God**, he withdraws from himself the living water for which **God** created him, without which he will not long have a life of grace.

2. I once inwardy desired to know from the **Lord** how I might best serve Him...

3. I sometimes reflect within myself that the love of **God**, which His Majesty <note>A common honorific for God in Spanish and German mystical traditions of this period, reflecting the Baroque view of God as a sovereign monarch.</note> gives me—even when it is [present in me] not so powerful and stormy as at other times, but rather very tender—it nonetheless causes, in part, a greater pain than a stronger one might otherwise.

4. Once on the 15th of December, this love became more steady and constant, and especially during the morning prayer hour so fervent that it seemed to me a person might easily die from the force of such a love of **God**. I would have wished that all people might have felt exactly what I found within myself. This comparison occurred to me: If perhaps in a wide field in the sand there are many springs of water, the water does not all burst out at once through one pipe or pond, but bubbles up here and there through the sand, and the finest, purest sand does not stop moving; the water boils over quite pure and clear like a crystal; and although the water covers this small sand, it does not stop jumping and moving quickly; just so I found my soul at this time—all its powers and movements were occupied by the love of **God**, and drowned in the same, so that it was as if it were consumed; it was also driven from all sides by this love to such an extent that, if **GOD** had not softened and stilled its force, I would have had to lose my life because of it.

5. This frees me from a great pain, namely that I am well aware that according to the measure **God** imparts His graces to me, He also exercises my soul in suffering.

6. Now for two or three years, I usually suffer great inner pain, which is so sharp and vivid that, if the goodness of the **Lord** were not so well known to me, I might lose courage and conceive a mistrust of His mercy; but let my sufferings and pain press upon me as hard as they ever will, I still remain at all times resigned to the will of God.

7. Some time before the previously mentioned excessive force of the love of **God** overwhelmed me, there came into my soul such a kind of darkness, which was darker than the night, and seemed to be more shadowy than anything that can be presented to the outward eyes. With such resignation this darkness takes place in the soul, which seems to be like a pain of death, and as if life were to come to an end; nevertheless, the soul, even if it were in its power, does not want to turn it away, but chooses much rather

### Eighth Part. The Life.

...to die, rather than to withdraw from such suffering or to resist it, so long as she may do **God** a pleasure.

I do not know how it happens that this takes away all my emotions and passions <note>original: "Passiones." In this context, "passions" refers to the passive states of the soul or external emotional disturbances.</note> to such an extent that I am within myself as if I were not within myself. Everything happens in an inner silence and stillness, and the soul finds itself in a freedom without knowing where it comes from, since the pain is so internal that it seems as if I were in a foreign land where one sees or hears nothing that could bring any joy, comfort, or delight; rather, everything is entirely dark and strange. The soul finds itself so oppressed and tormented as if it were truly in a press <note>This "winepress" metaphor is common in mystical literature, representing the "crushing" of the self to produce spiritual fruit.</note>, yet this comfort is present: such a soul is not easily moved by anything, as might happen in other circumstances or in other types of prayer. It is also so firm and constant that it finds itself inclined toward nothing in the world that might later cause a scruple. Death alone would indeed bring it some comfort and rest; yet it does not desire or wish for it, nor has it any thought or inclination to wish for anything else. It is only perfectly surrendered to the will of **God**, and our **Lord** gives it to experience the great abandonment <note>original: "Verlassenheit."</note> <margin>Or surrender.</margin> which He suffered in all things and occasions in this world, especially at the time of His bitter Passion.

This experience or sensation, as well as the light through which **God** gives me a taste of it, is such a delicate thing that it is not possible to explain it with words, nor to contemplate it as it is in itself; unless **God** should give someone the experience of it.

8. And when this sensation changes, I then receive another which is no less sensitive and wonderful: namely, His Divine Majesty gives me a taste of the extreme pains He suffered in all His wounds until He gave up His spirit.

9. On another occasion, I had found myself in such darkness and distress for three whole days that I did not know where I was. Thereupon, on February 25, 1624, I went into the choir in the evening, and as I sat down after prayer, a beautiful, shining little light came into my soul, in the manner that a bright sunbeam might pass through a crack into a dark room, and I understood that it was said to me: "Your Bridegroom loves you; He is well-disposed toward you, and is not well pleased to see you suffer." With this small light, my spirit rose up and broke out with these words:

## The Sixteenth Chapter.

### Her longing for death. Her humility and patience in her burdensome and painful illnesses. And her blessed passing.

-> I. <-

Up to this point, Mother Anna has described her own life by order of her superiors <note>original: "Obrigkeit." ### Eighth Part. The Life.

...to hope, and although she had miraculously recovered the last time, something of the illness always remained with her. This gave her hope that the imprisonment of her body would not last much longer, which was her entire wish and desire. Our <term>Blessed Mother</term> <note>German: "Gottselige Mutter." A title of respect for the superior of the convent, likely Ana de San Bartolomé.</note> (says one of her daughters) had an exceedingly great desire to see **God**, especially in the last years of her life. Usually, when she was dressing in the morning or lying down in the evening, she used to say with very deep and heartfelt sighs: "Oh, how this body burdens and weighs me down! Truly, it would be a singular joy to me if I could finally make an end of it."

2. She also took no more pleasure in anything on earth, but bore herself as if she were in a foreign land, sighing day and night for her desired homeland <note>In religious writing, the "homeland" or "fatherland" refers to Heaven.</note>. Her conversations were also generally about this; she could not hide it because she was now so detached from all created things that it was even a pain for her to speak of indifferent or external matters. Her body could no longer withstand the strength of her spirit without the special assistance of **God**.

3. During this time, she was attacked by many different and dangerous illnesses, in which her excellent humility and patience shone forth especially in every way. She could not bear that people made much noise <note>In this context, "noise" refers to public attention, fuss, or "commotion" regarding her health.</note> on her account, even in her gravest illnesses. When the **Most Serene Spanish Infanta**, Archduchess of Brabant <note>Isabella Clara Eugenia (1566–1633), the ruler of the Spanish Netherlands and a devoted patron and friend of Mother Anna.</note>, out of the most gracious affection she bore for Mother Anna, sent her doctors to her with orders to provide everything necessary for her health—and for that purpose even dispatched some of her ladies-in-waiting from Brussels—this humble soul became more sensitive and ashamed than can be expressed. She said to **God**: "How can you allow it, O my **Lord**! That a poor <term>Carmelite</term> <note>A nun of the Discalced Carmelite order, known for their commitment to poverty and enclosure.</note> should make such a great noise. Oh **God**! Do not permit this, but take me quietly out of this world." These were words she often repeated.

4. And thus, she had always been minded to show great displeasure toward the good opinion and high esteem people held of her. On the other hand, she had an incredible love, pleasure, and desire to be despised, rejected, and unknown to everyone. Those who enjoyed her blessed company testify to this; they say that when it happened that she was highly esteemed, she found it very painful and used to say to us: "Oh my daughters! What a shame it is that we are held for those we are not? Ask of **God** the **Lord** that He give me light to know myself, so that no one may be mistaken or deceived by me."

5. Regarding her patience, her spiritual daughters testify thus: although our mother’s illnesses were very grave and her pains very sharp, she nevertheless endured them with such great serenity, equanimity, and peace, that

### Of Anna Garcias. Chapter XVI. 161

...one might almost have said that the Cross and Suffering were her sole comfort and her life. She never complained in her illnesses, but instead felt a great joy to see herself in the hands of her **God**, often repeating these words: "Now I have nothing to do but to obey **God** and the nurse; I have nothing to wish for, but that **God** deal with me according to His pleasing will." She never desired anything for which she had a craving, but if the nurse gave it to her, she accepted it out of obedience to her. She never asked **God** to alleviate or take away her pains, but only that He would grant her patience and grace to suffer without causing unrest or inconvenience to others; for nothing was more distressing to her than when she saw us waiting upon her and serving her. In her final illness, this patience of hers shone forth even more remarkably, during which her sufferings and pains were also particularly intense, as we shall soon hear.

6. Several of her illnesses caused her at times to firmly believe that the longed-for hour of her departure had already come, of which she herself told a notable example at the end of the previous chapter, to which this should be added: that as she had been in a trance for a long time during the vision mentioned there and finally came back to herself, the <term>Father Provincial</term> <note>The regional superior of the Carmelite Order.</note> entered her chamber, to whom she said these brief words: "Ah, Father, how good is **God**!" She said no more; and believed entirely that her final hour was there, and that the **Lord** had appeared to her for the purpose of taking her with Him.

7. Another time someone spoke with her of the foundation in the city of *Liège* <note>Original: *Lüttig*.</note>, and said that they would take such nuns from *Antwerp* <note>Original: *Anthorf*.</note> for it as would please her; but she answered: "Before this happens, there will already be another who will travel" <note>She is implying her own "travel" or departure from this life.</note>. She also said that our departed Fathers would no longer find her alive; as indeed happened. However great her desires for death were, she always remained in <term>composure</term> <note>German: *Gelassenheit*. A key concept in German mysticism referring to a state of surrendered equanimity.</note> throughout her sufferings.

### Part Eight. The Life

...[suf]fer, and though she had miraculously recovered the last time, something of the illness always remained with her. This gave her hope that the imprisonment of her body would not last much longer, which was her entire wish and desire. Our Blessed Mother (says one of her daughters) had an exceedingly great longing to see **God**, especially in the last years of her life. Usually, when she dressed in the morning or lay down in the evening, she used to say with very deep and heartfelt sighs: "Ah, how this body burdens and weighs me down! Truly, it would be a special joy to me if I could finally make an end of it."

2. She also took no more pleasure in any earthly thing, but behaved as if she were in a foreign land, sighing day and night for her desired fatherland <note>A common Baroque metaphor for Heaven as the soul's true home.</note>. Her conversations were also usually about this; she could not hide it because she was now so detached from all created things that it was a pain for her even to speak of indifferent or external matters. Her body could no longer withstand the strength of her spirit without the special assistance of **God**.

3. During this time, she was attacked by many different and dangerous illnesses, in which her excellent humility and patience shone forth in every way. She could not bear for people to make a great fuss over her, even in her most severe illnesses. When the *Most Serene Spanish Infanta, Archduchess of Brabant* <note>Isabella Clara Eugenia (1566–1633), daughter of Philip II of Spain and sovereign of the Spanish Netherlands, who was a close friend and protector of Mother Anna.</note>, out of the most gracious affection she held for *Mother Anna*, sent her doctors to her with orders to provide everything necessary for her health, and even appointed some from her ladies-in-waiting in *Brussels* for that purpose, this humble soul became more sensitive and ashamed than words can express. She said to **God**: "How can You suffer it, O my Lord! That a poor *Carmelite nun* <note>original: "Carmeliterin"</note> should cause such a great stir. O **God**! Do not allow it, but take me quietly from this world." These words she often repeated.

4. And so she had always been of such a mind that she constantly showed great displeasure toward the good opinion and high esteem people held for her. On the contrary, she felt an incredible love, pleasure, and desire to be despised, rejected, and unknown to everyone. This is testified by those who enjoyed her blessed company; when it happened, they say, that she was highly esteemed, she felt it very keenly and used to say to us: "Ah, my daughters! What a shame it is that we are held for those whom we are not? Pray to **God** the Lord that He may give me light to know myself, so that no one may be mistaken in me or be deceived."

5. Regarding her patience, her spiritual daughters testify thus: Although our mother's illnesses were very severe and her pains very sharp, she nevertheless endured them with such great composure, equanimity, and peace, that
