# of Anna Garcias. Chapter XVI.

that one would almost have to say that the Cross and suffering were her only comfort and her life. She never complained in her illnesses, but felt a great joy to see herself in the hands of her **God**, and would then often repeat these words: "Now I have nothing to do but obey **God** and the nurse; I have nothing to wish for but that **God** acts with me according to His pleasing will." She never requested anything she had a craving for, but when the nurse gave it to her, she accepted it in order to be obedient. She never asked **God** to alleviate or take away her pains, but only that He would give her patience and grace to suffer without causing others unrest or inconvenience; for nothing was more sensitive to her than when she saw that we were waiting on her and serving her. In her final illness, this patience of hers shone forth even more remarkably, wherein her sufferings and pains were also especially great, as we shall soon hear.

6. Some of her illnesses caused her to firmly believe at times that the longed-for hour of her departure had already come, of which she herself told a notable example at the end of the previous chapter, to which this should be added: that, as she had been in a trance for a long time during the vision mentioned there, and finally came back to herself, the Father Provincial <note>The superior of a religious province within the Carmelite order.</note> stepped into her chamber, to whom she said these brief words: "Ah, Father, how good **God** is!" She said no more; and fully believed her last hour was there, and that the **Lord** had appeared to her for the purpose of taking her with Him.

7. Another time, someone spoke with her about the foundation in the city of Liège <note>original: "Lüttig," the French-speaking city in modern-day Belgium where a Discalced Carmelite monastery was being established.</note>, and said that they would take such nuns from Antwerp <note>original: "Anthorf," the city where Ana de San Bartolomé founded a monastery and eventually died.</note> as would please her; but she answered: "Before this happens, there will already be another who will travel." She also said that our departed Fathers would no longer find her alive; which indeed came to pass. However great her desires for death were, she always remained in a state of composure <term>Gelassenheit: a state of surrendered detached serenity</term> in her sufferings. "See, Lord," she said, "here I am; fulfill in me Your most holy will; I want and desire nothing else."

8. Until then, she had been sometimes better and sometimes worse, and so she went with constant fluctuations toward her blessed passing; but finally, on the Thursday before Trinity Sunday <note>The feast day celebrating the Christian doctrine of the Trinity, falling in late May or June.</note> in the year 1626, she was seized in the night by a strong fever, yet did not fail to get up the next day at the usual hour to receive Holy Communion <note>original: "H. Abendmal," literally the Holy Supper.</note>; as weak as she now was, she did not lie down in bed again until about five o'clock in the afternoon, when a fever and very violent pains seized her, so that the doctor had to be called, who nevertheless judged that there was no danger. Meanwhile, the pains in her left shoulder were so great, bitter, and excessive that she herself had to confess that if the **Lord** had not specially strengthened her, she would have lost her patience; these pains lasted the final three days of her life, though with some fluctuations; for thus it pleased her heavenly Bridegroom that

### Section Eight. The Life

that she should die with Him on the cross and in such pains, which in some way corresponded to those pains that He Himself had suffered on the cross.

9. She spent the night between Friday and Saturday in great misery; in the morning she was a little better, so that it seemed as if **God** wished to hide her illness; nevertheless, some medicines were prescribed for her. She passed the whole of Saturday reasonably well, without anyone sensing any danger; toward the night, however, the fever became so violent, and other symptoms <note>The original uses "Zufälle," which in a medical context of this period refers to sudden paroxysms or fits.</note> accompanied it, that the nurse constantly feared she might die in her hands. It was this evening, as she said in her violent pains: "Oh, my dear daughter! how bitter is my cup!" <note>A reference to the Cup of Suffering mentioned by Jesus in the Garden of Gethsemane (Matthew 26:39).</note> Whereupon one of the sisters, out of compassion, said: "What, Reverend Mother, is the cup not yet drained? How much longer shall it last?" She answered: "No, my daughter, it is not quite empty yet; I still have the bitterest part to drink." Just as she then had to suffer terribly before her end, it was in such a way that all those pains could not make her patience waver.

10. At five o'clock in the morning, on the Sunday after <term>Trinity Sunday</term> <note>The first Sunday after Pentecost, a major feast day in the Christian calendar.</note>, she began to change, so much so that the doctor found almost no more fever; the whole morning she held a conversation with some of the nuns about the mystery of the Holy Trinity, of its excellence and sublimity, with such spirit and zeal that her countenance changed because of it, and became as beautiful and lovely as an angel, so that everyone wondered greatly at it; one saw not a single wrinkle upon it, which commonly happened to her as often as she had received a special grace from our **Lord**, although she sought to hide such things as much as possible.

11. Around noon, the cold fever <note>Chills or rigors associated with a high fever.</note> came upon her with strong shivering, along with exceedingly great pains in the shoulder, as if the same were being pulled apart, just as in the previous days; but now they took the upper hand with ever greater violence, so that she said to a sister: "My daughter, if the **Lord** did not strengthen me in this pain, and if He had not given me to understand that it was in some way similar to that which He Himself suffered when His holiest arms were stretched out and nailed to the cross, then I would undoubtedly not have been able to endure it." Afterward, she requested that prayers be made for her; meanwhile, her countenance changed, so that the doctor as well as her confessor were called in the greatest haste; but a <term>stroke</term> <note>The original term "Schlagfluß" refers to apoplexy or a sudden stroke that causes paralysis.</note> had touched her tongue, so that she could no longer speak, though she otherwise gave it to be understood through signs that she had not lost her senses; her mouth and tongue were entirely swollen, and also as hard and stiff as if they had been made of iron. Afterward, her face changed once more, and she showed a very friendly and laughing mouth, and also opened her eyes, which were beautiful beyond measure, and lifted them toward the heights; thus she passed away in quiet peace, as if she had fallen into a sweet sleep, and went hence to enjoy **God**, in the year 1626.

# S u p p l e m e n t
## of several verses by Mother Anna.

Here follow several verses which Mother Anna composed on the Mystery of the Cross, to be distributed by lot among her daughters. Newly and faithfully translated from the Spanish.

<image-desc>An ornate vertical border separates the two columns of verse below.</image-desc>

1. Truly (a) love does not fear
Much work, toil, and hardship:
Though the Cross may look so bitter,
It can never become a burden to love.

2. Without love, I count all as just the Cross,
Our works are too meager;
Love makes them perfect,
Giving them their very essence, light, and strength.

3. Without the Cross, there is no rest here below,
Search where you will: where would you find it?
Therefore it is dangerous, believe me,
Not to bind oneself to the Cross in love.

4. When the Cross does not rule in the house,
Then your little cottage has no joys:
It is brought in with bitterness,
Yet only love it, and it brings sweetness.

5. When I incline toward you in love,
Then you, Cross, do not show yourself bitter to me:
When I show myself peevish toward you,
Then you show yourself so hard that I tremble.

6. Do I say yes or no to the Cross?
Should I love it or hate it?
It always involves itself in everything;
Wherever I turn, I find it in every street.

7. If I go to my cell to rest,
Thinking to sit there in safety,
And also shut my little door tight;
You press inside, like the point of a needle.

<column-break/>

8. Cross, whoever seeks you never has you;
If I do not seek you, you let yourself be found:
Therefore I know no better counsel
Than to bind myself to you quite willingly.

9. Lord, give me the Cross! This great gift
Is given to everyone who follows you:
Strip me of myself and everything else,
Let me live clothed with you alone.

10. I was lost entirely,
Were it not for you, O Cross!
But you have wonderfully
Snatched me from the enemy's hand and healed me.

11. You precious Cross, I love you,
I will choose you as my mistress <note>In this context, "mistress" (Meisterin) refers to a female teacher, guide, or authority figure.</note>:
In you there is always strength for me,
When it fails me in all things.

12. Cross, when I go and seek you,
You can beautifully hide your hardness;
Until I love you, you entice me,
Afterwards you leave me stuck, deceived.

13. Cross, although your burden presses upon me,
Yet you will not depart from me:
I feel you, and yet I am refreshed;
You are dear to me, even if it costs me dearly.

14. You are, O Cross! my crown of honor,
I will praise you and extol you;
Through you, my name stands written
With greater radiance in the Book of Life above.

15. —

Through the dark night, as I call this life.

### Rhymes of Mother Anna on several virtues.

1.
What should I call true humility?
To recognize ourselves, how and what we are,
The pure truth without appearance.
Whoever does not believe this must be deceived.

2.
The virtue of this very humility
Is only recognized and given in the Cross:
He has his life entirely in the Cross,
Who loves humility and was glad to be humble.

3.
Not to seek to be preferred,
Or to be loved more by others here on earth:
This brings into the ground of the soul
The greatest rest and peace at every hour.

4.
True gentleness <note>The original German "Sanfftmuth" implies a combination of meekness, patience, and a mild disposition.</note> can bend,
It is a cross in gentle silence,
It keeps itself immersed only in God,
Where it thinks nothing but good of everyone.

5.
Poverty and the solitary life,
Silence and being hidden besides,
When practiced in you, O Cross!
They make my heart love you heartily.

6.
The virtue of poverty is to be treasured,
It is a cross to lust and delight,
Which gives no burden nor disturbance,
If only the poor one himself loves poverty.

7.
Whoever has attained true chastity,
Resembles the Savior and the Virgin Mother:
If you possess this virtue purely,
The Cross will be light and lovely to you.

8.
Obedience, the crown of virtue,
Makes it so that she always dwells near humility,
Whereby love gladly joins her,
Which first makes her perfect before the Lord.
How good it is to practice therein,
To seek and to love being obedient!

<column-break/>

9.
The virtue of patience is loved,
Is much desired, and little practiced;
For without the Cross no one has it,
Nor can truly treasure its value.

10.
Not to grumble or complain at all,
Is a great virtue, I must say;
Oh, how well it pleases God!
Whomever it pleases: shall soon become peaceful.

11.
Whoever seeks to dwell constantly in prayer,
Will become a master of his passions,
Compassionate, who repays nothing evil,
Gives not a single word to him who reviles and scolds him.

12.
In your conduct always walk modestly <note>The word "züchtig" here suggests a disciplined, modest, and morally upright lifestyle.</note>,
Deal with everyone quite gently and kindly:
Then God gives Himself to you as a reward,
His blessing penetrates into your inner self,
Just as the dew brings the morning red.

13.
The chosen virtue of simplicity <note>The German "Einfalt" refers to a spiritual "singleness of heart" or holy simplicity, rather than a lack of intelligence.</note>,
Is only born in us by God's Spirit:
It looks at nothing according to its nature,
Except merely upon God’s loving presence.

14.
True faith must, before all,
Be the foundation pillar, should this house not fall:
On it all virtue is grounded,
In it they are all gathered into one.

15.
The last virtue is love,
A lovely salt of the virtue I practice,
It makes the bitter foods sweet,
So that I enjoy the most adverse things with pleasure.

1.
Beloved little Child, chosen one,
What will you do when you grow larger?
Now, since you are barely born a child,
You already pour out <note>literally: "wax" or "grow," but used here to mean the shedding of blood during the Circumcision, which traditionally occurred on New Year's Day.</note> your tender blood for us all.

2.
I see my child, who suffers even now,
Your whole life wakes out of pure love;
Though you have disguised yourself so poorly <note>Meaning Christ taking on the "lowly" form of human flesh.</note>,
Yet you will soon die in the war;
Quite dearly you will have to pay,
Gracious child, for the new suit of clothes,
With your blood you must atone for it,
Now that you are barely born in the night.

<header>Preliminary Report.</header>

# The Life
# of Brother Lawrence
### of the Resurrection.

## Preliminary Report.

What is shared here under the title of a biography of Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection was partly published in Paris in 1691, immediately following his blessed passing. Other parts came to light in 1694 by order of the Bishop of Chalon (who afterwards became the well-known Cardinal de Noailles <note>Louis Antoine de Noailles (1651–1729) was a powerful French bishop and later Cardinal who was deeply involved in the religious debates of his time, including the controversies surrounding Quietism.</note>). The author of the latter—and without a doubt of all the rest—was Mr. de Beaufort, Grand Vicar to the aforementioned bishop. He was not only a good friend of our Lawrence but also heard and recorded the "Conversations" cited here in Chapter VII from Lawrence’s own mouth.

The largest and most important part of these writings was attached to the first editions of the small works of Madame Guyon <note>Jeanne-Marie Bouvier de la Motte-Guyon (1648–1717), a French mystic and one of the key figures of Quietism, a movement emphasizing internal stillness and the passive contemplation of God.</note>, both in the French [1699] and German languages [1700, 1706], though they were omitted from the newer editions. However, they were printed together and separately in French in Amsterdam in the year 1710, under the title *The Theology of the Presence of God*. This edition was expanded by half, including an edifying treatise by Mr. Poiret <note>Pierre Poiret (1646–1719) was a French mystic and philosopher who edited and promoted the works of many great spiritual writers.</note> on the importance and usefulness of practicing the Presence of God. This treatise (along with the author's as-yet-unpublished additions) deserves to be published anew and translated into German again, as the 1714 German edition is certainly of little use.

<margin>
(a) History of the Reborn, pages 106, 102.
(b) See his Life, p. 51. <note>original: "Vid. ejus Vitam"</note>
(c) The same, on Erudition, Vol 2, p. 562. Library of Mystics, 337. <note>original: "Idem, de Erudit... Bibl. Myst."</note>
</margin>
These writings left behind by Brother Lawrence were not only printed with official approval and received with eagerness in the Roman Catholic Church; they were also loved and praised by Protestants. Gottfried Arnold <note>A radical Pietist historian famous for his "impartial" history of the church and heretics.</note> attached the eulogy regarding the simple path of faith and love of Brother Lawrence to his *Lives of the Faithful*. J. H. Reitz, who also briefly mentions this life story, calls these small works (a) full of the anointing <term>Anointing</term> <note>In this context, "anointing" (Salbung) refers to a perceptible sense of divine grace or spiritual power present in a text or person.</note> of the Holy Spirit. He further says: "This history is so excellent that no person, unless they be a truly blind zealot or sectarian, could take offense at it being placed here." Pierre Poiret, who, despite how learned he was, always (b) used to read our Brother Lawrence with singular pleasure, says: "The (c) method of Brother Lawrence is one of the most excellent that may be found, both because of its simplicity and because it goes to the heart, as well as for its ease and great thoroughness, etc."

In this present biography and its appendix, the reader will find everything that actually exists from Brother Lawrence, which has otherwise been seen under various titles such as the Eulogy, the Maxims, the Conversations, the Basic Rules, and the Letters. Thus, the entire "Theology of the Presence of God," both in theory and practice [in its teaching and its application], is presented and commended to us all for our blessed imitation.

Among all godly practices, there is none more universal, simple, sweet, or useful—nor one that more happily unites the entire sum of Christian duties into a single point—than the practice of the loving Presence of God. This is according to the testimony of all the saints: in this, Enoch, Noah, Abra-

<meta>Catchword: Abra- [Abraham]</meta>

<summary>This preface outlines the publication history of Brother Lawrence’s writings, noting their popularity among both Catholics and Protestants like Gottfried Arnold and Pierre Poiret. It introduces the "Practice of the Presence of God" as a central, simple Christian discipline.</summary>
<keywords>Brother Lawrence, publication history, Pierre Poiret, Madame Guyon, Gottfried Arnold, Presence of God, ecumenical appeal, mysticism, spiritual practice</keywords>

<header>Preliminary Report</header>

<margin>(a) Psalm 73:28.</margin>
Abraham, David, Asaph, and our Savior Himself have gone before us; and until now, all the godly testify that it is (a) good for them to keep themselves close to God <note>original: "nahe bey GOtt halten". This refers to the biblical concept of drawing near to the divine through inward devotion.</note>.

Now, this practice consists briefly in this: That we simply and devoutly believe that God is present everywhere, and also in our hearts. That He is present with us and in us for this purpose, so that we should worship, love, and serve Him there, just as He gladly wishes to communicate Himself to us there and take His pleasure in us. That we should therefore frequently remind ourselves of this truth of faith in a heartfelt way, and regard ourselves as being with God, before God, and in His presence. That we worship, glorify, and love this, our present God, with our heart, and surrender ourselves entirely to Him. That we strive to do, to deny, and to suffer everything in a gentle and quiet spirit, as if in His company, according to His dearest will, for His love and honor. That we converse with God in our heart in a loving and silent manner; and make ourselves familiar with Him, as with our dearest and best friend. And indeed at all times, and in everything that occurs to us inwardly or outwardly, be it good or evil. That we also for this purpose, amidst our business, pause for a moment now and then to strengthen or renew ourselves in this practice through a devout look of love toward God. That we perceive and respond to the drawings and enticements of love from God in our interior, through which He wishes to kindly remind, quiet, gather, and unite us with Himself. And finally, that after every distraction or unfaithfulness, we return at once to our previous practice with humble confidence, like a child to its dear father.

See then, what is simpler and easier to grasp than this sweet teaching on the way of our salvation, which our poor <term>lay brother</term> <note>A "lay brother" was a member of a religious order, like the Carmelites, who focused on manual labor rather than the formal liturgical duties of ordained priests.</note> Lawrence described more clearly and briefly than many a graduated doctor of theology would be able to do. And no wonder, for he practiced it at all times and in all places, both among his dishes in the kitchen and in the church and chamber; both in days of health and in the most violent pains and illnesses: so that we might also see in this example that not only so-called clergy and monastics, but everyone in their station and place, can live in the presence of God through His grace; indeed, that nothing is easier and lovelier than this very thing: whoever tries it will experience it.

So accustom yourself now to the Lord, my soul. May the company of this friend be dearer and sweeter to you than all things of this world. He is the faithful friend who will be your assistance and comfort in the hour of your death, when everyone leaves you. Yes, then you will truly begin to enjoy the glorious and blessed presence of your God, and be with the Lord in every way. Selah! <note>A Hebrew term often found in the Psalms, likely meaning a musical pause or a call to "stop and listen."</note>

# Chapter One.

## On his birth, soldier’s life, conversion, his desire for the monastic life, and entry into the same.

-> I. <-

Brother Lawrence, previously named Nicolas Herman, was born in Hériménil in Lorraine; <note>original: "Hermini in Lottringen". Hériménil is a village in the Meurthe-et-Moselle department in northeastern France.</note> his father and mother were very good people who led an edifying life and also implanted the fear of God in this their son from childhood. They took special care regarding his upbringing, teaching him nothing but holy doctrines in accordance with the Gospel. <note>original: "Evangelio"</note>

2. As Lorraine became entangled in the war turmoils of that time, <note>This likely refers to the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), which devastated the region of Lorraine.</note> he took up the life of a soldier, in which he walked in simplicity and integrity, so that God anticipated him with His goodness and mercy.

He was taken prisoner by a troop of German soldiers who were out on a raiding party <note>original: "auf Parthey giengen," a military term for a small detachment sent out for scouting or foraging.</note> and was held as a spy. In this distressing situation, he remained in the greatest patience and silence. They threatened to have him hanged, but he answered fearlessly that he was not the person they took him for, and since his conscience did not accuse him of any such vice, he would await death without terror; whereupon the officers then released him.

When the Swedes made an incursion into Lorraine and attacked the small town of Rambervillers <note>original: "Ramberville"</note> during their march, our young soldier was wounded. His wound necessitated that he return to his parents, who lived not far from there.

3. This accident caused him to leave the military life and undertake a holier one, namely to fight under the banner of Jesus Christ. These were not merely the impulses of a thoughtless devotion resulting perhaps from frustration with the restless life of a soldier; rather, it arose within him from a feeling of true godliness, which moved him to make the resolution to surrender himself entirely to the Lord and to improve his former life. This God of all comfort, who ordained him to a holy life, let him see then the vanity of this idle world and touched him through the love of heavenly things. However, these first stirrings did not immediately reach their full strength in him. He often considered within himself the danger in which he saw himself involved, the vanity and corruption of the world, the fickleness of men, the treachery of an enemy, the unfaithfulness of friends, and the like. All of this took place within him amidst many profound reflections, many hard struggles of the soul, and the pouring out of many tears and sighs, under which he was finally so overcome by the power of divine truth that he made the firm resolution to surrender unchangeably and to hold to evangelical exercises, and to follow in the footsteps of his holy uncle, a Discalced Carmelite <note>original: "Barfüßer Carmeliten," literally "Barefoot Carmelites," referring to the reformed branch of the order known for their poverty and devotion.</note> to—

### Ninth Part. The Life

...tread, as one who showed him how the world possessed a contagious air; and that even if it did not immediately kill those who lived within it, it nevertheless corrupted the morals of those who followed its basic rules.

4. The wise counsel of such an enlightened leader <note>The text likely refers to a spiritual director or mentor Herman met after his injury.</note> made the path to perfection quite easy for Herman, to which his own soul, by its inner tractable nature, contributed not a little. The great understanding and wisdom that shone from this man's face soon lifted for Herman all the difficulties that the devil and the world commonly place in the way of those who wish to change their lives. This prudent steadfastness, which was so uniquely his own, moved him to a bold resolution: that in a single moment, and almost miraculously, he drew himself out from the mire of the world.

This primarily occurred because he began to contemplate the promise of his baptismal covenant <note>original: "Taufbund," referring to the solemn vows made at baptism to renounce the world and the devil.</note>, the disorderly life of his youth, the mysteries of our Christianity, and especially the suffering of our Savior Jesus Christ. He never thought of the latter without great sensitivity, so that he became a completely different person through it, and the lowliness of the Cross appeared to him much more beautiful than all the glory of the world.

Otherwise, our Brother Lawrence himself says at the beginning of his *Conversations* <note>Referring to the "Conversations" recorded by Joseph de Beaufort, which alongside his letters form the core of *The Practice of the Presence of God*.</note> that the actual occasion of his complete conversion—which took place around the eighteenth year of his age—was the sight of a dry tree in winter. Upon seeing it, he received a deep vision of the Providence and Omnipotence of God, and through this was made completely free from the world, as can be seen below in the seventh chapter.

5. Subsequently, he now sought God in the simplicity and sincerity of his heart; his thoughts constantly drove him to seek solitude in order to weep for his sins there. Because of this, he reflected several times on how he might completely withdraw from the world, for which a convenient opportunity soon presented itself. There was, namely, a nobleman who, despite all his temporal happiness and wealth, could find no rest, but was always dissatisfied with himself. He had finally recognized that God alone could fulfill the breadth of his desires; this man had retreated into solitude, having denied everything else, to taste there "how sweet the Lord is" to those who seek Him in truth. <note>A reference to Psalm 34:8: "Taste and see that the Lord is good."</note>

As such a good opportunity arose for our Herman, he also resolved to go into the wilderness <note>original: "Einöde," referring to a hermitage or secluded place.</note>, as he was quite exhausted by his burdensome life, and there he surrendered himself to God more than he had ever done before. However, the manifold temptations and shakings of his still-weak spirit soon convinced him that the life of a hermit is not for everyone, nor for beginners in grace. For this reason, after some reflection and doubts within his spirit, he finally resolved to go to the Carmelite Monastery in Paris, where he was then also received...

# Chapter Two.

## His Zeal in Godliness. Tireless Diligence in Works of Obedience: as well as his ten-year inner trials and sufferings.

->I.<-

Right from the start of his probationary year <note>original: "Probierjahr," referring to the novitiate, a testing period for those entering a religious order.</note>, he devoted himself with great zeal to the exercises of a godly life; he placed his fear of God primarily in the diligent practice of prayer, in such a way that (no matter how great his business might be) he never allowed himself to be kept from waiting for the appointed time of these devotional prayer exercises. The presence and the love of God, which are the fruits of prayer, were his most beloved virtues. In a short time, these made him a model for his fellow brothers, who were also still novices in the probationary year with him; and the victorious grace of Jesus Christ moved him to embrace penance with great zeal and to choose that which corrupt nature most tends to abhor.

2. Although the superiors of the monastery assigned this Lawrence to the lowliest of tasks <note>This likely refers to his famous assignment to the monastery kitchen, which he initially disliked but turned into a spiritual practice.</note>, he never let a single complaint be heard from him; on the contrary, he possessed the grace (which never shrinks from that which is sharp and hard) to persevere constantly in all vexing business. No matter how much his nature otherwise felt a loathing for it, he nevertheless took it all on with pleasure and considered himself happy either to suffer or to be humbled following the example of our Savior. The good opinion that people formed of his service, and the respect he gained through his virtuous works, prompted the Master of Novices <note>original: "Meister der Probbrüder," the monk in charge of training new recruits.</note> to put his calling and the steadfastness of his spirit to the test by increasing his workload, weighing him down with various duties, and [in a word] testing him as one is accustomed to do with strong souls. However, instead of allowing such hard trials to deter or embitter him, he endured it all with complete faithfulness. This was also seen on another occasion when a brother came to him and said he had heard they intended to turn him out of the monastery; to which he gave this answer: "I am in the hand of God; let Him do with me as He pleases. In my actions, I have no regard for any man; if I do not serve the Lord here, I shall serve Him in another place."

3. In this manner his probationary years passed; but after that time it happened that

### Part Nine. The Life

3. He was placed into heavy inner suffering, partly by the ordinance of divine Providence—which allowed it for his purification—and partly from a lack of experience, as he wished to walk in the spiritual life according to his own way. He contemplated and observed the sins of his past life, and this sight filled him with great dread; it made him so small and contemptible in his own eyes that he considered himself unworthy of even the smallest signs of love from his Savior. Even though the Lord met him with many marks of favor, he did not dare to accept the offered heavenly gifts because he did not yet recognize that God could be so merciful as to share Himself with such a sinner as he believed himself to be. Thus it happened that his heart was strongly seized by the fear of deception <note>original: "Betrug," here referring to the fear of spiritual delusion or being misled by false religious feelings.</note>, and his condition seemed so doubtful to him that he did not know what to do. In the time that followed, this caused him such terrible agony that he was accustomed to compare it to the pains of hell.

4. In this distressing state, he often went to a hidden place near his workshop; there he used to pour out his anguished heart, swimming in tears, before his God, fervently calling upon Him not to let him be lost, for he placed his entire trust in Him and had no other purpose than to please Him alone. However diligently he prayed, his sufferings were nevertheless increased by all kinds of fear, sadness, and unrest, to the point that his spirit was suddenly driven into a narrow strait. The solitude, which he otherwise held to be a safe harbor, appeared to him like a sea raging with all kinds of storms. Now that his spirit was brought into such turmoil—not unlike a ship that, having been abandoned by the helmsman, is driven about by wind and weather—he did not know which way to turn or what resolution to make. On one hand, he felt a hidden inclination moving him to surrender himself to his Savior through a constant sacrifice; on the other hand, the fear he had that he might stray from the common path caused him to resist God unknowingly. All these insights, so vexing to his nature, placed him in great fear and terror. Indeed, his soul fell into such bitter sorrows and thick darkness <note>This description mirrors the "Dark Night of the Soul" described by other mystics, where a believer feels abandoned by God as a form of spiritual purging.</note> that he perceived no help from either heaven or earth.

5. As hard and severe as this guidance may be, it is often the means by which the Lord is accustomed to test the virtue of His true servants before He entrusts them with the inestimable treasure of His wisdom. And this is exactly the way God dealt with Brother Lawrence. One cannot believe how far his patience, his gentleness, his modesty, his constancy, and his stillness extended during these trials. Just as he was humble in his mind and conduct and thought little of himself, he truly esteemed nothing highly except suffering and humiliation; nor did he desire anything else but to drink the cup of the Lord <note>A reference to the "cup of suffering" mentioned in Matthew 20:22.</note>, which was indeed made bitter enough for him.

<meta>This page continues the biography of Brother Lawrence (born Nicolas Herman), detailing a decade of intense spiritual "dryness" and psychological distress following his entry into the religious life. ->Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection. Chapter III.<-

6. One might have thought that the Lord would have left him some of that anointing <note>original: "Salbung," referring to a sense of spiritual sweetness or divine favor.</note> which he had felt at the beginning of his penance; but no! Everything was taken from him. In the ten years that he spent in such fears and unrest, he felt very little relief; he found no taste for prayer, nor any easing of all his sufferings. This was what made his life so difficult and brought him to such great poverty of spirit that he became, as it were, a burden and unbearable even to himself, so that faith alone was his entire support.

7. Amidst this heap of various thoughts, which brought him to the utmost distress, he nevertheless did not let his courage sink. On the contrary, he took (whenever he was stuck in the highest need) his refuge in prayer, in the practice of the presence of God <note>original: "Vorstellung der Gegenwart GOttes," the foundational practice for which Brother Lawrence is famous.</note>, in the exercise of all Christian and upright virtues, in the mortification of the flesh, and in persistent sighing, weeping, and keeping watch—so much so that he spent entire nights in the church. Finally, one day, while reflecting on how much grief plagued his soul, he recognized that it was for the love of God and the fear of offending Him that he suffered all of this. He therefore made a brave resolution to endure all of this, not only for the duration of his life but also for all eternity, if it were so pleasing to God. "For it matters nothing to me," he said, "what I do or what I suffer, as long as I remain united in love with the will of God; for this is my entire work."

# The Third Chapter.

### How God delivered him from his anxiety and thereafter placed him in a firm state of mind: One of his letters, in which his entire guidance is contained.

1. In this complete abandonment <note>original: "völligen Ueberlassung," a spiritual term for the total surrender of one's will to God.</note> lay the actual condition of soul in which God wished to have him, in order to fill him with His graces. Thus, from this moment on, the firmness of his heart was increased more than ever before. Just as God does not need to make Himself known through a long passage of time, nor through many logical deductions <note>original: "Vernunft-Schlüsse," referring to intellectual or theological reasoning.</note>, He opened Lawrence's eyes all at once. Lawrence beheld a ray of Divine light, by which his mind was enlightened and all fear was driven away; his anxiety also vanished, and the grace he received made all previous sufferings sweet and forgotten.

### Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection. Chapter III.

> "...whom I regarded as always being near me, indeed, often even as present in the very depths of my soul. This gave me such a high veneration for God that faith alone was sufficient to satisfy me in this state.
>
> I did the same thing unnoticed in my prayer, which caused me great delights and consolations. See, through this I began. I will tell you nonetheless that in the first ten years I suffered much: the fear I had that I did not belong to God as I wished, my committed sins which were always before my eyes, and the great graces which God showed me were the cause and fountainhead of all my sufferings. In all this time I fell often, and stood up again immediately. It seemed to me that creatures, reason, and God Himself were against me, and faith alone was for me. Sometimes I was disturbed by the thought that it was an effect of my presumption that I wanted to be at once where others only reach with effort; and again, that I was willfully condemning myself, and no <term>salvation</term> <note>original: "Seeligkeit"; refers to eternal happiness or the state of being saved.</note> was to be hoped for.
>
> As I thought of nothing else but to bring my days to an end in this confusion and unrest (which had taken nothing away from the trust I had in God, and which only served to increase my faith), I suddenly found myself changed. My soul, which until then was constantly in unrest, found itself in a deep inner peace, as if it were in its <term>center</term> <note>original: "Centro"; a term in mystical theology referring to the deepest part of the soul where God dwells.</note> and at a place of rest.
>
> From that time on, I work simply before God in faith, with humility and love, and diligently strive to do, speak, or think nothing that could displease Him. I hope that when I have done what I can, He will then make of me what pleases Him.

This causes me at times such great inner, and often outer, pleasure and joy that I am forced to moderate and prevent them, so that they do not appear outwardly, and to do many childish things in my outward manner that seem to be more folly than devotion.
>

### Ninth Piece. The Life.

,,...that I do not weary you; meanwhile, I consider it useful to show you the way in which I view myself before God, whom I regard as my King.

,,I see myself as the most wretched of all men, torn by wounds, full of stench, who has committed all kinds of misdeeds against his King; and moved by a sensitive sorrow, I confess to Him all my wickednesses, ask Him for their forgiveness, and surrender myself into His hands, that He may do with me whatever pleases Him.

,,This King, full of goodness and mercy, does not punish me at all; instead, He embraces me lovingly, feeds me at His own table, serves me with His own hands, gives me the keys to His treasures, and treats me everywhere as His favorite. He converses and delights Himself with me in a thousand and thousand ways without ceasing, and says nothing of my forgiveness, nor does He take away my former habits. Although I ask Him to make me after His own heart, I see myself daily weaker and more wretched, yet I am all the more caressed by God. See how I view myself in His holy presence from time to time!

,,My most usual practice is this simple attention, and a general and loving looking upon God, in which I often find myself clinging with greater sweetness and pleasure than those felt by a child hanging at its nurse’s breasts. I would also gladly call this state, if I dared, "the breasts of God," because of the indescribable sweetness that I taste and experience there.

,,If I sometimes turn away from it out of necessity or weakness, I am soon called back by inner, loving, and pleasant stirrings, so that I am ashamed to speak of it. I ask you, Reverend Father, that you would rather look upon my great misery, of which you are fully informed, than upon the great graces with which God favors my soul, of which I am entirely unworthy and <term>unrecognizing</term> <note>original: "unerkenntlich"; can mean ungrateful or simply unable to fully grasp the magnitude of the grace.</note>.

,,As for my hours of prayer, they are nothing more than a continuation of this same exercise. Sometimes I consider myself there as a stone before the <term>sculptor</term> <note>original: "Bildhauer"; a classic mystical metaphor for the soul's passive surrender to God's transformative power.</note>, from which he wants to make a statue; so I place myself before God, and ask Him that He may form His perfect image in my soul, and make me entirely like Him.

,,At another time, as soon as I turn to prayer, I find my whole spirit and my whole soul elevated without any care or effort, and it remains quite firmly attached to God as if in its <term>center</term> <note>original: "Centro"; the mystical 'ground of the soul' where the human meets the Divine.</note>, and in a place of rest.

,,I know that some consider this state to be idleness, deception, or self-love. I confess it is a <term>holy idleness</term> <note>original: "heiliger Müssiggang"; this refers to the 'prayer of quiet,' where the soul stops its own busy reflections to simply be with God.</note> and a blessed self-love, if the soul were capable of such a thing in this state: for indeed, when the soul is in this rest...

3. A certain clergyman, whom he could not refuse to answer, asked him one day what means he had used to attain such a firm habit of the **presence of God**, wherein he could remain with such ease and constancy? To which he replied with his usual simplicity:

From the time I entered the monastery, I looked upon God as the ultimate goal and the end of all thoughts and all desires of my soul. In the beginning of my <term>probationary years</term> <note>original: "Probjahren" — the novitiate, a trial period for new monks before taking final vows.</note>, I occupied myself during the set hours of prayer with this: that I might obtain a firm conviction and impression of the truth of this Divine Being, and indeed more through the light of **faith**, than through laborious contemplations and reflections; and through this short and sure means, I increased in the knowledge of this lovable **object** <note>original: "Vorwurfs" — in older German, this referred to the "object" or "subject" of one's attention or love, rather than a "reproach."</note>, and resolved to remain with Him always. 

When I was now entirely permeated by the majesty of this infinite Being, I went and shut myself in the place assigned to me by **obedience**, namely in the kitchen. Just as I was alone there, I used to first attend to all the necessities of my office, and then use all the time remaining to me, both before and after work, for the practice of prayer; at the beginning of my tasks, I said to God with a childlike confidence: *My God, since You are with me, and I must, by Your ordinance, turn my mind to these outward things, I ask You to grant me the grace that I may also remain with You and keep You company; but so that this, my Lord, may happen all the better, work You with me, accept my works, and possess all my desires.* 

So I also used to continue in familiar conversation with Him in the midst of the work, offering Him my small services, and calling upon Him for His grace. When the work was at an end, I examined how I had done it; if I found something good in it, I thanked God for it; but if I noticed faults in it, I asked Him for forgiveness; and without becoming discouraged by it, I set my mind back in its uprightness, and began again with the Lord to...

> “Because you desire with such great zeal that I share with you the manner and way which I have observed to arrive at the state of the **presence of God**, in which our Lord through His mercy has willed to place me; so I cannot hide from you that it is with much restraint that I let myself be won over by your repeated urging, but even then only on this condition: that you shall share my letter with no one. I considered myself at times before Him as a poor criminal at the feet of his judge; at another time I looked upon Him in my heart as my Father, as my God; I worshipped Him there as often as I could and kept my spirit in His holy presence; I also called it back as often as I found it distracted from Him. I had no small amount of trouble with this exercise, which I continued against all the difficulties that I encountered, without disturbing or worrying myself when I was distracted against my will. I occupied myself with it no less during the day than during prayer; for at all times, hours, and moments, even during my greatest work, I drove away and removed from my mind everything that could take away the remembrance of God.
>

# Chapter Five.

## How he recommended this practice of the presence of God to each and every person through oral reminders, through letters, and through his own example.

->I.<-

Just as our Lawrence experienced what great benefit such holy practice brought to the soul, he was accustomed to advising all his friends to apply themselves to it with all care and the greatest possible faithfulness. However, to persuade them to do this with a constant purpose and invincible courage, he presented them with such concise and forceful reasons that he not only convinced the understanding but also so captivated the heart that they came to love this holy practice and began to engage in it with just as much zeal as they had previously viewed it with disregard.

2. He did not, however, stop at oral presentations; all the short letters from his hand are filled with nothing but heartfelt reminders and invitations to this divine exercise. It is a joy to read them and to see how he knew how to present and recommend this walk in the presence of God to everyone as something so necessary, useful, easy, and sweet; I cannot refrain from sharing a few of them here.

->My Reverend and Greatly Honored Mother!<-

“Today I received two books and a letter from Sister N., who is preparing to take her vows <term>Gelübde: formal promises made to God, usually of poverty, chastity, and obedience, when entering a religious order.</term> and desires for this purpose the prayer of your holy convent community, and yours in particular; she testifies to me that she places a very great and singular confidence therein. Do not deprive her of it. Ask God that she may make her offering with the sole intention of His love, and with a firm resolution that she wishes to be entirely His. I wish to [send] you one of these books

“I do not say that one must exert oneself with great violence for this; no, one must serve God in a **holy freedom**; one must work faithfully, without confusion or restlessness, and call our mind back to God gently and calmly as often as we find it has wandered from Him.

“Meanwhile, it is necessary to place all one's confidence in God and rid oneself of all other cares, even the multitude of specific, though good, devotional exercises with which one burdens oneself at the wrong time. For even these devotions are only means to reach the end; thus, when through this <term>Practice of the Presence of God<note>Lawrence’s signature method of maintaining a constant, silent conversation with God throughout the day's work.</note></term> we are with the One who is our end, it is useless for us to return to the means. Instead, we can continue our communion of love with Him and remain in His holy presence—now through an act of adoration, praise, or desire; now through an act of sacrifice, thanksgiving, and in all the ways our mind can devise.

“Do not lose heart because of the resistance you will find within your nature; you must <note>The phrase "Gewalt anthun" (to do violence to oneself) refers to the spiritual effort required to overcome worldly distractions and natural impulses.</note> force yourself. In the beginning, one often believes this is only **wasting time**, but one must continue and resolve to persevere in it until death and against all difficulties. I commend myself to the prayers of the holy society and to yours in particular; and I remain in our Lord.

->October 12, 1688.<-

5. He possessed a singular gift for convincing all those who came to him through his words, and those absent through letters; likewise, his good example gave no less emphasis and impression. When one merely looked at him, one was edified and placed in the **presence of GOD**, no matter how busy one might be.

6. He called this <term>Practice of the Presence of God<note>Lawrence’s signature method of maintaining a constant, silent conversation with God throughout the day's work, treating every moment as an act of worship.</note></term> the shortest and easiest way to attain **Christian perfection**; he said it was the form and life of virtue and the great safeguard against sin. He assured that to make this exercise easy and to gain a firm habit in it, one need only have a brave heart and good will; which is a truth he proved even more through his deeds than through his words, as we shall further hear in the following chapter.

## The Sixth Chapter.

### His walk with God even amidst his business; in whose union
### he lives quite contentedly, untouched by all unrest
### and suffering; his profound virtue; his humble and
### edifying interaction with his neighbor.

->I.<-

It has been observed in the conduct of Brother Lawrence that while he managed his duties in the kitchen—even when he had the most work to do there and found himself in the midst of very distracting occupations—he nevertheless remained collected in God within his soul. Even though his tasks were heavy and laborious, as he often performed alone in his office what was usually the work of two men, he was never seen to go about his work with haste. Instead, with a becoming order and measure, he devoted as much time to each matter as was required and always preserved his modest and calm nature. He worked neither with laziness nor with over-haste, and remained at all times in that same equanimity of mind and undisturbed peace.

2. He managed this office of his with the greatest possible love for about 30 years, until the providence of God arranged otherwise for him. Namely, he developed a large ulcer on his leg, which prompted the superiors to give him a lighter service. This change now gave him more time and leisure to adore his God in spirit and truth, according to his inner inclination, and to occupy himself all the better with His bare presence through the exercise of faith and love.

3. In such intimate union, which can only come from the two aforementioned virtues, the images of <term>creatures<note>In 17th-century spiritual writing, "creatures" refers to any created thing—people, objects, or worldly concerns—that might distract the soul from the Creator.</note></term>, which are otherwise so difficult to be rid of, were wiped from his memory. The powers of hell, which otherwise strive tirelessly against mankind, no longer dared to attack Brother Lawrence; his emotions became quiet and still, so that he almost no longer felt them. Or, if they did occasionally manifest themselves again with some slight stirrings to trouble him, he seemed like the high mountains, which, because of their height, hardly notice when all kinds of storms are stirred up down in the valley.

4. This is not mere eulogy or an exaggeration; Brother Lawrence himself admitted this unchangeable tranquility of mind and contentment in God when he opened up something of his inner condition to trusted friends. See how he expresses himself regarding this in two letters that have been preserved from him:

# Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection. Chapter VI.

> “Let us fear to depart from Him; let us stay with Him always, let us live and die with Him. Pray to Him for me. I will pray to Him for you.

-> Yours, etc. <-

-> November 28, 1690. <-

6. From this time on, it seemed as if virtue had become natural to him: he possessed a gentle nature, a complete sincerity, and the most honest heart. His lovely countenance, his affable and friendly manner, and his simple and modest conduct quickly inclined the respect, favor, and love of all those who saw him toward him. The more one associated with him, the more one discovered in him such a foundation of integrity and godliness as one would rarely find elsewhere.

It was observed that he was particularly diligent in letting no eccentricity be felt in his actions; he always maintained the simplicity of common life, nor did he allow any morose or severe manner to appear in his dealings, which might turn people away. Because he had nothing unusual, nothing contrived or pretentious about him, he was friendly and polite toward everyone, and was quite open and communal with his brothers and friends, without wishing to distinguish himself from them through affected holiness.

7. He was far from exalting himself because of the graces of God, or wishing to let his virtues be seen in order to gain the esteem of men; on the contrary, he strove in a particular way to lead a hidden and unknown life. Indeed, his humility—which one might call Brother Lawrence’s characteristic virtue—brought him to the point that he sometimes undertook something that seemed simple and childish, so that he might holily hide his virtue and cover its appearance. For he sought not the praise of virtue, but the essence of it; and just as he desired only God to be the witness of his deeds, so he set nothing before himself but Him as his goal and reward.

8. Although he was so private and reserved regarding his own person, he did not fail to open himself up communally for the edification of his fellow brothers—not, to be sure, with the clever, whose knowledge and "beautiful lights" <note>original: "schöne Lichter"; a metaphorical reference to intellectual or theological insights that can sometimes lead to spiritual pride.</note> often only puff up the heart, but with the small and most simple ones. Indeed, it was observed that when he encountered people of this sort, he kept nothing hidden from them; he revealed to them, with wonderful frankness, the most beautiful secrets of the <term>interior life</term> <note>original: "Jnwendigen Lebens"; the practice of focusing the soul's attention on the presence of God within.</note> and the treasures of divine wisdom. The unction <note>original: "Salbung"; a term used to describe a grace-filled, soothing, and persuasive power in someone's speech or presence.</note> that accompanied his words so powerfully stirred the hearts of those who had the good fortune to associate with him that they left him completely permeated with divine love and were set aflame with an inward desire to put into practice the great truths he had taught them in secret.

# Ninth Part. The Life

9. Since God led him more through love than through fear of His judgments, all his conversations were directed toward instilling this same love in others, in order to tear away even the subtlest bonds of <term>love for the creature</term> <note>In 17th-century spiritual writing, "love of the creature" (Creaturliebe) refers to an unhealthy attachment to worldly things or people instead of God.</note> and to kill the "old man" in such a way that the kingdom of the "new man" might be established. "If you wish," he said to his fellow brothers, "to make great progress in the life of the spirit, then pay no heed to the fine words and the ingenious speeches of the learned of this world; woe to those who seek to satisfy their <term>curiosity</term> <note>The original German "Fürwitz" implies a vain or meddlesome intellectual pride.</note> in the science of men! It is the Creator alone who teaches the truth, who in a moment instructs the heart of the humble, and gives them more to recognize of the mysteries of our faith, and of the Divinity Himself, than if they had meditated upon them for many years."

10. For this reason, it happened that he himself so carefully avoided answering inquisitive questions—those which aim at nothing important and serve only to carry away the intellect while leaving the heart dry and empty. But when his superiors required him to frankly open his thoughts on some difficulties presented in conversation, he answered so correctly and so orderly that his response allowed for no further opposition, as various scholars observed in him when they compelled him to answer the questions they put forward.

This gentleman committed these conversations to paper every time he had an interview with Brother Lawrence. 2. This was the first time I had seen **Brother Lawrence**. He told me how **God** had granted him a singular grace in his conversion when he was still in the world and 18 years old; one day in winter, he looked at a tree that was stripped of all its leaves, and considered how, after some time, the leaves would come forth again, followed soon by flowers and fruit. In this, he received a deep vision of the <term>Providence</term> <note>The protective care of God as a spiritual guardian.</note> and omnipotence of **God**, which was never again erased from his soul. This vision, he said, had completely detached him from the world and awakened such a love for **God** in him that he could not say whether this love had increased during the 40 years that had passed since he received this grace.

He had been a lackey—a servant—to the Lord Treasurer *Fieubet*, and was a large, clumsy man who spoiled everything and brought things to naught.

He had desired to enter the monastery, believing that he would be flayed alive there for the gross faults he would commit, and that he would thereby sacrifice his life and all his pleasures; but **God** had deceived him, because, on the contrary, he found nothing but pure pleasure therein; for which reason he often said to **God**: **Lord**, You have deceived me.

One must strive to be established in the **Presence of God**, and to that end, converse with Him without ceasing; it would be a shame to leave his company to think of all kinds of <term>trifles</term> <note>The original German "Lumpereyen" suggests worthless, ragged, or petty thoughts that distract from the divine.</note>.

One must strengthen and nourish one's soul through a high esteem for **God**, which would make it very joyful for us to think of Him.

One must make one's faith living within oneself; it was much to be regretted that we have so little faith; and that, instead of faith being our rule and our guide, we occupy ourselves with all kinds of minor devotional exercises which change every day. This way of faith was the spirit of the Church, and it was sufficient to attain a high state of perfection.

One must give oneself entirely to **God** with a pure and total surrender, both in spiritual and temporal matters, and take all one's pleasure in the fulfillment of His will; whether He leads us through suffering or through joy, everything must be equal to the one who has truly surrendered himself.

One must be faithful in times of <term>dryness</term> <note>A common term in mysticism ("dürre") for periods when one feels no emotional or spiritual consolation during prayer.</note> and abandonment, whereby **God** tests our love for Him; there we learn to practice beautiful acts of <term>Resignation</term> <note>original: "Gelassenheit." A central concept in German mysticism meaning a state of letting go, serenity, and yielding to God's will.</note> and surrender, a single one of which often helps us forward a great deal (a).

To reach the point where one surrenders oneself as fully to **God** as He requires of us, one must diligently watch over all the movements of the soul, which—

### II. Conversation. September 28, 1766.

3. He had always let himself be guided by love, without any other quest, and without worrying whether he would be saved or damned; rather, he had set this as the ultimate goal of all his actions: that he might do them all out of love for **GOTT**, and in this he found himself well. He would be well satisfied even if he could only pick up a straw from the ground for the love of **GOTT**; so that he sought Him alone, and nothing else, not even His gifts.

When the soul behaves in this way, it as it were <term>obliges</term> <note>Lawrence suggests a spiritual paradox: by seeking God alone, the soul "compels" God’s generosity.</note> **GOTT** to impart to her countless graces; but in accepting the fruit—that is, the love which arises from these gifts of grace—one must reject the <term>taste</term> <note>The emotional or sensory pleasure derived from spiritual experiences.</note> of them, saying that all this is not **GOTT**; since we know through faith that **GOTT** is infinitely greater and quite different from what we feel. When the soul acts thus, a strange conflict used to take place between **GOTT** and the soul: while **GOTT** is always giving, the soul is always saying that what she receives is not **GOTT**. In this conflict, the soul, through faith, was just as strong and even stronger than **GOTT**, because He could never give so much that she could not say that what He gave her was not He Himself.

The <term>ecstasies</term> <note>original: 'Entzückungen'—referring to mystical states of rapture or trance.</note> only come about because a soul lingers with the gift instead of rejecting it and going to **GOTT** beyond His gifts. One must also not allow oneself to be overcome by these, unless one is unexpectedly overwhelmed by them; yet **GOTT** is Lord and Master over all.

**GOTT** rewards everything done out of love for Him with such compliance and with such overflowing charity that he [Brother Lawrence] had sometimes wished he could hide something he did out of love for **GOTT** from Him, so that it might not be rewarded, and he would thus have the pleasure of doing something purely for **GOTT**'s sake.

He had experienced great <term>anguish of soul</term> <note>original: 'Gemüts-Angst'—a state of intense spiritual distress or "dark night of the soul."</note>, firmly believing he was damned; so much so that no one could take this opinion from him; but he had reached the following conclusion regarding it:

I entered the spiritual life only out of love for **GOTT**; I have strived to do everything only for His sake; whether I be saved or damned, I will always continue to do everything purely out of love for **GOTT**; at the very least, I will have this benefit: that I

...until my end, I would do everything within my power to love Him. This anxiety had lasted four years for him, during which he endured much.

Since that time, he had thought of neither heaven nor hell; and his whole life was nothing else but an unbound freedom and a perpetual delight; he placed his sins between himself and **GOTT** <note>original: "GOtt"</note>, to tell Him, as it were, that he was not worthy of His graces; but despite this, **GOTT** did not cease to overwhelm him with them. Sometimes He would take him by the hand and lead him before the entire heavenly host to show them the poor wretch on whom He took pleasure in bestowing His graces.

In the beginning, it costs a little labor to acquire the firm habit of constantly <term>conversing with God</term> <note>The German "umzugehen" implies a social interaction or keeping company with someone.</note> and directing everything one does toward Him; but after a little labor, one would feel oneself awakened to it by His love without any effort.

He did indeed expect that after the good days **GOTT** gave him, his turn would also come where he would have his share of the <term>Cross and Suffering</term> <note>A common Pietist and mystical reference to internal or external trials that mirror Christ's Passion.</note>; but he was unconcerned about this, knowing well that because he could do nothing of himself, **GOTT** would not fail then to give him the strength to endure it.

Whenever a virtue happened to be practiced, he turned to **GOTT**, saying: **My GOTT, I cannot do this, unless You work it in and through me;** and then immediately strength would be given to him, and indeed in abundance.

When he had failed, he did nothing else but confess his guilt before **GOTT** and say: **HErr <note>Lord</note>, I shall never do otherwise as long as You leave me to my own doing; it is Your work to ensure that I do not fall, and to better what is not good in me;** and thereafter he troubled himself no further about his failure.

One must deal quite simply with **GOTT** and speak to Him freely and openly, and as matters occurred, desire His assistance; **GOTT** would deny this to no one, as he had often experienced.

A few days ago, he was told he should travel to Burgundy and purchase the necessary wine there, which was very burdensome to him, because he was not only ill-suited for such tasks but also lame in one leg, so that he could not walk on the ship, but had to crawl over the wine barrels. He was, however, unconcerned about this, as well as about his entire purchase, and said to **GOTT**: It was His work; then he found that the matter was already done, and indeed done well. Last year he had been sent to Auvergne for the same reason, and he could not say how the matter was accomplished then; it had not been he who accomplished it, yet it had been found to have been done quite well.

### Part Nine. The Life

So it also happened in his kitchen, for which he by nature had the greatest aversion; but after he had accustomed himself to perform everything there out of love for **GOD** <note>original: "GOtt"</note>, and by looking to His <term>assistance of grace</term> <note>original: "Gnadenbeistand," referring to divine help given to complete a task.</note> on every occasion for the performance of his work, everything had become quite easy for him over the 14 years he had been employed there.

His current work was the mending of shoes or soles, which he did with great pleasure; yet he was ready to leave this work as well as any other, since he did nothing else anywhere but rejoice that he might do some small things out of love for **GOD**.

For him, there was no difference between the time of prayer and any other time; he did indeed keep his <term>seclusions</term> <note>Periods of private spiritual retreat.</note> when the <term>Father Prior</term> <note>The deputy head of the monastery.</note> told him that he should do so; but otherwise he did not desire it, nor did he seek it, because his greatest labor in no way drew him away from **GOD**.

Because he knew well that he must love **GOD** in all things, and labored toward the goal of properly fulfilling this duty, he had no need for a <term>spiritual director</term> <note>A mentor who provides guidance on the inner life.</note>; but he did indeed need a <term>confessor</term> <note>original: "Beichtvater," a priest who hears confession and grants absolution.</note> to absolve him of the faults he committed. He saw his failings quite well and was not surprised by them; rather, he confessed them before **GOD** and in no way sought to defend himself against Him or to excuse his mistakes; but when this was done, he returned in peace again to his usual exercise of love and adoration.

In his sufferings, he asked no one for advice; but merely with the light of faith, through which he knew that **GOD** was present, he let it be enough for him that he did his work for and before **GOD**, regardless of how things might go otherwise; and in this way, he wished to lose himself for the sake of the love of **GOD**, wherein he found himself well.

[Unnecessary] thoughts ruin everything: and this is the beginning of evil. But we must take care to reject them as soon as we become aware that they are of things unnecessary to our current occupation or to our salvation, and thus return to our <term>conversation with GOD</term> <note>Brother Lawrence's signature practice of constant internal dialogue with the Divine.</note>, wherein we find ourselves well.

In the beginning, he had often spent his entire prayer casting off the thoughts that occurred to him, only to fall back into them again.

He could never perform his prayer according to a prescribed rule, like others; yet in the beginning, he had practiced <term>meditation</term> <note>The German "Betrachtung" suggests a structured, intellectual reflection on scripture or religious themes.</note> for a time. Since then, however, he did not know how it went with him, and it would be impossible for him to give an account of it.

He had asked that he might always be left in the <term>state of a novice</term> <note>original: "Novitien-Stand," the introductory period of testing before a monk takes permanent vows.</note>, because he believed they would not want to admit him to <term>profession</term> <note>original: "Profession," the formal act of taking permanent religious vows.</note>; he also could not have imagined that his two years of probation had passed.

->**Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection. Chapter VII.**<-

He would not be bold enough to ask **God** <note>original: "GOtt"</note> to send him something for <term>penance</term> <note>original: "Pönitenz," refers to voluntary self-punishment as an outward expression of repentance.</note> or atonement; indeed, he did not even desire to perform any [self-chosen] penances. He knew very well, however, that he deserved to do much penance; also, if **God** were to burden him with it, He would give him the grace to carry everything out with patience.

All bodily austerities and all other exercises served only to help us come to union with **God** through love; therefore, after mature consideration, he found that it was an even shorter way to go straight toward this union through a ceaseless practice of love—namely, by doing everything solely out of love for **God**.

One must make a great distinction between the workings of the intellect and the workings of the will; the former count for little, but the latter for everything. Our entire work should only be that we might love **God** and delight ourselves in Him.

If we were to perform every possible work of penance, and these were separated from love, not a single sin would be erased by them. One must expect the forgiveness of sins through the blood of **Jesus Christ**, without making oneself restless; in the meantime, one should simply work toward loving Him with all one’s heart. It seems as if **God** chooses those who have been the greatest sinners to share His greatest graces more than others who remained in their innocence, because His goodness is made more manifest thereby.

He thought neither of death nor of his sins, neither of heaven nor hell; but only of how he might do one thing or another, however small, out of love for **God**, since he was not capable of doing anything great. Afterward, things might go with him as the **Lord** willed; regarding that, he was unconcerned.

He had endured so much in an internal <term>anguish of the soul</term> <note>original: "Seelenangst," a common 17th-century term for intense spiritual crisis or the "dark night of the soul."</note> that if one were to peel the skin off him while alive, such a thing would be counted as nothing in comparison—just as it was nothing compared to the great joy he had experienced and often still had. Thus, he troubled himself about nothing and feared nothing; all that he desired from **God** was this one thing: that he might not sin against Him.

He told me he very rarely had any <term>scruples</term> <note>original: "Scrupulen," a religious term for excessive guilt or obsessive worry that one has committed a sin where none exists.</note>; for, he said: "When I recognize that I have failed, I gladly admit it and say: 'This is nothing new for me; I can do nothing else but sin.' If, however, I have not failed, I thank **God** for it and confess that such a thing comes from Him."

### III. Conversation. November 22, 1666.

4. He told me: The first foundation of the spiritual life in him had been a high concept and esteem of **God** in faith. Once he had firmly grasped this, he had no other concern in the beginning but to faithfully reject all other thoughts, in order to do everything he did out of love for **God**...

### Ninth Section. The Life

Through our trust in **God**, He is greatly honored, and we obtain much grace through it.

It is impossible, not only that **God** should deceive, but also that He would for a long time allow a soul to suffer that is entirely surrendered to Him and determined to suffer everything for His sake.

He had reached the point where he had no thoughts other than of **God**; and when another thought or a <term>temptation</term> <note>original: "Versuchung"</note> tried to arise within him, he would soon notice its arrival. Because he was assured of **God's** immediate help through his own experience, he sometimes let them arrive until he knew it was time: then he turned to **God**, whereupon they immediately vanished.

Thus, from this same experience, when he had an external task to perform, he was not accustomed to reflecting on the matter beforehand. Instead, at the specific or necessary time for the task itself, he found in **God**, as in a clear mirror, everything that was necessary for him to do at that time. And indeed, for some time now, he had performed his duties in this way without prior reflection; however, before this experience of **God's** immediate assistance, he had used his own prudence in such matters.

He had no memory at all of the things he did; even at the time he performed them, he was hardly aware of them. When he rose from the table, he did not know what he had eaten; instead, remaining in the <term>simplicity of his vision</term> <note>original: "Einfältigkeit seines Gesichts," referring to a single-minded spiritual focus or "gaze" upon the divine.</note> (or turning toward Him), he performed everything out of love for **God**, thanked Him that He had ordered his works for him, and conversed with Him in countless other ways; yet all very simply, and in such a way that he was held firm and unmoved in the loving **Presence of God**.

When his external duties drew him away a little from the remembrance of **God**, a reminder was given to him from **God's** side which entirely occupied and permeated his soul. This awakened a far more powerful remembrance of **God** in him, by which he was sometimes so ignited and set on fire that he had to cry out loud and felt very violent movements in himself to sing and leap, like one who is not master of his senses.

He was much more closely united with **God** in his ordinary work than when he left it to set himself apart specifically for prayer; furthermore, he was usually in great <term>spiritual dryness</term> <note>original: "Dürre," a term used in mystical theology to describe a period where a person feels a lack of emotional or sensory satisfaction in their spiritual life.</note> when he came from such separation.

He believed that great suffering of the body or the mind lay ahead for him in the future; and his greatest misfortune would be to lose **God**, whom he had possessed for so long,

painfully to lose. But **God** gave him the assurance that He would not leave him entirely, and would give him strength to endure the evil that He would permit to befall him. This meant that he feared nothing, nor did he feel the need to discuss the state of his soul with anyone. If he had wished to do so, he would only have fallen into greater restlessness; and because he was willing to die and be lost out of love for **God**, he had no fear; complete abandonment to **God** was the certain way, and in that path there is never a lack of light to show how one should conduct oneself.

In the beginning, one must work faithfully and faithfully deny oneself, but afterward, nothing follows but pure, unspeakable pleasure. In times of need and difficulty, one must only run to <term>Jesus Christ</term> <note>original: "Christo JEsu"</note> and appeal to Him for His <term>grace</term>, with which grace everything becomes easy.

Many people occupy themselves with <term>works of penance</term> <note>original: "Bußwerken"</note> and special exercises, and yet neglect love, which is the ultimate goal; this is plain enough to see from their works, and it is the reason why one finds so little true virtue. To come to **God**, one has need of neither <term>cleverness</term> <note>original: "Klugheit"</note> nor <term>formal learning</term> <note>original: "Wissenschaft"; in this context, it refers to academic or theological scholarship</note>, but only a heart that is determined to concern itself with nothing but Him, and to act out of love for Him, and to love nothing except Him.

### IV. Conversation. November 25, 1667.

5. Brother Lawrence spoke to me with much zeal and sincerity about his way to **God**, of which I have already noted several points.

He told me that everything consisted in our renouncing, once and for all, everything that we recognize as not being directed toward **God**, and thus habituating ourselves to a constant conversation with Him, without any other mystery or subtle cleverness. We have nothing else to do but to recognize that **God** is present within our <term>innermost being</term> <note>original: "Inwendigsten"</note> and to speak to Him every moment, seeking His assistance so that we may recognize His will in doubtful matters and properly perform that which we clearly see to be His will; we should also offer all such things to Him before we perform them, and afterward thank Him that we have performed them for His sake.

In this constant conversation with **God**, one is simultaneously occupied in praising, loving, and worshiping **God** without ceasing, because of His infinite goodness and all His perfections.

We must implore Him for His grace with all confidence, without looking at our sins, relying instead on the infinite merits of our <term>Savior</term> <note>original: "Seligmacher"; literally "one who makes blessed"</note>. **God** does not cease to offer us His grace in every undertaking; Lawrence perceived this very clearly; and therefore he never failed, except when he distanced himself from the company of **God**, or when he forgot to call upon Him for His assistance.
