### Ninth Part. The Life of Brother Lawrence etc. Chapter VII. ###

In doubt and uncertainty, **God** never denies His light to those who seek nothing else but to please Him and to do all things for the sake of His love.

Our <term>sanctification</term> <note>original: "Heiligung"; refers to the process of being made holy</note> does not consist in changing our works, but rather in doing for **God** what we commonly do for ourselves.

It is to be regretted that so many people bind themselves to certain works, which they perform with much imperfection due to various human motivations, and thus they always mistake the means for the end.

He found no more excellent means to reach **God** than his ordinary tasks, to which obedience bound him, by purifying them as much as possible from all human intentions and performing them out of love for **God**.

One is greatly deceived if one thinks that the time of prayer must be distinct from the rest of the time; we are no less bound to be united with **God** during the time of work through our labor than during the time of prayer through prayer.

His prayer was now nothing other than the <term>presence of God</term> <note>original: "GOttes Gegenwart"</note>, wherein his soul was as if in sleep with regard to all other things, except for love; but even outside such times, he found little difference in himself, as he constantly kept himself with **God**, to laud and praise Him to the best of his ability, and thus he spent his life in unceasing joy; nevertheless, he hoped that **God** would give him something to suffer when he grew stronger.

One must once and for all truly entrust oneself to **God** and abandon oneself entirely to Him alone; He will not deceive us.

One must not grow weary nor cease doing even small things out of love for **God**, who does not look at the size of the work, but at the love; nor should one be surprised that in the beginning one often falls short in this regard; eventually, one attains the habit or steadfastness; then we would perform our <term>acts</term> <gloss>or turning toward God</gloss> <note>original: "Acten [oder Zukehr zu GOtt]"</note> as if by themselves, without thinking of it, and indeed with extraordinary pleasure.

We need only seek to maintain faith, hope, and love within us, in order to cling solely and exclusively to the will of **God**; everything else is immaterial and should only be like a bridge, so that we hurry across with all speed to immerse and lose ourselves in the only end, which is **God**, through trust and love. (a)

# Chapter Eight.

## On his Writings, his Reading, and his Virtues, among which Faith Shines Forth.

->I.<-

Just as his conversations were edifying, his writings were no less so; he wrote such sublime and heart-stirring things, both regarding the glory of **God** and the inexpressible communications of His love within souls, that those who caught sight of a few fragmented pages of his writings (which he let out of his hands only reluctantly and on the condition that they be returned as soon as possible) became quite enamored with them and were so edified that they never spoke of them except with admiration. And certainly, if one is to judge everything else he wrote from the little that remains of his letters and <term>fundamental rules</term> <note>original: "Grund-Regeln"; likely referring to the Spiritual Maxims often associated with Brother Lawrence</note>, one has reason to believe (as he himself is said to have confessed to one of his intimate friends) that his small works were, strictly speaking, nothing but outpourings of the **Holy Spirit** and brought forth from his love. Nevertheless, when he compared what he had written with what he desired to experience internally, it all seemed so insignificant to him, and so far removed from the high thoughts and experiences he had of the glory and goodness of **God**, that he would sometimes tear it up again immediately, as it had been written only to give his inner fullness some release and relief.

2. He did not read very much, and what he did read had to concern his one and only subject: the <term>presence of God</term> <note>original: "Gegenwart GOttes"; the central theme of Lawrence's spirituality</note>. In the little reading that he did, however, he preferred the **Gospel** over all other books, because he found therein that which could nourish his faith in the simplest and purest way through the very words of **Jesus Christ**.

3. Brother Lawrence’s virtue did not make him morose; he had an open manner which inspired confidence and let one feel from the very beginning that one could reveal everything to him and that one had found a friend. For his part, when he knew the person with whom he was dealing, he spoke with freedom and showed great kindness. What he said was simple, but always just and full of understanding. Through a rough exterior, one discovered a singular wisdom—a freedom that exceeded the common capacity of a poor <term>Carmelite lay brother</term> <note>original: "Carmeliter Leyen-Bruder"; a member of the order who focused on manual labor rather than clerical duties</note>, and an intellect that surpassed everything one might have suspected. While he was asking for alms, he showed a mind that was capable of managing the greatest affairs and which could be consulted on any matter. This was what was apparent from the outward appearance of Brother Lawrence.

Among the virtues which shone forth most in Brother Lawrence, one of the most prominent was his **faith**; just as the righteous man lives by this chief virtue, so it was also the life and nourishment of his spirit. It gave his soul such growth that he visibly made great progress in the internal life. This beautiful virtue was what made him trample the whole world under his feet and made it so contemptible in his eyes that he considered it completely unworthy to take up the smallest place in his heart. It was faith that led him to **God** and raised him above all created things, and made him seek his happiness solely in being able to possess Him alone. Faith was his great master-teacher, who alone taught him more than all books combined.

# Chapter Nine.

## His constant faithfulness in practicing the presence of **God**, and in performing everything out of love for Him, from which all his other virtues sprang.

->I.<-

Through the faithfulness of maintaining this sublime presence of **God** in his heart, contemplated through faith, Brother Lawrence began: he occupied himself with constant acts of worship, love, and invocation for the assistance of the **Lord** in whatever he had to do; he thanked Him after he had performed it; he asked His forgiveness for his negligences, which he confessed—as he said—without arguing with **God**; and as these internal acts were tied to his tasks in such a way, and the tasks gave him occasion for them, he performed them with all the more ease; and far from these acts drawing him away from his work, they rather helped him to perform it well. He admits, however, that in the beginning he found it difficult; that a noticeable amount of time would pass without him remembering his practice; but that after he humbly recognized his failure, he took it up again without agitation.

Among the virtues that shone most brightly in Brother Lawrence, faith was one of the most prominent; just as the righteous man lives by this principal virtue, so too was it the life and nourishment of his spirit. It gave his soul such growth that he visibly made great progress in the **interior life** <note>The "interior life" refers to the private, spiritual relationship and ongoing conversation between a soul and God, emphasizing internal prayer over external ritual.</note>. 5. His various and manifold acts were transformed into a simple attention, an enlightened love, and an enjoyment without interruption. “The time of action (he said) is not distinct from the time of prayer; I possess **God** as peacefully in the busy business of my kitchen, (where sometimes many persons demand different things from me at once) as when I lie on my knees before the altar. My faith itself becomes at times so enlightened that I believe I have lost it; it seems to me the curtain of darkness is drawn aside, and the day of that life, which is without end or clouds, begins to appear.” To this state our good Brother had been brought by the faithfulness he had in rejecting all other thoughts, so that he might devote himself to constant communion with **God**; and he had made this so habitual to himself that he said it was as if impossible for him to turn away from it and occupy himself with other things.

3. You will have found an important observation in his conversations regarding this, where he said: That this presence of **God** should be maintained much more through the heart and love than through the intellect and reflection. In the way of **God**, he said, thoughts are counted for little; love does everything.

And it is not necessary, he continues, to have great things to perform. [I am depicting for you a **Lay-Brother** <note>A member of a religious order who is not ordained as a priest and typically performs manual labor and secular duties within the monastery.</note> in his kitchen; permit me to use his own words]. I turn my little pancake in the pan out of love for **God**; when it is finished, and I have nothing else to perform, I cast myself upon the ground and worship my **God**, from whom the grace to make it has come; after which I rise up again more satisfied than a king. When I can do nothing else, it is enough for me to have picked up a straw from the ground out of love for **God**.

People seek ways and methods (he adds) to learn how one should love **God**; they wish to attain it through I know not how many different exercises; they take great pains to remain in the presence of **God** through a multitude of means; is it not much shorter and more direct to do everything out of love for **God**, to make use of all the works of one's station to demonstrate it to Him, and to maintain His presence within us through the communion of our heart with Him? Here no subtle trick <note>original: "subtiler Grif" — a clever technique or specialized method</note> is necessary; one need only go forward boldly and simply. I preserve his usual expressions with particular care.

4. Meanwhile, one must not think that, in order to love **God**, it is enough to sacrifice one's works to Him, to call upon His assistance, and to produce works of His love; our Brother reached the perfection of love in no other way than because from the beginning he was very attentive to doing nothing that could displease **God**, because he renounced everything else besides Him, and [surrendered] himself completely...

He advocates for a simple, heart-centered approach to God's presence rather than complex intellectual exercises.</summary>

<page-num>201</page-num>
<header>Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection. Chapter IX.</header>

...had completely forgotten. From the time of my entry into the monastery (these are his words) I no longer think of virtue, nor of my salvation. Since I have given myself entirely to **God**, and out of love for Him have renounced everything that He is not; I have believed that for the remainder of my days I had nothing else to do but to live as if there were nothing more in the world but **God** and I.

Thus Brother Lawrence began through that which was most perfect, by leaving everything for **God’s** sake and doing everything out of love for Him. He had completely forgotten himself; he no longer thought of Paradise, nor of Hell, nor of his committed sins, nor of those he might commit after he had prayed to **God** for their forgiveness. He did not think again on what he had confessed. He entered into a perfect peace once he had made his faults known to **God**; and he knew nothing else to do, after which he surrendered himself to **God**, as he said, for life and for death, in time and eternity.

We are made for **God’s** sake alone; He cannot take it ill that we leave ourselves to occupy ourselves with Him. We shall see better in Him what we lack than we could ever notice in ourselves through all our own reflection; and it <note>Brother Lawrence suggests that excessive self-scrutiny is actually a form of hidden pride or "self-love."</note> can be nothing else but a remnant of self-love which, under the appearance of our perfection, still binds us to ourselves and hinders us from rising to **God**. The Brother said that during those great sufferings which he endured for four years—which were so great that no one in the world could ever have removed the conviction from his mind that he would be damned—he nevertheless had not changed his first resolution. Instead, without reflecting on what might happen to him, and without occupying himself with his pain (as all suffering souls tend to do), he had comforted himself, saying: "Whatever may happen to me, I will at least do all my works during the remaining time of my life out of love for **God**." And thus forgetting himself, he was willing to lose himself for **God’s** sake, in which he found himself well.

5. The love of the **Divine Will** <term>Divine Will: The theological concept that everything that happens is either ordained or permitted by God for a greater purpose.</term> had taken the place of the attachment one usually has for one's own will; he saw in everything that happened to him only the command of **God**, which kept him in a constant peace. When he was told of some great disorder, instead of being shocked by it, he wondered on the contrary that there were not even more of them, considering the malice of which a sinner is capable. But he immediately raised himself to **God**, seeing that He could change such things, yet allowed these evils for reasons that were very just and useful to the general order of His government over the world; and after he had prayed for the sinners, he troubled himself no further and remained in his peace.

<margin>(a) This was the famous Archbishop of Cambrai, *Salignac de la Motte Fénelon*.</margin>
A man of very great dignity, (a) when he visited Brother Lawrence during a great illness, asked him what he would choose if God offered him: either to let him remain in life for some time longer so that his virtues might be increased, or to take him into heaven from this moment on. The good brother answered without hesitating: That he would leave this choice to God and that he had nothing else to do for himself but to wait in peace until God showed him His will.

6. This state of mind left him in such a great indifference toward all things and in such a total freedom that it approached that of the blessed <note>meaning the saints in heaven</note>. He belonged to no faction: one could discover in him no personal preference or <term>inclination<note>original: *Inclination*; a technical term in 17th-century spirituality referring to a natural leaning or bias toward specific people, places, or outcomes.</note></term>.

7. The natural attachment to one’s homeland, which people often keep even in the holiest of places, had no hold over him: he was loved equally by those who had completely different leanings than his own. He desired good in general, without regard for the specific persons through whom or for whom it was done. He was a citizen of heaven; nothing on earth held him back. His intentions were not limited by time; and since he had for a long time contemplated only the Eternal God, he had become eternal just like Him.

8. Everything was the same to him: every place and every task. The good brother found God everywhere, just as much while he was making shoe soles as when he prayed with the community. He had no urgent desire for special seclusion because he found the same God to love and worship in his ordinary work as in the deepest desert.

9. Because his only means of going to God was to do everything out of love for Him, it was all the same to him to be busy with this or that matter, as long as he performed it for God’s sake; he looked to God and not to the task itself. He knew that the more a task went against his natural preference, the more virtuous was the love that led him to offer it to God; that the smallness of the matter did not diminish the value of his sacrifice in the least, because God, who needs nothing, looks at nothing in our works other than the love with which they are accompanied.

10. Another quality of Brother Lawrence was an unusual firmness, which in another way of life might be called intrepidity, and which showed a great and noble mind elevated above the fear or hope of anything that was not God. He marveled at nothing, nothing startled him, and he feared nothing. This firmness of soul came from the same source in him as...

...all other virtues flowed. The high <term>concept<note>original: *Idée*; referring here to a foundational spiritual understanding or mental image of God’s character.</note></term> which he had of God presented Him to him as He truly is: as the highest equity and infinite goodness. Grounded in this, he was certain that God would not deceive him and would do nothing to him but good, because he, for his part, was determined never to displease Him, but rather to do and suffer everything for the sake of His love.

11. I asked him once who his guide was? He answered me: He had none, and did not believe he needed one. Because the rules and duties he had in the Order showed him what he had to do regarding external matters; and the Gospel showed him the duty to love God with his whole heart. Since he recognized this, a guide seemed useless to him; however, he had the greatest need for a confessor to absolve him of his sins.

# Chapter Ten.
## Of his Hope and Trust, as well as his Pure Love for God.

1. From this living faith was born the firmness of his hope in the goodness of God; a childlike trust in His providence; and a complete and total abandonment of himself into His hands, such that he no longer concerned himself with what might happen to him after his death. Regarding his <term>blessedness<note>original: *Seeligkeit*; refers to the state of eternal salvation and the soul's peace in the afterlife.</note></term>, he did not only rest upon the power of grace and the merits of Jesus Christ; rather, he finally forgot himself and all his own advantage, and threw himself as if lost, with closed eyes, into the arms of God's infinite mercy. The more desperate a matter appeared, the more he hoped; indeed, he even hoped, as the Scripture says, *against hope* <note>A reference to Romans 4:18, regarding the faith of Abraham who believed even when circumstances seemed impossible.</note>; therefore, he said that the greatest honor one could give to God consisted in completely despairing of one's own strengths and entrusting oneself perfectly to His protection. For by this, one both sincerely admits one's own weakness and confesses the omnipotence of the Creator in all truth.

2. And to such trust and abandonment to God and His providence, he also sought to awaken other souls, as the following short letter to a witness can serve as proof:

# Ninth Part. The Life.

„...the compassion which I have for your sufferings is sweetened by this: that I am convinced they are trials of the love which **God** bears for you; view them in such a light, and they will be easy for you to bear. My opinion is that you should let go of all human medicines and abandon yourself entirely to Divine Providence; perhaps **God** is waiting for nothing else but this surrender and perfect confidence in Him to make you healthy. Since the remedies, despite all your precautions, do not have the effect they ought to have, and since, on the contrary, the illness increases, then it is no longer a matter of 'tempting **God**' <note>To "tempt God" in this context refers to the theological concern of neglecting practical means (like medicine) and expecting a miracle; Lawrence argues that once medicine fails, total reliance on God is the only remaining pious path.</note> to leave yourself in His hands and expect everything from Him.

„I have already told you in my latest letter that He sometimes permits the body to suffer so that He may heal the diseases of our souls. Take courage; make a virtue out of necessity; ask **God** not for deliverance from the pains of the body, but for the strength to suffer courageously for the sake of His love, everything that He shall will, and for as long as it shall please Him.

„These prayers are truly somewhat hard for <term>nature<note>original: *Natur*; refers to "human nature" or the physical/egoic self, which instinctively recoils from pain.</note></term>, but to **God** they are very pleasing, and to those who love Him, they are sweet. Love sweetens pain, and when one loves **God**, one suffers for His sake with joy and courage. Do this, I beg of you; comfort yourself with Him who is the sole and only <term>healing remedy<note>original: *Geneß-Mittel*; an archaic term for a medicine or means of recovery.</note></term> for your illnesses. He is the Father of the suffering and always ready to assist us. He loves us infinitely more than we can imagine. Love Him then, and seek no other refreshment than in Him. I hope you will soon attain it; I commend you to **God**. I will help you with my prayer, as poor as it may be, and remain always in our **Lord**.

->Yours, etc.<-

3. Just as love is the queen and, as it were, the soul of all virtues, and imparts to them their proper weight and power, so one must not wonder that the virtues of Brother Lawrence were so perfect, since the love of **God** ruled so completely in his heart that—as <term>Bernardus<note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot and mystic known for his writings on the degrees of loving God.</note></term> says—he had turned all the inclinations of his love toward this Divine <term>object<note>original: *Vorwurf*; in 18th-century German, this often meant the "object" or "subject matter" of one's attention rather than a "reproach."</note></term>. While faith allowed him to recognize his **God** as the highest truth, and hope presented Him as his only goal and highest <term>blessedness<note>original: *Seeligkeit*; the state of eternal happiness in God.</note></term>, love revealed Him to him as the most perfect Being—or, to speak even better, as perfection itself.

He kept far from himself the idea of loving **God** only with a view toward himself; indeed, his love was so entirely without self-interested motives that he would have loved **God** even if there had been no punishment to fear nor reward to expect. This was because he sought nothing but the well-being and honor of **God**, and made his "heaven" out of being able to fulfill His holy will. This will be seen at the end, during his final illness, where he kept his mind so healthy and free until his last breath that he was able to explain the thoughts of his heart just as if he had been in perfect health.

# Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection. Chapter 10.

4. The purity of his love was so great that he wished, if it were possible, that **God** would not even be aware of all the works he performed in His service, so that he might have done them solely and alone for His honor and without any benefit for himself. Meanwhile, he often made a loving complaint, saying to his friends that **God** did not allow a single good work to happen without immediately rewarding it a hundredfold; for He often gave him such sensations and tastes <note>The German *Geschmack* (taste/savor) refers to "spiritual sweetness," a common mystical term for the emotional joy felt during prayer.</note> of His Divinity that he was at times, as it were, overloaded by them. Therefore, he said to **God** with reverence and in his usual intimacy:

> **Lord**, it is too much! It is too much for me; rather give such grace and comfort, if it pleases You, to sinners and to those who do not know You, in order to draw them into Your service. As for me, who has the happiness of knowing You through faith, it seems to me that this should be enough for me. But because I must not refuse such a rich and generous hand as Yours, I accept, **O my God!** such grace as You offer me; may it please You that, after I have received it from You, I give it back to you just as You have given it to me. For You well know that I do not desire Your gifts, but You Yourself, and that I can be satisfied with nothing less.

5. This purity of love and this renunciation of self-interest served only to cause his heart to be ignited more and more, and the flame of this **Divine Fire** to be increased, so that at times some sparks broke out externally. For although he used every effort to hide the intensity of the **Divine Love** that burned within him, it was not always in his power to halt its outbursts; thus, he was often seen, against his will, with a flaming face. But when he was alone, he let his fire break out in full flame and cried to **God**:

> **Lord**, give the powers of my soul more room and opening, so that I may also give more place to Your love; or at least support me by Your almighty strength, otherwise I might be consumed by the flames of Your love!

6. In the conversations he held with his brothers, he often said to the **Lord**, with regret for the lost time of his youth:

> **O Goodness**, who art both ancient and new! <note>original: *O Gütigkeit, die Du beydes alt und neu bist!* This is a direct reference to St. Augustine’s famous prayer in his *Confessions*: "Late have I loved You, O Beauty ever ancient, ever new."</note> How late I have begun to love You! Alas, my brothers! Do not do the same; you are still young, make use of this sincere confession of mine, which I have made regarding my former coldness in the service of **God**; sanctify all your years to His love. As for me, if I had known Him sooner, and if someone had told me what I am telling you now, I certainly would not have delayed so long in loving Him. Believe me, all that time is to be considered lost which is not spent in the love of **God**.

Ninth Part. The Life

## The Eleventh Chapter.
### Concerning his love for his neighbor, whom he was diligent to serve in body and soul.

->I.<-

Since the love of **God** and the love of neighbor are so closely joined together, one may judge the love Brother Lawrence had for his neighbor by the love he bore toward **God**. He was fully convinced of what our **Savior** says in the **Gospel**, that the slightest service done for the least of his brothers is regarded by Him as if it had been done for Himself <note>original: "Evangelio"; a reference to Matthew 25:40: "Truly I tell you, whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me."</note>; for this reason, he took extraordinary care to see how he might serve them in all the offices he held. This was especially evident when he oversaw the kitchens, where he faithfully provided for everything necessary for the brothers' sustenance. He took great delight in satisfying them according to their humble station, as if they were angels.

2. He helped the poor in their necessity to the best of his ability. He comforted them in their tribulations and assisted them with counsel, while at the same time encouraging them to seek the Heavenly when they were troubled by the Earthly. In short, he did all the good he could for his neighbor and never any ill to anyone. He became "all things to all people" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 9:22: "I have become all things to all people so that by all possible means I might save some."</note> so that he might win them all for **God**.

3. Then, just as the soul of the neighbor is infinitely higher in dignity than the body, Brother Lawrence likewise sought to prove his love toward the soul in particular—through earnest admonitions where necessary, and through comfort and strengthening where circumstances required it. Most especially, however, he did this through the most loving representations and encouragements toward an inner walk in the **Presence of God**, so that they all might share with him the bliss of this inward life. To prove what we say here, let us include a few more of his short letters written to various persons in different circumstances:

# The Eleventh Chapter.
### Of his love for his neighbor, whom he was diligent to serve in body and soul.

->I.<-

Just as the love of **God** and the love of neighbor are closely joined together, so one may judge the love that Brother Lawrence had for his neighbor by the love he held for **God**. He was fully convinced of what our Savior says in the Gospel: <note>original: "Evangelio"</note> that the least service done for the smallest of his brothers is regarded by Him as if it were done for Himself; <note>A reference to Matthew 25:40.</note> therefore, he took extraordinary care to see how he might serve them in all the offices he held. This was especially evident while he oversaw the kitchen, where he faithfully provided for everything necessary for the brothers' sustenance and took delight in pleasing them according to their humble station, as if they were angels.

2. He helped the poor in their necessity to the best of his ability. He comforted them in their tribulations and assisted them with counsel, while simultaneously urging them to seek the heavenly when they were worried about the earthly. In short, he did all the good he could for his neighbor and no evil to anyone. He became all things to all men, so that he might win them all for **God**. <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 9:22.</note>

3. Furthermore, just as the soul of the neighbor is infinitely higher in dignity than the body, Brother Lawrence sought especially to prove his love toward the soul through earnest admonitions where necessary; through comfort and strengthening where circumstances required; and especially through the most loving representations and encouragements toward an inward walking in the **presence of God**, so that they might all become partakers with him in the blessedness of this interior life. # Ninth Piece. The Life

### V.

### My Venerable and highly honored Mother!

8. "I do not ask **God** for the removal of your pains, but I pray to Him earnestly that He may give you strength and patience to suffer them for as long as it shall please Him; comfort yourself with Him who holds you fastened to the cross <note>In 17th-century spirituality, "being fastened to the cross" refers to the mystical union of one’s own suffering with the suffering of Jesus.</note>; He will set you free from it when He deems it useful. Blessed are those who suffer with Him; accustom yourself to suffering with Him, and ask Him for the strength to endure all that He wills, and for as long as He shall deem it necessary for you. The world does not comprehend these truths, and I do not wonder at it; this is because they suffer as worldly people and not as Christians. They view illnesses as plagues of nature and not as divine graces, and in this way, they find in them nothing other than what is harsh and contrary to nature. But those who consider them as coming from the hand of **God**, as effects of His mercy and means which He uses for their salvation <note>original: "Seligkeit," referring to both eternal happiness and the state of being saved.</note>, usually taste therein great sweetness <note>original: "Süßigkeiten," a common term in mysticism for the internal emotional or spiritual delights felt during prayer.</note> and sensible comforts.

"I wish you could persuade me that **God** is often much closer to us in times of sickness and weakness than when we enjoy perfect health; seek no other physician but Him; as far as I can grasp, He alone wishes to make you healthy. Set all your confidence in Him; you will soon see the effect of this, which we often delay through a greater trust in medicinal means <note>term: "Arzneymittel" (medicines). Lawrence suggests that while medicine can be used, one's primary faith must remain in the Divine.</note> than in **God**.

"You may use whatever medicines you wish, but they will only work as much as He allows. When pains come from **God**, He alone can heal them. He often lets us use the illnesses of the body to recover from the illnesses of the soul. Comfort yourself with the supreme Physician of souls and of the body.

"I foresee that you will say to me, 'Yes, you have it quite easy, you drink and eat at the **Lord's** table' <note>A reference to Brother Lawrence's role as a lay brother who worked in the kitchen, but also a metaphor for his constant experience of spiritual communion.</note>: you are right; but do you think it is a minor pain to the greatest wrongdoer <note>original: "Missethäter"</note> in the world to eat at the King’s table and be served by His hands, and yet not be certain of his forgiveness? I believe that he would feel a very great suffering because of it, which only confidence in the goodness of his Lord could alleviate; I can also assure you that, however much sweetness I feel in drinking and eating at the table of my King, my present sins as well as the uncertainty of my forgiveness always torment me before my eyes; though the pain is, in truth, pleasant to me.

"Be content with the state in which **God** places you; though you may consider me happy, I nevertheless carry envy toward you. Pains and suffering would be a paradise to me if I suffered with **God**. The greatest..."

## Chapter Twelve.

### His great patience and inner contentment in his illnesses; together with a letter from which his final state of mind can be seen.

-> 1. <-

Just as, according to the statement of Paul <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 13, where the Apostle Paul describes the nature of love (charity).</note>, love is patient, and triumphs over all difficulties, and endures all things for the sake of the one it loves, so we must in no way doubt the patience of Brother Lawrence, since he loved **God** so perfectly. The exercise of these two virtues showed itself particularly in him in the midst of the most sensitive illnesses with which it pleased **God** to visit and test this, His servant. I will not mention here a certain kind of hip pain <note>original: "Hüftschmerzen," likely referring to chronic sciatica.</note> (which caused him to become lame) and with which he was afflicted for approximately twenty-five years, and which later broke out into an ulcer that settled in his leg and caused him very violent pains; rather, I will dwell primarily on those three most severe illnesses which **God** sent to him in the final years of his life, in order to prepare him for death and to make him capable of that reward of grace <note>original: "Gnadenlohn," the spiritual reward given by God's favor rather than human merit.</note> which He had destined for him.

-> 2. <- With the first two occurrences that afflicted him, it almost came to the point

3. During his first illness, he demonstrated how he had some longing for death; in such longing, he also said to the physician (as he felt the power of the fever was somewhat broken): "Oh, my **Lord**! your medicine is working far too well for me; my happiness <note>original: "Glückseligkeit," meaning the supreme bliss of being united with God in the afterlife.</note> is only being delayed by it."

4. In his second illness, it almost seemed as if he had no preference left; he remained in a state of perfect indifference toward living or dying, because he had completely submitted himself to the will of **God**, and according to that will was just as ready to live as to die; he desired nothing but that which the Providence of **God** would ordain.

# Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection. Cap. XII.

5. Regarding his third illness, in which his soul was released from the body to be reunited with her Beloved <note>The soul is traditionally referred to as "she" in mystical literature, often depicted as a bride seeking her "Beloved," which is God.</note> in heaven, I can say that he displayed therein signs of an altogether extraordinary constancy, serenity, and joy. Just as he had long sighed for this blessed moment, he now became truly delighted when he saw that it had finally arrived. The terrifying sight of death, which often strikes even the boldest spirits with the utmost fear, did not make him lose heart at all; rather, he looked it boldly in the eye and, as it were, defied it. For when he once saw the humble deathbed being prepared for him and heard one of his friends say, "It is over for you, Brother Lawrence, you must depart!", he answered: "It is indeed true; see there my deathbed; but one shall soon follow me who thinks very little of it." And that truly came to pass as he had foretold; for although this brother was in perfect health, he became ill the next day and died on the very same day that Brother Lawrence was laid in the earth. On the following Wednesday, he was buried in the very same pit <note>original: "Grube," referring to the communal burial vault or grave used by the monastery.</note>, so that it almost seemed as if the love that had united these two brothers in life would not allow them to be separated in death, especially since at that time there was no other place available than the one used for the common burial.

6. Before we proceed further to speak in particular of his final illness and blessed passing, we wish to conclude this chapter with a precious little letter from this servant of God, which he wrote to a trusted person the evening before his illness and only six days before his departure. From this, one can see something of the state of mind in which he lay down and passed into a happy eternity.

->My good Mother!<- <note>Brother Lawrence is likely writing to a Mother Superior or a spiritual confidante.</note>

> “God knows very well what we need, and everything He does is for our
> “best; if we knew how much He loves us, we would be always ready to
> “receive equally from His hand both the sweet and the bitter, and the most
> “vexing and hardest things would be lovely and pleasant to us. The heaviest
> “sufferings usually seem unbearable only because of the way we look at them.
> “But when we are convinced that it is the hand of God dealing with us; that He
> “is a Father full of love who places us in such states of humiliation, pain, and 
> “suffering, then all bitterness is taken away, and they contain nothing but
> “sweetness.
>
> “Let us occupy ourselves entirely with knowing God; the more one knows Him,
> “the more one desires to know Him. And as the measure of love usually
> “follows the measure of knowledge <note>original: "Erkenntnis," referring to an experiential, spiritual understanding rather than just factual data.</note>; so the more depth and breadth the 
> “knowledge has, the greater the love will be. And when the love is great, 
> “we will love Him equally in suffering and in consolations. Let us not [halt...]

# Ninth Part. The Life

"...to seek or love GOD for the sake of the gifts of grace <term>Gnadengaben: spiritual blessings or favors bestowed by God</term> which He has either granted us—no matter how great they may be—or for those which He may yet grant us. These tokens of favor, as great as they may be, will not bring us as close to Him as faith brings us through a simple act <note>Brother Lawrence refers here to his "practice of the presence of God," a simple, constant turning of the heart toward the Divine.</note>. Let us seek Him often through this virtue. He is in our midst; let us not seek Him elsewhere. Are we not rude and even blameworthy to leave Him alone and occupy ourselves with a thousand trifles <term>Lappereyen: small, insignificant, or idle matters</term> that displease Him and perhaps even offend Him? He tolerates them nonetheless, but it is to be feared that they will one day cost us dearly.

Let us begin to become truly His, and to drive out of our heart and mind everything that He is not; He wishes to be alone. Let us ask this grace from Him. If we do our part as best we can, we will soon see the transformation in ourselves that we hope for. I cannot thank Him enough for the small relief <note>original: "Linderung," referring to a temporary easing of physical pain or spiritual burden.</note> He has given you. I hope, by His mercy, for the grace of seeing Him in a few days. Let us pray for one another. I am in our Lord,

-> Yours, etc. <-

## Chapter Thirteen.

### His constancy and desire for suffering in his last illness: and how he finally fell asleep <note>A traditional Christian euphemism for dying peacefully in the faith.</note> peacefully in GOD, in living faith, firm hope, and fervent love.

-> 1. <-

Fully four or five months beforehand, Brother Lawrence had already told various people that he would die before the end of the month of February. And in his two final letters, which were cited in the previous chapter, he had also prophesied this clearly enough. He concluded the first thus: "Commended to GOD, I hope to see Him very soon." And the other with these words: "I hope, by the mercy of GOD, for the grace of seeing Him in a few days."

-> 2. <-

On the very day that he became bedridden, he told a trusted clergyman that his illness would not last long, but that he would soon depart from this world; he was so certain of the day of his death that on the following day, which was Friday, he spoke even more clearly and told a brother that he would depart the next Monday, which indeed came to pass.

# Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection. Ch. XIII. 215

3. But let us return to the steadfastness <note>original: "Beständigkeit," referring to his unwavering patience and endurance.</note> which he showed in his illness, before we describe the circumstances of his death, along with his thoughts and words which he uttered in these final breaths. The only desire that remained for him was the wish to suffer something more for the love of God, which moved him to repeat what he had often said during his life: namely, that he had only one suffering, which consisted in his having no suffering <note>This reflects a common theme in mystical theology where the soul desires to share in Christ's passion to grow closer to God.</note>; yet he comforted himself with the thought that a purification was still at hand, as he would at least have something to suffer for his sins; he diligently had himself laid on his right side, because he knew that this side caused him the most pain, and so he wished to remain lying there to fulfill his burning desire <term>brünstige Begierde: an intense, ardent, or fervent longing</term> to suffer just a little. A brother who watched over him once wanted to give him a little relief, but he answered him twice:
> I thank you, my dear brother, I pray you, for the love of God, let me suffer a little.

In this painful state he said with burning zeal:
> O my God! I adore You in my weaknesses; so I shall now, O my Lord, suffer something for Your sake. Now then, let me suffer and die with You.

After this he frequently repeated these verses from the 51st Psalm:
> Create in me, O God, a clean heart: cast me not away from Your presence, restore to me the joy of Your help <note>original: "tröste mich wieder mit deiner Hülfe," which translates literally as "comfort me again with your help," corresponding to the spirit of Psalm 51:10-12.</note>, etc.

The pains he suffered from such a difficult bodily position were so cruel (because of a stitch <term>Seitenstechen: a sharp, stabbing pain in the side, possibly indicative of pleurisy</term> that remained in his right side) that he would undoubtedly have died if the nurse <term>Krankenwärter: a brother assigned to care for the sick within the monastery infirmary</term>, arriving just then, had not noticed this and immediately turned him to the other side, giving him relief once again through this change.

4. He had such a desire to suffer that he placed his entire comfort in it. He never once let it be noticed that he had grown weary for a single moment during his entire illness, even when it was at its most intense; rather, his joy in suffering shone forth not only from his face but from his whole manner of speaking. Because of this, the clergymen who visited him were prompted to ask if he truly had nothing to suffer? "Forgive me," he replied: "I do indeed suffer; the stitch in my side causes me pain, but my spirit is content." Whereupon they further said: "But dear brother, if it were God’s will that you should endure these pains for another ten years, would you also be satisfied?" "Yes," he gave as an answer: "not only so many years, but if it pleased God that I should bear these pains until Judgment Day, I would gladly submit myself to it and hope that the Lord would grant me the grace to be content at all times." See now how great the patience of Brother Lawrence was in the beginning and during the course of his illness, which lasted only four days.

5. But as the hour of his departure drew near, his zeal increased more and more. His faith became more vivid, his hope firmer, and his love more burning.

## Ninth Part. The Life
<meta>catchword: with</meta>

From the liveliness of his faith, one can judge by his many words of wonder, through which he testified to the extraordinary esteem he held for this virtue:
> O! faith, faith!
he exclaimed, and thereby expressed its excellence more than if he had spoken much about it. Thus entirely taken by its greatness and enlightened by its light, he worshiped the Lord incessantly, and said: that this adoration had almost become second nature to him. He once said to a brother: He almost no longer believed that God had His throne in his soul, but rather, by means of this bright faith, he already saw something of this inward presence.

6. The firm foundation of his hope proved itself no less: his undaunted courage during this passage—which is naturally full of terror—was so great that he answered one of his friends (who asked him about these matters): That he feared neither death nor hell, neither the judgment of God, nor all the power of the devil; for although he truly saw him <note>Referring to the devil.</note> walking back and forth around his bed, he only mocked him.

As people were fond of hearing such edifying talk from Lawrence, they presented him with more and more questions to answer; among other things, they asked him whether he also knew what a terrible thing it is to fall into the hands of the living God <note>A reference to the biblical verse Hebrews 10:31: "It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God."</note>, because no one is certainly assured whether they were worthy of love or of wrath? I admit it, he said, and I do not desire to know it either, for I would then have to fear that some imagination might interfere. His surrender was so great that he forgot himself and looked only upon God and the fulfillment of His will; so that he said:
> If it were possible that I could love God in hell, and He wanted to place me therein, I would ask nothing further; for He would be with me, and His presence would make a paradise out of hell; I have given myself to Him, He will do with me what pleases Him.

7. Since Lawrence had loved his God so fervently during his life, he loved Him no less in his death. He continued to practice acts of love: and when he was asked by a brother whether he loved God with his whole heart? He answered:
> Oh, if I knew that my heart did not love my God, I would tear it out immediately.
His illness visibly grew worse, so that they gave him the Communion <term>Abendmal: the Lord’s Supper or Holy Communion</term>, which he received joyfully with full consciousness and a sound mind (which he kept until his last breath).

8. Although he was not left alone for a single moment day or night, but was given every possible help that he could hope for from the love of his fellow brothers, they did let him rest a little after he had received the Holy Communion, in order to still make use of these final, highly-esteemed moments of life and to contemplate the high grace he had received from God. He also used this time very profitably and called upon God for steadfastness <note>original: "Beständigkeit"</note> until the end in His holy love. ...if his spirit were occupied with Him? To this he gave the answer: "I am doing now what I shall do for all eternity; I praise God, I laud God, I worship Him, and love Him with all my heart; this is our whole business, my brothers, that we worship God and love Him, without concerning ourselves with the rest."

9. To a clergyman, when he commended himself to Lawrence’s prayers and desired that he might obtain the true spirit of prayer from God for him, Lawrence replied that he must also contribute his own diligence and work on his own part to make himself worthy of it. The following day, Monday, the 12th of February <note>original: "Hornung," an archaic German name for February</note> 1691, at nine o’clock in the morning, Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection died, without a death-struggle, without any distortion or twitching of the limbs, in sound mind, in the embrace of the Savior. He surrendered his soul to his God in such peace and stillness as one who falls asleep. Indeed, his death was nothing other than a sweet slumber, which transported him from this miserable life—in which he had reached approximately eighty years of age—into eternal joy. There, his faith has now been exchanged for and crowned with clear vision, his hope with full possession, and the love he began here with an eternally perfect love.

All things are possible to him who believes, even more so to him who hopes; still more to him who loves; and most of all to him who practices all three of these virtues and remains constant in them.

2. When we devote ourselves to the spiritual life, we must fundamentally consider who we are, and we will find that we are worthy of all contempt and unworthy to bear the name of a Christian; that we are subject to all kinds of misery and countless accidents that plague us and make us unstable in our health, in our temperament, and in our external and internal conditions; in a word, we are such people whom God wishes to humble through countless adversities and <term>crosses<gloss>A common Christian metaphor for burdens, suffering, or trials endured in imitation of Christ.</gloss></term>, both inward and outward.

3. We must without doubt believe it is good for us and pleasing to God that we sacrifice ourselves to Him, and that His Divine Providence usually leads us through all sorts of conditions and paths, and ordains all kinds of pain, misery, and temptation over us for the sake of the love of God for as long as it pleases Him, because without this submission of the heart and mind to the will of God, piety and perfection cannot exist.

4. The more a soul strives for a high perfection, the more it must stand in a constant dependence on grace, and the more it needs God’s assistance every moment, because without Him it can do nothing. The world, nature, and the devil conspire against the soul and contest it so harshly and so incessantly that, without this actual assistance and without this humble and necessary dependence, the soul would be swept away even against its will. This indeed seems hard to nature, but grace finds its pleasure and rest therein.

## Necessary Exercises to Attain the Spiritual Life.

->I.<-

The holiest, most common, and most necessary exercise in the spiritual life is the **Presence of God**; namely, that one finds pleasure in and grows accustomed to His Divine company, speaking to Him humbly and conversing with Him with the heart’s loving affection—at all times, indeed every moment, without rule or measure, especially in times of temptation, adversity, <term>dryness<gloss>A state of spiritual desolation where one feels no emotional or spiritual "warmth" or connection during prayer.</gloss></term>, sorrow, and abandonment, and even in the midst of our unfaithfulness and sins.

2. We must apply ourselves at all times so that all our activities, without distinction, are little conversations with God; yet without artifice, but rather as they come from the purity and simplicity of the heart.

3. We must perform all our works with weight and measure, without turbulence and without haste, which are signs of a distracted mind. We must perform our work with God quietly, calmly, and lovingly, and ask Him that He would be pleased to accept the same. ### or Basic Rules, etc.

<note>original: "fen auf GOTT" - likely "Hoffen" (Hoping) or "Verlassen" (Relying). 4. During our work and other duties, even while reading and writing—even about spiritual things—and what is more, during external devotions and vocal prayers <note>Spoken prayers as opposed to silent, mental prayer.</note>, we must now and then, indeed as often as we can, stop for a tiny moment to adore GOD in the depths of our heart. We should taste Him there, even if only in passing and in a private way, because you know that GOD is present before you during your duties, and that He is in the depths and at the center of your soul. Why then would you not want, at least from time to time, to stand still for a little while during your external duties—and even during your vocal prayers—to adore Him inwardly within yourself, to praise Him, to call upon Him, to offer your heart to Him, and to thank Him?

What can be more pleasing to GOD than if we, thousands upon thousands of times throughout the day, leave all **creatures** <term>created things<gloss>In this context, "creatures" refers to anything created by God (people, objects, distractions) rather than the Creator Himself.</gloss></term> in order to turn into our interior and **withdraw**, adoring Him there? Not to mention that self-love is rooted out by this, because self-love can only survive among **created things**, from which many internal turnings toward GOD gradually, and without our even knowing it, make us loose and free.

In short: we can give GOD no greater testimony of our loyalty than when we renounce and despise **created things** thousands and thousands of times in order to enjoy the Creator for a single moment.

I do not mean to obligate you to always abandon external things, for that cannot be; rather, **Prudence** <note>Often called the "mother of virtues," meaning wise discretion in balancing duties.</note>, as the mother of virtues, must be our rule. Yet I say that it is a common error among spiritual persons that they do not now and then leave the external to adore GOD inwardly within themselves, and there enjoy His Divine presence for a few moments in peace. I see that I have departed quite far from our **subject**, yet it seemed necessary to me to explain the matter fully; let us now return to our exercises.

5. All these adorations must happen in and through faith; namely, that we believe that GOD is truly present in our heart; that He must be adored, loved, and served in spirit and in truth; that He sees everything that happens and will happen in us and in all **created things**; that He depends on nothing, and all **created things** depend on Him; that He is infinite in all His perfections, and because of His infinite majesty and highest sovereignty is worthy of all that we are, and all that is in heaven and on earth, to deal and rule with it according to His pleasure in time and in eternity; so that by right we owe Him all our thoughts, words, and works. Let us then see if we actually give them to Him.

### How one should adore GOD in spirit and in truth.

->This comprises three things which we must point out here.<-

->I.<-

Firstly, to adore GOD in spirit and in truth means to adore GOD as He must be adored by us. GOD is a Spirit; so we must then adore Him in spirit and in truth; that is, through a humble and true adoration of the spirit in the innermost **ground** <term>ground of the soul<gloss>A mystical term referring to the deepest, most essential part of the human spirit where it meets God.</gloss></term> and center of our souls. This adoration can be seen by no one except GOD alone, and we can repeat it often, so that at last it becomes, as it were, natural to us—indeed, even as if GOD were one with the soul and the soul one with GOD, as practice demonstrates.

2. To adore GOD in truth means to recognize Him for what He is, and to recognize ourselves for what we are. To adore GOD in truth means to recognize truly in deed and in spirit that GOD is what He is—that is, infinitely perfect, infinitely worthy of adoration, infinitely removed from evil, and infinite in all His Divine attributes. What person could be so irrational <note>original: "Vernunftlos" — literally "without reason" or "senseless."</note> that they would not gladly employ all their strength to pay this great GOD all possible reverence and adoration?

3. To adore GOD in truth means further still: to confess that we are entirely unlike and contrary to Him, and that He desires to make us like Him if we only wish it. Who then would be so unwise as to withdraw even for a single moment from the reverence, love, service, and adoration which we are bound to pay Him unceasingly?

# On the Union of the Soul with God.

->The union of the soul with God is of three kinds.<-

First, the soul is united with God habitually <note>original: "habitualiter"</note> through grace, so long as it remains in a state of grace. <note>In theology, "habitual grace" refers to a stable, supernatural disposition that perfects the soul, making it holy and pleasing to God.</note>

2. It is united with Him virtually <note>original: "virtualiter"</note> by virtue of a work, when it begins such a task and thereby unites itself with God, and consequently remains united with Him by virtue of this work for as long as the work lasts.

3. The third union is the actual <note>original: "actualis"</note> or active union, and this is the most perfect. Although it is entirely spiritual in itself, one can nevertheless feel its movement quite well, because here the soul does not lie as if in sleep, as in the other unions, but finds itself powerfully awakened. Its effect is more vivid than the effect of fire, and brighter than the sun when it is covered by no cloud. Nonetheless, one can also be easily deceived in this feeling, as it is not a mere expression of the heart—as if one were to say: "My God! I love You with all my heart," or other such words—but rather it is a "certain something" <note>original French: "un je ne sçai quoi"</note> or a certain disposition of the soul that is still, quiet, spiritual, reverent, humble, loving, and very simple. Through this, the soul is moved and compelled to love God, to adore Him, and indeed to embrace Him with such tender movements of love that they cannot be expressed and can be grasped by no one unless they have experienced it themselves.

4. All those who desire to reach Divine Union must know that everything that can please the will is indeed pleasant and delightful to it, or at least the will considers it so.

Everyone must confess that God is incomprehensible, and that to unite oneself with Him, the will must be deprived of all taste and all pleasure, whether spiritual or physical, so that, detached from all things, it can love God above all else. For if the will is to grasp or comprehend God in any way, this can happen only through love. However, there is a great difference between the "taste" and feeling of the will and the action of the will; because the taste and feeling of the will are and remain in the soul as their goal and end; but its actions—which is properly love—go out from the soul <note>original: "gehen aus der Seele hinaus"</note> and end in God, as their only goal and end.

### Appendix to Brother Lawrence, On the Presence of God.

->I.<-

**T**he Presence of God is a turning of our mind and heart toward God, or a remembering of the present God, which then occurs either through the imagination or through the understanding.

2. I know a person who for forty years has possessed and practiced an intellectual Presence of God, which they are accustomed to naming with several other names. Sometimes they call it a simple act; sometimes a clear and distinct knowledge of God; sometimes a general vision, a general and loving gazing upon God, a remembrance of God, an attentiveness to God, a silent interaction or conversation with God, a trust in God, and the life and peace of the soul. In a word, they say: that all these types of the Presence of God are one and signify one and the same thing, and that this Presence has now become natural to them; and indeed in the following manner:

3. They say that through manifold repeated acts, and by frequently calling their spirit back into the Presence of God, a firm habit has established itself in them to such an extent that as soon as they are free from their external duties—and indeed often in the midst of them, and even when they are most deeply immersed in them—the apex of their spirit, <note>The "apex of the spirit" or "fine point of the soul" is a term used by mystics to describe the highest faculty of the human soul where it meets the divine.</note> or the highest part of the soul, rises up into God without them doing anything on their part; and above all things it remains suspended and stands unmoving in Him as its center and place of its rest. Thus, they feel their spirit almost always in this elevation, accompanied by faith, with which they then let themselves be satisfied. This is what they call the actual Presence of God, which comprises all other types of this Presence and much more besides; so much so that they now live as if no one but God and themselves were in the world. They converse everywhere with God; they ask of Him what they have need of, and delight themselves with Him without ceasing in a thousand and thousands of ways.

4. It serves well to know, however, that this interaction with God happens in the ground <note>In German mystical tradition, the "ground of the soul" (Seelengrund) refers to the deepest, most essential part of a person's being, beyond thoughts and emotions.</note> and in the center of the soul. There the soul speaks with God heart to heart, and indeed always in a great and deep peace which the soul enjoys in God; everything that happens outside [outside of this inward ground] is to the soul nothing other than a straw fire, which goes out just as soon as it begins to burn, so that its inward peace may be disturbed by it almost never or very little.

5. To return to our Presence of God, I say that this silent and loving gazing upon God imperceptibly kindles a divine fire in the soul, which inflames it so fervently with the love of God that the person must often take up one thing or another externally to moderate it. <note>The author suggests that the internal spiritual heat becomes so intense that the person must perform physical tasks just to stay grounded or "cool down."</note>

6. Indeed, one would have to be highly amazed if one knew what the soul...

### Means to Attain the Presence of God.

->1.<-

The first means is a great purity of life, where one watches prayerfully to ensure that one does nothing, says nothing, or thinks nothing that could displease God; and if such a thing should happen, that one then humbly asks His forgiveness and performs penance for it.

2. The second is a great faithfulness in the practice of this presence and the inward gazing upon God in faith, which must always happen in a gentle, humble, and loving manner, without allowing any disturbance or unrest to take root within oneself.

3. One must take special care not to undertake any external tasks without this inward gazing upon God preceding us, even if it were only for a moment; that the same gaze also accompanies our tasks from time to time; and finally, that they all end with it. And just as much time and labor is required to fully attain this practice, one must by no means lose heart if one occasionally fails in this; for a firm habit is only established within us with effort; but as soon as it is there, everything will be done with joy.

Is it not right that the heart—which is the first thing to live and which holds dominion over all other members of the body—should also be the first and the last to love and worship God, both at the beginning and the end of all our spiritual and physical tasks, and in all the exercises of life? Thus, we must strive to practice this brief inward gazing with exactly that [namely, with the heart and in the heart]; yet, as has already been said, it should be done without strain and without artifice, so that it may be all the easier.

4. For those who are beginning to practice this, it will not be unhelpful to use a few words inwardly, for example: My God, I am entirely Your own! O God of love! I love You with all my heart;

<header>Appendix to Brother Lawrence,</header>

"Lord, make me according to Your heart!" <note>original: "HErr mache mich nach deinem Herzen!"</note> or other such words that love brings forth without long reflection. But one must take care that the intellect does not wander or return to the <term>creature</term> <note>As noted previously, "creature" refers to anything created—people, objects, or worldly distractions—as opposed to the Creator.</note>; therefore, they must keep it fixed on God alone, so that when the intellect sees itself urged as if by force through the will, it is finally compelled to remain with God.

5. This practice of the presence of God does indeed require a little effort in the beginning, but if it is practiced faithfully, it secretly produces wonderful and magnificent effects in the soul. It causes the graces of God to pour out abundantly upon her and leads her, without her even knowing it, to simple contemplation—or the loving vision of the omnipresent God—which is then the holiest, most profound, easiest, and most powerful form of prayer.

6. Note here that to reach this state, the mortification of the senses <note>The practice of "dying to" or denying the physical senses and worldly desires to focus on the spiritual.</note> is presupposed and required; for it is impossible for a soul that still finds some pleasure and delight in the <term>creature</term> to perfectly enjoy this Divine presence; for whoever wishes to be with God must necessarily leave the <term>creature</term> behind. *

### The Fruits of the Presence of God.

1. The first benefit the soul receives from the presence of God is this: that faith thereby becomes more living and effective in all circumstances of our life, especially in our needs. This is because we thereby easily obtain the assistance of God’s grace in all temptations and in our unavoidable dealings with <term>creatures</term>. For the soul that is accustomed to the exercise of faith through this practice sees and feels God as present through a simple remembrance; thus, she calls upon Him easily and powerfully and obtains from Him what she needs. One can say that in this state, she has something that corresponds in some measure to the state of the <term>Blessed</term> <note>The "Blessed" (Seelige) refers to the saints and souls already in heaven who experience the direct vision of God.</note> in heaven; the further she progresses, the more living her faith becomes, and finally it becomes so piercing that one might almost say: I no longer believe, but I see and experience.

2. The practice of the presence of God strengthens us in hope; our hope grows in proportion to the growth of our knowledge. And as faith, through this holy practice, penetrates more and more into the mysteries of the Godhead, it discovers more and more in God a beauty that infinitely surpasses all beauty—not only of the physical bodies we see on earth, but also of the most perfect souls and the angels. Thus, our hope grows and becomes ever stronger; and the glory of the great Good, the enjoyment of which it expects and which it already tastes in some measure, sustains and satisfies the soul.

3. She

3. It works in the will a contempt for the <term>creatures</term> <note>In this context, "creatures" refers to all created things—people, objects, and worldly distractions—as opposed to God the Creator.</note> and ignites in it the fire of holy love. For God, as a consuming fire <note>original: "verzehrend Feuer"</note>, in whose presence the soul always finds herself, destroys within her everything that might be contrary to Him; and this soul, thus burning with love, can no longer live in any other way than in the presence of her God. This presence impresses upon her heart a holy fervor, a holy impulse, and a powerful longing to see that this God of hers is loved, known, served, and worshipped by all creatures.

4. Through the presence of God and through this inward contemplation, the soul becomes so united with God that she spends almost her entire life in unceasing acts of love, worship, repentance, trust, thanksgiving, sacrifice, invocation, and the most excellent virtues. Indeed, sometimes it becomes only a single, continuous act that no longer passes away, as the soul finds herself at all times in the perpetual practice of this Divine presence.

I know well that few are found who reach this degree, and that it is a grace with which God favors only a few chosen souls, since this simple contemplation of God is purely a gift of His merciful hand. Yet, for the comfort of those who wish to devote themselves to this holy practice, I can say that God commonly gives this grace <insert>of unchanging, simple contemplation</insert> to those who make themselves ready for it; and if He perhaps does not give it, then at least the soul—with the help of His ordinary graces through this practice of the Divine presence—can reach such a manner or state of prayer that comes very close to this simple contemplation.

# Preface.

**N**othing is more beautiful, pure, delightful, powerful, and perfect than love; for God is love: by no means can God better take possession of the human heart than through love; and by no thing can man better please God than through love; for it is the fulfillment of the law. <note>original: "des Gesetzes Erfüllung"; a reference to Romans 13:10.</note> What could not be accomplished in man through all the severity of the law, and through all the fear of punishment—and still cannot be—is all easily accomplished wherever God commends His love to man in Christ Jesus, where He announces to him the forgiveness of his sins, redemption, and eternal salvation, and from such a foundation entices him toward repentance and reciprocal love. Just as the depths of God’s love have been opened again to straying man in the sweet name of Jesus-Immanuel <note>"Immanuel" means "God with us." The author uses this title to emphasize God’s presence within the soul.</note>; and even until this hour stand wide open in the soul of the poorest sinner, whether he knows it or not: so too is this eternal love constantly active in the depths of our souls, offering and commending itself to us, and seeking in a thousand ways to insinuate itself and find an entrance for our eternal happiness. All good thoughts and desires rising in the human heart, all sadness and woe over one's sins, all correction and guidance, all promptings to prayer, to true godliness, and to a thorough surrender to God, and the like, are the pure effects of this long-suffering love of God. Could even the most wicked sinner recognize but a thousandth part of it, he would have to surrender himself that very moment to this incomprehensible love; indeed, *"Love, show yourself even from afar to sinners, that You are Love, and they will all love You and follow You gladly!"*

If it now happens that a person allows himself to be drawn to repentance through God’s goodness and love, let him henceforth believe without hesitation that he can please God in no better or easier way through any work or exercise than through love: let him but carefully preserve and foster the hidden spark of God’s love in his heart through heartfelt remembrance of God, a childlike turning toward God, and a simple preoccupation with God and His perfections. Let him practice love: out of love for God let him give up himself and his most precious things, and let him entrust himself in faith to this pure love. Let him rejoice whenever he has a good opportunity to do, to deny, or to suffer something for the love and honor of this God. Let him accustom himself to doing everything he does out of love for this God; to receiving everything that happens to him in love from this God; to bearing everything he must suffer in love for the sake of this God. Everything must be sacrificed by love to Love. Through love, the most bitter sufferings become sweet, the most strange events become good, and the smallest works become great and divine.

But one should not think here specifically of an emotional and refreshing love: having love and feeling love are not always found together. True, constant love consists in an inward high esteem for God, such that we recognize Him through faith as the highest—indeed the only—one worthy of love; and therefore we willingly sacrifice and leave ourselves entirely, and whatever is in our power, to this God for His service and honor. This love, which the Holy Spirit pours into our hearts, can persist even in the midst of all dryness, darkness, and the deepest paths of purification, as these are nothing other than the blessed effects of the Pure Love of God. But I forget myself, and only hold back the eager reader with my dull expressions from reading that which one of the holiest souls has testified and proven in her life and writings in a powerful and vigorous manner regarding this matter of love and other magnificent truths. Read then, and be kindled!

### Foreword.

Nothing is more beautiful, pure, graceful, powerful, and perfect than love; for God is Love. There is no means by which God can better take possession of the human heart than through love; and there is nothing through which a person can better please God than through love; for love is the fulfillment of the law. What could not be achieved—and still cannot be achieved—through all the severity of the law and through all fear of punishment, is all easily accomplished when God commends His love to man in Christ Jesus, when He announces the forgiveness of sins, redemption, and eternal salvation, and from such a foundation lures him toward repentance and a reciprocal love. Just as the depths of God’s love are opened again to the straying human in the sweet name of Jesus-Immanuel <note>original: "JEsu-Immanuel"; Immanuel means "God with us."</note>; and even until this hour stand wide open in the soul of the poorest sinner, whether they know it or not: so too is this eternal love constantly active in the depths of our souls, offering and commending itself to us, and seeking in a thousand ways to introduce itself and find an entrance for our eternal happiness. All good thoughts and desires rising in the human heart, all sadness and woe over one's sins, all correction and guidance, all promptings toward prayer, toward true godliness, and a thorough surrender to God, and the like—these are pure effects of this long-suffering Love of God. If even the most wicked sinner could recognize but a thousandth part of it, he would have to surrender himself to this incomprehensible love in an instant; yes,

> "Love, show yourself even from afar to sinners, that You are Love, and they will all love You and follow You gladly!"

If it happens that a person allows himself to be drawn to repentance by God’s goodness and love, let him henceforth believe without hesitation that he can please God in no better or easier way, through any kind of work or practice, than through love. Let him simply preserve and cherish the hidden little spark <note>The "little spark" (*Fünklein*) is a classic term in German mysticism referring to the divine element remaining in the human soul.</note> of God’s love in his heart through a heartfelt remembrance of God, a childlike turning toward God, and a simple preoccupation with God and His perfections. Let him practice love: out of love for God, let him give up himself and what he holds most dear, and entrust himself in faith to this pure love. Let him rejoice when he has a good opportunity to do, to deny, or to suffer something for the love and honor of this God. Let him accustom himself to doing everything he does out of love for this God: to receiving everything that happens to him in love from this God: to bearing everything he must suffer in love for the sake of this God. Everything must be sacrificed to Love through love. Through love, the most bitter sufferings become sweet, the strangest events become good, and the smallest works become great and divine.

Yet one should not think here of a merely emotional or delightful love: having love and feeling love are not always found together. True, constant love consists of an inward high esteem for God, such that we recognize Him through faith as the highest—indeed, the only—one worthy of love; and therefore we willingly sacrifice and surrender our entire selves, and whatever is in our power, to this God for His service and honor. But I forget myself, and only delay the eager reader with my feeble expressions from reading that which one of the holiest souls has witnessed and proven in a powerful and vigorous manner in her life and writings regarding this matter of love and other glorious truths. Read then, and be ignited!
