confessors <note>original: "vater," likely "Beichtvater" (confessor)</note>, from the mouths of the Saints themselves, as can be seen more extensively in this history itself in *Chapter 17.* Initially, it was set down in the Italian language, and already more than a hundred years ago—namely in 1597—translated into French by the *Carthusians* in *Paris*, and has been reprinted many times: 1627, 1646, 1667, and so on. The earlier *editions* are somewhat unclear due to the language and contain many words that seem superfluous; in the later *edition*, which was published in *Lyon*, they sought to improve both, but took far too much liberty in changing and omitting things. For this reason, the later *edition* published in French by Mr. *Poiret* under the title of the *Theology of Love* <note>original: "Liebes-Theologie," referring to Poiret's "Théologie de l'amour"</note> at *Amsterdam in 1691*, rightly holds the preference in more than one respect.

It is from this *edition* that this concise biography has been prepared; however, as one of the oldest editions (1627) was also at hand, we have occasionally preferred to follow it where the changes were significant, marking such passages for the most part with a †. The dialogues of this Saint, which are exceedingly excellent and described by her own hand, have been included in this extract all the less because they were printed separately in the German language at *Halle in 1701*, although one cannot deny that the *translator*, for a particular purpose, occasionally took too much liberty. But because the circumstances of the Saint's conversion are only briefly touched upon in her "Life," and no sufficient concept of it is given there, we have deemed it entirely necessary to supplement such a deficiency here in several chapters from her dialogues; especially since her relapse into the vanities of this world, which occurred after her first conversion and is honestly recounted by herself, can still encourage many a feeble and stumbling soul to confidently take hold again of the hands of God’s tireless Love and be renewed to a double faithfulness.

*Gottfried Arnold* has published an extract of this life, and a still shorter extract was added to her German dialogues in *Halle*. Anyone who wished to take the trouble to *compare* <note>original: "conferiren"</note> these with the *original* as well as with this present extract would easily perceive the significant difference; however, that work is not held in low esteem because of this, as every *author* has his own particular intentions.

To repeat the *approvals* <note>original: "Approbationes"</note> and eulogies of this person and her writings from the Roman Catholics is superfluous, as she has been publicly *declared* a Saint. Through the aforementioned *editions* and extracts by Protestants, the same person and matters have also been sufficiently approved; space does not permit the citation of more testimonies. Mr. *Poiret*, who (a) can hardly believe that from the time of the *Apostles* until *Catherine* of *Genoa*, anything more divine, profound, and sublime has been produced than the writings of this Saint, concludes the preface to his *edition* with these sighs among others:

# Chapter One.

## Her Origins; Piety of her Youth; Unhappy Marriage and Miserable Relapse into the Vanities of this World.

I.

The holy Catherine of Genoa, whose father was Jacobus Fieschi, Vice-King of Naples, began even in her tender youth to trample her **carnal nobility** <term>carnal nobility<note>Her high-born social status and earthly lineage, as opposed to spiritual rank.</note></term> under her feet and to feel a loathing for worldly pleasures. This occurred in the eighth year of her age, as she was already being drawn toward penance; she thereafter despised all luxury, treated her body harshly, and felt her heart filled with repentance and pain whenever she contemplated the great sufferings which the Savior **JESUS** had endured for our sake. She lived in great simplicity, hardly speaking with others; she was entirely obedient to her parents and displayed a great longing for a virtuous way of life.

2. When she reached her twelfth year, the **Lord** granted her the gift of prayer, along with many living flames of His inward and heartfelt love, a great compassion for the sufferings He endured for us, and various other good impulses and insights into Divine matters. Because of this, she wished to enter a cloister in her 13th year, but because she was still too young, she was not accepted.

3. In the sixteenth year of her age, she was forced out of obedience to her parents to marry Julian Adorno, a nobleman from the same city of Genoa; he, however, was entirely contrary to her holy way of life and caused her much suffering for ten years through the profligate squandering of all his goods, by which they were placed in great poverty. The first five years she spent in great melancholy and tribulation; afterward, however, she sought to ease her sadness through external things and sought to delight herself in the vanities of this world, as is customary among ladies of her rank. But approximately the last three months of these ten years, her former sadness returned with great force, and she developed an extreme loathing for all things of the world, fled all society, and could no longer endure herself. And this sadness remained with her constantly.

4. [This is thus briefly reported concerning the first years of the life of this Holy Soul, up to her complete and irrevocable conversion to **God**, which occurred around the 25th year of her age. If we compare this more closely with the first chapters of the little book she wrote herself, called the *Dialogues* <note>original: "Gespräche [Dialogues]," referring to Catherine's "Dialogi del uigore et spirituale redentione."</note>, we see more properly the fragile beginnings and fluctuations of the work of grace in her soul: though she was moved early on by the drawing of the Father into sorrow and reflection regarding her salvation, and the soul had quite earnestly considered what serves its peace; yet because she was so tightly bound to the **body of death** <note>A reference to Romans 7:24, "Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?"</note>; and because too much ear was given to nature, reason, and self-love, she allowed herself to be drawn down again gradually into the...

# Section Ten. The Life
<meta>catchword: Body</meta>

Sensuality and distraction [prevailed], so that under the apparent pretext of fairness, necessity, and the glorification of **God** while enjoying earthly amusements, the soul was completely weakened. This was always paired with fear, doubt, and secret punishments from the chastening Spirit of Grace within. Initially, the soul was master for a time and the body was the servant; however, after several circumstances and changes, the body became the master and the soul the servant. Because of this, she finally fell into great sadness and **melancholy** <term>melancholy<note>In this historical context, "melancholy" (Schwermüthigkeit) refers to a deep spiritual despondency or depression resulting from a sense of separation from God.</note></term>, which corresponds to the state of her mind mentioned above during the first five years of her marriage.

To defend herself somewhat against this great melancholy, the soul gave itself over out of dejection to seek its life and comfort in the delights of the created world. She fell from one desire and vanity into another; she seems to have remained in such a state of backsliding until the following five years of her marriage came to an end, at which point **God** took pity on her again and powerfully drew her to Himself through His love. We wish to hear of the course of these events in more detail, using the very words of this Saint, as they are found in the aforementioned little book of her conversations.

5. The soul (she says) consented to everything the body said it needed. However, the cravings of the body increased day by day, as they united themselves with **self-love** <term>self-love<note>Known as *Selbst-Liebe* in German mysticism, this refers to an ego-centric attachment to one’s own will and comforts, which acts as a barrier to Divine union.</note></term>, and through it became so closely bound together that they would no longer allow themselves to be separated. Everything appeared to the body and to self-love as fair and necessary, and they did not want to ever lack for anything. If the soul did not daily consent to something new that might provide them with some fresh fodder, they grumbled against the soul and said she was doing them an injustice. In this way, she was dragged by them into an infinite sea of earthly love and lusts, which joined together and so transformed the soul into another shape that she could no longer think or speak of anything except those things which the body and self-love desired. If she tried to think for herself, she was so beaten back by her disorderly desires that she no longer dared to open her mouth.

6. Since the soul—which is created to love and to delight—still desired some nourishment and pleasure so as not to sink entirely into sadness and melancholy, she surrendered herself completely to earthly delights. Under a good pretense, she said to herself: "These beauties, this taste, these good things, these pleasures, this splendor and glory, and all this adornment of created things, are a means to reach the knowledge and enjoyment of Divine things." And while enjoying earthly lusts, she said: "O, how great must be the beauty, the excellence, and the goodness of heavenly things!" Meanwhile, as she thus followed the body and self-love, she lost more and more each day the impression of the Heavenly and her Divine nature, as she [mingled] with the...

...[the] body enjoyed the food of beasts; and thus, in a short time, the soul was most closely united with the body and with **self-love** <term>self-love<note>In mystical literature, "self-love" (Eigen-Liebe) refers to egoism or a preoccupation with one's own desires rather than the will of God.</note></term>.

7. One can now easily imagine how poorly treated the higher part of the soul must have been. There was no one left who spoke of it; the senses were turned toward earthly things. The taste, the inclinations, the amusements were all found in the worldly; spiritual matters seemed bitter to them—so much so that they no longer spoke of them, and could no longer bear to hear them spoken of, for fear that their earthly lusts might be interrupted.

8. This lasted so long that only a tiny gnawing <note>original: "Nagen"; this refers to the "gnawing of conscience," a persistent but ignored sense of guilt.</note> remained in the soul, which she also paid little heed to, except occasionally when the thought occurred to her of the danger she was in—of losing everything at once through death—which would then strike her with great terror. But once this good moment <note>A "good moment" here refers to a moment of clarity or conviction from God.</note> had passed, she would return to her previous ways.

9. Only one thing pained her: namely, that she could not satisfy her desires, no matter how much she pursued them. Because the soul has an infinite capacity, but all earthly things are finite, she could neither be satiated nor find rest through them. The more she sought such satisfaction, the less she found it, as she daily distanced herself more and more from **God**, who is her true rest.

Nevertheless, she was so blinded by earthly things that she lived under the delusion that she would be able to find her rest and contentment in the earth, and she applied all her diligence to satisfy herself with it. When a thing caused her disgust and frustration instead of the hoped-for satisfaction, she still hoped to find joy in another; so deeply was she internally blinded. And so she passed from one thing to another and deceived herself; and while moving from one hope to another, she lost her time without ever finding what she sought. **God**, in His mercy, allowed this to happen; for surely, if man could find his rest in earthly things, few souls would ever be saved.

3. ### of Saint Catherine of Genoa.

...left, but that God should draw her out through His infinite grace and goodness; for on her part, she desired nothing else but earthly things; they tasted sweet to her, she loved them, and she held them as her focus and her delight. She hated everything else and could no longer speak of it; she felt such a loathing for it that even that which had previously seemed sweet and pleasant to her had now become a very bitter food.

4. Now, after Divine Goodness had allowed this soul to wander about for a time in earthly things, and all creatures <note>In this mystical context, "creatures" refers to all created things—people, objects, and worldly pleasures—as opposed to the Creator.</note> had become wearying and loathsome to her—which, as she experienced, could not satisfy her, but rather only increased her suffering and disquiet from day to day—the Most Merciful finally had compassion on her. He sent her a light, whereby her understanding was opened, so that she perceived all her failings and the dangers in which she found herself, and it was given to her to recognize that no one but God alone could free her from them.

Then she saw where she was; she saw the path upon which she walked: on one side, bodily death, and on the other, the death of the soul; and how she found herself in the midst of so many enemies, through whom she allowed herself to be led like cattle to the slaughtering-bench, indeed, how she went toward it in good spirits. She became dismayed and entirely terrified by this, so that turning to God with sighs and piteous cries, she said:

> O miserable me! Who will pull me out of this abyss of wickedness if You alone do not do so? O my God! Lord, let me see the light, so that I may come out of so many puddles in which I sit imprisoned.

5. When the soul had thus fixed her gaze upon God and called upon His assistance, she immediately placed her entire trust in Him and let Him act thereafter as He always willed and for as long as it pleased Him, saying: "Henceforth I will accept everything that may happen to me from the gracious hand of God, except for sins, for those belong entirely to me, and one always acts against the Divine Will when one commits sin; therefore, sin comes entirely from us and from our own will; and all <term>own-will<note>German: *eigener Wille*. A central concept in German mysticism (Eigenwille), referring to the human ego's desire to operate independently of God's will, which is seen as the root of all sin.</note></term> is sin."

6. [And so it happened that this soul, through the vision of her misery and the incomprehensible goodness of God, was brought back from her wretched straying as if in a moment and was powerfully converted; in her life, this is told with the following circumstances]. It happened around this time that at the insistence of her sister, who lived in a convent, she wished to make her confession to her sister's confessor, a pious man; but she had hardly knelt down when her heart was wounded with a very great love of God, alongside such a clear vision of her misery and the goodness of God, that she almost fell fainting to the ground, and with a very fervent love she cried out inwardly: "Ah! No more world, no more sins"; and if she had had a thousand worlds in her...

### Tenth Part. The Life

...if she had possessed the power, she would have given it all up. Thus, in the presence of the confessor, she was almost entirely deprived of her senses by the sweetness of this wound <note>A common mystical term describing a spiritual experience that "pierces" the soul with intense love and longing for the divine.</note>, and she could not open her mouth because of the internal power of her longing and the great love she felt. After some time, however, she exerted so much force upon herself that she said to the confessor: "Dear Father, I would like to postpone this confession until another time." She then departed for home, carrying in her heart the arrow of this great love of **God** along with the recognition of her own miseries. She shut herself in one of the innermost rooms and broke out in flaming sighs to give vent to her internal fire, but could only bring forth these words: "O Love! Is it possible that You have called me with such great goodness, and in a single moment given me to know what my tongue cannot express?"

7. During these first days of her conversion, she did nothing else in her prayer but sigh; all her words consisted only of sobs and lamentations. Her contrition <note>deep regret for sins</note> and the pain of having offended this infinite Goodness was so deep that her heart broke with sorrow, and she would have given up the ghost at any moment had **God** not supported her in a wondrous manner.

8. The Savior, wishing to ignite the flame of her love even further, presented Himself to her mind as carrying His cross and shedding His blood in great abundance, and that out of pure love. By this, the glow in her heart was doubled, so that because of the intensity of the love and the pain, she seemed robbed of her senses. It was as if she always saw her sweet Love before her, nailed to the cross and bleeding; and as she simultaneously looked upon the offenses she had committed against Him, she cried out unceasingly: "O Love, never, never, nevermore to sin!" and out of hatred toward her [sinful] self she said: "O Love! I am ready to make my sins known to all the world, if it would be of use."

9. When she received that wound of love, it was to her as if she had been drawn to the feet of *Jesus Christ*, and in the spirit had seen all the graces and the paths through which He, by means of His pure love, drew her toward conversion. Even though **God** had forgiven all her sins in that very moment, consuming them in the fire of His unbelievable love, she nevertheless had to pass through a path of contrition for approximately fourteen months; after which time this vision of her sins was taken from her in such a way, as if they had all been thrown into the depths of the sea.

10. Afterward, she saw a much sweeter path, which contained many mysteries of a benevolent love that consumed her entirely in love, so that she frequently lost consciousness <note>The original German "von ihr selbst kam" refers to a mystical state of ecstasy or losing one's senses.</note>. And sometimes, without thinking about what she was doing, she licked the dust of the earth out of the deepest contrition and the sweetness of her love. And in this state she remained for three years.

11. After that time, she was drawn toward the most holy heart of **Jesus**, which appeared to her as being completely filled with fire, by which she felt herself ignited. Because of this, she was compelled to release sighs inflamed by the most fervent love without ceasing. She remained in these states of fervor for several years, and her heart and soul were so melted and consumed by this fire of love that she said: "I have no heart or soul any longer, but my heart and my soul is the heart and soul of my sweet love."

12. Finally, she was drawn to the most sweet mouth of her Savior, from which she was given such a kiss that she threw herself entirely into the bonds of this sweet Divinity. She lost herself within it to such an extent that she said: "I live no longer, but **Jesus Christ** lives in me" <note>This is a paraphrase of the biblical verse Galatians 2:20: "It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me."</note>. And because of this, she could no longer distinguish human actions within herself, whether they were good or evil; instead, she saw everything in **God**.

2. He gave her to understand how our sins can never anger Him in such a way that He should cease to do us good, so long as we are in this world; on the contrary, the more we distance ourselves from Him through sin, the more He calls us back through many reproaches of conscience and good inspirations. He does this to the end that we might not entirely deprive ourselves of His love, so that He may continually love us and do us good. And so that He may better win us over, He employs so many means and ways that when the soul perceives this in detail, it must cry out in astonishment: "Who am I then, that it seems **God** has no care but for me alone?"

3. Among other things, **God** showed her the pure love through which He created us, without demanding anything else from us than that we should love Him with the same love with which He has loved us.

4. He let her see the ardent love which our Savior **JESUS Christus** showed us on earth, from His Incarnation <note>original: "Menschwerdung," literally "becoming-human."</note> until His Ascension, in order to redeem us from eternal death. **God**, through His purest operation, allowed this soul to see all of this in a single moment.

5. He also showed her with what great patience He had waited for her and borne with her while she was laden with so many sins; had she died in that state, she would have been justly damned for eternity. He also showed her how she had been in many dangers of death, and how He had preserved her through His pure love to yet make her blessed, so that in time she might recognize her error and escape eternal damnation.

6. Accordingly, He also let her see how many good inspirations He had given her to draw her out of sin, even though she had not accepted them but had done the very opposite of what His Divine Will desired. He showed how, despite this, His goodness did not grow weary of reminding her and drawing her to Himself, now through one means, now through another, enticing and caressing her free will in such a way that He almost forced it to do what His goodness desired. He did all of this with such great care and patience that no act or demonstration of human love can be found that could be compared with such great care and heartiness of the Creator toward His poor creature.

7. **God** also let this soul see that, because of the great love He bears for man, He is never so angered against him that He does not still love him and unceasingly seek to unite Himself with him through love; on His part, He never fails to awaken such an inclination within the human being. It is true that **God** shows Himself fearsome and terrible toward sin, nor can the slightest imperfection exist within Him; but toward everything else, **God** harbors nothing but goodness. Sin alone is the object <note>The original German "Vorwurf" here functions like the Latin "obiectum," meaning the target or focus of an emotion.</note> of His hatred and His aversion; for sin alone stands in the way of His love

I will nevermore offend You again, nor do anything that is contrary to Your goodness; for this goodness shames me so, and binds me so much to You, that I am determined nevermore to separate myself from Your command and ordinance, even if I should lose my physical life a thousand times over it.

Look for once at the state you are in: alas! who will pull you out of so many miseries? Now you see how you are sunken in the filth of sins, and how terribly ugly you are, though you believe yourself to be so...

->### Tenth Part. The Life of Saint Catherine, etc. Chapter III.<-

...such a despair of herself that the sight of a human being was no less terrifying to her than the sight of the devil with all his malice; and if **God** had not tempered this sight, soul and body would have been annihilated and consumed by it, just as much as by the sight of Divine Love for humanity. And thus she so utterly lost all hope in herself that she considered her own human nature to be entirely incurable <note>The German "ungeneßlich" can mean "inedible" or "incurable," here referring to her soul's state as beyond human remedy.</note>; she wished henceforth to lose no more time thinking about it or seeking any remedies for it, but instead she placed her entire trust in **God** her Love, and said to Him: "Lord, I bring myself to You as a gift; for I know not what else to do with myself, since I am fit for nothing but to make a hell of myself. Therefore, O Lord! I would like to exchange with You, and give my malicious nature into Your hands, because You alone can hide and swallow it up in Your goodness; and that You might, in turn, give me Your pure and unadulterated love, so that it may extinguish all other love in me and completely annihilate me in You, so that nothing (†) more of myself may be seen, and thus keep me occupied in You so that nothing else ever finds time or space to remain in me." To which her sweetest **Lord** gave the answer: that He was satisfied with this, and in that very moment her malice was taken away from her memory in such a way that she no longer troubled herself about it.

18. At that very same time, a beam of love, so fervent, flaming, and piercing, was poured into her heart that it wounded and penetrated the soul in its innermost parts, to such an extent that she was stripped by it of all love, desires, pleasures, and self-will <note>Literally "Eigenheiten," referring to the ego-driven attachments that mystics believe separate the soul from God.</note> that she ever had or could have had in this world; she remained stripped of all things, with a certain consent and surrender <term>correspondence<note>original: Correspondance; in this context, it refers to a soul's harmonious responsiveness to divine grace.</note></term> to this Divine Love, which drew her to itself in such a way that she was completely stunned, possessed, transformed, and led away out of herself.

19. Now the sight of herself caused her no more distress, though she saw very clearly what she was of herself, for her (†) sweet and friendly **God** had taken all this distress away from her; and she saw how she was held and preserved by **God** in such a way that if He had left her to herself for even a little while, she would have been quite ready to bring forth just as malicious effects as the devil might have done; for she saw herself as an incarnate devil: but because she was surrendered into the hands of **God**, she could no longer have any fear.

# Chapter Four.
## Her Longing for the Holy Supper; Extraordinary Fasting; and Earnest <term>Mortification</term> <note>Original: *Abtödtung*—the spiritual practice of "killing off" or subduing the physical desires and ego to better serve God.</note> of Her Nature and Senses.

She was also overcome by a yearning desire for the daily enjoyment of the <term>Holy Supper</term> <note>The Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note>, which lasted steadily until the end of her life, so much so that if for some reason she did not receive communion, she had to spend that entire day in suffering, feeling completely weary and weak. For she said, “My heart is not like the heart of other people; it rejoices only in its Savior.” However, when she was commanded that she should not receive communion on this or that day, she abstained out of obedience, even though she suffered much because of it.

2. Once, God gave her such great comfort during the use of the Supper that she fell into a faint; and as the chalice was being handed to her and she was forcibly brought back to herself, she said: “My Lord, I do not wish to follow You for these delights, but only with a true and pure love.” Another time, when she found herself filled with such great sweetness after Communion that she thought she was in Paradise, she turned humbly to the Lord and said: “O my Love! Would You draw me to You through such tokens of grace? I do not desire such things. On the contrary, You well know that from the very beginning I have asked You never to give me any vision or sensory delight; because I see Your goodness so clearly that it seems to me I do not walk by faith, but in the actual experience of the heart.”

3. Not long after her conversion, her Love spoke to her inwardly: He wished for her to keep the fast with Him in the wilderness; and from that hour on, she could no longer eat, but had to remain without consuming physical food until Easter, after which time she could eat again like others without any discomfort of the stomach. In this manner, she kept the fast twenty-three times. Initially, she was in great fear because she could not eat and feared some deception; therefore, she forced herself to eat, but she always had to cast the food back up.

During this time that she could not eat, she practiced good works all the more; she slept better and was also fresher and stronger than usual. She went to the table like the others in order to avoid all <term>singularity</term> <note>Original: *Sonderlichkeit*—the act of drawing attention to oneself by acting differently from the group, which was considered a form of pride.</note> as much as possible; and when people wondered why she ate nothing, she said within herself: “O, if you knew the other matter that I feel within me! You would prize it far higher.” Namely, the pure and fervent love through which she was united with God in her heart.

# Chapter Four.

## Her Longing for the Holy Supper; Extraordinary Fasting; and Earnest Mortification of Her Nature and Senses.

She was also overcome with a yearning desire for the daily enjoyment of the <term>Holy Supper</term> <note>Original: *heil. Abendmals*—referring to the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note>, which continued steadily until the end of her life; it was to such an extent that when she did not <term>receive communion</term> <note>Original: *communicirte*.</note> for some reason, she had to spend that entire day in suffering, feeling quite faint and weak. For (she said): "My heart is not like the hearts of other people; it rejoices only in its Savior." But when she was commanded that she should not communicate on this or that day, she abstained out of obedience, even though she endured much suffering because of it.

2. Once, God gave her such great comfort during the use of the Supper that she fell into a faint because of it; and as the cup was offered to her and she was forcibly brought back to herself, she said: "My Lord, I do not wish to follow You with these <term>delights</term> <note>Original: *Ergeßlichkeiten*—mystical ecstasies or pleasant spiritual sensations that some mystics feared might distract from pure love.</note>, but only with a true and pure love." Another time, when she found herself filled with such great sweetness after Communion that she thought she was in Paradise, she turned humbly to the Lord and said: "O my Love! Would You draw me to Yourself through such testimonies of grace? I do not desire this. On the contrary, You know well that I asked You from the very beginning that You might never give me any vision or <term>sensible delight</term> <note>Original: *sinnliche Ergeßlichkeit*—physical or emotional pleasures felt during prayer.</note>; because I see Your goodness so clearly that it seems to me I walk not in faith, but in actual experience of the heart."

3. Not long after her conversion, her Love spoke inwardly to her: He willed that she should keep the <term>fast</term> <note>Original: *die Fasten*—specifically referring to the forty days of Lent.</note> with Him in the desert; and from that hour on, she could no longer eat, but had to remain without partaking of physical food until Easter. After that time, she could eat again like others without any discomfort to her stomach; and in this manner, she kept the Lenten fast twenty-three times. Initially, she was in great fear because she could not eat, fearing some deception; therefore, she forced herself to eat, but she always had to vomit the food back up.

During this time that she could not eat, she practiced all the more in good works; she slept better and was also fresher and stronger than usual. She went to the table like the others in order to avoid all <term>peculiarity</term> <note>Original: *Sonderlichkeit*—in mystical tradition, "singularity" or acting differently than others was often discouraged as it could lead to the sin of pride.</note> as much as possible; and when people wondered why she ate nothing, she said to herself: "Oh, if you only knew another thing that I feel within me! You would prize it far more highly." Namely, the pure and fervent love through which she was united with God in her heart.

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Catherine’s spiritual discipline following her conversion. The previous page described her overwhelming desire for the Eucharist and her rejection of "spiritual delights" in favor of pure love. This page details her extreme physical fasts, her practice of mortification, and the internal state of her soul during the first four years of her new life.</meta>

Tenth Part. The Life
<meta>catchword: so</meta>

One person grumbled, and another was amazed that she was unable to eat; she herself, however, made no great matter of it, but said:

> "One must value the inner workings of God much more highly than outward things. That I do not eat happens through God without my own will; no one should be amazed by this. The true Light teaches us that we must only pay attention to pure love, through which His Divine Majesty works within us. And when the soul sees the completely clear and pure workings of this love, and that it has no regard for any good we might perhaps do, then the soul must likewise love Him with a pure love, without looking toward any special gifts of grace she might receive. Rather, she must look to Him alone, who alone is worthy to be loved without measure and without secondary motives."

4. In the first four years of her <term>conversion</term> <note>Original: *Bekehrung*—her transformative spiritual awakening.</note>, she lived in great <term>austerity</term> <note>Original: *Gestrengheit*.</note> and <term>mortification</term> <note>Original: *Abtódtung*—literally "killing off" the impulses of the physical nature to prioritize the spirit.</note> of her nature; as soon as her flesh desired any thing, she took it away and gave it that which was repugnant to it. She did the same with her senses; whenever they wanted to have something, she resisted them immediately. At this time, she ate no fruit nor other tasty foods. And because she was by nature very talkative and knew well how to interact with people, she resisted herself most of all in this; and when her relatives visited her, she overcame herself and spoke as little as was ever possible, not caring at all if people were surprised by it. She never laughed; she almost always looked downward toward the earth and did not recognize those who passed by her, for she was so occupied internally that the outward world was as if extinguished. She always seemed to be sad, though she was actually very content. In sleeping, she also resisted her own comfort, for the fire of love was so burning in her interior that she paid little heed to outward matters, though without rejecting what was absolutely necessary. In this way, she <term>mortified</term> <note>Original: *mortificirte*.</note> all her senses without finding any difficulty in it. In these first four years, she remained in <term>prayer</term> <note>Original: *Gebät*.</note> for six hours every day; and although her physical senses felt much distress in this, they were nonetheless so obedient to the spirit that her heart did not have the will to resist him.

5. She was at that time so filled with internal sensations that she could not speak except so softly that one could hardly understand her; and she was so occupied and taken up within that she seemed dead to all external things. "I do not live," she said: "I do not feel that I have a soul, nor a body, nor a heart, nor a will, nor a taste, nor anything else, but only a pure love." Nevertheless, she lived in great submissiveness toward everyone, and sought only to do what was contrary to her own will, so that she would rather do the will of another than her own.

6. As she walked in such "dying away" of all her senses, she was sometimes asked: "Why do you do such things?" To which she answered:

> "I do not know: I only feel myself drawn inwardly and without any resistance to do so, and I believe that God wants it thus; but He does not want me to serve Him with an attachment to anything."

## The Fifth Chapter.
### Regarding various extraordinary gifts of grace, and certain rules that God gave her; her longing for death, and works of love within and outside the hospital in Genoa.

->I.<-

1. After those first four years of her conversion, a pure, free spirit <gloss>spirit <note>Original: *esprit*</note></gloss> was given to her, so filled with God that henceforth nothing foreign entered it. In the church and during sermons, she was so inwardly occupied that she neither saw nor understood anything of what happened or was said externally; but she saw and understood other things internally in the sweet Divine Light, where she was completely submerged in an internal taste and sensation that she could not cast off. Nevertheless, she did nothing unseemly outwardly, but as soon as it was necessary, she returned to herself and could even answer when she was called; for the Lord knew how to lead her so that no one had cause to grumble against her.

2. At times she was so ravished by the taste and feeling of the love of God that she was forced to hide herself, because she lost the use of her senses and remained as if dead. However, so that she might prevent such ecstasies <note>Original: *Entzückungen*—states of mystical rapture where one is "carried away" from sensory awareness.</note>, she did violence to herself and stayed among people as long as she could, saying to her Lord: "I do not desire that which comes from You <note>Meaning the spiritual "rewards" or pleasant feelings of ecstasy.</note>, but I want You alone, O my sweet Love!" But the more she wanted to flee such consolations, the more the Lord gave them to her.

3. Sometimes (as was said) she hid herself and stayed frequently in lonely places, because she was so consumed by the love in her interior that she could no longer associate with people. If she was then sought, she was found completely outside herself lying on the earth, keeping her face covered with both her hands, and indeed in such a lovely manner that it cannot be expressed; when she was called, she did not perceive it at all.

4. At other times she walked constantly up and down, without anyone knowing why she did so; but she did it as if outside of herself, and driven by the power of her love.

# Tenth Part. The Life

One person grumbled, while another wondered why she was unable to eat; she herself, however, made no great display of it, but said: "One ought to value the inner workings of God much higher than external things. That I do not eat happens without my own will through God; no one should wonder at this. The True Light teaches us that we must only pay attention to pure love <note>Original: *reine Liebe*—a central concept in Catherine’s mysticism, referring to loving God for His own sake without seeking reward or fear of punishment.</note>, through which His Divine Majesty works within us. And when the soul sees the so clear and pure workings of this love, and that it has no ulterior motive regarding the good we might perhaps do, then the soul must likewise love Him with a pure love, without looking for any special gifts of grace she might receive. Instead, she must look only to Him alone, who alone is worthy to be loved without measure and without [selfish] intent."

4. In the first four years of her conversion, she lived in great severity and the mortification <note>Original: *Abtödtung*—literally "killing off" the desires of the flesh.</note> of her nature. As soon as her flesh desired any thing, she took it away and gave it that which was contrary to its liking. She did the same with her senses; whenever they wanted something, she resisted them immediately. At this time, she ate no fruit nor any other flavorful foods. And because she was by nature very talkative and knew well how to interact with people, she resisted herself most of all in this regard; when her relatives visited her, she overcame herself and spoke as little as was ever possible, and cared nothing if people wondered at it. She never laughed; she looked almost always downward toward the earth and did not recognize those who passed by her, for she was so occupied within that external things were as if extinguished. She always appeared to be sad, though she was actually very happy. In sleep, she also resisted her comfort, for the fire of love was so fervent in her inner being that she paid little mind to outward matters, though she did not reject what was absolutely necessary. In this manner, she mortified all her senses without finding any difficulty in doing so. In these first four years, she remained in prayer for six hours every day; and although her physical nature felt much distress in this, it was nevertheless so obedient to the spirit that the heart did not have the will to resist.

5. She was at that time so filled with internal sensations that she could not speak except so softly that one could hardly understand her; she was so occupied and taken up within that she seemed dead to all external things. "I do not live," she said: "I do not feel that I have a soul, nor a body, nor a heart, nor a will, nor a taste, nor anything else, but only a pure love." Nonetheless, she lived in great submissiveness toward everyone, and sought only to do what was contrary to her own will, preferring to do the will of another rather than her own.

6. As she walked in such "dying away" of all her senses, she was sometimes asked: why do you do such things? To which she answered: "I do not know; I only feel myself drawn to do so inwardly and without any resistance, and I believe that God wants it so; but He does not want me to serve Him with attachment <note>Original: *Anklebung*—refers to spiritual "clinging" or being attached to specific practices or feelings rather than to God Himself.</note> to anything." This was indeed found to be true; for when these four years had passed, all such mortifications were

## The Fifth Chapter.

### Concerning various extraordinary gifts of grace, and some rules which God gave to her; her longing for death, and works of love within and outside the hospital in Genoa.

->I.<-

After those first four years of her conversion, she was given a pure, free spirit <note>original: *esprit*—the German text uses the French word here to denote a refined or spiritual intellect.</note> so filled with God that henceforth nothing foreign entered into it. # Tenth Part. The Life

5. At times she remained as if dead for as long as six hours; and when someone called to her, she stood up, answered, and went to perform whatever was necessary; for she shunned <term>self-will</term> <note>original: *Eigenheit*—referring to the ego's attachment to its own desires or possessions</note> like the devil himself. When she emerged again from the place where she had hidden herself, her face was quite reddish.

6. Once, her Love <note>Referring to Christ or the personification of Divine Love</note> said to her in the spirit: "My daughter, observe these three rules:

(1) Never say, 'I will,' or 'I will not.' Never say 'mine,' but always, 'ours.' Never excuse yourself, but be always ready to accuse yourself.

(2) When you say your prayer, always take as your foundation these words: 'Thy will be done' in all things, regarding the soul, the body, children, relatives, and in all that may happen to you, whether it be good or evil.

(3) Furthermore, take from the Holy Scripture as your support this word: **Love**, with which you will always be able to walk straight, pure, light, diligent, swift, enlightened, without error, and without the help or means of creatures; for love requires no help, as it can do everything without fear and without difficulty, so that even martyrdom seems sweet to it."

7. She lived as if taken out of her senses, and did not know whether she had a soul or a body; for they were so ignited in this furnace of divine love, and thus outside of themselves through a constant withdrawal <note>original: *Abziehung*—a mystical term for the soul's retreat from sensory perception into God</note> and union, that she could almost no longer see, nor hear, nor smell; at the very least, she could no longer take any delight in them. When she performed some manual labor, the work would fall from her hands out of faintness; and weeping, she said: "O God, my Love, I can do no more!" and sitting down, she remained for a time thus abandoned by her senses, as if she had been dead. This happened to her more at one time than at another, according to whether her purified love was more or less filled with this infused grace.

8. During the time that she tasted such <term>spiritual sweetness</term> <note>original: *geistliche Süssigkeit*—a technical term for the pleasant emotional or spiritual sensations felt during prayer</note>, and had such a great and lovely sensation that she was not at all able to perform anything or to use her senses, her spirit said to its humanity: "Are you satisfied that you are treated in this way?" She said yes, and that she would gladly exchange every other taste for this one.

9. These great sweetnesses, however, were only communicated to her in the beginning; for after that time, her heart felt such a great fire of pure and piercing love that one could hardly touch her, and it seemed to her that she had a wound in her heart, which beat so violently that she had to hold it with her hand. This was greater on one day than another; when this greatest heat had passed a little, her heart remained entirely melted in this divine and wonderful

10. At that time, she longed only for **Death**, so that she might go to see the truth of what she felt in her heart; for two whole years, she lived in this perpetual desire to die. She called death sweet, lovely, pleasant, beautiful, strong, rich, and worthy, and gave it many other titles of honor. Afterward, she said: "I find only this one thing to reproach in you, O Death! Namely, that you come all too slowly to those who desire you, but all too quickly to those who flee from you." Yet, I see well that you do everything according to the decree of **God**, in which there can be no fault; therefore, it is only our own disordered desires which cannot reconcile themselves with you. Were they peaceful and at rest, without grumbling against **God’s** will—just like death, which does nothing except what **God** wills—then we would reach a state where we would choose neither life nor death, as if we were already buried. Nevertheless, she confessed that if she could have chosen anything, she would have chosen death; because through it, the soul is placed beyond the fear of ever being able to do anything that might hinder her pure love, and is liberated from the prison of this miserable body and this world, which pull her toward their affairs in manifold ways and means.

11. In the beginning of her conversion, Saint Catherine practiced works of love most diligently. She sought out the poor in the city, in which she was guided by the so-called "Ladies of the Office of Mercy" <note>These were noblewomen in Genoa belonging to the *Mandatörie*, a charitable organization that distributed alms and assisted the poor.</note>, who gave her money and other necessities for that purpose. She served the sick; she cleaned them of their filth; their clothes, which were filled with lice and other impurities, she carried to her house and brought them back to them well-cleaned. She served the sick with the most burning affection, both in regard to their souls—by holding conversations with them on spiritual matters—as well as in regard to their physical needs; nor did she ever withdraw from any sick person, whoever he might be, or however dangerous his illness might be.

### Tenth Piece. The Life

III. When you are called to perform any works of mercy toward all kinds of poor and sick people, I desire that you should go and never refuse such a request; you should then go swiftly and leave everything else behind, and cleanse the sick of their filth; you should also not look to see who it is that calls you, nor what task is to be done for you.

IV. I do not want you to have any choice at all; the will of another shall be your will, but your own will you shall never carry out. And in this, I will exercise you for as long as I see it to be necessary; for I wish to kill and extinguish in you all disordered pleasure and displeasure that you can have in this life.

V. Whenever I command you to perform some work that is contrary to your nature, and I perceive that you still see and feel its difficulty, I will keep you at that work until you no longer see or feel it; and I will do the same in those things which may be pleasant to you.

VI. I desire that you love everyone without [human] love <note>original: "ohne Liebe." In this mystical context, it refers to a detached, divine love free from personal preference or selfish attachment.</note>, without affection, and with indifference—the poor as well as the rich, enemies as well as friends, strangers as well as relatives. Behold, this is the rule you should observe in your dealings with creatures on Earth.

13. For approximately three years, she persevered in these exercises; thereafter, she was requested, along with her husband, to come live in the Great Hospital in Genoa <note>This is the *Ospedale di Pammatone*, which Catherine would eventually lead. Her husband, Giuliano Adorno, had undergone a conversion after squandering their fortune.</note> to serve the sick. They then accepted this proposal [either because poverty compelled the husband to do so, since he had run through all her property, or because he was already a little more inclined toward it, as shall be told hereafter]. Now, while she was in the hospital, she had to be so submissive to those who presided over it, just as if she had been their maidservant. She hardly dared to open her mouth; she lived with her husband in a small chamber in silence and <term>Gelassenheit</term> <note>A key term in German mysticism meaning "yieldedness," "serenity," or "composure"—a state of letting go of one's own will to rest in God.</note>, and as one subjected to everything that was commanded of her. Whenever any matter was entrusted to her, she completed it with all diligence, even though those who lived in the hospital made nothing of it and held her in low esteem. She remained in this exercise for several years with great suffering.

14. Now, when the Spirit had tested her nature in all these miseries and saw that He was lord and master, she had to enter another, opposite trial. She was namely elected as the Directress of the hospital; and since she had to govern the same, the Spirit wanted to try for once whether her nature would still allow its malice to peek through in a state of honor and high regard. For several years she remained in this service; she took care of everything in the hospital; yet, no matter how much she worked in her office, she never lost the sensation of her sweet love, and the hospital never lacked the slightest thing, which everyone regarded as a miracle. At the same time, it was a wonder that despite this great immersion in divine love, she neglected nothing necessary; indeed, for many years she managed and submitted the great accounts of many sums of money, without the slightest

## The Sixth Chapter.

### Knowledge of self and of **God**; the Nothingness of the creature;
### the Allness of **God**; her humility, through which she attributes all
### good to **God**; the purity of her conscience; **God**
### and sin cannot exist together.

->I.<-

**This** holy soul was so purified, enlightened, united, and transformed in **God** her love, that the words she spoke (concerning their deeper meaning) were not human, but angelic, or rather divine. [What a deep knowledge both of herself and of her **God** our Saint possessed is shown by the following discourses:] "If it were possible," she said, "that I alone, for the sake of the love of **God**, had suffered all the deaths by martyrdom that all the martyrs together suffered—yes, and beyond this had endured all the pains of hell—and I then wished to entertain the thought that I had thereby done enough for **God**, I would thereby offend Him in the highest degree; specifically, if I weighed my suffering against the love and goodness with which He created, redeemed, and called us; for man, without the grace of **God**, is an incarnate devil."

2. "I see clearly that if there is anything good in me or in any other creatures, it is truly from **God**; but if I do anything evil, I do it alone; and I can attribute the blame neither to the devil nor to any creature, but only to my own will, evil inclination, pride, self-centeredness <term>Eigenheit: A technical term in German mysticism referring to "self-hood" or the soul's tendency to possess itself rather than being possessed by God.</term>, and sensuality. If **God** did not stand by me, I would never do any good; but as far as evil is concerned, I see that of my own accord I am more evil than **Lucifer** himself; and I see this with such great certainty that if all the angels wanted to persuade me that there was something good in me, I would not believe it, because I see clearly that all good is in **God** alone, and in me, without the grace of **God**, there is nothing but evil."

Tenth Part. The Life
<meta>catchword: 7. It</meta>

3. It seems to me, she said, that the love with which I love my sweet Love <note>original: "meine süsse Liebe"; Catherine frequently refers to God simply as "Love."</note> grows greater daily. In the meantime, I always consider it perfect; for it is the nature of love that it cannot tolerate the slightest defect. But after the time when my vision became clearer, I recognized that I have had many imperfections; had I recognized them at the beginning, I would have willingly taken upon myself every conceivable torture, even the pains of hell, to be rid of them. But God, my Love, did not allow me to recognize them then, but He wanted to do everything little by little; for if one had such deep insights all at once, one would take such excessive things upon oneself, which would so far exceed order and fairness <note>original: "Billigkeit"; here meaning spiritual balance or reasonableness.</note>, that one would become unbearable both to one's neighbor and to oneself. Now, since I see how everything that is truly perfect is entirely outside the creature <term>creature: in mystical theology, this refers to any created being, specifically the human self as distinct from the Creator</term> and in God alone, I am forced to say that everything the creature can possess of it is nothing but imperfection.

4. When our Catherine discoursed, she often had these words in her mouth: Friendliness of God, Purity of God, Goodness of God, Sincerity of God, and more such beautiful words. I see, she said, without eyes; I understand without understanding; I feel without sensation; I have neither measure nor form; for without seeing I see such a divine effect and virtue, <insert>or power</insert> that all these words of perfection, purity, or sincerity seem to me like mockery in comparison with this truth and with this righteousness. The sun, which previously seemed so clear to me, now seems to be dark; what previously seemed sweet to me now seems to be bitter; because all clarities, beauties, and sweetnesses are stained and spoiled by the mingling <insert>or effect</insert> of the creature. But when the creature finds itself purified and transformed in God, then it sees what is pure and true; and of this vision, which is actually no vision, one can neither speak nor think, and I can say nothing of it. God is mine, and all is mine.

5. I cannot call a single saint blessed in himself, but I see that all holiness and blessedness of the saints is outside of them and entirely in God in the most excellent way. I can see neither good nor blessedness in a single creature where it is not annihilated in itself in such a way, and so sunken in God, that God alone remains in the creature, and the creature in God.

6. Vain honor had no entrance into her soul, for she had the knowledge of the truth; <insert>from which arose in her</insert> a mistrust of herself, and a total trust in God alone, her sweetest Love, to whom she completely surrendered her soul and her body, saying to Him: Lord, do with me everything that You will. This she said with a firm trust that He would never forsake her, much less let her fall into any sin; for she would rather have endured all the pains of a thousand hells than have seen a single stain of the smallest sin in her; although, she said, no sin is small before God, nor simply great, but must be called truly great: because it is committed against such an immeasurable goodness.

She describes a mystical state of "seeing without eyes" where the soul is so united with God that the self is effectively annihilated.</summary>

### of Saint Catherine of Genoa. Chap. VI.

7. This soul felt not only no vain honor within her, nor any resistance toward humiliation; on the contrary, it was very dear to her when she was reminded or punished because of some evil inclination she might have had, and she never made excuses for herself.

8. 
> I would not like to see (she said) that a single meritorious work were attributed to me, even if I were assured that I would no longer fall into sin, but would infallibly be saved; because the sight of such a work would be like a hell to me. For if I should see that I alone had worked on my salvation, and that I alone had performed a single work which—insofar as it were mine—could help me toward my salvation without the grace of God, I would be worse than the devil, because in that way I would rob God of what is His; since all works of virtue which are not animated by sanctifying grace <term>sanctifying grace: original: "angenehm machende Gnade." In theology, this is the divine life in the soul that makes a person pleasing to God.</term> are nothing and worth nothing. Nevertheless, one must practice; for where we do not cooperate with grace, grace does not wish to save.

9. The hatred of herself that Saint Catherine had caused her to see clearly that all good came from God alone; she saw, she desired, and she willingly left all good in God alone.
> If I could (she said) find in any creature <term>creature: in mystical writing, this refers to any created being, specifically the human self as distinct from the Creator.</term> something good that was its own and originated from itself and not from God (which, however, is impossible), I would take it by force from the creature and lay it all back in God. All good movements and all good works of which we can even think or speak have all come down from this primal source of infinite love, which, it seems, has nothing else to do but to provide for our salvation through countless means; but the creature of itself can think of nothing but its sensuality and sins, according to the inclination which sin has imprinted upon nature, and which always pulls it downward, just as a stone thrown into the air has a ceaseless inclination to return to the earth.

10. 
> The purity of conscience (she said) can suffer nothing else but God alone, who is pure, clear, and simple <term>simple: in a theological sense, "divine simplicity" means God is not composed of parts but is a single, perfect essence.</term>.
Often she had the word *purity* in her mouth; in her speeches one sensed a wonderful purity and clarity; she wanted everything that the soul perceived inwardly to come forth quite clearly and purely, without appearance or pretense. She could not show herself outwardly as having compassion for her neighbor—such as out of friendship or where it was otherwise necessary—except only insofar as she experienced that she had an internal agreement [and freedom] for it.

11. She had such great humility, such great contempt and hatred of her self, that when, by divine permission, she was sometimes in such great mental suffering <note>original: "Gemüthsleiden"; this refers to periods of intense spiritual desolation or psychological distress.</note> that she could hardly open her mouth, she said:
> O Love! Let me always remain so, so that I may be lowered and humbled by it; grant that this state does not change, because otherwise I can do nothing but evil.

# Tenth Section. The Life

12. It is impossible for God and sin, however small it may be, to exist together; for this reason, the slightest sin prevents God from occupying a soul with His **glorifying light** <term>glorifying light: original: "herrlichmachendes Licht." This refers to the "beatific" light of God's presence that grants the soul a share in His glory.</term>; just as the smallest speck of dust makes the eye unable to see the sun. If, then, a soul wishes to be preserved from sin in this life and glorified in the next, it must be pure, clear, and **single-minded** <note>original: "einfältig." In mystical literature, this refers to a heart that is undivided and focused solely on God.</note>, so that nothing impure remains within it through its own will.

13. He who falls into sin must attribute the guilt to himself alone. God is always ready to help us, even if a soul has fallen into sin—no matter what kind of sin it may be—provided that the fallen soul allows itself to be helped and gives room to the grace that unceasingly calls it back. If the soul then repents of its sins with a sincere will never to commit them again, the Lord raises it up again from all its sins in that very moment; He also preserves it from all relapse, as long as it does not separate itself from God again through its own **malice** <note>original: "Bosheit." This implies a willful or wicked turning away from the divine.</note>.

14. I must therefore, she said, live without myself, for Love has shown me what I am. And I recognize this in such a way that I can no longer be deceived therein; indeed, I have so completely surrendered this whole "self-part" that I can value it no more than if it were a devil. After God has shared this light with the soul, it no longer can or will act with this "self-part," with this nature, with this **corrupt and hidden ground** <term>corrupt and hidden ground: original: "verderbten und bedeckten Grund." In German mysticism, the "ground" (Grund) is the deepest essence of the soul; here, Catherine describes it as being fouled by human ego.</term> which defiles everything, and even makes the pure water of God's grace turbid with its **slime** <note>original: "Schleim." A vivid metaphor for the "muck" of the human ego interfering with divine purity.</note> when one tries to draw it with this unclean vessel.

15. Therefore, where a soul is enlightened in this way, it offers itself up and abandons itself entirely to God, who then occupies His creature from within and without with Himself, so that it can no longer act except as much and in such a way as this **sweet Love** <note>In Catherine’s writings, "Love" (Liebe) is often used as a direct name for God.</note> desires and permits; such a soul then does not contradict God in the least because of the union it has with Him, and it performs no other works but those that are entirely clear, entirely pure and righteous, indeed pleasant, lovely, and delightful: because God removes all types of sadness and anxiety from it.

# The Seventh Chapter.

## The great Love and Care of God for mankind; the misery, malice, and cunning of our own will; visions of how the goodness of God communicates itself to His creatures, sustains them, and allures them to Himself.

1.

I see through the inner eye that God loves all His creatures with a love so perfect and so immeasurable that no angelic <note>original: "englischer." In this historical context, the word refers to angels (Engel), not the English nationality.</note> understanding can comprehend even the smallest spark of it. God has the greatest sympathy <term>sympathy: here used in the classical sense of an "affinity" or "natural resonance" between God and the human soul.</term> and uniformity with the rational creature; only take sin away from man, and then let the goodness of our God act, which, so it seems, has nothing else to do but to seek how it may unite itself with us. Indeed, one might almost say that He does violence to the freedom of man through the intimate and loving inspirations which He sends to him in abundance. The closer one comes to God, the more one recognizes that this is true; and one does not know how one can still remain alive after having recognized this.

2. When I behold (she said) with what love and care God provides us with all the necessary means to lead us back into His land, I am forced to say that this good God seems to be our servant. If man could only once see the care that God has for the soul, he would stand utterly confounded when he considered how the God of Glory, who stands in need of nothing as He who contains all things within Himself, takes such great care for the creature. And yet we, who receive all the benefit or harm from it, regard such things so lightly.

3. But if we do not hold that in high esteem which God prizes so highly, what then should we consider important? O you miserable man! To what ruin do you bring yourself? What are you doing with your precious time? With the wealth by which you could purchase heaven? <insert>If you would apply the same to repentance and faith.</insert> What are you doing with yourself, you who should devote yourself entirely to the salvation of your soul? And what are you doing with this soul, which should unite itself through love with its God? You have turned all of this toward the earth, which will produce nothing else for you but such a crop, and thereafter such damnable fruits, that you will have to eat of them with the devils in hell. There you will tear yourself apart in infinite despair because you have lost the glory for which you were created, and to which you were called by your sweet Savior with so many inspirations <insert>and the chastenings of His grace</insert>, so that you will recognize it was only up to you that you were able to enjoy this glory.

<meta>This page continues the spiritual testimony of Saint Catherine of Genoa (1447–1510), specifically focusing on her intense "holy hatred" of sin and the deceptive nature of the human "own-will" (ego). It follows from her description of God’s overwhelming love, contrasting it with the soul's struggle to release worldly attachments.</meta>

Tenth Part. The Life. 252

[The soul] would much rather choose to be in a burning furnace all his life than to tolerate [sin] within himself; and if the sea were made of pure fire, he would much rather plunge into the middle of it and down to its very bottom to escape sin; and he would not come out from there if he knew that he would have to see sin within himself upon coming out. This will seem unbelievable to most, as if one were merely exaggerating; but all this is almost nothing to a soul who recognizes the Truth as it is.

5. When I behold (she said): what God is, and on the other hand, what our misery is; and how God seeks through infinite means to pull us out of the same, provided we place no hindrance in His way, I become quite dismayed and go entirely out of myself. I see that the "own-part" <note>original: "eigene Theil." This refers to the self-centered part of human nature that remains separate from God.</note> of man is so contrary and rebellious toward God that He can hardly bring it to do His will, except through caresses and good words, promising it far greater things than those which it must leave behind—yes, even giving it a foretaste of the bliss of the next life already in this one. He does this because He sees that the soul loves visible and sensory things to such an extent that it would never let go of one thing unless it saw four others in exchange. And even then, the soul would still seek to flee if God did not constantly hold it back with some new grace [and benefit], whether external or internal. Without these, man, because of his evil nature, would not be able to preserve himself from evil; for the sting and the inclination to do evil—which arises from original sin as well as actual sin, and from our self-complacency—continually draws our senses toward earthly things.

6. Now, just as Adam desired to do his own will against the will of God, so we must have only the will of God as our object, so that it may annihilate our own will. And because we cannot annihilate this own-will through ourselves, due to our evil nature and self-love, it is very useful to subject oneself to someone else for the love of God, so that out of a pure and sincere intention for the honor of God, one does the will of another rather than one's own. The more one subjects oneself to such a person, the more one will find oneself in freedom and delivered from the dangerous plague of one's own will. This will is so subtle <term>subtle: in this 18th-century context, it means "crafty," "insidious," or "fine-spun" in its deceptions.</term>, so cunning, so malicious, so inward, and so deeply rooted in us, and knows how to cover itself through so many means and defend itself through so many apparent reasons, that it seems to be a devil full of malice. It is of such subtlety that where we cannot fulfill it in one way, we do so in another, under a thousand pretenses and cloaks of love, necessity, justice, or perfection; or under the appearance of suffering for God's sake; or to receive some spiritual comfort; or under the pretext of preserving our health, or giving a good example to our neighbor, or that one is "stooping down" to do or say something for the convenience of one who desires it of us. Thus, I see such a vast sea full of the poison of contrariness and rebelliousness against God, that no one but He alone can pull us out of it.

### of Saint Catherine of Genoa. Ch. VII. ###

7. Because He sees and recognizes this better than we do, He has such great compassion for us that He does not cease to send us good [means and] inspirations to deliver us from it, yet without forcing or doing violence to our free will; rather, He guides it through so many loving ways that a soul who opens her understanding and sees the great care God has for her is compelled to cry out and say: O my God! It seems You have nothing else to do but think of me. Who am I, that You should take such great care of me? You, who are God, for me, who knows not what I am! Oh, what care must I not take for that which You value so highly! With what diligence ought I not always submit myself to Your commandments, and pay heed to the sweet inspirations You incessantly send me through countless means?

8. I have (she said) had a divine vision <note>original: "Gesichte," referring to a mystical revelation or spiritual sight.</note> which gave me much pleasure. I saw in God the living source of all goodness, how the same had been entirely in Him alone from all eternity, without anything else having a part in it. Afterward, I saw that in the creation of the world, He began to make His creatures partakers of it, and for that reason, He created the beautiful company of angels, so that they might enjoy His unspeakable glory; and He required nothing else from them but that they should recognize themselves as creatures, created by His highest goodness, and that they had their whole being from Him—without whom all things would turn again to pure nothingness. The same must also be said of the human soul, which is also created immortal for this end: that it may enjoy this very same bliss. Now, since some angels (who are likewise immortal and cannot be annihilated) clothed themselves with sin through their pride and disobedience, God immediately withdrew from them the communion they had with His goodness; thus they became so hellish and terrifying that the hundred-thousandth part of their malice cannot be conceived, even by those who possess the light of God.

9. Yet God still bears with man, who is also His creature, although he is mired in sin; He governs him through His goodness, by which He allows us either to be plagued, chastened, and troubled, or else gladdened and comforted, according as it pleases Him to communicate this goodness to us, and according as He recognizes it to be useful and profitable for us—seeing that we are surrounded with flesh <note>The "flesh" here refers to the physical body and its earthly impulses, which the author views as a source of spiritual blindness.</note> which keeps us in much ignorance and frailty; therefore, He bears with us as long as we live here; He caresses us, He lures us incessantly through the participation of His goodness, which we can so poorly recognize.

10. But when the soul has departed from this life and finds itself in mortal sin <term>mortal sin: a grave sin committed with full knowledge and consent that separates the soul from God's grace</term>, then God withdraws this goodness of His from it and leaves the soul to itself. God has given me to see a small glimpse of His truth, so that I might recognize what man is without God; the soul is then infinitely more abominable and terrifying than can be thought or imagined.

# Tenth Part. The Life

<meta>catchword: passi</meta>

11. Therefore, no one should wonder at what I say and feel—namely, that I cannot live with myself, but that I must live without myself; that is, without any movement of my own <note>original: "ohne einige eigene Bewegung," referring to the mystical state of "holy indifference" where the soul no longer acts from personal desire.</note>, whether of the will, the understanding, or even the memory. When I speak, when I walk, when I stand still, when I sleep, when I eat, or when I perform any other task, I know and feel nothing of it in my inner being as if it came from myself. These things are further removed from me—that is, from the ground and interior of my heart—than heaven may be from the earth. On the contrary, if any of these things could enter into me through any means and give me the "taste" <note>original: "Geschmack," a common term in mystical theology for the sensory or emotional satisfaction found in worldly activities.</note> that they give to most people, it would cause an unbearable sadness in my inner being. All natural inclinations, both of the soul and of the body, are consumed in me one after another; everything of the "self" <note>original: "Eigene," meaning self-interest or the ego's ownership of actions.</note> must be consumed within us!

12. It was also shown to this holy soul how all actions of man, even spiritual ones, remain without fruit and are worth little—indeed, nothing—before God without supernatural grace. She also saw how God does not cease to knock at the heart of man in order to enter into it and begin His righteous works there; and that no man will ever be able to complain that God did not constantly knock at the gate of his heart. For God comes to all without respect of persons <note>original: "ohne Ansehen der Person," a biblical phrase meaning God does not show favoritism.</note>, and He calls and draws us.

## The Eighth Chapter.

### All Good is in God alone; the "Me" or "Self-hood" must be destroyed; the folly of man, who allows himself to be drawn into eternal misfortune by temporal trifles, from which God's goodness nevertheless seeks to preserve him.

->I.<-

I have always seen (she continues) and I see it better and better from day to day, that all good is in one place alone, namely in God; and that all other goods which are under Him and are received, are only goods through communication <note>original: "Mittheilung," the theological concept of God sharing His attributes with creatures.</note>. But Pure Love can desire no divided good from God; for she wants God Himself—entirely pure, entirely clear, and as great as He is. And if the smallest particle of Him were missing (which is nevertheless impossible), she would not be able to be satisfied, but would believe herself to be in hell.

Therefore, I desire to have no created love—a love that one can taste, understand, or indulge in. I will have no such love which passes through the means [or ways] of the understanding, the memory, or the will passi <note>The catchword "passi" likely leads to "passiv" (passively) or "passieren" (to pass through) on the following page.</note>
