# Tenth Piece. The Life

### of Saint Catherine of Genoa. Chapter XV.

5. ...row; but His Majesty does not let such a siege last longer than perhaps three or four days; and then He leaves her again in peace for just as many days, otherwise she would not be able to endure it, but would have to die of love.

6. When **GOD**, she said, has purified the spirit of its imperfections, which it has taken upon itself through innate and actual sin, then the spirit is drawn and goes to the place for which it was created. Because it finds itself so beautiful, so pure, so worthy, and so excellent, it can no longer find any place that is proper and fit for it except **GOD** Himself, who created it in His image and likeness, with whom it has such a conformity, and toward whom it has such an inclination, that if it could not be transformed and remain in Him, every other place would be a hell to it. When the spirit is thus reintroduced into its actual essence of purity with **GOD**, it is like a drop of water that has fallen into the sea, where, if one searches for it, nothing more can be found but the sea itself, and so forth. One cannot speak of this highest perfection, because all words, images, and examples would be nothing but confusion and untruths in comparison, and would have no agreement with the thing itself. One can only say that the soul that finds itself in this state already receives a part and communion with the blessed in this life (since it is in a deep contentment without taste <note>original: "Vergnügung ohne Geschmack." In mystical writing, "taste" refers to sensory or emotional feelings; "without taste" implies a state of pure spiritual joy beyond physical sensation.</note>).

7. But what this communion or participation actually is cannot be told. and you will never come to know it unless your spirit returns to that purity and clarity in which it was created by **GOD**.

8. But in order to arrive there, **GOD** must consume us from within and from without. To that end, the interior must necessarily die to itself, and its life and whole essence must be found hidden with Christ in **GOD** <note>A reference to Colossians 3:3.</note>, so that the soul itself no longer knows anything of it, nor can know or think of it, just as if it no longer had any life or essence. Yes, it must also become blind, deaf, mute, without taste, and without the operation of the intellect, memory, and will in the external world, and remain completely lost.

9. This creature dwells on earth, but is not of the earth; she has all inner and outer senses, but she can no longer act through them as through human senses, since she is completely transformed in the love of **GOD**. She no longer feels any individual desire or movement in her heart as she used to, but only feels such a subtle and piercing oppression [or siege, *alliégement* <note>The original text uses the French word "alliégement," meaning relief or lightening, alongside "Beklemmung" (oppression). This suggests a paradoxical spiritual state where the "weight" of God's presence actually makes the soul feel lighter.</note>] of the spirit, together with such a great spiritual effect by which she is inwardly consumed, that she no longer regards heart or body at all. She sees how the spirit daily separates itself from all bodily things and gathers itself in **GOD**, in whom it finds such a great, such an intimate, such a secret, and such an unknown abundance, that when it sees that it is still subject to so many adversities in this world, a longing comes upon it...

to cry out loud and say: **Lord**, I can no longer remain in this life, for it is just as impossible for me to remain here with a good will as it would be impossible for a piece of light (a) slipper-wood <note>original: "Pantoffelholz." > which I sense burning and consuming me within!

> Oh, dear mother! do tell us something of it. 
I cannot, she gave as an answer, find any words that would harmonize with such a great love; and everything I would say of it would be so unlike it that one would only do dishonor to this sweet love thereby. This alone I can say of it: that if a small droplet of that which this heart tastes were to fall into hell, hell itself would be transformed into a paradise.

12. Whereupon one who was present said to her: 
> Oh, dear mother! can you then not pray to **God**, your Love, that He might share some of these droplets with your children? 
But she answered with great joy: I see that this sweet love is so favorably inclined toward my children that I can ask nothing of Him for them; I only place them before His countenance.

13. At times she was submerged in this sea of infinite love; and just as it seemed as though nature <note>In this context, "nature" refers to the physical body and its survival instincts.</note> wanted to seek some relief so that she might live and endure in this great fire, it was said to her inwardly:
> Why do you seek relief for nature, and thereby prevent her from dying of too great a love? Why do you say that you can do no more; and what purpose do so many words and so much crying out for some relief serve? 
Then she turned afterward to her humanity and said: 
> If you want to die, then die; as for me, death is 
> better to me than life.

Tenth Part. The Life

# Chapter Sixteen.
## On the Goodness of God and the Wickedness of Man; and of the Great Care of Divine Love to Purify Us from the Imperfections of the Self <note>original: "eigenen Theils," literally "the own part," referring to the ego or the self-centered nature of a human being.</note>.

->I.<-

She said: Our Savior says: (a) No one comes to me unless the Father draws him; and the loving providence of **God** never fails in this regard, as He then speaks: I (b) stand at the door and knock. But our wickedness is so great that if **God** were to look upon it, woe to us! For then He would never be able to look at us or do us any good; but He looks only at His infinite friendliness and goodness, through which He seeks to lead us to the end for which He created us. Toward this very end, He brings forth in us, through His Pure Love <note>term: "Pure Love" (Reine Liebe). A mystical concept describing a selfless love for God that seeks no reward and is free from personal desire.</note>, all the effects that are necessary for us; if we make use of them, our affairs will go well; if not, things will be wretched for us in the hour of our death, and we will have to hear these words of **Jesus**:

> What could I have done for you, you wicked servant, that I have not done?

So that man, however wicked he may be, will not be able to excuse himself; for with the help of **God**, which is so very ready, he can leave his wickedness and say:

> (c) You, **Lord**, have torn my bonds asunder; to You I will bring sacrifices of thanksgiving.

2. And as I see it, that **God**—solely out of regard for His infinite goodness—continually does us good; even so, I also see that man continually fixes his eye on his own wickedness, and his will is always inclined toward evil. But when I see my wickedness subjected under **God's** power, I no longer regard it; rather, it gladdens me to see it subjected in such a way, so that it can no longer act according to its evil impulse.

3. Therefore I recognize that all honor and glory belong to **God**, and all wickedness to man; and that if **God** let him be, and did not hold him back through His mercy, all the wickednesses that are ever possible for a creature would all be found in man; and he would not be rid of them unless the hand of **God** freed him from them.

4. Therefore, I boast in this alone: that I find nothing in me in which I could boast. If there is anyone who believes he has in himself some cause to boast, his glory is vain; and he does not recognize that honor and glory are in **God** alone, and belong to **God** alone, but not to any creature; and thus vain glory arises from ignorance.

5. Since then, she said, Love has taken upon itself the care and the governance of everything within me, and it has never left me again. From that time on, I have taken no further concern for myself; I have also no longer been able to act through my intellect, nor through my memory, nor through my will, <note>In traditional theology, the "intellect, memory, and will" are considered the three primary faculties of the soul.</note> just as if I had never possessed any of these powers. From day to day, I have felt myself more occupied—or rather, consumed—by Him with a great fire. This arose because Love gradually liberated me from all my inner and outer imperfections and consumed them. Afterward, when He had consumed an imperfection, He showed it to my soul; through this, the soul, when it saw the flaw, was even more ignited in love and held in such a state that it could see nothing in itself that might hinder Love. For if it had seen these flaws earlier, the soul would have fallen into despair; instead, it had to live always in such purity as Love required. Whenever an imperfection was to be removed, it was not shown to the soul—indeed, it did not even enter the soul’s thoughts—just as if it did not concern the soul at all.

6. I had handed over the keys of the house <note>A metaphor for the total surrender of her life and will to God’s control.</note> to Love, with the greatest authority to do therein whatever it willed, without regard for soul, or body, or possessions, or relatives, or friends, or the world—only so that nothing might be lacking of all that the law of Pure Love requires. As I now saw that He had taken this care upon Himself (which I recognized well from the fruits it produced), I turned toward Him and kept my face directed there, to behold His necessary and lovely workings. He carried these out with so much love, with such great care, exactness, justice, and goodness, that He satisfied both the inner and the outer parts in whatever was necessary. As for me, I remained so remains so prayerful and occupied in beholding His work that it seems to me even if He had thrown me body and soul into hell, I would have found nothing therein but total love and total comfort.

7. I saw that the eye of this Love was so open and so pure, and its vision so subtle—seeing from such a distance—that I was astonished by the great imperfections it found and showed to me so clearly that I had to confess them. Love showed me many things which would have seemed right and perfect both to me and to many others, yet which Love recognized as wrong and imperfect; indeed, Love found faults in all things. Now, as the "self" <note>original: "eigene Theil," the ego or self-centered nature.</note> saw that it was thus caught in its own malice and peculiarities, and could no longer deny its imperfections which Love had uncovered, it turned to this Love and said: "Because you have such a subtle eye and such great power, I surrender myself to you; and even though my sensory nature is very oppressed by this, deal with everything according to your will and pleasure. My wish is that you strip from me this evil coat of self-love, and clothe me with the pure, clear, upright, strong, burning, and flaming love."

...step by step refined and examined every single thing, with such great care and such great power to reach its goal—namely, to annihilate all its own peculiarities, of which not a single grain can remain in its presence. Although I saw that this part belonging to the self <note>Original: "eigene Theil" – referring to the ego, self-will, or the "proprium" in mystical theology.</note> was more than devilish and of a terrible malice, I nevertheless saw in the end that it remained nearly annihilated through (†) the presence of Love, and through the power that Love used against it.

9. When this upper and spiritual part had done its best and thought it had overcome and suppressed the outer part—depriving it of all the hiding places and means by which it could nourish and maintain itself—and thought it had obtained all the gain for itself and could now enjoy it in peace, then this fierce and insatiable Love suddenly came upon it and said: "What do you then think you are accomplishing? I want both to remain naked and stripped of everything that is beneath me, and I will suffer nothing above me. Know that all these insights, feelings, and perfections that I have not approved are beneath me; and when I begin to sift a soul, I am so subtle that all perfection is a flaw in my eyes: therefore, I do not want a single thing to remain beneath me that may stay in existence, except that which I approve as good."

10. Pure love wants to be alone; and if any other love were in its company, the gates of Paradise would be closed to it; for they are open to pure love alone.

11. When this pure love wants to draw the soul toward perfection, it makes use of various means. First, when it sees that the soul is inclined toward some thing with love, it regards these things as its enemies—these things that the soul loves—and it resolves to consume them without having compassion for the soul or the body. And if Love were allowed to act according to its nature, it would root out all these objects <note>Original: "Vorwürfe" – here used in the archaic sense of objects of desire or things set before the mind.</note> in a single moment; but because it recognizes human weakness, it consumes them little by little; for man could not endure such a great and rapid effect, of which he, because of his imperfection, has as yet no knowledge. Otherwise, when he learns to recognize this divine work in its gradual progress, he takes it better to heart and is daily more and more ignited by this divine fire, which consumes and destroys all desires and imperfect love that might be found in man.

12. But if this divine love sees that we are so stubborn in holding fast to that which we have chosen to love and taken for ourselves—because we think it is so beautiful, so good, and so fair that we do not even want to hear anything spoken against this...

Now that I recognize the truth, I only mourn my own ignorance. And turning to you, O Divine Love, I leave all care for myself to you from now on, for I clearly see that you do everything for me much better than I ever could for myself. I will pay attention to nothing else but your work, which looks out for everything I should truly wish for and desire. It shows the soul how Love overcomes, deceives, compels, caresses, and nourishes her through a thousand lovely means, so that Love may lead her out of the tyranny of self-love and into true freedom."

Part Ten. The Life.

# Chapter Seventeen.

## The external and internal state of this holy soul in the final years of her life. Her longing for death. Certain ecstasies. By whom and in what manner her life story was written. How she was led by God step by step into divestment <term>divestment: the mystical process of "stripping away" (Entblössung) all ego and earthly attachments to be filled by God</term>.

->1.<-

This holy soul was accustomed to being constantly occupied, managing and providing for both the hospital in Genoa and her own household, until she was approximately fifty years old. At that time, she was forced to relinquish this care, both because of great physical weakness and because of the fire of love that burned unceasingly in her heart. Her spirit finally became so removed from earthly things that she could only attend to them with great difficulty. No sooner had she performed a task than her sweet Love <note>Catherine often referred to the Divine Presence simply as "Love" or "her Love."</note> would take it from her thoughts; yet if she was required to be occupied with it or speak of it, it was immediately brought back to her mind. In this way, God did not allow her to fail in any important matter, so that her neighbor would not be offended or hindered.

2. She did not dwell or rest in anything, whether earthly or divine; for she desired nothing but God alone. Thus it happened that she served the sick (†) <note>The cross symbol in the original text likely refers to her legendary service during the Great Plague in Genoa.</note> and scattered herself among the various businesses of the hospital to moderate her inner fire and to flee from all spiritual comforts. But the more she sought to flee them, the more abundantly she was showered with them, so that she was often forced to leave all external business and hide herself in a secret place. There was a singular delight in simply looking at her, and her face seemed like that of a cherub; so much so that those who visited her could not bear to leave her presence.

3. When she reached the sixty-third year of her age, her Love let her experience many fires of love. A spark of pure love was shown to her, and she said that if she had seen it even a little longer, she would have had to give up her life because of its great power. Through this vision, she was brought to a state where she could almost no longer eat, nor speak in a way that could be understood. This wound of love then became so piercing in her heart that it seemed like a physical wound on both sides, and every part of her body suffered pain from it. A few days later (†) she received yet another flame of love, and it always seemed to her that the latest was far greater than all those preceding it.

4. In the year 1507, while she was attending a church service, a longing for death came upon her; the soul desired to leave the body to unite itself with God...

It highlights her struggle to balance earthly duties with her overwhelming spiritual experiences.</summary>

She replied that since this was the pleasure of her sweetest Love, she was content with it, and that she would choose no one else but him, who had given her this counsel; although she knew well that it would be impossible to describe even the smallest part of the internal matters that occur between God and the soul, as few such things had manifested outwardly.

One day, this clergyman said to her that it might well happen that she would die suddenly one day. But such a thought was immediately silenced. Therefore, I tell you that I do not want even a tiny spark of my own desire to remain in this, neither for heaven nor for anything created; rather, I wish to leave everything to divine providence and pleasure."

From that day until her death, all personal desire was extinguished in her, and she was always united and transformed into the will of her sweetest Love.

2. She did not dwell or rest in anything, whether earthly or divine; for she wanted nothing but God Himself alone. Therefore, it happened that she served the sick (†) <note>This symbol likely refers to a marginal note or source citation in the original manuscript.</note> and otherwise scattered herself among the various tasks of the hospital to moderate her internal fire and to flee all spiritual comforts; but the more she wished to flee them, the more abundantly she was showered with them, so that she was often forced to leave all outward business and hide herself in some secret place. It gave a singular pleasure just to look at her, and she appeared in her countenance to be like a cherub; so much so that even those who visited her could not bear to part from her.

3. When she had reached the sixty-third year of her age, her Love let her experience many fires of love. A spark of pure love was shown to her, and she said that if she had seen it even a little longer, she would have had to give up her life because of its great power. Through this vision, she was brought to the point where she could almost no longer eat, nor speak so that one might have understood her. This wound of love became thereafter so piercing in her heart that it seemed to be like a wound on both sides, and all parts of her body suffered pain from it. A few days (†) later she received yet another flame of love, and it always seemed to her that the latter was far greater than all those that had preceded it.

4. In the year 1507, as she was once attending divine service, a longing to die came upon her; the soul longed to depart from the body to unite with

...to be united with God; and the body also longed for death, so that it might be rid of the great suffering caused by the fire of love. Her Love consented to this; and accordingly, for some time she went and saw all those who died in the hospital, both their dying and their burial.

5. It happened one year that she had some ecstasies <note>Original: "Entzückungen." These were profound mystical states where she became unaware of her surroundings.</note> in which she lost consciousness; several people then believed this came from a certain weakness of the head called vertigo <note>Original: "Schwindel."</note>. And she herself, once when speaking of these things with a clergyman, also called it vertigo, wishing for certain reasons to keep it hidden. He, however, said to her: "Dear Mother, it is not necessary for you to keep yourself hidden from me; rather, I ask you that for the glory of God you choose someone who is in harmony with your spirit to tell of the graces God has bestowed upon you, so that they may not remain unknown after your passing, but that God may be praised and glorified." She replied: that since this was the pleasure of her sweetest Love, she was well satisfied with it, and that she would choose no one else but him who had given her such advice; although she well knew it was impossible to tell even the smallest part of those inward matters which pass between God and the soul, even though few such things had outwardly occurred with her.

6. From then on, she began to tell him what had happened to her during her conversion, and everything else that has been faithfully gathered in this book. One day this clergyman said to her that it might well happen that she would die suddenly. (†) When he came to her again the next time, she said to him: "My son, when you told me that day that I might die suddenly, it seemed to me that I immediately felt a certain joy rising within me, and like an internal word which said with a deep sigh: O, that such an hour would come! But such a thought was immediately stilled again. And therefore I tell you that I do not want there to be even a spark of self-desire in this, neither for heaven nor for anything created; but I will leave it all to divine providence <note>Original: "Schickung."</note> and pleasure." From that day until her death, all desire was extinguished in her, and she was always united and transformed into the will of her sweetest Love.

# Section Ten. The Life

> “this human soul considered itself as satisfied as one who is given a drink in his great thirst.” The spirit was so strong and so deeply occupied in **God** that the slightest hindrance was a hell to it; and it had such great freedom and dominion over nature that if nature had wanted to resist it even a little, it would have pushed it back so harshly that anyone who witnessed it would have been dismayed.

8. She did not want anyone to suggest anything to ease her in this confinement <term>confinement: "Einsperrung," referring to a mystical state where the soul feels locked away from worldly comforts and even its own natural desires</term>; for the spirit, which held the reins in its hand, took no pleasure in it; and it seemed rather as if it took delight in tormenting and deceiving nature; specifically, it allowed nature a desire for everything from which it used to draw some refreshment, even letting it taste a bit of it; but soon after, it suddenly took away all taste for that thing; so that she was gradually deprived of all taste for earthly things, unable to find anything, either externally or internally, in which she might have nourishment. This spiritual nakedness <term>spiritual nakedness: "geistliche Blösse," a state of complete detachment where the soul feels stripped of all worldly and even spiritual consolations</term> caused in her a secret and great longing to hide herself; she wasted away little by little; sometimes she felt an impetuous urge to cry out and complain, though she still did not know what she was doing.

9. Her confessor was the only one with whom she had an internal and external agreement; but he was also later taken from her, so that she could no longer tell him anything, nor did she trouble herself about it; in the meantime, she remained in such great confinement that she could turn to nothing in heaven or on earth. She said: I am, as it seems to me, (†) <note>original: "†" – a mark in the manuscript likely indicating a significant theological point or a pause for reflection</note> just like those in this world who find themselves in a foreign land where they have neither home, nor friends, nor relatives; who have also completed the business for which they traveled and stand ready to depart again for their homeland, where they already dwell at all times with their heart and mind; and they have such a great and burning love and longing for their homeland that, because of the intensity of their desire, one day of delay seems like a year.

10. After that time, she was confined even more strictly than before; then she also lost the desire she had had to hide herself; instead, from day to day she found herself more and more restricted, until she could no longer even make known the extreme distress to which she was brought; and everything she had done before was set before her eyes as something in which she had sought her own refreshment and comfort. Nevertheless, to make her state known in some way, she said:

### Tenth Part. The Life

„...life, where you would not want to deprive yourself of the same? I cannot bear the pain that this memory gives me, and I would gladly do everything to let everyone know how terrible is the deprivation of God's love.„

2. This soul was led and instructed inwardly by God, her sweet Love alone, through His (†) <note>original: (†). This symbol usually indicates a cross-reference to a marginal note or a point of particular theological emphasis regarding the "inner word."</note> divine inner word, in everything she needed, without the mediation of any creature <note>This "direct guidance" is a hallmark of Catherine’s mysticism, where she felt God taught her spirit directly rather than through human teachers.</note>. And when she wanted to take refuge in someone, her Love made her feel such distress in her mind that she was forced to let it go, and she then said: "Lord, I understand you well." However, when someone once told her she would do better to submit to the obedience of another for her greater security, and she fell into doubt about it, the Lord gave her an answer in spirit: **"Entrust yourself to me, and do not doubt."** And so her sweet Love wanted to take care of her himself for a long time. He let her taste or understand no spiritual things except what He wanted and what He gave her. When she was at a sermon and delighted in some word she heard, the sensation of it was immediately taken from her, and she was drawn out of herself so that she might taste and understand only what pleased her Love; so that she understood little of the sermon, even if she went in. In this way of life she remained for twenty-five years, and was instructed and led by God alone with a wonderful effect.

3. After that time, either because of her age or her great weakness—since the soul could no longer endure the divine workings because she no longer had influence from the Spirit, which killed the soul in all its sensations <note>The author suggests that the intensity of the divine presence "killed" or numbed her natural senses, leaving her physically exhausted.</note>, and therefore the body remained without liveliness and as if quite abandoned—it happened that the Lord [as already mentioned above] sent her a priest who took care of both her soul and her body. This priest was a spiritual man of a holy life, well-suited for this office; to whom God also granted light and grace to recognize His workings in this soul, and who is the very same one who wrote a good part of the things contained in this book. <note>This refers to Father Cattaneo Marabotto, Catherine's confessor and primary biographer.</note>

4. The first time she was to confess to him, she said: „My dear Father, I do not know where I am, neither as to soul nor body: I would like to confess, but I can see no offense against God that I have committed.„ For regarding the sins she sometimes spoke of, she could not look at them as sins she had thought, spoken, or done; but it was with her just as with a child that had unknowingly done wrong in something; when one says to it, "you have done evil," it feels ashamed of what is said to it, although it does not even recognize that it has done evil.

5. When God worked something in her that caused her to be oppressed inwardly or outwardly, she left this entirely to the judgment of her confessor and spoke with him about it. He also understood it all, by means of the grace and the light...

For this reason, she also spoke to him with great openness, and had no peace until she had told him what she felt. If he happened to have some hindrance that prevented her from speaking with him (as (†) <note>original: (†). This symbol cross-references a marginal note or indicates a point of particular spiritual significance regarding the necessity of guidance.</note> such things often occurred), it seemed to her as if she were in a great fire; but as soon as she had spoken with him, she was content and at peace. His mere presence was a great comfort to her; for when they merely looked at each other, one could understand the other. One day she said to her confessor: "It seems to me that God has commanded you to take care of me alone, and that you should therefore pay heed to nothing but me. If it were not so, God—who sustained me for twenty-five years without the mediation of any creature <note>In this context, "creature" refers to any created being, such as a priest or teacher, as opposed to the Creator Himself.</note> in the spiritual way—would not have joined me to you. Nevertheless, when you have been with me and then go away from me, I cannot say to you that you should not go."

6. If she ever wanted to hide from her confessor what was happening within her, it was made known to him through a divine inspiration, and he said to her: "You have such and such a matter in your mind, and wish to hide it from me, but God does not want this"; at which she was then startled and confessed that it was the truth; and through this she was then freed from her oppression, which she had wanted to conceal.

7. Mention has already been made above how she (†) was married in the sixteenth year of her age to Julian Adorno, who was indeed of noble descent, but of such a peculiar nature and dissolute life that he brought himself and his wife into great misery and poverty. She was nevertheless always obedient to him, and God granted that she endured everything without murmuring, in silence and great patience, despite his strange and disorderly character and conduct; but she suffered so much in the process that she became quite thin, withered, and sickly from it. For the first five years, she was kept so strictly that she was almost not allowed to leave the house. But for the following five years she had freedom, and sought relief among ladies of her own rank through worldly society and amusements, until she was suddenly converted by God, as can be read in more detail above in Chapters I and II. Afterward, she obtained from her husband the agreement that she could live with him in abstinence <term>Enthaltung: specifically refers to a "Josephite marriage," where the couple lives together in perpetual chastity</term> like brother and sister; indeed, he himself eventually entered a religious order <note>Julian became a member of the Third Order of St. Francis.</note>. Finally, he was visited by God with a very painful illness—a retention of urine—which lasted a long time and brought him to great impatience. As he was now near death in this state, Catherine feared greatly that his soul might be lost; for which reason she locked herself in a chamber and, praying for her husband with sighs and tears, said to her sweet Love: "*O Love! I desire this soul from you, I pray you, that you would grant it to me, for indeed you can grant it to me.*" Scarcely had she continued for about half an hour in such prayer with many tears, when she was finally inwardly assured that she had been heard; and entering again into the chamber where her husband lay, she found him completely changed and peaceful, as he then also testified that he was now fully satisfied with the will of God.

# Tenth Piece. The Life

8. After her husband had died, people told her that she was finally freed from the many sufferings she had endured while with him. She replied, however, that she was aware of none of that; she cared for nothing but the pleasure of God, otherwise she took no heed of whatever might happen to her, whether it be good or evil. Her brothers and sister also died not long thereafter; but because she was entirely united with the sweet will of God, she felt no pain because of it. <note>Catherine’s detachment is a hallmark of her "Pure Love" theology, where the soul becomes so absorbed in God’s will that personal grief is eclipsed by divine peace.</note>

9. A friend of Catherine, named Thomasse, renounced the world only gradually at the beginning of her calling, and Catherine could not wonder enough that she proceeded so slowly in it; but the former answered that Catherine hurried toward God with a foolhardy courage; as for herself, she feared that she might perhaps return to the world and only gain great shame from it. Catherine wondered even more at such fear and could not comprehend it, but said: "If I were ever to return, I would wish that my eyes were torn from my head, that my whole body were dismembered and cut into pieces, and that I were torn apart by everyone through all kinds of mockery and shame." Both, however, attained perfection—one gradually, and the other as if in a single moment.

10. There was a man named Marcus du Vel, who was terribly plagued by cancer of the nose and was provoked to an almost desperate impatience. His wife, Argentina, then went to Catherine with a request that she might visit her sick husband and pray to God for him; which she did immediately, for Catherine was of such great compassion and so obedient that if even an ant, so to speak, had requested her to come and perform a work of mercy, she would have allowed herself to be led there at once. When she arrived there, she comforted the sick man humbly and with devotion; afterward, she was accompanied back to the hospital by Argentina, where, throwing herself onto her knees in the corner of a church, she felt strongly impelled to pray for the sick man in Argentina's presence. When Argentina returned home, she found her husband so changed that it was as if a devil had become an angel, saying to his wife: "O Argentina! Tell me, what kind of saint is this whom you have brought to me?" She gave the answer: "That is Catherine Adorna, a woman who leads a very holy life." Thereupon he requested that his wife might lead her to him once more. The following day, Catherine came again, having already recognized the condition of the sick man through the revelation <note>original: "Oefnung" (opening); a term used in mystical literature to describe a sudden spiritual insight or a "channel" opening between the soul and God.</note> she had felt the previous day during prayer. When she came to the sick man, she was embraced by him with many tears, and he then told her how, the previous day after she had left him, the Savior had forgiven him all his sins and reminded him that he should prepare for death because he would soon die: "Therefore," he said, "I beg you, dear mother, that you would take Argentina as your spiritual daughter and keep her with you always." With this, they were both well satisfied, and it was fulfilled accordingly thereafter.

## The Nineteenth Chapter.

### Her way of life. The wondrous effects and the fire of the love of GOD. Her approaching final martyrdom is shown to her in spirit, to the consternation of her outward humanity.

->1.<-

About nine years before Catherine’s passing, she was visited with a completely unknown illness, which indeed did not seem to be a bodily sickness, yet one could also not say that it was an effect of the spirit; thus, no one knew how she should be treated. Medicines were of no use to her, nor was the physical food; those who attended her did not know what to do with her. Her body continually decreased in strength; at times it was thought she must die, but soon thereafter she was well again. She had such violent attacks in body and mind that they seemed to be unbearable.

->2.<-

A year before her death, she no longer ate as much in a week as another person would in a single meal. Half a year after that, she took only a little chicken broth, and nothing more.

->3.<-

The intensity of her spirit, filled with pure love, was so great that her entire body was as if crushed from head to foot; to such an extent that all her limbs and veins were inflamed by the internal fire, causing the greatest pains. Afterwards, she cast up much blood and whatever else she had in her body; they washed her mouth with plain water, but she did not have the power to let a single drop go down. She could not sleep because of her great pains, which made her cry out loudly. She burned from within and without. She could not move herself, but had to be moved by others. This spirit of love <term>Liebesgeist: a common Pietist term for the Holy Spirit acting specifically through the attribute of Divine Love</term> also tested her in this: that He often awakened in her a desire to eat or drink this or that, and when it was then present, the desire was taken from her again, and she could taste none of it.

->4.<-

She remained thus imprisoned and oppressed, appearing to be crucified with an unspeakable martyrdom. On the other hand, however, she was also in the greatest internal contentment, and spoke truly burning words of divine love, with such great power and anointing <note>original: "Salbung" — a spiritual quality of grace that makes speech persuasive and moving</note>, that everyone was dismayed by it and moved to weep with devotion. Many came from afar to see her, to hear her, and to speak with her, all of whom admired her and commended themselves to her prayers. And thus, in her soul was Paradise, and in her martyred body was Purgatory. <note>Catherine of Genoa is most famous for her "Treatise on Purgatory," in which she argues that Purgatory is not an external prison but an internal state of purifying fire caused by the soul's longing for God.</note>

->5.<-

She recognized what was hidden in the hearts of men, and she also revealed such things at times. Often one saw how she was outwardly enraptured, and meanwhile her face was entirely bright and shining; then, when she came to herself again, she would deliver such sublime discourses on the love of GOD that they could be understood by almost no one

However, when she began to speak of this divine love, she became so inflamed that her body became faint and ill from it, and the outward person fell into such a state of abandonment that she recovered only with great difficulty. All her life-force was drawn toward God, and she appeared as if dead, though she lived in Him in quiet peace, according to the word of the Apostle:

6. A year before her passing, she was visited with various graces and divine workings. Just as it was God’s intention to lead this, His chosen one, through a great martyrdom <term>Marter: refers here to "martyrdom" or "torment," describing Catherine's intense physical and spiritual suffering as a purifying sacrifice</term> into eternity, He once let her see the entire order of His work within her in an instant, and what a great and long-lasting martyrdom she had to expect, so that it might surprise her all the less. At this insight, her nature was so dismayed and oppressed that it seemed as if she must die from it. She could find no words to express what had been shown to her; but from her whole being and every movement, one could sufficiently conclude that they were cruel and terrifying things—indeed, things at which the whole world might tremble. This terrifying vision was no sooner over than she uttered such fervent speeches of love that those standing around were filled with consternation, even though they were unable to grasp such words.

7. Another time she had a most terrifying vision; for she saw how her spirit remained so firmly and with such great fervor attached to the beam of divine love that it said to the outward humanity <note>original: "Menschheit" – here referring to her physical body and mortal nature as opposed to her immortal spirit</note>: 
> *I will no longer go away from here, for this is my true place of rest; if you wish to die, so be it, I will remain here with God.* 

At this, her humanity was quite dismayed by this great fire of love and said to the spirit: 
> *How can you do such a thing without causing my death? Since God does not wish for me to die yet, you will surely do nothing against God's will. Because I am to live longer, you must withdraw yourself a little from this so-intense fire and, whether willingly <note>original: (†) - This symbol in the text likely indicates a specific emphasis or a note in the original manuscript</note> or unwillingly, let yourself down to carry me as long as it shall please God, though I am sufficiently assured that you will cause me much suffering, as I see how you become more fervent and stronger from day to day to reach your intended goal, which you will finally attain.* 

But the spirit gradually consumed the natural part and brought it to such great inward and outward weakness that it could almost no longer complain.

8. At a certain time, her mouth said nothing more than these words: *Love of God, sweetness of God, purity of God*; at times she also said nothing but such words: *Love, union, peace*; at another time she said nothing more than *God, God*; finally, she said nothing at all, because everything was locked and imprisoned within.

Love ignited her so intensely that she could not bear it; indeed, it seemed as if her whole body must crumble into dust. In such a state, she turned toward a picture where the Samaritan woman was depicted with our Savior by the water well <note>A reference to the biblical story in John 4, where Jesus offers "living water" to a woman at a well in Samaria.</note>; she then called upon the Lord JESUS and said: "Oh my Savior, I pray You, give me just one little drop of that water of which You spoke with the Samaritan woman, for I can no longer endure such a great fire that burns and consumes me entirely, both inwardly and outwardly." In an instant, her prayer was heard, and she was refreshed both inwardly and outwardly in an inexpressible manner; and thereby she enjoyed some rest for a short time.

10. Regarding the struggle between her spirit and her humanity <term>Menschheit: here referring to the lower, physical nature and earthly inclinations</term>, it occurred to her one day as if she were hanging in the air, and the upper spiritual part desired to fix itself firmly in heaven and pull the soul along with it; but the lower part, or the humanity, desired to remain clinging to the earth. In this way, it seemed to her as if these two parts were struggling with one another, yet in such a way that neither of the two reached its goal, but remained hanging continually in the air. Finally, after the struggle had lasted a long time, the upper part, which pulled toward heaven, seemed to obtain the victory over the opposing part, and pulled it upward little by little with force; and she saw how it removed itself further and further from the earth from hour to hour. Although at the beginning this happened with much resentment from the lower part, nevertheless, once it was so far removed from the earth that it could no longer see it—that is, when all hope of returning to its previous desires was taken away—it began to lose all inclination and drive toward the earth, and to gain a taste for those things which the upper part experienced and tasted. Meanwhile, the spiritual part did not cease to pull it ever further toward heaven, until they finally agreed with one another entirely and were satisfied with the same food, even though the human part still frequently remembered the earth. However, after it found itself raised so high, it also lost such remembrance; it remained firmer, more constant, and more content, both because of the new revelations of heavenly things which were frequently shared with it, and because it gradually lost its natural drive and inclination toward the earth; so that finally it no longer burdened the upper part, which pulled it ever toward heaven to dwell there with it in peace.

...to have, finally to move from the prison of the body into eternal freedom and rest; to touch upon just a little of it here, it happened once at the beginning of the year 1510, that she went one night and locked herself in a chamber, wishing to have neither food, nor conversation, nor refreshment from any creature <note>In this context, "creature" refers to any created thing or being, as opposed to the Creator.</note>; because her spirit drove her to entirely consume and annihilate the human part, so that it might no longer be hindered by it from being able to unite itself freely and perfectly with God. For some time she remained thus locked away, refusing to open the door; but as she once had to go out, her confessor crept into the chamber and hid himself within it; when she then came back, and thought she was still alone in the chamber, she said with a moving voice to the Lord: Lord, what do you want me to do longer in the world? I see no more, I hear no more, I eat no more, I sleep no more, I know no more what I should do or say; all my inner and outer sensibilities are lost; I find in myself neither an inner nor an outer part, like other creatures, because I have entirely forgotten and lost myself in You. Every person finds something to do, to say, to think, or otherwise something to busy themselves with. I see that they still take delight in something, be it something external or internal; but as for me, I find myself as if dead; and yet I still live, because I am held in this life as if by force. There is no creature that understands me; I find myself abandoned, unknown, poor, naked, stripped of all things, removed from the world, and even opposed to it; indeed, I no longer understand what "world" is. Therefore, I can no longer live on the earth among creatures.

2. Afterward, she was visited by another divine operation <term>Wirkung: a theological term for the way God acts upon or "works" within the soul</term>, which was even more subtle and piercing than the previous one; to such an extent that she was almost always like one who is incessantly ill, without obtaining any remedy, neither physical nor spiritual; everyone stood dismayed at these effects, although no one but she herself understood what it was.

3. Afterward, she was wounded by an even subtler and more piercing arrow <note>The "arrow of love" is a common image in Christian mysticism, representing a sudden, intense experience of God's presence that "wounds" the soul with longing.</note>; her body contorted with such terrifying anguish that those standing around were dismayed by it and did not know what they should do. She gave them to understand, though without words, that she felt something great; this attack lasted two hours in its intensity, and no kind of remedy could be brought to her; when it was over, she was asked what she had seen? To which she gave the answer: that she had seen her spirit separated both from all created things and from herself, in such great bareness and purity as it had been created by God, and as it must again possess in order to be perfectly united with God.

4. On another day, she experienced an even more piercing effect of divine love; she was taken by such a fire that she burned entirely and lost her speech because of it. She only gave signs of herself through her head and hands, and it was truly piteous to see her lying so; this lasted about three hours.

5. Another time she was wounded by an even more powerful and subtle arrow of divine love, which worked secretly within her to purify her. This wounding was so great and so mighty that for several hours she lost both her speech and her sight, and it was thought that she would have died. She was struck several times by these divine wounds <note>The "divine wound" is a common mystical concept (often called the *transverberation*) representing an intense spiritual experience that feels like a physical piercing of the heart by God's love.</note>, which were so terrifying that it was a wonder how it was possible that she could still live in such martyrdom.

6. Afterwards she once had a truly difficult day, with much anxiety and such a great internal burning <note>The original German "Entzündung" refers here to a spiritual fever or "inflammation" of love that manifested as physical heat.</note>, that she could not remain in her bed; it seemed as if she were in a great, burning fire; and one could not see her suffer such great martyrdom without weeping, which lasted a whole day and night. No one was permitted to touch her body because of the great pains she endured in all her nerves.

7. After a short relief, she was as if abandoned by God, stripped of all things, and deprived of divine support and comfort; so that nothing remained to her but an impression of the will of God, and indeed only just as much as was necessary for her to maintain her life. In this great stripping <term>Entblössung: a mystical state of being "naked" or emptied of all spiritual consolations</term> she said to God: "Ah! my Lord, thirty-five years have now passed that I have asked nothing of You for myself; but now I pray You, that You would not wish to separate me from You. You know well, my Savior, that this would be unbearable to me. Ah, my Lord! everything is easy for me to bear, except for this separation; for the same is so entirely contrary to the essence of a soul, that it seems she could not subsist therein; but Your divine decree lets her live almost against her nature." These and similar words she spoke in such a moving and heartfelt manner that even the hardest hearts could not refrain from weeping.

8. As God had granted her some rest for a day and a night, there came again a new and even more violent attack than the previous one had been, so that the joy of her spirit might be tempered thereby; for her spirit was right well-pleased as it saw that it was coming ever closer to its desired goal. Her whole body trembled at this attack, especially the right shoulder, which seemed to be entirely separated from the body; a rib also seemed to be separated from the others, with such cruel pains that it seemed impossible for a human body to bear. This attack lasted again twenty-four hours; after that time she had indeed a little relief; but she remained quite weak and full of pain; she ate nothing, she drank nothing, she could also hardly sleep, and it was a miracle that she was still able to remain alive.

9. For several following days she had ever greater and greater pains, and everyone believed she must die. This attack was accompanied by a convulsion <gloss>or cramp-like movement</gloss> in the neck and in the mouth, so that she could neither speak, nor open her eyes, nor draw breath; as she came to herself again, she led

...she spoke with those standing around truly divine words, which kindled hearts in devotion; and everyone stood astonished that she maintained such a calm and contented mind under such terrible martyrdom.

10. On a following night, she had four consecutive seizures <note>The original German "Zufälle" refers to sudden medical episodes or fits common in hagiographies of this period.</note>, each one more violent than the last; she lost her speech and her sight, all her nerves <note>original: "Sehnadern," literally "sinew-veins," a term used at the time to describe the nervous system or tendons.</note> were tormented, and her body seemed to be entirely consumed by the violence and by the great fire. And yet, through it all, she said:
> I find myself in such great pleasure in the spirit, and I feel such great peace in the soul, that no tongue can express it, and no understanding can comprehend it.
She smiled and said to those standing around that they should not be distressed on her account, for she was entirely content; they should only see to it that they lived piously, because the way of God was very narrow <note>A reference to Matthew 7:14: "strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life."</note>.

11. Now, when she had been in great suffering for another four days, it ceased a little; but when her pains returned as before, the physicians <term>Medici: the Latin-derived term for doctors</term> insisted that she should use a medicine; but this medicine caused her so many seizures for eight days in a row that she was not far from death. All who saw her only wished that she might die, so that she might be relieved of the great agony; so that the physicians finally judged that her illness was supernatural.

12. But because the report of this person and her wonderful illness spread here and there, it also moved the excellent physician <term>Giovanni Battista Boerio <note>original Latinized: "Iohannem Babtistam Bocrium"</note>: a famous Genoese physician who served Kings Henry VII and Henry VIII of England.</term>, who had been for a long time in the service of the King of England, to go to Catherine, because he could not believe that her illness was not natural; when he had seen her, he immediately said to her:
> I wonder very much, honored lady, that since you are of such great reputation and esteem in this city, you do not diligently guard against causing offense <note>original: "Aergerniß," meaning a stumbling block or public scandal in a religious sense.</note>, but rather cause so much of it by pretending that your illness is not natural and has no need of medical remedies. Consider that this is a kind of hypocrisy and presumed holiness.
Upon this, she answered in great humility and spoke:
> I am heartily sorry that anyone takes occasion from me to be offended. If a remedy can be found against this illness, I am ready to use it. If you think, my lord, that you can cure me, then I will gladly do everything that you shall command me to do.
To which the physician replied:
> Well, if you will allow yourself to be treated, then I hope that you will be helped.
He therefore prescribed many and various medicines, which she allowed to be given to her without any contradiction; he persisted for a time and prescribed one medicine after another, but not one of them would take effect. When she had persisted for twenty days with the careful use of the prescribed medicines, she finally turned to the aforementioned Boerio and spoke:
> My Lord, have I not now followed all your orders, and done everything that you have wanted? But I find, as you see before your eyes, not the slightest improvement in me. Since I have until now done everything that has pleased you, in order to give no person any offense, you will then from henceforth...

## Chapter Twenty-One.

As this holy soul finally drew closer to her blessed death, her pains also increased, as one suffering followed another. Yet she was also inwardly visited by God with manifold graces. One day her spirit was uplifted by God and drawn to Himself: she kept her eyes fixed steadily on the wall and remained thus motionless for about an hour without speaking a word; but she smiled so sweetly and lovely that one had to conclude she was inwardly in great joy. When she returned to herself and was asked what she had seen, she gave as her answer: The Savior had shown her a tiny spark <note>original: "Fünklein." In mystical literature, the "spark" often refers to a glimpse of the divine essence or the core of the soul's joy.</note> of the joys of eternal life, at which her joy was so great that she could not refrain from laughing. She said nothing more about it, other than these words: Lord, do with me whatever pleases You.

2. On another occasion, when she had been in such great torment the previous day that everyone thought nothing else but that she would die, she again fell into such great and overflowing joy of heart that it expressed itself through a pleasant smile on her face. Everything within her seemed to laugh and rejoice, so that people looked upon her with pleasure and wonder. When the vision was over, she said upon being questioned: I have seen charming faces <note>The word "charming" (original: charmirende) here conveys a sense of divine beauty or enchantment, likely referring to angelic beings.</note> which had such simple, such pure, and such clear eyes that their appearance showered my heart with joy. This supernatural joy remained with her for seven days and was so powerful that such great improvement was seen in her as if she had come alive from the dead. But as soon as this was over, she became even worse than before, as she drew closer to her redemption daily.

3. Afterward, she had a truly difficult day of great heat and pain; she could not move one hand at all, and then she became as if dead for sixteen hours. She was almost always in a very great fire: she felt such a violent thirst that it seemed to her she could have drunk the whole sea, and she thought the entire world was on fire; nevertheless, she could not take a single drop of water, nor could any created thing refresh her, because her

all taste for things was taken away. One day she saw an apple and had a great desire to take some of it; but no sooner did she have it in her mouth than she brought everything back up again with great vomiting.

4. On the twenty-fifth of August, they wanted to give her some cordial <note>original: "Herzstärkung," a restorative tonic or medicinal drink intended to strengthen the heart and spirit.</note>; she took it, though with the utmost effort and purely out of obedience, so that she might not follow her own will; for she had such great esteem for obedience that to satisfy it, she would have accounted all pains, even death itself that might have come upon her for its sake, as nothing. But the restorative she took caused her such great suffering and weakness that she could no longer open her eyes; afterwards, she had the windows opened so that she could look at the sky; and when night came, she had various candles lit and sang, as well as she could, the hymn: *Come, God Creator, Holy Spirit* <note>original: "Komm GOTT Schöpfer, Heiliger Geist," the German translation of the Latin hymn "Veni Creator Spiritus."</note>, and they helped her to finish singing it. When it was over, she kept her eyes fixed toward heaven for about an hour and a half, made various movements with her hands and eyes, and had a very joyful and radiant countenance, but was so weak that they believed she would die. Finally, she came to herself again and said several times: "Well then, let us go, let us go;" adding also: "No, no more earth, no more earth." Following this vision, her body remained entirely crushed; and when asked what she had seen, she replied that it could not be expressed: but that they were excellent and divine things that caused a truly heavenly joy.

5. On the twenty-eighth of August, she again had a difficult night; and during the day she was as if in a great fire, by which she was consumed with unspeakable pain. No kind of medicine or cordial could serve her in the least. All the water of the sea could not have given her the slightest refreshment in her great fire; for she could not take it into herself, and when she finally could let a drop pass, it was consumed in an instant by the internal blaze, so that she was not refreshed by it. Her tongue, her mouth, hands, feet, the left side, and her entrails were sometimes all in such extraordinary torment for three or four hours that she had to cry out vehemently. Her lips and mouth were like a burning oven, and her entire flesh so burning that one dared not touch it—not even her hair or the linen sheet <term>Lailach (or Leylach): an archaic German term for a bedsheet or linen cloth.</term> with which she was covered—without increasing her pain so that she began to cry out loudly. She became as reddish-yellow as saffron because of the great fire; but soon a change would come again so that she was completely cold.

6. On the second of September, she was very weak, and because her great fire, her pains, and sufferings continued to persist, she spoke very little; she also could not bear for anyone to speak to her, nor could she take anything. When she had nevertheless taken a little broth the following day, she remained for about twelve hours as if sleeping and without any sensation.

7. On another day, she experienced a great coldness in her right arm, followed by unbearable pains in the same for eight consecutive hours, so that she cried out with a loud voice. Yet she said during this: "Regarding my higher will <note>In mystical theology, the 'higher will' refers to the rational soul’s decision to align with God, even when the 'lower' physical senses are suffering.</note>, I welcome all suffering for God's sake." The following day, she stretched out her arms because of the great pain, just like one who is nailed to the cross. Lying in such a form of a crucified person, and in such exceedingly great pain, she said: "Let this suffering be welcome, along with every other plague sent to me by the sweet decree and providence of God. Thirty-six years have now passed since you, O sweet Love, enlightened me! From that time on, I have always desired to suffer both internally and externally. Because of this desire, it always seemed to me that I found nothing that caused me suffering; rather, for the sake of your pleasure and providence, everything appeared entirely lovely and most delightful to me. But now I feel such an overwhelming suffering, which tortures me inwardly and outwardly, from head to foot, in such a way that it seems incredible to me that a human body, however strong it might be, could endure such immense pain. Indeed, if it were a body of iron or diamond, it would have to be consumed and annihilated by such suffering. Therefore, it is certain that just as You govern all things according to Your holy and righteous will and providence, You also will it that I should not yet die. For although I endure such immense martyrdom without having any remedy or relief, I nevertheless find myself in such strength that I cannot say that I suffer; rather, it seems to me that I am in such great delight that it is beyond words or thought."

8. On the sixth of September, after she had received the Holy Communion <note>original: "Abendmahl." Catherine was famous for her practice of daily communion, which was very rare for laypeople in the 15th century.</note>, she was not only unable to consume anything further, but could not even draw breath. In her heart, however, she had such a new and overwhelming joy that it expressed itself through a lovely smile for about two hours. Afterward, she saw a new ray of divine love, which was unbearable to her external humanity because of its weakness; and the more her spirit united with this ray, the more her external humanity was disturbed and consumed by it, because it was left to its natural frailty without support. After this, she saw a great ladder of fire <note>The "ladder of fire" is a traditional mystical image representing the soul's ascent to God through the purification of divine love.</note>, by which she was drawn up bit by bit. The entire following night, she was again in such a great fire that she certainly thought the whole world was ablaze with her, and the windows had to be opened because she wanted to see if this were not so.

9. On the ninth of September, she had a vision of her former miseries <note>This likely refers to Catherine's life before her conversion in 1474, which she often recalled with deep humility.</note>, which caused her spirit great consternation. Afterward, it was shown to her what a pure and clean spirit is, when it can no longer have any memory except for divine things; and at this, she said: "O, that one might find oneself in such a state at the hour of death!" As if she had wanted to say: how blessed such a soul would be! Following this, she remained lying motionless and in ecstasy, with a joyful face.

# Tenth Part. The Life of St. Catherine etc. Chapter XXI.

10. On the tenth of the same month, she was presented with various impressions and images of such sins that she had never even thought of, and for which her conscience did not even accuse her; nevertheless, these mere images caused her great suffering. On this same day, she was in such great heat that she thought she was burning entirely. Water was constantly put into her mouth for her refreshment, but she could not swallow a single drop, instead spitting it out again immediately.

11. The following day she lay for a long time without speech; but when her mouth was washed out once, she said: "I am suffocating." This occurred because a small droplet of water had entered her throat, which she could not swallow. This entire day she did not open her eyes, took nothing into herself, and said nothing, but indicated by signs what she wanted. Otherwise, her intellect remained unimpaired, her pulse was so regular, and her face so very beautiful that one would have considered her completely healthy. But at ten o'clock at night, she fell into a great heat; and after she had passed entirely black blood through her mouth, it was seen that she developed black spots over her whole body, accompanied by very intense pains. Her sight was so weakened by this that she could no longer recognize anyone.

12. In the evening of the thirteenth day of this month, and through the whole night, she again passed much hideous blood, which was so burning that the vessels in which it was placed became quite hot from it; and everyone who looked at the quantity of this blood wondered how she could still be alive.

13. As the fourteenth day of this month finally approached, the burnt blood <note>In the medical theories of the time, "burnt blood" (melancholia adusta) was thought to be blood scorched by internal heat, becoming toxic or black.</note> gushed from her in such great quantity that it was judged she would have none left in her body. Accordingly, she had so little pulse movement that it often could not be found; but her mind remained undisturbed. This night she spoke much, and also received the Holy Supper <note>Holy Communion or the Eucharist.</note> toward morning; in this state she remained through the day and a part of the following night. At two o'clock after midnight, she was asked if she wished to partake of the Holy Supper. But when she perceived that her usual hour had not yet come, she stretched one of her fingers toward heaven to indicate that she was going to the Marriage Supper of the Lamb <note>A reference to Revelation 19:9, symbolizing the union of the soul with Christ in heaven.</note> and would now unite herself entirely with her Love, to triumph with Him for all eternity. At that very moment, this blessed soul departed from here in great stillness and peace, and laid herself down in the bosom of her sweet Love for eternal rest. This occurred on September 14, 1510, at the age (as is probably concluded) of sixty-three or sixty-four years.

# The Life
## of
# Angela of Foligno.

### Preface.

The life and writings of this blessed soul, Angela of Foligno, were described in Latin by her confessor and subsequently printed in Paris, as well as in Cologne in 1601. They are also found in the *Acta Sanctorum* of the Bollandists <note>The Bollandists are a group of Jesuit scholars who have published critical editions of the lives of saints since the 17th century.</note> under January 4th. Similarly, they exist in Italian (Venice, 1680), as well as in French (printed in Paris) and in the Brabantian dialect (Antwerp, 1628). Finally, because French copies were no longer obtainable, Mr. Poiret published them under the title *Theology of the Cross* <note>original: "Theol. de la Croix"</note> in Amsterdam in 1696. A noble young woman in Madrid, Francisca de los Rios, is said to have translated these same writings from Latin into Spanish at the age of twelve and published them in 1618.

When one examines the form and orderly arrangement of these writings, one must not assume that they were written down in such a sequence (regarding either time or subject matter) by Angela herself or her confessor. We have at hand a manuscript written on parchment from the year 1415 which teaches us otherwise. This manuscript consists of various pieces, some of which her confessor recorded from her own mouth, while others were written down by a female companion of Angela, also from her dictation. Everything was later read back to her by her confessor. To this are added various original writings and letters by Angela herself. From all these fifteen to twenty pieces, the material was later compiled and (especially in the most recent French edition) brought into a very suitable order. Nonetheless, we have diligently utilized the aforementioned manuscript while preparing this biography and have inserted various parts from it here and there that have never before been printed. Such instances, or where there was a significant variation in the manuscript, have mostly been marked with an asterisk (*).

Although the writings of this holy soul were unknown to many prominent authors who have written bibliographies, they have nevertheless been cited and praised with honor by many others. Thomas à Jesu says: (a) She was a person enlightened by divine light and experienced in spiritual matters. Another (b) calls her: a divine contemplator. See further in the works of Sandæus, Sales <note>Saint Francis de Sales, a Doctor of the Church known for his spiritual writings.</note>, Gelen, Bona, Rodriguez, Bernieres, Boudon, etc.

Among the Protestants (c), I shall cite only the unique Johann Arndt <note>A famous German Lutheran theologian (1555–1621) whose work "True Christianity" became a cornerstone of Protestant devotion.</note>, who not only made good use of Angela's writings for himself but also took much from them (as from other similar writings) for his books on *True Christianity*, which are famous for good reason. As proof of this, I will list several chapters of his second book here, along with the corresponding pages from the *Theology of the Cross*; perhaps this might awaken a thirst to further trace such clear little streams that lead us to the Source of Life from which they sprang.

It is fitting, and useful as proof of the certainty of these matters, that we cite one thing and another here regarding the manner in which these things were initially written down, and what happened to the **Author** <note>The "Author" here refers to Brother Arnaldo, Angela’s confessor and scribe, who recorded her visions.</note> in the process. Thus reads his own report: “When this holy **woman** <note>original: "Weibsperson." In this period, this was a neutral term for a female person, here used with reverence for her spiritual status.</note> began to reveal her divine **mysteries** to me, she told me the most astonishing and wonderful things in the world; she used unusual but emphatic and luminous words. She was distressed that she could not reveal the matters to me exactly as she perceived them. Sometimes, when I had written down what I had heard from her mouth as best as I could and read it back to her afterward so that she might correct it where I had perhaps failed, she would say, not without amazement, that she could no longer understand any of it. Another time she said, to my dismay: I was writing without power and without flavor. Another time she said: ‘Your words remind me well of what I said, but they are quite dark and do not actually express the matter as I perceive it.’ Yet another time she said: ‘You have written the very worst, and left out the most important and precious.’ All of which by no means occurred because I had intentionally changed anything, but only because I could not sufficiently understand her due to my own **unfitness**, or could not write fast enough what she said, and therefore, to my great regret, had to leave much out.

“But in that which I have written, **God** has assisted me in a sensible <note>In this context, "sensible" means perceptible or tangibly felt.</note> way with His grace, which is why I also wrote with great respect and fear, so that from beginning to end, I might not add a single word of my own; for that reason, I also preferred to keep her own **Italian idioms** <note>original: "Italiänische Redarten"</note> in the Latin. I always read back to her what I had written, indeed sometimes more than once, so that I might put down nothing but her own words.

“After I had written everything, I asked this faithful servant of **Jesus Christ** to call upon the **Lord** and ask whether I had perhaps written anything incorrect or superfluous, so that He might reveal it to her, etc. To which she replied: ‘I have already asked the **Lord** for this many times before you told me, that He might make known to me if there were an untrue word or anything superfluous in what I said and you wrote. But He answered: Everything is true; there is nothing false or superfluous in it.’ He also said: I had greatly **(a) moderated** myself; for He had said much to me that I should say, which I nevertheless had not said; also, everything had been spoken to me far **(b) more perfectly**. **God** Himself also said to me: ‘Everything that is written, it is all written according to my will; it comes from me.’ And afterward He said: ‘I will set the **seal** upon it.’ Since I did not understand what that was meant to say, *I will set the seal upon it*, He said again: ‘I will confirm it.’

“Once, this faithful servant of Christ confessed to me, who writes this, as she was accustomed to do; this happened with such perfect knowledge of her sins, with such great **contrition**, with such deep humility and sincerity, and with so many tears from beginning to end, that I too could not refrain from weeping; so that I also held it in my heart as completely certain that even if the whole world were deceived, **God** could nevertheless never allow this soul, whom I saw so full of truth and sincerity, to be deceived.

“Furthermore, **God** has permitted that everything I have written was not only examined by two other trustworthy brothers, but that they also heard it from her own mouth and spoke with her about it.”

May He **(c)** who through the eternal Spirit offered Himself to **God** as a spotless sacrifice, cleanse our **conscience** from dead works to serve the living **God**! Amen.

---

(a) I had spoken temperately. <note>original: "Temparate dixeram"</note> (b) Much more fully. <note>original: "Magis plena multum"</note> (c) Hebrews 9:14.

Eleventh Part. The Life

## The First Chapter.

### Account of the origins of Angela, of the author of her biography, and of the first nine stages of her conversion.

->1.<-

This holy Italian woman, Angela of Foligno, is so named after the place of her birth, Foligno, in the Duchy of Spoleto; where she also lived at the end of the thirteenth century. At the beginning of her conversion, she still had a husband and many children, but they all died one after another; thereafter she entered the Third Order of St. Francis <note>The "Third Order" allowed laypeople to follow Franciscan spirituality while living in the world.</note> and ended her holy life in 1309. We have little information regarding her external circumstances, but her inner character and spiritual guidance—which is our primary concern here—were (as we have already seen in the preface) mostly recorded from her own mouth by her confessor, a Friar Minor <term>Friar Minor: A member of the Franciscan Order, literally "Lesser Brother."</term> named Arnold. He compiled these accounts, along with her personal letters, into a book, which he begins as follows:

[ (a) <note>original: "M. 8." refers to a section in the manuscript sources.</note> Just as God allows His faithful to truly taste, see, and touch through experience the Word of Life that became flesh] as He Himself spoke in the Gospel: (b) <note>John 14:23</note> Whoever loves Me will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him; and again: Whoever loves Me, to him I will reveal Myself. Thus has God recently allowed testimony of this experiential teaching to be given through one of His faithful, namely the blessed Angela of Foligno.

In the name of the most blessed Trinity, I, an unworthy brother, then begin to describe what I was able to obtain from the mouth of this blessed woman with great effort and much pleading, notwithstanding that I was very familiar with her and closely united in the love of Jesus. For she was very reserved and secretive regarding the gifts of God, so much so that I likely would never have obtained anything from her had she not been moved to it by compassion, seeing my sadness because we suddenly had to be so far apart from each other, and it was uncertain whether I would ever see her physical face again. However, she was also entirely compelled by God to tell me these things, just as I, her unworthy scribe, also believe that I was urged by God to describe them.

Otherwise, she also frequently said to me: that because of the loftiness of these matters, she could find no human words to sufficiently express herself, especially when they were things that occurred within her during (c) an extraordinary ecstasy of the mind <note>original: "sonderbarer Gemüthsverzückung," translated from the Latin "in excessiva mentis alteratione." This refers to a state of mystical trance.</note>; for such a thing is entirely inexpressible.

[ Once, (d) while I was writing, she suddenly said: listen to what is being said to me right now;

Another time she said: "I would have a troubled conscience about telling all these things, were it not that a certain word was spoken to me, namely: 'The more you say of these things, the more will remain for you to say.'" <note>This suggests the infinite nature of divine experience; the more she describes it, the more she realizes how much remains unsaid.</note>

II. Afterwards I fell into bitter repentance and shame for my sins, so much so that I could not even bring myself to confess them properly, and for that reason I was punished in my conscience day and night; finally, through God's providence, I confessed all my sins to a preacher and received absolution <term>Absolution: The formal forgiveness of sins pronounced by a priest in the sacrament of Penance.</term>. However, I still felt no love, only shame and pain.

III. The third step consisted in the performance of the penance imposed upon her, which was still done with pain.
