4. Hence it also comes to pass that they are grieved when they have no tribulations; and conversely, the more they are overwhelmed with suffering, the more joy and sensation they have in **GOD**. I, for my part, have experienced this countless times; whenever I have been in suffering on account of the brothers, or despised by other people, I cannot express the sweetness and the comfort in which I found myself at that time; and how the tears I then shed were like a precious balsam to me, which permeated me with pure delight and joy.

5. Another time, when I was very sick, weary, and full of suffering, the God-man <note>original: *Gottmensch* — a theological term referring to Jesus Christ being simultaneously fully God and fully human.</note> **JESUS** Christ came and revealed Himself to me. Just as if He had great compassion for my misery, He said to me: "I have come here to serve you." Now, all the service He rendered me was this: that He stood upright before my bed and showed me such a loving, gracious countenance that it is impossible to describe. I saw Him with the eyes of my soul much clearer than one can see any physical thing, which caused me an altogether exceeding delight and pleasure.

6. Therefore, I say that although one finds trouble and distress in the beginning of penance, and in the sufferings and tribulations that one takes upon oneself for the love of **GOD**, one finally finds a very great comfort in all of it.

7. Another time I was inwardly very tormented, and it seemed to me as if I had no feeling of **GOD** at all, and as if I were entirely abandoned by **GOD**; I could not even confess my sins. On the one hand, I wondered if this might be happening to me because of my pride; and on the other hand, I saw my sins so deeply, and so many of them, that it seemed to me I could not confess them with sufficient contrition <term>Zerknirschung: a deep, heart-felt sorrow for sins, motivated by love for God rather than fear of punishment</term>, no, not even be able to confess them merely with my mouth. I also could not praise **GOD**, nor persevere in prayer. This alone remained to me of **GOD**: that, in my estimation, I did not yet have as much suffering as I well deserved; and also that I would not have wanted to depart from **GOD** through any sin; yes, even if I could have won all the goods of the world thereby, or had to suffer all the martyrdoms of the world for it, I would have consented to nothing evil.

<margin>(a) The Manuscript has *adjuta*, meaning "helped."</margin>

8. Now, when I had been tormented in a truly intense and terrible manner for four weeks and more, the **Lord** said to me: "My dear daughter, you who are loved by **GOD** the Almighty! **GOD** has placed His love in you, and He loves you more than any other woman in this region of Spoleto." <note>Spoleto is an ancient city in the Umbria region of Italy, near Foligno where Angela lived.</note> Then my soul answered Him and cried out: "**Lord**, how can I believe such a thing, when I am so full of suffering and torment that I think I am abandoned by **GOD**?" He replied: "When you think that you are most abandoned, it is precisely then that you are most loved by (a) **GOD**, and **GOD** is precisely then nearest to you." He also added: "A father who has a very beloved child gives the same only a tempered <note>meaning moderate or measured</note> nourishment; he allows the child no pu-

...drink wine, nor eat anything that could harm him, but rather he tempers the wine with water for the child’s benefit. <note>The image here compares God to a careful guardian or nurse who dilutes strong wine so it does not overwhelm a child; similarly, God "dilutes" spiritual joy with suffering to keep the soul humble.</note> So also God does with the soul: He mixes its comforts with temptations and sufferings, and in these very temptations He supports and preserves the soul, which would otherwise fall and be lost. Therefore, when the soul thinks it is most abandoned, it is then most loved.

9. Another time, when I was also in heavy suffering and thought I was abandoned by God, these words were spoken to me: "O my Beloved! Know that you are not abandoned by God, but rather you are now in tribulation, and He is much closer to you." To which my soul replied: "If it be so, that I am much closer to God in tribulation, then I pray to God that it may please Him to take all sin away from me, and to announce to me the forgiveness of the same through the merits of His suffering, and His blessing both to me and my companion, as well as to the brother <note>Likely Brother Arnold, Angela's confessor and scribe, who recorded her visions.</note> who writes down my words." Whereupon He replied: "Your sins are taken away from you; and I give you my blessing with the very hand that was nailed to the cross." Thereupon I also saw this divine hand placed upon our heads, blessing us; the sight of this hand delighted me greatly. And then He said to us three: "The blessing of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit be eternally with you and in you!" He also said: "Tell the brother who writes your words that he should strive to become small. <note>To "become small" is a common mystical term for practicing extreme humility and recognizing one's own insignificance compared to God.</note> Tell him also that he is greatly loved by God the Almighty; and therefore let him strive that he also may love."

10. # of Angela of Foligno. Chapter XII.

1. ...he would not at the same time have some knowledge of her discourses and evangelical teachings. For this reason, we find ourselves compelled to share a brief sketch of her "Doctrine of the Cross" as well; since not everyone is able to read it in Latin or French <note>original: "Lateinischen oder Französischen"</note>; and also because it is a food that is indeed healthy, but at the same time so bitter to the sensory man that even among the "called souls" in these days, almost everyone is disgusted by it. One person slinks past it under one pretext, another under a different seemingly plausible excuse, and politely excuses themselves; thus, it is in great need of recommendation. You poor, crippled, lame, and blind, come with me to the feast. <note>This is an allusion to the Parable of the Great Banquet in Luke 14:21.</note>

2. In the *Theology of the Cross of Jesus Christ* (for this is how the most recent French editor titled the little works of our holy Angela), the content and purpose of the entire teaching of these souls is first summarized in these, her own short words: "Behold here, my children! All that I have to say to you; know and keep it well: that you need nothing but God alone. To find God, to gather your heart to Him, and to unite with Him—see, that is your only important and necessary business."

3. In order to reach this point of gathering and turning your heart toward God, it is (I.) necessary that you take a complete leave of all your old habits, all vain and unnecessary friendships and social interactions with other people, all * superfluous talk, all unnecessary sciences and types of knowledge, and the desire to know much news of what might be happening in the world, all worries and non-essential business; in short, you must separate yourself from everything by which the soul might be scattered. Then (II.) you must go within to recognize the abyss of your great and manifold miseries. No less (III.) must you seek to recognize the great mercy of God, and never forget the immeasurable goodness that Jesus Christ showed us, since He willed to become a companion in all our miseries.

4. Our entire perfection consists only in these two points: namely, in the knowledge of God and in the knowledge of ourselves.

5. As for me, * I am so bound that I can write no letters to you, my dear children, nor to others, except concerning this; indeed, nothing in the whole world delights me to speak of except only this twofold knowledge of God and oneself. Whoever stays with this always lies in his prison and does not go out of his prison. <note>The "prison" is a common mystical metaphor for the "interior cell" or a state of focused spiritual enclosure where the soul is protected from worldly distractions.</note> But should he perhaps wish to go out of his prison, let him seek only with pain and true contrition to return again into his prison. "For I believe that it never goes well for the one who does not know how to stay in his prison, but looks outward at others and does not examine himself, and that he does not possess the true Good."

# Eleventh Part. The Life

...the soul cannot attain through itself, nor through any created thing, neither through letters and words of Scripture, nor through any other <term>science</term><note>German: "Wissenschaft"; in this historical context, it refers to human learning, academic study, or intellectual knowledge rather than modern physical science.</note>. Such things can serve as means and preparation to a degree, but the true knowledge itself comes solely through the communication of divine light and is a special gift of divine grace. And I believe most certainly that no way can be found to attain this divine light and this divine grace from **GOD** Himself—the highest Good, the highest Light, and the highest Love—sooner and more easily than through devout, pure, humble, persistent, and earnest prayer; not prayer that happens merely with the mouth, but the prayer of the spirit and the heart.

7. Therefore, a soul that desires to attain this cornerstone of true knowledge of **GOD** must devote itself entirely to prayer, and alongside this, diligently study, read, and meditate in the true **Book of Life**, which is the entire life of **JESUS Christ** as long as He walked here on earth.

8. Now, the adorable wisdom of the Most High has willed it so that His beloved Son, throughout the entire course of His life, always had this threefold company with Him: first, a perfect **poverty**; second, a perfect, extreme **humiliation and contempt**; third, constant, supreme **sufferings**. The **LORD JESUS** willed to have this company during the time of His life here on earth to teach us by His example that we too should prefer, choose, love, and endure this company above all other things of this world, even unto death.

9. **GOD*** the Father has made this way to union with Him through His Beloved—that is, through His Son, whom He made a Son of poverty, of pain, of contempt, and of obedience. <insert>First, Christ was a Son of poverty.</insert> Through the path of pride, the first Adam fell, and through the path of poverty, the second Adam <note>A common theological reference to Jesus Christ, who "undoes" the fall of the first man, Adam.</note> has raised us up again. Now, while there is indeed no greater poverty than not knowing **GOD** or oneself—which is precisely the pride through which man fell—the **LORD** has found another poverty that we must maintain. We must possess a threefold kind of poverty within ourselves:

First, a **poverty of temporal things**, which Christ possessed perfectly. Therefore, he who is able must follow Him in this; but he <margin>(a)</margin> who cannot do so entirely—such as a count or someone who manages a household—must nevertheless love poverty in his heart and seek to cast off the love for and attachment to earthly things. 

The second poverty is a **poverty of relatives**, which Christ possessed in such a way that, for the sake of His friends or blood relatives, not a single slap <note>original: "Maulschelle"; refers to a physical blow or cuff to the face, emphasizing Christ's lack of protection from family status.</note> would have been spared Him; thus we too must become poor in friends and in all creatures that wish to hinder us in following Christ. 

The third poverty that was in Christ is this: that He was also **poor in regard to Himself**; for though He was the Almighty **GOD**, He became so weak and lowly so that we might follow Him, not by hiding our strength—for we have none—but rather...

### Of Angela of Foligno, Chap. XII.

...our weakness and need must become manifest so that we may see them, [not only through experience] but through devout contemplation and lamentation of our failings, insignificance, and misery. Therefore, a soul that seeks to do the will of the Beloved, which He showed through His example in poverty, must strive to be **transformed** into this very poverty as perfectly as is ever possible for it.

10. Such a soul also desires to be transformed into the pains that Christ endured; for **GOD** the Father made Him the <term>Son of Sorrows</term><note>Often referred to in Latin as the *Vir Dolorum* (Man of Sorrows), a reference to the prophecy in Isaiah 53.</note>, and He was ever in pain; for from the moment of His conception, He was in the highest sadness, because divine wisdom showed Him even then everything He would have to suffer. Thus, His pains began then and lasted until the separation of His soul from His body; as He also showed when He spoke: <note>original: "Meine Seele ist betrübt bis in den Tod"</note> *My soul is sorrowful even unto death*; for by saying that death would be the end of His pains, He also gives us to understand when they took their beginning. Since man was the cause of such pains, we too must be transformed into these pains. And we do this according to the measure of our love. Thus we must now be followers [of the sufferings of Jesus] for the sake of His pains, which were above all pains. We should always be in pain and be eager for the same, and when they come upon us, bear them patiently, whether it be that we are reviled, or ill-treated, or that we fall into temptations; for as long as we do not consent to evil, we must also patiently endure the temptations that **GOD** permits to come upon us. Just as when we fall into any other tribulation or sadness, or otherwise receive pain or suffering through any other thing. We should regard all of this as coming upon us for the sake of following our Beloved, who was always in suffering; only we must see to it that we give no cause for it and suffer as the guilty.

11. Christ was also a <term>Son of Contempt</term><note>A term describing Christ’s state of being despised and rejected by society during His Passion.</note>; for He was despised, reviled, and abandoned by everyone. In this we must follow Him if we truly love Him; for love causes one to desire one and the same thing as the Beloved. But whoever rightly considers his poverty, and is truly poor, also enters into suffering; and whoever is poor and in suffering is despised, so that poverty is the root of it all.

12. Christ was also a Son of Obedience; for obedience drew Him from the bosom of the Father, to whom He was also obedient even unto death. In this we must follow Him, that we be obedient, not only to the commandments of **GOD** and the commandments of our <term>superiors</term><note>Refers to ecclesiastical or monastic authorities.</note>, where we have such; but also to the "messengers" of **GOD's** will, that is, the good inspirations of **GOD** in our souls; let us be quickly obedient to them without any sloth.

Eleventh Part. The Life

I say that we should by no means keep a good peace with our faults and sins, or with that which is harmful to our souls; rather, we should be like lions in driving such enemies out of ourselves. We must also follow Christ in His friendliness and gentleness, not only toward our good friends, but toward everyone, as is their due; only we must not make ourselves too familiar with vain, worldly people, except insofar as it may provide an occasion to call them back from their evil ways; for in such a case, one must also be at their service. We should also be friendly and gentle in the sense that we do not repay or answer evil with evil, but bear it patiently; indeed, we should seek to perform acts of love for the one who has done us wrong or reviled us; but let this be done quietly and not by the opposite [of what he did to you], so that he does not come to shame because of his evil. For all acts of love that we perform for those who offend us must be done with a quiet nature and a calm mind; just as I know a certain person (a) <margin>She means herself.</margin> who would have liked to kiss the feet of those who offended her. To attain this virtue, one need only look at the Lord Jesus, how He suffered everything so kindly and gently; for when we look at this example, we receive the strength so that we will no longer retain any resentment against our enemies. We must also follow the Savior in this, that we preserve ourselves in <term>integrity or simplicity</term><note>The German *Einfalt* implies a holy single-mindedness or lack of guile, often contrasted with worldly "cleverness."</note> in our speech and in our actions, without any pretense or double-meaning.

# of Angela of Foligno, Chapter XIII,

Look * but once, my dear children, with the deepest devotion of your soul, whether we are not duty-bound to show the greatest loyalty in return to the most faithful suffering <term>God-man</term><note>The term "God-man" (Gottmensch) refers to the Christian doctrine of the Incarnation—that Jesus is simultaneously fully divine and fully human.</note>? Who has most humbly and completely subjected Himself not only to rational but also to irrational creatures, because of His most faithful and purest love for us.

3. He gave the devil the power to tempt Him and lead Him about. He gave humans full power over Himself. He gave their hearts the power to think the most wicked and cruel things against Him. He gave their senses power to counsel against Him, to blaspheme Him, to strike, to scourge, to unmercifully nail, to crucify, and to kill Him. Therefore, O children of God! never turn your eyes away from this most faithful humility, which this suffering God-man had for your sake; O with what great and most faithful loyalty has the uncreated God served His creature! since He became obedient solely for its sake, even to the lifeless creatures! <note>The "lifeless creatures" refer to the physical instruments of the Passion, such as the wood of the cross, the iron nails, and the thorns.</note> Solely for your sake, O human! was He obedient in all tribulations; solely for your sake was He obedient in all insults; solely for your sake was He obedient in all shame; solely for your sake was He obedient to all punishment; solely for your sake was He obedient to all pains; solely for your sake was He obedient to all death!

4. [Both this point and all the other points concerning the **poverty of Jesus** are further explained by our Saint in a moving manner, after which she makes the following dedication:] And all this He did so that He might teach us—we who are but a wretched food for death, and who must suffer anyway, whether willingly or unwillingly—to yield ourselves patiently to the tribulations that encounter us. He did this so that He might henceforth raise us out of the state of powerlessness into which we had fallen, to make us eternally invincible, and to place us in a state where we are no longer capable of suffering, through the power of His glorious resurrection.

5. The Lord and Master of all things, the Invincible One, placed Himself in a state where He could suffer; the Creator of all things made Himself powerless and willingly subjected Himself to all creatures, all tribulations, all scorn, pains, and suffering. He did this so that He might shame us in our wretched "tenderness"—we who are so far from being willing to take tribulations and exercises of penance upon ourselves, that we even cast far away from us all the suffering and adversity that God sends us according to His healing divine decree, and for that reason even murmur sinfully against the Almighty.

6. The Son of God made Himself poor in regard to His own wisdom, and wished to be seen by the people of this world as a lowly, ignorant man—even as a fool—so that He might show us the way of simplicity and truth which we must take. He showed us how much we should avoid boasting or exalting ourselves under the pretext of wisdom or learning, and before

7. Jesus Christ became poor in regard to the glory of His holiness, His purity, and His innocence; and He was held as a sinner, as a friend of sinners, as a deceiver and a blasphemer. 8. The Son of God was poor in regard to His sovereignty over all creatures. **14.** The second companion, who always kept the Son of God company here on earth, was perfect contempt for himself <note>The German *Verachtung seiner selbst* refers to voluntary self-abasement or "lowliness"—choosing to be viewed as insignificant or shameful by the world.</note>, and the fact that He lived as an outcast in voluntary, extreme disgrace and shame. He chose this state so that, as a man, He might attain the state of the glorious resurrection and also raise us through that very same path to the state of highest glory.

If anyone were to be excepted, it could be no one but the person who is united with Christ as their head through a true and living love. For when a soul filled with the love of Christ * sees that He Himself, her King, Master, and Head, loved this company [of contempt], she also loves and desires to have the same, because of the love she bears for Him.

### of Angela of Foligno. Chapter XIII.

**17.** Indeed, someone might say: "As for me, I love *Christ*, and I want to love Him more and more; therefore, I care very little for the honors of this world. But I cannot bear to be dishonored; I do not want to be brought low, disgraced, or reviled before the world." See, is this not a clear sign that one still has a small faith, a fragile righteousness, a very narrow love, and a very great lukewarmness! Whoever speaks this way should consider whether he has committed things for which he deserves disgrace and shame (and there are likely few who are innocent in this regard), or whether he has not committed such things.

If he has committed them, whether secretly or publicly, and if he wishes to act as a true penitent <note>A person who is sincerely repenting of their sins through acts of contrition.</note> and not like a false devotee, it is most fitting that he not only endure the shame with patience but also find a certain delight in it. But if he has committed nothing evil, neither in will nor in deed, then he must carry the disgrace and shame—when God ordains it for him—with a hundred times greater patience and joy than if he were guilty. This is because all such shame serves only to increase the grace within him, and the increase of grace brings about a greater glory.

And it is not to be doubted in the least: holy souls and true friends of God grow toward perfection in this manner—namely, when all sorts of opportunities for humiliation come upon them without their own fault, and they endure them with patience. In the same way, those who endure poverty or other sufferings for the love of God also become more perfect. Truly, the Lord Jesus Christ loved disgrace and shame and fled from honor for this very reason: so that He might teach His friends that they could grow in grace and glory by following Him in this.

**18.** The third companion, who accompanied the Lord Jesus at all times and in the most sensible manner, was the highest of pains and sufferings. <insert>Here, the blessed Angela presents in detail the magnitude and variety of the Savior's sufferings, and finally concludes with this application:</insert> He suffered all of this so that He might make known to mankind the way of truth and destroy lies along with the entire dominion of the devil; so that He might make known to us the humiliations of true repentance and draw us toward them; in short, to show us that the blessedness, the true good, and the glory of man are enclosed within the patient endurance of pain and tribulations.

**19.** O divine goodness! O infinite mercy! O incomprehensible friendliness! Where an infinite wickedness is abundant, there an eternal and immeasurable grace becomes even more abundant! <note>A paraphrase of Romans 5:20: "But where sin abounded, grace did much more abound."</note> But why then, O goodness without end? O mercy without limits? Why then have You revealed such a strange and supernatural mystery to us? It has happened, my children, so that it might serve as a model for us in all our tribulations and adversities. We should not only refrain from repaying our enemies evil for evil, but we should also do good to them, because of the love of our Redeemer.

### Eleventh Section. The Life

**20.** The Son of God has not only blessed those who suffer, but He has also embraced suffering in body and soul with total willingness, bearing greater pains than any human could ever endure. He has testified to us that, just as He entered into His glory and Kingdom through suffering, we too must enter eternal glory through this very same path of pain, suffering, and tribulations; it is impossible to enter by any other way. Since God Himself chose this path, we see clearly that it is the true **Royal Way**. <note>The "Royal Way of the Holy Cross" (Latin: *via regia sanctae crucis*) is a traditional Christian concept suggesting that the path of suffering is the most direct route to God.</note>

**21.** The Son of God knew very well what a great good lay hidden beneath pain and tribulations; therefore, He chose and embraced them, while fleeing and abhorring all worldly delights, comforts, and consolations. In former times, it might have been somewhat excusable to flee from tribulations and seek out pleasure and prosperity; but now, since the Son of God has chosen so many adversities and such great tribulations, how could man still be so foolish and miserable as to doubt a wisdom so clearly proven and constantly made known? Truly, one would have to have lost their senses, and in such a state, one would make themselves guilty of the very deepest damnation.

**22.** Since this is undeniable, what shame and damnation are we not worthy of—we poor and harmful sinners! For we are not only negligent in taking up the tribulations that meet us with a repentant spirit, but we flee them with great impatience, pushing them away from us with grumbling and complaining.

**23.** O, what miserable and unhappy creatures we are! Sufferings and tribulations are indeed the healing medicine <term>remedy; original: "Genesmittel"</term> for our sins, but when the divine Physician of our souls—who is Wisdom itself—prescribes them and offers them with His own hand, we reject them. If we are only a little cold, we immediately run to the fire and seek out the weight of heavy clothes; if we are a little too warm, we must immediately have refreshment and cooling; if we feel even the slightest pain in the head or the stomach, look, that is already enough to cause complaining, sighing, and screaming, running to doctors and for medicines, comforting ourselves with soft beds, and inventing all kinds of delicacies. Indeed, people even besiege God with their prayers for relief; in those moments, they pray from the bottom of their hearts. But that is how one *should* pray for the forgiveness of sins and the healing of the soul—not for liberation from the **Cross** and the pains that are so beneficial to our salvation and are so lovingly dealt to us by the hand of the Most High.

**24.** We act in exactly the same way when the Lord allows someone to treat us poorly or insult us for the benefit of our souls: see there, we are immediately indignant, disturbed, and angered. We immediately complain about such a person; we judge presumptuously that they did it out of malice; we speak evil of them; we revenge ourselves to the best of our ability. In a word, we do not want to learn to suffer with patience and willingness the slightest pain, the slightest tribulation, the slightest of those adver- <note>The text breaks here; the catchword "Wider-" indicates the continuation of the word "Widerwärtigkeiten," meaning adversities or hostilities.</note>

### Of Angela of Foligno. Chapter XIII.

->**Adversities which the heavenly Physician of our souls sends us out of love and for our true benefit.**<-

**25.** Oh, what labor and effort do we not take upon ourselves, and what great costs do we not incur, to ward off or shake off the sufferings, tribulations, and adversities that God so graciously allows to come upon us? Yet, if we took these upon ourselves and bore them with a willing heart, they would without doubt be far more healing and much more useful to us than the many other <term>penances|Self-imposed acts of discipline or atonement, such as fasting or hairshirts.</term> which we might impose upon ourselves by our own will. For the heavenly Physician knows incomparably better than the sick and senseless human which <term>mortifications|The practice of "dying to the self" by enduring physical or emotional discomfort to strengthen the spirit.</term> and adversities are most suitable to purify and improve the soul. Self-sought penances and denials are often subject to vain self-complacency; whereas those that come upon us through divine providence, and which we accept from His hand with true patience and total willingness, are hidden from the eyes of men under the veil of necessity, making it seem as though we only bear them because we must.

Therefore, I earnestly recommend to my children that they should patiently endure the cold, the heat, the disorders of the seasons, and the small inconveniences—now a bout of sweating, now a cold, a headache, a stomach ache, and similar mortifications which do not actually destroy one's health. I would wish that we were not so quick to run to doctors and medicines, except when the need is great and the soul is obviously suffering harm because of it. I also advise them that when, by divine permission, they are overtaken by poverty, the loss of friends, oppression, persecution, shame, unjust treatment, the theft of their goods, and the like, we should not be distressed by these things. We should not only take them upon ourselves with patience but embrace them with such sincerity as if we had sought them out and chosen them of our own free will; or better said, as graces that our supreme Physician and Savior has chosen for us and offers to us through His pure love and for our highest happiness.

**26.** But how do we poor wretches behave in this matter? We strive for exactly the opposite. We do nothing but meditate day and night on how we might obtain all kinds of comforts, amusements, and tenderness for our senses; we are intent, with all diligence and care, on seeking every kind of worldly comfort and delight. No, truly—such a path was not trodden by Him whom we call our Savior, the <term>God-man|A theological term (German: Gottmensch) referring to Jesus Christ being both fully divine and fully human.</term>, JESUS Christ, blessed forever! If He Himself was the Way—a way of sorrows—as well as the model we must follow, how then is it possible for a wretched soul that seeks comfort in this world to reach Him? Truly, a soul who is rightly in love with her beloved JESUS desires no other gain, nor any other status here on earth, than that which He Himself had. I mean the gain of pains, hardships, and tribulations, in which she should place all her joy and all her comfort.

2. The more you are tempted, however, the more you must pray. The * gold must be refined and purified. Whoever prays uprightly will be tempted, and whoever prays uprightly will also constantly be delivered from temptation. For through prayer you are enlightened, through prayer you are purified, through prayer you are united with God.

3. Prayer, however, is nothing other than a revelation or discovery of God and of oneself. This revelation of God and of oneself is perfect and true humility. For this is the state of humility: namely, when the soul sees God and itself; then it is in deep humility, and out of this deep humility divine grace grows and sinks ever deeper into the soul; and conversely, the more divine grace increases, the more the soul will be deepened and remain lying in true humility.

4. When divine grace and <term>heat|Spiritual fervor or a "burning" emotional intensity felt during devotion.</term> occasionally drive you to prayer, or to other exercises, see to it that you do not receive this grace of God in vain. But if it pleases God to withdraw this <term>fervor|In German, "Brunst," referring to an intense, passionate spiritual state.</term> from you—whether it be because of your failings (as is most often the case) or because He wishes to increase and strengthen His grace within you thereby—then practice no less in prayer and good works than before: even if you should have to experience suffering and temptations at the same time. You only do your part, my child; God will surely do His.

5. Persevere then in prayer, and when you feel yourself perhaps more completely drawn by God than usual, and a sublime light is given to you to see God and yourself, then surrender yourself to that drawing, and do not entangle yourself in any other occupations; at that time, do not even occupy yourself in the instruction of your neighbor, and guard yourself, that you do not give yourself to * any <term>creature|In this context, "creature" refers to anything created (people, animals, objects) as opposed to the Creator.</term> until you have learned to be able to separate yourself from all creatures. Take care regarding your zeal, and do not follow it until you have first well understood the beginning, middle, and end, and as far as it agrees with the <term>Book of Life|A biblical reference (e.g., Revelation 20:12) to the record of those destined for heaven, used here as a metaphor for divine truth.</term>, follow it that far and no further.

6. [She says this with an eye toward the immature desire to convert others found in beginners. She gives a similar reminder in another place, which is especially useful for teachers to take to heart.] I pray you, that you * remain masters of yourselves, and do not give yourselves entirely to any creature; but give yourselves entirely to Him Who Is. And when one of you preaches or hears confession, or shares counsel with other people, let his heart not be with the creature, but with the Creator. We should not act like fools, for where the fool’s eye is, there also is his whole heart. If flattering men or women come before you, saying: "O my dear brother! through your words I have been converted to repentance"; then do not look upon such creatures, but look upon the Creator, and thank the Creator for such a benefit.

# Eleventh Part. The Life

### Section 59 (Continued)

7. For there are many preachers of falsehood who preach either out of greed, or for money, or for their daily bread; but you, my dearest children, I desire from the very depths of my heart that you be preachers of the holy truth, and let the <term>God-man|A theological term for Jesus Christ (German: *Gottmensch*), emphasizing the union of His divine and human natures.</term> be your book. I do not say that you must give up your physical books, only that you must be as willing to give them up as you are to keep them. I do not want you to preach only with learned words, or to recount the deeds of the saints with dry words; by no means—you must preach with that same divine <term>anointing|In German, "Salbung," referring to a spiritual presence or grace that makes speech feel divinely inspired rather than merely intellectual.</term> possessed by those whose works you recount. For those who have had the preaching happen within themselves through such an anointing are the ones truly fit to preach to others.

8. [Regarding the deception caused by a false appearance of holiness and <term>free-thinking|The German "Freygeisterey" here refers to "Free Spirits," a medieval and early modern movement often accused of believing that the spiritually perfect were exempt from moral laws.</term>, she gives the following important reminders:] Take care to guard yourself against those who use sweet, enticing words, who seek to make themselves pleasant to others through spiritual talk, and who claim to have revelations. These are the snares of malice used to draw others to themselves. Also, take care to guard yourself against those who have an appearance of holiness and an appearance of good works, lest they draw you to themselves through this path. Therefore, watch carefully, consider and test everything well, and follow no one except insofar as they resemble the path of the <note>original: "Buch des Lebens" (Book of Life), referring to the life and example of Christ.</note> Book of Life, and no further.

9. Guard yourself also against those who say they possess the spirit of freedom, while they are meanwhile clearly living in opposition to the life of Jesus Christ. God the Father had His Son—who was not bound by the law, who was indeed above the law, being the Lawgiver Himself—submit to the law; He was free, yet He became a servant. Therefore, everyone who wishes to follow Christ must make themselves conform to the life of Christ, and seek no freedom in the loosening of the Law and the divine commandments, as many are accustomed to do; rather, they must submit themselves to the Law, the commandments, and the counsels of God. The Holy Spirit gives such people a rule and order for how they should live, and He binds them; though many things might be permitted to them which are not against God, the Holy Spirit nevertheless does not allow them to do these things because of the precise order that the Holy Spirit prescribes for them.

10. Therefore, if you find any among those who say they have the spirit of freedom, and they say to you: "Why do you judge me? How do you know what I have in my heart?"—then rebuke them, and answer them boldly: the Holy Spirit teaches us to judge those whose works are evil. "For when the Holy Spirit is poured directly into the soul, He organizes the outer man perfectly according to the perfect order He gives to the soul. Where that does not happen, it is false."

11. [Regarding essential knowledge and divine truths, she says:] The soul that wishes to know something essential of God and divine things must first be entirely <term>transformed|The German "vergestaltet" implies being reshaped or "re-formed" into the likeness of God.</term> into God through love; and when it is thus transformed into Him, it must place itself in His presence, and stand there and look upon <gloss>the object it wishes to know</gloss> inwardly within God, and not outwardly outside of God.

<summary>Angela of Foligno warns against "preachers of falsehood" and the "Free Spirit" heresy, emphasizing that true spiritual freedom involves submitting to Christ's example and the Law. She argues that internal spiritual transformation must be reflected in outward orderly conduct and that true knowledge of God only comes through union in love.</summary>

One must therefore [first consider what he is in himself, and when he is then raised above himself in God, he can then see Him who is invisible, and recognize Him who is unknowable, and comprehend Him who is incomprehensible: the unknown Good. And when the soul, according to her capacity, comprehends, sees, recognizes, and feels God Himself, then she expands herself through love into Him, and is filled with God Himself; she expands herself in God <note>original Latin: "in Deo"</note> and God in her and with her. And then the soul receives and possesses a greater sweetness from that which she does not comprehend than from that which she does; from that which she does not see than from that which she sees; and from that which she does not feel than from that which she feels; and from that which she does not know than from that which she knows. And this seems to have its cause in this: that even if a soul were perfect—yes, even the most perfect of all—it is still nothing, all that she knows of the uncreated and infinite God; she sees, feels, and recognizes through the sight of that which she can neither comprehend, nor see, nor feel, nor recognize.]

12. [Speaking of humility, she uses, among others, the following expressions:] O my beloved! she says, above all things I desire this one thing from you: that you be always of one mind, and that no kind of division or separation be found among you. I also wish only that the <term>essential remedy|In German "Grundmittel," referring to the fundamental spiritual practice that cures the soul of pride and division.</term>, which brings all diversity into unity, remains deeply rooted in your souls. This essential remedy, however, is nothing other than **being little**. <term>Smallness|The German "Klein seyn" (literally "being little") is a core concept in Angela's mysticism, describing a state of radical humility and self-emptying.</term> ensures that one does not look upon one's own satisfaction, wisdom, or own opinion; rather, it brings the soul only to the point where she looks upon her own failings and miseries, as well as ensures that she quarrels or disputes with no one, except against her own vices, to discover and improve them. Being little ensures that one desires to be preferred over no man, nor to be higher than any single person; it ensures that one does not become vexing or burdensome to anyone, whoever they may be, nor starts a quarrel with any single person. Conversely, it ensures that one can always bear with everyone, * even though the life of such a soul strikes and hits all those who are contrary to this smallness.] I wish for you, my dear children, that you may possess this poverty and smallness so thoroughly that your whole life, without much chattering, may be a true mirror to all those who desire to follow it, but a sharp sword to the enemies of the truth.

13. O my beloved! I would wish to hear this good news from you: that this being little had made you into one heart and one soul; how then would my spirit be so peaceful on your account? For I do not see how you could please God in any other way, unless you are united in such a manner.

14. [Of the love of God, she speaks, among other things, the following:] The love of God has many kinds of properties. For first, the soul that loves God is made tender or soft through this love. Secondly, she becomes faint and weak thereby. Thirdly, she is made strong thereby. It happens with her as with a piece of limestone that is thrown into the kiln; at the beginning, before it is dissolved, it makes a rattling sound, but as soon as it is "cooked," the thumping stops: so too a soul, when

### Section Eleven. The Life. ###

...when it feels the heat of divine love, it makes a noise and a cry. Initially, the soul seeks <term>divine comforts|In mystical theology, "comforts" or "consolations" (Tröstungen) refer to the pleasant emotional and spiritual feelings that often accompany early stages of prayer.</term>; however, if these are withdrawn, the soul becomes soft; it cries out and complains against God Himself, asking why He treats it so?

15. In this state, the soul enjoys quite a few divine comforts—indeed, it sometimes receives excellent and inexpressible comforts—which the soul, to tell the truth, must not demand with impetuousness, but neither should it despise them when God gives them; for through them, it receives the courage and strength to run after its Beloved. However, in the *absence of these comforts, love grows, and the soul begins to seek the Beloved; and since it does not yet find Him, it becomes faint and sick, and can no longer be satisfied with divine comforts as before, so long as it does not participate in the presence of the Beloved.

16. But when the soul is perfectly united with God and is established in the <term>seat of truth|A term used to describe the deepest part of the soul where God dwells, often called the "ground" or "apex" of the soul in mystical tradition.</term>, which is the soul's proper seat, then it no longer cries or complains; it no longer has those tender feelings and faintings. Much more, it *recognizes itself as unworthy of all good and of all the gifts of God, and worthy of a greater hell than hell itself;] rather, a certain wisdom and ripe maturity is placed within it. It becomes firm and ordered in God—indeed, so strengthened in Him that out of love for the Beloved, it would willingly go to its death. It possesses God as fully as it is capable of, and God also expands its heart and the powers of its mind so that it may be capable of what He wishes to place within it. It seeks Him who is, and sees also that everything else is nothing, except insofar as it has its being from Him who is.

17. At that point, it regards everything that came before as nothing in comparison to what it now possesses. All created things are also nothing; it is troubled neither by sickness nor death, nor by honor or shame; it is so completely satisfied and at peace that it desires nothing more. It loses its desires and can no longer "act" <note>In this context, "acting" or "working" refers to the soul's own self-directed spiritual efforts, which cease when it is moved entirely by God.</note>, because it is overcome and united with God in this inexpressible contemplation. In this divine light, it sees that God does all things in the order that is proper; therefore, it no longer faints over His absence. Indeed, it unites itself with His divine will so completely that it does not even seek Him again when He is absent; rather, it is satisfied with everything He does and leaves it entirely to Him.

18. This* however only holds its truth when the soul has been strengthened and calmed in love in the aforementioned manner, so that it loses its longing and can no longer "act" because it experiences the aforementioned contemplation of God in its stated fullness. But if this is again withdrawn—for to no soul in this life is it given to remain in this state continually—then a new and fervent desire is shared with it to perform <term>works of penance|Acts of self-discipline or service performed to express sorrow for sin and love for God.</term> even more than before, and without any difficulty; for this state is far more perfect than all the others.

19. Now, the more perfect the state in which one finds oneself, the more one strives—

She told us that this would be the final writing that one would compose for her; for she had known of her blessed passing for a long time. Therefore, she pressed me—I who was so sluggish in writing—to write, as she then spoke the following words with great fervor:

2. "O my God! Grant me the grace to recognize Your most high mystery, which Your fervent and inexpressible love has brought about—namely, the most high mystery of Your holy <term>Incarnation|Menschwerdung: The Christian doctrine that God the Son became human in the person of Jesus Christ.</term>, which took place for us and is the beginning of our salvation.

3. "This Incarnation achieves two goods for us: First, it fills us with love. Second, it gives us the assurance of our <term>salvation|Seligkeit: Referring to eternal happiness or the state of being 'saved' in the presence of God.</term>. O incomprehensible love! There is no love greater than this love: that my God becomes flesh so that He might make me God." <note>This reflects the ancient theological concept of 'theosis' or divinization, suggesting that the purpose of God becoming human was to allow humans to participate in the divine nature.</note>

4. "O heartfelt love! You annihilate Yourself and become as nothing, so that You might make me once again. You take on the form of a despised servant to acquire for me a royal dignity and a divine beauty! Yet, You lost nothing of what You were; nothing was taken from Your divinity. The abyss of Your deep <term>abasement|Erniedrigung: The voluntary act of lowering oneself in status or dignity; here, it refers to Christ’s humility.</term> during the Incarnation forces only these words from my inner being: O incomprehensible Being, behold, You have become comprehensible! O Uncreated One, for me You have become a creature! O my Lord, grant me the grace to recognize the depth of Your highest love, which You have shown us in Your most holy Incarnation! O happy guilt—<note>original: "O glückselige Schuld" — This is a reference to the 'Felix Culpa' (Happy Fault), a phrase from the Catholic Easter liturgy suggesting that the sin of Adam was 'happy' because it led to the coming of Christ.</note> (not in itself, but because of the <term>mercies of God|Erbarmungen Gottes</term>)—which gave cause for the most hidden abyss of divine love to be revealed to us, which would otherwise have remained hidden from us! O love! No, I can conceive of no greater love! O Most High! Make me capable of conceiving this highest and inexpressible love."

> "O Lord! There are five mysteries that You have worked for us; O my God, make us capable of understanding them."

(I.) "The first is the mystery of Your most holy Incarnation, which is pure, inexpressible love. O highest love, transformed into a creature! O Divine! O inexpressible contemplation! Blessed be You, Jesus Christ, <note>original: "JEſu Chriſte"</note> for letting me know that You were born for me. O glorious knowledge! To truly understand what I now see and understand: namely, that You were born for me. This knowledge is sweet and full of delight. O wonderful God! How wonderful are Your mysteries that have happened for us!"

(II.) "The second mystery, which flows from the birth of the Son of God, is that we thereby receive a certain direction for how we should live; and that in His Incarnation, birth, and life, we have before our eyes the teachings of <term>poverty|Armuth</term>..."

(III.) "The third is the mystery of His death; for to this end was He born,
that He might die for us. Five points are to be considered in the death of Jesus Christ. 
First, the outworking and revelation of our salvation. Second, 
our strengthening, and the victory over our enemies. Third, the fullness and the 
overflowing of the love of God, which became especially manifest in this death. 
Fourth, we are thereby filled with a deep, inward, and sublime knowledge; 
for we see, recognize, and grasp herein how God reveals and glorifies His Son 
to us, just as in His <term>Incarnation|Menschwerdung: The theological concept of God taking on human flesh.</term> and birth, so also preeminently 
in His death. Fifth, we must consider how the Son of God revealed 
Himself to His Father, as He was obedient to Him throughout the entirety of His 
life, even unto death on the cross; through which obedience He acted as a mediator 
before God His Father for the entire human race.

"O <term>uncreated God|unerschaffener Gott: A philosophical term for God as the eternal source of all things, who was not Himself created by anything else.</term>! grant me the worthiness to recognize the abyss of Your 
fervent love; make me worthy to understand Your unspeakable love, which You 
poured out upon us when You showed us Your Son Jesus Christ in the flesh; 
and when Your Son revealed to us that You are our Father! O wonderful 
love! O lovely love! In You is all taste, all sweetness, all delight! 
The contemplation of this love calls my soul away from the world, raises it above itself, 
satisfies and calms it.

(IV.) "The fourth mystery is the resurrection of the Son of God. In which 
we consider two points: First, it gives us a firm hope for our own 
resurrection; second, it allows us to recognize the <note>In mystical theology, "spiritual resurrection" refers to the soul being raised from the "death" of sin or worldly attachment into a new life of grace while still on earth.</note>spiritual resurrection. O sublime, 
wonderful, unknown, unspeakable, holy mystery! Through it, 
our perfection has been completed. O Lord! give me the grace to rightly 
understand the greatness of this mystery.

(V.) "The fifth is the mystery of the Ascension. O Love! make me 
worthy and capable of understanding this mystery, in which our entire salvation has 
been completed; for thereby, O my dear Lord Jesus Christ! You have placed Yourself in 
possession of the goods of Your Father and ours.

"See, these five mysteries are learned in the school of the true disciples of 
Jesus, and the true school in which they are taught is perpetual prayer.

"Ah, my Lord! grant me the worthiness that I may recognize and grasp Your 
highest love, through which You created and redeemed me! O incomprehensible 
God! make me capable of recognizing Your priceless and fervent love, along with the 
heartfelt affection through which You have willed to choose the human race from eternity 
to see Your saving countenance, and through which You, the Highest Being, have 
deigned to look upon us! Grant that we may recognize our debt, 
so that * we may thereby be brought to the knowledge of Him whom You have sent 
to redeem us from our guilt."

## The Sixteenth Chapter.
### Her final speeches, testament, and blessed passing.

->I.<-

<margin>(b) This chapter is arranged entirely according to the manuscript.</margin>
**A**fterward, the blessed (b) Angela spoke little more, and indeed only intermittently, now and then; partly because of great weakness in her fatal illness, and partly because she found herself more than usually swallowed up in the abyss of divine infinity; nevertheless, we who were present have briefly collected as much of her words as we could understand and grasp. One day (it was around Christmas, at which time she also passed away to the Lord) she said: *The Word became flesh.* A good while later she spoke again, as if returning from another place: "O, no creature can reach this! O, the understanding of all angels is insufficient for it!" We asked her, what is it that no creature can reach, and for what is the understanding of the angels insufficient? She answered: "To comprehend this." Afterward she said: "O in truth! Behold, my God keeps for me what He promised me: for Christ, His Son, has now presented me to His Father." Previously she had said: "Do you well know that..."

that Jesus was in the boat, even though the storm was great? Truly, it is also this way at times in the soul, when temptations strike against it and the Lord seems to sleep. A little while afterward she said: Truly, God sometimes allows it to happen that the temptations and the storm do not subside until the person is broken, crushed, trodden underfoot, and as if annihilated; and He allows such things to happen especially to His right and true children.

2. Another time she said to us: O my dear children! I would gladly speak a few words to you, if I did not fear that God would refuse me His promise. She understood the promise regarding her departure <note>Angela refers here to her "departure" from this life—her impending death.</note>. Afterward she said: That which I wish to say to you, I say only to the end that you might better progress in the way in which I have walked so little. And this I say only so that God may be honored, and because I also do not wish to take anything under the earth <note>A common idiom for being buried or dying.</note> with me that could be useful to you. Behold, God speaks to the soul: All that is mine, is yours. Oh, who could ever earn this—that all the goods of God should be theirs? Oh, in truth! nothing can earn this; love alone is deemed worthy of it. O my dear children, fathers, and brothers! strive to love one another, and that you may also have this divine love in truth. For through this love for God and for one another, the soul is made worthy to inherit the goods of God. I make no other testament <note>In the sense of a "last will and testament" for her spiritual followers.</note> than that I commend to you love for one another and deep humility. And I leave you my entire inheritance: namely, the life of Christ, which is **poverty**, **suffering**, and **contempt**. Those who now accept this inheritance—namely, the inheritance of the life of Christ—and are true children of prayer, they will without doubt attain the inheritance of eternal life.

After this, the blessed (b) Angela spoke very little more, and then only intermittently, now and then; partly because of great weakness in her terminal illness, and partly because she found herself swallowed up more than usual in the abyss of divine infinity. ### of Angela of Foligno. Chapter XVI.

1. ...that **JESUS** was in the ship, even though the storm was great? <note>This refers to the biblical story from Mark 4:35-41, where Jesus sleeps during a storm on the Sea of Galilee, testing the disciples' faith.</note> Truly, it is sometimes the same in the soul when temptations strike it and the **Lord** seems to sleep. A little while later she said: Truly, God sometimes allows it to happen that the temptations and the storm do not subside until the person is broken, crushed, trampled underfoot, and as if annihilated <note>The term "annihilated" (German: *vernichtiget*) is a technical term in medieval mysticism, referring to the "naughting" of the self-will so that only God remains.</note>; and He lets such things happen especially to His right and genuine children.

2. At another time she said to us: "O my dear children! I would gladly speak some words to you, if I did not fear that God would deny me His promise." She understood this promise to be regarding her departure <note>Her impending death.</note>. Afterward she said: "That which I wish to tell you, I say only to the end that you may better progress in the way in which I have advanced so little. And I say this only so that God may be honored, and because I do not wish to take anything with me under the earth <note>To the grave.</note> that could be useful to you. See, God speaks to the soul: 'All that is mine is yours.' O, who would be able to deserve this—that all the goods of God would be theirs? O, in truth! nothing can deserve this; love alone is deemed worthy of it. O my dear children, fathers, and brothers! exert yourselves to love one another, and that you may also have this divine love in truth. For through this love for God and for one another, the soul is made worthy to inherit the goods of God. I make no other <term>testament</term> <note>A spiritual will or final instruction for her followers.</note> than that I commend to you mutual love and deep humility. And I leave to you my entire inheritance, namely the **Life of Christ**, which is **poverty**, **suffering**, and **contempt**. Those who accept this inheritance—namely the inheritance of the Life of Christ—and are true children of prayer, they will also without doubt attain the inheritance of eternal life."

3. And then she laid her hand upon the head of each one of us and said: "Be blessed, my dear children, by God and also by me, both you who are present and the others who are not here. And just as the Lord has given me permission and has shown me this eternal blessing, so I give to you all this blessing. May He Himself, **Christ JESUS**, confirm it to you with the hand that was nailed to the cross."

4. Afterward she said: "In what I say to you, I have nothing to do with it myself, but it is all God’s; for it has pleased the Divine Goodness to lay upon me the care of all His sons and all His daughters who are in the world, those across the sea and those on this side of the sea; and I have protected them according to my ability; I have felt their sufferings, and the sufferings I have endured for them have been far greater than you know." And thereupon she turned to God and said: "Now, O my God! now I lay them back into Your hand, and I pray You that You may protect them from all evil!"

# Eleventh Part. The Life
<meta>catchword: 10. Also</meta>

...all people; for I say to you in truth, that my soul has received more graces from **GOD** when I have suffered with all my heart and wept for the sins of my neighbor, than when I have wept for my own sins. Truly, there is no greater love on earth than to suffer for the sins of one's neighbor. I know well that the world mocks what I say, because it seems contrary to nature that one should suffer as much, or even more, for the sins of a neighbor as for one's own; but the love that does this is not of this world.

6. O my dear children! strive to have this love, and judge no man, even if you should see someone commit a heavy sin. I do not say that the sin should not displease you, indeed, you should abhor it; but I say this: you should not judge the one who sins, because the judgments of **God** are unknown to you. For many seem blessed in the eyes of men who are yet condemned by **God**; and conversely, many seem condemned in the eyes of men who are yet blessed by **God**. I could name several such persons to you whom you have despised because they abandoned the good they had begun, of whom I nonetheless have the firm hope that **God** will lead them back into His way.

7. Also, she said at another time: Now my soul has been immersed, washed, and purified in the blood of **Jesus Christ**, which was still as fresh and warm as if it were just then flowing out of the body of the Crucified One <note>This vivid, visceral imagery of Christ's "warm blood" is a hallmark of late medieval mysticism, emphasizing the immediate, physical reality of the atonement.</note>; and with this, it was said to my soul: This is what has purified you. Whereupon my soul replied: O my **God**! is there no deceit in this? <note>Angela frequently expresses a fear of "deceit" (Betrug), reflecting the common mystical concern that spiritual visions might be demonic delusions rather than divine revelations.</note> And it was answered: No.

8. My soul also heard these words being said to it: O my bride! O my beautiful one! O my beloved with a true love! I do not wish for you to come to me draped in these sorrows, but with jubilation and unspeakable joy, as it is fitting that a great King should lead in his much-beloved and long-awaited bride with royal garments. And he showed me this royal garment, just as a bridegroom might do for his much-beloved and longingly awaited bride. This garment was neither of purple nor of scarlet, neither silk nor velvet, but it was a wonderful light with which the soul was clothed. Then the bridegroom himself was also shown to me, namely the **Word** <note>original: "das Wort"; referring to the Greek *Logos*, the divine reason or person of Christ as described in the Gospel of John.</note>, so that I now recognize what the **Word** is, and what it means when one says "the **Word**." And then He said to me: This is the **Word** that willed to become flesh for you.

9. Then this Word also permeated me; it touched me entirely and embraced me, saying: Come, my beloved, my beautiful one, who is loved by me with true love; come, for all the saints await you with great joy. He also said this: I will give orders to neither angel nor saint to fetch you, but I will come in my own person for your sake and take you to myself; for you are suited for me, and are high in the eyes of my **Majesty**.

10. Angela also said at another time: Cursed be all privileges in the world which puff up and corrupt the soul—such as all power, all honors, and high positions. O my children! strive so that you may be small. Yes, be so humble that you always regard yourselves as a pure <term>Nothingness</term> <note>original German: "pures Nichts." In the mystical tradition, "Nothingness" refers to the total stripping away of the ego so that only God remains.</note>. After this, she cried out and said: O you unknown Nothingness! O you unknown Nothingness! I tell you in truth, that a soul can have no better vision in this world than to see its own nothingness and to remain within it as if in its prison.

11. She said: There is a far greater danger and deception in having a "privilege" in spiritual matters than in worldly ones—for instance, when someone has a gift for speaking about **GOD**, performing great works of penance, understanding the Scriptures well, and always being occupied with spiritual things. For such people are even more easily deceived and led astray, and are brought back to the right path with more difficulty than those who only have some advantage in worldly matters. And she cried out once more and said: O you unknown Nothingness! O you unknown Nothingness!

12. On the day before her departure, she said many times: Father, into your hands I commend my soul and my spirit <note>original: "Vater, in deine Hände befehl ich meine Seele und meinen Geist," a translation of the Latin "In manus tuas, Domine, commendo spiritum meum" from Luke 23:46.</note>. Once, when she had spoken these words, she said to us who were present: Now, in response to this word, it is said to me: "What was impressed upon your heart during your life, it is not possible that you should not also have it in your death." Thereupon we asked her: "Do you wish then to go from here and leave us?" To which she gave the answer: Until now I have kept it hidden from you, but now I conceal it no longer, but say it freely: yes, I must go from here.

On that same day, all her pains ceased, by which she had previously been martyred for many days in the most terrifying way in all the members of her body, internally and externally; and she lay in such great peace of body and such inward joy of spirit that she seemed to already taste something of that joy and <term>jubilation</term> <note>original: "jubiliren." In mystical theology, this refers to an ecstatic, wordless joy of the soul in the presence of God.</note> promised to her. We asked her whether **GOD** had granted her the aforementioned jubilation? Whereupon she answered: This jubilation has already begun. In this rest and joy of mind she remained lying quite contentedly until Saturday evening, while various brothers stood around her, until at the last hour of that same day she entered into her rest as if through a gentle sleep; this occurred in the year of Christ 1309.

<meta>This page transitions from the biography of Angela of Foligno to a new section focusing on the life and works of Johanna Maria (Jeanne-Marie) von Cambry (1581–1639), a Flemish mystic and nun known for her rigorous asceticism and spiritual writings. # The Life of Johanna Maria von Cambry.

## Preface.

Two learned and well-known friends of Johanna von Cambry had intended, even during her lifetime, to bring the history of her life to light; they had already collected and composed the necessary reports for this purpose. However, because there were hesitations about making public the virtues of a person who was still living and facing persecution, and because many respectable people, also still living, would not have been mentioned in the most favorable light, the work remained unfinished. These collected reports, along with what our Johanna’s spiritual guides left behind of her writings, later came into the hands of her biological brother, Pierre de Cambry, a <term>Canon</term> <note>A priest serving in a cathedral or collegiate church.</note> at Renaix; who publicly testified that, next to God, he owed his conversion to the prayers of this, his sister. From the aforementioned reports, and from what he otherwise knew of his sister and held in his hands, he composed her life and finally published it in Antwerp in 1659, with many preliminary <term>approvals</term> <note>original: "Approbationen." Official endorsements by Catholic Church authorities confirming that the work contained no theological errors.</note>. I have never become aware of any other edition of it; much less have I seen any of it in the German language.

Concerning this extract of her life, it consists, for the greatest and most important part, of documents from her own hand, written to her guides or trusted friends; the rest was reported by irreproachable eyewitnesses and earwitnesses. It is to be regretted that the written reports of the final years of her life were lost in the wartime unrest of that time. Meanwhile, the remainder is far too beautiful not to find a small space in these collections of such histories.

The remaining writings of this godly person were printed all together in <term>quarto</term> <note>A book size where the sheets are folded twice to create four leaves.</note> in Tournai (or Dornick) in 1665 under the following title: *The Spiritual Works of Sister Jeanne-Marie of the Presentation, formerly Jeanne de Cambry;* <note>original: "Les Oeuvres spirituelles de Soeur Jenne Marie de la Presentation, premierement Jenne de Cambry"</note> and they consist of six treatises, which were also each published individually: (1) Short Exercise to Attain the Love of God. (2) The Four Books on the Destruction of Self-Love and the Building Up of the Love of God. Specially printed in 1622 and 1627 at Tournai, as well as in 1645 at Paris, in <term>octavo</term>. This is her largest and a truly important treatise; in which not only various hiding places of self-love are thoroughly uncovered, but also the successive states of the Inner Life are described quite orderly and from deep experience. (3) The Mystical Torch, also specially printed at Tournai, 1631, in <term>duodecimo</term>. After the author has given some necessary reminders to spiritual guides in the first chapters of this treatise, she thereafter explains mystical matters and idioms in a completely thorough and excellent manner. (4) A Treatise on the Improvement of the Married State. (5) Lament of a Captive Soul in its Mortal Body. (6) On the Excellence of Solitude. The manner in which she wrote these books of hers can be read remarkably below at the end of Chapter III.

She, like all other pious souls, had her enemies and persecutors, yet there is no lack of those who loved and praised her and her writings. From many, we wish to cite only a couple.

Monsieur Coriache, Vicar General of the Archbishop of Mechelen, gives the following testimony regarding her *Mystical Torch*:
> “The clarity of the *Mystical Torch* blinds my coarse sight, and makes me confess that this torch must have originally come from the Father of Lights, with whom there is no respect of persons, and who works wonders in the weaker sex. May He be blessed into all eternity, primarily through these purified spirits, who are most partakers of His divinity.”

This Coriache was a trusted friend of the famous and renowned maiden Antoinette Bourignon (a), at whose insistence she also composed her *Inner Life* or *The Word of God*, and to whom she wrote several letters, which are found in her book *The Light Shining in the Darkness*.

Andreas Catulle, Vicar General of the Archbishop of Tournai, who also [regarded] the said maiden

---

<note>(a) Whether our Johanna was acquainted with Antoinette Bourignon, I do not find to be certain; yet it may have been so. For Johanna came to Lille <note>original: "Ryssel," the old German name for the city of Lille.</note> in 1625 and died there in 1639, shortly before the maiden Bourignon, in the 23rd year of her age, left from there for the second time.</note>

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the life of Johanna Maria von Cambry (1581–1639). It provides testimonies from other notable mystics and scholars of the 17th century, such as Pierre Poiret and Antoinette Bourignon, who defended her spiritual path despite its outward severity.</meta>

<image-desc>A symmetrical horizontal woodcut ornament featuring a central floral motif surrounded by scrolling, acanthus-like foliage and vine patterns.</image-desc>

Bourignon, in seeking to defend her during her persecutions, brought to light more than one testimony regarding the life and writings of our Johanna von Cambry, from which we can cite only a few: "I am (so he writes to Johanna's biological brother) almost the only one remaining of those who, besides yourself, had a close acquaintance with your sister. I still remember the sufferings she endured with such great patience and incredible steadfastness; for because she was pleasing to GOD, she had to be proven through temptation. I visited her often in Lille <note>original: "Rissel," the historical German name for the city of Lille in modern-day France.</note>, and always perceived a deep humility in her and in her spiritual conversations. In her enclosed little chamber, she spent almost all her time in prayer or in writing godly and excellent books. From her countenance, nothing but godliness and devotion shone forth, so that I never returned from a visit with her or from her venerable presence without feeling <term>contrite</term> <note>Feeling deep sorrow and remorse for sin.</note> within myself and gathered in spirit, etc."

Petrus Poiret (a) calls her profound and enlightened. Her life, he says, contains many important things regarding GOD's dealings with souls devoted to Him, and so forth. To say nothing of other testimonies (b), some of which are even cited in this biography itself.

Against the severe and solitary lifestyle of these godly souls, many readers in particular will have no small objection. However, such a life is not imposed upon anyone for imitation; her guidance and life story are reported only in a historical manner—not to transform us into her outward form of life, but to stir up our sluggish hearts toward an earnest faith and a burning love for GOD. How little these and similar souls otherwise placed their trust in their outward way of life, good works, and exercises can be seen in the single short letter from this person (c), with which we conclude this book, serving as a powerful testimony. Let whoever wishes read it, and then judge whether a deep evangelical foundation did not lie in her soul; one which, however, is never attained through mere parroting, but is first born within us through much suffering and dying <note>A mystical term for the "death of the self" or "dying to the world."</note>. For truly, neither Christ nor His saints have any other Gospel for the "old Adam" <note>A biblical reference to the sinful, unregenerate nature of humanity.</note>. They know that all who wish to belong to Christ (d) must crucify their flesh, along with its passions and desires, without thereby ceasing to place their entire salvation in Christ alone. Whereupon there comes to my mind an important reminder concerning a false love of GOD, with which this soul concluded her books on the destruction of self-love, and with which we also wish to conclude here:

> "There are people," she said, "who take upon themselves the most beautiful appearance of the love of GOD in words and manners, so that one would say it is all fire and pure holiness. However, my dear friends, look at the end; see what works they proclaim to you beneath their words. One must, they say, love GOD and one's neighbor. GOD demands only our heart, and not our blood. One must care for the body so that one (e) can endure the inner workings of divine love. It is better that one loves GOD for many years than that one shortens one's life through severities, etc. See there, does it not go quite well that way? We shall thus stroll into Paradise with all comfort; the people who treat their bodies kindly will go straight in. See, that goes most excellently indeed. Poor souls! Soon they will be caught in the net. They do not see the poison which is hidden under such a beautiful appearance, leading us only to a false freedom, and from there down into hell, etc. JESUS Christ calls out through His whole life nothing other than repentance and poverty, as He Himself did not have a place to lay His head. By this path, all holy souls have followed Him. There is no other way than the way of the cross. Love must be crucified. Do not think that you will attain perfect love through a dainty life and the coddling of your body. Living well and rattling off one's prayers is indeed not enough to love GOD and become holy. Watch out for the false prophet. I do not say, of course, that everyone should perform such great acts of penance; let each behave therein according to their strength and calling, etc.
>
> "It is also the truth that all acts of penance without love are but dead works; but acts of penance with love are means to attain and preserve love, etc. And why do we need to care so much for our body, which will soon rot in the earth? Let us only care for our soul, which shall live eternally. If we wish to enter heaven, let us seek the way to heaven which JESUS Christ prepared, and which all the saints have walked after Him, and which shall remain the same until the end of the world. May GOD give us His grace, that we may fulfill it all to His honor! Amen."

(a) *The Mystical Library*, pages 225 & 328. (b) See *The Library of Illustrious Women*. Antoine Arnauld, *Tradition of the Church*, page 402. (c) Below, Chapter XIV. (d) Galatians 5:24. (e) Compare Johannes Tauler's *Meditation of the Soul*, Chapter 23, throughout.
