Twelfth Part. The Life of Johanna von Cambry. 383

## The First Chapter.

->Her origin. Pious childhood and youth. Her vision<-
->of the earthly paradise and others more. Her relapse<-
->into vanity. Complete conversion, and serious conduct.<-

1. Johanna von Cambry, or of Cambrai <note>original: "Camerich," the historical German name for the city of Cambrai.</note>, was born in Douai <note>original: "Douay"</note> on November 15, 1581. Her father was Michel von Cambry, chief counselor of the city of Tournai <note>original: "Dornich," the historical German name for the city of Tournai in modern-day Belgium.</note>, and her mother was Louisa von Gouyon; not long after her birth, she was brought to Tournai and raised there in the fear of GOD.

2. Of her childhood and youth, we find indeed little recorded for information; yet a few things shall be mentioned. One thing is certain: from childhood, her heart turned toward godliness, as she herself confesses somewhere, that from her early youth the Holy Spirit drew her to prayer and instructed her in it.

When she was three years old, and did not yet know at all what the supernatural gifts of GOD were, only that she loved Him dearly, it happened that she once fell into an <term>ecstasy</term> <note>A state of intense spiritual focus or trance, often involving visions.</note>, in which the Savior appeared to her hanging on the cross; she saw with the eyes of her soul that the cloud in which the Lord JESUS was leaned down until He came near to her; by which she was so greatly comforted that from that time until her death, she always remembered it with the greatest joy.

3. In the tenth year of her age, she was led in the spirit one day into a very delightful and so magnificent garden <margin>(a) See Ch. 12, §. 12.</margin> (a) that the loveliest summer time compared to it would be regarded as nothing but darkness; yet it was a place so created that everywhere she turned her eyes, she saw nothing else but this garden, as large and wide as her sight could reach, without a single house being inside it. The sun in this garden was incredibly more brightly shining than it could ever be at high noon; nonetheless, its great light did not dazzle her eyes, and its heat caused not the slightest discomfort. The trees and fruits were incomparably beautiful to look upon. Some were laden with ripe fruits, others with blossoms, without any change of seasons or any other variation; everything there was wonderfully beautiful and delightful. As she came back to herself from this ecstasy and vision, she found herself full of joy, and it was given to her to understand that the place she had seen was a representation of the earthly paradise.

4. Some time after, she had a beautiful vision in which GOD let her see in what manner He was present in the beauty of all His creatures, both rational and irrational <note>In the context of 17th-century theology, "rational" refers to humans and angels, while "irrational" refers to animals and plants.</note>, from which she later drew great benefit, so that she found the presence of GOD in all created things.

These and similar visions more, which she had at that time, caused all the pleasures of the world to become bitter and quite repulsive to her. Even when she found herself in company where there was dancing or feasting out of kindness toward her parents, she always had to weep bitterly, because her soul was filled with the beauty of the things she had seen.

5. Yet, see the danger in which a good soul <note>original: "Gemüth," referring to the inner disposition or spirit.</note> lives in the world and among the people of the world. As our Johanna grew more mature and a bit older, she allowed herself to be gradually seduced into social interaction and fellowship with the vain world by several young women of her own age and status. Although she took no real pleasure in it, she nevertheless fell into vain curiosity and fashionable finery, as she always wanted to go about dressed quite elegantly and according to her rank. She remained in this folly for two years, during which time she lost the love she previously held for GOD and divine things, as well as the heavenly graces and visitations of GOD which she had experienced manifold from the third year of her age until then. After these two years had passed, she finally noticed the deception and harm through GOD’s mercy, and decided to completely give up all such vanities; whereupon her previously held gifts of grace gradually returned.

6. Among these, it is particularly remarkable that once, in a state of spiritual ecstasy <term>ecstasy</term> <note>A trance-like state of deep prayer or "Gemüthsentzückung" where the mystic experiences a vision of the divine.</note>, the Child JESUS appeared to her as if very near; at the same time, it seemed to her as if she herself had become a little child again and played with the little JESUS. He had two crowns in His hand, one of which was made of beautiful flowers, but the other of prickly thorns. He held them out to her with a smiling face, so that she might choose one of these two crowns or wreaths. Through GOD, she saw that these flowers represented the luck and prosperity she could have in this life, and that if she chose them, she would be tormented in the next world with much pricklier thorns than those of the other crown the little JESUS offered her. In this crown of thorns, she saw countless hardships, persecutions, crosses, and sufferings that she would have to endure in this world; but at the same time, she also beheld the reward of grace of eternal life. Since she recognized that it was the pleasure of JESUS that she should take this crown of thorns—even though He left the choice to her—she seized it with great courage and thereafter came back to herself with inexpressible comfort. From that time until her death, she had to endure all kinds of plagues and sufferings, as various instances shall be cited in this life story; although her heavy external persecutions have been largely covered up for certain reasons.

7. Accordingly, she resolved to live henceforth in the single state and under the obedience of a spiritual leader, until such time as her father and mother might come to die; in which case she intended to distribute her temporal goods among the poor, to have her meager living from the work of her hands, and should she perhaps become ill, to let herself be carried into an almshouse, so that she might thus live in the highest

She gave up all her vain clothes and used simple ones; she began to practice abstinence and moderation, using no more wine—indeed, eating and drinking became a burden to her. She was by nature very much inclined toward anger, but now began to resist it with such force that she often thought her bones would be broken by the effort. But it happened not long afterward, as an opportunity for marriage arose, that her father strongly pressured her to choose one of the two: namely, either to marry or to enter a convent. However strange this proposal of her father seemed to her, she nevertheless had to make a decision, and for that purpose requested three months for reflection. During this time, the aversion she felt toward the cloistered life gradually faded and was transformed into a great longing for this way of life.

## Chapter Two.

### A brief sketch of GOD’S initial ways with a called soul. The frail state of the first conversion, under the Law. The necessity of a second conversion, which places the soul into GOD’S grace, fellowship, and as if into a beautiful spring.

->I.<-

We find only this brief account of the first years of her life and her Christianity until her entry into the convent. In the aforementioned books on the *Destruction of Self-Love*, she describes the successive stages of conversion, sanctification, and union with GOD as she herself experienced them, in more detail, under the symbol of the four seasons. We wish to provide at least a very brief sketch of the initial ways and leadings of GOD from this treatise of hers and share it for contemplation. After she has thoroughly uncovered the various and hidden malices of self-love in the entire first book, and thereafter dealt with the initial conversion of a sinner to GOD, she further gives us the following report on the ways of GOD here and there:

2. After the first conversion of a soul, by which it has surrendered the world and sin and begins to devote itself to prayer, it receives from GOD small perceptible comforts and sweetnesses to strengthen it in the struggle, “so that often

(so her own words state) the soul does not know how to find itself therein, and thinks it is already in a small paradise, because it has never tasted anything other than the bitterness of sensual and earthly pleasures.

> “The more she now sees the great goodness of GOD, the more she is set in contrition <note>original: *Zerknirschung*. A state of deep remorse and repentance for one's sins.</note> over the fact that she has so greatly offended such a GOD; and then tears become her bread day and night, which, however, appear to the soul as pure sweetness and refreshment.

3. “Afterward, she receives strong impulses toward the mortification <term>mortification</term> <note>original: *Castenung*. The practice of self-denial or physical discipline, such as fasting, to strengthen spiritual focus.</note> of her body through vigils, fasting, and the like. But when these impulses come, she must choose an experienced guide <note>A spiritual director or mentor, common in early modern religious life to prevent "spiritual pride."</note> to whom she may reveal such desires, and of her own impulse undertake no external penitential exercises without the permission of her guide, so that, under the appearance of great devotion, self-love does not sneak in with them, or the devil deceive her through indiscreet penitential exercises.

4. “The new soldier of JESUS Christ, who desires nothing else than to become truly faithful to her bridegroom JESUS, and to overcome everything that might be displeasing to Him, finds on one side sensible sweetness in prayer, but on the other side experiences [gradually] that in her conduct and way of life she is often overcome by her passions <note>original: *Affecten*. At this time, "affections" or "passions" referred to strong emotions like anger, pride, or lust that were seen as obstacles to the soul.</note> and falls into many small sins, to her utmost sorrow. Therefore, she resolves a thousand times again not to want to offend GOD further; but this resolution is no sooner made than she falls into them anew. She returns to prayer, she weeps for her previous sins; and her new sins seem even heavier to her than the previous ones, because she now has love for GOD and the knowledge that she did not have before.

“In this manner, the soul is sometimes driven about for many years without progress in the spiritual life. For because she does not know the interior, she walks like a blind person, and indeed for lack of an experienced guide. If the soul now does not have such human help, she should ask GOD for His Holy Spirit, surrender herself to GOD, and choose Him as her guide, and then fight against herself as a brave soldier of JESUS Christ.

5. “Many are deceived in this, who think they have progressed far in the spiritual life because they feel the aforementioned sensual comforts in prayer, although they still feel their usual desires of anger and lust within them. They think it is enough if they guard themselves against opportunities for an outburst, though the root has not been removed. The root must be lifted through a true [or internal] dying-to-self <term>dying-to-self</term> <note>original: *Absterbung*. A central concept in mysticism where the ego or "self-will" is eliminated to make room for God.</note>, without lingering on or leaning upon the sweet sensations; these one should only accept from GOD in humility and use them as aids toward dying-to-self; firmly believing that one cannot be pleasing to GOD where one is not purified from all sin.

> “[opposing] them, their disordered emotions <note>original: *Gemüthsbewegungen*. This refers to the passions or stirrings of the soul that can lead one away from spiritual focus.</note> and desires dampened, behold, there appears the beautiful dawn <note>original: *Morgenröthe*</note>, and begins to enlighten this soul—I mean the Grace of God—which leads her in all her actions according to His holy will. And once she has reached this first step <note>original: *Staffel*</note> of perfection, she abandons herself entirely by consenting to everything God desires of her, who becomes the sole object <note>original: *Vorwurf*. In this historical context, this refers to the "object of focus" or "aim," rather than a "reproach."</note> of all her desires, thoughts, and love; in short, God is the beginning, the middle, and the end of all internal and external actions and deeds. Then the beautiful flowers of the virtues appear, which this soul brings forth, making her far more beautiful than all created lights. Then the lovely song of the birds is heard, in perpetual praise and love of God, through elevations of the spirit and inward outpourings of the mind into God, so that He may be praised by all creatures. This is a lovely song that delights not only humans but even the angels; indeed, God Himself takes all His pleasure in it. The Lord also makes Himself so intimate with this soul that she seems to be one with God through a precise union <term>union</term> <note>The mystical *unio mystica*, where the human soul feels entirely joined with the Divine.</note>, not only of her will but also of all other faculties of the soul and her purest spirit with her God. From this union, she receives such divine and piercing comforts that she no longer seems to be on earth; she almost no longer remembers her natural existence, except only in God, in whom she sees all things. My dear reader, if one could comprehend the graces that this soul enjoys, one would find no one who would not gladly leave a thousand worlds behind just to experience such enjoyment for a single day.”

10. Following this, the author uses fifteen chapters to describe the various divine growths of this lovely springtime of the soul; which is followed afterward by a hot summer (by which she means the state of abandonment and inner suffering), when thunder, lightning, and all kinds of weather pass over the desolate soul; but which is finally crowned blessedly in autumn (the unity and transformation <note>original: *Vergestaltung*. A theological term for being "re-formed" or transformed into a new shape in God.</note> into God) with a rich and ripe harvest. She treats this in an excellent manner in the last book of this treatise, which is called *The Holy Cabinet of the Purest Love of God* <note>original: *Das heilige Cabinet der Reinsten Liebe GOttes*</note>. However, we shall return to the order of our biography, having only intended to encourage the reader to faithfully pursue this noble jewel <note>original: *Kleinod*</note>, which the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus sets before us.

## Chapter Three.

*She enters the convent in 1604, where she is visited with many gifts of grace during the first years; thereafter, however, she had to walk in a state of abandonment and suffering for four whole years. She is delivered from this and writes her books on the Destruction of Self-Love.*

->1.<-

Thus it happened that Johanna, in November 1604 and in the twenty-third year of her age, entered a convent of the Augustinian Order in Tournai <note>original: *Dornich*</note>, called the Abbey of Pré, and was there clothed in the habit with great joy. As she now found herself freed from the cares and hindrances that had previously kept her distracted and entangled, she began to be frequently drawn away, receiving heavenly lights and visions, spiritual drunkenness <note>original: *geistliche Trunkenheiten*. A common mystical term describing a state where the soul is so overwhelmed by divine love that it loses its sensory orientation, much like intoxication.</note>, and similar extraordinary graces. It reached such a point that she could no longer read, nor hear the name **JESUS** pronounced or sung, without falling into such an ecstasy <term>ecstasy</term> <note>In this context, ecstasy refers to a trance-like state where the person becomes unresponsive to the physical world while focusing entirely on a spiritual vision.</note> that she had to be led or carried away. Hardly a day passed in which something of this nature did not occur; indeed, divine love burned so intensely within her that she also received a wound in her heart, which caused her very great, yet most pleasant, pains.

2. Her spiritual guide had indeed forbidden the sisters who were around her to speak with her during her spiritual drunkenness, but rather to leave her in peace until she should come to herself again. Nevertheless, some were so curious that they questioned our Johanna about many things concerning her internal state. Because she was not herself <note>original: *nicht bey ihr selbst*. Meaning she was in a trance or altered state of consciousness.</note> and was unaware of what she was saying, she often spoke of the secret things of her heart in this heat of love. Afterward, when this was repeated to her by the sisters, she would weep bitterly that others knew of her secrets.

3. Among other things, it happened one afternoon that she was in a long ecstasy in the presence of the Mistress of the Novices <note>original: *Meisterinne der Probtöchter*. The "probationary daughters" or novices were women in their first stage of convent life.</note>. Upon coming to herself, she found this Mistress dissolved in tears. When Johanna asked the cause of her distress, the Mistress replied that she was so moved because she had witnessed this ecstasy and could not doubt that it was God working within her; she had seen in Johanna's countenance an extraordinary and more than natural beauty and clarity, from which she certainly judged that Johanna must be experiencing great things from God in her interior. This made our novice feel quite ashamed. And it was at this very time that she received the command from God to write her books on the *Destruction of Self-Love*.

### Twelfth Part. The Life

4. Around this time, she was truly caressed by GOD; soon He came to her and corrected her faults, just as a father comes to his child, which happened with unspeakable power and love. At other times, He instructed her on how she should walk; He strengthened her and encouraged her to confidently devote herself to the practice of the virtues.

This took place in the first years of her life in the convent. She remained in this way of refreshments <note>original: *Erquickungen*. In mystical literature, this refers to periods of intense spiritual joy or consolation.</note> and loving visitations from GOD until approximately 1612, for six or seven years in succession. During this time, although she also faced many adversities and sufferings, she was able to bear them all with delight and joy, because everything was swallowed up and consumed in the fire of divine love, with which her soul was ignited.

5. During this time, she also had various visions and revelations of future things, which our "Savior (she says) promised to give me, through obscure prefigurations <note>original: *dunkele Vorbildungen*. These are symbolic images that are not immediately clear to the recipient.</note> that I did not understand at the time, nor where they were leading. Thus it happened once, while I was in prayer, that GOD showed me a small, very glorious little tree that grew out of the center of a burning heart. Its trunk was divided into four branches, and on its leaves stood golden letters, so glorious that I have never seen the like in the world. And it was given to me to understand that the four lowest branches signified these four virtues: namely **Humility**, **Faith**, **Hope**, and **Love** <note>original: *die Liebe*. In this context, it refers to Charity or Divine Love.</note>; and upon the leaves these virtues were written. And our Lord said to me: **Your heart must be similar to this heart.** Whereupon I gave as answer: My GOD! how can it be possible that my heart should bear such virtues? But He replied: **It is I who will water it with my grace.** When it was over, I remained very comforted by it and received great strength for self-denial."

6. After these years of pleasure, it pleased GOD to test her and to refine her like gold in the furnace of affliction <note>original: *Ofen der Elenden*. A biblical allusion, likely to Isaiah 48:10, "I have refined thee... in the furnace of affliction."</note>, and to place her in a state of abandonment and suffering. For four whole years, she could not obtain even a single word of outward comfort, assistance, or instruction from a living soul, because of the confusion and hindrances that were placed in her way.

At this time, she sometimes fell into such weakness <term>fainting fits</term> <note>original: *Ohnmacht*. This implies both physical fainting and a state of spiritual collapse or ecstasy.</note> that she could not keep herself upright. She went to and fro through the house or through the garden, lamenting and whimpering as if she had been dealing with tyrants who wanted to pierce her body; and she would have quite gladly suffered such a thing—indeed, she would have prized it as a refreshment—in comparison to what she had to suffer; for the pains she suffered internally in her soul, she also had to feel externally in her body.

7. She was compelled at times to pour out her complaints before her fellow sisters; but because they could not comprehend her state and her suffering, and only passed all sorts of perverse and audacious judgments upon her, this only brought her greater distress. Sometimes she stood up at night and ran into the nearest chamber to a sister, saying that she saw Hell open before her and stood in the greatest danger—

to sink into [it]; she wept incessantly, and it was a small relief to her if she could pour out her lamentation a little.

8. Her distress and suffering were so great throughout these four years that, as she herself often said, if GOD had not specially protected her, there would have been no sin so great into which she would not have fallen; for she was tempted against faith, against hope, against her election <note>Election refers to the theological concept of being chosen by God for salvation; doubting this was a common and terrifying spiritual trial for mystics.</note> and so forth. Nevertheless, in all these shakings and confusions, she did not cease to surrender herself patiently to God’s will; she said to Him full of love that she was content to endure all this, if it so pleased Him, until the end of the world, if only He could be glorified thereby, and if He granted her the grace not to offend Him.

During this time of abandonment, she did indeed have some internal strengthenings and lights every now and then, but these did not last long at all; as it then happened that once it was said to her: Daughter, Satan wants to sift you like wheat <note>A reference to the Gospel of Luke 22:31, where Jesus warns Peter of coming trials.</note>: But I will protect and preserve you.

9. This state of her four years of heavy suffering and abandonment is only mentioned here briefly; however, she later described it herself more circumstantially in the entire third book of *The Destruction of Self-Love*, which third book bears this title: **The Secret Purifying Fire of Faithful Souls, who Consume Themselves in the Fire of Divine Love.** Time and space forbid us from inserting an extract of it here; but since she made a general sketch of the sufferings of this state in the first chapter, we wish to briefly set it down here:

10. > “Here now,” she says, “the soul has reached the third state, that is, the state of

# Twelfth Piece. The Life
## of Johanna von Cambry.

> "...patience, her humility, her love, and so forth, in all circumstances. Just as this third state of perfection is represented by the summer, when the sun’s heat is in its full power; so also the intense love which this soul possesses in its heart will not be diminished in the slightest by all these storms and tempests, nor by all kinds of persecutions from men, from herself, and from the hellish spirits; even when it seems as if the heavenly spirits and **GOD** Himself have joined together to make this soul suffer. Amidst all of this, however, her love grows ever more, and nature <note>In mystical theology, "nature" refers to the unrefined human ego and worldly desires as opposed to the "spirit."</note> is annihilated on all sides."

11. All of this the author explains in great detail and order; however, she provides this important reminder near the beginning:
> "Everything discussed in this third book is not for souls who have only made a little progress in the spiritual life; various occurrences happen here that would cause an inexperienced person to wonder how things so contrary to virtue and perfection could be found in such an elevated state. Therefore, one could easily be deceived—namely, if someone who has not yet practiced the dying-off <note>The term "Absterbung" (mortification) refers to the process of killing off one's selfish impulses.</note> and overcoming of self, and in whom the desires of anger and lust were still fully alive, should imagine that he was in this third state simply because he was moved by a small moment of devotion. Such a person would certainly take winter for summer, and summer for winter."

12. After she had endured this martyrdom for four years in the manner described, it happened one day, as she turned in prayer to **GOD**, who was her only refuge, that it was said to her internally in a most gentle and lovely way: > Be comforted, my daughter, for you must become a pillar of religion. <note>In this context, "religion" refers to the established religious life or the Church's spiritual foundation.</note>
Upon these words, the dark black cloud of sadness and tribulations that had covered her for so long suddenly vanished, and she was so completely freed from all her sufferings as if she had never been in that state at all. Some time later, she did experience a new onset of these anxieties, but within eight days all sadness and oppression disappeared again, never to fall upon her in that way again. This occurred on St. Augustine’s Day <note>August 28th.</note> 1616, with such a singular change in her state of mind that she always used to call it a "second baptism." This dark night of suffering had not long passed when she received a rebuke from **GOD** because she had not yet begun to write her book on the *Destruction of Self-Love*, as she had been commanded to do six or seven years earlier. She then set herself to the work and described this excellent treatise with incredible speed and a singular influence of the grace of **GOD**, who can make tongues eloquent and give His instruments the pen of a ready writer. Although our Blessed one was hindered and disturbed in the work by the Evil Foe <note>The devil.</note> in various and extraordinary ways, she nevertheless brought the first book of this writing to a close in the year 1617, thinking that perhaps the benefit readers would draw from this text might be the fulfillment of the words spoken to her—that she should be a "pillar of religion."

of Johanna von Cambry. Chapter III.

13. Somewhere, our saint remarkably recounts the manner in which she wrote her books:
> “Everything I have written,” she says, “has always happened after I had first prayed to **GOD** for the grace to do so, and after I had first immersed myself in my <term>nothingness</term> <note>In mystical tradition, "nothingness" refers to a state of total humility where the soul recognizes it has no power or identity of its own without God.</note>; for despite all the insights that **GOD** was pleased to give me, I was nevertheless quite mute when I was supposed to go and write, unless I first of all immersed myself in my nothingness and humbled myself before **God**. But as soon as I surrendered myself to **GOD** and said in humility: ‘My **GOD**! speak through me what it pleases You that I should speak,’ my eyes were immediately opened. Never in any other way have I been able to write even the slightest thing.”

14. Regarding her internal state, after the aforementioned <term>martyrdom of abandonment</term> <note>A period of intense spiritual trial where the soul feels completely forsaken by God's presence.</note>, she was caressed by the **Lord** in a strange and entirely new way. In previous times, **GOD** had always shown Himself to her in a certain form, which happened rarely thereafter; similarly, any visions she received possessed a far greater clarity, whereas before they were always surrounded by images and obscurities.

->I.<-

We shall now observe in succession how she further spent her time in this, her first convent, until roughly the end of the year 1619. During this time, she indeed received many remarkable graces from **GOD** internally, but externally she was forced to follow the **Lord** through constant persecution, pressure, and trials.
> “In the year 1618 (so her own words say), there were violent divisions, confusion, and rebellion against the superiors in our convent. These were caused by a pure addiction to high status and positions of honor, and they stirred up great quarreling and discord among the sisters. In the midst of these thorns, I sought only contempt <note>In this context, "seeking contempt" means intentionally choosing the lowest, least respected roles or accepting insults to cultivate humility.</note>, and in that I found my **God** far more than in all high status and honorable positions. The most difficult thing for me in all of this was that I could speak with no human being about my state of mind, except for the Father <note>The "Pater" or father refers to the convent's appointed male confessor or spiritual director.</note> in the convent, who was, however, quite unskilled at leading souls to whom **GOD** communicates special graces. Yet the kind **GOD** arranged it so that—after I had been unable to reveal my heart and the secrets **GOD** told me to anyone for over six years—I finally obtained the freedom with a certain

### Twelfth Part. The Life

“...theologian <note>original: "Gottesgelehrten"</note> to act, who helped me greatly to learn to learn to know the Spirit of **GOD**, both through his good life and through his instruction; just as he had also been helpful to me with his good advice eight years earlier.

“When I gave him, along with other writings, the third book [On the Destruction of **Self-Love**] <note>In 17th-century mysticism, "self-love" (Eigenliebe) refers to the ego or self-will that prevents total union with God.</note> which I, unworthy as I am, had written at the command of **GOD**, this man gave me the assurance that it had come from **GOD**. After I had further related to him my entire guidance and circumstances, he wished one day that I should pray to **GOD** with him to see whether it might not perhaps be His will that I should leave my current convent and enter a stricter one; which I then did with such simplicity, without knowing his intention; for as far as I was concerned, although there were great disorders in our convent, I was nevertheless content therein, because many tribulations came upon me due to their divisions, which only incited me like so many thorns to love **GOD** so much the more, and in the midst of those persecutions I found the hidden pearl of divine grace.”

2. **GOD** also finally revealed to our Johanna that she would depart from this convent, although the time when, nor the means and ways by which this should happen, were not shown to her.

3. One day, when she had been reproached by the Superior in the presence of all the other sisters and punished quite innocently, she took her refuge in the **Lord**, who touched her so inwardly with His divine love that she found herself compelled to leave everything where it lay and go to ask Him that He might take her into the wound of His holy side! Whereupon she received as an answer:
> Come, my dove, make your nest in this secure rock, and dwell therein.
By which words she was then most powerfully encouraged to take upon herself all kinds of tribulations and adversities.

It is quite inexpressible what she then felt in her soul; the fervor of divine love caused her such great pain that she thought her whole heart was but a single wound; she was so withdrawn <term>withdrawn</term> <note>A state of ecstasy or "rapture" where the soul is so focused on God that it loses awareness of the physical world.</note> the whole day until seven o'clock in the evening that she could not speak at all, and could not rightly remember what was spoken to her inwardly by the **Lord**; even more so was she estranged from external things; and when she came back to herself, it was to her as if she had come from Paradise into Hell, so much did the things of the world seem to her to be contrary to divine things; nevertheless, she remained estranged in spirit from all things that are not **GOD**, possessing in spirit an inexpressible good, along with a longing to die so that she might enjoy **GOD** without hindrance. But **GOD** said to her that she must yet remain in life, and at the same time gave her to understand how she would yet have to endure many persecutions from men, along with an assurance that it should all be fruitful for her, and she would be overcome or brought to a fall in none of it. The Savior showed her His wounds and spoke:
> My daughter, my well-beloved, these five

### Of Johanna von Cambry. Chapter IV.

...Bonds shall henceforth be your support and your defensive wall; be of good cheer!

Concerning what else occurred during this divine visitation, our Johanna could say nothing further, except that the enjoyment of a single little drop of this pure divine love <note>original: "Gottesliebe"</note> which she had tasted is a good without beginning and without end, so beautiful, so great, and so delightful that if only the smallest drop of it could fall into Hell, it would necessarily turn it into Paradise and the devils into angels; for, she said, it would be impossible for either sin or the punishment for sin to coexist with this good of pure love.

4. Such divine strengthenings and caresses, amidst outward sufferings and trials, she received several times at this time. “Once (she says herself) **GOD** embraced me just as a father embraces his child, and said to me: 
> My dear daughter, be of good cheer! Suffer gladly for my name's sake, and persevere.
Which word of **GOD** caused me such uncommon comfort that I immediately fell into an ecstasy <note>original: "Entzückung," a state of mystical rapture where the soul is perceived to be outside the body</note> because of it; then I was plunged so much deeper into my own nothingness and pleaded for the forgiveness of my sins; whereupon it was said to me quite kindly: 
> My daughter, all your sins are forgiven you.
This occurred on the 27th of September, 1618.

5. Never were any sufferings or tribulations inflicted upon her that she did not take upon herself with joy in her heart, and there the **Lord** always showed her a special grace. One day she was accused of a certain matter of which she was entirely innocent, and during a harsh punishment it was said to her, among other things, that the books she had written were worthy of being burned. Now, whatever else had been said against her person and honor, she bore with all willingness; but concerning what was said about the books, which she had written by divine command, she was distressed this time because she thought it concerned the honor of **GOD**, for which reason she also complained to **GOD** about it in prayer, meanwhile thanking Him that He showed her the grace to suffer for the sake of His love. Then the **Lord** appeared to her entirely wounded, with the open wound of His side, and embraced her, whereupon she then sucked from His side—not blood, but such a sweet and exceedingly lovely essence <note>original: "Saft," literally "juice" or "sap." This vivid, physical imagery of nursing from Christ's wound was a common motif in medieval and early modern mysticism, symbolizing the soul receiving direct spiritual nourishment from the Savior.</note> that no human heart would be able to comprehend it. After this divine visitation, she had no further sadness about it, nor has she since been able to weep over any tribulation, however great it might be.

6. How her conduct in general shone in the eyes of the discerning at that time, I will indicate only through this short testimony, which one of her fellow sisters in the same convent allowed to flow into a letter:

> Where there is division or disorder, she is skilled at reuniting minds and bringing them back within bounds through her exemplary and holy life. She is like a sun in our midst through her bright-shining virtues: and though she be covered with shame and mockery, all the more do her virtues shine forth, especially her steadfastness in bearing all kinds of slander with a magnanimous heart—

# Twelfth Part. The Life
<meta>catchword: "will"</meta>

...pains and to endure with invincible patience, indeed even with a wondrous love toward her greatest persecutors, to whom she repays good for evil. She possesses a deep humility, a high level of contemplation <term>contemplation: a form of deep, wordless prayer focused on the presence of God</term>, a sound judgment, and a great modesty, the likes of which one does not easily find among women. I cannot say enough about it, or rather, she surpasses all that I can say. I consider her another Catherine of Siena <note>Catherine of Siena (1347–1380) was a famous Italian mystic and member of the Dominican Order known for her spiritual influence and writings</note>, etc. She is friendly, affable, and pleasing in her speech and outward behavior; from which something divine shines forth, so that whoever merely looks upon her is moved to love and praise GOD, etc.

7. The usual effects that occurred within her at this time consisted of an everlasting flame of the love of GOD, which brought about such an ardent longing for the Heavenly in her that everything she had to use for the necessary support of the body—such as eating, drinking, sleeping, and the like—caused her pure suffering; she had to perform her prayers aloud and while walking to and fro, so that she might not be too much taken away by any ecstasy <term>ecstasy: a state of being "outside oneself," common in mystical traditions where the soul is perceived to be absorbed in the divine</term> or similar effects that arose from the constant flame of divine love; for as soon as she lay down on the ground to pray, she was so gathered up in spirit that she could no longer bring forth a single word.

8. Between Easter and Ascension Day <note>The Christian feast commemorating Jesus's ascent into heaven, occurring 40 days after Easter</note> in the year 1619, GOD gave her for fourteen days together such a vivid experience of His holy love that her spirit was more in Paradise than on earth; she saw nothing but love, she tasted nothing but love, she breathed nothing but love; she saw GOD not only in the innermost part of her heart and in the highest part of her soul, but she saw herself entirely in GOD, and with body and soul as if submerged in GOD.

9. She also received at that time the knowledge of high mysteries, which she did not write down for fear that others might get to see them. Indeed, she even had to distract herself from this close union with GOD because she became quite ill from it; then this inward fire was ignited even more when some of her fellow sisters mocked and reviled her, even when she was sick unto death. She was not at all distressed by this; on the contrary, she was full of joy and praised GOD for the mockery and shame; she was seen, in the midst of all her bodily torment, laughing for joy, so that people did not know what to think of it; all of which then caused a great longing for solitude in her, so that she might have complete freedom to converse with GOD day and night.

10. Around this time, she also had a vision in which she recognized how GOD is present in all things that have being, how He sustains all things, and how they all exist through His power. “GOD,” she said, “is everywhere glorious in Himself; He is everywhere in His pure and simple divine essence, without being comprehended by the creatures. We are all in GOD; even Hell itself is in GOD, although it is deprived of His holy presence <note>original: "Anschauens," referring to the Beatific Vision, the direct perception of God's essence which is denied to those in Hell</note>; for if Hell were not in GOD, there would have to be another essence than the essence of GOD, who alone is the One who is, and consists and [remains] in this sole divine essence...

# of Johanna von Cambry. Chapter IV.

> “...all created being is sustained; sin alone has no being <term>being: in this context, "Wesen" refers to ontological existence—the idea that because God is the source of all existence, and God is good, evil/sin cannot have a "substance" of its own but is rather a lack of good</term>, it is a pure nothingness, and for that reason, sin is also not in God.”

Our Johanna recognized many such things through divine revelation and wrote them down, though she later burned them out of fear that they might be seen by others.

11. Before we accompany our saint into her second convent, let us say another word about her physical exercises: The care for her soul did not allow her to pamper her body much; for her, the body had to follow the spirit as a servant, not the spirit follow the body. She says so herself:

> “I have (she says) throughout my entire life given very little rest to this wretched body, which is destined to rot in the earth; I devote the greatest part of the night to prayer, unless I am sick; at such times I am secluded from all creatures, and then I feel myself more drawn by God to pray, as much for my own sins as for the whole world and other needs. I do this so that I do not resist the Holy Spirit, who has drawn me to prayer since the years of my childhood and has instructed me in the same.”

Specifically, she was accustomed to using only three hours of the night for sleep and the remaining time for prayer; a habit she had held at all times since her youth, both while she was in the convent and while she was still outside.

12. She was also accustomed to numbing her body in every other way and keeping it quite strictly. Her appearance was such that one of her acquaintances pointed out—what was otherwise said of the Church Father **Basilio** <note>original: "Basilio." Referring to Saint Basil the Great (c. 329–379 AD), an influential theologian and monastic leader known for his asceticism</note>—that because she lived only according to the spirit, her entire body seemed to consist of skin and bone. She was very moderate in eating; indeed, it was a burden to her that she had to nourish and care for her body: she did not eat to enjoy herself in the food, but merely to sustain her body and life. Before she was in the convent, she drank no wine at all; afterwards, she had to conform to the others. She was accustomed to eating dry bread with salt, although she also took a little of her portion so that people should not think she did this out of self-denial; indeed, some actually said she was following her "corrupt appetite" in doing so, which then gladdened her, that people held such a judgment of her. However, she only did this in her first convent; when she came to her second convent in the year 1619, she ceased such habits upon the advice of the Superior, although she otherwise retained enough other maneuvers to crucify her corrupt desires through abstinence. She practiced such abstinences whenever she thought of them; but most of the time, her spirit was so transported into the heavenly essence during meals that she often, when rising from the table, would not have known what she had eaten if she had been asked about it, [and that was indeed the best kind of fasting.] Often her spirit was so powerfully drawn and kept occupied within during the meal that she sometimes had enough to do just to keep her eyes open, and did not know how to behave so that it would not be noticed.

# Twelfth Part. The Life

### The Fifth Chapter.

#### Entry into her second convent. The fire of love within her. Visions of the virtues and the justice of God. Various sufferings and persecutions.

---

->I.<-

In November of the year 1619, Johanna was led into another convent in the same city of Tournai <note>German: "Dornich"; a city in modern-day Belgium where Johanna spent much of her religious life</note>, called Sion. There, she initially enjoyed more outward peace and was also frequently visited by God with extraordinary graces. She describes this herself in the following manner, in a letter written to her spiritual guide:

> “Beloved Father in our Savior! I feel a fire within me that burns and
> consumes me. Dying I live, and living I die; yet this
> fire is so sweet that it gives me life even as it devours me. But one thing
> is lacking in this inner fire, and that is what oppresses my soul: namely,
> the inward longing for the perfect enjoyment of my God, which it
> causes in me, cannot be fully stilled in this life. If only, in
> these flames, in these violent attacks, I could have just one single person
> who understood me, to whom I could open my heart and with whom I could speak of this
> presence of God, which causes me these inward oppressions,
> it would be a relief to me; but no, I must rather take pains to
> cover up this fire, for fear that it might be noticed outwardly. Or if I could
> give space to the inner <insert>impulse and effect of love</insert>, then I would
> enjoy God as much as one can enjoy Him in this life; but no, I must
> withdraw myself by force, as one pulls a child from its mother's arms, since I am
> compelled to interact with people who do not know my sickness, and whom
> I would rather offend than edify? What? Must I then live to please
> men, when I have no other desire than to please the living God?
> Must I still interact with men, when my citizenship <note>original: "Wandel"; a reference to Philippians 3:20, "Our citizenship/conversation is in heaven"</note> is in heaven?
> Must I still give nourishment to this body, when I only groan for
> Him who can sustain and satisfy my soul?
> 
> “This fire has various effects; I sometimes find myself in such a
> blaze that I must cry out loud to have a little air. At present, I 
> do not have ecstasies <note>original: "Entzückungen"; states of mystical trance</note> quite as often anymore—I mean to say, where I completely lose
> consciousness of myself—but more often I feel, in a sensible way, something like a wound in my heart,
> which arises from the hot desire of a soul inflamed in the love of God;
> afterwards, this wound causes either a certain weakening of the breath or a 
> stream of tears that I cannot hold back; then people think I am
> sad, because I find it impossible to hide it. I no longer know what to 
> do; I am not understood.” etc.

of Johanna von Cambry. Chapter V.

2. There is also something remarkable about this soul, in that God occasionally allowed her to see the essence <note>German: "Wesen"; here meaning the spiritual reality or true core</note> of this or that virtue. Thus it happened once, as she was in conversation with a certain spiritual person, that she saw a virtue hidden within his soul, namely virginity or chastity, which shone forth even from this person’s face. She saw this although she did not look at his face with her physical eyes; however, the remarkable delight she enjoyed from the beauty of this soul compelled her to lift her downcast eyes and look this person in the face. There she then saw in the exterior a certain extraordinary but non-physical beauty, which to her was altogether ineffable. She was most highly astonished that she beheld such beauty in this person’s face, which she had never seen before. Specifically, she saw in the interior the essential beauty of virginity, so that it was thereafter no longer a wonder to her that the Savior had wished to be born of a virgin. Johanna had indeed seen this person often before, but had never perceived in their face the virtue hidden in their soul. When this had passed and she thought no more of it, she received the vision of this virtue once again the following day, and in a more perfect manner. This lasted for a considerable time, with such great consolation for her soul that she thought she was no longer in this world. When the vision had entirely passed, the whole world appeared to her like pure darkness; and "if I" (she said) "had the whole world, even a thousand worlds, in my power, I would give them all up just to preserve this virtue, indeed just to see the beauty of this virtue once more, if it were otherwise permitted to ask for such graces."

3. Another time (while she was still in her first convent), she also saw the essence of humility and of human nothingness <note>a common mystical concept referring to the total dependence of the creature upon the Creator</note>, regarding which she said that if one had seen the essence of humility only once, it would be enough to never again attribute anything good to oneself. And a vision of our nothingness brings greater benefit to the soul than if it had meditated on humility for an entire year.

4. In June of this same year, she had a vision of the justice of God, in which she saw the entire earth flooded with the wickedness of men. In this vision, God said to her: "My daughter, if I were to exercise my justice over men according to their merits, I would have to exterminate the entire world, and the good would have to suffer along with the wicked."

Afterward, God showed her that among a thousand million people, scarcely any are to be found who perfectly fulfill God's will in everything. And if perhaps five or six such souls were in a country, God would preserve the entire land for their sake.

5. In addition to this, God showed her which goods and graces He was willing to communicate to the children of men; but all of them, except for a small number, resisted these. Because of this, she could almost no longer rejoice, since she had seen how corrupt human nature resists God and His graces in such a manner.

<summary>Johanna von Cambry experiences profound mystical visions revealing the spiritual essence of chastity and humility, as well as a divine warning about human wickedness and the protective power of a few holy souls.</summary>

# Part Twelve. The Life

### 6.
Just as it is an unavoidable necessity that all who wish to live godly in Christ Jesus must suffer persecution, so too was our godly Johanna vigorously shaken in this sieve <note>A biblical metaphor from Luke 22:31, referring to the "sifting" or testing of a believer's faith by the devil.</note>, both in her first convent and throughout the rest of her life. In this convent at Sion, the evil enemy <note>A common term for the Devil.</note> stirred up some of her fellow sisters, who spread rumors that the books she wrote did not come from her own mind, but that she was merely copying them from others. To discover the truth of the matter, a small opening was made in the floorboards above her chamber, through which someone had to watch secretly to see what she was doing and how she wrote her books—just as she had been tested in this manner in her previous convent. While this resulted in some beginning to love and highly esteem her, others held her to be a sorceress who was in league with the devil. This was believed especially because a bright light was often seen in her room at night, illuminating the entire chamber, even though they were certain she could have no natural light <note>Meaning a candle or lamp.</note> with her at that time.

### 7.
These and many other slanders and persecutions our poor Johanna had to endure at this time, which the biographer of her life—for reasons that can easily be guessed—wishes mostly to keep silent. At that time, among other things, she wrote the following little letter regarding this matter to her biological brother:

> “I pray you, my brother, do not be distressed by all that I suffer and all that I shall yet suffer; rather believe that when GOD burdens me with tribulation, it is a sign of His love. I have not yet been condemned like St. Teresa <note>Likely referring to St. Teresa of Avila, whose mystical experiences were frequently investigated by the Inquisition.</note>, nor yet exorcised <note>German: "beschworen." Teresa was famously subjected to adjurations and exorcisms by confessors who feared her visions were demonic.</note> like her, of whom it was also said that she was ruled by the devil, and that her visions and revelations were from the devil and nothing but dreams. Do not wonder that I am persecuted and will be persecuted in the future; for there is no other way to heaven than the Way of the Cross. Blessed be the Cross that prepares us for the enjoyment of GOD! As for me, the Cross and tribulation are my daily food. In the Cross, I find the grace of GOD hidden.”

### 8.
As she was at prayer one certain evening, she was overtaken by terrible suffering; namely, she saw in the spirit what her adversaries intended against her innocence. She was indeed surrendered to everything in GOD <term>Gelassenheit: a core mystical concept of "letting go" of self-will and accepting God's will with inner peace</term>, but inwardly she had to endure an agony which (as she thought) was equal to that which her bridegroom Jesus endured on the Mount of Olives. “My GOD,” she said, “I am willing to suffer; but how is it possible that You allow my enemies such power against my innocence?” But in these anxieties, GOD said to her: “Fear not, my daughter, I preserve you as the apple of my eye.” By these words she was greatly comforted and strengthened, although otherwise the inner agony still persisted. She knew nothing [externally] of what her adversaries intended; she saw it only in the spirit. However, everything was later found to be true, except that the plot they had forged against her was discovered in time and thus thwarted.

# The Sixth Chapter.

## Her distressed misery, into which she was placed by her spiritual director, along with other sufferings.

-> I. <-

Of those immediate persecutions which she had to endure from the evil enemy <note>The Devil.</note>, I will say nothing here; I only cannot think without painful compassion of how this inward heart was confused and truly martyred by unwise <term>spiritual directors</term> <note>Confessors or mentors assigned to oversee a mystic's spiritual life; in Johanna's case, they often doubted her visions.</note>. She suffered far more from them than from the persecutions of evil men and hellish spirits. I will merely insert various extracts from her own handwritten letters in succession, from which the reader may be convinced of this themselves, and also simultaneously see something of the diverse communications and visitations of God which this dear soul participated in during the year 1621. In March of this year, she wrote the following to her director:

> 2. "When God unites Himself with the soul, the effect of it is hidden and inward—indeed, so much so that it seems to me I am entirely in God. I do not believe that anyone else can produce such an effect, except only He who is All, and who can do all things, toward such a one who has not deserved it. And when I see or feel such wonderful things—namely, that the **Nothing**, which I am, is united with Him who is **All**, without any action on my part other than giving my will to it and surrendering myself to Him who is All—then I cannot doubt that it must be God. Because I now believe this, I adore Him, I love Him, and I enclose Him in the midst of my heart.
>
> "At that time, it does not enter my thoughts that it might be the devil; for if I were in doubt about it, I would not be able to do such things. But because I am then certainly assured that it is God, I adore Him. And even when the doubts return afterward, I still feel an impression in the innermost part of my heart telling me that it is God. Even if I sometimes weep for fear that I might be deceived, I nevertheless feel an impression in the spirit telling me: I should not doubt, it is God. So much so that even if all <term>creatures</term> <note>In mystical writing, "creatures" refers to all created beings and worldly things as opposed to the Creator.</note> told me the opposite, I would not be able to believe them, but I feel how I must hold to Him alone above all creatures; that same impression also tells me that I linger too much among the creatures, and when

5. On May 30th of this same year, as she had to give a precise report to her guide of what was occurring within her, she wrote, among other things, the following:

> „I know well that I am entirely imperfect, and it is precisely my imperfections, together with the suspicion that I see in you, that cause doubt to penetrate, whether it be God who rules me, because I deem myself unworthy of such great graces. Nevertheless, if I were to know any willful and sinful imperfection in me, I would surely need no other judge than my own conscience; for I know, God be praised, from experience, that the graces of God are so delicate that a very small imperfection hinders them. I speak, however, of this union; for I feel it immediately when I fall into any weakness. For example, when out of fear of displeasing our Superior <note>Original: *Vorsteherin*. The female head of her religious house.</note> or the sisters, I accommodate myself to their mind or nature <note>Original: *Naturel*. Referring to their temperament or personality.</note>, and divert myself with them, I do so so very much against my will that I would rather weep than laugh; nonetheless, God then withdraws Himself from me for perhaps three or four hours; I mean to say, as far as His unifying presence is concerned, for the act of perpetual love, of which I said that it makes me die, that same act lasts forever. And when I afterwards return to myself, it happens that our God, who is so kind and well sees that I cannot conveniently avoid such opportunities, forgives me and embraces me like a father his child. “

6. At this time, she had a constant longing to die, so that she might enjoy God and be freed from the opportunities to offend Him; for if she committed even the slightest fault, she suffered incredible distress; therefore it was the greatest joy to her when she heard the bells tolling for a dead person. Although, in all of this, she was resigned to God’s will to live as long as it might please Him.

7. At times, it seemed as if the guide had attained better insight into the ways and workings of God in and over her soul, as may be seen from the following letter which Johanna wrote to him.

> „I have been comforted to the highest degree; for because I have now received a little more assurance that it is the Spirit of God who works in my soul, I shall now have so much more occasion to inflame my will and desires in the love of God, and to yield myself so much more freely, fully, and without any fear...

### Twelfth Piece. The Life

...things <note>Original: "-chen". This is the end of a word like *Sachen* (things) or *solchen* (such), continuing from the previous page.</note> I have had a very great compassion for her, as I saw and heard the persecutions, contempt, and blasphemies inflicted upon her by the three eldest convent sisters, who are yet her own subordinates, etc. Upon her request, I advised her that she should seek to win them over through gentleness and friendliness; which she then did at all times, with such great patience, gentleness, and wisdom, that the citizens themselves stood astonished by her immense wisdom and fortitude <note>Original: *Tapferkeit*. Here meaning spiritual strength and courage in the face of adversity.</note>, yet without being able to soften the hardness of those sisters' hearts through all of this, etc.

5. Amidst all these and other trials and vexations, the fire of divine love nevertheless burned incessantly in her heart, and indeed with such assaults that her heart seemed ready to burst from the heat of these pure flames; this she called the spiritual martyrdom <note>A term in mystical theology for the suffering caused by the soul's intense longing for God, which is both painful and joyous.</note>; wherefore she also took as her motto: **My Love is crucified.** <note>Original: "Meine Liebe ist gekreuziget." This is likely a reference to the Latin phrase *Amor meus crucifixus est*, attributed to St. Ignatius of Antioch.</note> These visitations of love from her heavenly Bridegroom were so persistent and intense that, because her body was sometimes not strong enough to endure them, she was forced to cry out: "Cease, my God, cease, I cannot endure your delightful presence in this frail body!" She was entirely bewildered by this and praised God that He was so kind as to descend so deeply to her soul, which well recognized its own deep nothingness <note>The concept of "nothingness" (*Nichts*) refers to the humility of realizing that the creature is nothing compared to the Creator.</note>; and that He granted her the grace to preserve His presence in her soul and remain united with Him in the midst of all the business of the house.

6. In such a manner was she led inwardly by the Lord at the beginning of her office as superior at Menain, and for some time thereafter; later she sometimes felt heavy internal sufferings, in which she was exercised with alternations; but it did not last long before she was visited again even more lovingly by God. What actually occurred between God and her soul at such times, she knew no other way to describe,

> „than that she, in an entirely spiritual manner, embraced her heavenly Bridegroom 
> „in the center of her heart, and with Him all souls united with God and 
> „living in His grace, especially those whose state was known to her.

> „She said that in these assaults and unions of divine love, the soul 
> „opens itself and gives itself entirely to her Beloved; and if it were possible, 
> „she would wish to make God infinitely greater, more glorious, and more powerful than He is, 
> „which is however impossible, because He is All, just as He is. These effects, she 
> „said, were entirely divine, and it was God more than the soul who was acting, as the soul 
> „only added her full consent, and let God work through His love 
> „everything He willed. The fruit of these effects was that the soul 
> „was thereby placed in a state of great loathing for all the vanities of this world.„

> „My Father, it is difficult for me to write to you of the abstractions [<term>Abstractiones</term> <note>In this context, "abstractions" refers to mystical states where the soul's attention is "drawn away" from the physical senses and focused entirely on God.</note>] of divine love since I have been here. ### Of Johanna von Cambry. Chapter VII.

„...comprehend what God wants from me. I always find myself in my inward being. The innermost part of the soul, the spirit, and all its powers have no other beginning, middle, or end than love; my whole body and outer senses breathe nothing but love, so that if all parts of my body were turned into tongues, they would all cry out unceasingly: Love! Love! Sometimes because of the absence of my beloved Jesus, and sometimes from the pleasure of His divine presence, which I carry enclosed in the center of my heart. In such a state, it is an incredible pain to me to attend to temporal matters <note>Refers to worldly or administrative tasks as opposed to spiritual ones.</note>, and to deal with people, for whose sake I must forcibly withdraw myself from God: but I return to myself as soon as I can break free, and there I find my divine Bridegroom without searching, in the center of my heart.

„In short, whether I speak with people with whom I am obliged to deal by virtue of my office; or whether I perform something else, my heart always goes up to my Beloved.

„I am nothing, I am of no use, and I deserve nothing but hell; I am not worthy to love God; nevertheless, I cannot deny that I love Him with all my heart, and am sick with His holy love, which makes me live like a martyr. O Love! sweet and lovely beyond all delights. O Love! more cruel than death. Yes, my dear <term>Father</term> <note>Original: "Pater". Her spiritual director or confessor.</note>, divine love is sweet and cruel: it is sweet to the spirit, but cruel to nature <note>In mystical theology, "nature" refers to the physical body and human ego, which often suffer under the intensity of spiritual experiences.</note>, which is not able, of itself, to endure its loving and completely divine effects.„

8. Through all such visitations of love from her heavenly Bridegroom, she was only made ever more courageous to take upon herself all kinds of adversities and sufferings with good cheer, so that she used to say: „I want to live on the Cross, and die on the Cross; I hold the Cross to be my mother, my beloved, my trusted and best friend; I praise the Cross, I glory in the Cross: blessed Cross, I want to sing your praise, and I pray to the beloved Bridegroom that I may end my days on the Cross.„

9. In this year of 1622, our dear Johanna had a powerful urge to write a treatise on the *Triumph of the Cross*, to show what blessings the Cross brings to a soul; however, she only recorded the contents of a few chapters and was prevented from finishing the work itself.

10. In January 1623, when she was asked by her guide how she understood the words in one of her previous letters, that **God is All**? She gave the following answer:

„Through these words, **God is All**, I understand that all things without God are pure nothingness; for God alone is He who is, and without God we can neither be nor exist. Jesus Christ I recognize thus: that God took our human nature upon Himself and became a mediator between God and us. As God, He [made] man perfect and in the state of righteousness...

# Part Twelve. The Life

created; but as man had made himself an enemy of God instead of a child of God, Jesus clothed himself with the mantle of our nature <note>A theological way of describing the Incarnation—God taking on human flesh.</note>, and placed us once more in God's grace and favor, so that now our nature, through the grace and merits of Jesus Christ, can again be united with God in love.

> „And so, when I have said, God is everything, and Everything is God, I marvel at the Everything and the Nothing, how they are united with one another through love and grace; and I could not contain myself from crying out: O wonderful work of God! who through his incomprehensible love and goodness deigns to unite himself with such a Nothing <note>In mystical tradition, "the Nothing" refers to the human soul or the self, which has no existence or value independent of God.</note>.

11. In June of the year 1625, God gave her a vision of the hideousness of sin and the malice of the corrupted nature of man, a vision which she thereafter had frequently. This produced in her an extreme hatred of sin and a disgust for all things of the world, except for those souls who walk according to God's pleasure; she even found herself unbearable if she perceived the slightest bit of this corrupted nature within her. Furthermore, from that time on, she did not wonder so much that so many sins occur, but rather that even more sins are not committed.

12. Her state of mind and the graces received from God in this year of 1625 can otherwise best be seen from several writings by her own hand, composed around this time. In August, she wrote the following comforting little letter to her leader <note>Original: "Führer". Referring to her spiritual director or confessor.</note> at the time:

> „How is it, why do you hide your inner sorrow from me? How, my Father, does the mere memory of your nothingness already put you in fear that you should be separated from God? Should such a thing prevent you from entering into the holy land? No, no, my Father, we are all sinners. As for me, even if I had as many heavy sins upon me as there are droplets in the ocean and grains of sand in the abyss of the sea, and I had once confessed them, I would lay myself down comforted before the crucified God-man. There, in living contrition <term>contrition</term> <note>Deep, sincere remorse for one’s sins arising from a love of God rather than fear of punishment.</note>, I would wash them all away in the blood of the holy wound in the side of the crucified Jesus; and so I would then throw myself into his arms full of love, sink myself into his love, and burn all my sins therein, without ever thinking of them again. And if the devil should bring them back into my thoughts...

### of Johanna von Cambry. Chapter VII.

> „...bring, and tried to set me in fear, to separate me from God, I would laugh at him and say: Go away, Satan, you shall have nothing but my sins for your portion; go away, and burn together with this chaff <note>A biblical metaphor for something worthless that is burned away, representing the sins Johanna discards.</note>: you shall have nothing in me, for I belong to my God.

> „God, my Father, if God, who is our Love, wishes to test you through such fear, it will also be wholesome for you; but from now on, think no more of the past. As I read your letter, I fell into a powerful detachment <gloss>original: Abstraction</gloss> wherein our gracious God let me feel the flames of his burning love in such a manner that I was as if utterly shattered by it the whole night and the following morning; and there I once again had such an assurance of your election <note>In this context, "election" refers to the theological belief that a person is chosen by God for salvation.</note> that I can in no way doubt it. But let us forget everything, and only remember that we may be perfectly united with God in his holy love. One must remember one’s sins in no other way than only in love.

13. In the month of September, the opened side of Jesus was shown to her in prayer; she saw herself and her guide dipped into the wound of the side of Jesus, and how they both were washed of all their sins through his blood, and drank their fill of it; afterward she saw quite clearly how the fleshy heart of Jesus was changed into a golden heart, and gave off a wonderful radiance through the opened side.

14. On the 30th of this same month, she wrote the following to her guide:

> „God does not want me to desire to know such things further; He also does not want me to crave revelations; it is enough that I did it once out of obedience for your reassurance concerning my inner state; God has not forgotten it, and you can certainly still remember it. Concerning the assurance of your and my election, which God has given me: know that, as far as I am concerned, I never look back upon myself to wonder whether I shall be damned or saved; but I am in God in such a way that when I behold myself in God, and living in God, so I <unclear>see</unclear> myself also dying in God, wanting nothing but God, and nothing <unclear>outside</unclear> of God, without me distinguishing whether I should be damned or saved. I do indeed feel an assurance within me that I shall enjoy God, both in heaven <unclear>as</unclear> on earth, without me, as I said, making any <term>reflection</term> <gloss>original: Reflexion; here meaning an intellectual over-analysis of one's spiritual state</gloss> upon it. I cannot make myself better understood.

> „I see in God the abyss of my nothingness, without thinking of election, although I see that, because of my malicious nature, I do not at all deserve to enjoy God, neither in heaven nor on earth. I would make no reflection at all upon myself nor upon you; but because I see you in sorrow and doubt, God has, for your particular comfort, given me the assurance of your election. „

Around this same time, the heavenly Bridegroom gave his beloved Johanna to understand that we would have a different name in heaven than our baptismal name; and that just as we were created for the purpose of refilling the places from which the devils <note>original: "Teufel"; here referring to the fallen angels who left their positions in the celestial hierarchy.</note> were cast down, so she recognized in God that we would also have those very same names that the fallen angels had, as well as their place in Paradise. Indeed, we would constitute the same hierarchy and possess the same graces and the level of essential glory <term>essential glory: a theological term (Latin: gloria essentialis) referring to the fundamental happiness of the soul in the direct presence of God</term> that they were meant to have; and moreover, we would enjoy an increase of accidental glory <term>accidental glory: additional happiness in heaven (Latin: gloria accidentalis) resulting from one’s good deeds or specific trials endured on earth</term>.

## Chapter Eight.

->A remarkable writing on the state of innocence. God’s assistance in things physical and spiritual. She is enclosed at Lille <note>original: "Rissel"; the historical German name for the city of Lille in modern-day France, where Johanna lived as an anchoress.</note>, November 25, 1625.<-

->I.<-

In this very year, our Johanna also composed the following remarkable writing concerning a state of innocence that can still be attained in this mortal life, from which we can learn much.

> “One can in no way doubt that God, who is so utterly kind, could not fail to impart such a singular grace to the soul of his beloved, through which she could be raised to a state very near to that from which our first parents fell, which was a state of perfect innocence. I say that a soul can reach such a state that comes close to the state of innocence; but how does this happen? And how can one recognize a soul that has arrived there? This we wish to point out, without however dealing here with the ways to get there, because that is sufficiently addressed in our four books on the *Destruction of Self-Love*.

> “We wish, then, to show here the nakedness <note>meaning the complete stripping away or absence</note> of all passions and desires from which this soul is freed, so that nothing in the whole world, nor anything created, of whatever kind it may be, can prevent her from entering into this holy land <note>original Latin: "Terra Sancta"</note> which is like the state of innocence.

> “Yes, it is a holy land; one cannot enter it as long as one is stained with any passions of the mind or desires outside of God. This is the burning bush that burned and was not consumed, of which God said to Moses: Take off your shoes. This bush is the very state spoken of here, and this holy land is the body or the humanity of Jesus Christ, with which the soul is already united in this life.

<meta>This page continues the specific treatise written by Johanna von Cambry in November 1625 regarding the "state of innocence." ### of Johanna von Cambry. Chapter VIII.

2. “What, I ask, is this burning bush? It is the fire of the love of the Godhead, as united and bound with that humanity with which the soul is already united in this life, since the body is placed in that state through this union, as mentioned above. This state is no longer one of toil, but rather fruitful—that is to say, the soul [is no longer the one acting, but rather she] enjoys here the fruits of her labor; she enjoys the reward of the freely given graces <note>original: "umsonst geschenkten Gnaden"; in theology, these are "gratia gratis data," gifts given by God for the benefit of others rather than for the person's own holiness.</note>, whereby she also possesses the enjoyment of an earthly paradise. But what must one not abandon, and what must one find, in order to reach the possession of this holy land? This earthly paradise, where one lives as if in the state of innocence? One must leave **Everything**; one must possess **Everything**.

3. “When the soul has left everything to enjoy everything, she remains steadfast without change, and without turning away in any matter from union with her God; neither the world, nor the self, nor friends, nor enemies, loss of goods, or whatever else it may be, can in the slightest turn her away from her God.

4. “O blessed innocence! But what does corrupt nature do here? It is entirely obedient and subject to the spirit, yes, so bowed down that it no longer seems to be nature.

“But what does this word 'innocence' mean? A child is commonly considered innocent because it cannot sin; and the Savior says: *Unless you become like children, you cannot enter the kingdom of heaven.* But how? Should one then remain without judgment? <note>The author refers here to a state of "holy indifference" or "non-judgment," where the soul is so focused on God's perspective that it stops using the human ego to categorize and condemn.</note> I say yes, as far as sin is concerned; for a soul is so much more perfect, the more she becomes without judgment in regard to sin; which then happens when we are so dead to sin in ourselves that the soul no longer sees or judges sin, neither in one's neighbor nor in herself, nor even her past sins, except only outside of God and outside of herself, where she views sins only in their own nothingness <note>The "Nothingness" (Nichts) is a central theme in German mysticism, referring to the void of the creature when separated from the Being of God.</note>. These souls can no longer reflect upon their own sins so as to have sorrow over them, except only out of divine love, outside of God and outside of themselves, and in their own nothingness.

“I say once more, that even if these souls look upon hell and its terrible torment, they do not see sin therein otherwise than outside of God; so that even their own past sins, or the sins of their neighbor, or of their relatives who are in hell, no longer cause them any distress, because they view everything through love, through which they are placed as if in a state of innocence outside of sin.

5. “But by what can one recognize the innocence of the earthly paradise, where one enjoys and possesses **Everything**? A soul that has and possesses **Everything**—that is to say, God—no longer thinks or acts in any matter, whether it concerns the soul or the body, except only in this **Everything**, through this **Everything**, and for this **Everything**.”
